exp.4:0:
God invites the people to run through the streets and squares of Jerusalem to look for just one person who practices justice and seeks the truth. If they find one, God promises to pardon the city. "Run" means to go back and forth through the streets. "Do justice" means to act with fairness and uprightness.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people considered themselves faithful, but they lived in deceit and refused to correct themselves. The verses that follow say that they swore in God's name without sincerity and hardened their faces. The request shows how serious the situation was, and also the mercy of God, who is ready to forgive.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are people who seek the truth and act with justice, even when no one else does. Begin with one concrete act of honesty today.
exp.3:15:
This verse is a command to give warning. The message must be announced to the nations, and also to Jerusalem, that an army is coming from a distant land. Here "watchers" means besiegers or sentries who surround a city. The phrase "give out their voice" means to shout against them, like a battle cry. The cities of Judah will be attacked.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier he called Jerusalem to cleanse its heart so that it might be saved. Now he warns that judgment is drawing near because of its rebellion. Many understand this to be the army of Babylon, although the text does not give the name in this verse.

For today: God gives warning before he corrects, because he desires that we return to him. Today you can examine your heart with sincerity, acknowledge what you need to leave behind, and come to God without delay.
exp.50:2:
God gives an order against the army of Babylon. It speaks of the archer who draws his bow and of the soldier who boasts in his armor. Here the armor is the one the verse calls "brigandine." "Young men" are the young warriors. The order is to show no mercy and to destroy its whole army.

The one speaking is the Lord, through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been an instrument of judgment against Judah, but it grew proud and mistreated God's people. Now God himself judges it. The verses that follow remind us that Israel was not abandoned by its God, even though it had sinned.

For today: no human power, however strong it may seem, stands above God. Trust that he does justice in his own time, and avoid the pride that puts its confidence in its own armor.
exp.16:8:
It says that the human heart, that is, the innermost part of a person (their desires, thoughts and decisions), can deceive us more than anything else. "Desperately wicked" here is also understood as sick or twisted, and the question "who can know it?" means that no one can fully understand it by themselves.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah, who trusted in human alliances and in their own strength. Earlier, the person who trusts in God is compared to a tree planted by the water. Then God says that He indeed searches the heart and gives to each one according to his deeds.

For today: do not blindly trust your feelings or your justifications. Before deciding, pray, ask God to examine your heart, and compare your decisions with His Word.
exp.47:19:
Moab is put to shame because it has been broken down. The call to "howl and cry" is a command to weep out loud, with grief. "Tell ye it in Arnon" is the instruction to announce the news of the ruin, so the word of the downfall would reach as far as the river Arnon, which marked the border of Moab. Here the phrase "that Moab is spoiled" means that the country has been completely ruined.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, delivering God's message against Moab, a neighboring country of Israel. The passage describes the fall of its cities, such as Dibon and Aroer, and the people who flee and report what has happened. Many understand that the judgment came because of Moab's pride and its trust in its fortresses and riches, something the same chapter mentions. The exact historical details of how it was fulfilled are debated.

For today: do not place your security in your achievements, money, or strength. All of that can fall. Seek humility before God, because only in Him is there a firm refuge.
exp.20:11:
God speaks to the royal family of Judah, the descendants of King David. He commands them to judge with justice "in the morning," meaning promptly, without putting it off. They must rescue the oppressed person from the one who mistreats him. If they do not, God's anger will burn out like a fire that no one can put out, because of the evil of their deeds. The word "deliver" in the verse means to set free or to rescue.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah at a time when Jerusalem was threatened by Babylon. God denounces that the rulers had allowed injustice. Even so, this message offers an opportunity: if they changed, there was hope. Some scholars think the punishment was already very near; others see here a sincere call to repentance.

For today: if you have any authority or influence, even a small amount, do not delay in doing what is right. Defend the person who is mistreated or ignored, and do it soon.
exp.43:27:
It says that a few survivors from Judah will escape the sword and return from Egypt to their land. Then all those who went to live in Egypt will know whose word was fulfilled: God's or theirs. The "remnant" means those who are left over, the rest. The "knife" refers to the sword, to war.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The Jews who fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem kept worshiping the queen of heaven and said things were going better for them that way. God warns them that his judgment will come upon them, and the outcome will show who was right.

For today: we can ask ourselves whose advice we are following more, our own ideas and excuses or the word of God. Opinions change, but what God says endures. It is wise to obey him before we learn the hard way.
exp.16:22:
The explanation says that the people of Judah did not listen to God or pay attention to him. "Made their neck stiff" means they became stubborn, like an ox that will not let the yoke be put on it. "Obeyed not" and "inclined their ear" go together: they refused to listen or to let themselves be taught.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who addresses the people of Jerusalem. He had asked them to keep the Sabbath as a day set apart, without burdens or work, as he had commanded their ancestors. The Sabbath was a sign of trust and obedience to God. This verse shows that their underlying problem was not just a rule, but a heart that did not want to listen. God offers them blessing if they obey.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are willing to listen to God when something makes us uncomfortable. This week, choose a moment to read the Bible calmly, and ask God for a heart willing to receive correction.
exp.27:11:
This verse tells how Hananiah, who claimed to be a prophet, broke the wooden yoke that Jeremiah wore on his neck. After that, God spoke to Jeremiah. "The word of the Lord came" means that God gave him a message.

Jeremiah wore the yoke as a sign that Judah had to submit to Babylon. Hananiah said, in God's name, that Babylon would fall within two years. Jeremiah went away without arguing any further, and then God gave him an answer. In this way we see that God himself corrects falsehood, and his servant does not need to win by shouting.

For today: not every message that sounds cheerful and claims to come from God is true. Test it against the Bible, pray calmly, and patiently wait for God's direction.
exp.8:14:
God says that he will feed his people wormwood and give them water of gall to drink. Wormwood is a very bitter plant, and gall is a bitter, poisonous liquid. They are images of suffering and pain.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before Judah was taken into exile. God explains the reason: his people abandoned his law, did not listen to his voice, and followed their own desires and the Baals, false gods. The verses that follow speak of scattering among the nations and of the sword. This is not a whim of God, but the consequence of persistent rebellion.

For today: when we turn away from what God says, we usually reap bitterness. Today we can ask ourselves what stubborn desires of the heart we are following, and return with humility to his Word, which invites us to repentance.
exp.37:13:
This verse tells how King Zedekiah secretly had the prophet Jeremiah brought to a certain entrance of the temple, a place we cannot identify with certainty. He said to him, "I will ask you a thing; hide nothing from me."

Jeremiah had just been rescued from a muddy cistern by Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian official. Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon. Zedekiah was afraid and wanted a word from God, but he was a weak king, pressured by his leaders. Jeremiah distrusts him and reminds him that he had not listened to him before.

For today: we often want to hear from God, but only if the answer suits us. Let us ask God not only for counsel, but also for a heart willing to obey him, even when it costs us.
exp.47:36:
In Moab, everyone will show their grief: heads shaved bald, beards cut off, hands marked with cuts, and rough cloth worn at the waist. Shaved means cut away or cut short.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel, trusted in its riches and its gods, and God announces its fall. These customs were signs of mourning in that time. It is striking that God says his heart will moan like a flute, meaning he grieves even over this judgment.

For today: God does not delight in human suffering, even when it is just. We can trust that he judges with truth, but we can also ask him for a compassionate heart rather than a proud one, and not place our security in material things, which pass away.
exp.13:16:
God tells Jeremiah to say these words to the people: let their eyes overflow with tears day and night, without stopping. The "virgin daughter of my people" is a poetic way of speaking of Judah, like a beloved young woman. She is broken, that is, shattered, struck with a very heavy blow.

Jeremiah speaks, yet his words reflect God's own grief. There is drought, hunger and war, and false prophets had promised peace when God had not sent them. Even so, the message of judgment does not come from a cold heart, but from someone who weeps for his people.

For today: when someone suffers the consequences of their mistakes, we can speak the truth without harshness or pride. Let us ask God for a heart that weeps with those who suffer and also prays for them.
exp.23:6:
God promises to give his people a new heart so that they truly know him. Here, "know" means a close relationship, not just having information. Then they will be his people and he will be their God, because they will return to him with their whole heart, that is, with complete sincerity.

God speaks through Jeremiah after Babylon took the first exiles of Judah captive. In a vision of two baskets of figs, the good figs represent those exiles: God did not abandon them, but would watch over them and bring them back. The bad figs represent King Zedekiah and those who stayed behind or fled to Egypt.

Today, we cannot change our own heart by sheer willpower alone. We can ask God to renew it and return to him sincerely, even in difficult times.
exp.6:1:
God tells Jeremiah to stand at the entrance of the temple and announce a message to all of Judah. The old wording is easy to clarify: "Stand in the gate" is in the verse as "stand in the gate," "proclaim" is in the verse as "proclaim," and "Hear" is in the verse as "Hear." The message is addressed to those who came in to worship God.

God is speaking, and Jeremiah is his messenger. The place was chosen on purpose: that is where the religious people were. According to the verses that follow, God wanted to correct the false confidence of those who believed they were safe simply because they had the temple, while they lived without obeying him.

For today: before going to church or praying, ask yourself whether your everyday life reflects what you say you believe. Truly worshiping includes listening to God and obeying him, not only keeping a religious custom.
exp.20:2:
Here Jeremiah answers the king's messengers. He tells them to carry a message to Zedekiah, and that message comes from God.

Context: Babylon, under King Nebuchadnezzar, had Jerusalem under siege. Zedekiah sent Pashur and Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to inquire of God, hoping for a miracle like those of the past. Jeremiah speaks as a prophet, and what follows is not what the king hoped for: God says he will not fight on their side, because the people had turned away from Him.

For today: It is easy to seek God only when we are in trouble and to expect him to give us the answer we want. It is better to approach Him with humility and be willing to listen, even when His word confronts us and calls us to change.
exp.39:10:
This verse tells that the Jews who had fled to Moab, Ammon, Edom and other lands heard something: the king of Babylon had left a group of people in Judah and had appointed Gedaliah, son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan, as governor.

Jerusalem had fallen to Babylon. The one telling the story is the author of the book, who continues the account after the destruction. Gedaliah, from a respected family, had encouraged the people to stay, to serve Babylon, and to gather the harvest. That news reached the scattered people and gave them hope of returning.

Today, the news that there is a place to start over can encourage someone who feels far away and scattered. If you are in a season of loss, do not close the door on an opportunity to rebuild. Ask God for wisdom to take the first step with humility.
exp.22:26:
God says that those prophets want his people to forget his name through the dreams they tell one another. The comparison is made to what Israel's ancestors did: they too forgot his name by following Baal, a false god of Canaan.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. There were prophets who said, "I dreamed, I dreamed," and presented their own ideas as messages from God, but they were false. By doing so they turned the people away from the true word of God. Then God makes it clear that his word is like fire and like a hammer, not like a mere dream.

Today we can examine what we hear in God's name. An experience, an impression, or an opinion does not carry the same weight as Scripture. The safest course is to compare everything with the Bible and ask God for the humility to obey it.
exp.6:4:
If you truly change your ways and your actions, and if you practice justice fully between a person and his neighbor, then God says you will be allowed to stay in this place. The verse has four key words to explain. "Change" here means changing your conduct for the better. "Fully" means completely, not halfway. "Neighbor" is the person who is close to you. "Do justice" means acting fairly.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses those who came into the temple in Jerusalem confident that the place would protect them, while they lived unjustly. God asks them for a real change, not just religious words. The promise is that they could continue living in that land.

For today: faith is not measured only by attending church or saying the right phrases. Think of a relationship or task where you have been unfair or careless, such as at work, in your family, or in a dealing with a neighbor, and this week make it right with honesty.
exp.41:4:
Here the people promise Jeremiah that they will obey everything God tells him to say. They ask that the Lord be a faithful witness, meaning a witness who will judge them if they do not keep their word. It is a solemn oath, and the phrase "if we do not" simply means "if we do not do it."

The speakers are the army leaders and all the people who remained in Judah after the fall of Jerusalem. They are afraid of the Babylonians and want to know whether they should flee to Egypt. They ask Jeremiah to pray for them. Later in the text, when God answers, they do not accept his answer (chapter 43). This suggests that their promise was not sincere.

It is easy to say "I will do whatever God says" before you know what he will say. Before asking God for direction, ask yourself whether you are truly willing to obey, even if the answer is not the one you hoped for.
exp.31:6:
Jeremiah recounts what God had told him: his cousin Hanameel, the son of his uncle Shallum, would come to ask him to buy a field in Anathoth. The words "inheritance" and "right of redemption" refer to the family property and the right of the relative who redeems it, so that it would not leave the family.

Jeremiah is held prisoner in the courtyard of the guardhouse, while Jerusalem is besieged by the Babylonians. God warns him beforehand, and when Hanameel arrives, Jeremiah recognizes that it was the word of the LORD. Buying that field in a land about to be conquered was a sign that, after the punishment, God would bring His people back to the land.

For today: even when everything seems lost, we can take small steps of faith and obedience, trusting that God keeps His promises. He warns us and guides us, even in difficult times.
exp.4:22:
He says that the people of Judah had a heart that was "false," meaning twisted and stubborn, and "rebellious," one that does not want to submit to God. "Turned aside and gone" means they turned around and walked away from Him, instead of drawing near.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier He showed them that the sea obeys the limit He set for it, yet His people, who can think and decide for themselves, do not obey Him or fear Him. Then He reminds them that God gives them the rain and the harvest, and that their sins have taken good things away from them.

Today we can ask ourselves: is there something God has spoken to me about, and have I turned away from it? Today we can return to Him with humility, thank Him for what He gives us each day, and obey Him in something specific.
exp.34:6:
This verse records the command that Jonadab, ancestor of the Rechabites, gave to his family: not to build houses, not to sow seed, not to plant vineyards or own them, but to live in tents all their lives. In this way they would live many years in the land where they were foreigners.

Here the Rechabites speak, explaining to Jeremiah why they refuse the wine he offers them. God used this scene to contrast their faithfulness to a human command with the disobedience of Judah toward Him. Scholars do not know for certain why Jonadab gave those rules.

For today: let us ask ourselves whether we are as steadfast in obeying God as these men were in obeying their father, and let us practice that faithfulness in one concrete decision this week.
exp.30:3:
God promises his people that he will raise them up again, like someone rebuilding a fallen house. He calls Israel "virgin," a tender way of speaking of a beloved people. The "tambourines" are instruments of celebration, and the "circle of dancers" is a ring of joyful people dancing. The promise is that the celebration will return.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were in pain, struck down by destruction and exile. God reminds them of his everlasting love and announces restoration. Scholars often see here the people of the northern kingdom (Ephraim and Samaria), though the promise embraces all of Israel.

For today: if you feel your life has been left in ruins, God has not forgotten you. He knows how to rebuild. Trust in his love and leave room for joy to return, even if it comes slowly.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that God, with just his voice, causes the heavens to fill with water. He lifts up the clouds from the ends of the earth, makes the lightnings together with the rain, and brings out the wind from his treasures, that is, from his storehouses. The words "the ends of the earth" refer to the most distant places.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah, surrounded by nations that worshiped idols. Just before this, he says that the false gods did nothing, and afterward he mocks the cast idols, which have no breath in them. By contrast, he presents the true God as the Creator who governs nature.

For today: when you feel that your life is moving through storms or things beyond your control, remember that the God who commands the wind and the rain cares for you. Trust in him and do not place your security in money, success, or passing things.
exp.41:5:
The explanation says that the people promise to obey whatever God answers, whether it is pleasant or hard. The phrase "whether it be good, or whether it be evil" means the same as "whether it be good or whether it be evil." The word "that" in the verse is simply the link to the next clause, and "it may be well with us" means "it may go well with us." They recognize that obeying God is the way to have things go well for them.

The people speaking are those who remained in Judah, together with Johanan and the military leaders. After the fall of Jerusalem, they are afraid of Babylon and plan to flee to Egypt. They ask Jeremiah to pray and they swear loyalty to God. But the following text and the rest of the chapter show that, when the answer arrives, they do not like it and do not obey as they promised.

It is easy to say "I will do whatever God says" before knowing what he will say. Today you can examine your heart: am I willing to obey even when the answer is not convenient for me? Pray with sincerity and ask God for a heart that is willing beforehand.
exp.47:32:
It says that in Moab the harvest celebration will come to an end. The fruitful fields will no longer have joy, and the wine will stop flowing from the winepresses (the places where the grapes were trodden). Before, the grapes were trodden while singing; now, if someone shouts, it will no longer be a joyful song but a cry of disaster. The phrase "the song will not be a song" means that the sound will resemble a song, but it will be full of pain.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on Moab, a neighboring people of Israel, known for their abundance and their pride. Even so, the prophet does not speak with mockery: he says he will wail and weep for Moab. God judges, but also shows grief.

For today: let us not place our security in what we produce or enjoy, because it can end soon. Let us thank God for what we have and live with humility. And if someone suffers the consequences of their mistakes, let us not rejoice; rather, let us pray with compassion.
exp.11:8:
God compares his people to a strange bird with unusual colors, which other birds surround to attack. Then he calls the wild beasts of the field to come and devour her. "Heritage" means his cherished possession, and "round about" means on every side.

God speaks through Jeremiah about Judah. The people had turned against him, and for this reason he allows enemy nations to attack them. The image of the bird is difficult: some understand a spotted bird of prey, others a bird attacked for being different. Even so, the tone shows God's grief, not coldness.

Today, do not take your relationship with God lightly. If you have drifted away, return soon, because he suffers over what he loves. And take care of what he has entrusted to you: your faith, your family, your service.
exp.50:24:
God speaks directly against Babylon, which he calls the "destroying mountain" because it laid waste to many nations. He promises to stretch out his hand, to roll it down from the rocks (to bring it down from its height), and to leave it as a "burnt mountain," that is, like a dead, scorched volcano.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, and God promises to repay Babylon for the wrong done to Zion. Some understand the image of the mountain as the power of the empire; others see it as a reference to its lofty capital. The text does not specify.

For today: do not lose heart when pride and injustice seem to prevail. God sees, and no human power is eternal. Trust in his justice, refrain from taking revenge on your own, and seek to live with humility.
exp.17:19:
Here Jeremiah brings a complaint to God: "Shall evil be recompensed for good?" He says that his enemies have dug a pit for him, that is, they have prepared a trap to make him fall or to kill him. Then he asks God to remember how he stood before Him to speak on their behalf and to turn away His wrath from them.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the middle of a very sincere prayer. Some people of Judah were planning to silence him with accusations and slander, because they did not want to hear his message of judgment. Jeremiah feels hurt because he had interceded for them. What follows is a very harsh prayer against them; it is an honest cry, not a model to imitate without thought.

For today: when people repay you with evil for having done good, do not keep the pain to yourself. Bring it to God with sincerity, as Jeremiah did, and let Him take care of your cause and heal your heart.
exp.3:13:
The explanation says that Jerusalem must cleanse its heart of wickedness if it wants to be saved. God asks sorrowfully, "How long shall thy vain thoughts lodge within thee?" because the people kept holding on to thoughts of wrongdoing, that is, crooked plans and ideas. The word "vain" in that question refers to thoughts that are empty and misguided. To be saved means to be delivered or rescued.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah had turned away from God, and the arrival of an enemy army, swift as a whirlwind and coming from the north, was being announced. Even so, God offers a way out: a change within, not only in outward behavior. Many understand that the judgment was coming because of the people's rebellion, but the invitation to repentance remained open.

Today we can ask ourselves what wrong thoughts we are feeding, such as resentment, envy, or deceit. Instead of justifying them, let us ask God to cleanse our hearts and obey him today.
exp.30:13:
It says that God will give the priests such abundance that they will be fully satisfied, like someone who eats until they are full. The verse's word for filling up here does not speak of drunkenness, but of filling completely. The word for fatness refers to the best and richest part of the food, especially in the sacrifices. All the people will be satisfied with God's goodness.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter announces the restoration of Israel after the exile. The people had suffered greatly, but God promises to bring them back, turn their weeping into joy, and give them provision and comfort. The priests were the ones who lived from the offerings of the temple, so the promise includes that worship would flourish again.

Today we can remember that God not only forgives and restores, but also provides generously. When we go through sorrow or scarcity, we can come to Him with confidence and gratitude, trusting that He will satisfy us with His goodness.
exp.31:1:
This verse says that Jerusalem was surrounded by the army of the king of Babylon, and that the prophet Jeremiah was shut up in the court of the prison, an area under guard inside the royal palace. The word "shut up" means held inside, kept from going out or coming in.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, describing the situation in which Jeremiah received a word from God, in the tenth year of King Zedekiah. The king had locked him up because Jeremiah was announcing that the city would fall into the hands of Babylon. Jeremiah was in prison for saying what God commanded him to say, even though nobody liked it.

For today: the truth of God does not lose its value by being surrounded by problems or rejection. Even when everything seems closed off, we can remain faithful and trust that God is still speaking and working. Ask him today for the courage to be honest and faithful.
exp.15:2:
This verse explains the reason for a difficult command God gave to Jeremiah: not to marry or have children in that place. God speaks of the fate of the children who would be born there, and of their mothers and their fathers. The phrase "bare them" refers to the mothers who gave birth, and "begat them" refers to the fathers who had children. "This place" is the land of Judah.

God speaks to Jeremiah, His prophet, at a time when the people had turned away from Him through idolatry and wickedness. Jeremiah's solitary life was a visible sign of the judgment that was coming. The verses that follow describe a calamity so great that there would not even be normal funerals.

For today: God speaks with seriousness about sin, but He also gives warning before He acts. If we sense His correction today, let us not ignore it; let us return to Him with humility, because His desire is to restore us.
exp.50:21:
God says he will use an instrument of his, like a hammer, to destroy Babylon. The "break in pieces" language means to smash into fragments. The words for "young men" and "young women" refer to the young, and the unmarried girls are included. The list covers every age and both sexes, to show that the judgment would be total.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed nations and had harmed Judah and Jerusalem. Scholars do not agree on who the "hammer" is: many think of the Medes and Persians who would defeat Babylon, and others see a more general image. What is clear is that God promises justice for the wrong that was done.

Today we can trust that God sees injustice and does not forget it. Instead of taking revenge, we can hand our pain over to him and wait for his justice, without losing compassion for people.
exp.22:17:
This verse asks a challenging question: which of those prophets truly stood in the counsel of the Lord, that is, in his inner circle, to see and hear his word? The implied answer is that none of them did.

God speaks through Jeremiah. The false prophets said "you will have peace" and "no harm will come," even though the people were living in sin. They made up pleasing messages from their own hearts. God reminds them that he will judge, and that his storm will fall on the wicked.

For today: before accepting a message as coming from God, compare it with the Bible. A word that only sounds comforting is not necessarily from God. Set aside time to hear his Word with careful attention and humility.
exp.36:5:
God spoke to the prophet Jeremiah at a specific moment. The phrase "the word of the Lord came" means that God gave him a direct message. The phrase is only an introduction: the important part comes in the verses that follow.

Jerusalem was surrounded by the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). When the army of Egypt arrived, the Chaldeans withdrew for a time, and the people and King Zedekiah were filled with false hope. The king sent to ask Jeremiah, and God answered that Egypt would return to its own land and that the Chaldeans would come back. Jeremiah speaks what God says, not what the people want to hear.

When circumstances seem to improve, that does not always mean the danger has passed. Let us seek the word of God sincerely, even when it is hard to hear, and not simply trust in what looks like momentary relief.
exp.51:15:
This verse says that Nebuzaradan, the captain of the Babylonian guard, left some of the poorest people in the land to work as vinedressers (those who tend the vineyards) and husbandmen (those who farm the fields). The rest were taken into exile.

Chapter 52 is a historical summary of the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. The one telling the story is not a prophet speaking in the first person, but the account that reviews how Babylon destroyed the city and the temple. The Babylonians probably left these poor people behind so that the land would keep producing and would not be left abandoned, although the text gives no further reasons.

For today: God sees and remembers those whom the world overlooks. Even in the midst of judgment, the poor were not forgotten, and their simple work kept the land alive. Value humble work, yours and that of others, and seek to care for those who have less.
exp.48:31:
It says that the camels and the large herds of Hazor will be taken as plunder by their enemies. God says he will scatter his people in every direction, to the farthest corner, that is, the most distant remote place. He also states that he will bring ruin on them from every side. "Spoil" means what is taken away from the defeated.

The message is spoken by the Lord through the prophet Jeremiah, against Kedar and Hazor, desert peoples who lived off their flocks. They lived in confidence and without walls, but Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, planned to attack them. It is not known exactly where Hazor was; it is understood as a region of Arab tribes, not the city of Israel with the same name.

For today: wealth and a sense of security cannot protect us from everything. It is wise to trust God more than our possessions, and to live with humility and gratitude.
exp.38:17:
God promises Ebed-melech that he will rescue him. He will not die by the sword; instead he will keep his life as a prize, that is, as the spoil of war: the only thing a person takes with them when they come out alive from a disaster. God gives him this reason: because he trusted in Him.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah. Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian who served in the palace, had defended the prophet when he was thrown into a cistern (chapter 38). Now Jerusalem is about to fall to Babylon, and God promises to care for him in the midst of that judgment. This is not stated in the text, but it is fulfilled within that same account.

For today: God sees acts of courage and trust, even when no one else notices them. If you do what is right and it costs you, rest in the knowledge that He cares for you. His care may not spare you every difficulty, but it will not abandon you.
exp.26:0:
The verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah. The phrase "this word came from the Lord" means that the message came directly from God. Jehoiakim reigned from about 609 to 598 B.C.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who presents Jeremiah receiving a divine command. A curious detail: the verses that follow speak of King Zedekiah, not Jehoiakim. Many scholars think "Jehoiakim" may have been a copyist's error, and that the message was given in the time of Zedekiah. Others explain it in a different way. There is no complete agreement.

For today: God speaks at specific moments in history, and he expects obedience even when his message is uncomfortable. Let us ask for attentive ears to hear him.
exp.11:5:
They say that even Jeremiah's own relatives, his kinsmen and the house of his father, have dealt treacherously with him. They rose up against him and cried out after him, that is, they accused him and pursued him loudly. God warns him: do not trust them, even when they speak with kind words to you, that is, do not put your faith in them even when they speak to you in a pleasant way.

Here God answers Jeremiah's complaint about the wickedness of the people. It is thought that his relatives were from Anathoth, his hometown, though the text does not say this in detail. God tells him that the opposition will be harder and closer than he imagines, and that he must prepare himself to remain faithful.

For today: when someone very close to you wounds you, do not be surprised or stop obeying God. Be wise about whom you trust, ask for wisdom, and rest in God, who never betrays you.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that the people used their tongue the way someone uses a bow: just as an arrow is shot from a bow, they shot out lies. "Shot" means launched or fired. They did not stand firm for the truth, but went from evil to evil. "They have not known me" means that they did not truly want to know God or take him into account.

God speaks here, and he does so with the grief of the prophet Jeremiah, who weeps for his people. Judah lived with deceit, injustice and unfaithfulness. The verses that follow show that there was no trust even among brothers or friends, because lies were everywhere.

For today: truthfulness is practiced in small things. Before you speak, ask yourself whether what you are about to say is true and whether it helps or hurts. Ask God to teach you to speak honestly, even when lying seems easier or more convenient.
exp.30:24:
He says that God will give rest and joy to the one who is worn out and sad. "Satiated" does not speak of wine in a bad sense, but of filling completely, as when someone drinks until fully satisfied. "Replenished" is an older way of saying filled. God promises to fill the weary soul and the sorrowful soul.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah were living in exile in Babylon, tired and with broken hearts. God promises them that they will return to their land, that there will be blessing and normal life again. Some think the following verse, "awoke," is Jeremiah saying that his vision of comfort was sweet to him.

Today, if you feel exhausted or sad, bring that weariness to God honestly. He does not tire of you. Ask Him to fill you with peace and strength, and seek to rest in His faithfulness, one day at a time.
exp.3:22:
He says that the prophet looked at the earth and saw it destroyed and empty, that is, ruined and without life. He also looked at the heavens and there was no light. The word "destroyed" means leveled, left in ruins. The phrase recalls Genesis 1:2, where the earth was without form and void.

Jeremiah speaks here, recounting a vision God gave him. Judah had become foolish: it knew how to do evil but not how to do good. For this reason the prophet announces a judgment that would be like a return to chaos. Scholars agree that it is an image of the disaster that was coming, probably through an invasion; not all agree on how literal the scene is.

For today: sin undoes what God has ordered, but He continues calling us to return. Today you can ask yourself in what area you have ignored God and take a concrete step of repentance and obedience.
exp.8:25:
God says he will hold accountable Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and the peoples of the desert, those who live in the farthest corners, probably those who shave the sides of their heads or live in remote areas. "Uncircumcised" means not having been circumcised. All these nations are uncircumcised in the body, but Israel is uncircumcised in the heart: their inner self has still not surrendered to God.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Several of those peoples practiced circumcision, and yet God treats them alike with the uncircumcised. Judah trusted in that outward sign as a guarantee, but lived without mercy, judgment, or justice. For this reason God announces that he will visit them all alike.

For today: a religious sign is not enough, such as being baptized, attending church, or knowing the Bible. Ask God for a sincere heart and examine whether your life reflects mercy and justice toward others.
exp.50:45:
God tells his people not to lose heart or grow afraid when reports of war arrive. "Rumour" here means news or a report. First a warning will come one year, and the next year another, along with violence in the land and one ruler rising up against another ruler.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to his people who live among the Babylonians. He announces that Babylon will fall and that God will judge its god Bel. He warns them ahead of time that there will be disturbing news and violent changes, so that they will not lose heart or be caught off guard.

For today: when alarming news arrives, do not let fear rule your heart. Remember that God sees everything and still governs. Breathe, pray, and trust that his word will be fulfilled.
exp.34:7:
Here the Rechabites explain that they have obeyed their ancestor Jonadab, son of Rechab, in everything he commanded them. They have never drunk wine, neither they, nor their wives, nor their sons and daughters.

The people speaking are the Rechabites, a family that lived in tents. God asked Jeremiah to bring them into the temple and offer them wine. They refused. God used their faithfulness as a contrast: they obeyed a man, but Judah did not obey God.

Today, this passage invites us to ask whether we are consistent in obeying God. We can choose a clear command from the Bible that we have neglected and commit to keeping it with perseverance this week.
exp.41:7:
Jeremiah, after receiving God's answer, called together Johanan the son of Kareah, the military leaders who were with him, and all the people, from the least even to the greatest. The phrase "called together" is the same as "called," and "military leaders" refers to the captains of the army.

Jeremiah is the one who speaks and acts here. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors asked him to pray for them, promising to obey God whatever his answer might be. Ten days later, the word of God came, and Jeremiah gathered everyone to announce it. His message was not only for the leaders but for everyone.

For today: when we ask God for direction, it is good to be willing to obey before we hear his answer. Praying with an open heart, and not merely seeking approval for what we have already decided, prepares us to receive his guidance with humility.
exp.31:30:
God says that Jerusalem, from the time it was built until that moment, has been a cause of his anger and his fury. Therefore he announces that he will remove it from his presence. The phrase meaning that he will cause it to be taken away means that he will remove it or take it away from before him.

God spoke through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the Chaldeans (Babylonians) destroyed Jerusalem. The people had worshiped Baal and other gods, and they had not listened to God's warnings. Some scholars understand the words "from the day they built it" as a strong expression that sums up a long history of disobedience, not as an exact date.

God is patient and speaks to us again and again, but he is not indifferent to sin. Today we can ask ourselves: is there something God has pointed out to me that I have let pass? Listening in time and correcting our course is a sign of humility and of love toward him.
exp.51:11:
On the tenth day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan came into Jerusalem. He was captain of the guard and served close to the king of Babylon.

The account presents this as a historical record of the end of the kingdom of Judah. Babylon had already captured Zedekiah, and now its officer comes to carry out the destruction of the city. The parallel passage in 2 Kings 25:8 gives the seventh day instead, and it is not known for certain why. Some think these are two different moments of the same event. The chapter seems to be a summary added to the book, and its exact author is not certain.

Today, this passage reminds us that God speaks seriously, but he also does what he says. Listening in time is a sign of wisdom.
exp.43:23:
Jeremiah speaks again to all the people, and in a special way to the women, who had been the ones most involved in worshiping the "queen of heaven." He asks them to hear the word of the Lord. He addresses all of Judah who were living in Egypt with the words "Hear" (listen).

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet of God to the Jews who fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem, even though God had told them not to go. They kept offering incense to another deity and refused to acknowledge their error. That is why Jeremiah calls them to hear a message of judgment.

For today: listening to God is not just hearing, but being willing to change course. Today you can ask yourself whether there is something God shows you in his Word that you have been putting off obeying.
exp.0:9:
God tells Jeremiah that he has placed him this day with authority over nations and kingdoms. "To root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down" speaks of removing what is wrong; "to build, and to plant" speaks of raising up something new.

The LORD speaks to Jeremiah, a young man called to be a prophet. He had just touched his mouth and put his words in it. Jeremiah had no power of his own: his authority consisted in announcing what God said, and those words would bring judgment and also hope. God promises to be with him, so that he would not fear.

For today: God does not call us only to point out what is wrong, but also to build. Ask him to show you what attitude you should let go of and what good habit you should sow, and trust that he walks with you.
exp.42:5:
This verse continues the list of the people whom Johanan and the military leaders took with them to Egypt: men, women, children, and the king's daughters. It also includes everyone that Nebuzaradan, captain of the Babylonian guard, had left in the care of Gedaliah. Among them were the prophet Jeremiah and Baruch, his helper. "Persons" here means people.

The narrator is describing what happened after Gedaliah was murdered. The people had asked God for counsel through Jeremiah, and God told them to stay in Judah. But Johanan and the leaders did not believe that word, and they went to Egypt out of fear of Babylon. Jeremiah and Baruch were carried off with them as well, though we do not know in detail how this happened.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we seek God's direction only so that he will confirm what we have already decided. Obeying his word when it frightens us is better than fleeing toward a false sense of safety.
exp.29:1:
God speaks to Jeremiah and tells him to put in writing everything He has said to him. "Write thee in a book" means that he should record those words so they will not be lost. "Jehovah" is the name of the God of Israel.

God Himself is speaking, and the one who listens is the prophet Jeremiah. According to the verses that follow, what he must write is a promise: God will bring back Israel and Judah from captivity and will make them return to their land. Many understand that it is written so that the people, in the middle of exile, would have something firm to trust in. The book serves as a witness that God will fulfill what He has promised.

God wants His words to be kept safe. Today we can do something similar: write down what God teaches us in the Bible and go back to it in difficult moments, to remember that His promises still stand.
exp.4:29:
This verse says that something horrible and scandalous is happening in the land. The colon at the end announces that what this terrible thing is will be explained right away.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Judah. Earlier He accused the rich of growing fat while they did not defend the orphan or the poor. What follows in verse 31 reveals the matter: the prophets prophesied falsely, the priests ruled by their own authority, and the people loved it that way. The most serious thing was not only the sin of the leaders, but that the people accepted it.

For today: let us not accept comfortably what sounds good but is not true. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible, and let us defend, with concrete actions, those who have no voice, like the orphan and the poor.
exp.39:12:
This verse tells that Johanan, son of Kareah, came with all the captains of the troops who were out in the countryside. They went to see Gedaliah at Mizpah. The fighting men are the armed men, and the word for captains here means leaders or commanders.

Jerusalem had fallen to Babylon, and the Babylonian king appointed Gedaliah as governor over the Jews who remained in the land. Here the narrator speaks, introducing Johanan, who comes to warn Gedaliah of a plot to kill him. Gedaliah did not believe them, and that had very painful consequences.

For today: when someone brings us a serious warning, it is wise to listen with humility and check it carefully. Ignoring an alert out of excessive confidence can cost dearly.
exp.29:11:
God says that the wound of his people is hopeless, meaning there is no hope of cure by human means. A "bruise" is a fracture or severe blow, and a "wound" is an open sore. The word for "hopeless" means very hard to heal. The harm runs deep, and no remedy people can offer reaches it.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Israel, who was suffering punishment for their sin and exile. Earlier, God had promised to save them and not destroy them completely. Here he explains that their allies had abandoned them and that he himself had disciplined them for their wickedness. In this passage God is honest about how serious the problem is, and that honesty sets the stage for his promise of healing (v. 17).

For today: do not minimize your wounds or your sin, and do not look only for human remedies. Acknowledge honestly what hurts you and bring it to God, the only one who can heal what seems beyond repair.
exp.50:39:
He says God will bring the Babylonians down like lambs led to the slaughter, like rams together with male goats. It is an image of weak and defenseless people walking toward their fate. The phrase "I will bring them down" is the same idea stated in the verse above. Before this they were like roaring lions, but now they will not be able to defend themselves.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He is announcing judgment against Babylon, the proud empire that had destroyed nations and carried Judah into captivity. The verses before speak of feasts and an everlasting sleep, and the verses after refer to a code name for Babylon. The message was a comfort to God's people.

For today: do not lose heart before the power of the proud. No human power lasts forever, and God sees injustice. Trust that He governs history and acts in His own time.
exp.6:10:
Is God asking whether the temple, where his name is called upon, has become for the people like a den of robbers, that is, a hiding place where criminals feel safe? Then he adds: "I too see," meaning that nothing escapes him. The phrase "called by my name" means that the place belongs to him and bears his name.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah were stealing, murdering, and worshiping Baal, and then they went to the temple saying "we are delivered," as if the building would protect them. God reminds them of what happened at Shiloh, an earlier place of worship that was destroyed because of the people's wickedness.

For today: going to church or using God's name does not replace an obedient life. Before we worship, let us honestly examine whether there is something we need to correct, ask forgiveness for, or make right, because God sees the heart.
exp.15:5:
It says that in the land of Judah people of every age will die, great and small, and no one will give them a proper burial. No one will mourn for them. Wailing aloud, cutting the skin, and tearing out the hair were gestures of grief, as when one wounds oneself or pulls out one's hair.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had left God for idols, and judgment was coming because of their rebellion. God forbids Jeremiah to attend funerals and feasts, as a sign that there would no longer be peace or comfort for that generation. Many understand that this points to the invasion of Babylon.

For today: God is serious about sin, but He still calls people to repentance. Do not harden your heart; if God shows you something, return to Him today, while there is still time for mercy.
exp.25:14:
Jeremiah warns them firmly: if they kill him, they will be shedding innocent blood, and the guilt would fall on them, on the city, and on its inhabitants. He affirms that the Lord himself has sent him to speak these words to them.

Jeremiah speaks in the temple, before priests, prophets, officials, and the people. They had seized him and were demanding his death for announcing that Jerusalem would be destroyed if they did not turn back to God. Even so, he does not defend himself out of fear: he places himself in their hands, but reminds them that his message came from God and that they could still repent. The officials and the people declared him innocent.

For today: God calls us to speak the truth with humility and courage, even when it costs us. He also invites us to listen to correction carefully, without attacking the one who brings it.
exp.11:16:
It says that if a nation does not listen to God, He will pull it up completely, the way a tree is pulled up by the root, and destroy it. The words "but" and "would not hearken" stand in for the source's wording, and "that nation" refers to the nation in question. The name of God is "the LORD."

God is speaking, answering Jeremiah's complaint about Israel's neighboring peoples who mistreated them. God says that although He will judge them, afterward He will have compassion on them. If they learn to follow His ways and to swear by Him instead of Baal, they will be included among His people. This verse is the final warning: the offer of mercy is real, but rejecting it has consequences.

Today, this verse reminds us that God's mercy is an invitation, not something we can ignore without consequences. If there is something in your life that God is asking you to correct, do not postpone it: respond to Him today with humility.
exp.5:22:
It says that an enemy army is coming against Jerusalem, called here "the daughter of Zion." Its soldiers take hold of the bow and the spear, they are cruel and show no mercy. The noise of their advance sounds like the raging sea, and they come riding on horses, ready to fight.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. For a long time the people ignored his warnings and continued in their sin. Therefore he announces a judgment coming from the north. The text does not name the invader here; many think of Babylon, though some debate this.

For today: do not ignore God's warnings out of convenience. If something in your life draws you away from him, do not put it off; return to him sincerely, because God corrects in order to restore, and his mercy remains open to whoever repents.
exp.37:27:
He says that Jeremiah stayed in the courtyard of the guard until Jerusalem was taken. The word translated "guard" here is the one the verse uses as "prison." The phrase "Jerusalem was taken" is the same event described in the verse. In other words, he was not released earlier, and he was there when the city fell.

The narrator tells what happened after Jeremiah spoke privately with King Zedekiah and then gave a careful answer to the officials who questioned him. Jeremiah had been warning for a long time that Jerusalem would fall if it did not surrender to Babylon. That is why he had been mistreated. This verse closes that episode and prepares the account of the city's fall, which most historians date to 586 B.C.

Jeremiah remained faithful even though his situation did not improve. God does not always rescue us from difficulties right away, but he is with us in them. Today we can keep doing what is right even when things seem stuck, trusting that God sustains those who obey him.
exp.1:24:
God asks his people to stop running after idols until their feet are bare and their throat is dry. It is as if he were saying, "Stop, you are wearing yourself out." But the people answer, "There is no hope," that is, "there is no remedy." They say, "No, I will not stop," because they love strangers, that is, foreign gods, and they intend to follow them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just compared Israel to a wild female camel or donkey in heat, running out of control. Israel denied its idolatry, and God shows them what they are really doing. The people's answer sounds like stubbornness and false hopelessness.

For today: when something wears us down and we still say, "I can no longer change," let us remember that God keeps calling. It may be an addiction, an anxiety, or an idea that has taken the place of God. Today you can stop, be honest with him, and ask him for help.
exp.1:16:
God asks his people a question that already contains its answer: was it not your own choice to abandon the Lord that brought these troubles upon you? He says this while reminding them that he himself had been leading them along the way.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. The verses before describe ruin and humiliation, and they mention Egypt (Noph and Tahpanhes were Egyptian cities). Judah sought security in alliances with Egypt and Assyria instead of trusting God. The Lord shows them that their problem was not bad luck, but having left him.

For today: when something in your life falls apart, ask yourself honestly whether you have been looking for support in other things before looking to God. Returning to him with humility is always possible.
exp.36:9:
What it says: God declares that the fall of Jerusalem is certain. Even if the people managed to defeat the whole army of the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), and only wounded men were left, those wounded men would rise up from their camp and burn the city.

Context: The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to King Zedekiah. The Chaldeans had lifted the siege because the army of Pharaoh of Egypt was coming, and the people thought the danger had passed. God warns them not to deceive themselves: the Chaldeans would return, because the judgment had already been decided.

For today: It is easy to trust in temporary relief and to believe that everything is fine. God invites us to listen to his truth even when it is uncomfortable, and to turn back to him with honesty, instead of leaning on false hopes.
exp.1:35:
It says the people keep moving back and forth, changing direction and looking for help in different places. The verse's "why gaddest thou about so much" points to running from one plan to another, and "to change thy way" means shifting their plans and alliances. God warns that Egypt will also leave them ashamed, just as Assyria did before.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people considered themselves innocent and, instead of turning back to God, sought protection from powerful nations. God tells them those alliances will fail. Scholars agree on the general point, although the exact historical details of those alliances are explained in several ways.

For today: when you face a problem, do not run from one solution to another looking for security everywhere except in God. Before deciding, stop, pray, and honestly acknowledge your faults. He offers a firm trust that will not leave you ashamed.
exp.48:22:
Concerning Damascus. The explanation says that the cities of Hamath and Arpad were confounded, or full of shame and fear, because they received bad news. The phrase "they melted in waters of fainting" means they lost all their courage, like someone who falls apart with fear. The phrase "they cannot be quiet" means they cannot calm down, like a troubled sea.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a series of messages about the nations neighboring Judah. Damascus, the capital of Syria, would face judgment. Hamath and Arpad were cities in northern Syria, and their panic announces that disaster is approaching. Scholars often connect this with the advance of Babylon, although the text does not give all the details.

For today: bad news can overcome someone who trusts only in their own strength or in their city. Let us learn to place our security in God, and in the face of sudden fear, to pray before we let ourselves be overwhelmed.
exp.21:29:
God commands that Coniah be written down as "childless," that is, without children who will reign after him. "Seed" means offspring, and "to rule" means to govern. None of his children would prosper on David's throne.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Coniah, also called Jehoiachin, was king of Judah and ended up exiled to Babylon because of the disobedience of the people and their kings. He had children, so the text is understood to mean that none of them would reign. Some see here a difficulty for the line of Jesus, and scholars explain it in different ways.

Today we can remember that positions, inheritances, and family names do not secure the future. What sustains life is obeying God with humility and trusting in his promises.
exp.50:58:
This verse presents a message that the prophet Jeremiah gave to Seraiah, son of Neriah. Seraiah was accompanying King Zedekiah to Babylon in the fourth year of his reign. He is called "the quartermaster," a title that some translations render differently, and the exact meaning of the title is uncertain.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet of God. He entrusts to Seraiah, who was travelling to the capital of the empire that dominated Judah, the word of judgment against Babylon. In this way the message would reach the very place it spoke about. The Bible gives no further details about the reason for the king's journey.

For today: God can use ordinary people, in difficult places, to carry his word. Trust that he rules over the powers of this world, and obey faithfully wherever you find yourself.
exp.6:25:
This verse says that the people did not listen to God or pay attention to him. The phrase "inclinar el oído," which literally means bending the ear, refers to paying attention with a willingness to obey. "Endurecer la cerviz," or stiffening the neck, means becoming stubborn, like someone who holds his neck rigid so as not to bow his head. The verse also says that this generation did worse than their ancestors.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in Jerusalem, before the fall of Judah. The people believed they were secure because they had the temple, but they continued in injustice and idolatry. God reminds them that for generations he had sent them prophets persistently, and yet there was no change.

For today: when a word from God makes us uncomfortable, we should not reject it out of pride. Let us ask him for a heart ready to listen, and let us obey promptly, even when changing is costly.
exp.7:0:
This verse announces a very harsh judgment. God says that, at that time, enemies will open the tombs of Jerusalem and bring out the bones of the kings, the princes, the priests, the prophets, and the ordinary people. Being left in one's grave was a great dishonor, because in that culture a proper burial was very important.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah had turned away from God and worshiped the sun, the moon, and the stars, as the following verse says. This announcement is a warning about the consequences of that sin. Many understand it to refer to the invasion by Babylon, although the text does not give exact details.

For today: whatever we put first in life ends up ruling over us. Today you can ask yourself to whom or to what you are giving your trust, and return to God with humility while there is still time.
exp.3:1:
If Israel returns to him, God says, they will be able to swear "as the Lord lives" sincerely: with truth, with good judgment, and with righteousness. To "swear" is to affirm something by calling God as witness. The phrase "they will bless themselves" can be understood as the nations being blessed by God or as using him as the example of blessing. "They will glory" means they will rejoice in him and be proud of him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. Many people used God's name with their mouths, yet they kept their idols and their injustices. God asks for a real change, not just words.

For today: let us make sure that what we say about God matches how we live. This week, try to keep your promises and be honest, even when no one notices.
exp.13:6:
It says the people recognize that their sins are a real accusation against them. Even so, they ask God to act, not because they deserve it, but for the sake of his own name, that is, for his reputation and his faithfulness. Their wrongdoing is what the verse calls iniquities, and their repeated acts of disobedience are the rebellions they confess. They admit that these have multiplied and that they sinned against God.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of the people of Judah during a great drought. The animals are suffering for lack of grass, and the people cry out for help. Instead of defending themselves, they confess their guilt and rest on the character of God. The verses that follow show this: "Thy name is called upon us; leave us not."

For today: when you fail, do not hide or make excuses for yourself. Acknowledge your sin honestly and come to God trusting in his mercy, not in your own merits.
exp.48:18:
God says that he will come like a lion coming up out of the thick thickets along the Jordan when the river overflows, and he will attack a place that looks fine and secure, a green and safe pasture. God will make its people run away from there and will appoint whoever he chooses to take charge. He will make them run, and whoever he calls to account cannot match him or resist him.

The message is spoken by the LORD through the prophet Jeremiah, against Edom. Edom was a neighboring nation of Israel, known for being proud and secure in its mountains. God announces that its confidence will not protect it from judgment. Scholars discuss some details, such as who the one "chosen" is, but the central message is clear: God rules over the nations.

For today: do not put your security in your strength, your achievements, or your position. Trust in God, who is just and is above all things, and live with humility before him.
exp.11:15:
It says that if the neighboring nations of Israel carefully learn the ways of God's people, and swear "As the Lord lives" sincerely, just as they once taught Israel to swear by Baal, then they too will be prospered, or made to grow strong, in the midst of his people. "Swear" here means committing oneself to God as the true God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on the wicked neighbors who harmed Israel and led them into idolatry. But he also leaves open a door of mercy there: if they turn back to the Lord, they will be received. If they do not, the following verse speaks of their destruction.

For today: God offers a new opportunity even to those who have harmed us or led us astray. We can pray for them and live with integrity, so that our example invites them to know the Lord.
exp.50:33:
Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, devoured and tore apart God's people. He left them empty like a vessel, swallowed them up like a monster, and filled himself with the best they had. Then he cast them out.

The explanation of the words used here is as follows: to tear apart means to break into pieces; a dragon here is a great monster or serpent; and the finest things are the most valuable and refined possessions.

The speaker is Jerusalem, that is, the people of Judah, who describe their grief after the Babylonian conquest. Nebuchadnezzar plundered the city and carried many people into exile. The verses that follow show that God hears this cry and promises to defend their cause and punish Babylon.

For today: when you feel that someone has left you empty or harmed you, you can bring your complaint to God honestly. He sees injustice, and He does not ask you to take revenge yourself; He invites you to trust that He judges with justice.
exp.23:1:
Jeremiah sees two baskets of figs. One holds excellent figs, "even like the figs that are first ripe," which are the first figs of the year, early and highly prized. The other holds figs so spoiled that they "could not be eaten, they were so bad," meaning they were so damaged that they were no good to eat.

Jeremiah is speaking, recounting a vision that God gave him. It takes place after the first deportation to Babylon, when Nebuchadnezzar carried away King Jeconiah, the princes, and the craftsmen. God will use these baskets, set in front of the temple, to explain his judgment and his care for two groups of people.

For today: God sees reality beyond appearances and circumstances. Those who go through hard trials are not forgotten by Him. Ask Him to teach you to look at your life and the lives of others as He sees them, with truth and hope.
exp.15:11:
The explanation says that the people of Jeremiah's time were worse than their ancestors. "Imagination" means what the heart invents or desires, and "evil" indicates that it is inclined toward wrong. Each person followed their own desires and did not listen to God. "To me" is "to me."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, before the exile in Babylon. The people would ask why such punishment was coming. God answers that their fathers abandoned him to serve other gods, and that they, instead of learning, followed their own path even more. For this reason he announces that they will be carried off to another land.

For today: it is not enough to say that we are better than others or that we have inherited a good faith. It is worth asking ourselves honestly whether we really listen to God or simply follow what our heart dictates. Read his Word, pray, and ask for direction to obey him.
exp.24:37:
God comes out of his hiding place like a young lion to bring judgment. A "covert" is the den where the lion lives. "Desolate" means destroyed and left in ruins. "Oppressor" and "fierce anger" speak of strong, violent wrath. In this rendering, the land is laid waste by that fury. Some scholars think "the oppressor" refers to Babylon, and others to God's own judgment itself; the phrase can be understood in either way.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God. This chapter closes a long warning to Judah and the nations: they did not listen to the prophets, and judgment would come. The "shepherds" are the kings and leaders, who now mourn because their people, like a flock, are being destroyed.

For today: God is patient, but he does not ignore injustice. If this gets your attention, do not harden your heart; listen to him today and turn your path around with humility.
exp.10:12:
It says that Judah had as many false gods as it had cities, and that in Jerusalem there were as many altars as there were streets. Those altars were for Baal, a Canaanite god who was very popular at that time.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had broken their covenant with Him and worshiped idols everywhere. For this reason God announces a punishment: when trouble comes, they will cry out to those gods, and those gods will not be able to save them. It is a serious warning to a people who did not want to return to God.

For today: examine what you place your trust in, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Anything that takes the place of God can become an idol. Give that place back to Him today in prayer.
exp.0:15:
God says he will pronounce his sentences against his people for all their wickedness. The older wording means this: "will declare his judgments" means to announce their condemnations; "burned incense" means offering incense in worship; "the works of their hands" are idols made by them; "bowed down" means bending low to worship them.

The Lord speaks, and answers Jeremiah, a young prophet called to speak in Judah. God explains why he will send an army from the north: the people abandoned him and worshipped other gods. The judgment is not arbitrary; it has a clear reason. Even so, God strengthens Jeremiah so that he speaks without fear.

For today: examine what things are occupying the place of God in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Right now you can return to him sincerely and put him first in your decisions.
exp.25:4:
He says that God asks the people to listen to the words of the prophets whom he has sent to them. The phrase "rising up early" means that God kept sending them again and again, with persistence, without growing tired. The word "á" is an old form, and "no habéis oído" means that they have not paid attention to them.

Here the LORD speaks, and he tells Jeremiah to repeat it in the temple. It is a warning: God wants the people to turn away from their evil way so that he will not have to punish them. If they do not listen, Jerusalem will suffer the fate of Shiloh, a place where the sanctuary once stood and which lay in ruins. Many understand that God gives them another chance because of his mercy.

For today: God still speaks to us with patience, through his Word and through people who advise us. Let us not harden our hearts. Today, read the Bible with a desire to obey and correct something that God shows you.
exp.51:13:
It says that the Babylonian army, which was with Nebuzaradan, the captain of the king's guard, broke down all the walls that surrounded Jerusalem. The word "Chaldeans" is another name for the Babylonians. "Round about" means "all around." Without walls, the city was left defenseless and exposed.

This chapter is a historical account that closes the book of Jeremiah. It tells how Jerusalem fell, approximately in the year 586 BC. Jeremiah had warned for years that, if the people kept turning away from God, this judgment would come. Here the narrator simply describes the events: first the temple and the houses were burned, and then the walls were broken down.

For today: God's warnings are not empty threats but calls to return to Him in time. If today we feel that God is speaking to our hearts, let us not put it off. Let us respond with humility, and He is patient and generous in forgiving.
exp.35:9:
Baruch, Jeremiah's assistant, read the book of the prophet's words aloud. He did it in the temple, in the room of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, who was a scribe (the one who wrote and handled official documents). That room was in the upper court, near the new gate, and all the people could hear.

The writer tells how Baruch obeyed Jeremiah's command. Jeremiah could not enter the temple, so Baruch read on his behalf. It was a day of fasting, so many people from Jerusalem and Judah had gathered. It was a good moment for them to hear God's message, which called them to turn back to Him. This public reading would carry the news as far as the officials and the king.

Today too it is fitting to give others the Word of God faithfully and boldly, without changing or softening it. And when we hear it, let us not let it pass as if nothing happened: let us ask God for a heart ready to obey.
exp.45:24:
God, the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, declares that he will bring punishment on Amon of No (the name of Thebes, the great city in southern Egypt, and of its god Amon), on Pharaoh, on Egypt, on its gods and its kings, and on all who trust in Pharaoh. The word "punish" here does not mean a friendly visit, but a judgment.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter announces the defeat of Egypt before Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Egypt seemed strong and many trusted in its power, but God shows that no king or idol can stop his plans. Then the same passage comforts Israel with the promise that it will not be completely destroyed and will rest again.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, power, or people. All of that can fail, but God remains faithful. Trust in him first.
exp.13:21:
This verse asks three questions to show that only God can give rain. "The vanities of the Gentiles" refers to the idols of the nations, which are worth nothing. The heavens cannot make rain by themselves either. So the people say, "Art not thou he, O Lord our God?" and confess that they wait on Him, because He made all these things.

The people of Judah are speaking, and the prophet Jeremiah prays on their behalf. There is a great drought (Jeremiah 14:1-6). Before this verse they acknowledge their sin and ask God to remember His covenant. Here they stop looking to idols and place their hope in God alone.

For today: when something important is missing, such as work, health, or peace, do not run first to what cannot help you. Acknowledge your failings honestly and wait on God, who has power over all things.
exp.8:6:
It says God himself will melt them down and test them, the way metal is melted to prove it and remove its impurities. The closing question, "What more can I do with the daughter of my people?", means something like: "What more can I do with my beloved people?" Many read it with sorrow, as if God saw no other way out.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah lived full of lies: they deceived their neighbors, spoke peace with their mouths while plotting harm within, and did not want to know God. That is why this judgment comes, aimed at purifying and correcting.

For today: ask God to examine the way you speak. Try to tell the truth with love, without false words or deceit. If God corrects you, remember that He does it to cleanse you and draw you close to Him.
exp.42:11:
He says that God himself will set fire to the temples of the gods of Egypt. The idols will be carried off as captives, and Nebuchadnezzar will wrap the land of Egypt around himself the way a shepherd puts on his cloak: he will take it with ease. Then he will go out from there in peace, that is, without being stopped.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf in Tahpanhes, Egypt. A group of Jews had fled there, against the prophet's advice, out of fear of Babylon. God warns them that Egypt will not be a safe refuge. He calls Nebuchadnezzar "my servant," because he would use him as an instrument of judgment, even though that king did not know the Lord.

For today: do not place your security in places, people, or things that seem strong. Only God is a firm refuge. Before making a decision out of fear, pray and seek his guidance.
exp.45:23:
Egypt, here called "the daughter of Egypt," is said to be left humbled and without defense. The verse's word "confounded" means that it suffered shame and dishonor. The phrase "the people of the north" refers to a people who would come from the north and gain control over it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that Egypt, a power that trusted in its own strength, will be defeated by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who came from the north. The text compares the army to locusts and woodcutters to show that they would be many and unstoppable. God also promises that, afterward, Egypt will be inhabited again.

For today: let us not place our final trust in power, money, or prestige, for these can fall. Let us rest in God, who rules over all and also restores.
exp.13:12:
Jeremiah says to God, in distress: "Ah, Lord God!" because the prophets are telling the people that there will be no war or famine, but a secure peace. The word "sword" stands for war itself. The phrase "peace" can also be understood as a steady and lasting peace.

Jeremiah, a prophet of Judah, speaks in a time of drought and threat. God had already told him not to pray for a people who did not want to return to Him. Jeremiah responds by pointing out that other prophets say the opposite. God clarifies that those prophets speak lies in His name, although He did not send them.

Today, not every message that sounds encouraging comes from God. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and seek the truth even when it is uncomfortable, because God calls people to repentance before He gives firm comfort.
exp.21:17:
God announces that when Jehoiakim, son of Josiah and king of Judah, dies, no one will truly mourn him. His family will not cry out, "Ah my brother! or, Ah sister!", and the people will not cry out, "Ah lord! or, Ah his glory!" It will be a death without grief or honor.
