The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Shortly before, he compared Jehoiakim with his father Josiah, who defended the poor and the needy, and that was what it meant to know God. Jehoiakim, on the other hand, sought his own gain, shed innocent blood, and oppressed others. That is why he receives this judgment.

For today: greatness is not measured by position or money, but by how we treat the weak. Ask God to show you whom you can defend or help this week, and do it with justice and kindness.
exp.24:34:
This verse says that the shepherds and the leaders of the flock will have no place to run or to hide. "Shepherds" and "chiefs of the flock" refer to the rulers and leaders of the people and of the nations.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on the word of the LORD. Just before this passage, God announces judgment on many nations for their wickedness, and calls their leaders to weep. Many readers understand that the image of the shepherd who cannot escape shows that neither power nor position spares anyone from being held accountable before God.

For today: if you have responsibility over others, in your home, your work, or your church, carry it out with humility and honesty, remembering that God sees how you care for those who have been entrusted to you.
exp.48:36:
God says he will cause Elam to be dismayed before their enemies, those who seek to kill them. He will bring disaster upon them and his fierce anger, and he will send war, the sword, until he has consumed them. "Seek their life" means that they want to take away their lives. "Dismayed" means that they will be filled with terror.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message against several nations. Elam lay east of Babylon, and was famous for its archers. Breaking their bow shows that God would take away their strength. It is not known with precision how each detail was fulfilled. But the passage ends with hope: God promises to restore Elam in the end.

For today: no human strength is as secure as it seems. Trust in God, not in your own power, your money, or your success. And remember that his judgment is not the final word, because he also offers restoration.
exp.13:9:
God answers the people of Judah with judgment. "Loved to wander" means they delighted in going from place to place, running after other gods and alliances, and not "refraining their feet," that is, not stopping or turning back to God. For this reason the Lord "does not accept them," meaning He takes no pleasure in them. "Visit their sins" means He will hold them accountable for them.

Jeremiah has just prayed for the people during a great drought, asking that God not abandon them. Here God responds. The people were saying "do not forsake us," but their lives remained far from Him. For this reason, in what follows, God tells Jeremiah not to pray for them.

For today: it is not enough to ask God for help in a crisis if we are not willing to change course. If there is something God shows you that you must leave behind, stop your feet today and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.26:8:
It says that the people should not listen to those who speak to them in God's name or in the name of hidden powers and assure them that they will not have to submit to Babylon. Those who foretell the future by omens are among the kinds of speakers named there; those who practice magic or spells are another; and those who try to uncover what is hidden are another. The phrase about dreams refers to the dreamers who presented their dreams as messages from God.

God speaks through Jeremiah to Judah and to the neighboring nations, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. He had allowed Nebuchadnezzar to dominate the region. Many false prophets promised an easy way out, but God warns that those words were lies and would lead the people to lose their land.

For today: let us not believe a voice simply because it sounds spiritual or because it comforts us. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible, pray with humility, and be willing to hear also what we do not want to hear.
exp.50:18:
God, the "portion of Jacob," is not like the idols. A "portion" is the share or inheritance that someone receives. He is the Creator of all things. Israel is described as the people who belong to him. His name is the Lord of hosts, the Lord with all power.

Jeremiah announces judgment against Babylon. Earlier, the text shows that the idols made by craftsmen are false and have no life. Here it contrasts the true God with them, and reminds his people that they are not abandoned. Who the hammer of the following verse is has been interpreted in several ways.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: money, success, or things we ourselves have built. God is the Creator and can be our true inheritance. Trust in him.
exp.32:23:
God asks Jeremiah whether he has taken notice of what the people are saying: that the two families the Lord chose, he has now rejected. "Notice" here means to perceive or realize. "Rejected" means cast off or abandoned. So that people despises God's people and no longer regards them as a nation.

The Lord speaks to Jeremiah when Jerusalem has fallen or is about to fall, and the people are discouraged. There is discussion about which "two families" is meant: many believe they are Israel and Judah, others the line of David and that of the Levites. God answers with promises: just as day and night remain, his covenant with Jacob and David will stand, and he will restore their captivity with mercy.

For today: when others say your situation has no remedy, or you yourself think it, remember that God's faithfulness does not depend on opinions or circumstances. Trust his word.
exp.39:15:
Gedaliah firmly answers Johanan, "Thou shalt not do this thing." He does not believe that Ishmael is a traitor, and he tells him that what Johanan claims is false. With this, he rejects the plan to kill Ishmael in secret. In this verse, the word "smite" means to kill.

Gedaliah was the governor whom the Babylonians left over the poor people who remained in Judah. Johanan and other leaders warned him that the king of the Ammonites had sent Ishmael to murder him. Gedaliah did not believe them. Afterward, Ishmael did kill him (Jeremiah 41), so his trust proved to be a serious mistake. His intention seemed good, but he was naive.

For today: kindness and trust are valuable, but they need wisdom. When someone warns you of a danger, listen with humility, pray, and investigate carefully, instead of dismissing it just because you don't want to think badly of others.
exp.24:7:
God, here called "the Lord of hosts" (the Lord who has power over all), begins to pronounce a judgment. The reason is simple: "you have not listened to my words." In other words, the people did not want to hear or obey what he had told them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah and Jerusalem. For many years he had warned them to give up their idols and return to him, but they kept on as before. That is why this "therefore" introduces the consequences: the coming of Babylon, which God would allow as a judgment.

Today, this verse reminds us that listening to God is not only hearing, but obeying. If we feel that his Word corrects us, we should not ignore it: let us respond with humility and change, while there is still time to return to him.
exp.34:4:
Jeremiah tells us that, inside the temple, he set before the Rechabites pots full of wine and cups, and told them to drink.

Jeremiah speaks here on God's command. The Rechabites were a family who, by the order of their ancestor Jonadab, lived in tents and did not drink wine. They had come to Jerusalem fleeing from an invading army. God uses this test to show a contrast: they obeyed a human father, but Judah did not obey God.

For today: let us ask ourselves whether we are as faithful to the Word of God as this family was to its commitment. Constant obedience, even when temptations are in plain sight, honors God and strengthens our character.
exp.28:13:
He says that God promises to let himself be found by his people. He assures them that he will change their captivity, that is, he will bring their exile to an end. He will gather them from all the nations and places where he had driven them, and he will bring them back to the land from which they were taken away. Where the explanation comments on a word, "turn away" means "bring back" or "restore." The phrase "I have driven you" shows that God recognizes the exile as part of his judgment.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a letter to the Jews who were carried captive to Babylon. They wanted to return soon, and false prophets were promising them exactly that. God tells them that the return will come, but later on (verse 10 mentions seventy years). In the meantime, they are to seek him with their whole heart.

For today: when you are in a difficult season that does not get resolved quickly, do not stop seeking God sincerely. He has not forgotten you. Pray with perseverance and trust that his timing and his restoration are more reliable than your hurry.
exp.50:11:
It tells them to prepare to attack Babylon: raise the banner or signal of war on its walls, strengthen the watch, post sentries (soldiers who keep guard), and set ambushes, which are surprise traps. The reason given is that the Lord has decided it, and he will carry out what he said against the people of Babylon.

The prophet Jeremiah announces God's judgment against Babylon, the empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and carried the people into captivity. The text mentions the kings of Media as instruments God would stir up. Babylon, trusting in its walls and wealth, would be judged for its pride and its violence.

For today: you can trust that God keeps his word, even when it takes time or seems impossible. When you see injustice that seems to have no end, do not fill yourself with resentment; pray, do good, and wait patiently for God to act in his time.
exp.50:46:
He says that God will "visit" Babylon, that is, step in to judge her. Her "carved images" are the carved idols she trusted in. Her land will be put to shame, because those gods cannot save her, and her slain will fall in the midst of her.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been a proud and idolatrous empire that oppressed other peoples, among them Israel. The text announces that God does not overlook that injustice and calls his people to leave the city. Many understand it as referring to the fall of Babylon before peoples from the north.

For today: do not place your trust in things that seem strong but cannot save, such as money, prestige or power. Trust in God, who is just and cares for his own.
exp.50:59:
This verse says that Jeremiah wrote down in one scroll all the disaster that would come upon Babylon. There he gathered all the words God had spoken against that city and that empire. "Evil" here does not mean wickedness, but disaster or judgment.

Jeremiah was God's prophet in Judah. He wrote this message for Seraiah, an official who traveled to Babylon with King Zedekiah, in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah was to read it there, aloud, as a sign that God would carry out what had been announced. Many believe it was also a message of hope for the exiles.

For today: God does not forget what He promises, and so it is worth writing down and keeping His words. Even when evil seems strong, we can trust that God has the last word.
exp.25:0:
This verse says that at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah and king of Judah, God gave a message to the prophet. The phrase "came this word from the Lord" means that God spoke directly. "The Lord" is the usual English name for God.

The one speaking is God, and he is speaking to Jeremiah. This was a delicate moment: a new king was beginning his reign, and the people needed to return to God. According to the verses that follow, God asks Jeremiah to speak in the temple, holding nothing back, in the hope that the people will turn from their ways. Some scholars see here the start of a message that continues through the rest of the chapter.

For today: God still speaks with clarity and with hope that we will return to him. Today we can hear his word with humility, without trimming it or bending it to suit ourselves, and let it correct us with love.
exp.29:20:
The explanation says that Israel's leader will come from within his own people; he will not be a foreigner. God says he will bring him near to himself and asks: who is this that engaged his heart to approach unto me? In other words, no one would dare to come near to God on his own; it is God who permits it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He promises to restore Israel after the exile: he will multiply the people, punish their oppressors, and renew his relationship with them, so that they will be his people. Many Christians see here a sign of the Messiah, but the text also speaks of a future ruler in general, and it has been interpreted in various ways.

Drawing near to God does not depend on our courage or our merits, but on his initiative. If today you feel a desire to pray or to seek God, thank him, because he himself has been softening your heart. Come near with confidence.
exp.50:19:
It says that God uses someone as his battle axe and weapons of war. With that instrument, he himself will break in pieces nations and destroy kingdoms. To break in pieces means to shatter or destroy, and to destroy means to tear down completely.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah, in his message against Babylon. The verses before it contrast idols, which are worthless, with the God of Jacob, creator of all things. Not all scholars agree on who the battle axe is: some think of Israel, others of the Medes and Persians who would overthrow Babylon. In either case, the one who acts is God.

For today: God can use ordinary people as tools in his hands. Ask him to use you, and remember that the power is not yours, but his.
exp.7:17:
This verse says that the pain is so great that the heart feels without strength.

The speaker is Jeremiah, the prophet, although some think the voice of God is also heard, feeling the pain of his people. The text does not make this fully clear, and it is interpreted in several ways. Judah faced judgment for its idolatry, and an invasion from the north was announced. Jeremiah does not speak coldly: he grieves over the ruin of his people. That is why he is known as the weeping prophet.

For today: you do not have to hide your pain before God. You can bring him your sadness honestly, and also learn to feel compassion for those who suffer the consequences of their own mistakes.
exp.16:5:
This verse describes how the person ends up who trusts only in human strength and turns away from God. He will be like a dry shrub of the desert. He will not notice when something good arrives. He will live in dry, barren places, in a land without people where nothing grows.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. They had put their security in alliances with other nations and in their own strength, and had left the LORD. God warns them with this image of the desert, which contrasts with the tree by the water in the following verse.

For today: when you face pressure, do not place all your hope in money, connections, or your own effort. Make prayer and trust in God your first support, and you will see your life take root where there is water.
exp.24:13:
It says that Babylon, which had conquered and enslaved other peoples, would also be brought low. The phrase about other nations using them as servants means that other mighty nations and kings would make them serve them. The idea of repayment means giving a fair reward, and the phrase about according to their deeds indicates that the punishment would match what they had done.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had gone for years without listening to his warnings, and God announced that Babylon would be his instrument of judgment for seventy years. But Babylon would not go free either: its pride and its violence would also be judged. Scholars understand in different ways how these seventy years were fulfilled, but the central message is clear.

For today: God sees every injustice and does not forget it. We can trust that he judges with justice, so there is no need for us to take revenge. And he invites us to live with humility, treating others as we would want to be treated.
exp.9:6:
This verse asks who would not fear and honor God, called "King of the nations," that is, of all the nations. The phrase "to you it belongs" means that this fear and honor are rightly yours. Neither the wisest of the nations nor their rulers have anyone equal to God.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, addressing God in the middle of a message to the people of Israel. Earlier, he mocked the idols: they are like scarecrows, they neither speak nor walk, and they can do neither good nor harm. Jeremiah contrasts that powerlessness with the greatness of the living God, so that his people would not copy the religious customs of the nations.

For today: when you feel pressure to trust in money, success, or the opinion of others, remember that none of these compares to God. Take a moment today to thank him and to put him first.
exp.30:30:
God announces that days are coming when he will make a new covenant, that is, a new agreement, with all his people: with Israel (the house of Jacob) and with Judah. The name of God is "the LORD," and the promise comes from him and does not depend on human effort.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were living through a hard time, with judgment and exile, because they had broken the earlier covenant made in the days of Moses. Even so, God does not abandon them. He promises them a fresh beginning, in which his law will be written on the heart and there will be a close relationship with him.

For today: even if you have failed or feel far from God, he still offers a new beginning. Christians see this covenant fulfilled in Jesus. Ask God to change your heart from within, not only your behavior on the outside.
exp.28:1:
This verse is a parenthesis that tells us when the letter was written: after King Jeconiah left Jerusalem. Leaving with him were the queen mother, the court officials (the royal attendants), the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen and the smiths (according to others, the blacksmiths or locksmiths; the term is understood in several ways).

The one speaking is the narrator, who places the letter of the prophet Jeremiah. This happened around 597 B.C., when Nebuchadnezzar carried the most capable people of the kingdom off to Babylon. Jeremiah writes to the exiles to bring them God's word in the midst of their grief.

For today: God does not forget those who live through circumstances they did not choose. Even far from what is familiar, we can receive his word, pray, and keep trusting in him.
exp.22:35:
God says that the expression "burden of the Lord" should no longer be used. The word in the original can mean "burden" but also "a solemn prophecy or message." God says that whatever each person says will become a burden to that very person, because they had twisted the words of the living God. The phrase "shall ye mention" means "you will bring up." "Perverted" means "distorted" or "changed."

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf against prophets, priests, and people who used that phrase in a mocking way or to give authority to their own ideas. Many interpreters see a play on words here, though some understand it in a slightly different way.

Today, we should be careful not to say "God says" to support our own opinions. Before speaking on God's behalf, it is wise to listen to his Word with humility and to compare it with the whole Bible.
exp.5:19:
The explanation says that God does not value lavish offerings when the heart is far from him. The costly perfumes that came from distant lands were prized goods, and Sheba is usually placed in the south of Arabia, though its exact location is debated. Whole burnt offerings were sacrifices burned completely on the altar. The idea that God does not accept them, and that they do not please him, is what the verse conveys.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah kept performing their rituals in the temple, yet they rejected God's word and his law, as the preceding verse says. For that reason God announces judgment. The sacrifices could not cover their disobedience.

For today: before looking for impressive things to offer God, such as songs, services or donations, check whether you truly listen to him and obey him. God seeks a sincere heart, not merely a good religious appearance.
exp.1:12:
God says that his people committed two evils: they abandoned him, who is the fountain of living waters (water that flows and gives life), and they began digging their own cisterns, that is, pits for storing water. But those cisterns are broken: they have cracks and do not hold the water.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, his people. He rebukes them for exchanging their living God for idols and human alliances that could not help them. Not even the pagan nations change their gods, and yet Israel exchanged the true one. The following verses show the consequences: invasion and destroyed cities.

For today: we all seek something to quench the thirst of the heart, such as success, money, approval, or pleasure. Those things can be useful, but they fail when we ask them for what only God gives. Today, before you run after something to feel full, take a few minutes to pray and read the Bible, returning to the fountain.
exp.12:8:
God says that just as the linen belt hidden by the Euphrates rotted and became useless, He will cause the pride of Judah and of Jerusalem to rot. Pride means thinking more of yourself than you should and refusing to submit to God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He had been commanded to use a linen belt as a sign for the people. God wanted to show that Judah, made to stay close to Him, had drifted away by refusing to listen and by following other gods. The text does not make clear whether the trip to the Euphrates was literal or a vision, and scholars understand it in both ways.

Today, pride pulls us away from God and ruins us from within. We can ask God in prayer where we struggle to listen to Him, and obey Him with humility.
exp.2:3:
God invites his people to return. "At least from now on" means "at least now, even though it is late." God asks whether they will not cry out to him, calling him "my Father" and "the guide of my youth," meaning the one who accompanied and led them from the beginning as a nation. "You will cry out" means asking for help with force.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah and Israel, who had turned away from him through idolatry, which is described as unfaithfulness in a marriage. God reminds them of their sins and of the drought as a sign of judgment, yet still opens the door to repentance. His words show both grief and patience.

For today: if you have turned away from God, do not wait until you are better before returning. Cry out to him today with sincerity, as to a Father who is still waiting for you and wants to guide you again.
exp.12:5:
It says that a long time passed after Jeremiah hid the linen belt by the Euphrates. Then God tells him to go and get it. A "belt" is a sash or girdle, and the phrase "after many days" means "after a long time." Jeremiah is to return and take back what he had hidden at God's command.

Here the Lord speaks to the prophet Jeremiah, and this action is a symbolic sign for Judah. Later on, God explains that the rotten belt represents the people's pride and their refusal to hear his word. Scholars debate whether the journey was physical or a vision, because the text does not make this clear.

For today: God wants us to stay close to him, like a belt held snugly around the waist. If we drift away and harden our hearts, we wear down inside. Today you can set aside a few minutes to read the Bible and pray, so that you remain close to God.
exp.32:11:
God says that this place, now a desert with no people and no animals, will once again be full of life. There will again be shepherds' huts, that is, simple shelters where shepherds look after their flocks. The image speaks of peace, ordinary work, and everyday life restored.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah at a time when Jerusalem and Judah had been destroyed by the Babylonian invasion, and the people were either in captivity or on the way to it. In the middle of the ruin, God promises to bring them back and restore joy. Many understand that this was fulfilled in part with the return from exile, and others also see a greater fulfillment in Christ.

For today: when something in your life seems empty or lost, do not treat that scene as the final word. God can raise up the simple and ordinary once again. Trust Him and take one small step of faith today.
exp.47:23:
This verse follows a list of Moabite cities that will be reached by God's judgment. Here Kerioth and Bozrah are named, and then all the cities of Moab are included, both far and near. In other words, none would be left out. Some believe that Bozrah here is a Moabite city and not the well-known Bozrah of Edom, although there is no complete certainty.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, carrying the message of the LORD. Moab, a neighbor of Israel, trusted in its own strength and exalted itself against God, as the following verses say. For this reason its downfall is announced.

For today: God sees every place and every attitude, however great or small they may seem. We can examine whether we trust in our own strength and, with humility, hand over to God our pride and our sense of security.
exp.6:26:
God tells Jeremiah to repeat to the people everything He has told him, but He warns him ahead of time that they will not listen to him. Even if he calls out to them, they will not answer him.

God speaks to Jeremiah in the temple in Jerusalem, where the people relied on rituals while they lived in injustice and idolatry. God had sent prophets to them again and again, and they stiffened their necks, meaning they became stubborn. Jeremiah receives a difficult assignment: to speak without any guarantee of being heard. The text does not say the message is not worth delivering, but that the people's hearts were closed.

Today it reminds us that obeying God does not depend on the results. If you share the truth with love and people do not pay attention to you, do not be discouraged. Remain faithful, pray for those people, and trust that God is working in hearts.
exp.42:7:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah while he was in Tahpanhes, a city in Egypt. The phrase "the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah" means that the Lord gave him a message. The words "came" and "unto" are older forms of how English is written today, but the meaning is simply that the message arrived for him.

Jeremiah had warned the people not to flee to Egypt, but they did not obey, and they took the prophet with them. Even there, God kept speaking. After this verse, the Lord tells him to set up a sign with stones to announce that Nebuchadnezzar would reach Egypt. Scholars agree that this is a announcement of judgment, although they discuss the historical details of how it was fulfilled.

For today: God does not stop speaking even when we go wrong or are far from where we should be. We can listen to him again and obey him today.
exp.18:14:
Thus says the Lord of hosts, meaning the Lord of all power, that he is going to bring upon Jerusalem and its surrounding towns all the punishment he had already announced. The reason is that the people have hardened their necks, a way of saying they were stubborn, like an ox that refuses to bow its neck to take the yoke, and so they would not listen.

Jeremiah had just broken a clay jar in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, next to Topheth, as a sign of the judgment to come. Then he returns to the temple and speaks to all the people. He does this because God commanded him to. The people had worshiped false gods, and the earlier warnings meant nothing to them.

God speaks before he acts, and his warnings are a sign of patience. Today we can ask ourselves whether there is something God has told us in his Word that we have been ignoring. Listening in time, with humility, prevents much pain.
exp.24:25:
God says he will make all the kings of the north, near and far, one after another, and all the kingdoms of the world drink the cup of his judgment. The north is the direction referred to here, and the surface of the earth is the whole face of the world. At the end, the king of Sheshach will drink as well. Many understand "Sheshach" to be a code name for Babylon, although the text does not explain this here.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, around 605 B.C. Judah and the neighboring nations had rejected the calls to turn back to God. The "cup" is an image of divine punishment: no one is left out, not even Babylon, which would be used as an instrument.

For today: God is just with everyone, without favoritism. Instead of believing that our power or our nation protects us, it is wise to live with humility, listen to his correction in time, and repent with sincerity.
exp.48:2:
Jeremiah calls on Heshbon to wail because the city of Ai has been destroyed. He also tells the women of Rabbah to put on sackcloth, the clothing of mourning, and to lament. Mourning here means crying out with sorrowful songs. Running back and forth along the walls probably means running frantically from one side to the other in despair. Their king, with his priests and princes, will go into exile.

God speaks through Jeremiah against Ammon, a people neighboring Israel, who had taken over the territory of Gad. Some believe the king mentioned here is the god Milcom. It is also not certain which Ai is meant here.

Today, this passage reminds us that no power or wealth can protect us from God. We can examine whether we trust in what we have more than in Him, and live with humility and justice.
exp.8:15:
It says that God will scatter the people of Judah among unfamiliar nations, nations that neither they nor their ancestors had known. In addition, He will send war after them, and the phrase about the sword going after them means that it will pursue them, until they are destroyed. The word translated here as "destroy" means to bring to an end or to consume completely.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had turned away from God to follow their own desires and to worship the Baals, false gods, just as their fathers had taught them. That is why this judgment comes, which history shows fulfilled in the exile in Babylon. The verses that follow speak of mourning over this tragedy.

For today: what we inherit or follow out of habit is not always what is right. It is wise to examine our lives in the light of God's Word, and to return to Him with humility before error costs us dearly.
exp.50:52:
Even if Babylon were to climb up to heaven and make the height of her strength secure, God says he would send destroyers against her. The word for "should mount up" in the old text simply means would climb, and the phrase about making her strength firm means would strengthen or secure. Those who tear down and lay waste are the destroyers. Nothing, however high it may seem, is beyond God's reach.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had invaded Judah and defiled the temple in Jerusalem, and the people felt shame and grief. God answers by promising that he will judge Babylon and its idols. The image of climbing to heaven recalls the pride of those who think they are untouchable. The verses that follow announce the fall of the city.

For today: when pride, injustice, or power seem unbeatable, do not lose hope. God is just and has the final word. Trust in him, keep doing good, and do not rely on your own strength.
exp.19:4:
God says that everything of value in Jerusalem will be handed over to its enemies. The wealth and goods of the city are what he means by "strength"; "labours" refers to what the people had produced with effort; "precious things" and "treasures" are objects of great value, including those belonging to the kings of Judah. The enemies will plunder them and carry them off to Babylon.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Pashur, a priest with authority in the temple, had struck Jeremiah and left him imprisoned in the stocks (an instrument of punishment) for announcing judgment. When he was released, Jeremiah answered him firmly: God was warning that Judah would be taken captive to Babylon because it did not turn back to him.

For today: what we value most, such as money, position, or security, is not firm forever. It is good to ask ourselves where we are placing our trust and to return to God, even when his word is sometimes hard to hear.
exp.1:23:
It says that Israel is like a wild donkey, raised in the wilderness, that sniffs the wind with desire, and no one can restrain her. "Breathes as she wants" speaks of an uncontrollable impulse. "Her occasion" is her moment of heat, and "her month" is her season of mating. When it comes, there is no need to tire yourself searching for her: she herself lets herself be found. "They will find her" means "they will find her."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses his people of idolatry, of running after the Baals, false gods of Canaan. They denied their guilt, but God shows them with this image how unrestrained their desire is to go after other gods.

For today: when a passion dominates us and we justify it, it is wise to stop, be honest before God, and ask him for help. He does not condemn us to humiliate us, but to bring us back to himself.
exp.22:22:
It says that God is not a God limited to one place. The phrase that means "near" is not something your verse uses, and the phrase that means "far" is also not used, so these explanations are dropped. God asks whether he is only near and not also far away. The answer is clear: he is everywhere and sees everything.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah. He condemns the false prophets of Judah, who claimed to have messages from God without having been sent by him. They presented their dreams as if they were divine word. They believed their lies would go unnoticed, but God reminds them that nothing is hidden from him.

For today: since God is near and far, nothing we do or say escapes his sight. That invites us to be sincere, not to use his name to back up our own ideas, and to test every teaching against the Bible. It also comforts us: he is always near us.
exp.9:21:
The explanation says that a report is coming, a great roar from the north. The phrase used for the report means a rumor or news that spreads, and the word for "north" is an old term. That army will turn the cities of Judah into desolate places, so abandoned that only snakes will live in them (other versions say jackals).

Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah before the invasion by Babylon. The verses just before show Judah mourning like a tent that has been torn down. It says that their leaders, called shepherds, were foolish and did not seek God, and for that reason the people were scattered. Many understand the north to refer to Babylon, although the text does not name it here.

For today: when we make decisions, let us seek God first, and not only our own wisdom. If we are leaders at home, in the church, or at work, let us care humbly for those who depend on us.
exp.45:22:
He says that the enemy cuts down Egypt's forest, that is, brings it down, and that it cannot be counted because their soldiers are more numerous than the grasshoppers.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God to Egypt, after its defeat by Babylon at Carchemish. The "forest" can represent Egypt, with its people and its power, although some understand it in another way. The Egyptian soldiers seemed strong, but they fled. God shows that He rules over the nations.

For today: let us not place our security in what seems great and firm, such as money, power or fame. All of that can fall. Let us trust in God, who endures, and ask Him for wisdom and humility to live each day.
exp.16:18:
God tells Jeremiah to go and stand in one of the gates of Jerusalem, the gate through which the kings of Judah came in and went out. He is also to stand in all the other gates of the city.

Here "the Lord" is the name God uses for himself. "Á" is an old spelling of "a".

Speaking is God, and Jeremiah is the prophet who receives the assignment. The gates were very busy places, where kings and ordinary people passed through. That made them an ideal place to deliver a message to everyone. What follows is a call to keep the Sabbath. It is not known for certain which gate this was.

For today: God wants his word to reach everyone, without distinction. We can speak of him simply in the places where we live each day, with respect and with love, and first obey him ourselves.
exp.5:29:
This verse says the people will be called "rejected silver," that is, silver with no value, which is thrown away because it is no good. The reason is that God himself has rejected them. The word "rejected" means cast aside or set off to one side as something no longer useful.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He compares Judah to a metal that is put through the fire to be purified. But however hard the refiner worked, only dross was left: the people did not give up their wickedness, and their leaders kept deceiving and corrupting. That is why the people were rejected as worthless. Some scholars see here a judgment that announces the coming invasion of Babylon.

For today: it is not enough to look valuable on the outside. God looks for a heart that lets itself be corrected. When He confronts us, it is wise to answer Him with humility and repentance, instead of hardening ourselves.
exp.35:0:
In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah and king of Judah, God spoke to Jeremiah. The verse says that the word came to Jeremiah from the Lord. The Lord is the name of God.

The one speaking is God, who gives a message to his prophet Jeremiah. From the verses that follow we see that he will ask Jeremiah to write on a scroll everything he had already said to him. The fourth year of Jehoiakim is usually placed around 605 BC, although the exact dates can vary depending on the calculation. God wanted the people to listen, to turn back, and to be forgiven.

God does not tire of speaking to us or of offering us a way out. Today we can open his Word with a willing heart, asking ourselves which path we need to change, and trusting that he wants to forgive.
exp.16:13:
Here Jeremiah asks God to heal him and to save him. He says that if God does this, he will truly be healed and saved. He ends by saying that God is his praise, that is, the reason for his gratitude and trust.

The text does not make clear whether the healing is physical, emotional, or spiritual.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. He has just said that those who turn away from God will be put to shame, because they abandon the source of living water. Right after this, he reports that people mock him and ask him where the word of the Lord is. For this reason he prays out of his pain, seeking from God what no one else can give him.

When you feel hurt, tired, or criticized, make a simple and sincere prayer like this one. Do not depend only on your own strength or on the opinion of others. Bring your need before God and trust that he alone can give you true healing and salvation.
exp.15:7:
It says God commands Jeremiah not to enter a house where there is a feast or banquet, nor to sit down to eat and drink with the people. "Feast" means banquet or party. "Likewise" means "in the same way," because earlier God had already forbidden him to marry and to attend funerals.

God speaks, addressing the prophet Jeremiah. His solitary life was a sign to the people: soon a judgment so great would come that there would no longer be ordinary weddings, feasts, or funerals. God wanted the people to wake up and return to Him before it was too late.

For today: let us not take God's warnings lightly. Take a moment to listen to His voice and correct whatever needs correcting, instead of carrying on as if nothing were happening. He warns because He desires to restore, not merely to punish.
exp.26:19:
This verse says that when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, carried away captive Jeconiah (son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah) and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem, he did not take certain objects from the temple: the pillars, the bronze sea, the stands, and other vessels. The word "carried away" means taken into exile.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf, around the year 594 B.C. Some false prophets were claiming that the objects from the temple would soon be returned. Jeremiah answers them: if you truly have a word from God, then pray that what is still left will not be taken away. God warns that Babylon will take those things too.

For today: do not cling to comfortable promises that merely sound good. Test what you hear against the Word of God, and trust that He has a plan even in difficult times, and that He keeps what He promises.
exp.40:5:
This verse tells how Ishmael, son of Nethaniah, went out from Mizpah to meet some travelers. He was weeping as he went, but his tears were false. He said to them, "Come to Gedaliah," even though he had already killed him. "He went out to meet them" means that he went out to receive them.

The narrator recounts the event. Gedaliah was the governor placed by Babylon over those who remained in Judah, and Ishmael murdered him in secret. The eighty men were coming in mourning, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn, to bring offerings to the temple in ruins. Ishmael pretended grief to draw them into the city, and there he killed them. The text does not explain all of his motives.

Today the passage warns us that tears and kind words do not always reveal a sincere heart. Let us ask for wisdom to discern, and let us make sure that our own compassion is genuine.
exp.5:16:
God says that he set watchmen over the people, that is, sentinels who warned of danger, so that they would hear the sound of the trumpet, which was the alarm signal. But the people answered with firmness: "We will not listen." The explanation of the old wording is removed, since the reader's verse does not use those words.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, shortly before judgment came. God had already shown them the good way and promised them rest, but they said: "We will not walk in it." Watchmen are usually understood as the prophets who warned the people. Their refusal brought consequences, as the following context shows.

Today, God still speaks through his Word and through people who advise us with love. Think of some warning you have been ignoring, and ask God for a humble heart to listen to it and obey in time.
exp.17:2:
Jeremiah obeys what God commanded him: he goes down to the potter's house, the craftsman who makes clay vessels. There he sees him working at the wheel, the spinning device on which the clay turns while the potter shapes it.

God himself had told Jeremiah to go there, to give him a message. Jeremiah was a prophet in Judah, a people who had turned away from God. The Lord uses an everyday scene as a visual lesson, which is explained in the verses that follow: he has the right to deal with his people as the potter deals with the clay.

For today: God often speaks to us through the simple things of each day. Today, as you look at your work or your home, ask him to teach you something. And let him shape you with trust.
exp.34:3:
Jeremiah brought the Rechabites into the temple and led them into a chamber, or room, belonging to the sons of Hanan, a man called "a man of God," that is, a man recognized as a servant of God, perhaps a prophet. That room was next to the chamber of the princes, or leaders, and above the chamber of Maaseiah, the keeper of the door.

Jeremiah speaks here, following God's command. The place is public and clearly identified, so that there would be witnesses. God wanted to use the faithfulness of the Rechabites, who obeyed their ancestor Jonadab, to show by contrast that Judah was not obeying God.

Today we can ask ourselves: if these people keep the word of a human father, how do I obey the Word of God? Choose a clear command of God today and keep it faithfully.
exp.15:3:
This verse announces a very harsh judgment on Judah. Many will die of terrible diseases, and no one will mourn them or bury them. Their bodies will be left lying like refuse on the ground, and they will become food for birds and wild animals. There will be war and famine.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He is commanded not to marry or have children, as a living sign of what would come upon that land. The people had abandoned God and followed other gods, and God withdraws his peace. Many understand this as a warning given before the fall of Jerusalem, although the text does not give details of each scene.

For today: God is serious about sin, but his warnings are meant to bring us back to him. Today you can ask yourself what you have put in God's place, and, in prayer, return to him sincerely before the harm grows.
exp.4:8:
This verse is a question that God asks. "Visit" in the sense of calling to account is an older way of saying that God comes to bring punishment for wrongdoing. The phrase about God's soul being avenged means that God Himself responds with justice. God asks: how could I not act against a people like this?

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. Earlier, He accuses them of abandoning Him, of swearing by false gods, and of living in unfaithfulness and excess. Even after receiving prosperity, they turned away from Him. Then He announces judgment, yet asks not to destroy them completely. So the warning comes after great patience, not from a sudden anger.

For today: God takes faithfulness seriously, but He is also patient. Do not take advantage of His goodness; if He shows you something you need to change, respond quickly with repentance and return to Him.
exp.16:26:
This verse is a warning. God says that if the people do not obey him by keeping the sabbath as a holy day, and keep carrying loads and bringing things in through the gates of Jerusalem on that day, he will send a fire into those gates. That fire will destroy the palaces and will not go out.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message addressed to the king and the people of Judah. The verses before this one promise blessing if they obey: the city would remain and people would come to worship. This verse shows the other side: disobedience would bring judgment. The sabbath was a sign of the covenant between God and his people.

For today: God invites us to set aside time to rest and to remember that he is our provider. You might reserve one unhurried moment each week, free from work and rush, to pray, rest, and be with your family or your church.
exp.46:4:
Gaza is said to have become bald, and Ashkelon is said to have been brought to silence or destroyed. Mourning practices of the time involved tearing out or cutting one's hair as a sign of deep grief, and the verse's image of baldness and self-cutting pictures that grief. The prophet asks, "how long wilt thou cut thyself?", as if to say that their sorrow has no end.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf against the Philistines, who lived along the coast. An invading army is announced that comes with chariots and a loud tumult, and it brings such terror that fathers do not even stop to help their children. It is not stated here with certainty who the invader is; some think of Egypt and others of Babylon. What is clear is that God allows it.

For today: let us not trust in our own strength or security, because everything can fall suddenly. It is better to trust in God and to live in humility before Him.
exp.37:25:
King Zedekiah tells Jeremiah what he should answer if the officials ask him what they discussed in private. He should say that he begged the king not to send him back to Jonathan's house, so that he would not die there. The word "return" is used here for going back to a place.

The king speaks with Jeremiah in private. Zedekiah is afraid of the officials, who already wanted to kill the prophet. Jeremiah had been held prisoner in Jonathan's house, a place in poor condition. The answer the king suggests is partly true, since Jeremiah had indeed asked for this before, but it does not tell the whole conversation. Some scholars see here discretion in the face of a real danger; others notice the king's weakness.

For today: one can keep discretion without lying, and under pressure it is wise to act with prudence, yet with honesty and courage, trusting that God cares for those who are faithful to him.
exp.27:12:
He says God sends Jeremiah to go to Hananiah and give him a message. Hananiah broke wooden yokes, but God says that now iron yokes will come, much harder and impossible to break. The yoke is the piece placed on the neck of working animals; here it stands for submission to Babylon.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Hananiah, a prophet, had announced that Babylon would fall within two years, and he broke the wooden yoke that Jeremiah was wearing as a sign. But God had not sent him. His false hope did not remove the punishment; it would make it heavier.

Today, listening only to what comforts us can turn out to be very costly. Before we believe a pleasant message, let us compare it with the Bible and ask God for a humble heart, ready to hear the truth even when it hurts.
exp.21:1:
God tells Jeremiah to say to the king of Judah: "Hear the word of the Lord." The message is not only for the king but also for his servants (his attendants and officials) and for all the people who enter through the palace gates. "Sitting on the throne of David" means ruling as a descendant of David.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. God sends him to the royal palace to call the rulers to account. The verses that follow explain the reason: God requires justice, help for the oppressed, and protection for the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. Whoever reigns is not an absolute owner; he answers before God.

Whoever has authority, whether in government, at work, or in the home, must listen to God. Today we can ask ourselves: do I use my influence to protect the weak, or only for my own benefit?
exp.38:1:
This verse tells that, after a long siege, the walls of Jerusalem were broken down. "The city was broken up" means that the Babylonians made a breach in the wall and were able to enter. About eighteen months passed from the start of the siege, and the date is the ninth day of the fourth month of the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.

The one who tells the story is the book of Jeremiah, which records what the prophet had warned about for years. God had called Judah to return to Him, but the king and the people did not heed it. The fall of the city shows that God's words are fulfilled, even though it takes time.

For today: let us not postpone obedience, thinking there will always be time. When God speaks to us through His Word, listening in time spares us much pain. He remains merciful to whoever turns back to Him.
exp.16:1:
Here the text says that the children of Judah fondly remember their altars and their groves, which were sacred poles or trees used to worship idols. Those places stood beside leafy trees and on the high hills, where that false worship was practiced.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just said that Judah's sin is engraved as with an iron chisel on their heart. The children inherited idolatry from their parents and felt it as part of their identity. That is why the judgment announced afterward would come.

For today: what we repeat and love over time is engraved on the heart. It is worth asking ourselves which inherited or learned "altars" are occupying God's place in our lives, and asking him to write his truth on our hearts.
exp.49:43:
He says that God will bring an enemy like a lion that comes up out of the thick thickets along the Jordan toward a safe pasture. The reference to the Jordan's thick banks points to the crowded, overgrown edge of the river, where lions used to live. Babylon is the place that seemed secure, and God says he will make them run away from it suddenly, and he will set over it whomever he chooses. The word for calling someone to account, to demand an answer, means that no one can challenge him, not even a shepherd, that is, a ruler.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment against Babylon, which had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed Judah. Much of what is said here nearly repeats what was said against Edom (Jeremiah 49:19). Scholars understand the "chosen one" as a people or leader whom God raises up, commonly associated with the Medes and Persians.

For today: no human power is beyond God's reach. If you see injustice or abuse that seems unbeatable, you can trust that God governs and will do justice in his time. Meanwhile, seek to live with humility and do not rely on your own strength.
exp.9:3:
What it says: The verse describes how a wooden idol is made. It is "decked" or adorned with silver and gold, and it is "fastened" or secured with nails and hammers so that it will not fall or move from its place.

Context: God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to his people, surrounded by nations that worship idols and practice astrology. He warns them not to imitate those customs or fear those signs. With a certain irony, he shows that a god made by human hands, which needs nails so that it does not fall, has no power at all. At the end, the text contrasts this with the greatness of the Lord.

For today: Today idols can be money, success, or image. Ask yourself: what do you trust more than God? What we build and adorn cannot sustain us; only God, living and powerful, can do that.
exp.29:9:
God tells his people, here called "Jacob" and "Israel," not to be afraid or dismayed. He himself will save them, even though they are far away, in the land where they were taken as prisoners. He will bring them back, they will live in rest and quiet, and no one will frighten them again.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were suffering the consequences of their disobedience and were living in exile, far from their home. God promises them freedom, restoration, and a future of peace. He also makes clear that he will discipline them, but he will not destroy them completely.

For today: when you feel trapped by guilt, fears, or difficult circumstances, remember that God corrects with love and does not abandon you. Pray with confidence and rest in his promise to help you.
exp.1:6:
God says he brought his people into a fertile land. The word "Carmel" here means a land of orchards and fruitful fields, and the word "inheritance" is the property God gave them as their portion. The words "defiled" and "abomination" refer to making the land unclean and turning it into something repugnant. God gave them blessing, but they answered with contempt.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Israel of forgetting him after he brought them out of Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness. The leaders also failed: priests, shepherds and prophets went after Baal, a false god. So God brings a formal charge, as in a court case.

For today: it is easy to forget God when everything is going well. Today we can stop and thank him for what we have, and care honestly for what he has entrusted to us: family, work, health and faith.
exp.25:8:
Here the people challenge Jeremiah: "Why did you say in the name of God that this temple will become like Shiloh, and that the city will be destroyed and empty?" Their word for "destroyed" is the one in the verse that reads "desolate," meaning laid waste and ruined. "Without an inhabitant" refers to having no one living in it. Then all the people gathered against him in the temple.

The priests, the prophets, and the people are speaking. Jeremiah had just announced that, if they did not repent, God would leave the temple like Shiloh, a place where the sanctuary once stood and which, according to Jeremiah 7, was judged. They trusted that the temple would protect them, so his message seemed to them an offense.

For today: sometimes God's truth is uncomfortable, especially when it touches what we believe is secure. Let us ask for humility to hear correction without attacking the messenger, and for courage to speak the truth with love.
exp.40:7:
This verse tells how, among a group of men that Ishmael was about to kill, ten begged him not to do it. They told him that they had supplies hidden in the field: wheat, barley, oil, and honey. Ishmael spared them and did not kill them along with the others. The word "treasures" here means hidden stores or reserves of food.

Ishmael, of the royal family, had murdered Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon. Then he deceived a group of pilgrims who were coming from the north, pretending to weep and offering to take them to Gedaliah. The ten men spoke to save their lives. The text does not explain why Ishmael accepted; perhaps he wanted that food, but the Bible does not say so.

For today: in the middle of a dangerous situation, what we have can help us save lives, but the account reminds us that violence and deceit are terrible. Let us ask God for wisdom, and use our resources to care for others, not to bargain with evil.
exp.34:1:
God tells Jeremiah to go and find the Rechabites, a family that lived as nomads, and to bring them into the temple, into one of its side rooms. There he is to offer them wine to drink. The words "speak to them" simply mean inviting them, and the name of God is the Lord.

The one speaking is God, in the time of King Jehoiakim of Judah. The Rechabites, by command of their ancestor Jonadab, never drank wine. God wants a public test: they obey a man even when wine is offered to them, while the people of Judah do not obey God. This contrast is made clearer later in the chapter.

For today: ask yourself whether you are as steady in obeying God as this family was in keeping their promise. Choose one specific thing God has asked of you and carry it out this week, even if there is pressure or temptation around you.
exp.10:22:
This verse says that none of that group will be left alive. God announces that he will bring disaster on the men of Anathoth, and he calls that moment "the year of their visitation." "Visitation" here does not mean a friendly visit, but a time when God steps in to judge.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The men of Anathoth, his own townspeople, wanted to kill him if he kept prophesying in the name of the LORD. God responds by defending his servant and announcing judgment on those who wanted to silence his word. The Bible presents this as God's justice, not as Jeremiah's revenge.

For today: it is not wise to keep quiet about the truth out of fear of pressure, even from family or acquaintances. And whoever rejects God should not take his patience lightly. We can trust that God cares for those who are faithful to him and acts with justice in his time.
exp.28:22:
It says that God judges Ahab and Zedekiah for three things: they did wickedness in Israel, they committed adultery with their neighbors' wives, and they spoke words in God's name that He never commanded them to speak. God affirms that He knows this and is a witness to all of it, even though no one else has seen it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He writes to the Jews taken captive to Babylon. There, these two men were giving them false hopes that the exile would be short. God announces that Nebuchadnezzar will punish them. The text says nothing more about how these sins became known, only that God saw them.

For today: God sees what we do in secret, and speaking in His name is something very serious. Before saying "God says this," let us examine His Word and live with integrity, knowing that He is a witness to everything.
exp.26:12:
He says God asks King Zedekiah a question: "Why will you and your people die?" The old words "by the sword" mean "by the sword," that is, by war. "Pestilence" is a disease that spreads. God had already warned that this would happen to the nation that did not submit to Babylon.

The prophet Jeremiah, sent by God, speaks to King Zedekiah of Judah. Jeremiah wore a wooden yoke as a sign that Babylon would rule over those nations. Other prophets were saying the opposite, that there would be no submission. With this question, God invites the king to choose to live and not to harden himself.

For today: sometimes we prefer the voices that tell us what we want to hear. This week, compare any advice with what God says in his Word, even when it is hard to accept, and choose the obedience that gives life.
exp.12:3:
Here God asks Jeremiah to take the linen belt he bought, the one he wears around his waist, and go to the Euphrates River. There he must hide it in a hole in a rock.

The Lord speaks, and gives an order to his prophet Jeremiah. It is a symbolic action, like a parable acted out. Later in the same chapter, God explains that the belt represents Judah, a people who were meant to cling to him but became proud. Some debate the exact location of the Euphrates, since it is far away, and it is not certain whether this was a real journey or a vision.

For today: God wants us close to him, like a belt held snugly against the body. We can set aside a moment each day to pray and read his Word, so that we do not drift away from him.
exp.34:8:
It says that the Rechabites did not build houses to live in, nor did they have a vineyard, nor any land of their own, nor a field sown with seed.

Here the Rechabites speak, a family that God sets forth as an example before Judah. They explain that they obey their ancestor Jonadab, son of Rechab, who ordered them to live in tents and not to drink wine. They kept that command for generations. They took refuge in Jerusalem only because of the invasion by Babylon. God uses their faithfulness to show that Judah did not obey Him.

For today: ask yourself whether you obey God with the same steadiness that others show in keeping a promise. Choose today one single instruction from God that you have put off, and begin to carry it out faithfully.
exp.37:20:
It says that if King Zedekiah refuses to surrender and go out to the officers of Babylon, God has shown Jeremiah what will happen. It is a serious warning: there is one good choice and another that brings suffering.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks with the king during the siege of Jerusalem. Zedekiah was afraid of his own people and of the mockery of the Chaldeans. Jeremiah offers him a way out: obey God and save his life, his family, and the city. Then he describes, as a vision, the consequences of resisting.

For today: sometimes we know what God asks of us, but fear of what others will say holds us back. Obeying may seem humiliating, but it is safer than giving in to fear. Ask God for the courage to obey him today, even when it costs.
exp.3:23:
Jeremiah describes what he sees in a vision: the mountains were trembling, and the hills, which are not named in the verse, were moving and being destroyed. What is firmest in the land was shaking and collapsing. "Devastated" means laid waste, and "fury" is a very strong anger.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to Judah, before the fall of Jerusalem. God has just said that his people are foolish: they knew how to do evil, but not how to do good. The vision shows the effect of God's judgment, as if everything were returning to emptiness. Many think it speaks of an invasion that was approaching, and the image is very poetic.

For today: do not put your security in things that seem firm, such as money, success, or your own wisdom. Seek to know God truly and to obey him, because only he does not move.
exp.47:26:
God asks Moab: "Was not Israel a derision unto you? Was he found among thieves, that you shake your head with scorn every time you speak of him?" He adds that whenever Moab spoke of Israel, Moab shook its head in contempt. "Derision" means cruel mockery. "Thou skippedst for joy" points to Moab's gleeful reaction when Israel was in trouble. "Thou shakest the head" probably refers to that gesture of disdain, though some interpret it differently.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment against Moab, a neighboring people of Israel. Moab had become full of pride and mocked Israel when things went badly for it. God takes this as an offense against himself, since Israel was his people, and so the punishment falls on Moab.

For today: God sees how we treat others, especially when they fall or suffer. Before we mock or criticize, let us ask him for a humble and compassionate heart, one that helps rather than despises.
exp.13:2:
The verse tells how the nobles of Judah sent their servants to fetch water. The servants went to the pools, or water reservoirs, but found nothing. They returned with their vessels empty. They felt shame and dismay, and they covered their heads, a gesture of grief and humiliation.

God spoke to Jeremiah because of a great drought. All the people were in mourning. Here it is shown that not even the rich and powerful were spared from the scarcity. In other passages of Jeremiah, this drought is connected with the sin of the people, although this verse only describes the distress.

For today: when our resources run out and nothing we have is enough, we can set aside pride and seek God with humility, recognizing that only he can give what we truly need.
exp.25:3:
This verse is the beginning of the message Jeremiah was to deliver. God asks him to say: "If you will not listen to me and walk according to my law, which I have set before you..." The sentence is left incomplete and continues in the next verse. The word "hearken" means "listen" or "pay attention," and "say" here means to tell or deliver a message.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He commands him to go to the court of the temple and speak to the people who came to worship, holding nothing back. God wanted them to repent, and so He says that perhaps they would listen and turn away from their evil way. In this way He could hold back the punishment He had planned.

For today: it is not enough simply to go to a place of worship; God expects us to listen to His word and put it into practice. This week, read a passage of the Bible and decide on one concrete action to obey it.
exp.12:11:
God commands Jeremiah to tell the people that every bottle (a leather bag for storing wine) will be filled with wine. The people answer with a mocking or weary tone: "Doesn't everyone already know that?"

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah. The people had refused to listen and kept following false gods. What seems like an obvious statement is a coded message: in the following verse, the wine stands for God's judgment, which would fill everyone, from the kings down to the common people, until they stagger and fall.

For today: let us not take God's warnings lightly just because they sound familiar. Listening with humility, and not with an attitude of "I already know that," leads us to change course in time.
exp.48:14:
God tells Edom that he has made it small among the nations, that is, weak and of little importance. The word "despised" in this verse means looked down on, treated as someone of no worth.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Edom, the people living next to Israel. Bozrah was one of its main cities. Edom trusted in its strongholds in the rocks and in its pride, as the following verse says. God announces that this pride will be brought low. Some understand that this was already taking place in the prophet's vision, and others that it refers to a judgment still to come; the text does not give exact dates.

For today: let us not place our security in what we have, in our reputation, or in our own strength. Let us ask God for a humble heart, because He cares for the humble and opposes pride.
exp.16:11:
It says that the place where God makes himself present among his people is glorious and high, and that it has been so from the very beginning. "High" means very lofty and worthy of honor. A "sanctuary" is the holy place where God is worshiped. The prophet calls it a "throne of glory," as if God himself reigned there.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. Earlier, God warned that unjust riches are lost, and that he examines the heart of every person. Then Jeremiah says that whoever abandons God will be put to shame. Between those two warnings, the prophet praises God as a secure refuge. Scholars debate whether he is speaking of the temple in Jerusalem or of God's throne in general.

For today: when you feel that what you have could be lost, return to God as your secure place. Set aside a moment each day to pray and remember that he reigns and does not change.
exp.17:3:
It says the potter was working a clay vessel, and it was spoiled in his hands. But he did not throw it away: he began again and remade it into another vessel, as seemed good to him.

God sends the prophet Jeremiah to the house of a potter to teach him something. Then God applies the scene to Israel: the people are like the clay in his hand. In the verses that follow, we see that God can respond according to how the people respond, whether with repentance or with rebellion.

For today: if something in your life has been broken, such as a failure or a mistake, it does not mean that God is finished with you. Humbly surrender what you are to him, allow yourself to be corrected, and trust that he can form something new and good.
exp.40:10:
This verse says that Johanan and the army officers who were with him heard about all the harm that Ishmael had done. The words "the army officers who were with him" simply mean the captains or leaders of the forces. "Evil" here refers to the murders and the taking captive of the people of Mizpah.

The book of Jeremiah recounts here what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. Babylon had left Gedaliah as governor, and Ishmael murdered him and carried the people away captive. The narrator reports that Johanan learned of this, and so he gathered his men to go after Ishmael, as the account goes on to tell.

For today: when we learn of an injustice, it is not enough simply to grieve over it. God calls us to act with wisdom and courage, according to what we are able to do, to help those who are suffering, whether by praying, by speaking out against wrong through proper means, or by coming to the aid of the victims.
exp.18:13:
Jeremiah returns from Topheth, the place where God had sent him to prophesy. Then he stands in the courtyard of the house of the Lord, that is, the temple court, and speaks to all the people.

Here the narrator of the book tells what Jeremiah did. In Topheth, a valley where false worship was practiced, the prophet had announced judgment. Now he carries that message to the temple, where the people gathered, so that everyone may hear it. What follows is God's warning because of their stubborn hearts.

For today: God sometimes asks us to speak the truth in uncomfortable places, not only where it is easy. We can ask him for courage and love to say what is true with humility, while remaining faithful to him.
exp.41:20:
Jeremiah says that he has already told them today what God commands, but they have not obeyed. Here "declared" simply means that he made it known to them. God had sent his message to them through the prophet, and they did not carry it out.

Jeremiah speaks to the survivors of Judah, after the fall of Jerusalem. They had asked him to pray and promised to obey whatever God said. God answered that they should not go to Egypt, but they had already made up their minds to go. Jeremiah shows them that their words did not match their actions.

For today: let us not ask for God's guidance only to receive permission for what we already want. Before we pray, let us decide to obey his answer, even when it costs us or is different from our plan.
exp.9:19:
It says that the house of the one speaking has fallen into ruin. The "tent" was the home of shepherds and of people in that time, and the "cords" held it up. If they are broken, everything collapses. Its children, that is, its people, have gone away or died, and no one is left to raise the tent again or its coverings, which were the cloths that covered it.

The one speaking is the voice of Judah, the people, or perhaps the prophet Jeremiah speaking on their behalf. They mourn the destruction that comes with the invasion from the north and the exile. The text that follows says that their leaders did not seek God.

For today: when everything falls apart, we do not need to pretend we are fine. We can lament honestly before God. And if the leaders, or we ourselves, have stopped seeking Him, this is a good moment to return to Him.
exp.30:12:
It says that a time will come when the young women will dance with joy, and the young men and the old will celebrate together. God promises to turn their mourning into joy and to comfort his people. Where the explanation gives the meaning of an old or unusual word, I will keep it to the words of the verse above: "virgin" is the young woman, and "mourning" is the grief that is turned into joy.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel was suffering the consequences of its disobedience and of the exile. In this chapter, sometimes called the book of comfort, God announces that he will rescue his people and restore them. Christians often see in this promise a foretaste of salvation in Christ, although there are different ways of interpreting it.

For today: if you are going through pain, bring it honestly to God. He does not ignore your tears, and he promises comfort. While you wait, lean on others, both young and old, and keep hope alive.
exp.37:19:
Jeremiah tells King Zedekiah that the Jews who had defected to the Babylonians will not hand him over to them. He asks the king to listen to the voice of the Lord, that is, to obey what God says through the prophet. If he obeys, things will go well for him and his life will be spared. The phrase about his life surviving means that he will keep his life.

Jeremiah speaks during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem. The king is afraid of his own countrymen and does not dare to surrender. Jeremiah urges him to give himself up to the Babylonian officials, just as God had indicated, so that he and the city might be saved. Interpreters see here a genuine offer from God, which the king had to decide whether to accept.

For today: sometimes fear of what people will say weighs more heavily than the voice of God. Before deciding, stop, listen to what God says in his Word, and obey with confidence, even when the path is frightening.
exp.31:34:
This verse says that the people of Judah built altars to Baal in the valley of Hinnom, a place near Jerusalem. There they made their sons and daughters pass through the fire as an offering to Molech, a false god. God makes clear that He never commanded this, and that it never came into His mind that they would do something so terrible. The word "abomination" means something deeply detestable.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before Jerusalem falls to Babylon. He reminds them that although He taught them again and again, they turned their backs on Him and refused to correct themselves. Even so, the passage that follows announces that God will bring them back.

For today: we should measure our customs by what God says, not by what most people do. If there is something that harms others, and God does not endorse it, we must leave it behind and return to Him in humility.
exp.43:26:
God says that he is "watching over" the Jews who went to Egypt, but not to care for them, rather to punish them. "Watching over" here means keeping close and vigilant attention. "By the sword" means they will fall by the sword, and "completely perish" means that almost all of them will die. Even so, the next verse mentions that a few will escape and return to Judah.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The Jews had fled to Egypt and there were worshiping the "queen of heaven," a pagan goddess, keeping vows made to her. God warns them because they had abandoned him despite many warnings.

For today: God takes our faithfulness seriously. It is worth examining whether we give him first place or seek security in other things, and returning to him with humility while there is still time.
exp.6:17:
This verse shows whole families working together in idolatry: the children gather the wood, the fathers light the fire, and the women prepare the dough. With it they make cakes for the queen of heaven, a pagan goddess (many believe she was Astarte or Ishtar, though this is not certain). The phrase "that they may provoke me to anger" means making God angry on purpose.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. He tells him that he should no longer pray for the people, because they do not want to return to Him. What is serious is that the whole family takes part, and this is not a hidden sin but one in plain sight in the streets.

For today: ask yourself what things your family does together. Make sure their faith, their customs, and their example at home point toward God and not toward other things that take His place.
exp.21:3:
God tells the king of Judah that if he truly obeys what he has just commanded (to do justice, to defend the one who is oppressed, and not to harm the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow), the line of David will continue to reign. The word "if ye do this thing" means "if you do this." Kings would enter by the gates of this house with honor, security, and authority, riding in chariots and on horses, together with their servants and their people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who is to carry this message to the royal palace. God offers a conditional promise: the continuation of the throne depends on obedience. He then warns that if they do not obey, the palace will be left desolate. History shows that Judah eventually fell before Babylon.

For today: those who hold some kind of authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, should use it to protect the vulnerable. God's blessing is not sustained by religious appearance, but by practical justice and mercy.
exp.31:38:
God promises to give his people "one heart, and one way," that is, one shared desire and one direction for life. The phrase "I will give them" is simply the verse's "I will give." "That they may fear me" does not speak of terror, but of respect and reverence toward God. And "that it may go well with them" means that things will go well for them. This blessing would reach their children as well.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah faced exile because of their disobedience, but God promises to gather them, bring them back, and make an everlasting covenant with them. Here the change comes from God himself: he puts that heart and that reverence within them.

For today: if you find it hard to obey or to keep a steady course, ask God to give you a united heart to follow him. And remember that your faithfulness can also bless your family.
exp.37:24:
Here King Zedekiah, the king of Judah, tells Jeremiah that the princes might find out about their secret conversation.
