If that happens, he asks Jeremiah to imagine how they will question him: "Tell us what you said to the king, do not hide it from us, and we will not put you to death." The word "declare" in that verse means "tell," and "hide" means "keep back."

Jeremiah had announced that Jerusalem would fall into the hands of Babylon if the people did not surrender. The princes wanted him dead for this. The king, afraid of them, asks Jeremiah to keep quiet and suggests an answer to protect himself. Jeremiah, according to the text, said what the king had told him to say about his request not to be sent back to the house of Jonathan, though he did not tell them everything that had been discussed.

For today: fear of people can lead us to crooked decisions. Let us ask God for the courage to act with wisdom and truth, without letting what others think control us.
exp.15:17:
God says that, before restoring his people, he will justly punish their wickedness and their sin. "Pay double" probably means a complete and abundant repayment, though some understand it as an expression of great severity. He speaks of "carcases": this refers to the lifeless idols, which polluted the land that God had given them as their inheritance, that is, their possession.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had filled the land with idolatry, and God announces that exile will come, for he sees all their ways. But the nearer context also points to hope: afterward, nations will come to acknowledge that the idols are a lie.

For today: God sees what we hide and calls us not to fill our lives with empty things that take his place. Today we can ask ourselves what we are putting first, and bring it honestly to God, who forgives and restores.
exp.49:5:
The passage says that God's people were like a lost flock. Their shepherds, that is, their leaders, led them astray and took them over the mountains. They wandered from mountain to hill without rest, and they forgot their resting place, which is the fold, the safe place where the flock lies down to rest.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message against Babylon. He announces that Babylon will fall and that Israel and Judah, united, will return weeping to seek God. The verse describes how they were lost: their leaders misled them, and for that reason they suffered harm from their enemies.

For today: those of us who guide others, in the home, the church, or the workplace, must care for those who follow us and lead them toward God. And if we find ourselves lost, we can always return to the Shepherd, who receives us with grace.
exp.49:29:
It says that the young men of Babylon will fall in her streets, that is, in the public spaces of the city. Her soldiers will also be "cut off," a word that means cut down or destroyed, the way a tree is cut down. This will happen "in that day," the time of God's judgment.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and its temple, and had grown proud against the Holy One of Israel. For this reason God announces that he will judge her, and his people receive hope that evil will not have the last word.

For today: let us not trust in our strength, success, or power, because none of these protects us from God. We can ask him for humility in what we do, and rest in the knowledge that he will do justice in his own time, without our having to take revenge.
exp.16:0:
This verse says that the sin of the people of Judah is not something temporary or easy to erase. It is written as if with an iron tool and a diamond point, that is, carved into hard stone. That sin is marked on the heart of the people and also on the horns of their altars (the reference to the altar's corners is what the verse describes).

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who warns Judah before the judgment. The people practiced idolatry at altars and high places, and their children followed the same custom. That is why God announces that there will be consequences.

For today: do not downplay the bad habits of the heart, because they become custom and are passed down. Ask God to renew your heart and to teach you to leave in your family a mark of faith, not of sin.
exp.51:16:
This verse tells how the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, broke up the large bronze objects of the temple. The columns were two huge pillars at the entrance. The stands were the supports with wheels for the water basins. The "bronze sea" was a large basin of water for the priests. Then they carried all that metal off to Babylon.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, closing the account of the fall of Jerusalem, around 586 B.C. Jeremiah had warned for years that the people would suffer for abandoning God. This account shows that those warnings came true. The symbols of God's presence did not protect the people on their own.

For today: let us not trust in places, objects, or religious routines as if they were a guarantee. What God seeks is a faithful and obedient heart. Examine today where you are placing your security.
exp.40:13:
This verse says that all the people whom Ishmael had carried off as captives from Mizpah turned around and went over to Johanan, son of Kareah. The words about turning back and going are rendered here as "turned around and went." Johanan's coming to rescue them is why they were glad when they saw him.

This is part of the account in Jeremiah. Ishmael had murdered Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, and he took many people of Mizpah captive. Johanan and the military leaders pursued him and caught up with him at Gibeon. The text does not say there was a battle with the captives; they simply went over to Johanan's side. Ishmael escaped with eight men.

For today: when someone sets us free from an oppressive situation, let us thank God and turn toward what is good without hesitation. Even so, we need to ask him for wisdom about what comes next, because the rescue was only the beginning.
exp.49:39:
It says that Babylon will be destroyed just as Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities were, when God overthrew them, that is, brought them down completely. No one will live there again, not a single person. "Son of man" is another way of saying "human being."

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been a proud empire, full of idols, that oppressed Judah. The prophet announces that a people from the north will come to judge it. Scholars explain that the total desolation was fulfilled gradually, and some still debate how to understand each detail.

For today: no human power, however great it may seem, is above God. This invites us not to trust in money, success, or modern idols, but in the One who is just and cares for his people.
exp.31:13:
God tells Jeremiah to take the two documents of the purchase of the field: the sealed copy, which was the official one and was kept closed, and the open copy, which could be read. They were to be stored in a clay jar so that they would last for many days.

Jeremiah is held in the courtyard of the prison while the army of Babylon surrounds Jerusalem. God had asked him to buy a field from his cousin Hanameel, something that seemed absurd in the middle of the war. Jeremiah gives the documents to his assistant Baruch, and God explains that this purchase is a sign: one day people will again buy houses and fields in this land.

For today: even when everything looks lost, God invites us to plant hope through concrete steps of faith and obedience, trusting that He does what He promises.
exp.2:6:
God says he waited for Israel, the northern kingdom, to return to him after all her unfaithfulness. He said to her, "Turn back to me," but she was not willing. The word "rebellious" here means that she turns her back and walks away. Meanwhile, her sister Judah, the southern kingdom, was watching what was happening.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the days of King Josiah. God compares the idolatry of his people to an unfaithful wife. Israel had already fallen, and God wanted Judah to learn from that example. As we will see in the verses that follow, Judah saw, but did not repent.

For today: it is not enough to see the consequences in the lives of others; God invites us to correct our course in time. If there is something that pulls you away from him, listen today to his call to return, because his patience is real.
exp.46:5:
This verse is a lament addressed to the sword of the Lord, which represents God's judgment carried out through war. The speaker asks how long the destruction will last and calls on the sword to return to its sheath, to rest and be still.

The speaker is the prophet Jeremiah, announcing judgment against the Philistines, especially Gaza and Ashkelon. His plea comes from grief at so much ruin. But the next verse answers that the sword cannot rest, because the Lord himself sent it with a purpose. Many understand the invader to be Babylon, though the text here does not name it.

For today: we can cry out to God honestly in the middle of pain, asking him how long. We can also learn to trust that he governs history and acts with justice, even when we do not understand it.
exp.26:9:
What it says: God declares that the prophets who announce that Judah will not have to serve Babylon are lying. "To remove" means to take away from the land, and "to drive out" means to force out. These false promises would end in exile and ruin for the people.

Context: The LORD speaks through Jeremiah, toward the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah. Babylon already dominated the region. Many prophets, diviners, and enchanters claimed that everything would turn out well. God asks them to accept the yoke of Babylon as the way to keep living in the land.

For today: Do not believe something just because it sounds encouraging. Before following a message, compare it with what the Bible teaches and ask God for wisdom. Sometimes the truth is hard, but it leads to life.
exp.5:24:
This verse is a very serious warning: it is not safe to go out into the fields or travel the roads. "Sword of the enemy" means there are armed soldiers ready to kill, and "fear on every side" means terror surrounds everyone. There is no quiet place.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, and the message comes from God. He announces that an invading army from the north will come against Jerusalem, the city called the daughter of Zion, because of the people's persistent disobedience. The verses before and after show anguish, mourning, and a call to repent. Scholars often connect the enemy with Babylon, though the text describes it without naming it.

For today: let us not ignore God's warnings until disaster arrives. If He calls us to return to Him, let us answer now with humility and sincerity, trusting that His mercy remains open to whoever repents.
exp.30:22:
Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: when he brings his people back from captivity, the people in the land of Judah and in its cities will once again speak this blessing: "The Lord bless you, habitation of justice, holy mountain." "I will turn their captivity" means to restore or bring back the captives to their land. "Habitation of justice" refers to Jerusalem or Zion, the place where God dwelt among his people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were in exile, or were about to be, because of their sin, and these chapters bring comfort and hope. God promises that punishment will not be the final word: there will be a return, rest for the weary, and joy for the sorrowful.

For today: if you are going through a time of pain, failure, or exile, remember that God knows how to restore. While you wait, pray with confidence and bless again what belongs to God, without losing hope.
exp.47:8:
It says Moab needs wings to flee away in flight, because its cities are going to be left empty, with no one living in them. "Give wings" is a poetic way of saying that its only way out would be to escape very quickly.

It is Jehovah speaking through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and it trusted in its riches, its fortresses, and its god Chemosh. The message announces that a destroyer would come and that this false sense of security would not save it. Scholars debate which invasion is in view; the text presents it as a judgment from God.

For today: check where you truly rest your trust. Money, achievements, or comfort may seem secure, but they do not sustain life when crises arrive. Trusting God gives you a foundation that does not collapse.
exp.40:15:
This verse tells how Johanan and the army officers with him gathered all the survivors they had rescued from Ishmael: soldiers, women, children, and court officials (men who served in the royal household). Ishmael had killed Gedaliah, the governor, and had carried the people of Mizpah away as captives.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah is speaking. Gedaliah had been placed by the king of Babylon over the people who remained in Judah. After his murder, the people were afraid that the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) would take revenge. For this reason Johanan began to consider fleeing to Egypt, as the next verse shows.

For today: rescuing and caring for those who are in danger is good, but fear should not make our decisions for us. Before taking a major step, it is wise to pause and seek God's direction, and not simply run from what we are afraid of.
exp.8:20:
This verse describes death as if it were a thief that climbs in through the windows and slips into the houses. It reaches even the palaces, which seemed like safe places, and it takes away the children playing in the streets and the young men gathering in the squares.

Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah, before the fall of Jerusalem. God asks him to call for the women who mourned the dead so that they may teach a funeral song. In this way God warns that the judgment for the people's unfaithfulness is real and will reach everyone, regardless of their position.

For today: let us not trust in our security, wealth, or strength, because life is fragile. The verses that follow say that what truly matters is to know God. Today you can take a few minutes to thank him for your life and to ask him to teach you to live with humility and to value those you love.
exp.34:10:
This verse tells how the Rechabites, a family that lived in tents, had to take refuge in Jerusalem when King Nebuchadnezzar invaded the land. They were afraid of the army of the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) and of the army of Syria.

The Rechabites are the ones speaking, answering Jeremiah. Their ancestor Jonadab had ordered them not to build houses, not to sow fields or plant vineyards, and they had obeyed him for generations. They made only one exception because of the war, and even so they remained faithful in everything else. God uses them as an example to rebuke Judah, which did not obey its God.

For today: if a family kept the word of a father faithfully for years, how much more can we obey God with steadfastness. Ask yourself today which clear command of God you have set aside, and take one concrete step to fulfill it.
exp.27:9:
Hananiah, who claimed to be a prophet, takes the wooden yoke off Jeremiah's neck and breaks it. The word "brake" is an old form of "broke." A yoke is the wooden frame placed on oxen for work.

Jeremiah wore the yoke as a sign that God allowed Babylon to rule over Judah. Hananiah contradicted that word and promised that within two years the yoke would be broken. He broke the symbol in front of all the people, and Jeremiah left without arguing. Afterward, God gave Jeremiah a message about this event.

For today: not every pleasant message comes from God. Before believing a promise of comfort, compare it with what the Bible says and ask God for wisdom. God's truth sometimes hurts, but it takes care of us.
exp.22:11:
It says that the path of these prophets and priests will be like a slippery ground in complete darkness. They will not see where they are stepping, they will be pushed, and they will fall. The word "slippery places" refers to places where one slides. "Visitation" means the moment when God intervenes to call to account. God himself will bring that evil upon them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The religious leaders of Judah had pretended to serve God, but they lived in wickedness, even inside the temple. They encouraged the people to continue in sin instead of calling them back to God. For this reason he announces certain judgment against them.

For today: whoever teaches or guides others has a great responsibility before God. Let us examine whether our lives match what we say we believe, and ask God to let his light guide our steps so that we do not walk in darkness.
exp.32:25:
This verse continues the thought of the previous verse: "If my covenant with day and night does not stand, then I would also reject the descendants of Jacob and David." In other words, God is saying that this is impossible. The explanation of "seed" as descendants and "cast away" as rejecting has been removed, since those words do not appear in the verse you are reading. Because the order of creation remains firm, God will bring his people back from exile and show them compassion.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were in captivity, and some were saying that God had rejected Israel and the family of David. God answers with a promise of restoration.

For today: when you feel that your failures or your hard times have pulled you away from God, look at the sunrise and the sunset. God sustains his creation faithfully, and he also keeps his promises. Return to him with confidence.
exp.50:32:
The explanation says that God, the Lord of hosts, compares Babylon to a threshing floor, that is, wheat spread on the ground of the threshing floor so that it can be beaten and the grain separated from the chaff. The time has come to tread and beat it. Very soon the time of the harvest will also arrive, that is, the reaping, and with it the final judgment on the city.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been a power that oppressed Judah and destroyed Jerusalem. The verses that follow show the pain of God's people. Here he promises that this injustice will not go unanswered and that Babylon's power will come to an end.

For today: when you see injustice that seems never to end, do not take revenge with your own hands. Trust that God sees, that he has his just timing, and that he cares for his own. Meanwhile, keep doing good with patience.
exp.37:2:
This verse says that God announces, through Jeremiah, that Jerusalem will certainly be handed over to the army of the king of Babylon, and that this army will capture it.

Jeremiah speaks to the people while Babylon has the city under siege. Some officials hear him and become angry, because they believe his words discourage the soldiers. Jeremiah does not speak for personal gain or out of disloyalty, but repeats what God has shown him, even though it costs him rejection and nearly his life.

For today: speaking the truth in love can be costly, but it is better than lulling others to sleep with pleasant words. It also invites us to listen with humility, even when the message is uncomfortable, because God corrects in order to give us the chance to change.
exp.30:29:
It says that each person will answer for their own sin. The explanation's word for the unripe grapes would be sour grapes, very tart green grapes, and the feeling of their sourness set on the teeth is the bitter sensation that is felt in the teeth. The word "set on edge" in the verse refers to that same feeling. It was a popular saying: the parents eat the sour fruit and the children's teeth ache. God says that this will no longer be the case: each person will face the consequences of their own wrongdoing.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to a people who were suffering in exile. Many thought they were paying only for the mistakes of their ancestors. God promises to restore them and announces a new covenant, one that is more personal. Some think that he does not deny that the decisions of some affect others, but rejects using that as an excuse.

For today: do not blame your past or your family to justify your mistakes. Acknowledge your responsibility, ask God for forgiveness, and trust that he can give you a fresh start.
exp.43:0:
This verse introduces a message from God to Jeremiah. It is addressed to all the Jews who were living in Egypt, in several cities and regions: Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph (also called Memphis), and Pathros, which was southern Egypt. "Dwelt" here means "lived."

Jeremiah was a prophet of God. After the fall of Jerusalem, many Jews fled to Egypt, and Jeremiah was taken there with them. God gives him this message because the people were still caught up in idolatry, even after seeing the punishment that fell on Jerusalem. The verses that follow explain this clearly.

For today: God speaks to us to correct us and also to protect us. If we have seen the consequences of turning away from Him, let us not repeat the mistake. Today you can ask yourself, with humility: what things are pulling me away from God? Listen to His word and return to Him.
exp.21:9:
It says that it is not worth weeping for the one who has already died, nor finding comfort for him. Rather, one should weep with great sorrow for the one who goes away into exile, because he will never return or see again the land where he was born.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had left the covenant with God and worshiped foreign gods. The following verse makes clear that the one carried into exile is Shallum (also called Jehoahaz), son of King Josiah, taken captive. Josiah, already dead, was spared from seeing that ruin; Shallum would live through the loss. It is an announcement of God's judgment on the people.

For today: the decisions to turn away from God have painful consequences. Today you can return to Him sincerely, before the pain arrives. We can also accompany with compassion those who suffer deep losses, not only those who have already rested.
exp.49:40:
It says that a people is coming from the north, a great nation, and that many kings will rise up from the farthest corners of the earth. The word "north" here in the older wording is an old term for the north, and the phrase about the sides of the earth means the far ends or remote places.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter announces God's judgment against Babylon, which had been a cruel and proud power. Commentators often connect this invasion with the Medes and the Persians, though some also see a broader meaning. The text does not give every detail, so it is wise not to claim more than it says.

God rules over empires, however powerful they may seem. If today you see injustice or arrogance that seems to have no end, trust that God sees and acts in his own time. In the meantime, live with humility and justice, without relying on human power.
exp.4:6:
God asks how he could pardon a people who turned away from him. His children abandoned him and swore by gods that are not gods. The phrase "when I had fed them to the full" means that God gave them everything they needed, and yet they committed adultery. They gathered in crowds at the houses of prostitutes. Some understand this as literal unfaithfulness, and others also as idolatry, which the Bible often calls spiritual adultery.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, shortly before Babylon invaded it. God accuses the people of rebellion and of lying when they swear by idols. Even so, the question shows pain, not only anger.

For today: when God blesses us, it is easy to forget him. Think about what he has given you, and thank him with a concrete decision of faithfulness, such as keeping your promises and your honesty.
exp.19:12:
This verse is an invitation to sing and praise God. The reason is that He has rescued the life of the poor from the power of the wicked. The word "praise" in the verse is the one the explanation refers to, and "wicked" describes the people who do evil.

The speaker is the prophet Jeremiah. He had just suffered blows and humiliation for announcing God's message. Even so, he expresses his confidence that God is with him. It is striking that, just after this, in the verses that follow, Jeremiah goes so far as to curse the day of his birth. This shows that faith and deep sorrow can live together in the same person. Some understand this praise as a certainty of faith, and others as a brief moment of relief.

For today: even when the distress has not passed, you can choose to praise God for what you already know of Him. Be honest with God in your pain, and also thank Him for His care.
exp.13:10:
God said to Jeremiah: "Pray not for this people for their good." That is, do not ask God any longer to bless them or to spare them from punishment. "Pray not" means "do not pray," and "for their good" means "asking good things for them."

The Lord spoke to his prophet. Judah was suffering a great drought, and Jeremiah had prayed for the people. But they loved to wander, that is, they liked to stray far from God, and they did not change. Their fasts and offerings were only outward, and the false prophets promised them peace without repentance. God, therefore, announces judgment.

For today: God takes sin seriously, and he is not pleased with rituals while the heart remains far away. Examine whether your life of faith goes beyond the outward, and turn to God with sincerity while there is still time. He always receives those who truly repent.
exp.19:3:
God tells Pashur that He will make him a "terror," that is, a cause of dread, to himself and to all his friends. They will fall by the sword of their enemies, and Pashur will see it with his own eyes. In addition, all of Judah will be handed over to the king of Babylon, who will carry the people away captive and put some of them to death. Here "sword" is the weapon meant by the verse; "friends" refers to his companions and close associates.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Pashur, an official of the temple, had struck the prophet and put him in the stocks for announcing judgment. Jeremiah answers him with this message and gives him a new name, which is usually understood to mean "terror on every side." Pashur denied God's warning and trusted in a false sense of security.

Today: do not silence or ignore correction just because it is uncomfortable. Ask God for a humble heart, willing to hear His truth even when it hurts, because His warning seeks our good.
exp.4:28:
God asks a pointed question: will he not call these things to account? The word "visit" here means to step in to judge and correct. "Shall my soul not be avenged" is not a fit of anger, but God, with his whole being, will respond to evil with justice. The question has a clear answer: yes, he will.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. The powerful were growing rich through deceit, and they did not defend the orphan or the poor. In addition, prophets and priests were failing in their duty. God does not ignore injustice, even when it seems the guilty are doing well.

Today, this invites us to examine how we gain what we have, how we treat the weak, and whether we defend what is right. It also comforts us: God sees injustice and does not forget it.
exp.35:25:
This verse tells that King Jehoiakim, angry at the message of the scroll, ordered three men to arrest Baruch, the secretary or scribe, and the prophet Jeremiah. The word "capture" is what the order meant by "take." But the Lord hid them, and they could not be found.

It is part of the account where Jeremiah dictated to Baruch the words of God, and Baruch read them publicly. The king, instead of repenting, burned the scroll and tried to silence the messengers. The text does not say where or how God hid them, only that it was God who protected them.

For today: when obeying God brings opposition, remember that He cares for His own and that His word cannot be erased. Remain faithful, trusting in His protection, even when you do not always know how He will provide it.
exp.6:29:
God says that the people of Judah did evil in His sight. They placed their detestable idols and practices inside the temple, the house that bears God's name, and so they defiled it, making it impure and unclean.

God speaks through Jeremiah, who preached in the temple at Jerusalem. The people felt secure because they had the temple, yet they still did not obey. The verses that follow mention Topheth, a place where they sacrificed their children, something God never commanded. For this reason He announces judgment.

For today: it is not enough to appear religious or to attend church. God looks at the heart. We can ask ourselves whether there is something we have placed in the position that belongs to Him alone, and give it to Him sincerely.
exp.27:13:
This verse says that God himself, the Lord of hosts, placed an iron yoke on all those nations so that they would serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. The word "nations" here refers to the peoples and kingdoms surrounding Judah. A yoke is the wooden frame placed on the neck of working animals. God adds that he has also given the beasts of the field to Nebuchadnezzar.

Jehovah speaks through Jeremiah. Hananiah, another prophet, had broken the wooden yoke that Jeremiah wore as a sign, and had promised that Babylon would soon fall. God answers that this false hope would only bring a heavier yoke, one of iron. The people were to accept the judgment that was coming.

For today: sometimes we prefer to hear words that comfort us rather than the truth that corrects us. Ask God for the humility to listen to his voice, even when it is difficult, and trust that his correction seeks our good.
exp.10:9:
The explanation says that the people repeated the same sins as their ancestors. It refers to the people who "turned back" to their old ways, and it means they have turned back to their former conduct. They did not want to listen to God and preferred to serve other gods. So both Israel (the northern kingdom) and Judah (the southern kingdom) broke, that is, violated, the covenant that God had made with their fathers.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The covenant was the agreement made in the time of Moses: God would be their God, and they would obey him. God accuses them of a conspiracy, a shared agreement to rebel. For that reason he announces the consequences of having broken what was promised.

Today we can learn that it is not enough to know what God has said; we must listen to him and obey him. Ask yourself whether there is something God has already shown you that you keep putting off. Ask him for help today to take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.41:15:
It says that the things the people want to avoid by going to Egypt, the war (the sword, which is to say the sword) and the famine, will overtake them right there. "The sword" in the verse means the same thing: the sword that you feared will overtake you there in the land of Egypt. The famine will follow close after them, not letting them go. And "there ye shall die" is a serious warning: running away on their own will not save them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, the remnant of Judah asked God for counsel, but they already planned to go to Egypt out of fear of Babylon. God had told them to stay in the land, and here he shows them that disobeying would not bring them safety.

For today: sometimes we look for refuge in our own solution, even when God has already shown us another path. Before deciding out of fear, it is wise to pray, listen to his Word, and obey, trusting that his direction is safer than our plans.
exp.39:0:
This verse says that God gave a message to Jeremiah after Nebuzaradan, captain of the Babylonian guard, released him at Ramah. Jeremiah had been brought there in chains, bound in irons among all the prisoners from Jerusalem and Judah. The bound prisoners are the captives taken away from their land to another country.

The one speaking here is the narrator, who presents God's word to Jeremiah. Jerusalem had already fallen to Babylon, and the people were going into exile. Jeremiah had spent years warning that this would happen, and almost no one had believed him. The details of how he ended up at Ramah are told somewhat differently in the nearby accounts, so it is worth reading them carefully.

For today: God does not abandon those who are faithful to Him, even in times of grief. You can keep trusting Him and obeying His word, even when everything around you seems to be falling apart.
exp.23:7:
It says God will make Zedekiah, king of Judah, like the bad figs, so rotten that they cannot be eaten. The same will happen to his officials, to those who were left in Jerusalem, and to those who went to live in Egypt.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jeremiah saw two baskets of figs: some good, representing those carried off into exile in Babylon, and some bad. Zedekiah and the others felt secure, but God says their stubbornness would bring judgment. Interpreters agree that the image contrasts those who accepted correction with those who rejected it.

For today: let us not trust in our position or in appearances. God looks at a heart willing to listen and turn back to Him. When He corrects us, accepting it with humility can be the path to a new life.
exp.27:16:
This verse tells us that Hananiah, the prophet who had spoken in God's name without God having sent him, died that same year, in the seventh month. In this way the warning Jeremiah had given him two months earlier came true. The seventh month refers to a month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly between September and October.

The narrator recounts the end of a confrontation. Hananiah had announced that Babylon would fall soon and that the exiles would return right away, and he had broken the wooden yoke that Jeremiah was wearing as a sign. Jeremiah replied that God had not sent him and that his message was false. The people were trusting in a promise that God had never given.

For today: it is not enough for a message to sound pleasant or hopeful. We should compare what we hear with God's Word and ask him for wisdom. This keeps us from trusting empty words, and it reminds us to speak with responsibility whenever we mention God's name.
exp.50:7:
It says that Babylon, the great power, suddenly collapsed and was broken to pieces. It calls people to wail over her, and to take balm, a medicine to ease the pain of her wounds, in case she might be healed.

Jeremiah announces what God will do to Babylon for her wickedness. Earlier, God had used her as a golden cup that made the nations drunk. Now her judgment arrives. The verses that follow show that it was already too late to heal her. Many read the words about the balm as an ironic or sorrowful call, and not everyone interprets it the same way.

No human power lasts forever, and God remains just. Do not place your security in what seems strong, but in God. If something harmful surrounds you, ask Him for wisdom to get out of it and return to Him.
exp.30:35:
God says that if the laws that govern the sun, the moon, the stars, and the sea were to stop working, then the descendants of Israel would also cease to be a nation before Him. "Descendants" means offspring, and "cease" means to stop existing. Since that does not happen, the promise will not fail either.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were in crisis and exile, and God promises them a new covenant, in which everyone will know Him and He will forgive their sin. To assure that He will keep this promise, He uses the steady order of creation as a sign. Many Christians also see here an announcement of the work of Christ.

For today: when you doubt that God is faithful, look at the sunrise and remember that He sustains creation and also sustains His promises. Rest in His faithfulness, not in your own strength.
exp.20:7:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to the people of Jerusalem. He sets before them two ways: one that leads to life and another that leads to death. "I set before you" means "I place in front of you," so that they may choose.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by the army of Babylon, and King Zedekiah had asked for a word from God. The answer is hard: the city would fall. Even so, God leaves a door open. According to the verses that follow, whoever went out and surrendered to the Chaldeans would save his life. It was a call to accept the judgment with humility.

For today: God does not force us down only one road; He invites us to choose with responsibility. When He corrects us, the wisest thing is to listen in time, even if it costs our pride, because His correction seeks that we may live.
exp.50:23:
God promises that he will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea for all the harm they did to Zion, and he will do it "in your sight," that is, in such a way that his people will see it. Here "repay" means to give just recompense. "Chaldea" is another name for the land and people of Babylon.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and taken the people of Judah into captivity. Before this verse, God uses Babylon as his hammer that breaks nations, and now he says that she too will answer for her violence. Scholars understand that the fulfillment came with the fall of the empire, though some also see a broader meaning.

For today: when we are wronged unjustly, we can hand our pain over to God and not take revenge ourselves. He sees every injustice, and his justice comes in its time. That frees us to forgive and to keep trusting.
exp.35:18:
The leaders of the kingdom tell Baruch to go and hide along with Jeremiah, and to make sure no one knows where they are.

These officials had just heard God's message written on the scroll. They were frightened and decided to report it to King Jehoiakim. They knew the king could react violently against the prophet and his scribe, so they advised them to protect themselves. The text does not say whether they fully believed the message, but it does show that they wanted to look after them.

Today we can learn that obeying God does not always mean exposing yourself without wisdom. Sometimes prudence, such as withdrawing from a dangerous conflict, is a way of caring for the life and the mission God has given us. Let us pray for discernment to know when to speak and when to take shelter.
exp.35:17:
Baruch answers the officials that Jeremiah was dictating all these words to him with his own mouth, and that he was writing them with ink in the book, that is, in the scroll. He invented nothing; he only put in writing what he heard.

The officials of Judah had just heard the scroll read and were frightened, because they knew King Jehoiakim would not receive a message of judgment well. That is why they ask Baruch how he had written everything down. He, a faithful scribe, explains his role clearly. Then the officials advise him to hide with Jeremiah, for they feared the king's reaction.

Today we can learn to be faithful and honest with the truth of God: to convey it as it is, without adding or taking away, even when it causes discomfort. God cares for those who are faithful to him, even in difficult times.
exp.35:2:
God says that he hopes the people of Judah will hear the warning of the punishment he plans to bring. The word "perhaps" shows that God gives them a real chance. If each one leaves his evil way, that is, his wrong manner of living, God promises to forgive their wickedness and their sin. "I purpose to do" means "I have planned to bring."

God speaks, giving instructions to Jeremiah in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim. He asks him to write on a scroll all the messages he had given him over many years. Jeremiah was in prison and could not go to the temple, so he used Baruch to write. God did not want only to punish; he wanted the people to respond and return to him.

For today: when God shows us something wrong in our lives, it is an invitation to change, not only a threat. Today you can recognize a bad habit, ask for forgiveness, and trust that God hears those who return to him with sincerity.
exp.22:23:
Here God asks whether anyone can hide in secret places so that He will not see them. And He answers with another question: does He not fill heaven and earth? The word "fill" in this verse is the key idea: God is present everywhere and sees everything.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. At that time there were prophets who spoke lies in God's name and presented their dreams as if they were divine messages. God reminds them that He hears them and sees them, even though they think their deceptions go unnoticed. Moreover, if they had truly stood in His counsel, they would have turned the people away from their evil ways.

Today we can live with sincerity, knowing that God sees even what no one else sees. This should not frighten us, but encourage us to be honest with Him and always to speak the truth.
exp.7:21:
Jeremiah asks whether there is no balm in Gilead, that is, a resin used as medicine, and no physician there. If there was a remedy and a healer, why did the people not recover? "The daughter of my people" is a tender way of referring to Judah, seen as a wounded daughter.

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, grieved by the sin and suffering of his people. Times of judgment were coming, and they still would not turn back to God. Gilead was a region known for its balm. Some understand the question to point out that God offered healing, but the people would not accept it.

For today: if you are wounded inside or by your own mistakes, do not stay silent or hide it. God offers forgiveness and healing, so come to Him in prayer and also seek the help of fellow believers and trained people.
exp.12:19:
Look up, it says, and see those who come from the north. Where is the flock that was given to you, the flock that was your pride? That people is no longer there, for it was taken into exile.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses Jerusalem, and probably the royal house, before Judah fell to Babylon. Many understand that the invaders were coming from the north. God warns that the ruin is not an accident, but the result of a persistent wickedness, as the following verses say.

For today: if God has entrusted people to us, such as children, students, or a congregation, let us care for them with faithfulness and humility. Let us not wait until a crisis arrives to turn back to God; let us listen to his correction in time.
exp.9:8:
It says that idols are made from costly materials: beaten silver brought from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz. A craftsman and a founder work the metal, and then they dress the image in cloth of dark blue and purple. All of it is the work of skilled hands, yet it is still human work.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, sent by God to Judah. He mocks the idols of the nations, which tempt his people. Tarshish and Uphaz were distant places from which precious metals came, though no one knows for certain where each one was. The contrast comes right after: the LORD is the living God, not a fashioned figure.

For today: let us ask which beautiful and well-made things, such as money, success, or image, we are treating as if they could give us security. Only God, who made us, deserves our trust.
exp.47:45:
It says that Moab is in great disaster. Chemosh was the chief god of the Moabites, and here it is announced that his people, the ones who followed that god, will be destroyed. Their sons and daughters will be taken away as captives. To perish means to be destroyed, and captivity means being carried by force into a foreign land.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab, a neighbor of Israel, had trusted in its gods and in its pride. God announces the time of his judgment on them. But the chapter ends with hope: God promises to restore Moab in the latter days. How this is fulfilled, interpreters explain in various ways.

For today: nothing other than God can truly sustain us. Examine where you place your trust, and turn your heart back to the Lord, who judges with justice but also offers restoration.
exp.31:36:
God promises that he will gather his people from all the countries where he scattered them. He says he drove them out in his "fury," his "anger," and his "great wrath," strong words that speak of his intense displeasure with sin. But now he promises to bring them back, to return them to this land, and that they will live in safety and without fear.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon, and the people have fallen into idolatry, including the horrible sacrifices made to Molech. The exile was a deserved punishment. Even so, God does not end with judgment: he adds a promise of restoration and of a renewed covenant.

For today: God disciplines, but he does not abandon. If you have turned away from him or are living through the consequences of your mistakes, you can return to him with confidence. His discipline seeks to heal and restore, not to destroy. Pray sincerely today and let him lead you back.
exp.43:10:
This verse says that God, the Lord of hosts, sets himself against those who remained in Judah. "I will set my face against you for evil" means he decides to act against them and not in their favor. "And to cut off all Judah" refers to the rest of the people who still lived there.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. A group of Jews fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem, and there they continued to worship other gods. God reminds them that their fathers, their kings, and they themselves did not repent or obey his law. His warnings were ignored again and again.

For today: let us not harden our hearts when God corrects us. If he points out something to us, it is better to repent soon and return to him, rather than seek security somewhere else.
exp.6:5:
It says that God asks his people for three things: not to oppress the stranger, the fatherless, or the widow; not to shed the blood of innocent people in this place; and not to follow false gods, because that would bring them harm. To oppress means to mistreat someone through abuse. Foreign gods are idols of other nations.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people believed the temple would protect them, even though they lived in injustice and idolatry. God tells them that repeating "the temple of the LORD" is not enough; they must change their behavior. If they do, they will be able to keep living in the land.

For today: true faith shows in how we treat the most vulnerable. This week, you could concretely help someone who is alone or in need, instead of relying only on going to church.
exp.31:19:
This verse says that God performed signs and wonders, that is, miracles and astonishing deeds, in Egypt. It says those works continued to be remembered down to the present day, both in Israel and among other nations. In this way God made himself a name, a reputation that was still alive in the time of Jeremiah.

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, in prayer. Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon, and he is a prisoner. God had told him to buy a field, something that seemed absurd at that moment. Jeremiah recalls what God did in the past, such as the exodus, to support his confidence that God can keep his promises.

For today: when everything seems to have no way out, remember what God has already done in your life and in his Word. Recalling his past faithfulness can give you the courage to trust him today.
exp.49:17:
God says that he will punish the king of Babylon and his land, which means he will come to call them to account and bring judgment on them. He will do it in the same way he earlier punished the king of Assyria. "The Lord of hosts" is a title that shows God as the Lord of all power.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Assyria had devoured Israel, and Babylon had then stripped it bare, as the previous verse says. God used these nations, but they were cruel and proud. So now it is their turn to answer. The text that follows promises that God will bring his people back and forgive them.

For today: even when evil and injustice seem to win, God sees everything and will do justice in his time. We can trust him and leave in his hands what we cannot fix.
exp.50:8:
It says that people tried to heal Babylon, but she did not get better. That is why the call is to leave her and for each person to return to their own land. "We tried to heal" means "we tried to heal"; the word for "forsake her" is "leave her"; and "let us go" is "let us go away." Her judgment is so great that it reaches "unto heaven," that is, her guilt is enormous and God already sees it.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, or the voice of the foreigners who lived in Babylon. Many understand that they are the exiles of Israel and other peoples who were cared for by Babylon, but she did not change. God had already decided to judge her for her pride and her violence. The text does not fully make clear who is speaking, and so it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: there are situations or environments that do not change even when we have done our part. After praying and doing what we can, we can let go of what is not ours to fix, step away with wisdom, and trust that God does justice.
exp.31:9:
Jeremiah describes how he closed the deal for buying the field. He wrote the deed of sale and sealed it so that it would be protected. He had some witnesses confirm the transaction, and he weighed out the silver on a scale, because that was how payment was made back then.

Jeremiah was a prisoner in the courtyard of the guard while Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon. His cousin Hanamel offers him the field, and Jeremiah recognizes in this the word of God. Buying land at that moment was a sign that, after the punishment, God would once again give hope to his people.

Today, this verse encourages us to act with order and honesty, even when things seem lost. We can trust God's promises by faithfully doing what is ours to do: keeping agreements, being clear, and acting with hope.
exp.41:13:
This verse shows what some of the people might say: "We will not stay here; it is better for us to go to Egypt." There, they believe, there will be no war, no sound of the trumpet (the alarm signal in battles), and no hunger for bread. "We will dwell" means "we will live there," and "we will go in" means "we will go and settle there."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, bearing the word of the LORD. After the fall of Jerusalem, the survivors of Judah ask him to pray for them. God promises to care for them if they remain in their land, but He warns them what would happen if they disobey and go to Egypt seeking safety.

Today, we sometimes look for security by our own way and not by God's way. Before deciding out of fear, ask yourself: "Am I seeking comfort or obeying God?" His direction is always safer than our plans.
exp.49:26:
It says to slaughter all of Babylon's bullocks and have them taken to the slaughter. The bullocks are young bulls, strong and well fed. The "time of their visitation" is the moment when God steps in to judge. That is why the words "woe unto them!" announce that their day has come to give an account.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Babylon, the empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and the temple. Interpreters often see in the bullocks an image of the empire's warriors or leaders, though the text uses poetic language. The reason the passage gives is Babylon's pride against the Holy One of Israel and its treatment of his people.

For today: power and prosperity do not make us untouchable before God. We can live with humility and justice, and trust that he sees every injustice and acts in his own time.
exp.30:10:
This verse says that God rescued Jacob, that is, the people of Israel, and freed them from the power of someone stronger than they were. The word "redeemed" means that God paid the price or acted with power to free his people from slavery or oppression.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter is a message of hope for Israel, a people scattered and suffering in exile. God promises to bring them back, to lead them with care, and to turn their weeping into joy. Many understand the "stronger" one to refer to the nations that dominated Israel, such as Babylon. The text does not name it here, so this is a reasonable interpretation.

For today: when you feel trapped by something stronger than you, such as fear, debt, or an addiction, remember that God knows how to rescue. Ask him for help with confidence and take the step you can take, knowing that you are not alone.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that when God's people are multiplied and grow in the land, no one will speak anymore of the ark of the covenant. They will not remember it, nor miss it, nor visit it, nor make another one. "Shall come to pass" means "will happen," and "visit it" here can be understood as "go to it" or "miss it."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to an unfaithful people, yet He invites them to return. The ark was the symbol of God's presence. Here He promises a new time when Jerusalem itself will be called "the throne of the Lord." Some see in this a closer divine presence; others, an announcement of the Messiah. Interpreters explain it in several ways.

For today: do not cling to symbols or traditions as if they were God Himself. Seek His presence sincerely, because He wants to be near you.
exp.6:0:
This verse is only the opening of a new message. It says that a word from God came to Jeremiah. The word "came" is an older form of the word "came," and "the Lord" is the name of God. Here the content of the message is not yet stated; the verse only announces that it is coming.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is the prophet who receives and passes on his word. According to what follows, God will send him to the gate of the temple to speak to the people of Judah who were coming in to worship. The message will be a call to change their conduct, not just to keep up their religion.

For today: before speaking, it is good to listen. We can ask God to let his word reach us first, and be willing to correct our ways, not just to attend church.
exp.36:7:
It says that the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, will come back. They will attack Jerusalem, capture it, and burn it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to King Zedekiah. The Babylonians had stopped besieging the city because the Egyptian army was approaching. The people felt relieved and thought the danger had passed. But God warns them that this lull is temporary and that the announced judgment still stands.

A passing calm does not always mean the problem has been resolved. When God speaks to us through his Word, it is better to listen and correct our course than to trust human solutions or momentary relief. Today we might ask ourselves: is there something I need to acknowledge before God, instead of ignoring it?
exp.36:1:
This verse says that King Zedekiah, his servants (his officials and advisers), and the people of the land of Judah did not pay attention to what God was telling them through the prophet Jeremiah. The word "But" begins the verse, and the name of God appears as "the Lord."

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. Zedekiah was placed as king by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, when Judah was already under his rule. Jeremiah had been warning the people for years, but the people would not listen to him. Soon after, the king asks Jeremiah to pray for them, which shows that they wanted God's help without obeying his word.

For today: it is not enough to ask God for help in a crisis if we are not willing to listen to him in our everyday lives. Today we can ask ourselves what his Word tells us and take a concrete step of obedience.
exp.37:16:
Here Jeremiah tells King Zedekiah, on God's behalf, that there is a way out: if he surrenders and goes out to the princes of the king of Babylon, his life will be spared, Jerusalem will not be burned, and his family will also live.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet at a very hard moment: Babylon had surrounded Jerusalem. The king, out of fear, consults him in secret. Jeremiah asks for assurance because he had already been punished for saying uncomfortable things. Even so, God's message offers mercy. Later on, Zedekiah does not obey, out of fear of the people.

For today: when God shows us a path of humility and obedience, even when it costs our pride, it is better to follow it than to let fear of what others will say make the decision for us.
exp.1:29:
It says that God struck the people's children, but it was in vain, because they did not accept the correction. The phrase "in vain" in the verse is the word for "without result," which is why it is used here. Being "smitten" speaks of painful discipline. It also says that the sword killed the prophets, like a lion that tears apart its prey. The prophets were messengers of God, and the people rejected them and killed them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, accusing Judah of having abandoned him to worship idols. God reminds them that the earlier punishments did not bring them back to him. Some understand that this refers to prophets killed by the people's own violence, as other passages of the Bible also tell; the text does not give names here.

Today, this verse invites us not to harden our hearts when God corrects us, whether through his Word, through wise counsel, or through the consequences of our mistakes. Ask yourself: what is God trying to teach me through this? Listening with humility leads us back to him.
exp.26:16:
It says that the people of Judah should not pay attention to the false prophets. Instead of resisting Babylon, they should submit to its king and so keep their lives. Jeremiah asks: "why should this city be laid waste?", that is, why let Jerusalem lie in ruins? Here "hearken" means to listen to and obey, and "live" means to stay alive.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God to King Zedekiah, to the priests, and to the people. The false prophets said that the vessels of the temple, carried off to Babylon, would soon be brought back. Jeremiah warns them that this is a lie. God offers them a hard path, but one that saves lives.

For today: before following a voice that tells us what we want to hear, let us compare its words with what the Bible teaches and seek wise counsel. The truth sometimes makes us uncomfortable, but it cares for us.
exp.46:1:
God says he is announcing a great invasion. The waters that come from the north are waters rising out of the north, and the word "north" is the term the verse itself uses. These waters swell until they become a flood that overflows the whole land, its cities, and its people. Everything that is in it is swept along with them. The men cry out, and all the inhabitants of the land wail, that is, they cry out in pain and despair.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, and his message is against the Philistines. The waters are a poetic image of an army that advances and sweeps everything away. Many think this refers to Babylon, although the text does not name it here, and some see it differently. The passage speaks of judgment on peoples who did not turn to God.

For today: no one and nothing is beyond God's reach. We can trust that he governs history, and not place our security in things that can suddenly come to an end. Let us seek refuge in him.
exp.4:24:
It says that the people's sins were the reason God withheld good things. Their "wrongdoings" are their crooked actions, and "turned away" means that they blocked or held back. "These things" refers to the rain and the harvest of the previous verse. "Good things" are the blessings God wanted to give them.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on God's message to Judah. He rebukes them because, although God gave them rain and harvest in their season, they did not honor or thank him for it. Furthermore, the text that follows shows that there was deceit and injustice among them. Some scholars see here a covenant-style language, where disobedience brought consequences.

For today: not all suffering comes from a personal sin, but it is wise to examine our hearts. We can thank God for what we receive each day and humbly correct what displeases him, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.35:21:
This verse describes the scene: King Jehoiakim was sitting in the winter house, a part of the palace used during the cold months. It was the ninth month (roughly November or December), and in front of him was a brazier, a vessel with coals to give warmth.

God had told Jeremiah to write his warnings on a scroll. Baruch wrote them down, and now they were being read to the king. The author mentions the fire on the hearth in detail because it will be key: the king will burn the scroll in that fire. This shows that he heard the word of God but did not want to obey it.

For today: we can be very close to the Word of God and still harden our hearts. When something in the Bible makes us uncomfortable, instead of burning it or ignoring it, let us ask God for a humble heart that listens and changes.
exp.1:15:
It says that even the people of Noph (Memphis) and Tahpanhes, cities of Egypt, "broke the crown of the head" of Israel. The crown of the head is the top part of the skull, so the phrase means they struck Israel down and humbled it severely.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to his people. He shows them that their ruin was no accident: they had left God and sought protection in Egypt and Assyria. The very nations they trusted ended up harming them. Scholars do not agree on the exact historical event the verse refers to, but the message is clear.

For today: when we look for security in money, people, or human powers instead of in God, sooner or later they fail us and hurt us. Today you can hand over to God whatever you trust most and return to him with sincerity.
exp.33:17:
God says that he is going to hand over the people who broke his covenant. They had made a solemn promise in his presence, cutting a calf in two and passing between the halves. "Broke" means violated, and "carried out" means fulfilled.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at a time when Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. The people had set free their Hebrew servants, as the law required, but then they took them back into slavery. Passing between the parts of the animal was an ancient way of sealing a covenant, as if saying: "may this happen to me if I do not keep my word." God takes that promise seriously.

Today, this reminds us that our word matters before God. If we have promised something, especially something that protects or frees others, we should keep it. If we have failed, it is good to acknowledge it and make it right with humility.
exp.43:4:
This verse says that the people did not pay attention to God's warnings. They did not listen or take heed so as to turn away from their wickedness. They kept burning incense to other gods.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the Jews who were living in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. He reminds them that from earlier times He sent prophets again and again, rising early and sending them with urgency. Even so, the people continued in idolatry, and that brought the destruction of their cities.

For today: God speaks to us with patience, and ignoring His voice hardens the heart. When something in your life competes with God or pulls you away from Him, do not put it off: listen, recognize it, and change course today.
exp.44:4:
God asks Baruch whether he is seeking great things for himself, and tells him not to seek them. He will bring calamity upon "all flesh," that is, upon all people. But to Baruch he promises that his life will be given to him as a prize: like plunder rescued from war, meaning that he will survive wherever he goes.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah, probably in the days of King Jehoiakim, when Judah was about to fall. Baruch, the scribe who wrote down the prophet's words, was exhausted and discouraged. God corrects him with tenderness and invites him to see the whole picture.

For today: in difficult times, be careful not to dream only of your own success or comfort. Ask God to help you be content with his daily care. He does not promise an easy or famous life, but he does promise to sustain you and keep you safe in the middle of trial.
exp.37:4:
Zedekiah, king of Judah, answers the officials who are asking for Jeremiah's death. He says to them, "Here he is; he is in your hands." He admits that the king can do nothing against them. The reader needs no separate explanation of the old wording here, since the verse itself says what the king means: the king is not able to act against them.

Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon. Jeremiah has said that the city will fall, and the officials accuse him of discouraging the soldiers. Zedekiah, a weak and fearful king, does not defend the prophet and leaves him in their hands. They throw him into a cistern full of mud.

For today: when we know what is right, fear of people can lead us to keep silent or to give in. Let us ask God for courage to defend the truth and the innocent, even when it costs us.
exp.12:20:
God asks Judah, who is presented here as a woman: "What will you say when He comes to call you to account?" "Visit" means that God will come to judge. The ones she taught to be "leaders and head" are allies who will now dominate her. And the pain that is coming will be like that of a woman in labor: sudden and intense.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. Judah had sought alliances with other nations instead of trusting in God. Many understand that these "allies" were powers such as Babylon, which would come from the north. The exact details of who is meant are debated.

For today: the decisions we make without God can turn against us. Today you can examine what you have placed your trust in and return to God with humility before problems grow.
exp.49:0:
This verse opens a new section of the book. It says that what follows is a word from the Lord directed against Babylon, which is also called "the land of the Chaldeans." The Chaldeans were the people who ruled Babylon. The phrase "by the hand of Jeremiah" means that God used the prophet as his messenger to deliver and write down this message.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah only passes on what he receives. Babylon was then the power that had conquered Judah and carried people off into exile. This message announces that that empire would also be judged. Many understand it as a comfort to God's people, for it showed them that Babylon's power was not eternal. Chapters 50 and 51 are devoted entirely to this theme.

For today: when evil seems powerful and invincible, remember that God still governs history. Trust that his justice will come in its time, and in the meantime remain faithful.
exp.16:23:
It says there will be blessing if the people obey God. Dios's wording is rendered here in plain terms: God asks them not to carry burdens through the gates of Jerusalem on the sabbath, but to set that day apart for Him and do no work at all.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Judah and Jerusalem. Shortly before this, he says that their ancestors would not listen and stiffened their necks, meaning they were stubborn. The sabbath was a sign of Israel's covenant with God. The text then promises that the city would remain standing and that the people would come to worship in the temple.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and put God first, without letting work and hurry push Him aside. Christians understand differently how the sabbath applies to them, but the principle of trusting God in rest still holds.
exp.25:11:
Jeremiah speaks to the leaders and to all the people. He tells them that God himself sent him to announce a message against the temple and against Jerusalem. "Princes" are the leaders or those in authority. "Prophesied" means that he spoke on behalf of God.

The priests and the prophets had just accused Jeremiah and were demanding that he be put to death, because he announced that the temple and the city would be destroyed if the people did not change. Now Jeremiah defends himself before the judges, without denying anything. He makes clear that he does not speak on his own, but because God commanded him.

For today: speak the truth with courage, even when it costs, and do so with humility. Jeremiah does not mock or attack; he calls for change and trusts in God. We can ask him to give us courage and gentleness together.
exp.50:9:
It says that the Lord has brought our righteousness to light, that is, he has shown everyone that his people were in the right and that he defends them. That is why everyone is invited: "Come," and let us declare in Zion, that is, in Jerusalem, what God has done. To bring something out into the light means to make it visible, to reveal it.

Here the Israelites in exile are speaking, or the prophet on their behalf, in view of the fall of Babylon. That nation had oppressed them, and now God is acting against it. Some understand the "righteousness" as the vindication of the people, not as meaning they were perfect; the text does not elaborate further.

For today: when you go through injustice, trust that God sees and can act in his own time. And when he works in your favor, do not keep it to yourself: tell it in your church or with your family, to encourage others and to give him thanks.
exp.47:11:
Thus says the Lord that days are coming when he will send people who pour out wine from one vessel to another, and they will make Moab leave its place, empty its vessels and break its jars, which were leather bags used to keep wine.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab had lived at ease, like wine that rests on its dregs (the sediment) and is never disturbed. That comfort made it proud and confident in its god Chemosh. With this image, God announces that this calm will end in judgment.

For today: long-lasting comfort can make us self-sufficient without our noticing. Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and receive with humility the changes God allows, for at times he shakes us to draw us closer to himself.
exp.38:11:
It says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, gave orders for Jeremiah to be looked after. "Take him" means "take him away," "look well to him" means "take good care of him," and "do him no harm" means that no one should do him any harm at all. "Do unto him even as he shall say unto thee" means that they were to give him whatever he asked for.

The king speaks, and gives the order to Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, when Jerusalem fell. Jeremiah had been imprisoned by his own people for announcing this judgment on behalf of God. Now the enemy king orders that he be protected. The Bible does not explain why he did this; it may be that he knew what Jeremiah had said, but that is not stated clearly. What we do see is that God took care of his servant.

For today: God knows how to care for those who are faithful to him, even in difficult times and in unexpected ways. Remain faithful, and trust that he sustains you.
exp.33:10:
Here, the people and officials of Judah turned back on what they had done. They had first set free their Hebrew servants, but afterward they changed their minds. They made the men and women they had released come back, and they forced them into slavery again.

Jeremiah records this during the siege of Jerusalem by the army of Babylon. King Zedekiah and the people had made a covenant before God to free their Hebrew brothers, as the law of Moses required. Many believe they did it out of fear of the crisis, and when the pressure eased, they broke their word. God answers by reminding them of his covenant with Israel when he brought them out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.

For today: keeping what we have promised to God and to others, even after the trouble has passed. We might ask ourselves whether our obedience is sincere or only appears when we are afraid.
exp.13:15:
It says that the people who listened to the false prophets will be cast out into the streets of Jerusalem, dead from famine and war. No one will bury them, nor their families. "Sword" means war, and "I will pour their wickedness upon them" means they will receive the consequences of their own evil.

God speaks to the prophet Jeremiah, in a time of drought and threat. The false prophets promised peace and said there would be no war or famine, but God had not sent them. The people believed them because it was what they wanted to hear, and so they also share the responsibility. Even so, God himself weeps for his people in the verses that follow.

For today: let us not believe something just because it sounds pleasant. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible and ask God for discernment, even when the truth is difficult.
exp.9:11:
This verse says that God made the earth by his power, set the world in order by his wisdom, and stretched out the heavens by his understanding. The words "power," "wisdom," and "understanding" translate the same ideas that appear in the verse above: power is strength, wisdom is knowledge, and understanding is good judgment. Everything created shows that God works with strength and with a mind.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah. Around this passage, he compares the living God with idols made by human hands, which cannot do anything. He wants to remind them that only the Creator deserves trust and worship, and that they should not let themselves be impressed by the religions and customs of the neighboring nations.

Today we can remember that the God who holds up the universe is also wise enough to guide our lives. When something worries us, we can pray and trust that his power and his wisdom never fail. And we can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts.
exp.3:20:
Here the question is asked: "How long will I have to see the battle standard and hear the sound of the trumpet?" The "standard" was a signal to gather troops or to warn of danger, and the trumpet sounded the alarm. The phrase "will have to see" is a cry of weariness and anguish before a war that does not end.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, the prophet, and his grief is very deep, as his earlier words about his inner being show. He announces the judgment that is coming upon Judah. The verses that follow explain the cause: the people did not know God and became skilled at doing evil. Some understand that Jeremiah also expresses God's grief over his people.

For today: do not ignore the alarms God sends, such as your conscience or his Word. And if the evil around you grieves you, weep and pray for others, as Jeremiah did.
exp.50:25:
It says that Babylon will be so completely destroyed that no one will ever again take from its ruins a stone for a corner or a stone for a foundation. At that time, the corner stone and the foundation stone were the strongest and most valuable parts of a building. "Ruin" here means total ruin and desolation. The phrase "for ever" means it will last forever.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon, here called "the destroying mountain," had laid waste to nations and also to Jerusalem and its temple. God promises to bring justice to his people. The verses that follow call on peoples such as the Medes to rise up against it. Scholars understand the prophecy in different ways as to how and when it was fully fulfilled.

For today: do not despair before the abuse or injustice of the powerful. God sees, remembers, and judges with justice. Rest in Him, and avoid personal revenge.
exp.20:13:
God says he will punish Jerusalem according to what its people have done. Here "punish" means calling them to account, not paying a friendly visit. "The consequences of your actions" is what the phrase about the fruit of their deeds means. The word translated as "forest" refers to a thick forest or dense woodland, and almost everyone understands it to mean the city itself or its proud sense of safety. The fire that consumes everything around it speaks of a destruction that reaches beyond the city itself.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before Jerusalem falls to Babylon. He had called the royal house of David to do justice and to rescue the oppressed. But the people trusted that their city, set high up, could not be reached by any enemy, asking who would dare come against them. God answers that no wall protects them from his judgment.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we use our position, work, or influence to help those who suffer injustice. God does not ask us for our own security, but for justice and mercy toward others, beginning today.
exp.29:10:
God tells his people: "I am with you to save you." The nations where he scattered them will be completely destroyed, but he will not completely destroy Israel. The explanation that "full end" means total destruction is rendered here as: the nations will be utterly brought to an end. A word for cutting down a tree is not needed, since the verse does not use it. The phrase about correction with justice is conveyed by the verse itself: he will correct you in measure, and will not leave you altogether unpunished.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel was under God's judgment and would soon be taken into exile. Even so, God promises restoration: the people will return and live in peace. The verse that follows shows that the wound is serious, but God does not abandon his people.

For today: when God corrects us, his aim is not to destroy us but to heal and restore us. If you are going through discipline or a hard consequence, do not lose hope. Come to God with humility, because he remains with you.
exp.16:9:
In this verse God says that He examines the deepest part of each person. "Searching the heart" means investigating thoughts and desires thoroughly. "Trying the reins" is an old expression for the innermost emotions and conscience. God gives to each person according to their ways and according to the fruit of their deeds, that is, the consequences of what they do.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. He has just said that the human heart is deceitful and that no one knows it well. Here He answers that He does know it. Earlier He contrasted the one who trusts in God, like a tree beside the water, with the one who trusts in man.

For today: do not be content with looking good on the outside, nor trust only in your feelings. Ask God to examine your heart and correct you with love, and trust in Him sincerely.
exp.27:10:
Hananiah says before all the people that God will break the yoke of the king of Babylon from all the nations within two full years. Then Jeremiah simply goes away.

Hananiah is a prophet who contradicts Jeremiah. Jeremiah had announced that Judah должна submit to Babylon, and to show it he wore a wooden yoke. Hananiah breaks that yoke and promises a quick deliverance. Jeremiah does not argue at that moment; he withdraws, and shortly afterward he receives an answer from God.

For today: an encouraging message does not always come from God. Before believing an easy promise, compare it with what the Bible teaches, pray calmly, and take time to discern.
exp.14:17:
Jeremiah asks God why his pain does not end. He speaks of a wound that is hopeless, without any prospect of healing, and that refuses to be cured.
