Then he dares to ask God whether he will be to him like something false, a deception, like a stream that dries up and gives no reliable water just when it is most needed.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. He had been faithful: he received God's word with joy, did not join with the mockers, and stood alone, filled with indignation at the sin of the people. Even so, he suffered rejection and persecution. That is why he complains with honesty. God does not rebuke him harshly, but calls him to trust again and promises to be with him and to protect him.

You can bring your complaints and doubts to God with sincerity, without pretending. He listens, corrects with love, and reminds you that he remains with you, even when the pain lasts longer than you expected.
exp.25:20:
It says that King Jehoiakim and his leaders heard what the prophet Uriah announced, and the king wanted to kill him. Uriah became afraid and fled to Egypt. The phrase "sought to put him to death" means that he looked for a way to kill him. "Mighty men" and "princes" refer to the men of authority in the government.

The speakers here are the leaders and the people of Judah, who cite the case of Uriah while they debate whether Jeremiah deserves to die. Uriah had prophesied the same thing as Jeremiah: judgment against Jerusalem. Jehoiakim, instead of repenting, pursued him. Later they caught up with him in Egypt and killed him.

For today: speaking the truth can cost dearly, and even the faithful feel fear. Let us ask God for courage and wisdom to speak with humility and firmness, and let us listen to correction instead of silencing the one who gives it to us.
exp.10:8:
God tells Jeremiah that he has discovered a common plot and rebellion among the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

The Lord speaks to the prophet Jeremiah. He had warned their fathers, from the time he brought them out of Egypt, to obey him and keep his covenant. Now the people were repeating the same disobedience: it was not just an isolated mistake, but a shared decision to return to idols. That is why God announces that judgment will come.

For today: disobedience sometimes becomes a collective habit and stops seeming serious to us. Ask yourself humbly which practices accepted around you move away from what God says, and ask him for the courage to listen to him and obey, even when others do not.
exp.34:0:
This verse says that God gave a message to the prophet Jeremiah. The word "Jehovah" is the name of God. It is made clear that this happened when Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, was king of Judah.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is the one who receives and passes on his word. Jehoiakim reigned in a time of disobedience among the people, and Jeremiah had spent years warning them. The verses that follow show that God will use the Rechabites, a family faithful to the instructions of their ancestors, as an example for Judah.

For today: before we listen to opinions or pressure, let us look carefully at what God says in his Word. If he speaks clearly, our response should be to obey him with sincerity and steadiness.
exp.51:20:
Here, according to the text, each of the temple pillars was eighteen cubits tall (about eight or nine meters, since a cubit was roughly half a meter). A cord of twelve cubits went around it, meaning that was its circumference. The wall of the pillar was four fingers thick, and it was hollow inside.

This chapter closes the book of Jeremiah with an account of the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, around 586 B.C. We do not know for certain who wrote it; many believe it is a historical summary added later, similar to 2 Kings 25. The detail about the pillars, made by Solomon, shows how much was lost when the Babylonians destroyed the temple.

For today: what seems large and secure, such as a sacred building, can be lost. Place your trust in God himself, not in places or things.
exp.37:15:
The explanation says that King Zedekiah made a solemn promise to Jeremiah in private. He swore by the Lord, the God who gives life, that he would not kill him and would not hand him over to the men who wanted to kill him. "Seeking your life" means they were looking to take his life. The word "sware" means he promised with an oath.

The king speaks with Jeremiah at one of the entrances of the temple, in the last days of Jerusalem before it fell to Babylon. Jeremiah had been mistreated for announcing hard messages from God. Zedekiah was afraid and wanted to hear a word from the prophet, but he did it in secret, because he feared his own officials. Jeremiah did not trust him, and with good reason.

For today: a promise is worth as much as the obedience that goes with it. Zedekiah promised to protect the prophet, but he did not obey his counsel. Let us ask God for courage to listen to his truth and live it, even when it is uncomfortable.
exp.13:19:
Here the people speak to God and admit their guilt. "Wickedness" means living with your back turned to God, and "iniquity" is evil or injustice. They recognize that they, and also their ancestors, have done wrong, and they state it plainly: "we have sinned against thee."

These words come in the middle of a great drought, with famine, sickness, and war in Judah. Many understand that Jeremiah prays on behalf of the people, though some think it is the people themselves who speak. They ask for mercy, but their repentance may be incomplete, since later God does not immediately change his decision.

For today: when things go wrong, it is not enough to ask only for relief. It is good to stop, to be honest with God, and to call sin what it is, without excuses. That honesty opens the way to his forgiveness.
exp.16:21:
God tells the people of Judah not to carry loads out of their houses on the sabbath day and not to do any work. He asks them to set that day apart as holy, just as he commanded their ancestors. "Sanctify" means to treat something as set apart for God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the kings and inhabitants of Jerusalem, who gathered at the city gates. At that time there was a great deal of trade and transport of goods. God reminds them of an ancient command to rest. The verses that follow show that the problem was the hardness of their hearts: they did not want to listen or to be corrected.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and stop your worries, trusting that God cares for you. Ask yourself whether work or money is occupying the place that belongs to him. Obeying gladly is more important than keeping a practice out of habit.
exp.45:12:
This verse serves as a heading. It says that God gave Jeremiah a message about the coming of Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon, who would come to attack the land of Egypt. The phrase "the Lord spake to Jeremiah" corresponds to the original wording, and "smite" means strike down or defeat.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, the text describes Egypt as a nation wounded beyond cure, and afterward it announces the alarm in several Egyptian cities. Many understand this to refer to the Babylonian campaigns against Egypt, but scholars debate the exact moment it refers to. What is clear is that God directs history, including the history of the great powers.

For today: do not place your final security in power, money, or prestige, because all of these can fall. Trust in God, who remains in control and cares for those who seek him.
exp.43:11:
God says he will take the group of Jews who decided to go to Egypt to live there, and that they will die right there, by war or by hunger, from the lowest to the highest. "Sword" means war. "They will become an oath, a horror, a curse and a disgrace" means that their fate will stand as an example of punishment and shame, something people will mention with dread.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group fled to Egypt, even though God had asked them to stay in Judah. In Egypt they continued to worship other gods. God reminds them that they did not change or obey, and for that reason he warns them of the consequences.

For today: it is not enough to look for safety far from God. If we already know what he asks of us, it is wise to obey him promptly and humbly, and not to trust in our own plans.
exp.15:19:
This verse asks a question that already contains its answer: can a person make gods for himself? Of course a person can make images, but those images are not real gods. The phrase "for himself" means he made them to suit his own taste and convenience, which the verse itself conveys in the words "unto himself."

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, in the middle of a prayer. God has just announced punishment for the idolatry of Judah. Jeremiah looks ahead and says that people from other nations will recognize that their fathers inherited nothing but falsehood. Then God promises to show his power so that they will know that his name is the LORD.

Today we may not carve statues, but we can still make "gods" to our own measure: money, fame, success, or comfort. Ask yourself honestly what thing gives you more security than God does, and hand it over to him in prayer.
exp.45:20:
The explanation says that Egypt's hired soldiers, who lived well fed like fattened calves, did not hold their ground in the battle. They all fled without stopping, because the day of their ruin had come. "The day of their ruin" here is the day of their destruction. "Visitation" in this verse means a time when God acts to judge.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing the word of the LORD. Egypt trusted in its strength and its reputation, but God says that Babylon will come against it. Many understand this to refer to the Egyptian defeat before Nebuchadnezzar. Some scholars debate whether the "soldiers" were foreign mercenaries, since the text does not make this completely clear.

For today: do not place your security in your comfort, your money, or your strength. All of these can fail in a difficult day. Trust in God, who sustains life when everything else collapses, and live with humility and responsibility.
exp.31:42:
In the very land that people today see as a destroyed and empty place, handed over to the Babylonians (the Chaldeans), fields and property will once again be owned. A portion of land, held and passed down to one's children, is what is meant here.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon, and the people feel that everything is lost. Even so, Jeremiah buys a field at God's command, as a sign that there will be a future. God promises that just as He allowed the punishment, He will also bring the good He has promised, and that the people will return from captivity.

For today: when a situation seems empty or without a way out, do not take what you see as the final word. You can take small steps of faith and obedience, trusting that God is faithful and can raise up hope where today you only see ruins.
exp.31:40:
God says that he will delight in doing good to his people. The explanation of the wording: the verb in the original is the one for "I will rejoice," so the sentence reads "I will rejoice to do them good." "I will plant them" is an image: God will settle them in the land the way someone plants a tree so that it takes root. He will do so "assuredly," that is, with firmness and sincerity, "with my whole heart and with my whole soul," meaning with his entire will.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by the Babylonians (Chaldeans), and the people were heading into exile because of their disobedience. Even so, God promises an everlasting covenant and a return to the land. Jeremiah had bought a field as a sign of that hope.

For today: God does not help you grudgingly. He takes joy in doing you good. If you feel you have failed or that everything is lost, trust that his love is steadfast. You can come to him with humility, knowing that he desires to restore you and to let you take root in him.
exp.29:15:
He says God will bring justice on the enemies of his people. Those who "devour" (eat up, destroy) will be devoured; those who afflict (cause suffering) will go into captivity; those who trampled will be trampled; and those who plundered will be plundered.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Israel, who was suffering the consequences of its sin, as God's discipline. Even so, God does not forget his people. This verse opens the promise of restoration: after the punishment comes healing, the return from captivity, and the rebuilding of the city.

For today: when others have harmed you, do not take revenge with your own hands. Trust that God sees, judges with justice, and also heals. And if you have failed, remember that his discipline is not the end, but the path toward his restoration.
exp.29:16:
God promises to bring healing and to mend the wounds of his people. The word "Outcast" means someone who has been rejected or thrown away. The nations mocked Zion, saying that no one cared and that no one sought her. Here the verse's "but" marks the point where God answers that scorn with a promise of restoration.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to a people in exile and wounded. Earlier the text says their suffering came because of their sins, but now God changes course: he will punish their oppressors and bring his people home. The verses that follow speak of rebuilding the city and of joy returning.

For today: when others make you feel discarded or worthless, you do not have to accept that label. God does not define your worth by what others say. Bring your wounds to him honestly, even the ones you yourself caused, and trust that he can heal and raise you up again.
exp.32:22:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that God spoke again to Jeremiah. The word "Moreover" links it to what came before, and the phrase "the word of the Lord came to" shows that what follows is not the prophet's own idea but a message that comes from God.

Jeremiah was speaking to the people in a very hard time, when Jerusalem had fallen and many believed that God had abandoned them. God himself speaks and promises that he will not forget his covenant with David or with the Levites. He will soon answer those who said that God had rejected the two families he had chosen.

For today: when you feel forgotten or doubt God's promises, do not rely only on the opinions of other people or on your circumstances. Take time to listen to what God says in his Word, because he remains faithful.
exp.28:19:
This verse is a direct call from God to the exiles of Judah who live in Babylon. The word "hear" in the verse conveys what the original text meant, and the people who were carried off by force to another country are the ones being addressed. God asks for their attention, because what follows is important.

It is the Lord who speaks, through the prophet Jeremiah, who writes to the exiles. Many of them were listening to false prophets who promised a quick return. God reminds them that the exile came because His people ignored the true prophets He sent to them again and again. Now He invites them to listen once more.

For today: even in difficult situations, God asks us to listen to His voice with humility. Before following any spiritual message, compare it with the Bible and ask yourself whether it truly reflects what God has said.
exp.35:6:
Jeremiah hopes that the people will bring their plea humbly before God and that each one will turn away from his evil way. The phrase "it may be" means that perhaps their request will reach God. The word "return" in the verse means turning back from the wrong path. Jeremiah warns that the anger of God against this people is very great.

Jeremiah speaks from prison and cannot go into the temple. So he asks Baruch, his scribe, to read the scroll with God's messages aloud in public. He takes advantage of the day of fasting, when many people would be gathered together. He says "it may be" because the turning back depended on the people's response; it was not guaranteed.

For today: God speaks to us clearly because he desires that we return to him. If there is something in your life that God shows you, do not harden your heart against it. Come to him with sincerity, pray, and take one concrete step of change.
exp.50:56:
God says he will make the leaders of Babylon drunk: her princes, her wise men, her captains, her rulers, and her mighty men. Here "make drunk" is a picture of judgment: they will be left without strength or judgment, like a drunk man. Then they will fall into a sleep from which they will not wake, which is death. The one who speaks is the King, the LORD of hosts, that is, God with authority over all powers.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been a proud empire that oppressed other peoples, including Judah. The message, sent with Seraiah, announces that God will repay with justice and that not even the most powerful will be able to escape it.

For today: let us not place our trust in human power, fame, or intelligence, because all of that is temporary. Let us trust in God, the just King, and live with humility, knowing that he has the last word.
exp.29:23:
It says that God's anger will not stop until he has finished what he set out to do. "Fierce anger" is an old way of speaking of his righteous wrath, and "the intents of his heart" are his purposes and plans. And "in the latter days" points to a future time, when the people will understand what they do not see clearly today.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the name of the Lord. The people of Judah faced judgment for their sin, but this chapter also announces restoration. God promises that he will be their God and they will be his people. The storm falls on the wicked, and the verse shows that God finishes what he begins. Interpreters differ on what exact time "the latter days" means.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, trust that he has a just and good purpose. Keep obeying him with humility and ask him for patience, because some answers come with time.
exp.22:18:
It says that God's judgment comes like a strong storm, and that it is already prepared. The storm will fall on the wicked, that is, on those who persist in evil without repenting.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. At that time, several false prophets were telling the people that they would have peace and nothing would happen to them, even though they lived following their own desires. God makes clear that He did not send them and did not speak to them. His warning is serious, but it also shows that God does not ignore lies or injustice.

Today it invites us not to seek only words that comfort us, but the truth of God. Before accepting a message, we can compare it with the Bible, pray, and examine our hearts with humility, ready to correct our course.
exp.30:31:
God says that the new covenant will not be like the one he made with Israel's ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt. He speaks of taking them by the hand, the way a father guides a child. They broke that covenant, even though God was a faithful and committed husband to them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a time of crisis for Judah, when the people had been unfaithful. Even so, God promises something new. The verses that follow explain that this covenant would work in the heart and would bring forgiveness. Christians see its fulfillment in Christ (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8).

For today: our relationship with God does not rest on our own strength, but on his faithfulness and his forgiveness. When you fail, return to him with confidence and ask him to transform your heart.
exp.51:9:
The explanation says that the king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, had the sons of Zedekiah killed before the eyes of their father. He also had all the leaders of Judah killed, in a place called Riblah.

The explanation of the quoted word "slew" is removed, since the verse already uses that word. The quoted word "princes" is explained as the leaders and authorities of the people, so the note is rewritten to match the verse's wording: "All the princes" here means the leaders and authorities of the people.

The book ends with a historical account of the fall of Jerusalem. It is told as a fact, probably to show that the warnings Jeremiah had given for years were fulfilled. Zedekiah had been king of Judah, and his flight ended in capture and punishment. Afterward his eyes were put out, so the last thing he saw was the death of his sons.

For today: This passage reminds us that ignoring the voice of God has painful consequences, and that our decisions affect others, especially our own family. Today we can listen to God with humility and obey him in time.
exp.35:24:
This verse tells us that three officials at court, Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah, pleaded with the king not to burn the scroll containing God's word. But the king would not listen to them. "Pleaded" means they begged urgently, and "would not listen to them" means he refused to heed them.

We are in the time of King Jehoiakim of Judah. Jeremiah had spoken God's words, and his assistant Baruch wrote them on a scroll. When the scroll was read to the king, he cut it up and threw it into the fire. These officials, unlike the king, were alarmed and tried to stop him. Even so, God's word was not destroyed, because afterward God commanded that it be written again.

For today: do not harden your heart when the Bible confronts you. If someone warns you with care, listen to them, and before the word of God respond with humility rather than rejection.
exp.28:10:
God says that he knows very well the plans he has for his people. They are plans of peace and not of evil. The word "thoughts" in the verse means plans or purposes, and the phrase "expected end" refers to a future full of hope, a good outcome.

Jeremiah writes a letter to the Jews exiled in Babylon. False prophets were telling them the exile would be short, but God says they will last seventy years. Even so, he promises that he will not abandon them and that he will bring them back. This promise was first given to that people in that specific situation.

For today: even if you go through long and difficult times, you can trust that God remains good and faithful. This does not mean everything will come easily, but it does mean you can seek him in prayer, as the next verse says, with all your heart.
exp.27:1:
Here speaks Hananiah, a prophet from Gibeon, and he says that the LORD, the God of Israel, has already broken the king of Babylon's yoke. The yoke was the wooden piece placed on oxen to bring them under control; here it stands for Babylon's rule over Judah.

This happens in the fourth year of King Zedekiah, in the temple and in front of the priests and the people. Hananiah promises that within two years the vessels of the temple and the exiles would return. But Jeremiah had announced that submission to Babylon would be long. The chapter shows that Hananiah was not speaking on God's behalf, even though he used God's name.

Today, not every message that sounds encouraging comes from God. Compare what you hear with the Bible, pray calmly, and prefer the truth, even when it costs you, over easy promises.
exp.49:18:
God promises that he will bring his people Israel back to their land, to their dwelling place, that is, to their home. There they will graze like sheep in good pasture, on Carmel, in Bashan, on the hill country of Ephraim and in Gilead. These were regions known for their fertile land. Their souls will be completely satisfied, meaning they will be fully content.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had been like a scattered and mistreated flock, first by Assyria and then by Babylon. God announces that he will judge Babylon and that he will spare those of his people who remain. Some understand this promise as the return from exile, while others also see a future fulfillment.

For today: if you feel lost or worn out, remember that God knows how to restore. He cares for his people like a good shepherd and can give you back peace and rest. Trust in him and return to his care.
exp.45:27:
God tells his people, called "my servant Jacob," not to be afraid, because he is with them. He promises to put an end completely to the nations where he scattered them, but not to Israel. He will correct Israel with measured justice, that is, with fairness and due limit. To destroy completely means to wipe out entirely, like cutting down a tree until nothing is left. Full destruction means total annihilation.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah were under the threat of Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar, and many would be taken into exile. God comforts them: the punishment would be real, but it would not be the end. He keeps his promise to restore them and bring them back.

For today: when God corrects us, he does so as a Father who seeks to heal us, not to destroy us. If you are going through a hard consequence, do not think that God has abandoned you. Come to him with humility, trust that he is with you, and let his correction lead you to change and to rise again.
exp.17:12:
He says that God invites people to ask the nations around them whether they have ever heard anything like this. The word for the surrounding peoples refers to those who are not Jewish. Horrible shame is something hideous and disgraceful. The phrase "the virgin of Israel" is a poetic way of naming God's people, as if they were a pure young woman who ought to have been faithful. What they did is so strange that not even the pagan nations would do it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He had just offered Judah a way out: to leave their evil path. They answered with stubbornness, saying that it is no use, that they will keep following their own desires. So God points out how absurd it is to abandon Him.

For today: when God calls us to change, let us not harden our hearts by saying it is too late or that we will do as we please. Today you can ask Him to show you a crooked path and take one concrete step to correct it.
exp.39:5:
It says that Jeremiah went to Mizpah, where Gedaliah, the son of Ahikam, was, and he stayed with him. There were the poor people who had not been taken away to Babylon. The sentence about "went" and "dwelt" explaining the old wording is removed, as it refers to words not in the verse.

It is the account of the prophet after the fall of Jerusalem. The Babylonian captain Nebuzaradan had freed him from the chains and gave him the choice of going to Babylon or staying. Jeremiah chose to stay with his people, beside Gedaliah, whom Babylon had appointed as governor. No other reason is given here, but his decision shows his love for those who were suffering.

Today we can learn that serving God often means staying beside people in need, even when more comfortable options exist. We can ask ourselves: whom can I accompany with patience and faithfulness?
exp.35:20:
The explanation says that King Jehoiakim sent a man named Jehudi to bring the scroll. Jehudi took it out of the room (the chamber) of Elishama, the secretary or scribe, and read it aloud before the king and all the princes (the high officials) who were standing beside him.

The scroll contained the words God had given to Jeremiah, and Baruch had written them down. The princes, frightened by the message, told the king, and they advised hiding Baruch and Jeremiah. The account does not explain everything the king was thinking when he asked for the scroll, but what follows shows that he did not want it in order to obey it.

Today we can ask ourselves how we receive the Word of God. We can listen to it carefully and still not let it change us. Let us ask God for a heart ready to obey, especially when his message makes us uncomfortable.
exp.15:10:
God tells Jeremiah what to answer when the people ask why such a great punishment is coming. The reason is that their ancestors abandoned God, followed other gods (false gods of other nations), served them, and bowed down before them, that is, they bent low to worship them. In this way they stopped obeying his law.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the fall of Judah. The people believed they were innocent and asked what wrong they had done. God reminds them that idolatry went back many generations, and the next verse says that they were doing even worse.

For today: it is not enough to say "I have done nothing wrong." It is worth asking ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts, such as money, success, or comfort, and listening again to his Word with sincerity.
exp.30:26:
God promises that days are coming when He will "sow" Israel and Judah, that is, He will repopulate them and make them grow. The "seed of man and seed of beast" speaks of people and livestock: the land will once again have families, herds, and life.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had suffered destruction and exile. That is why, in this chapter, God announces hope and restoration. The verses that follow say that just as God watched over them to uproot and tear down, now He will watch over them to build and plant.

For today: if you are going through a season of loss or ruin, remember that God knows how to sow again. Trust that He can raise up something new in your life, and walk with patience while He makes it grow.
exp.7:11:
Is it a question that God asks whether his people felt shame after doing detestable things? The answer is no: they no longer knew how to blush. "They have been ashamed" means that they felt sorrow, and "I will visit" here means that God is coming to call them to account. For this reason they will fall together with those who fall in the judgment.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Judah. God accuses everyone, from the least to the greatest, including prophets and priests, of deceit and greed. They kept saying "peace, peace" to calm the wounds of the people, without truly healing them, even though there was no peace.

For today: do not get used to sin or treat it lightly. If you feel conviction, do not put it out; it is a gift of God. Come to Him with sincerity, ask for forgiveness, and let Him truly heal you.
exp.5:17:
God calls all the nations to listen. The opening words are an invitation to pay attention. The second part is hard to translate: some understand it as addressed to the congregation or assembly (perhaps of the nations), and others render it in different ways. Even so, the central idea is clear: pay attention!

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. His people rejected the good ancient path and would not heed the watchmen who warned them. Therefore God makes the nations witnesses that the punishment coming is the consequence of their rebellion. Moreover, he rejects their sacrifices, because they were religion without obedience of the heart.

For today: it is not enough to practice religious acts if we do not listen to God. Today you can stop, read his Word, ask yourself what he asks of you, and then obey him simply, without hardening your heart.
exp.17:13:
God asks two questions whose answer is "no": will the snow of Lebanon stop being there? Will the cold waters that come from far away dry up? These things are constant and reliable. Note: the Hebrew of the first sentence is difficult, and translations understand it in several ways.

God speaks through Jeremiah to Judah. The people had said they would follow their own plans and their stubborn hearts. God contrasts the faithfulness of nature with the unfaithfulness of his people, who had forgotten him to go after empty things, such as idols.

If creation is so constant, how much more can we trust God. Today we can ask ourselves: do I follow my impulses, or do I stay firm in God? Let us return to him with humility and steadiness each day.
exp.7:8:
The explanation says that those who considered themselves wise were left ashamed, dismayed, and caught, like prisoners. The reason is that they rejected the word of God. Then God asks: if they reject his word, what kind of wisdom do they really have?

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people said, "We are wise, and we have the law." But God says that the scribes copied it or handled it in vain, because they did not obey it. Even the birds know when to migrate, but the people did not recognize God's judgment.

Having the Bible or knowing a great deal about it is not the same as obeying it. Today we can ask ourselves: is there something God has already told me clearly that I am avoiding? True wisdom begins by listening to him and heeding him.
exp.19:15:
He says that the man who brought the news of Jeremiah's birth should be like the cities that the Lord destroyed without changing His mind. "Destroyed" here means wiped out or left in ruins. "Without changing His mind" means God did not change His mind. And that this man should hear "a cry in the morning," that is, alarm and weeping from early hours, and "a shout at midday," that is, an outcry in the full light of day.

Jeremiah speaks at the height of his anguish. He had just been beaten and put in the stocks by the priest Pashhur for announcing God's judgment. His pain is so great that he curses the day of his birth. It is often read as an exaggerated outburst rather than a calculated wish. Some see here poetic language of lament.

For today: God is not shocked when we honestly tell Him our pain. Bring your complaints to Him in prayer, and do not carry them alone.
exp.34:18:
God promises that the family of the Rechabites will never lack a descendant of Jonadab who stands before Him. The phrase "to stand before me" means to serve God, to live at His disposal. The phrase "for ever" speaks of a lasting promise.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The Rechabites had for generations obeyed the command of their ancestor Jonadab not to drink wine or live in houses. God holds them up as an example before Judah, which did not obey its God. It is not known with certainty how this promise was fulfilled afterward; some think it speaks of continuous service, others of a descendance that would endure.

Today, this encourages us to be faithful and obedient. If we do so with God, who deserves more than any other authority, He sees and values our steadiness, even in the small things of each day.
exp.42:12:
Here it says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, will break the images of Beth-shemesh, a city in Egypt, and burn the temples of the gods of Egypt. The "images" here are sacred columns or pillars. The name Beth-shemesh means "house of the sun," and it is usually identified with Heliopolis.

God speaks through Jeremiah. A group of Jews fled to Egypt seeking safety, even though God had told them not to go. Jeremiah warns them that Egypt will not save them, and that the gods they trusted there will be unable to defend themselves or defend them. God uses Babylon as an instrument of judgment.

For today: let us ask ourselves where we look for security apart from God, whether in money, power, or our own plans. All of that can fail, but God remains faithful. Trusting in Him and obeying Him is the firmest refuge.
exp.3:9:
Jeremiah cries out to God in pain and surprise. He says that the Lord has deceived this people, because they were promised peace, and now the sword has reached the soul, that is, to the very depths of life. Jerusalem is Jerusalem.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, distressed by the judgment that is coming upon Judah. Interpreters explain his words in different ways: some think the false prophets proclaimed peace in God's name and the people let themselves be deceived; others think Jeremiah voices his complaint in very strong language, without really accusing God of lying. In both cases, the people ignored the warnings.

Today, let us not trust comfortable messages that avoid the truth. Let us seek God's Word with humility, even when it corrects us, and bring our complaints to Him with sincerity, as Jeremiah did.
exp.43:21:
This verse says that God could no longer put up with the people's wickedness and their detestable practices. That is why the land of Judah was left in ruins, turned into a horror and an example of a curse, and without inhabitants, just as it stood at this day.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to the Jews who had gone down to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. They said they were better off when they burned incense to the queen of heaven. Jeremiah answers them that the ruin of their land was no accident, but the result of their idolatry and of not obeying God.

For today: God's patience is real, but we must not mistake it for indifference. If God shows us something we need to leave behind, it is wise to repent today and return to Him with humility.
exp.30:23:
This verse says that when God brings his people back, the people of Judah will again live in their land. Not just in one place, but in all its cities. It mentions farmers, that is, those who work the land, and shepherds who go out with their flocks. The word rendered "dwell" in the verse above is the word the explanation glosses; no further gloss is needed here.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter is part of the promises of comfort for Israel and Judah after the punishment of exile. God announces that he will turn their captivity into blessing. What is described is a simple, ordinary life: work, fields, livestock, and peace. Some see here a promise about the return from exile; others also see a foretaste of the final restoration. Scholars understand it in several ways.

For today: God knows how to restore the everyday as well. If you are going through a hard time, trust that he can give you stability again, and give thanks for daily work as a gift from him.
exp.7:14:
We looked for peace and well-being, but nothing good came. We expected a time of healing and relief, and instead we found terror and disorder. The word "trouble" in the verse means terror, confusion and distress.

These words are part of a lament of the people of Judah, facing the threat of an enemy coming from the north. Before this, God had warned through Jeremiah that his people would suffer for having turned their backs on him. Many expected that everything would turn out well without changing their lives. Some scholars think Jeremiah also speaks with grief on their behalf, but the text does not always make clear who is speaking in each line.

For today: it is not enough to wish that things would get better if we keep ignoring God. True hope begins when we return to him with sincerity and humility.
exp.35:1:
God tells Jeremiah to take a scroll, that is, a long sheet rolled up that was used for writing, and to put in it everything God has said to him. It includes messages for Israel, Judah, and the other nations. It covers the period from when Jeremiah began to speak, in the time of King Josiah, up to that moment.

The Lord speaks in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim. Jeremiah had spent years warning the people, and now God wants his words set down in writing. According to the verses that follow, the hope was that the people would listen, turn away from their wrongdoing, and that God would forgive them. His Word was not only meant to condemn, but to give an opportunity to return.

God does not grow weary of speaking to us or of offering forgiveness. Today we can read the Bible with a willing heart, asking ourselves which path we should change. Listening to God in time is always better than ignoring him.
exp.8:24:
This verse says that God announces a time when he will call to account, or "punish" in judgment, everyone: both those who bear the sign of circumcision and those who do not. "Punish" here means that God will step in to judge. The "uncircumcised" are those who do not have that physical sign.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier he had said that the only thing worth boasting about is knowing him and his mercy, justice, and righteousness. The verses that follow name Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, and Moab, and say that Israel was "uncircumcised in heart": having an outward sign without a heart given to God.

For today: having religious signs, such as baptism, church membership, or customs, is not enough. Ask yourself honestly whether your heart truly seeks to know God and to live with mercy and justice.
exp.0:14:
God says that he will call all the peoples of the kingdoms of the north. They will come, and each king will set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, around its walls and against the cities of Judah. It is an image of armies surrounding and taking the city.

The LORD speaks to the young Jeremiah at the beginning of his calling as a prophet. He showed him a boiling pot tilting from the north, a sign of a judgment that is drawing near. According to the text that follows, the cause is that the people left God and worshiped idols. Many think it refers to Babylon, although the text does not name it here.

God does not ignore sin, but neither does he act without warning: he sends his prophets to call people to repentance. Today we can listen with humility when his Word corrects us, and return to him before the consequences arrive.
exp.34:9:
They say they live in tents, not in fixed houses, and that they have kept everything their ancestor Jonadab commanded them.

These are the Rechabites, a family whom Jeremiah tested by offering them wine. They refused, because Jonadab, son of Rechab, had given them rules of simple living. When the Babylonians invaded, they took refuge in Jerusalem. God uses their faithfulness as an example to rebuke Judah, which did not obey its Lord.

For today: if this family was so steadfast in keeping the word of a human father, how much more should we obey God? We can choose today a clear command of Jesus and practice it with firmness, even when it costs us or others do not do the same.
exp.1:20:
God says he planted his people as a choice vine, of the very best kind, from entirely good seed. Then he asks with grief: how is it possible that they now produce branches of a strange, degenerate vine? One of the old words in the verse is explained here as a vine of choice quality, and another as the branches of the vine. The word "strange" here means foreign, degenerate, or of poor quality.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He reminds them that he freed them and gave them a good beginning, but they said "I will not serve" and went after other gods, the Baals. His question does not seek information; it expresses sorrow and accusation, because the fruit does not match what he planted.

For today: God has given us his care and a good beginning. It is worth asking ourselves what fruit we are bearing and returning to him sincerely, without excuses, so that our lives reflect his care.
exp.24:0:
This verse presents a message from God to Jeremiah, addressed to all the people of Judah. It says that it came in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and that this same year was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon.

Jeremiah was a prophet who spoke in a very tense time. Babylon was becoming the dominant power, and Judah still would not listen to God. The following verse says that Jeremiah had been warning the people for about twenty-three years, but they did not pay attention to him. That is why the date is recorded so carefully: God speaks within real history.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are listening to God in time. Often he speaks to us through his Word, through wise counsel, or through our conscience, and we put it off for later. Today is a good day to obey with humility.
exp.2:7:
Here God says that he saw everything Israel, the northern kingdom, had done. Through her unfaithfulness she "committed adultery," that is, she went after other gods. For this reason he "put her away" and gave her a "bill of divorce," which was the legal document of divorce. But Judah, her sister, saw this and felt no fear; she also was unfaithful in the spirit.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah in the days of King Josiah. God uses the image of a broken marriage to show that Israel was unfaithful to him through idolatry. Israel had already been taken into captivity, and Judah should have learned from that, but it did not.

For today: let us not minimize sin because others have already suffered its consequences. God invites us to return to him with our whole heart, not merely in appearance, before our hearts grow hard.
exp.6:27:
This verse says that the people of Judah did not obey God nor accept being corrected. To "accept correction" means to let oneself be taught and to change. The phrase about faith being lost means that truth and faithfulness had disappeared. The phrase about the truth being cut off from their mouth means that they no longer even spoke of it.

God speaks to Jeremiah at a time when the people trusted in the temple and its rituals, yet lived in injustice and idolatry. God tells him in advance that his message will be rejected. Even so, Jeremiah must keep speaking faithfully. Then comes a call to mourn over the judgment that is approaching.

For today: when a word from God makes us uncomfortable, let us not set it aside right away. Let us ask for humility to listen, to recognize what we need to change, and to obey. A sincere faith shows itself in how we respond to correction.
exp.44:3:
God commands Jeremiah to tell Baruc a clear message: the Lord is going to tear down what he himself built and uproot what he himself planted, and this reaches the whole land. Uprooting means pulling something out by its roots, and the land means the whole country of Judah.

The Lord speaks, through Jeremiah, to Baruc, the prophet's scribe. Baruc was worn out and discouraged by so much suffering. God reminds him that the judgment on Judah is very great, and so he should not expect an easy life or seek personal greatness.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart, we can remember that God still is the one who governs. Instead of striving for status or comfort, we can trust that He cares for our lives, as He promised Baruc.
exp.50:51:
God himself says he is going to step in. The word "visit" here means coming to call someone to account, that is, to judge. The "graven images" are the carved idols of Babylon. "The wounded" are those who fall under that judgment, and their groaning will be heard throughout the land of Babylon. God announces that the false gods will not be able to defend anyone.

Jeremiah prophesies against Babylon, the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and defiled the temple. Earlier, the people confessed their shame over that humiliation. God responds by promising that Babylon too will be held accountable. The verses that follow say that neither its height nor its strength will save it.

For today: no power and no modern "idol", such as money, fame or control, can save us. We can trust that God sees injustice and will act in his time. In the meantime, let us place our security in him alone.
exp.24:36:
This verse says that the peaceful flocks, which seemed safe, will be destroyed by the fierce anger of God. The sheepfolds are the places where the livestock rest, and the flock itself is also called by that name. The word for "destroyed" means laid waste or ruined. The shepherds and chief herdsmen, that is, the leaders of the people, cry out and weep because they no longer have any way to escape.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, sent by God. In this chapter he announces judgment on Judah and on several nations. The "shepherds" represent kings and rulers. God judges them for their rebellion and injustice, and for not having listened to the prophets over many years. Scholars understand the images of flock and shepherd as figurative language about leadership.

Today it reminds us that outward calm does not always mean we are right with God. It is a good time to examine the heart, listen to His Word, and turn back to Him with humility, for He is patient and desires to forgive.
exp.39:6:
This verse tells that the military commanders who had been scattered across the countryside, along with their men, heard something important: the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah as governor of the land. Furthermore, he had entrusted to him, that is, placed in his care, the men, the women, the children, and the poorest of the land, those who had not been carried away captive to Babylon.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jerusalem had already fallen, and the Babylonians left in Judah the most humble people to work the land. Gedaliah, from a respected family, stayed in Mizpah to lead them. The officers who had fled now approach to see what they will do.

For today: God cares for the most vulnerable, and those who lead should protect the weak, not take advantage of them.
exp.10:18:
Here Jeremiah says that he felt like a gentle lamb being led to the slaughter. He did not realize that some were scheming against him. Those who plotted did so in secret, planning evil, and they wanted to destroy him along with everything his life produced. They wanted to cut him off from the living, so that no one would remember his name.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. God had shown him that there was a conspiracy, and it is later known that these were his own fellow citizens from Anathoth. They rejected his message, which called the people to abandon the worship of Baal. They wanted to silence him so that he would prophesy no more.

Today, if you suffer opposition for doing what is right, you are not alone. Jeremiah did not take revenge on his own, but placed his cause before God. You can do the same: pray sincerely, remain faithful, and trust that God sees what others do in secret.
exp.41:18:
He says that God has already spoken to the people who remained in Judah, the survivors. His message is clear: do not go down to Egypt. The phrase that the KJV renders as "know certainly that I have admonished you this day" means that they should be sure they are being warned with full seriousness, today itself.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in God's name. After the fall of Jerusalem, the survivors feared Babylon and wanted to flee to Egypt. They had asked Jeremiah to pray so they would know what God wanted, and they promised to obey. But it seems they had already decided to leave, and God warns them before they take the step.

For today: when we ask God for direction, it is good to do so with hearts ready to obey, not merely seeking his approval for what we have already decided. Listening with humility spares us from paths that seem safe but are not.
exp.14:0:
God tells Jeremiah that even if Moses and Samuel, two great intercessors for the people, were to stand before him pleading for them, his decision would not change. The phrase about casting them out of his sight means that God commands Israel to be sent away. The phrase about his will not being toward this people means that at this time he will no longer show compassion to them.

The Lord speaks to Jeremiah in the midst of a drought and a crisis in Judah. Moses and Samuel had interceded for Israel before (Exodus 32; 1 Samuel 7). Here God shows that the people had persisted so long in their idolatry and disobedience that judgment was already decided. The verses that follow describe death, the sword, famine, and captivity.

For today: the prayers of others are valuable, but they do not replace our own repentance. Do not delay turning to God; today you can draw near to him with sincerity and obedience.
exp.30:34:
This verse presents God as the Creator who sustains the universe. He gives the sun to light the day, and sets the order of the moon and the stars for the night. He also divides the sea, that is, he stirs the waters so that its waves roar. "The Lord of hosts" is his name, a title that speaks of his power over all that he has made.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just promised a new covenant, in which his law will be written on the heart and sin will be forgiven. To give Israel assurance that he will keep that promise, he appeals to the faithful order of creation. The verses that follow say that as long as that order endures, Israel will not cease to be his people.

Today, when you doubt God's promises, look at the sun and the stars. The One who sustains them every day is also faithful to forgive you and to fulfill what he has said.
exp.22:16:
They say with boldness to those who despise me, "God says you will have peace." To those who follow the desires of their own stubborn heart, they promise, "No harm will come to you." "They irritate me" means that they offend me or treat me with contempt. The phrase "the imagination of their heart" refers to their own will and their own ideas.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Before the exile in Babylon, Judah lived in sin, and many prophets gave reassuring messages that God had not given them. That is why God rebukes them, since their words came from their own minds and not from his presence.

Today it is wise to be wary of messages that only tell us what we want to hear. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and accept that sometimes God corrects before he comforts.
exp.13:5:
It says that even the wild donkeys, which usually endure drought well, climbed onto the hills and gasped for air like jackals. Their eyes grew dim, meaning their strength of sight failed, because there was no grass left at all.

Jeremiah describes a great drought in Judah. Shortly before, he speaks of the cracked ground, the ashamed farmers, and the does who abandoned their young. Soon the people acknowledge their sin and cry out to God. Many understand this drought as a consequence of the people's disobedience, although the text here mainly describes the suffering and the prayer that follows.

When things dry up inside or outside us, we do not have to pretend to be strong. We can do what the people did: recognize our need, be honest about our failings, and cry out to God, who is our hope.
exp.16:4:
This verse says that God declares under a curse the person who puts their trust in human beings and leans on the strength of flesh, that is, on what is weak and temporary. "Man" means a person, and "arm" stands for strength or support. The problem lies in the fact that their heart turns away from the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. They had fallen into idolatry, with altars on high places, and they sought security in alliances with other nations instead of turning to God. The next verse compares such a person to a dry shrub in the desert, and then contrasts them with the one who trusts in the Lord.

For today: value the help of other people, but do not make them your final foundation. Before deciding something important, pray and ask whether your heart is resting in God or only in your own resources and connections.
exp.50:26:
God calls for a banner to be raised and a trumpet to be sounded to gather armies against Babylon. He names the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz, peoples to the north of Babylon. "Summon" means to prepare or call together. "Captain" is a military leader. The image of horses coming up like swarming locusts suggests an unstoppable multitude, though scholars debate the exact meaning of "rough."

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed nations and plundered Judah. God announces that he will judge her and will use other peoples to do it. The verses that follow mention the Medes, and this was fulfilled with the fall of Babylon before the Medes and Persians.

For today: God rules over empires, and injustice will not last forever. If you suffer something unjust, trust that God sees and acts in his time, and avoid taking revenge on your own.
exp.2:8:
It says that Israel took her unfaithfulness lightly, and that this defiled the land. Those images for unfaithfulness toward God are rendered in the verse as whoredom and adultery. The word "lightness" in the verse means a lack of seriousness, a treating of things as small. "Stones and stocks" are the idols made of stone and of wood.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He compares his people to an unfaithful wife. Israel, the northern kingdom, had already been punished and sent away. Even so, Judah, the southern kingdom, saw this and did not learn from it, but did the same. God calls them to return, but they do not do so from the heart.

For today: It is easy to treat sin as something small, and it becomes a habit. Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken the place of God in our hearts. If there are any, let us return to Him with sincerity, not just with words.
exp.49:30:
Here Got says he himself is against Babylon, which he calls "most proud," meaning arrogant and full of itself. The phrase "thy day is come" means the time of judgment has arrived. "The time that I will visit thee" here is not a friendly visit; God comes to call Babylon to account and to punish. "The Lord God of hosts" is a title that emphasizes his power over all things.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had oppressed Israel and Judah, and the nearby passages say it grew proud against the Holy One of Israel. God promises that its pride and its violence will not go unanswered. Scholars connect this with the historical fall of Babylon, though some also see in it a symbol of human pride in general.

For today: pride makes us believe we do not need God. Today you can ask him to give you humility and to recognize that everything you have comes from him.
exp.16:7:
The explanation says that the person who trusts in God is like a tree planted by the water. Its roots reach the stream, so when the heat comes it does not fear, its leaves stay green, and in the time of drought it is not anxious and does not stop bearing fruit. The phrases about the verse's wording have been left out, since your reader sees the King James text.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. Shortly before, he warned that whoever trusts only in people is like a dry shrub in the desert. Then he contrasts that life with the life of the one who leans on the Lord. Afterward he speaks of how deceptive the heart can be.

For today: in your hard times, do not wait for the drought to arrive before seeking God. Set aside time each day to pray and read the Bible, so that your roots are firm and you find calm when the pressure comes.
exp.50:28:
This verse says that the land will tremble and suffer, because God keeps his plan against Babylon firm. His purpose is to leave the land of Babylon a desolate place, with no one living there. The word "sorrow" in the verse means that the land will be in anguish, and "inhabitant" refers to someone who lives there.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing the word of the Lord. God calls several nations, such as Ararat, Minni, Ashkenaz and the Medes, to attack Babylon. Babylon had dominated and oppressed many peoples, and God declares that its power will come to an end. The text uses poetic and strong language to describe that judgment.

For today: even when it sometimes seems that the powerful will never fall, the Bible reminds us that God governs history and his purposes are fulfilled. We can rest in him, live with humility and trust that his justice comes in its time.
exp.5:27:
These verses say that the leaders of the people have become rebellious. "Rebellious princes" are leaders who do not obey God. "They walk with slanders" means they go around spreading false accusations and deceiving others. "Brass and iron" are common, hard metals, not precious ones: this is how God describes their character, hardened and without worth. "Corrupters" are those who damage and spoil others.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Before this verse, he announces that a destroyer is coming upon Judah and calls the people to mourning. God appointed Jeremiah as one who examines, like someone who tests metals. Then the image continues: the refiner's fire fails to remove the impurity, and the people are left as rejected silver.

For today: when we have influence over others, at home, in the church, or at work, let us ask God for a sincere heart. May our words and example build up, not corrupt. Let us allow Him to examine and correct us.
exp.28:12:
It says that God promises to let himself be found by those who seek him sincerely. "You will find" means "you will find." "With all your heart" means seeking him with your whole will and desire, not halfheartedly or out of habit.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He is addressing the Israelites who were carried off captive to Babylon. He had already told them the exile would be long, but he promises them that he has not forgotten them and that he has plans for peace for them. Then he announces that he will bring them back to their land.

For today: if you are going through a difficult time, do not turn away from God. Set aside a few minutes each day to pray and read the Bible sincerely, without rushing, trusting that he answers those who seek him truly.
exp.21:27:
God asks with sorrow whether Coniah is like a broken idol, a thing to be despised, or a vessel that no one takes pleasure in. He asks why he and his children have been thrown out into a land they do not know. "Despised" means held in contempt, and "takes pleasure in" means finds delight in.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Coniah, king of Judah, also called Jehoiachin, was taken captive to Babylon because of the disobedience of the people and their kings. The message says that none of his descendants would sit on the throne. Some understand the phrase about having no children to mean that none of them would hold the throne.

For today: power, office, and prestige do not last, and God does not measure worth by them. Live with humility and obedience, and remember that God remains the one who gives and takes away.
exp.32:9:
God says that the place people see as a wasteland, with no people and no animals, in the towns of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem, will once again be full of life. The phrase "again there shall be heard" refers to the sound of life returning to the place. The verse leaves the sound open, and the verses that follow tell what will be heard: voices of joy and praise.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had suffered the destruction of Jerusalem and the exile, and Jeremiah himself was in prison. God answers with a promise of forgiveness and restoration, just when everything seemed lost.

Today, you may see areas of your life as a desolate place. This verse invites you not to let what you see have the last word. God can forgive, heal, and restore joy. Bring to him in prayer whatever seems hopeless, and trust in his goodness.
exp.35:23:
This verse says that King Jehoiakim and his servants heard all the words of the scroll and were not afraid. Neither did they tear their garments. In that time, tearing one's clothes was a sign of grief, humility, and repentance. Here "servants" means his officials or attendants.

Jeremiah had dictated to Baruch the messages of God, warning of judgment if the people did not return to Him. The narrator contrasts this reaction with that of King Josiah, who did tear his garments when he heard the law (2 Kings 22). Jehoiakim chose to burn the scroll rather than listen.

When the Word of God confronts us, we can harden ourselves or respond with humility. Today, instead of looking for excuses, let us ask God for a tender heart willing to change.
exp.49:4:
It says that God's people will ask the way to Zion, that is, to Jerusalem, and will walk toward it with determination. They urge one another: "Come" and "join yourselves" to the Lord in an everlasting covenant, a bond that shall never be forgotten.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, passing on what the Lord says. The message announces the fall of Babylon, the people from the north, who would be destroyed. Then Israel and Judah, once divided, would return together, weeping and seeking God. Many understand this as the return from exile, and others see in it a broader hope that is fulfilled in Christ. Interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: if you have drifted away, you can return to God with humility and without delay. Ask for the way, seek the company of other believers, and renew your commitment to Him.
exp.33:5:
This verse says that the prophet Jeremiah personally delivered to Zedekiah, king of Judah, the whole message God had given him. He did this in Jerusalem, the capital. The words "spake all these words" refer to what came before: the warning that Babylon would conquer the city and the promise that the king would not die by the sword. Zedekiah is the king named in the verse, and Jerusalem is the city where it all took place.

Jeremiah was the prophet who spoke on behalf of God. Babylon already had Jerusalem surrounded, and the king was in a very difficult situation. Even so, Jeremiah did not soften the message or change it to please the king. He told it to him directly, just as he had received it. Some scholars debate exactly how the promise that the king would die "in peace" would be fulfilled, but the text emphasizes that God had spoken.

For today: when you must say a hard truth, do it with respect, but do not distort it out of fear. And when God speaks to you through his Word, listen with humility, even when it is not comfortable.
exp.22:7:
This verse says that God will bring back the descendants of Israel from the north, and from all the countries where he had scattered them. They will live again in their own land. And people will say "the Lord lives" because of this new deliverance, more than because of the exodus from Egypt.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The kings and leaders of Judah had failed, and the people would go into exile. Even so, God promises a future of return and hope. This appears alongside the promise of a righteous King, "the Lord our righteousness," whom many Christians see fulfilled in Jesus.

For today: even if you feel far away or lost, God remains faithful to restore. Trust that he can raise up a new story, and remember with gratitude his past and present rescues.
exp.41:3:
Jeremiah answers them plainly: "I have heard you," that is, he has understood their request. He says he will pray to the Lord, "your God," and that he will tell them everything God answers. "I will keep nothing back from you" means he will not hide anything from them, whether it is pleasant or hard.

After the fall of Jerusalem, a small group of survivors asks Jeremiah to seek God's guidance. They fear Babylon and are unsure whether to stay or flee to Egypt. They promise to obey. Later in the chapter it becomes clear that their hearts were already leaning toward Egypt, although here they sound sincere.

For today: before asking God for direction, honestly decide that you will obey his answer, even if it is not what you hope for. And if someone advises you from the Bible, be thankful that they speak to you with frankness.
exp.27:0:
This verse sets the scene. Jeremiah tells us that in the fourth year of the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah, in the fifth month, a prophet named Hananiah, son of Azur and a native of Gibeon, spoke to him in the temple. He did so in the presence of the priests and all the people.

Jeremiah is the one speaking, telling the story in the first person. Judah was under pressure from Babylon, and some of the treasures of the temple had already been carried away. Hananiah presents himself as a prophet of God and gives a message that the people wanted to hear. The next verse announces a swift deliverance. Later in the chapter, the text shows that his message was false.

For today: not every pleasant message comes from God, even when it sounds religious and is delivered in a sacred place. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and ask God for wisdom to discern.
exp.24:16:
Jeremiah tells that he obeyed God. He took the cup that God handed him and gave it to drink to all the nations to which he was sent. The word "gave" is what the verse means by "took," and "nations" refers to the peoples or nations.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks and tells what he did after receiving God's command. The cup represents God's judgment, called "the cup of wrath." To drink from it means to receive the consequences of sin. The list begins with Jerusalem and Judah, and continues with Egypt and other nations. Many understand this as a symbolic or prophetic vision, not a literal journey through all those places, although the text does not fully clarify this.

God speaks with seriousness, but also with justice, and no one stands outside his gaze. Today we can listen to his Word with humility, without thinking ourselves exempt, and turn back to him in time. If he sends us to say something difficult, may we do so with faithfulness and love.
exp.41:17:
It says that God, the Lord of hosts, warns the people: just as his anger fell upon Jerusalem, so it will fall upon them if they go into Egypt. The words "horror," "curse," and "shame" are the terms the verse uses for what they would become; "curse" is a word of bad luck, and "shame" means disgrace. Furthermore, they would not see their land again.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, the survivors feared Babylon and planned to flee to Egypt. They asked Jeremiah to pray and promised to obey God. But he noticed that they were already inclined to leave, and that is why he speaks to them with such firmness.

For today: before asking God for direction, let us check whether we are truly willing to obey the answer, even when it is not the one that gives us the most security.
exp.30:25:
He says that someone wakes up from a sleep and realizes it was pleasant and restful. "Upon this I awaked" means that rest was sweet to him and did him good. The word "awaked" is an older form of "awoke."

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks after receiving a message of hope for Judah and Israel, who were suffering under judgment and exile. God promises comfort to the weary and joy to the sorrowful. Some understand the sleep as a vision God gave him; others, as an expression of relief after so many harsh announcements. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: when you are exhausted or sad, remember that God can bring rest and hope into your life. Trust his promises, even if you do not yet see the complete change.
exp.36:12:
This verse tells that Jeremiah came to the gate of Benjamin, one of the gates of Jerusalem. There a captain of the guard, named Irijah, stopped him. He accused him of going over to the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians.

A narrator recounts the events. The Chaldeans had stopped besieging Jerusalem because the army of Pharaoh was coming. Jeremiah was going out toward the land of Benjamin, probably on some personal matter, and the captain thought he was a traitor. Jeremiah had announced that Babylon would win, and for that reason they suspected him. But he denied the accusation.

Today, we are sometimes judged unfairly or accused without reason. Jeremiah remained faithful to God even though others did not understand him. We can speak the truth, keep calm, and trust that God knows our heart.
exp.10:13:
God tells Jeremiah that he should no longer pray for the people of Judah. He warns him not to raise a cry or a prayer on their behalf, because when they call to Him in their distress, He will not listen to them.

God is speaking to his prophet Jeremiah. Judah had broken the covenant: they filled the cities and streets with altars to Baal and to other gods. This command is very harsh and shows how serious their persistent rebellion was. God had warned them many times, but they did not change. Now, only in the crisis, they wanted to seek Him.

For today: God does not want us to seek Him only when trouble comes. True faith is cultivated every day, with obedience and sincere repentance. Let us not wait for pain before returning to Him; let us draw near today with humility.
exp.17:5:
God asks whether he does not have the right to deal with Israel as the potter deals with his clay. He says the people are in his hand, just as the clay is in the hand of the craftsman.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jeremiah saw a potter remake a damaged vessel, and through that picture God explained his message to Judah and Israel. The verses that follow make clear that this is not a blind fate: if a nation turns away from its wickedness, God changes his mind about the punishment. Scholars understand that expression in different ways, but all see an invitation to return.

We can allow ourselves to be shaped by God with humility. If something in our life has been broken or needs to change, it is not too late: God can form us again, and we are called to respond with a willing heart.
exp.6:18:
God says that his people think they are offending him with their idolatry, but in reality they are harming themselves. The question is a way of saying: "Is it really me they are hurting?" The phrase "confusion of their own faces" means shame and ruin. "Provoke me to anger" means making him angry.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah practiced a cult of the "queen of heaven," a pagan goddess (scholars debate exactly who she was). Entire families took part. God warns them that his judgment will come because they abandoned him.

For today: when we turn away from God, the greatest harm falls on us ourselves. His commands protect us. Today we can ask ourselves what things are taking God's place in our lives and return to him with sincerity.
exp.49:33:
Their Redeemer is strong; the Lord of Hosts is his name. He says that the Redeemer of Israel and Judah is strong, and that his name is the Lord of Hosts. A redeemer is one who rescues and defends his own people. He will plead their cause like a lawyer, to bring rest to the land of his people and to bring unrest and fear upon the inhabitants of Babylon.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel and Judah had been oppressed and taken captive, and their captors did not want to let them go. God promises to judge Babylon for that oppression. The verses that follow show that the judgment would reach its rulers, wise men, and soldiers. Scholars understand this as speaking of the fall of Babylon, though they do not all agree on how and when each detail was fulfilled.

When you feel trapped or unfairly treated, you are not alone. Entrust your cause to God in prayer, trust in his justice, and avoid taking revenge yourself.
exp.22:20:
God says that there were prophets who rushed out to speak in his name, but he never sent them and never gave them any message. The word "ran" describes people who were in a hurry, very busy and active. "Prophesied" means they announced messages as if they came from God.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah in the days before the fall of Judah. Many prophets told the people that everything would be fine, even though they were still living in sin. God rebukes them because their words came from their own imagination and not from his presence. That is why the people did not repent.

Today we can learn not to trust a voice just because it sounds confident or is full of activity. It is wise to compare what we hear with the Bible and to spend time in God's presence. And if we speak on his behalf, let us do it with humility and faithfulness to his Word.
exp.14:2:
God announces that he will send four kinds of punishment upon his people: the sword that kills, the dogs that tear apart, and the birds and the beasts that devour and leave everything ruined.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the time of Judah before the fall of Jerusalem. The people had rejected God again and again. Not even the prayers of Moses and Samuel, great intercessors, would change the decision. The text mentions the sins of Manasseh, a king who led the people into idolatry and violence.

For today: God is patient, but he takes seriously the sin that is not abandoned. Let us not wait for the consequences to arrive. If there is something God has shown you that you should leave behind, do it today with humility, trusting in his forgiveness and his mercy.
exp.45:2:
He says: "Order the small shield and the large shield, and draw near to battle." "Order" means to prepare or get ready. The small shield was carried by the soldier, and the large shield was a great one that covered nearly the whole body. It is a military command given to the Egyptian soldiers.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message against Egypt. It refers to the battle of Carchemish, near the river Euphrates, where Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, defeated the army of Pharaoh Necho. The tone is ironic: Egypt prepares with all its equipment, but the verses that follow show that it will flee in defeat.

For today: we can have good preparation, plans, and resources, but none of them saves us if God is not on our side. Prepare yourself with responsibility, but place your trust in God and not only in your own strength.
exp.22:28:
God asks whether his word is not like fire and like a hammer that breaks the rock. With these images he says that his word has power: it burns away what is false, purifies, and breaks down hardness of heart.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Some prophets told their own dreams as if they came from God, and in this way they led the people away from him. God distinguishes between the chaff (human dreams, which have no value) and the wheat (his word, which nourishes). Then he rebukes them for stealing messages from one another and saying "Thus says the Lord" when God had not spoken.

For today: it is not enough that something sounds beautiful or spiritual. Test what you hear in the light of the Bible, and let it confront you and transform you, even when it sometimes makes you uncomfortable.
exp.9:13:
Jeremiah 10:14 says that the person who worships idols acts without understanding. The explanation says such a person becomes foolish and stops reasoning. A "knowledge" here means understanding or insight. A cast image is a figure of molten metal poured into a mold, and the one who makes it is the metalworker. The metalworker should feel shame, because his work is a deception: the figure has no breath, that is, no life in it.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, sent by God to warn Judah not to imitate the religions of the surrounding nations. Just before this, the text shows the Creator who made the earth, the heavens, the rain, and the wind. The contrast is strong: the living God creates, while the idol is made by human hands.

For today, let us ask what we put in the place of God, such as money, success, or image. These things promise security but have no life. Let us return to trusting the Creator, who hears and sustains.
exp.17:15:
It says that, because they had abandoned God, the land of Judah will be left in ruins. The phrase about constant hissing refers to mocking or horrified whistles that will be heard again and again. Anyone who passes by there will be astonished and shake his head, a gesture of pity or scorn at seeing such a disaster.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He compares the steady faithfulness of nature, such as the snow of Lebanon and the cold flowing waters, with the inconstancy of his people, who forgot him and burned incense to empty idols. The old paths are the road of faithfulness that their ancestors walked. The verse announces the consequences of leaving that road.
