For today: God calls us to return to the firm and tested character of his Word, instead of chasing empty things that promise much and hold up nothing. Today you can ask yourself what has taken God's place in your heart, and turn back to him.
exp.49:24:
He says that God opened his armory, that is, the place where he keeps his weapons, and brought out the instruments of his anger, which are the tools with which he carries out his justice. "Treasury" here means storehouse. He also states that this is the work of the Lord, the God of hosts, in the land of the Chaldeans, that is, Babylon.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon, called the hammer of the whole earth, had oppressed many peoples, including Judah, and had become proud against God. Now judgment is coming to it. Scholars understand that God uses other nations as his instruments, although the text does not name them in this verse.

For today: God does not overlook injustice, even if it takes time. This invites us to trust that he will do justice, and to live with humility, without abusing whatever power we have.
exp.17:7:
This verse says that if a nation turns away from its wrongdoing, God will change the plan of punishment he had for it. The word "But" in the verse is a connecting word meaning "however" or "yet." "Turn" in the verse means to turn back or change direction. "Repent," when said of God, expresses that he changes his mind and does not carry out the punishment he had announced.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has sent him to the potter's house to show that God is like one who shapes clay. His message to Israel and to other nations is clear: his warnings of judgment are not fixed sentences, but calls to return. The verses that follow show that the opposite can also happen: if a people turns away from what is good, God will change the blessing he promised.

For today: God responds to the heart that changes. If there is something in your life that does not please God, do not think it is too late. Today you can leave it behind and return to him with sincerity.
exp.47:7:
This verse says that a destroyer will come upon every city of Moab, and no city will escape. The valley and the plain will also be ruined. The word "destroyed" means destroyed, and the plain is the open countryside, with its crops. All of this will happen because the Lord has already said it.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf against Moab, a neighboring people of Israel. The preceding text points out that Moab trusted in its riches and in its god Chemosh. For that reason, the judgment would reach both the people and their gods. Scholars often connect this with the Babylonian invasion, though the text does not name the destroyer.

For today: examine where you place your security. Money, possessions, or success can fail, but God remains faithful. Trust in Him first, and use what you have with humility and generosity.
exp.28:18:
God explains why the punishment is coming: his people did not want to hear his words. He sent them through the prophets, sending them early and often, which is a way of saying he did it with persistence and from the beginning, without growing tired. At the end he repeats the charge that they would not hear, so the accusation reaches those who were listening to him at that very moment.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. He addresses Judah, and especially those taken into exile in Babylon. He announces beforehand that those who stayed in Jerusalem would be like bad figs, too spoiled to eat. The cause is not bad luck, but a long refusal to heed God's warnings.

For today: God keeps speaking with patience. Today we can set aside time to read his Word carefully and obey what we understand, without putting it off until later.
exp.16:14:
Here Jeremiah reports what the people say to him in mockery: "Where is what God says will happen? Let it happen now!" They doubt God's word because they still do not see it fulfilled. The phrase "let it come now" means "let it come right away, let it be fulfilled this very moment."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, in Judah. He had announced judgment because of the people's disobedience, but time went by and nothing happened. That is why they mocked him. Jeremiah, hurt, brings his complaint to God and asks him to heal and sustain him, trusting that God knows he spoke with sincerity.

For today: when God seems slow, or when others mock your faith, do not lose heart. Bring your pain to God honestly, as Jeremiah did, and keep trusting that his word is true, even when his timing is not yours.
exp.17:6:
It says that God has the right to announce judgment against any nation or kingdom. The phrase "at any moment" in the source would be rendered here as "at whatever instant" God decides it, with the word "instant" taken from the verse itself. The verbs "pluck up, pull down, and destroy" are like those of a farmer who pulls up a plant and ruins it.

The Lord speaks to the prophet Jeremiah, who is in the potter's house watching how the clay is worked. God uses that scene to tell Israel that He is the one who shapes the nations. But the verses that follow make clear that the warning is not a fixed fate: if the people turn from their evil, God changes His mind and does not send the punishment.

For today: when God warns us through His Word or through our conscience, we should not take it as a final sentence, but as an invitation to turn back. Right now we can recognize a wrong path and ask Him for help to change.
exp.47:20:
This verse says that God's judgment has already come upon the open plain country, that is, the flat tableland of Moab. It then names three towns that were reached: Holon, Jahazah, and Mephaath. The plain country means open, level ground, and judgment refers to the punishment that God pronounces.

The speaker is the prophet Jeremiah, announcing what God says about Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Specific places are named, as in a list, to show that the punishment would reach the whole territory. The prophets explain that Moab trusted in its pride and its riches. The exact location of some of these towns is not fully certain.

For today: God sees what happens in every place, even the smallest. We can examine whether we trust in our own strength or in Him, and draw near with humility.
exp.11:10:
The explanation says that God's land was turned into ruins. Destroyed and left as a wasteland is the sense here. The land "mourneth unto me," as if it were crying out before God. And the whole land suffered because no man laid it to heart, meaning nobody took it seriously or cared about it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. His inheritance is the people of Judah and their land. God describes how the shepherds, who were the leaders, trampled it, and how the enemies came to devour it. What is serious is that no one saw it as a judgment from God or repented. Some believe that "laid it to heart" means taking it to heart.

For today: do not overlook the signs that something is wrong in your life or your surroundings. Stop, pray, examine your heart, and return to God before the harm grows.
exp.42:1:
Here we see that Azariah, Johanan, and other proud men accuse Jeremiah of lying. They say that God did not send him to warn them not to go into Egypt. The explanation of the word "proud" is not needed in the translation, and the explanation of "sojourn" is replaced by the verse's own wording: "to sojourn there" means to live there for a time as a foreigner.

After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors asked Jeremiah to pray so that they could know what to do. They promised to obey. But when God told them to stay in Judah and not go to Egypt, they already had another decision in their hearts. That is why they reject the message and blame the prophet, later saying that Baruch is manipulating him.

For today: before asking God for direction, let us check whether we are truly willing to obey. If we have already decided everything, it is easy to call what God tells us a falsehood.
exp.45:11:
The nations heard of Egypt's shame, and her cry of pain was so loud that it was heard throughout the earth. The word "shame" here means humiliation, and "filled" means the cry spread through the whole land. The strong soldier stumbled against another strong soldier, and the two of them fell down together.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Egypt had been defeated by Babylon at Carchemish, beside the river Euphrates. Egypt trusted in its power and its fame, but God tells them that their defeat is unavoidable. It has no cure, like a wound without remedy.

For today: let us not place our trust in strength, money or prestige, because all of that can fall in a moment. Let us instead seek refuge in God, who is the only one who never fails and who sustains the humble.
exp.1:27:
God asks Judah with irony: "Where are the gods you made for yourself?" He invites them to arise and save them when trouble comes. And he adds that Judah had as many gods as it had cities.

Here "rescue" is simply the same idea as saving someone from danger, and "trouble" is a time of distress. The phrase "let them see if" means the same as "let them see whether."

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. His people had turned away from him to worship idols of wood and stone, but when crisis came they cried out to God: "Arise and deliver us." God exposes that contradiction: they had turned their backs on him, not their faces, and yet they still expected to be rescued.

For today: we can ask ourselves where we truly place our trust: money, work, reputation, and other things. These things may help a little, but they do not sustain the soul in a crisis. It is wise to seek God now, not only when trouble arrives.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that when the announced day of judgment comes, the leaders of the people will lose their courage. "The heart will fail" means they will lose their nerve and their strength. "Astonished" means struck dumb with terror, and "wonder" here expresses amazement and horror, not admiration.

God speaks through Jeremiah to Judah and Jerusalem. The lion and the destroyer of nations are commonly understood to refer to an invader from the north, though the text does not give its name here. The people had trusted false promises of peace, and the leaders who were meant to guide them did not see the danger coming. That is why the blow catches them unprepared.

For today: do not rest in easy assurances. If you have any responsibility, whether at home, in the church, or at work, seek God's truth with humility, even when it is uncomfortable, and not only what soothes you.
exp.21:19:
This verse is a painful command. Jerusalem is told to climb the mountains of Lebanon and the region of Bashan, and to cry out loudly from there. "Lovers" refers to the political allies the people trusted, and "destroyed" means they were defeated and broken.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the fall of Judah. He has just announced a shameful end for King Jehoiakim. God reminds Jerusalem that He spoke to her when everything was going well, but she would not listen. Scholars usually understand that those high places serve to make the lament heard far away, and that the lovers were the neighboring nations.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: money, people, or reputation. All of these can fail. Let us listen to God today, in the good times, and not wait until the crisis arrives.
exp.25:1:
The Lord tells the prophet Jeremiah to stand in the court of the temple and speak to all the people who come from the cities of Judah to worship. He must tell them everything God has entrusted to him, without leaving out a single word.

The Lord speaks at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, a king who did not faithfully follow God. The people kept going to the temple, but their lives were not changing. God sends his message in the hope that they will repent, as the following verse shows.

For today: when God shows us a truth in his Word, we should share it with love and honesty, without trimming it to look good. We can also ask ourselves whether our lives match what we say at church.
exp.11:13:
Thus says the Lord concerning the wicked neighbors, the nations close by that attacked and harmed the land God gave Israel as an inheritance. God promises to uproot them from their land, that is, to drive them out of it. He also says he will pluck Judah out from among them, which can be understood as rescuing Judah from those nations.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had been judged, and the neighboring nations took advantage of its fall. But God does not leave them unaccountable: they too will answer for what they did. The verses that follow show that, after the judgment, God will show mercy and restore those who turn back to him.

For today: God sees injustice and also offers a new beginning. We can trust that he executes justice without our taking revenge ourselves, and we can draw near to him with humility, knowing that his mercy remains available.
exp.47:22:
This verse continues a list of cities of Moab on which God's judgment falls. Three more are named here: Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon. The names appear in an older spelling in the text this explanation is based on, but they are real places in the Moabite region. It is not known with certainty where each one was located today.

The one speaking is the LORD, through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and God announces punishment for it, partly because of its pride and its trust in its own riches and fortresses (v. 7, v. 29). Naming so many cities shows that the judgment would be complete: no one would be left out, whether far away or close by.

For today: God sees and knows every place and every situation. Nothing we build to make ourselves feel secure, whether money, success, or fame, can protect us from Him. Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and humbly hand that pride over to God.
exp.50:48:
It says that Babylon made many of Israel fall dead, and for that reason people from all over the earth will now fall dead in Babylon.

The prophet Jeremiah announces what the LORD says against Babylon, the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and its temple and carried the people into captivity. God promises that he will "visit" them, that is, he will call Babylon to account for its violence and its idols. The exiles receive hope: God has not forgotten their suffering and does not ignore the injustice. The text does not say that Israel was innocent; other passages show that God also disciplined them.

For today: when you suffer an injustice, do not take revenge. Hand your pain over to God, who judges with justice, and ask him to help you forgive and to keep trusting in him.
exp.33:9:
This verse tells that the leaders and all the people heard about the agreement made in Jerusalem: each person would let go their male and female servants, and would no longer use them as slaves. They obeyed and let them go.

King Zedekiah made this covenant when Jerusalem was threatened by the army of Babylon. God, through Jeremiah, was reminding them that the law of Moses commanded that enslaved Hebrews be set free. It is not known with certainty why they did it at that time; some believe it was out of fear of the danger. Sadly, they later changed their minds and enslaved them again.

For today: obeying God is not only making a good decision in a difficult moment, but keeping it when the pressure passes. Ask God for the steadiness to fulfill what you have promised.
exp.51:27:
This verse begins a list of the Jews whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away, that is, took into exile in Babylon. It says that in his seventh year there were 3,023 people. It is a brief record, with precise figures.

Jeremiah 52 is a historical appendix that reviews the fall of Jerusalem. We do not know for certain who wrote it. Some think it was Jeremiah or one of his associates. The dates and numbers differ from other biblical accounts, and many scholars explain this by different ways of counting the years. The purpose seems to be to leave a record that what God had warned through the prophets was fulfilled.

For today: God does not overlook the pain of his people, not even when it is reduced to figures. You can trust that He sees your situation, and his word deserves to be taken seriously and with humility.
exp.51:23:
This verse tells how Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, seized Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, together with three keepers of the door of the temple.

The chapter describes the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, and the writer tells it as a historical event. Earlier, the text details how the temple was plundered, including its bronze pillars. Now its religious leaders are carried away. According to the account that follows, these prisoners were brought before the king at Riblah, where they were judged. It is a sign that the judgment announced by the prophets had been fulfilled.

For today: God takes his announced word seriously. We can listen to his Word with humility and not trust only in offices, buildings or traditions, but in a sincere and obedient faith.
exp.17:21:
It says that Jeremiah asks God to let cries of pain be heard in the houses of his enemies when an army suddenly arrives. The reason is that they dug a pit to catch him and hid traps along his path. The verse uses "snares" for the traps and "take me" for the act of catching him.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. The people of Judah, angry over his messages from God, planned to harm him, even though he had pleaded on their behalf. This is one of his most raw and sincere prayers. Some understand these words as a cry for justice, and others as a human outpouring of pain. The Bible does not hide it.

For today: when someone repays you evil for good, bring your pain honestly to God, without holding it in or taking revenge yourself. Then let Him be the judge, and ask Him for a heart free of resentment.
exp.4:13:
God says that, because of what the people spoke, he will make his words in Jeremiah's mouth a fire, and this people will be like wood. "Wherefore" means "for this reason." "Wood" refers to pieces of dry timber. "Devour" means to burn them up completely.

The LORD, the God of hosts, speaks to Jeremiah. The people had denied God, saying: "He does not exist, and nothing bad will happen to us." They also despised the prophets, saying they were only wind. God answers that his message will be real and powerful, and that judgment will come through a foreign nation, as the following verses say.

For today: do not make light of God's word or think there will be no consequences for ignoring it. Read the Bible with humility, let yourself be corrected, and respond quickly when God speaks to your heart.
exp.24:27:
Some nations will refuse to take the cup that Jeremiah offers them. The cup represents God's judgment, like a drink that leaves a person staggering. Then God tells Jeremiah to say to them that they have no choice: "Ye shall certainly drink."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at the time when Judah was falling. God announces that the punishment will begin with his own people, and that the other nations will not be free either. No one can escape his justice.

For today: we should not believe that we can avoid the consequences of our decisions just because we do not want to see them. It is better to humble ourselves, acknowledge our faults and seek God while there is still time, for his mercy remains open to whoever repents.
exp.17:8:
This verse says that God can, at any moment, announce blessing over a nation or a kingdom: to build it up is to raise it and strengthen it, and to plant it is to give it roots and growth. "I will speak" means that God declares what he will do.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, the prophet saw the potter reshape a damaged vessel. God teaches that his announcements are not a blind fate: they depend on how the people respond. If a nation turns from its evil, God changes the punishment announced; if it turns away from him, he changes the blessing. It is a call to Judah to turn back.

For today: do not give up on your future, and do not rely on your past blessings. Today you can return to God, correct a wrong path, and obey his voice with humility.
exp.18:3:
God says that the people abandoned him and turned this place into something that no longer belonged to him. There they burned incense to foreign gods, gods that neither they, nor their ancestors, nor their kings had known before. The sentence about the word "estranged" is removed, since it explains a word not in the verse. They also filled the place with the blood of innocent people.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the Valley of Hinnom, near Jerusalem. He warns the kings and inhabitants of Judah that punishment is coming because of their idolatry and violence. The following text clarifies that children were offered there to Baal, something God never commanded.

Today we can ask what things occupy the place that belongs to God in our lives. Returning to Him means leaving behind what harms others and living with justice and compassion.
exp.0:18:
God tells Jeremiah that the people will attack him with words and with deeds, but they will not be able to destroy him. The reason is a promise: "I am with you." "Deliver" means to rescue you and keep you safe. God does not promise that there will be no opposition, but that opposition will not have the final word.

The Lord, who is speaking, calls Jeremiah as a prophet. He sends him to speak to kings, princes, priests, and the people of Judah, who had turned away from God. His message would be harsh and would not be well received. That is why God compares him to a fortified city, an iron pillar, and a bronze wall.

If you do what is right and are criticized or rejected, you are not alone. Obey with humility and confidence, remembering that God's presence sustains you even when others oppose you.
exp.43:16:
They say the people refuse to obey Jeremiah. They insist on doing everything they promised: burning incense to the "queen of heaven" and pouring out drink offerings to her. They claim that they did this, and their ancestors, their kings, and their leaders did it too. According to them, back then they had plenty of food, were well, and saw no evil.

They are Jews who had taken refuge in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. Jeremiah warned them in God's name to abandon idolatry. They answer with rebellion. The exact identity of the "queen of heaven" is debated; many think she was a goddess of the ancient Near East, such as Ishtar or Astarte.

Today we can learn not to measure what is true by what went well for us before. A comfortable memory can deceive us. Let us ask God for humility to listen to his Word, even when it confronts us.
exp.6:2:
Thus says the Lord, through Jeremiah, to the people: "Amend your ways and your doings." That is, change the way you live and act. If they do, God promises to let them keep living in this land.

Jeremiah speaks at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem, and the message is for the people of Judah who came in to worship. God warns them not to trust in empty religious phrases like "the temple of the Lord," for they believed the temple would protect them even while they lived wrongly. God asks for a real change, above all justice toward one's neighbor.

Today we can ask whether our lives match what we say we believe. Going to church or using spiritual words is not enough. Let us ask God for help to change one specific attitude or habit, and to treat those around us with justice and kindness.
exp.50:27:
This verse is a command to prepare several nations and their rulers to attack Babylon. The word "Prepare" in the verse means to get ready or set in order. The verse names the kings of the Medes, their captains, all their rulers, and the whole land under their dominion. In other words, God calls a whole people with their leaders to rise up against that city.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah, who announces judgment on Babylon, the powerful empire of his time. Babylon had destroyed nations and had mistreated Judah. The text presents God as Lord of history, who uses other peoples to carry out his purpose. The Medes appear here as the instrument of that judgment. Later history shows that Babylon fell, although the details of how this was fulfilled are explained in different ways.

For today: no human power is eternal, but God remains faithful. We can trust that he sees injustice and acts in his time, and in the meantime we can live with humility and hope.
exp.45:1:
This verse opens a prophecy addressed to Egypt. It speaks of the army of Pharaoh Necho, which was by the river Euphrates at Carchemish. There Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, defeated it in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This message is part of the oracles against the nations, that is, against the neighboring nations of Judah. Egypt was a very proud power, and its defeat at Carchemish (around 605 BC) changed the balance of power in the region. The verses that follow describe the soldiers preparing for war.

For today: no human power, however strong it may seem, is above God. We can trust that He governs history, and so we do not need to place our security in money, fame, or power.
exp.50:61:
Jeremiah tells Seraiah what he must say when he arrives in Babylon: a prayer addressed to God. He acknowledges that God himself announced that this place would be destroyed completely. He says that neither person nor animal would remain, and that it would be left a wasteland, desolate and in ruins, forever.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet and writes God's words in a book. Seraiah, who was traveling to Babylon with King Zedekiah, was to read it aloud there. It was a message for the exiles, a reminder that Babylon, so powerful, would not have the final word. Some understand the total destruction as prophetic and gradual language; others expect a more complete fulfillment.

For today: when evil seems great and unconquerable, we can pray with confidence, remembering that God still governs and fulfills what he says.
exp.22:13:
God says that he has seen horrible things among the prophets of Jerusalem. They committed adultery and lived in lies, and they encouraged evildoers so that no one turned away from their wickedness. Where the source said that they "strengthened the hands" of the wicked, the meaning is that they gave encouragement and support to them. That is why God compares them to Sodom and Gomorrah, cities famous for their sin.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Earlier he had condemned the prophets of Samaria, who followed Baal. Now he says that those of Jerusalem are even more serious, because they were meant to guide the people and instead deceived them with false messages. Then comes the judgment against them and the warning not to listen to them.

For today: it is not enough for someone to speak about God with confidence. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and also look at how that person lives. If you have influence over others, take care that your life and your words do not encourage wrongdoing.
exp.4:16:
It says that an invading people will devour everything Israel had worked for: the harvest, the bread meant for their sons and daughters, the flocks and herds, and the vines and fig trees. Even the fortified cities, where the people felt safe, would be destroyed by the sword.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that a foreign nation, whose language they do not know, will come as a consequence of the people having abandoned him to serve other gods. Many understand this to refer to Babylon, although the text does not name it here. The following verse makes clear that God would not destroy them completely.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether it is your work, your savings, or your strongholds. All of that can fail, but God endures. Trust in Him first, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.48:11:
God says that he will judge Edom. He speaks of the "cup" as an image of punishment, something bitter that must be drunk. If even those who did not deserve such suffering will drink it, Edom will not escape. "Absolved" means declared free of guilt. "Surely" means without any doubt.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Edom, the people descended from Esau. Edom was a neighbor of Israel and, according to other passages in the Bible, showed hostility when Judah fell. Here God announces that his judgment reaches all the nations, and the context adds a comfort: he cares for orphans and widows.

For today: let us not confuse God's patience with indifference. If he judges with justice, we can leave in his hands the injustices we suffer, instead of seeking revenge, and examine our own hearts with humility.
exp.31:23:
They say the Babylonian armies have already raised siege ramps and are attacking Jerusalem. Soon the city will fall into the hands of the Chaldeans, who are the Babylonians. Inside it the people suffer because of war (the sword), hunger, and disease (the pestilence). What God had announced is coming true, and Jeremiah acknowledges it.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, in prayer to God. Jerusalem is under siege, and God had asked him to buy a field, something that seemed absurd. Jeremiah remembers that the people disobeyed, and that is why the punishment came. He appears confused: why buy land if everything is being lost?

For today: when things make no sense, pray honestly. God is not offended by your questions. Bring your confusion before Him and keep obeying, trusting that He has a greater plan than what you can see.
exp.22:5:
This verse promises that, in the days of the righteous King whom God will raise up from David's family, Judah will be saved and Israel will live in safety. The phrase "shall dwell safely" means he will live calm and without fear. The King will be called "THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS," that is, "the Lord is our righteousness."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were being misled by unjust shepherds (leaders), and soon they would be carried into exile. God promises better shepherds and a righteous King. Christians see in this branch Jesus; Jews have understood it in other ways.

For today: when you feel guilty or insecure, remember that your worth before God does not depend on your achievements, but on Christ, our righteousness. Rest in Him and live with confidence, doing good.
exp.41:11:
It says that God promises to deal with the people with compassion. The phrase "I will shew mercies unto you" means that He will show them kindness, and "that he may have mercy upon you" means that the king of Babylon will also treat them with leniency. Finally, "and cause you to return to your own land" means that He would bring them back or would let them continue living in their land. Note: in some readings, the subject is God working through the king.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, the survivors fear Babylon's revenge and want to flee to Egypt. They ask God for counsel, and He answers that they should stay in Judah and not be afraid.

For today: when fear pushes you to look for a quick way out, stop and ask God what He wants. Obeying sometimes means staying still and trusting, even when the situation seems threatening.
exp.46:2:
It says that the noise of the hoofs of the strong horses, the rushing of the chariots and the rumbling of the wheels will be so terrible that the fathers, overcome with panic, will not even turn back to help their children. "Hoofs" are the hooves of the horses, "strong" refers to the mighty steeds, and "feebleness of hands" is the weakening that fear brings.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing the Philistines. He announces a judgment coming from the north like a flood. Scholars often see there an invading army, and many think of Babylon, although the text does not give the name. The passage shows that God rules over all nations, not only over Israel.

For today: let us not place our security in the strength, power or resources of this world, because they can vanish. Let us trust in God, who remains a firm refuge when everything shakes.
exp.50:6:
Babylon was like a golden cup in God's hand. It was beautiful and powerful, but God was the one who used it. Its wine made all the nations drunken, that is, left them confused and under its control. The word "drunken" in the verse is the same as "mad," meaning the nations were left stunned and unable to think clearly.

The prophet Jeremiah announces a message from God against Babylon, the empire that had conquered Judah. God had not abandoned his people, even though they had sinned. Now he calls them to leave Babylon, because its punishment was coming. Some understand that God used Babylon as an instrument and then judged it for its wickedness.

For today: The bright and powerful things of this world can confuse us and dull the heart. Ask yourself what influences are making you drunk on ideas or desires that pull you away from God, and take one concrete step to separate yourself from them.
exp.43:13:
God says that the Jews who fled to Egypt to live there will not escape the punishment. None of them will be left alive to return to Judah, even though they long to go back. The final phrase, "no volverán sino los que escaparen," suggests that only a few fugitives would manage to return.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group went to Egypt, against God's counsel, and there they worshiped other gods. God warns them that Egypt will not be a refuge. Instead of repenting, the people reject the message, as the next verse shows.

For today: do not seek security far from God, and do not harden your heart when He corrects you. Listening in time and returning to Him is wiser than insisting on our own way.
exp.50:22:
He says that God will use Babylon like a hammer to destroy all kinds of people: the shepherd with his flock, the farmer with his oxen (the "yoke of oxen" are the pairs of oxen that plowed), and also the rulers. "Dukes" here means governors or chiefs, and "princes" are lesser officials. No one is left out: neither the field nor the government.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been an instrument of God and had also oppressed many peoples, including Judah. This passage announces that its power will come to an end and that God will repay it for the evil it did in Zion. Some understand that God will use another people, the Medes, to carry this out.

For today: no human power is eternal or escapes the justice of God. If you suffer from an injustice, you can rest in the knowledge that God sees and judges with righteousness. And if you have authority, use it with humility and justice.
exp.5:18:
God calls the whole earth to witness what he is about to do. He will bring "evil," that is, disaster or calamity, upon Judah. That evil is "the fruit of their thoughts": the natural result of their decisions and of their hearts. The reason is plain: they did not listen to God's words and they looked down on his law.

The verse says they "rejected" it, meaning they turned it away with contempt.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier he had sent watchmen, that is, prophets who warned of danger, but the people answered, "We will not listen." Afterward, God says that their sacrifices and their incense do not please him, because their religion was only outward and their lives did not obey.

For today: it is not enough to practice religious rituals if we close our ears to the voice of God. Today you can read his Word with humility and obey something concrete that it shows you.
exp.17:18:
Jeremiah asks God to look at him closely and to listen to what his opponents are saying. The phrase "Look after me" is rendered here simply as the request itself, and the word for those who oppose him is "contend" in the sense of arguing against him or setting themselves against him.

The prophet is speaking. The people of his town, together with religious leaders, were planning to harm him and silence him, because his message of judgment troubled them. He does not defend himself alone but brings his case before God. The verses that follow show his pain and a very harsh prayer against them. This can be understood as a sincere complaint, which God allows him to express before him.

For today: when someone criticizes you or treats you unfairly for doing what is right, you do not have to repay blow for blow. Bring your case to God honestly, tell him how you feel, and ask him to see and to act.
exp.3:25:
He says that Jeremiah saw a vision: Mount Carmel, which was a fruitful hill full of greenery, was now a wilderness. Its cities lay in ruins before the Lord himself, that is, before God himself. The word "destroyed" in this verse means completely laid waste, reduced to nothing. The phrase "fierce anger" speaks of a very strong wrath against sin.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet, and God shows him what the land of Judah would become because of its rebellion and idolatry. It is a warning of judgment, probably through an invader from the north. But the following verse makes clear that God will not make a full end of his people.

For today: do not take lightly God's call to return to him. His patience is real, but we must not take advantage of it. Today you can examine your life, repent of what you know displeases him, and trust in his mercy.
exp.35:5:
Jeremiah tells Baruc to go to the temple and read aloud the scroll on which he wrote what God had spoken to him. He is to read it before the people gathered on the day of fasting, and also before those who come in from the cities of Judah. A scroll was an ancient book made from a long strip rolled up.

The speaker is Jeremiah, God's prophet, who is in prison and cannot enter the temple. For that reason he sends his assistant Baruc. God wanted to warn the people of his judgment, in the hope that they would turn back. This is believed to have taken place in the time of King Jehoiakim, although the exact details are interpreted in different ways.

For today: God still uses ordinary people to share his Word. If he places in your heart to say something true and good, do it with courage and humility, even when others cannot or will not.
exp.26:3:
This verse says that Jeremiah is to give a message to the envoys so that they carry it back to their kings. It is a command with authority: "Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel." The phrase "the Lord of hosts" presents God as the Lord of all power.

God speaks, and Jeremiah is his messenger. Envoys from several neighboring nations were in Jerusalem, probably to plan a rebellion against Babylon. Through Jeremiah, God sends them a message: it is not the time to rebel. The verses that follow say that God is the Creator and that he allowed Nebuchadnezzar to have authority for a time.

For today: before making ambitious plans, it is good to stop and listen to God. He sees beyond what we see, and his word calls us to humility and trust.
exp.33:6:
This verse tells us that the army of Babylon was attacking Jerusalem and the last fortified cities of Judah that were still holding out: Lachish and Azekah. "Fought against" means that they were waging war or attacking. "Remained" means that the other strong cities had already fallen.

Jeremiah is speaking to King Zedekiah in Jerusalem while the Babylonian siege was advancing. God had warned him that the city would be handed over, but he also promised that the king would die in peace and with honor. The verse shows how serious and how near the situation was. Shortly afterward, the people made an agreement to free their Hebrew servants, but then they did not keep it.

For today: when the pressure is great, it is easy to promise change and forget it once the danger has passed. God expects sincere and steady obedience, not only in a crisis. Today you can keep a pending promise you made to God or to someone else.
exp.26:7:
The explanation says that God warns any people or kingdom that refuses to submit to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. A yoke is the wooden frame placed on the neck of working animals; here it stands for submission. Plague is a deadly sickness that spreads, and the phrase "I will visit" means "I will send punishment." Resistance would bring war, famine, and disease.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah in the days of King Zedekiah of Judah. God had allowed Babylon to rule the region for a time, and the false prophets were saying there would be no submission. Jeremiah urged people to accept this reality in order to save lives.

For today: when God allows a difficult situation, listening to his voice with humility is worth more than comfortable but false words. Before following a popular message, compare it with what the Bible teaches.
exp.22:12:
God says he saw "folly" among the prophets of Samaria, meaning foolish and senseless things. They spoke in the name of Baal, a false god, and so they led the people of Israel astray. Here "err" means to lose the way.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom, Israel, which had already fallen to Assyria. God uses it as an example to accuse the prophets of Jerusalem, who according to the context were even worse. The leaders who were supposed to guide the people led them down the wrong path, and God announces that he will hold them accountable.

For today: do not follow someone just because they speak with confidence or hold a religious position. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and if you teach others, do so with humility and faithfulness to the Word of God.
exp.51:25:
He says that Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard of Babylon, gathered the important prisoners from Jerusalem (priests, officials and other men) and brought them to the king of Babylon, who was at Riblah. "Captain of the guard" was a high military commander. The sentence about the word for "took them" is removed because it does not appear in the verse above.

The chapter tells, as a historical account, the fall of Jerusalem in the time of King Zedekiah. Jeremiah had warned for years that the people would be judged for their disobedience and for not listening to God. Here the announced judgment is seen fulfilled: the religious and military leaders are taken away as prisoners and executed at Riblah, in the land of Hamath.

For today: God speaks seriously, but he is also faithful to his word. If today we sense his call to correct something in our lives, it is better to listen in time and return to him with humility, without waiting for the consequences to arrive.
exp.0:4:
God says that he knew Jeremiah before he was formed in his mother's belly. Before he was born, God set him apart, that is, he dedicated him for a special purpose. And he appointed him as a prophet to the nations.

The explanation of the old wording is removed here, since the phrases it discusses do not appear in the verse you are reading.

The LORD speaks, and he addresses these words to Jeremiah, a young man from a priestly family who lived in the final years of the kingdom of Judah, until the fall of Jerusalem. God calls him to a difficult task: to speak his message to a people who had turned away from him. Jeremiah answers with fear, saying that he is too young and does not know how to speak, but God does not change the call.

For today: God knows you and has valued you from the beginning, before your achievements or your failures. When you feel that you do not measure up to what he asks of you, remember that his calling comes with his support. Take the first step by trusting him.
exp.16:24:
God promises that if the people obey and keep the Sabbath, kings and their princes will continue to enter through the gates of Jerusalem, riding in chariots and on horses, seated on the throne of David. The men of Judah are the people of Judah, and the inhabitants are those who live in the city. The city will remain forever as long as there is obedience.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had become stubborn and refused to listen. God offers them a choice: obey and receive blessing, or disobey and see the city burned, as the following verse says. The Sabbath was a sign of trust in God.

For today: God invites us to trust Him and not to live enslaved to work. Set aside a regular time to rest, pray, and thank Him, believing that He sustains your life.
exp.2:5:
God spoke to Jeremiah in the days of King Josiah and asked him to look at the behavior of Israel, the northern kingdom. He calls her "unfaithful" because she was disloyal to him. Her unfaithfulness is a spiritual one: worshiping other gods. The high mountains and the leafy trees were places where pagan worship was practiced.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Israel had already fallen before Assyria, and God compares her to an unfaithful wife. He shows this to Judah, the southern kingdom, which saw what had happened and still followed the same path. God wants Judah to learn and to turn back.

For today: let us learn from the mistakes of others before we repeat them. If anything takes the place of God in our hearts, let us return to him soon, because he still calls us with patience.
exp.45:10:
He says that Egypt, called the "virgin daughter," must go up to Gilead, a region famous for its balm, a resin used as medicine to heal wounds. But God warns her that it will be useless: no matter how many remedies she multiplies, there will be no cure. "In vain" is the sense here, meaning to no purpose. "Virgin" here alludes to a nation that thought itself unspoiled and invincible.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. Egypt had been defeated by Babylon at Carchemish, beside the river Euphrates. The text presents that fall as a judgment of God, and with irony it shows that no human resource could undo that wound.

For today: let us not trust in our strength, reputation, or resources to fix what only God can heal. When we recognize our need and return to Him in humility, there is hope, because He is able to restore.
exp.48:8:
In the verse, the prophet says that when grape harvesters come to a vineyard, they usually leave some grapes behind for the gleaners. Even thieves at night take only what they need. But with Edom it will be different: the destruction will be total, as the next verse shows. "Enough" in the verse means what is sufficient.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah with a message of judgment against Edom, the people descended from Esau. Teman and Dedan were regions or cities connected with Edom and its reputation for wisdom. God announces that neither their wisdom nor their hiding places will save them. Many understand that the judgment comes because of their pride, although here the text focuses on the punishment.

For today: let us not trust in our intelligence, resources, or security as if they were our refuge. Let us place our trust in God, who also cares for orphans and widows, and use what we have with humility.
exp.1:34:
The people of Judah claim: "I am innocent, so God is no longer angry with me." But God answers that he will bring her to judgment, precisely because she says "I have not sinned." Bringing someone to judgment means presenting a formal case against them. "Turned away from me" means that his anger has already passed.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had sought other gods and political alliances, and even had the blood of innocent people on her clothes. Even so, she considered herself free of guilt and did not repent. That is why God confronts her.

For today: denying our failures keeps us from forgiveness. We can ask God to show us honestly what is in our hearts, and confess it without excuses, trusting that he forgives those who repent.
exp.16:3:
God tells his people that they will lose the land he himself gave them. The phrase "discontinue from thine heritage" means that they will no longer possess it. They will be slaves to their enemies in a country they do not know. The "anger" is his burning wrath, and the "fire" that burns "for ever" is an image of judgment. Some understand "for ever" as a very long and harsh punishment, not necessarily one without end.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people had built altars and high places to worship idols, and their children grew up remembering them. That is why the punishment comes, which was fulfilled in the exile to Babylon.

For today: God calls us to trust in him alone, not in false gods or in passing things such as money or people. Today you can ask yourself where you are placing your security, and hand it over to God in prayer.
exp.34:16:
This verse says that God, the Lord of hosts and God of Israel, is going to bring upon Judah and upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem the punishment he had already announced to them. The reason is simple: God spoke to them and they did not listen; he called them and they did not answer.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. In this chapter, God holds up as an example the Rechabites, a family who faithfully kept the command of their ancestor Jonadab not to drink wine. If they obeyed a man, how much more should the people obey God, who had sent them prophets again and again?

For today: when we sense that God is speaking to us through his Word or through our conscience, we should not delay our response. Listening and obeying humbly today is better than hardening the heart.
exp.0:12:
God spoke to Jeremiah a second time and asked him what he saw. He answered that he saw a boiling pot, tilted toward the north. The word "north" in the verse is the direction the pot faces, so the pot appears to be pouring over toward the south.

God speaks to Jeremiah at the beginning of his call as a prophet. Through this vision he announces that a disaster will come from the north upon Judah and Jerusalem because of their disobedience. The verses that follow explain it as nations that would come to surround the city. Tradition often connects this with Babylon, although the text here speaks in general of kingdoms from the north.

For today: God warns us in love before the consequences arrive. If today you feel that He is calling you to correct something, do not put it off; respond with humility and trust that He remains faithful.
exp.9:23:
This verse is a prayer. The speaker asks God to correct him, but with justice and measure, not in burning anger. "With judgment" means with justice, with balance. "Fury" is a very strong anger. "Bring me to nothing" means that you destroy me completely.

The one praying is Jeremiah, speaking on behalf of his people. An invasion is announced from the north that will leave the cities of Judah in ruins. Jeremiah acknowledges that human beings do not control their own path and asks for mercy in the midst of punishment. Some understand that he prays for himself, and others, that he prays as the voice of the people.

For today: when you recognize a mistake, do not run from God. Come near with humility and ask him to correct you with his love, trusting that his purpose is to restore you, not to destroy you.
exp.50:41:
The sea has risen against Babylon and covered her with the multitude of its waves. It is a poetic image: Babylon is buried and destroyed like a city under a flood.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on what God announces against Babylon, the empire that had oppressed Judah. God promises judgment for its pride and violence. The "sea" most likely represents enemy armies arriving like waves, although some understand it only as a figure of total destruction. Babylon was not literally covered by a sea, as far as we know.

For today: no human power lasts forever, however great it may seem. We can trust that God sees injustice and has the final word. This invites us to live with humility and to rest in Him when evil seems to be winning.
exp.47:39:
God announces that an enemy will swoop down on Moab suddenly, like an eagle that drops on its prey with its wings spread wide. The image speaks of a sudden attack, one from which no one can escape.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Moab, a neighboring people of Israel, east of the Dead Sea. The text does not say here who the eagle is; many think it refers to an invading army, probably Babylon. God explains the reason for the judgment: Moab "exalted itself against the Lord." Its pride and its rejection of God led it to its fall.

For today: pride makes us trust in our own strength, achievements, or securities. Today you can hand over to God whatever you trust in most and ask him for a humble heart that depends on him.
exp.24:1:
This verse says that Jeremiah the prophet spoke God's message to all the people of Judah and to all who lived in Jerusalem. The words "spoke" and "inhabitants" mean that he said it out loud to those who lived in the city. No one was left out: it was a message for everyone.

Jeremiah speaks in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, when Nebuchadnezzar was beginning to reign in Babylon. God sends him to warn the people that, after so many years of not listening, serious consequences would come. Jeremiah had insisted for twenty-three years, according to the verses that follow, but almost no one paid him any attention.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we are listening to God when he speaks to us through his Word, even when the message is uncomfortable. A good practice is to read the Bible with a heart willing to obey, not just to receive information.
exp.28:6:
It says that the exiles were to seek the good of the city where God had sent them, and to pray to the Lord for it. The word "seek" means to strive to obtain something. "Carried away" here means being taken off into exile. To "pray" is to ask earnestly. The reason is simple: if the city has peace, they too will have peace.

Jeremiah writes a letter to the Jews who were taken captive to Babylon. God tells them to settle down, start families, and live normal lives, because the exile would last a long time. At the same time, he warns them not to believe prophets who promised a quick return. Those promises were false.

For today: even when we are not in the place we dreamed of, we can serve and pray for our city, work with honesty, and care for our neighbors. God can use that place to take care of us and to shape us.
exp.24:14:
God tells Jeremiah to take from his hand a cup full of the wine of his anger. He is to make all the nations to whom God sends him drink from it.

The Lord, the God of Israel, speaks and gives his prophet a command. Jeremiah lived in days of great wickedness, and God warns that judgment would reach Judah and also other peoples. The cup is a picture of the punishment each nation would have to drink. Some scholars understand that Jeremiah did this in a vision, and others that it was a spoken message. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: God is just with everyone, not only with a few. This invites us to live with humility, to listen to his correction in time, and to turn back to him before our hearts grow hard.
exp.8:21:
This verse describes a very harsh scene: the bodies of the dead will lie scattered on the open field like dung, or like the sheaves that the reaper leaves fallen on the ground, and no one will gather them. "Surface of the field" means the open ground of the field. A "handful" is a bunch of cut stalks of grain.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces the judgment that would come upon Judah for its rebellion, with death and mourning everywhere. For this reason he calls the women to raise laments. Many scholars connect this with the Babylonian invasion, although the text gives no further details.

For today: the things we tend to trust in, such as talent, strength or money, do not save us from everything. What is most valuable is to know God and to live as he pleases, with mercy, justice and righteousness.
exp.6:24:
God says that, from the time Israel came out of Egypt until the days of Jeremiah, He sent them all His servants, the prophets. "Rising up early" means He did it with persistence and care, never tiring, like someone who gets up early so the day does not slip by. "Fathers" refers to their ancestors.

God speaks through Jeremiah in his message at the temple. The people trusted in their rituals and in the temple, but they did not obey. God reminds them that from the beginning His covenant was: "Hearken unto my voice, and I will be your God." The prophets were a sign of His patience, but the people hardened their hearts.

Today, God still speaks with patience. Ask yourself: is there something God has already shown you in His Word that you have put off obeying? Today you can listen to Him with an open heart and take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.50:36:
This verse says that Babylon will be turned into ruins. "Heaps" are rubble piled up; "jackals" are wild animals like dogs; "terror" is something that frightens whoever sees it; a "hiss" is the whistling sound people make when they mock or are amazed; "without an inhabitant" means without people living in it.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had oppressed Judah and destroyed Jerusalem, and the people cried out for justice. God answers that he will judge the cause of his people. It is a prophecy of judgment against a proud and violent nation. Scholars debate how and when it was fulfilled in exact detail, but the central message is clear.

For today: God sees injustice and does not forget it. We can hand our pain over to him without taking revenge, trusting that he judges with justice, and examine whether we ourselves walk in pride.
exp.6:31:
God announces that a time is coming when the place called Tophet, in the valley of the son of Hinnom, will no longer bear that name. It will be called "the valley of slaughter." So many will die that they will be buried there until there is no room left.

The word "defile" in the verse means to make something dirty or unclean.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people had done terrible things: in Tophet they burned their own children in rituals, something God never commanded. They had also filled the temple with their idols. The announcement is a judgment: the place of their sin would become the place of their punishment.

For today: God takes seriously the harm we do to the innocent and false worship. It is worth asking ourselves what things we put above God, and whether for their sake we neglect those we are called to care for. He also always calls people to repentance before judgment.
exp.31:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah on a specific date: the tenth year of King Zedekiah of Judah, which matched the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. The word "Lord" in this verse is the name of God used in this translation.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is the prophet who receives the message. According to the verses that follow, Jerusalem was surrounded by the Babylonian army, and Jeremiah was imprisoned because he had announced that the city would be handed over to Babylon. Scholars usually place this around 587 BC, although the exact dates can vary depending on the calculation.

For today: the Bible places God's word within real events and difficult moments. When life feels enclosed or without a way out, we can remember that God continues to speak and act in the middle of crisis. Look for his voice in Scripture and trust that he does not lose control.
exp.4:4:
It says that the prophet thought to seek out the great ones, that is, the leaders and important people, to speak with them. He expected that they, at least, would know the way of the LORD, that is, what God requires and how he judges. But he discovers that they too had broken the yoke and burst the bonds. The yoke and the bonds are the straps with which an ox is joined to the plow; here they stand for obedience to God.

The one speaking is Jeremiah. Earlier he thought that the poor did not understand God because they lacked instruction. Then he turns to the leaders, but they too were unwilling to submit. For this reason God announces judgment: it was not ignorance, but rebellion.

For today: knowing what is right is not enough. Knowing the Bible, or holding a position of responsibility, calls us to obey. Let us ask God for a heart willing to accept his correction, rather than hardening ourselves.
exp.46:3:
It says a day is coming that will bring destruction on all the Philistines. That day will also cut off the help that Tyre and Sidon, allied cities, could offer them. "Spoil" means to lay waste or cut off completely. "Caphtor" is probably the island of Crete, though some think of another region of the Mediterranean; the Philistines came from there.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The flood that rises from the north is an army that comes down like an overflowing river. Many understand this to be Babylon, though the text does not name it here. God announces judgment on a nation neighboring Judah, and the grief is so great that parents do not even turn to look at their children.

For today: do not trust in alliances, money, or people as your ultimate security. When every human helper fails, God remains the firm refuge. Place your trust first in Him.
exp.48:25:
It says that the young men of Damascus will fall dead in the city's streets, and that all its soldiers will die on the same day. The word translated as "young men" in the verse above means young people or lads. The soldiers are the men of war. It is spoken by the LORD of hosts, a title that shows his authority over every kind of power.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, within a message against several nations that were neighbors of Israel. Damascus, the capital of Syria, appears frightened and without strength, like a woman in labor. The texts do not explain each step in detail, but the message is that God judges the nations and that no strong city is outside his hand. Scholars debate which exact historical events are meant.

For today: do not place your security in your strength, your money, or your youth. All of these can fail. Trust in God, who is just and sustains what truly endures.
exp.14:3:
It says that God will hand over his people to be shaken and carried back and forth among all the nations. "Agitated" means tossed about, with no safe place to rest. The cause it gives is what King Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, did in Jerusalem.

The words are spoken by the LORD through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Judah. Manasseh had promoted idolatry and violence (2 Kings 21). Although his grandson Josiah carried out reforms, the people kept walking the same path. Interpreters explain in different ways how Manasseh's guilt relates to that later generation, but the text shows that his sin left deep marks.

For today: our decisions can affect others, even those who come after us. Take care what you sow in your family, and return to God with sincerity while there is still time.
exp.9:15:
God is not like the idols at all. The phrase "the portion of Jacob" refers to the people of Israel, who belong to God and are his own possession. He is the Creator of all things, and Israel is "the rod of his inheritance," that is, the people who belong to him, set apart as his own. His name is the Lord of hosts, the Lord of all power.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, sent by God to Judah. Earlier he mocked the idols made by craftsmen: they have no life and no breath. Now he sets those lifeless things against the living God. Then comes a warning that judgment and exile were drawing near, because the people had trusted in what was false.

For today: check where you place your security, whether in money, success, or the opinions of others. All of these fail. Rest in the God who made you and calls you his own.
exp.30:9:
This verse calls all the nations, even the most distant ones, to hear a message from God: the same God who scattered Israel will gather them again and take care of them. The word "nations" refers to peoples, and "the isles afar off" refers to faraway lands. The image of the shepherd who cares for his flock shows constant protection.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf to a people who suffered exile because of their sins. This chapter is part of what is called the "Book of Consolation," where God promises to restore his people with tenderness. God himself is presented as the Father of Israel. Some see here the return from Babylon; others also see a broader and future hope.

For today: if you feel that your life is scattered or broken, trust that God cares like a good shepherd. Tell him your situation in prayer, and take a step of obedience today, trusting that he knows how to gather what was lost.
exp.20:6:
This verse announces a very harsh judgment. God says that after the pestilence, the famine, and the war, he will hand over King Zedekiah, his servants, and the people who survive in Jerusalem into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon. The "edge of the sword" here simply means the sword itself, and the phrase about showing no pity means that the enemy will show no mercy.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah shortly before the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. King Zedekiah had asked for a favorable word, but God answered with a warning. This came after years of refusing his calls to repentance. Even so, the next verse offers a way out: surrender and live.

For today: when God warns us, it is wise to listen in time and not to trust in our own defenses. His truth may hurt, but it always leaves a door open to return to him.
exp.49:12:
Because of God's anger, the explanation says, Babylon will be left without inhabitants and completely destroyed. Anyone who passes by will be amazed and will whistle, that is, make a sound of mockery or horror, when they see all the wounds the punishment left behind. The word for the disasters that fell on the city means blows or calamities. Being laid waste means being torn down to ruin.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and mistreated Israel, whom God calls his own inheritance. Babylon had filled itself with pride and joy over its conquest. Now God announces that this empire will be judged for its wickedness. Scholars understand the fall of Babylon in different ways regarding when and how it was fulfilled, but the central message is clear: God holds it accountable.

For today: do not lose heart when injustice seems to win. God sees everything and will bring justice in his time. Meanwhile, avoid pride and do not rejoice in the misfortune of others.
exp.8:1:
He says that the prophet wishes he had, out in the wilderness, a lodging place of wayfaring men, that is, a simple shelter where travelers spend the night. He wants to go there and leave his people behind. The reason is that he sees them as adulterers, unfaithful to God and to one another, and as an assembly of treacherous men, people who betray and break what they have promised.

The speaker is Jeremiah, the prophet who suffers for his nation. In the verse before, he wished he could weep day and night for the dead of his people. His grief is mixed with weariness at so much lying and betrayal. Many understand that it also reflects the grief of God himself.

For today: when it hurts us to see injustice or unfaithfulness around us, let us not flee in bitterness. Let us bring that pain to God in prayer, and ask him to keep us sincere and faithful, even when others are not.
exp.16:19:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to the kings of Judah, to all the people, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem who pass through the city's gates. The verse's word "hear" means listen closely and pay attention.

Here the Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He sends him to stand at the gates, where all the people came and went, so that no one could say they did not hear. The message that follows is about keeping the Sabbath and not working on that day, as God had commanded their ancestors.

For today: God speaks clearly and wants his word to be heard. We can set aside a fixed time each day, or each week, to pause, read the Bible, and listen with humility, ready to obey what God shows us.
exp.35:27:
God tells Jeremiah to take another scroll and write down again all the words that were in the first one, the one King Jehoiakim burned. The word "write" here means that Baruch, the scribe, would put them down in writing again, as he had done before.

The Lord speaks to Jeremiah after the king burned the scroll containing messages of judgment. Jehoiakim was angered by the warning that Babylon would come, and he tried to silence it by destroying the document and seeking to arrest the messengers. But God hid them and ordered the writing to be made again. The passage shows that burning the message does not cancel it.

For today: God's truth does not depend on being accepted. If there is something in his Word that makes you uncomfortable, do not hide it or ignore it; instead, listen to it with humility and let it correct you in time.
exp.1:33:
God says that the blood of the poor and innocent is found on the edges of the people's clothing, that is, in plain sight of everyone. The edges of the garment are the hems. The word for the hole in the wall probably refers to a break-in, as a thief would make at night. God did not catch them hiding: the guilt was in full view. The Hebrew is difficult, and some translators understand it differently.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. Earlier, he rebuked them for forgetting him, something unthinkable, like a bride who forgets her dress. Now he accuses them of injustice and violence against the weak. And, moreover, they say: "I am innocent."

Today, let us ask God to show us whether our decisions harm others, especially the most vulnerable. Acknowledging sin with humility is better than justifying ourselves.
exp.16:12:
It says that the Lord is the hope of Israel, and that those who abandon him will be put to shame. "Those who turn away from me" refers to those who draw away from the Lord. "Shall be written in the earth" means that their names will soon be erased, like something written on the ground. "Fountain of living waters" is a spring of fresh, flowing water, and that spring is God himself. "Foolish" means senseless.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the middle of a people who trusted in riches and other supports. First he praises the sanctuary and God as hope, and then he warns about the consequences of leaving him. The shift to "from me" makes it seem that God himself is speaking, though some understand it as Jeremiah speaking. Right after this, the prophet asks to be healed, and the people mock him.

For today: when you feel dry inside, do not look first to other sources. Return to God with simple prayer and reading of his Word.
exp.21:0:
This verse says that God orders the prophet Jeremiah to go down to the palace of the king of Judah and announce there a message from Him. "Lord" is the name of God, and "go down" indicates that he was to go down from the temple or his place of ministry to the king's house. The words "said" and "speak" show that the message was not Jeremiah's own idea, but God's.

The one speaking is God, and the message is addressed to the king of Judah, his servants, and the people. We do not know with certainty which king is meant at the beginning, although the following verses suggest that the kingdom of David was in danger because of its injustice. God wants rulers to act with justice and to protect the weak.

For today: if you have authority, even if it is only in your home or at work, use it to protect and treat well those who have less power.
exp.43:1:
God speaks to the Jews who live in Egypt and reminds them of what they themselves saw: the destruction of Jerusalem and of the cities of Judah. Today those cities are a ruin, with no one living in them.

It is the Lord who speaks, through the prophet Jeremiah. This group of Jews had fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. Places such as Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph and Pathros were locations in Egypt. God reminds them of the past so that they do not repeat the same mistake: worshiping other gods. The verses that follow explain that this was the reason for the punishment.

For today: learn from past experiences, our own and those of others. If God has already shown us the consequences of turning away from him, it is wise not to go back to the same path. It is better to listen to his voice and return to him in humility.
exp.13:18:
This verse is a prayer full of pain. Questions are put to God: "Hast thou utterly rejected Judah? hath thy soul lothed Zion?" To reject utterly is to cast away, and to loathe is to despise. Then they say: "why hast thou smitten us, and there is no healing for us?" They looked for peace and well-being, and terror arrived instead. Healing is restoration, and trouble is dread.

Here the people of Judah speak, and Jeremiah is often the one who puts that prayer into words. There is drought, famine and the sword, and the religious leaders did not understand what was happening. The next verse shows that the people acknowledge their sin and appeal to God's covenant.

For today: when you suffer and feel that God is far away, you can bring him your questions with honesty. But pray also with humility, acknowledging your faults and trusting in his faithfulness.
exp.31:29:
This verse says that God's people, both Israel and Judah, lived doing what was evil from their youth as a nation. "Provoked me to anger" means making God angry, and "the work of their hands" refers above all to the idols they made.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem is under siege by the Babylonians and will soon fall. God explains that this judgment is not unjust: the people had been given over to idolatry for a long time, even offering incense to Baal on the rooftops. Yet in this same chapter God promises to restore his people.

For today: we should not minimize sin or let it become a habit. Today we can examine what things made by our own hands or desires have taken the place of God, and turn back to him with humility, trusting that his mercy is still open.
exp.33:11:
This verse is a brief introduction. It says that God spoke to the prophet Jeremiah. The phrase "the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah" means that the message did not come from Jeremiah himself, but from God.

Here the narrator speaks, and then God speaks. The princes and the people had set free their Hebrew servants, as the law required, but afterward they changed their minds and enslaved them again. God intervenes to point out that betrayal, recalling the covenant he made with their ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt.

For today: God sees whether we keep what we promised. Before going back on a commitment, especially one that protects another person's dignity, it is good to remember that God listens and expects faithfulness.
exp.30:14:
God says that a voice was heard in Ramah: a very bitter weeping. It is Rachel, weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are no longer there. "Weeping" means crying, and the phrase about them being lost or dead refers to those who were taken away and no longer present.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah to a people wounded by the fall of Judah and the exile. Rachel, mother of the tribes of Joseph and Benjamin, appears as a mother who weeps for her children carried far away. Ramah was in the territory of Benjamin. Matthew 2:18 quotes this text in connection with the grief over the children of Bethlehem. But in Jeremiah, the pain comes with a promise: the children will return.

Today, God does not ask you to hide your pain or hurry your mourning. Weep honestly before Him and do not isolate yourself. Trust that He sees your loss and can sustain you with hope.
exp.42:9:
God tells Jeremiah to say to the Jews that He will send for Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, whom He calls "my servant." This king will set his throne over the stones that Jeremiah hid, and he will spread his royal canopy, a kind of awning or royal covering, over them.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah at Tahpanhes, in Egypt, where many Jews had fled out of fear of Babylon, even though God had told them not to go. The stones hidden in the clay at the entrance of Pharaoh's palace were a visible sign: Egypt would not be a safe refuge. Calling Nebuchadnezzar "servant" does not mean he was righteous, but that God would use him to accomplish His purpose.

For today: do not look for security in places or people that God did not direct you to. Trusting and obeying God, even when it is frightening, is safer than any refuge we choose on our own.
exp.9:24:
Here the prophet asks God to pour out his anger on the nations that do not know him and do not call on his name. The reason is that those nations ate up and devoured Jacob, that is, the people of Israel, and made their home desolate.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of his people, before or during the Babylonian invasion. He has just acknowledged that a person does not control his own path, and he has asked for correction that is just, not destruction. Now he cries out for God to act against those who attacked Israel with cruelty. It is a prayer of pain, and this kind of cry also appears in some of the psalms.

For today: when you suffer injustice, you can bring your pain honestly to God and leave justice in his hands, instead of taking revenge yourself.
exp.34:13:
It says the commands of Jonadab, son of Rechab, were carried out faithfully. He ordered his sons not to drink wine, and to this day they have not drunk it, out of respect for their father. But God spoke to the people of Judah, rising early and speaking to them again and again, and they would not listen.

God speaks through Jeremiah. The Rechabites had kept their ancestor's custom for generations. God uses them as an example to show Judah its disobedience, even though He is far more worthy of being obeyed than any human father.

For today: if there are people who faithfully keep a family rule, how much more should we listen to and obey God! Today you can choose one instruction from the Bible that you have let slip by and put it into practice with consistency.
exp.6:21:
When God brought Israel out of Egypt, the first thing he asked of them was not to talk about burnt offerings and sacrifices. A "burnt offering" was an offering that was burned whole on the altar, and the animals offered are the "victims." God does not deny that sacrifices exist; he marks what mattered most from the beginning.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the temple at Jerusalem. The people carried out ceremonies, but they lived in disobedience. So God tells them, with irony, to add more offerings and eat the meat: without an obedient heart, these are of no use. Interpreters explain this statement in various ways, but almost all agree that God puts obedience first.

For today: it is not enough to attend church, give, or sing. Ask God to show you where you need to obey him from the heart, and start there.
exp.17:0:
God spoke to Jeremiah. The phrase about the word coming to him is an old way of saying the word came to Jeremiah. "Jehovah" is the name of God in this translation. The verse is only the introduction, and the teaching comes in the verses that follow.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is the prophet who receives the message. Jeremiah ministered in Judah in very difficult times, before the fall of Jerusalem.
