God sends him to the potter's house to teach him a lesson through something he could see. Later in the text, that image is used to speak about the way God deals with his people.

God still speaks today through his Word. We can ask him for an attentive heart and read the Bible calmly, willing to listen and obey, even in the simple things of each day.
exp.8:17:
It says the mourning women, women who were skilled at weeping at funerals, should hurry to raise a lament over the people. The verse uses the word "make haste," meaning to hurry up. "Eyelids" are the edges of the eyes, and "gush out" means the water flows out, that is, tears. It is a weeping that runs without stopping.

The LORD of hosts speaks through Jeremiah. He announces that Judah will be scattered and destroyed because of its unfaithfulness. He calls for the women who knew how to lament, because the pain will be so great that it will take a deep and shared weeping. Some believe Jeremiah himself joins in that grief, since he is known as the prophet who wept for his people.

Today we can learn that weeping in the face of sin and suffering is not weakness. If there is pain in your family or your community, do not hide it: bring it to God and tenderly accompany the one who suffers.
exp.24:17:
Jeremiah gave the cup of God's judgment to drink first to Jerusalem, to the cities of Judah, to their kings and to their princes. The result would be ruin: they would become a desolation, an astonishment, a hissing and a curse. The phrase "as it is this day" suggests that, at the time this was written, that ruin was already seen or regarded as fulfilled.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, sent by the LORD. The "cup" is an image of God's anger. Judah had rejected many warnings and practiced idolatry. That is why the judgment begins with God's own people and then reaches the other nations, as the following verses show.

For today: God takes seriously the faithfulness of those who say they believe Him. Ask God to show you what you should correct, and respond promptly, because His warning is also an invitation to return to Him.
exp.4:30:
It says that the prophets were announcing lies in God's name, and that the priests ruled "by their means," that is, relying on their authority or following their direction. What is most sad is that the people loved it that way. The phrase "in the end thereof" refers to what will happen when all of this comes to its final result. God asks: "And what will ye do in the end thereof?"

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at a time when Judah was living in injustice and idolatry. Earlier, God says that he must call to account this "terrible and vile thing." The problem was not only false leadership, but also a people who preferred comfortable messages. Some interpreters understand "by their means" in different ways, but the central idea is clear.

Today, it is good to examine what we hear in the light of the Bible. Let us seek not only words that comfort us, but the truth that brings us near to God.
exp.39:11:
This verse tells that the Jews who had fled to other countries came back to the land of Judah. They arrived where Gedaliah was, in Mizpah, and gathered a great deal of wine and summer fruit. The word "returned" in the verse is the one that means coming back, and "driven" means scattered, and "gathered" here means harvested.

It is part of the account of the prophet Jeremiah after the fall of Jerusalem. The Babylonians had left poor people in the land and had appointed Gedaliah as governor. When they heard this, many scattered Jews came back. The text does not say that God approved everything that happened afterward, but it shows a brief time of calm and provision.

Today we can see that God can give us moments of rest and abundance after difficult times. We should receive them with gratitude, but also with attention, because the account that follows shows that Gedaliah did not heed the warnings. Let us be thankful and wise.
exp.49:6:
The explanation says that Israel's enemies devoured everyone of the scattered people who came across them. They also justified themselves, saying: "We are not guilty, because they have sinned against the Lord." Some old words: the verb "found" in the verse is what the explanation calls "found" in the sense of come upon; "devoured" is used as a figure for destroying or taking advantage of; "the habitation of justice" is the place where what is just dwells; "the hope of their fathers" is the one in whom their ancestors put their trust.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, announcing the fall of Babylon. His people were like lost sheep, badly led by their shepherds. The enemies used Israel's sin as an excuse, but God does not leave them without blame: he will judge Babylon for its violence. Then he calls his people to return to him.

For today: to recognize our own failings without using other people's failings as an excuse to do harm. And if we have drifted away from God, we can return to him with humility, because he remains our hope.
exp.20:9:
God says he has decided to act against Jerusalem, not to bless it but to discipline it. The city will be handed over to the king of Babylon, who will set it on fire. To "set one's face against" someone means to confront them firmly. "Will burn it with fire" is the phrase "will burn it with fire."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by the Babylonians, and the people refused to change course. Earlier, God offered them a choice between life and death: surrendering meant living. Then he calls the house of David to do justice and rescue the oppressed. The punishment is presented as the result of their wickedness.

For today: God warns us out of love before the consequences arrive. If something in your life pulls you away from justice or truth, do not harden yourself with pride. Listen, acknowledge your mistake, and change today.
exp.35:3:
Jeremiah calls for Baruch, the son of Neriah. Baruch was a scribe, that is, someone who knew how to write. While Jeremiah speaks to him, Baruch writes on a scroll everything that God had said to the prophet. A scroll was a long sheet of papyrus or leather that was rolled up.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks during the time of King Jehoiakim, about twenty years after his ministry began. God wants his warnings to be put in writing, because Jeremiah was prevented from going to the temple. God's aim was not only to punish: he wanted the people to listen, to turn back, and to receive forgiveness.

For today: God takes care that his word is preserved and reaches people. We can value it by reading it carefully and, if something corrects us, responding with humility. We can also write down what we learn so that we do not forget it.
exp.11:0:
Jeremiah acknowledges that God is righteous, yet he dares to bring a complaint before Him. He wants to speak with God about matters of justice. His question is: why do the wicked prosper, and why do those who act treacherously live at ease? Here, bringing a complaint before God means presenting one's grievance to Him, and acting treacherously means with betrayal or a lack of faithfulness.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, in the midst of his ministry in Judah. He was suffering rejection and opposition for proclaiming God's message. So, with pain and sincerity, he lays his confusion before God. The verses that follow describe people who speak of God with their mouths, but keep Him far from their hearts.

For today: when injustice confuses you or hurts you, you do not have to stay silent. You can bring your questions to God with honesty and respect, as Jeremiah did, trusting that He is just even when you do not yet understand.
exp.1:36:
It says that Judah will go out from Egypt with their hands on their heads, a gesture that normally shows grief, shame, and defeat. The reason is that the Lord has rejected the things they trusted in, that is, whatever they were placing their security in. Therefore they will not prosper in them, meaning things will not go well for them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people claimed to be innocent and sought alliances with foreign powers, such as Assyria and Egypt, instead of turning back to God. He warns them that these alliances will leave them ashamed. Scholars understand the gesture of the hands on the head as a sign of mourning or humiliation.

Today we can ask ourselves where we are placing our security: money, work, influence, or our own righteousness. All of these can fail. The wisest course is to acknowledge our faults with humility and to trust God first.
exp.12:7:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah once again. "Then the word of the Lord came unto me" means "I received a message from God." It is a transition phrase: the action with the rotten belt ends, and now the explanation comes.

The speaker is Jeremiah, a prophet of Judah. God had told him to hide a linen belt by the Euphrates, and when he went back to get it, it was ruined. That object was a visible sign. The following verses explain that Judah, because of its pride and because it followed other gods, would be ruined just like that belt. Scholars debate exactly where that place was.

God does not stay silent: he explains what he is doing and why. Today we can approach his Word with humility, letting him correct us in time, before pride wears us down from the inside.
exp.14:20:
God promises Jeremiah: "I will deliver you from the power of wicked people, and I will rescue you from the hands of the violent." The words "deliver" and "rescue" are the verse's own wording here, and in this verse "rescue" means to free or save someone from danger.

The Lord speaks, and answers Jeremiah, who felt alone and rejected for preaching a message that no one wanted to hear. God had asked him to be faithful and not to be swept along by the pressure of the people. Now He assures him that, although they attack him, they will not overcome him, because God is with him.

For today: when being faithful to God brings opposition or loneliness, do not rely on your own strength. Pray, keep doing what is right, and remember that God walks with you and knows how to care for you, even when it is not always in the way you expect.
exp.18:6:
God says that he will make void, or bring to nothing, the plans and decisions of Judah and Jerusalem. They will fall by the sword before their enemies, and by the hands of those who seek their lives, meaning those who want to kill them. Their bodies will be left unburied, as food for the birds of the heaven and the beasts of the earth.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the valley of Hinnom, near Jerusalem. There the people had worshiped Baal and offered their children in the fire, something God never commanded. This message is a judgment for that idolatry and violence. It was fulfilled with the siege of Jerusalem by Babylon.

For today: the best plans without God do not hold up. Before deciding, ask yourself whether your path honors God, and return to Him with humility when you have gone astray.
exp.5:15:
God tells the people of Judah to stop, like someone who has come to a crossroads, and to look and ask about the old paths, that is, the ways of faithfulness God showed them from the beginning. There is the good way, and whoever walks in it finds rest for their souls, that is, peace and inner calm. But the people answer firmly: "We will not walk therein."

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, God denounced leaders who healed the wound of the people lightly, saying "peace, peace" when there was no peace. Later, God sends watchmen to warn them of the danger, and they also say: "We will not hearken." It is a call to return before judgment.

For today: before making an important decision, stop for a moment, pray, and seek God's guidance in the Bible, instead of following only what is fashionable or what comforts you for a little while.
exp.47:12:
It says that Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, its national god, because that god will not be able to save it. The comparison is with Israel, which was ashamed of Beth-el, the place where it had placed its trust. This probably refers to the golden calves that Jeroboam set up there, which failed to protect them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab had lived at ease and without disturbance, like wine that rests undisturbed in its jar. That comfort gave it a false sense of security and pride. God announces that judgment is coming, and with it will fall what Moab believed was firm: its military strength and its god.

For today: examine where you place your confidence. Money, comfort, success, or even a routine of religious habit can give us a security that does not hold up in a crisis. Rest in God, who remains faithful when everything else begins to waver.
exp.29:4:
This verse says that God himself announces a cry that is heard: a voice trembling with fear. It speaks of terror, not of peace. The words "voice of trembling" describe people terrified, and "we have heard" shows that the message is received by the whole people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Just before this, he promises that he will bring Israel and Judah back from captivity. But before that restoration there will come a very hard time, which the text calls "a time of trouble for Jacob." Interpreters apply it in different ways: to the fall of Babylon, to other historical events, or to a time still future. Even so, the passage ends with the promise that Jacob will be delivered.

Today it reminds us that pain does not have the final word. If you are going through fear or distress, you can hold on to the fact that God still guides your story and has a purpose of rescue.
exp.21:2:
God commands the king of Judah and his people to act with justice and righteousness. They must rescue the one suffering abuse from the hands of the one who mistreats him. They must not cheat or take what belongs to the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow, nor kill innocent people. The phrase "execute judgment" means deciding fairly, and "deliver" means to rescue or defend.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who receives the order to go to the royal palace. The message is for the king, his servants, and the people. God reminds them that ruling is not only about having power, but about caring for the most defenseless. He then promises blessing if they obey, and warns that the palace would fall into ruins if they do not.

Today we can ask ourselves who near us is at a disadvantage: an immigrant, a child without support, or a widow. We can help them, deal with them honestly, and defend their rights.
exp.45:0:
This verse opens a new section of the book. It says that God gave a message to Jeremiah, his prophet, and that this message was directed "against the Gentiles," that is, against the nations that were not Israel.

The Lord, the God of Israel, speaks through Jeremiah. Chapters 46 to 51 gather messages about several foreign peoples. The verses that follow begin with Egypt and recall its defeat by Babylon at Carchemish. In this way it is shown that God rules over all the nations, not only over Judah.

For today: although the powers of the world may seem immense, none of them is outside the care and authority of God. We can trust that he remains just and sovereign when the news frightens us.
exp.23:5:
God promises to care for a group of people with kindness. "I will set my eyes upon them for good" means that he will look on them with favor. He says he will bring them back to their land, will build them up and not tear them down. He will also plant them and not pluck them up, like someone tending a garden.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks for God. Judah was carried off captive to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans. God uses the image of two baskets of figs: the good figs represent those taken into exile, whom God did not abandon, and the bad figs represent those who stayed behind with King Zedekiah. In this way he gives them hope in the middle of exile.

For today: even when you go through a painful season, God may be working for your good. Trust that he has not forgotten you, and turn back to him with your whole heart.
exp.2:14:
God promises that he will give his people leaders who think and feel as he does. "Feed" here means to care for and nourish, the way a shepherd looks after his sheep. In this verse, that nourishment is knowledge and understanding for living well.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had been unfaithful to him, like a wife who leaves her husband, and had gone after other gods. Even so, God calls them to return and promises to restore them. This promise shows that his desire is to heal and guide his people, not only to rebuke them.

For today: value leaders who teach God's Word with truth and humility, and pray for them. And remember that God himself wants to nourish you with his wisdom if you return to him with sincerity.
exp.12:24:
God tells Jerusalem that this is what she has coming, the portion He has measured out for her. The word "lot" here means what falls to a person as their share, and "portion of your measures" is the fair part that she receives. The reason is clear: the people forgot God and put their trust in a lie, that is, in false gods and deceptive securities.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Judah and Jerusalem. Earlier He said they were so used to doing wrong that it was hard for them to change, just as a leopard does not change its spots. Then He announces that their shame will be exposed, and yet He asks with sorrow, "How long?"

For today: check where you place your trust. When we forget God, false securities fail us. Today, spend a few minutes in prayer and leave in His hands what worries you most.
exp.14:16:
Jeremiah says he did not join the mockers for their amusement, nor did he think himself superior for being a prophet. He preferred to remain alone, because God had filled him with bitterness, a deep indignation and sorrow. Being filled with anger here is the sense of what the verse describes.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the middle of a sincere complaint to God. He had received the word of the Lord with joy, but announcing it brought him mockery, rejection and loneliness. His pain was great, and he even dares to ask God whether He has left him without help. God answers by calling him back to Himself and to remaining firm.

For today: if obeying God brings you loneliness or mockery, do not hide your pain. Tell Him honestly, and ask Him for strength to remain faithful without being carried along by the crowd.
exp.29:22:
It says that God's judgment comes like a strong storm, already prepared, and it will fall on the heads of the wicked. The first quoted phrase in the source means that it is ready. The word for the wicked there refers to people who live without respect for God and practice evil. The word translated here as the verb to rest means that it will remain, and that it will fall with weight.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a passage of comfort for Israel. Before this, he promises to restore his people, give them a ruler of their own, and renew the relationship: "You shall be my people, and I will be your God." The judgment on the wicked shows that God does not ignore injustice. The next verse says that his anger will not cease until he has accomplished his purpose. Some see this fulfilled in part with the return from exile, and others also look toward the future.

Today we can trust that God sees evil and will bring about justice. So we do not have to live with resentment or take revenge. It also reminds us to examine our own hearts and to draw near to God with humility.
exp.15:6:
The explanation says that when judgment comes, people will no longer be able to observe the customs of comfort for the dead. Sharing a meal with mourners, and the cup that was offered to them to encourage them, even when they had lost a father or a mother, will be impossible. There will be so many deaths that not even this will be possible.

God speaks through Jeremiah before the fall of Jerusalem. He orders the prophet not to attend funerals or feasts, as a living sign for the people. God says he has taken away his peace because of Judah's persistent disobedience. It is a serious warning, not a mockery of grief.

Today, we can see how valuable it is to be present with someone who suffers. If you have the opportunity today to comfort someone with a meal, a visit, or a prayer, do it, and remember that true peace comes from God.
exp.50:49:
Says that the survivors of the sword, those who managed to escape the slaughter, must leave without delay. It also asks them to remember the Lord for a long time, and to keep Jerusalem in mind. The word "go away" conveys the sense of moving on, and "remember" means to keep something in mind.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that Babylon, which had destroyed Israel and defiled the temple, would be judged. The Israelites living in exile there receive an order: leave before the city falls. Scholars understand this as a literal call to leave Babylon, and some also see it as a message of faithfulness in a foreign land.

When God rescues us from danger, it is not wise to keep looking back or hesitating. We can act with obedience and keep the memory of God alive: set aside a moment each day to thank him and to recall what he has done for us.
exp.32:7:
This verse says that God promises to cleanse his people from all their wickedness. "Cleanse" means to purify, like washing away a stain. He also promises to pardon all their sins, both those of disobedience and those of turning away from God on purpose. God does not make light of what happened, but he offers to erase it completely.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah was in ruins and many had been taken captive, something the Bible connects with their sin. Even so, in the midst of that pain, God announces healing, peace, and restoration. Forgiveness is the foundation of that new stage: first he cleanses the heart, and then he rebuilds what was lost.

For today: if you feel that your mistakes are too big, bring them to God with sincerity. He offers cleansing and a fresh start. Confess what weighs on your conscience and receive his forgiveness without continuing to carry the guilt.
exp.12:2:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah a second time. The word "came" in the verse is how the message reached him, and "the word of the Lord" is God's message. Jeremiah had already obeyed the first instruction, to buy and wear the linen belt, and now he receives new instructions.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking, and God is the one giving the message. All of this is part of a sign God uses to teach Judah. The linen belt represents something close to God, and the text explains this later. Some scholars debate whether the journey to the Euphrates was real or a vision, and the text does not make this clear.

For today: God keeps guiding us step by step. Be faithful in obeying what He has already shown you, and stay alert and ready to listen for what He asks of you next.
exp.34:12:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to the people of Judah and of Jerusalem. He asks them a question that sounds like a rebuke: will they not learn the lesson and obey his words? In the phrase about "the men" and "the inhabitants," the sentence simply refers to the men of Judah and the people living in Jerusalem, and the name of the city is Jerusalem.

The Lord, the God of Israel, speaks through Jeremiah. The Rechabites, a family that fled to Jerusalem because of the Babylonian invasion, had faithfully kept the command of their ancestor Jonadab not to drink wine. God uses their example to show that Judah, by contrast, did not listen to God, even though he spoke to them again and again.

Today we might ask ourselves: do I obey God with the same constancy with which I respect the people I esteem? A good practice is to read the Bible every day and choose one specific thing God asks of you, so you can put it into practice that same week.
exp.5:12:
It says that everyone in Jerusalem, from the lowest to the highest, was ruled by greed, that is, by the desire to gain more at any cost. And the religious leaders, the prophet and the priest, instead of guiding the people, were deceiving them. The word "deceivers" speaks of falsehood and trickery.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the invasion of Babylon. God warns that judgment is coming because corruption had reached everyone. Most serious of all, those who should have taught the truth twisted it and said that all was well, as the next verse shows: "Peace, peace; when there is no peace."

Today it invites us to examine our hearts: do we seek to gain at any cost? It also encourages us to prefer the truth even when it is uncomfortable, and not to stay silent or disguise what is wrong, whether at work, in the family, or in the church.
exp.3:28:
At the sound of the horsemen and archers approaching, the whole population flees the city, the explanation says. They hide in the thickets (very dense woodland) and climb up onto the rocky crags. The cities are left forsaken, meaning abandoned, with no one living in them at all.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on Judah for its rebellion. The nearby verses describe an invading army from the north. The text does not name it here, and many connect it with Babylon. God says he will not change his mind about what he has announced, but also that he will not bring a complete end, that is, total destruction.

For today: we should not trust in appearances or in false securities. It is better to turn back to God sincerely while there is still time, since his warning comes from his desire to restore.
exp.49:3:
It says that when Babylon falls, God's people will come back together: Israel and Judah, who had been divided. They will not return in pride, but weeping, and they will seek the Lord, their God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message against Babylon. He announces that this empire will be defeated by a people from the north, and that its idols will be put to shame. Scholars understand in different ways how much of this was fulfilled with the return from exile, and how much points to a future time. What is clear is that God promises to restore his people.

For today: when you have moved away from God, sincere weeping is not the end but a good beginning. Come back to seek him with humility, and try to do it together with other believers, not alone.
exp.21:13:
He says this man thinks: "I will build myself a large house with spacious and elegant rooms." He makes windows for it, lines it with cedar wood, and paints it a bright red. "Spacious and elegant rooms" are tall, showy halls; "vermilion" is a very striking red, a sign of luxury.

Jehovah speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses the king of Judah who followed Josiah, probably Jehoiakim, although the text of this passage does not say so in full. He rebukes him because he was building his palace with other people's labor, without paying the workers. The problem is not the house, but the injustice with which he was building it.

For today: ask yourself whether what you achieve or build rests on justice. Pay with honesty, treat well those who work for you, and do not seek your own comfort at the expense of others. For God, knowing him is shown in how we treat the needy.
exp.7:16:
God says he will send venomous snakes against his people, and that no charm will be able to stop them. Charms were words or practices used to calm snakes. The verse's word for these snakes is one that the explanation says was the name of a feared serpent, though it is not known for certain which species is meant. The verse is figurative language for a punishment that cannot be escaped.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had fallen into idolatry and did not want to return to God. Before this verse, the arrival of an enemy army from the north is described. Afterward, the prophet shows his deep sorrow for his people.

For today: we cannot deceive ourselves with a false peace while we remain far from God. He calls us to return in time, with humility and repentance, because his heart also suffers for us.
exp.7:3:
God tells Jeremiah to ask the people two very simple questions. If someone falls, does he not get up? If someone turns away from the road, does he not come back to it? The word "turn back" means "come back," and "turn away" means to stray from the right path. The obvious answer is yes; that is the natural thing to do.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Just before this, the text announces judgment on a people who served the stars and false gods. With these questions, God shows how strange Judah's attitude is: falling and straying are human, but refusing to come back is not. The verses that follow say that even so, they would not repent.

For today: if you have fallen or moved away from God, do not stay there. He invites you to come back. Acknowledge your mistake, ask yourself "what have I done?" and today take a step back toward Him.
exp.48:0:
God asks the Ammonites whether Israel had no sons and no heir. In other words, the land of Gad had rightful owners. Even so, their king seized that land, and the Ammonites stayed in its cities. An inheritance is land received as a family's portion. Some translations read Milcom, the god of Ammon, instead of "king."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. It is a message against Ammon, Israel's neighbor east of the Jordan. The Ammonites took over territory belonging to the tribe of Gad, probably when part of Israel was taken into exile, though the text does not give all the details. God defends what he gave to his people and announces judgment.

For today: God sees injustice, even when someone takes advantage of another person's weakness. We can trust his justice and check that we are not holding on to what does not belong to us.
exp.3:11:
It says that an even stronger wind is coming than the one before, and that God himself is sending it. "Vehement" means violent, very intense. The phrase about God speaking judgments means that God will pronounce sentence against them for their wickedness. The phrase "shall come unto me" can be understood as "comes from my part," since the Hebrew phrase has several possible translations.

The one speaking is God, in the middle of the words of the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, Jeremiah complains that the people expected peace and received a threat. This dry desert wind represents the invasion that was drawing near. It was not meant to winnow the wheat, but to destroy. God warns that the punishment would be worse, because the people did not want to leave their sin.

For today: let us not confuse God's patience with approval. If He points out something to us in our conscience, it is wise to repent soon, before the consequences grow.
exp.24:26:
God commands Jeremiah to tell the nations to drink until they are drunk, vomit, and fall, never to rise again. It is an image: the cup stands for God's judgment, and the sword is the war that He allows. "Drink" is not an invitation to sin, but to swallow the consequence to the very end.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at a time when Babylon posed a threat. Earlier, God had shown this cup of His anger to Judah and Jerusalem, and then to many nations. God judges everyone, not only His own people. Some details, such as the exact identity of the name in this passage, are understood in several ways; many see it as a coded name for Babylon.

For today: God takes sin seriously, beginning with His own people. Instead of justifying ourselves, we can ask Him to correct us and turn back to Him with humility.
exp.51:31:
This verse says that Evil-merodach, king of Babylon, treated Jehoiachin, the king of Judah who was in prison, well. He spoke to him kindly and gave him a place of honor, higher than that of the other kings who were also living in exile there. "Kindly" means with good and gentle words. "Throne" here means a seat of honor, a place of importance.

This is the end of the book of Jeremiah. It is not God or the prophet who speaks here, but the account reports a historical event. Jehoiachin had been a captive for thirty-seven years. After so long, a new king brought him out of prison. Many understand this as a sign that God had not forgotten his people, although the text gives no further explanation.

For today: even in long and dark times, God can open an unexpected door. We keep waiting on Him, without losing hope.
exp.22:9:
It says the land of Judah is full of adulterers, both literally and, probably, in the sense of unfaithfulness to God. Because of a curse (an "oath"), the land is dried up and desolate. The pastures of the wilderness have withered. Their "course" means the direction of their lives, which is evil, and their "force," or power, is not used with justice.

Jeremiah speaks, grieved by the false prophets. God makes him feel a deep anguish, like someone staggering from wine. The religious leaders were deceiving the people and living in wickedness. Some think the "oath" refers to curses brought on by sin or to false oaths; the text allows several readings.

For today: examine how you use your influence, whether at home, at work, or in church. Ask God that your life be faithful and that your strength be used to do good and to speak the truth.
exp.12:12:
God says he will fill all the inhabitants of the land with a staggering confusion: the kings who sit on David's throne, the priests, the prophets, and all the people of Jerusalem. This is not about drunkenness from wine, but a picture of God's judgment: they will be confused, stumbling, unable to defend themselves.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, with the image of the linen belt, God had reminded them that he had bound his people to himself so that they would honor him, but they would not listen. The image of the wineskin full of wine announces that this judgment will reach everyone, without exception, not even the leaders.

For today: let us not trust in our position or our religion; let us listen to God with humility and obey while there is still time.
exp.37:5:
The verse says that they took Jeremiah and put him into the cistern-pit of Malchiah, son of Hammelech, which was in the court of the guard. They let Jeremiah down with ropes. There was no water in it, only mud, and Jeremiah sank into the mud.

The officials of the king were angry because Jeremiah was prophesying that Jerusalem would fall to Babylon. They said his words discouraged the soldiers and the people. King Zedekiah, weak and fearful, gave them permission to do with him as they wished. Jeremiah suffered for speaking what God had commanded him.

For today: speaking the truth with love can bring misunderstanding or rejection. Even so, God does not abandon those who are faithful to him; in the next verse he sends unexpected help through Ebed-melech. Today we can stand firm and trust God.
exp.47:38:
They will cry out in grief, saying, "How broken Moab is! How it has turned its back in shame!" So Moab will become an object of mockery and horror to all the nations around it.

The explanation says that Moab has fallen completely, and that everyone should weep aloud. Crying out is a loud wail of pain. "Broken" means shattered to pieces. Turning one's back, or fleeing defeated, is what the phrase about turning the back means. The neighboring nations see Moab as a reason for mockery and amazement.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a prophecy against Moab. Earlier, the text mentions Moab's pride and its trust in itself. God says he has broken Moab like a vessel that is not pleasing. The gestures of mourning, such as shaving the head and wearing sackcloth, show deep grief. The verses that follow announce the invasion.

For today: do not trust in your success or your pride, because they can fall. Place your security in God, and treat with humility those who suffer, without mocking them.
exp.38:8:
This verse tells that Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, carried into Babylon those who were left in Jerusalem. He also took those who had gone over to the Chaldeans. The word "carried away" is simply the verse's way of saying "took them far away," and "fell to him" means they had joined themselves to them.

Here the narrator of the book is recounting the fall of Jerusalem, around 586 B.C. For years, Jeremiah had warned that this judgment would come because the people had disobeyed God. The verses before this one show the ruin of the city and the capture of King Zedekiah. Then a contrast appears: the poorest people were left behind and received land.

For today: God is serious when he warns, but he also cares for the humble. Listen to his voice in time, before the consequences arrive.
exp.1:18:
The verse says that the consequences of doing wrong will fall on the very people who did it. "Your turning away" means turning away from God. "Will condemn you" means that this very path will show that you were wrong. God invites you to recognize how evil and bitter it is to leave Him, and that there was no longer any fear of Him in you, that is, reverence and awe.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people had left God to seek help from Egypt and Assyria, neighboring powers, and to follow other gods. God reminds them that He had cared for them, and that their choices were hurting them.

For today: when you feel yourself drifting away from God, stop and examine what you are asking to keep you safe. Return to Him sincerely, because far from Him, what seems like freedom ends in bitterness.
exp.3:24:
Jeremiah says that he looked and there was no human being, and that even the birds of the heavens had fled. It is a picture of complete desolation: the land was left without people and without life. The phrase "no man was seen" means that no one could be seen.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, describing in a vision the judgment that would come upon Judah for its idolatry and its rebellion against God. The images recall creation undone: an empty earth, skies without light, mountains trembling. Many understand that it foretells the invasion from the north. Even so, God makes clear in verse 27 that he will not finish off his people completely.

For today: God is patient, but he takes sin seriously. If something in your life is drifting away from him, do not ignore it; return to him soon, because his mercy remains open to anyone who repents.
exp.48:9:
God says he will leave Esau, that is, Edom, without protection. The word that means stripping him bare says that he will be left exposed. The places where he used to hide will no longer serve him. Esau's descendants are the ones who would have carried on his line. His brothers and neighbors, the nearby peoples, will also fall, and Edom will cease to exist as a nation.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message of judgment against Edom. This people descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob, and lived in lands that were hard to reach, where they felt safe. Earlier, God compares this judgment to grape harvesters and thieves, who leave something behind; here nothing will be left. Even so, God cares for the fatherless and the widows.

For today: do not put your security in your resources, your position, or the places you hide in. Trust in God, who sees everything and protects the weak.
exp.47:27:
He tells the people of Moab to leave their cities, which are no longer safe, and to seek shelter in the rocks and the cliffs. He asks them to be like the dove that makes its nest at the mouth of a cave, hidden and safe.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. Moab was filled with pride and rose up against God, and it also mocked Israel. Because of this, judgment is coming upon them. Some understand that the invasion would be so severe that only fleeing to hidden places would offer any hope. The exact historical details of how this was fulfilled are not entirely clear.

For today: pride makes us feel strong, but humility leads us to seek refuge in God. Today you can bring to God in prayer whatever you trust in most for yourself.
exp.9:14:
They say the idols are worth nothing. "Vanity" means something empty, without value or power. "Work of mockeries" means they are a work fit for ridicule, something deceptive. "Time of their visitation" is the moment when God steps in to judge. Then those idols will vanish, because they have no life or strength to save.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah, who were surrounded by nations that worshiped images made by craftsmen. Earlier, the text shows the great power of God over the rain, the clouds, and the wind. It compares this with cast idols, which have no breath. He wants the people not to be impressed by those religions and to trust only in the true God.

Today we do not usually carve statues, but we can still put our trust in things that cannot sustain life: money, success, or the opinions of others. Today you can ask yourself where your security rests, and turn your trust back to the God who truly has power and endures.
exp.28:9:
God has not forgotten his exiled people, says this passage. When seventy years are complete in Babylon, he will "visit" them, meaning he will act on their behalf. He will fulfill his "good word," his promise to restore them, and bring them back to Jerusalem. The phrase about bringing them back refers to returning them to their homeland, and "to this place" refers to Jerusalem.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a letter addressed to those taken into exile in Babylon. False prophets were telling them the exile would be short and filling them with hopes of a quick return. God corrects that lie: the exile would be long, but it would have an end. Scholars debate whether the seventy years is an exact figure or an approximate one.

For today: God sometimes allows long seasons of waiting, but he does not abandon us. Instead of clinging to easy promises, trust his true word, pray with patience, and keep serving him where you are while you wait.
exp.31:11:
He says that Jeremiah handed Baruch the deed of purchase for the field. He did this in the sight of his cousin Hanameel, of the witnesses who had signed, and of the Jews present in the courtyard of the prison. "Deed of purchase" means the written document or contract of sale. "Signed" means the witnesses had put their names to it.

Jeremiah speaks while he is imprisoned in Jerusalem, as the army of Babylon surrounds the city. God asked him to buy a field in Anathoth, even though the land seemed lost. It was a sign that, after the judgment, the people would return to their land. Baruch, his secretary, would keep the documents with care.

For today: God invites us to trust his promises even when the situation looks dark. We can take concrete steps of faith, with order and honesty, waiting for God to fulfill what he has said.
exp.6:7:
It says that the people trust in false words that are of no use. To trust in something means to place one's security in it, and the verse's point is that these words bring no benefit at all. In other words, they felt safe because of things that were not true.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people kept repeating that the temple would protect them, while they went on stealing, murdering, swearing falsely, and worshiping Baal. God asks them to change their way of living, to care for the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, and to return to Him.

For today: let us not put our trust in religious phrases or in attending church as if that alone guaranteed us anything. Let us examine whether our lives reflect what we say we believe, and ask God to correct us with sincerity.
exp.47:30:
The explanation says that the one speaking is filled with grief for Moab. To howl, to cry out, and to lament are ways of weeping loudly, as was done in times of mourning. Kir-heres was a city of Moab, perhaps the same as Kir of Moab; this is not known with complete certainty. The "men of Kir-heres" are its inhabitants.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab had been very proud and trusted in its lies, and for that reason judgment comes. Even so, the text shows God (or the prophet speaking in his name) feeling sorrow over the destruction that is coming. The judgment is just, but it is not presented with joy.

For today: when we see someone fall because of their pride or their mistakes, we should not celebrate. We can recognize what is just and, at the same time, feel compassion and pray for that person.
exp.50:43:
God says he will punish Bel, the chief idol of Babylon. "I will punish" means coming to call someone to account. The phrase about bringing out of his mouth what he has swallowed refers to the riches and peoples that Babylon had seized as plunder. In addition, the nations will no longer come to pay him honor, and his wall, the symbol of his security, will fall.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had conquered Judah and looted the temple. Bel (another name for Marduk) was its protecting god. God shows that this idol cannot defend anyone and that he rules over empires. Immediately he calls his people to leave that place.

For today: the things we place our security in, such as money, power, or reputation, can fall. Ask yourself what you truly trust in, and place your trust again in the God who endures and cares for his own.
exp.46:6:
This verse is the answer to a question. The prophet had asked the sword of the Lord to be still, and now he is given a reply: how can it be quiet, when God himself has given it a charge against Ashkelon and the sea shore? The phrase "the sea shore" refers to the edge of the sea. "It" refers to the sword, and "there hath he appointed it" means that God assigned it that place.

Jeremiah speaks of God's judgment on the Philistines, who lived in coastal cities such as Gaza and Ashkelon. The text does not say precisely which army carried this out, and scholars have interpreted it in different ways. What is clear is that the prophet presents the punishment as something God directs, not as a simple accident of war.

For today: we can trust that God governs justice with purpose and timing. When we see violence or injustice that seems never to end, let us pray honestly, yet rest in the knowledge that God remains in control.
exp.39:1:
Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, took Jeremiah and spoke to him. He acknowledged that the Lord, the God of Jeremiah, had announced the punishment that was now falling on Jerusalem. The phrase "so he took" means "then he took," and the words "he said to him" are simply "he told him." The phrase "this place" refers to Jerusalem and Judah.

The speaker is a foreign officer. Jeremiah had been bound among the captives who were being taken to Babylon, and he was set free at Ramah. For a long time Jeremiah had warned that the people would be punished for their disobedience. We do not know how Nebuzaradan knew that prophecy; the text does not explain it.

For today: God's truth is sometimes recognized where we least expect it, and when trouble comes, people do not always listen to us. If God speaks to us through his Word, it is better to respond in time with humility, rather than waiting to see the consequences.
exp.30:6:
God invites his people to celebrate with joy and to shout for gladness. "The chief of the nations" means the foremost of the nations, and "sing with gladness" means to sing with strength. They are to announce and praise, and also to pray: "O Lord, save thy people, the remnant of Israel." The remnant are those who survived and were left behind.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had suffered exile and destruction because of their disobedience. In this chapter God promises to restore them, bring them back, and comfort them. This joy is announced before the full fulfillment is seen; it is a hope based on God's promise.

For today: even in difficult times, we can praise God in advance, trusting that he keeps what he promises. As you pray for what you need, add gratitude and song, because God hears and rescues his own.
exp.33:19:
God says that he will hand over those who broke their covenant to their enemies, the people who want to kill them. Their corpses will be left unburied and will become food for the birds and the animals. "Seek their life" means that they are looking to take away their lives.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem. The people had set free their Hebrew servants, as the law commanded, but then they enslaved them again. They had sealed that agreement with an ancient rite: passing between the parts of a calf that had been cut in two. By breaking the promise, they took on the curse that this rite symbolized.

For today: God takes our promises seriously, especially those made before him. Before promising something, let us think carefully; and if we have already promised, let us keep our word with integrity and justice toward others.
exp.31:20:
This verse reminds us that God brought his people out of Egypt in a powerful way. "Signs and wonders" were miracles that showed his power. "Strong hand and outstretched arm" is a way of saying that God acted with great strength on Israel's behalf. "Great terror" speaks of the fear the Egyptians felt when they saw what God was doing.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, praying to God. Jerusalem was surrounded by the Babylonians, and the prophet had just bought a piece of land at God's command. Before receiving an answer, Jeremiah goes over the history: God had rescued and cared for his people, but the people did not obey him.

For today: when you find yourself in a situation with no way out, remember what God has already done for you and for his people. Before asking him for help, thank him for his past faithfulness. That strengthens trust and helps you obey him with more humility.
exp.30:19:
God asks whether Ephraim is not his precious son, his dear child. He says that every time he speaks of him, he remembers him with affection. Because of this, his heart (his inmost feelings, the deepest part of his being) is moved, and he promises to have mercy on him.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Ephraim represents the northern kingdom, Israel, which was in exile. Shortly before, the people had wept with regret, acknowledging their rebellion and their shame. God responds with tenderness, not rejection. Then he invites them to come home by the way they had traveled.

For today: when you feel ashamed of your mistakes, do not run from God. Come close to him with sincerity, because he does not look at you only as someone who failed, but as a beloved child whom he wants to forgive and restore.
exp.48:30:
God calls an army to rise up and attack a peaceful people who live without worry and without defenses. "Get you up" means advance against them. The "gates and bars" are the locks on their doors, and "dwell alone" suggests they lived apart, trusting in their remoteness.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in his message against Kedar and Hazor, peoples of the desert of Arabia. According to the text, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, would attack them. Their false sense of security would not save them. Scholars cannot determine with certainty all the historical details of these places.

For today: feeling secure is not the same as being safe. If we trust only in our calm, our wealth, or our isolation, we can neglect what matters most. Let us put our trust in God, who is a firm refuge, and live with humility, attentive to his voice.
exp.45:15:
He made many stumble, and they fell one upon another. And they said, "Get up, and let us go back to our own people and to the land of our birth, away from the enemy's sword."

The explanation says there were so many fallen soldiers that they stumbled over one another. The ones still standing encouraged each other to go home, to their own people and their native land, away from the enemy's sword. The word "he made many" refers to God, who allowed many to fall. The "companion" is a fellow soldier in arms, and the "victorious sword" is the army that is winning.

Jeremiah announces a prophecy from God about Egypt, defeated by Babylon (see verse 2). The people speaking in this verse appear to be foreign soldiers serving in the Egyptian army, either mercenaries or allies. They see that everything is lost and want to flee home. Some interpreters understand that "he made many" refers to God, and others to the disorder of the army itself. The text attributes it to the fact that the Lord "pushed him down," that is, He thrust him down.

For today: no human force, however great it may seem, can stand against God. Trust in Him more than in your own strength, your money, or your alliances, and return to Him before everything falls apart.
exp.12:9:
God says this people is evil because they refuse to listen to his words, follow the wishes of their own stubborn heart, and go after other gods, to serve them and bow down before them. So they will be like this waistband: good for nothing.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He had asked him to take a linen waistband, hide it by the Euphrates River, and later it rotted there. Through that sign he shows that Judah, which should have clung to God like a waistband to the waist, was ruined by its pride and disobedience.

For today: God wants us close to him, not just out of habit. If we stop listening to his Word and follow only what our heart dictates, we wear ourselves down from the inside. Today you can set aside a few minutes to read the Bible and obey one concrete thing.
exp.5:11:
This verse announces a harsh judgment. The houses, the fields, and even the wives of the inhabitants will pass into the hands of others.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people had rejected his word, regarded it as shameful, and did not want to hear it. Moreover, from the least to the greatest, everyone was seeking gain, and the leaders deceived with a false peace. Many understand this as a warning that was fulfilled with the Babylonian invasion.

For today: let us not harden our hearts when God corrects us. If his word makes us uncomfortable, it is better to listen and change in time, rather than soothing our conscience with false calm.
exp.32:21:
It says that God will make the descendants of David, his servant, and the Levites who serve him grow until they are as countless as the stars of the sky and the sand of the sea. The phrase about the stars is explained here as referring to the host of heaven, meaning the stars themselves.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah, who is in prison, while Jerusalem falls to Babylon. The people feel that God has rejected the two chosen families: the royal family and the priestly family. God answers with a firm promise, comparing his covenant to the order of day and night. Christians often see here a announcement fulfilled in Christ, although there are different ways of understanding it.

For today: when your situation seems lost, remember that God is faithful to his promises even when you cannot see how. Trust his word and keep serving him with hope.
exp.30:32:
God makes a promise of a new covenant with Israel. Instead of a law written on stone, he says he will put it "in their inward parts," that is, in the deepest part of their being, and write it "in their hearts." The phrase "I will write it" is the same promise restated. At the end he repeats the old promise: "I will be their God, and they shall be my people."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in a time of crisis, when Judah was facing judgment for breaking the earlier covenant made at Sinai. In the middle of that punishment, God announces hope: a new covenant based on forgiveness and on a personal knowledge of God. The New Testament takes up this promise again, especially in Hebrews 8.

For today: it is not enough to keep rules on the outside. Ask God to transform your heart, and spend time in his Word so that he shapes you from within.
exp.50:0:
God says he himself will stir up a destroying wind against Babylon and against the people who live in the middle of those who rise up against him. The phrase "rise up against me" shows that Babylon had set itself against God. Some scholars note that in the original the expression "those who rise up against me" could be a code name for Chaldea, but not all agree. The wind is an image of judgment that sweeps everything away.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been used by God to discipline Judah, but it was also proud and cruel toward the nations. So God announces that now Babylon itself will receive justice. The verses that follow speak of winnowers, people who shake and empty the land, the way wheat is cleaned.

For today: no human power or pride lasts forever. We can trust that God sees injustice and has the last word. In the meantime, let us ask him for humility so that we do not rise up against him.
exp.30:1:
This verse says that God speaks of a people who survived the destruction and found his favor in the middle of the wilderness. "Found grace" means they received kindness they did not deserve. Where the verse uses "sword," it refers to war and violence. And "to cause him to rest" means giving Israel rest and peace.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter brings hope to a people struck by judgment and exile. Some understand that the "wilderness" recalls the departure from Egypt; others, that it refers to the exile. Perhaps it includes both ideas. In any case, God promises to be their God again and to restore them with everlasting love.

Even in your dry seasons or after deep wounds, God can meet you with his grace. If today you feel worn out, do not strain to appear strong: draw near to him and receive his rest.
exp.42:4:
This verse tells how Johanan and all the army commanders gathered the survivors of Judah. These were people who had been scattered among other nations and had come back to live in their land. The military leaders are the men in charge of the armed forces. The word "driven" means forced out or scattered.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. God, through Jeremiah, had told them to stay in Judah and not to fear Babylon. But Johanan and the others accused Jeremiah and Baruch of lying, and they did not obey. So they took everyone, including the prophet, and set off toward Egypt.

For today: fear can lead us to disobey God even when He has already shown us the way. Before deciding something under pressure, it is wise to pray, search the Bible, and listen to wise counsel, rather than choosing what seems safest.
exp.48:26:
God announces that he will set fire to the wall of Damascus, and that this fire will destroy the palaces, or fortified houses, of Ben-hadad. The wall is the barrier that protected the city. Ben-hadad was a name used by several kings of Syria, so here it stands for his whole dynasty and its power.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, within a message against several neighboring nations. Damascus, the capital of Syria, appears as a city full of fear and defeat. The verses that follow mention Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, and many understand that he would be the instrument of this judgment, although the text gives no further details about how it happened.

For today: no human stronghold, no wealth or power, is safe before God. We can examine where we place our trust and seek refuge in him, who remains when everything else falls.
exp.26:15:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to the priests and to all the people. He warns them not to listen to the prophets who promise: "Soon the vessels of the Lord's house will be brought back from Babylon." God says that is a lie.

Jeremiah speaks in Jerusalem, shortly after Babylon carried away part of the temple's articles and some of the leaders. Many wanted to hear that everything would be set right quickly. But God commanded them to accept Babylon's rule for a time, so that lives and the city could be saved.

Today we can learn not to believe something just because it sounds pleasant. Before accepting a spiritual message, it is wise to compare it with the Bible, pray with humility, and ask whether it calls us to obey God, even when the truth is hard.
exp.24:8:
God says that he is going to send and gather all the peoples from the north, along with Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, whom he calls his servant. They will come against Judah, against its inhabitants, and against the surrounding nations. The destruction will be complete: the land will be left as an object of mockery, a thing that people stare at in astonishment and whistle at in amazement, and as ruins that remain desolate forever.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. For years he had called the people to turn away from their evil ways and give up their idols, but they would not listen. That is why judgment is coming. Calling Nebuchadnezzar God's servant does not mean that he was righteous; it means that God was using his power to carry out God's purpose.

For today: God speaks with patience and does not stay silent about what harms us. If you feel today that he is calling you to correct something, do not put it off. Listening in time is a sign of humility and spares you greater pain.
exp.32:1:
It says that the one speaking is the LORD, the God who made it and formed "it," that is, the city or the land that the context is talking about, and that he did this in order to establish it, that is, to make it firm and secure. It ends with a statement of identity: the LORD is his name. Old wording: "saith" means "said," and "establish" means "make it stable."

Jeremiah is held prisoner in the courtyard of the guard, while Jerusalem faces the siege of Babylon. The houses are being torn down, and the people feel that everything is being lost. God speaks to the prophet a second time and presents himself as Creator and Lord of history. Some understand that "it" refers to Jerusalem; others, to the land in general. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when your situation seems to be falling apart, remember who God is. Before asking him for something, pause to recognize that he made, sustains, and can restore. That brings calm to pray with confidence, as he invites in the following verse.
exp.33:2:
He says that King Zedekiah will not be able to flee from the Babylonians. He will be taken captive and handed over to the king of Babylon. He will see him face to face, and speak with him face to face (that is, directly and personally), and he will end up carried off to Babylon. "Captured" is the meaning of the word "taken" here.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon was already attacking Jerusalem and other cities of Judah. God tells Jeremiah to warn the king that the city would fall. Zedekiah had earlier ignored the prophet's warnings. The following verse adds a note of mercy: he would not die by the sword, but would die in peace and with honor. Other passages in the Bible describe a harsher end for Zedekiah, and scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: God speaks the truth even when it hurts, and his warnings aim to get us to respond in time. Today we can ask ourselves what advice we have been avoiding hearing, and respond with humility and obedience, trusting in his mercy.
exp.33:7:
This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to proclaim liberty to them. The covenant consisted of proclaiming liberty, that is, publicly announcing that the Hebrew slaves would be set free. A covenant means an agreement or pact, and the explanation of the old spelling of the word "was" is not needed here.

The army of Babylon was attacking Jerusalem and the few strong cities that remained in Judah. Jeremiah, the prophet, spoke on behalf of God to the king. The verses that follow say that the leaders and the people obeyed and freed their servants. Historians and commentators do not agree on the exact reasons, but the danger of the siege probably weighed heavily.

For today: doing what is right should not depend only on crises. We can ask whether there is some injustice that God is calling us to correct, and do it steadily, not only when we are afraid or under pressure.
exp.11:12:
The passage says that the people worked hard and sowed wheat, but reaped thorns. They had the land that God gave them, but it did them no good. The word "reap" here means to harvest what has been sown, and "inheritance" is the land received as a family's portion. In the end, they will be ashamed of what they produced, because of God's burning anger.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, describing the Lord's judgment on Judah for turning away from Him. The land was left desolate, and no one took it seriously. Even so, the verses that follow show that God does not abandon them completely: He promises to have mercy and to bring them back to their land.

For today: whatever we do without God, however much effort it takes, can end in emptiness. Before you keep running ahead, ask yourself whether your plans are placed before Him. And if you have wandered away, remember that His mercy remains open for the one who returns.
exp.28:30:
God sends a message to all the exiles in Babylon. "Captivity" means the group of people taken away from their land. God speaks about Shemaiah, from the family or town of Nehelam, and says that this man prophesied to them without God having sent him. In this way he caused them to trust in a lie.

Jeremiah had written to the exiles, telling them to settle down in Babylon and wait there for many years. Shemaiah, on the other hand, sent letters from Babylon to Jerusalem against Jeremiah, criticizing that message. When Zephaniah read the letter to Jeremiah, God answered and denounced Shemaiah as a false prophet.

Today we can learn not to believe something just because it sounds encouraging or comes from someone with authority. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible and pray with humility. God's truth can be difficult, but it sustains better than a comfortable lie.
exp.7:12:
God says he will completely put an end to his people. The phrase that means "I will gather them all together, as one gathers the whole harvest" describes destroying them all at once. He uses the image of a vine with no grapes, a fig tree with no figs, and leaves that wither and fall: signs of a dry field with no fruit. The words that say "what I have given them will pass away from them" mean that they will lose the blessings God had given them.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah were living in sin, and their leaders kept saying "peace, peace" to calm the people, even though there was no true peace. They felt no shame for their wrongdoing. Some scholars see here a warning of the judgment that would come upon Judah.

For today: God looks for real fruit, not just appearance. If something in your life is wrong, do not cover it with pretty words. Acknowledge it with humility, ask God for forgiveness, and let yourself be corrected before the damage grows.
exp.34:15:
The explanation says that the descendants of Jonadab, son of Rechab, did keep their father's command firmly, which was not to drink wine. By contrast, the people of Judah did not listen to God. The phrase "have performed" in the verse means they kept the command and carried it out without changing it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. God told Jeremiah to offer wine to the Rechabites, and they refused out of respect for their ancestor. God uses this example to show Judah's disobedience. If a family obeyed a human father for generations, how much more should the people obey God, who spoke to them again and again through his prophets?

For today: look at an area where you know what God asks of you but have gradually let it slide. Choose one concrete step of obedience and take it this week, with humility and trust in his care.
exp.14:11:
This verse is a question: can iron break iron that comes from the north, or bronze? The suggested answer is no. The word "north" here is an older way of saying north, which is not used in the verse your reader sees, so the wording of the question stands on its own. Scholars interpret it in two ways: as a reference to Babylon, which would come from the north with great force, or as an image of Jeremiah's firmness, since God made him strong.

Jeremiah complains to God because everyone rejects him for preaching a hard message. God answers him that his life will have a good ending. Then God announces judgment on the people for their sins. The text is difficult, and there is no single explanation that is certain.

For today: when people reject you for doing what is right, do not rely only on your own strength. God sustains those who are faithful to him, and you can bring your complaints to him honestly, as Jeremiah did.
exp.36:6:
God commands Jeremiah to give an answer to the king of Judah, who had sent to ask him what was going to happen. The message is that the army of Pharaoh, which was coming to help Jerusalem, had already returned to Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by the Chaldeans (Babylonians), but when the Egyptian army came near, the Chaldeans withdrew for a time. King Zedekiah asked Jeremiah to pray and consult God, hoping for good news. God answers him that this help would not last and that the Chaldeans would return.

Today, we often place our hope in human help that seems secure, but it can fail. We can accept help with gratitude, but our firmest trust must be in God, and we should listen to his truth even when it is not what we hoped to hear.
exp.33:20:
God says that he will hand King Zedekiah and his officials over to their enemies, that is, to those who want to kill them. He will also hand them over to the army of the king of Babylon, which had withdrawn from Jerusalem for a time.

The phrase in the verse that means "those who seek their life" means that they are trying to take away their lives.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had made a solemn agreement to free their Hebrew slaves, passing between the parts of a divided calf, but later they enslaved them again. God judges them for breaking their word and for not obeying his law. The withdrawal of Babylon was only temporary.

For today: God takes seriously what we promise. If we make a promise before him, we should keep it, especially when it concerns treating others with justice and freedom. Let us ask him for help to be people of our word.
exp.9:10:
This verse says that the false gods, the ones that did not make the heavens and the earth, will disappear from this world. The word "perish" means to be destroyed or to cease to exist. It is a forceful statement about the difference between the true God and idols.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to his people, who lived surrounded by nations with idols of silver, gold, and wood. The verses before this one mock those images made by craftsmen. It is notable that this verse is written in Aramaic, not in Hebrew, as if it were a message meant for neighboring peoples to understand. Scholars explain this in different ways.

Today we do not carve statues, but we can put our trust in things we make ourselves: money, success, or recognition. Ask yourself where you are placing your security, and turn your trust back to the Creator.
exp.51:12:
This verse tells that Nebuzaradan, captain of the Babylonian guard, set fire to the temple, the king's palace and the houses of Jerusalem. The word "burned" here means he destroyed everything completely by fire, and "every great house" refers to every important building in the city.

Jeremiah 52 is a historical summary that closes the book. The writer records the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, just as Jeremiah had warned for years. The people had ignored God's calls to return to Him, and judgment came. It is a sad account, but it shows that God's words are fulfilled.

For today: let us not take the voice of God lightly. If He corrects us through His Word or through wise people, it is better to listen in time and return to Him. His correction seeks to heal us, and His mercy is always waiting for us.
exp.20:3:
God tells the people of Jerusalem that the weapons they use to defend themselves against the king of Babylon will become useless, as if He were turning them back against them. "Your hands" refers to their soldiers and their strength. "Besieging" means surrounding. The Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, will not be stopped outside the city; God will bring them in to the very center of it.

King Zedekiah asked Jeremiah to inquire of God, hoping for a miracle like those of the past. But God answers through the prophet with a message of judgment: the city had persisted in disobedience, and now He Himself would not fight on its behalf.

For today: it is not enough to ask God for help when trouble comes if we keep ignoring His voice. Today you can examine your heart, acknowledge where you have failed, and return to Him with humility, before seeking only quick solutions.
exp.40:2:
This verse tells that Ishmael, after murdering Gedaliah, also killed all the Jews who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean soldiers who were there. "Slew" here means that he killed them, and "Chaldeans" are the Babylonians.

The one telling the story is the book of Jeremiah, which recounts what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. Babylon had appointed Gedaliah as governor over those who remained in the land. Ishmael, who was of royal lineage, took advantage of a shared meal to betray and kill. The Bible does not fully explain his motives; many think resentment and political ambition played a part, and that he may have had foreign backing (the king of the Ammonites is mentioned in verse 40:14).

Today, this account warns us how destructive resentment is when it is not surrendered to God. It also invites us to seek peace and not to let ambition or bitterness lead us to harm others.
exp.4:1:
The explanation says that although the people of Jerusalem say "The Lord liveth," a phrase used to make a solemn oath, they actually swear falsely. "Surely they swear falsely" means that their words sound religious but are not true. They use God's name without honoring it with their lives.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, God challenges them to search Jerusalem for a single person who practices justice and seeks truth, and promises to pardon the city if such a person is found. Then Jeremiah laments that the people did not accept correction. The problem was a faith of lips, without obedience.

For today: it is not enough to say Christian phrases or to name God. Today you can examine whether your words, promises and daily decisions agree with what you say you believe, and ask God to make you a sincere and faithful person.
exp.8:23:
If someone wants to feel proud of something, the verse says, let it be that they truly know God. God says that He is the Lord, who acts with lovingkindness (kindness toward those who are weak), with judgment (right decisions) and with righteousness in the earth. And He adds: "in these things I delight," meaning this is what pleases Him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah trusted in their wisdom, their strength and their money, while the nation was heading toward disaster. God shows them that none of that would save them, and that what mattered most was knowing Him and living as He is.

For today: instead of boasting about your achievements, seek to know God through His Word, and practice kindness and justice with the people around you.
exp.51:4:
This verse says that the armies of Babylon kept Jerusalem surrounded and shut in for almost two years, from the ninth year to the eleventh year of King Zedekiah. "Besieged" means surrounded by an army, with no one allowed to come in or go out.

Here the book's narrator is recounting the fall of Jerusalem. He explains that this happened because of God's anger against Judah, after many warnings that the people did not heed. Zedekiah rebelled against Babylon, and the result was this long siege, which ended with famine and the city taken.

For today: the consequences of ignoring God sometimes take time, but they come. If God speaks to you through his Word or your conscience, do not wait until you are surrounded by problems to listen. His forgiveness is always near to those who repent.
exp.20:10:
Here the explanation says that God commands Jeremiah to speak directly to the family of the king of Judah. "Hear the word of the Lord" is an order: listen to what God says. "The house of the king" refers to the king and his family, the ones who governed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was surrounded by the armies of Babylon, called the Chaldeans, and God had already announced judgment. Before giving his sentence, he calls the rulers to listen. Next he asks them for justice: to defend the one who is oppressed. This shows that the responsibility of the leaders was great.

God expects that those who have authority or influence, in the home, at work, or in the church, will listen to his word before deciding. Today we can ask ourselves: am I using what I have to care for the one who suffers, or only for my own comfort?
exp.32:4:
God says that the houses of Jerusalem were torn down, and that the people went out to fight against the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). Those houses would be left full of the bodies of the dead. The phrase about filling them means the houses would be packed with corpses, and striking down the enemy is the picture of the destruction. The phrase about God hiding his face means that God withdrew his favor and his protection. The Hebrew text is difficult, and some scholars understand it in somewhat different ways.

The words come through Jeremiah, who was held prisoner while Babylon was laying siege to Jerusalem. God explains that the city is suffering because of its persistent wickedness, not because He has forgotten it without reason.

For today: the harsh consequences of sin are real, but they are not God's final word. Right after this, He promises healing, peace, and restoration. If you are going through a hard time, be honest with God, acknowledge whatever you need to, and cry out to Him. He invites us to do so and promises to answer.
exp.0:7:
God tells Jeremiah not to be afraid of the people he will be sent to. The reason is simple: God himself is with him and will deliver him, that is, rescue and protect him. "The Lord" is God's name, and "saith the Lord" stresses that the promise comes from him.

God speaks and answers Jeremiah, a young man who felt unable to speak in public. God does not accept the excuse of his young age, for he will give him the words and send him with a difficult message for the people and the kings. The promise does not say there will be no opposition, but that God will be with him.

When God calls you to do something difficult, such as telling the truth in love or standing firm, do not wait until you feel capable. Take the step trusting that he is with you.
exp.27:15:
God, through Jeremiah, tells Hananiah that he is going to remove him from the earth. "I will cast you from off the face of the earth" means he will be taken out of this world.
