Hananiah would die that same year, and the reason is that he taught rebellion against the Lord, that is, a message that went against what God had said.

Jeremiah speaks to Hananiah, a prophet who had promised that Babylon would soon fall and that everything would return to normal. But God had said that the people must submit to Nebuchadnezzar. Hananiah gave the people false hope in God's name. The following verse tells that he died in the seventh month of that year.

Speaking in God's name is a serious matter. Before repeating or teaching something as "the word of God," it is wise to compare it with the Bible, even when the message is more comfortable or pleasant to hear.
exp.30:17:
God listened closely to Ephraim's lament. Ephraim here stands for the northern people, Israel. They acknowledge that God corrected them, and that they were like an untamed young bull, that is, a stubborn calf that will not let itself be led. They ask God himself to bring them back, because they cannot do it on their own, and they confess that the Lord is their God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were in exile because of their disobedience, but God promises comfort and return. Before and after this verse, God asks them to stop weeping, and then calls them a precious son, with a heart moved by mercy.

For today: when you feel far from God or ashamed of your mistakes, do not wait until you have fixed yourself on your own. You can pray sincerely: "Turn me, Lord." He listens, corrects with love, and receives the one who returns to him.
exp.32:17:
God promises that there will always be Levite priests standing before Him to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to present sacrifices every day.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah, who is in prison and writes to a people discouraged by the fall of Jerusalem. God promises restoration: a king from the line of David and a priesthood that continues. Christians often see here a sign pointing to Christ, the King and High Priest; others understand it in a more literal way. It is interpreted in several ways.

For today: if God keeps His promises even when everything seems lost, we can trust Him. Today, in the middle of your difficulties, come to God in prayer every day, with thankfulness and hope.
exp.29:18:
God promises that out of the people will come thanksgiving, and the voice of those who make merry will be heard. He also promises to multiply them so that they will not be few. He will glorify them, so that they will not be small.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Israel were in captivity, wounded and looked down upon, and others were saying that no one cared for Zion. In the middle of that pain, God announces healing, return, and rebuilding. This promise was first read as hope for the return of those who had been exiled, and many Christians also see in it a foretaste of the restoration God gives in Christ.

For today: if you are going through a season of hurt or loss, do not hold on only to what others say about you. God knows how to restore. Learn to give thanks to him now, because praise can be a first step of hope.
exp.17:4:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that, after what Jeremiah saw in the potter's house, a message from God came to him. The explanation's quoted wording is an old way of saying "came to me," which is already how the verse reads, so no separate comment is needed.

Here the narrator is Jeremiah, and he presents God as the one who is about to give the explanation. First the prophet watched the potter remake a damaged vessel. Then God shows him that this scene is a lesson for Israel: He can deal with His people according to His justice and His purpose, and the people need to return to Him.

For today: before drawing quick conclusions about what we are going through, it is worth pausing to listen to God in His Word. He can give meaning even in broken situations, and He invites us to let ourselves be shaped with humility.
exp.1:4:
God asks his people a question: what fault or injustice did their ancestors find in him that they should go so far from him? They followed what is worthless, that is, empty idols and things without value, and they ended up empty and without purpose.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He reminds them that Israel was set apart for him, that he brought them out of Egypt, led them through the wilderness, and brought them into a fertile land. The question does not seek information; it is a painful complaint that shows how unjust their turning away from him was.

For today: when something pulls us away from God, it is wise to ask ourselves whether he truly gave us anything better. Remembering his past faithfulness helps us return to him and not chase things that leave us empty.
exp.24:35:
The explanation says that a cry and a wail are heard from the shepherds and the leaders of the flock. The reason is that the Lord has left their grazing lands ruined. "Cry" means a loud outcry, "wail" is a heartbreaking lament, "leaders" are the chief leaders, and "sheepfolds" are the places where the sheep rest.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in God's name within a announcement of judgment on Judah and the nations. The "shepherds" are the rulers and leaders of the people, who, according to the context, did not care well for the flock. Many understand that the judgment came through Babylon, although this verse does not name it.

For today: whoever has some responsibility over others, in the church, the family, or the workplace, should care for it with humility and truth, remembering that one day they will give an account to God.
exp.36:8:
God warns the people not to deceive themselves. Some were saying, "The Chaldeans have already left; we are safe." But God says it is not so: they will return. Here "deceive" means to fool your own selves, to mislead your own hearts. "Chaldeans" is another name for the Babylonians.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing King Zedekiah. Babylon had besieged Jerusalem, but it withdrew for a time when the army of Pharaoh came from Egypt. The people felt relief and believed the danger had passed. God tells them that Egypt will not save them and that the city will be taken.

For today: a temporary relief does not always mean the problem has been resolved. Before we put our trust in something, it is wise to listen honestly to God and to correct what He points out to us, rather than comfort ourselves with illusions.
exp.31:24:
Jeremiah speaks with God and expresses his confusion. He reminds God that he was told to buy a piece of land, to pay for it with money, and to have witnesses sign the purchase. But now the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, are about to conquer the city. It seems strange to him to buy something that appears to be lost.

Jeremiah is in prison while Babylon besieges Jerusalem. God asked him to buy the field of his cousin Hanamel as a sign that, after the punishment, the people would return to live in their land. Jeremiah obeyed, but he prays honestly and without understanding everything. God answers by reminding him that nothing is hidden from him.

For today: when God's instructions seem to make no sense, you can obey and also express your doubts with sincerity. He is not bothered by your questions, and his promises still stand even when the situation looks dark.
exp.49:21:
This verse describes the sound of war coming into the land, and a very great destruction. The word "destruction" conveys the idea of ruin, collapse, or a blow that leaves everything broken to pieces. It is as if one could hear the noise of an army and of a city falling.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah and announces judgment against Babylon, the power that had oppressed other nations. The verses before it mention Merathaim and Pekod, names that probably refer to regions of Babylon, though scholars debate their exact meaning. At the same time, God promises to forgive his people who remained.

For today: God sees injustice and does not allow human pride to last forever. We can rest in the fact that he governs history, and at the same time receive his forgiveness with humility.
exp.35:30:
God says that he will punish Jehoiakim, his children, and his servants for their wickedness. "Punish" here means to come and call them to account, that is, to bring judgment. "Descendants" means offspring, and "men" refers to the men. God will also bring upon Jerusalem and Judah the evil he had announced, because no one would listen to him.

God speaks through Jeremiah. King Jehoiakim had burned the scroll with the prophet's warnings, as if destroying the message could cancel it. God answers that his word still stands, and that the king and the people would face the consequences of rejecting it. Then Jeremiah writes another scroll, and the word of God continues.

Today we might ask ourselves whether there is something God tells us through his Word that we prefer to ignore or silence. It is better to listen in time and correct our course, because God is patient, but his warnings are real.
exp.31:27:
God announces that he is going to hand Jerusalem over into the hands of the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, and of their king Nebuchadrezzar. He says the city will be taken.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah while Jerusalem is under siege and King Zedekiah has the prophet imprisoned. Shortly before this, Jeremiah bought a field as a sign of future hope. God reminds him that he is the God of all flesh and that nothing is hidden from him. The judgment comes because the people fell into idolatry and wickedness.

For today: God speaks the truth even when it hurts, and he also keeps promises of restoration. We can trust that he sees everything, so it is wise to turn to him honestly, hiding nothing, and to wait for his mercy.
exp.35:8:
It came to pass in the fifth year of Jehoiakim, in the ninth month. They announced a public fast, meaning a time of going without food in order to seek God. The people of Jerusalem were called to it, along with those who came from the other cities of Judah.

Jeremiah had received words from God warning of judgment on the people. He could not enter the temple, so his helper Baruch was to read the scroll aloud. The text does not say who ordered the fast, but it gathered many people, and so it was a good moment for them to hear the message.

Today, when we humble ourselves before God, we should also be ready to listen to his Word and obey it. Praying without listening is only half done.
exp.1:9:
God tells his people to cross the sea to the islands of Chittim, which probably refers to Cyprus and the lands of the Mediterranean to the west, and to send messengers as far as Kedar, a desert tribe to the east. "Pass over" means "go" or "cross over," and "consider diligently" means "look carefully." They are to search whether anything like this has ever happened.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. Its leaders, priests, shepherds, and prophets, had forgotten God and were following Baal. God points to the far west and the far east to show that no nation changes its gods the way Judah did with the living God.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we have put in place of God, even if they seem good or ordinary. It is good to devote time to prayer and to the Bible in order to return to Him, who is the source that never fails.
exp.40:17:
This verse explains why the people wanted to go to Egypt: they were afraid of the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians. Ishmael had killed Gedaliah, the governor whom the king of Babylon had placed over the land. Here, "slain" means killed. They feared that Babylon would punish them.

The account is told by Jeremiah. After the killing, Johanan rescued the people that Ishmael had carried off, and he stopped near Bethlehem. They planned to flee to Egypt, but they had not yet asked God for direction. The Bible shows here a very strong human fear.

Today, when something frightens us, it is easy to decide quickly and look for an escape of our own. Before acting, let us pray, ask for wise counsel, and seek the will of God. Fear should not be our guide; trust in God should.
exp.8:5:
It says that the people live surrounded by lies. The word for "dwelling" refers to the place where one lives. Therefore, deceit is the atmosphere of everyday life. And because they deceived so much, the people refused to know God. The name of God is the one written in the verse above.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah was full of lies, even among brothers and friends. The verses before show that they had become accustomed to lying. God says that this falsehood kept them away from Him. Then He announces that He will test them the way metal is tested in fire, and it grieves Him to have to do it.

For today: honesty brings us closer to God. Today you can choose to tell the truth with love, even in small things, and ask God to cleanse you from all duplicity.
exp.12:13:
God says that he will break his people, causing some to crash against others, fathers and sons alike. He announces that there will be no forgiveness, compassion, or mercy to stop the punishment. The phrase "to keep from destroying them" sounds strange; the meaning is that nothing will hold him back from destroying them.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah and Jerusalem, including kings, priests, and prophets. The image of wineskins full of wine announces that everyone will be left reeling from the judgment, stumbling with no way out. The cause is their pride and their persistent rebellion, despite the warnings. The verses that follow call them to humble themselves and give glory to God before the darkness comes.

For today: do not harden your heart when God speaks to you. If He corrects you through His Word, respond quickly with humility and repentance, while there is still time and light.
exp.17:11:
The explanation says that the people of Judah responded with hopelessness and stubbornness to God's call. They said there was no point in trying, and they chose to follow their own plans and do what their evil heart asked of them, without caring what God said.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, right after the image of the potter who can reshape the clay. He offers Judah a way out: turn from their wrong path and improve their deeds. But the people reject the invitation. Here we do not hear God, but the voice of the people, who shut the door to repentance.

For today: when we feel that change is pointless, or we prefer to keep walking our own way, let us remember that God still invites us. Today we can listen to his voice and take a concrete step toward correction.
exp.43:2:
God explains why Jerusalem and the towns of Judah were left in ruins. The cause was the people's wickedness: they provoked him to anger by burning incense and by worshiping other gods that neither they nor their ancestors had known. "Other gods" means the gods of other peoples.

God speaks through Jeremiah to the Jews who were living in Egypt, in places such as Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph, and Pathros. They had seen the destruction of Judah, yet they continued in the same idolatry. God reminds them of the past so that they may learn and turn back to him.

For today: let us not wait to suffer the consequences before we correct our course. If anything occupies in our heart the place that belongs to God, we can recognize it today and return to him with humility.
exp.14:13:
God says that he will cause the enemies of Judah to carry the people away into a land unknown to them. The reason is that God's anger is like a fire that has been kindled and will burn against them. The phrase about making them pass over is about being taken away or carried off to another place. The word for the people carried away refers to being taken as captives, and to handing over to plunder.

Here God speaks to the people of Judah through Jeremiah. They had fallen into idolatry and disobedience, and God announces the consequences. Some scholars see here a reference to the exile in Babylon, but the wording of this verse presents certain difficulties, and for that reason there are different ways of translating it.

For today: God speaks with seriousness about sin, but his warnings aim to wake us up in time. If today you feel that God is calling you to change something, do not harden your heart; return to him with humility, because his mercy remains open to whoever repents.
exp.50:57:
He says that God, the Lord of hosts, will utterly break down the great walls of Babylon and burn its high gates with fire. The phrase "with fire" is simply "with fire." The nations will labor and grow weary, but it will all be in vain, because their work will not last.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message against Babylon. This city was a powerful empire that had oppressed Judah. God promises it justice, for He is the God who repays. The verses that follow say that Jeremiah put these words in writing to send them to Babylon with Seraiah.

For today: We can rest in the knowledge that no human power, however strong it may seem, is above God. Trust Him when you see injustice, and avoid placing your security in things that do not last.
exp.28:15:
This verse introduces a message from God for those who stayed in Jerusalem: the king who sits on the throne of David, and all the people who live in the city. They are the brothers of the exiles, the ones who were not taken captive to Babylon. The phrase "but" in this verse simply connects it to what came before, and the words "thus saith the Lord" mean that this is a direct message from God.

Jeremiah writes a letter to the exiles in Babylon. Some prophets there were promising a quick return. God asks them for patience, because restoration would come later. Now he also speaks to those who remained in Jerusalem, who believed they were safe and did not listen to his warning. The next verse announces the judgment that awaited them.

For today: let us not trust in our position or in voices that only say what is comfortable. Let us receive the Word of God with humility, even when it corrects us.
exp.14:4:
God asks Jerusalem three questions: who will have pity on you, who will mourn for you, who will go aside to ask how you are doing? The phrase "to ask how you are doing" was a way of greeting someone and showing concern for their well-being. The implied answer is that no one will.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces the punishment coming upon Judah for its idolatry and its rebellion. He mentions the sin of Manasseh, the king who led the people into great evil, and recalls that the people did not turn from their ways. The verse shows the pain of a judgment that would leave the city alone.

For today: let us not harden our hearts when God calls us to return. And in the meantime, let us be people who care about others, who visit, comfort, and ask with kindness how they are.
exp.21:22:
It says that someone lives calm and secure, like a bird that builds its nest high in the cedars of Lebanon. But that comfort will not last. When the pains come, they will cry out with a pain as strong as that of a woman in labor. The word "cry out" here means they will complain with deep suffering.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses Jerusalem and its royal family, and the following verse mentions Coniah, king of Judah. The cedars of Lebanon probably point to the luxurious royal palaces, built with that wood. God spoke to them when things were going well, but they would not listen to him. That is why judgment will come through Babylon.

For today: when everything is going well, it is easy to ignore God. Use times of calm to listen to him and obey him, instead of trusting only in your own security.
exp.5:25:
It says that God's people should dress in sackcloth, roll in ashes, and mourn with the deepest grief, as one who has lost his only son. Sackcloth and ashes were signs of mourning and repentance. The word "suddenly" is what the verse says about the invading army that is about to come upon them without warning.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The verses before this one describe fear and anguish in the face of an enemy coming from the north. Judah had rejected God's warning, so the call is to grieve in earnest, not to pretend. The text that follows shows that Jeremiah was to examine the people's wickedness.

For today: do not minimize your mistakes or get used to them. When you see something that pulls you away from God, come to Him with humility and a sincere heart, before the consequences arrive.
exp.5:4:
The explanation says that the invaders encourage one another: "Arise," that is to say, "get up!" and they propose to attack by night and destroy the palaces of Jerusalem. "Let us go up" is a way of saying that they advance toward the city, which stood on high ground. The "palaces" are the strongholds and important houses.

Here the enemy armies speak, the ones God announces from the north. Earlier, in verse 4, they had wanted to attack at midday, but the time has run out on them, so now they decide to attack by night. According to the next verse, it is the LORD who backs them, for Jerusalem is full of violence, injustice and robbery. It is a judgment for the people's persistent wickedness, after many calls to return to God.

For today: let us not think that God's time of grace is endless. If God points out something wrong in our life, let us not leave it for later. Let us repent today, while there is still time.
exp.21:25:
He says that God himself will drive out Coniah and his mother from their own country and carry them off into a foreign land, where they were not born. There they will die. The phrase "I will carry thee" means "I will make you be carried away," and the words "a land not their own" mean a foreign country.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Coniah, also called Jehoiachin or Jeconiah, was king of Judah. God had already compared him to a signet ring on his hand, and yet he rejects him because of the wickedness and pride of the kingdom. He was taken captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, and his mother went with him.

For today: holding a place of power or privilege does not protect us from the consequences of turning away from God. It is better to live with humility and to listen to his voice in time, before things are lost.
exp.3:16:
The explanation says that the enemy armies will surround Jerusalem like the watchmen who guard a field or a harvest: they keep watch on every side and do not let her escape. The reason is clear: the city rebelled against God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Before this verse, it is announced that an army is coming from far away and that the warning of danger runs from Dan to Judah. God explains that this is not bad luck: the people turned their back on him. Afterward, the prophet shows grief over what is coming.

For today: when something in your life goes wrong, do not stay only with the complaint. Ask God to show you whether there is something you should correct. He corrects with pain, but he always invites you to return to him.
exp.47:1:
It says that Moab will no longer be a source of pride or fame. Against Heshbon, a Moabite city, others planned evil and said to one another: "Come, and let us cut it off from being a nation." "Devised" means that they made plans. Madmen too will be cut down, that is, silenced or destroyed, and the sword will go after it. The name Madmen resembles a Hebrew word meaning "dung," and some believe there is a play on words here, though this is not certain.

The one speaking through Jeremiah is the LORD, the God of Israel. This message announces judgment on Moab, a neighboring people who trusted in their cities, their riches, and their pride. The texts do not say exactly who the attackers would be, and interpreters explain this in various ways.

Today we can remember that no human fame, strength, or security lasts forever. It is wise to place our trust in God and not in what we boast of, and to live with humility.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that God compares the two kingdoms of the Hebrew people. Israel, the northern kingdom, was openly rebellious and turned away from God. But Judah, the southern kingdom, was faithless, that is, treacherous. The phrase "has justified herself" means that Israel was less guilty than Judah.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had already fallen to Assyria, and Judah saw it, but did not learn from it. Judah returned to God only in pretense, with a religion that was merely for show. With this comparison God does not excuse Israel; rather, he shows how serious Judah's falsehood is. Right after this, God invites Israel to return, because he is merciful.

For today: it is not enough to appear faithful before others. God looks for a sincere heart. If we know the truth and still pretend, our failure is serious. But the door remains open: we can acknowledge our sin and turn back to God with all our heart.
exp.12:6:
Jeremiah obeys God and goes to the Euphrates River. There he digs in the place where he had hidden his linen belt, and he finds it ruined. It was no longer good for anything. The quoted words "Fuí," "fui," and "escondílo," along with "lo escondí," are not needed here, and "podrido," which means damaged and falling apart, can be rendered as "ruined," the word that appears in the verse.

God had asked Jeremiah to use this belt as a sign for the people. A belt is worn close to the body, and God wanted Judah close to Him. But the people became proud and turned away from God. The following verse explains that in the same way the pride of Judah and Jerusalem would be ruined. Some scholars debate whether the journey was real or a vision, and the text does not make this clear.

For today: pride pulls us away from God and leaves us useless. We can ask Him for a humble heart and stay close to Him every day, in prayer and in His Word.
exp.48:21:
It says that someone will come up and fly like an eagle, spreading his wings over Bozrah, which was an important city of Edom. On that day, the bravest soldiers of Edom will have as much fear and pain as a woman about to give birth.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Edom, a neighboring people of Israel, trusted in its strength and its high places. God announces that he will send judgment upon them. The eagle is not clearly identified in the text; many think it represents an invading army, such as Babylon, and that God uses it as his instrument.

We can learn that no human strength, reputation, or security protects us if we leave God out. Today it is good to ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and to place our hope in the Lord, the only refuge that does not collapse.
exp.51:30:
This verse tells that, after thirty-seven years of exile, the new king of Babylon, Evil-merodach, brought Jehoiachin, king of Judah, out of prison. "Lifted up the head" means that he honored him and gave back his dignity. "Came to pass" means "happened." This took place on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, in the first year of that king's reign.

Jeremiah 52 is the end of the book and repeats much of what is told in 2 Kings 25. The account closes with this news, after speaking of the fall of Jerusalem and the deportations. Many understand that the author leaves a sign of hope: the family of David had not been forgotten.

Even in long and dark times, God can open an unexpected door. We can keep trusting and waiting with patience, without thinking that everything is lost.
exp.22:19:
This verse says that God's anger will not stop until he has done everything he planned in his heart. The word for his intense anger is rendered in the verse as "anger," and "the thoughts of his heart" refers to his purposes. The phrase about the final days means the last times or later on, and the verse says that people will understand it fully. God promises that when everything happens, the people will understand it well.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were listening to prophets who said that everything would be fine, but God declares that he did not send them and did not speak to them. For this reason he announces judgment like a storm falling on the wicked. Some understand "the last days" as the near time of the exile in Babylon, and others see a broader scope as well. Interpreters explain it in different ways.

Today we can learn to measure every religious message by the Word of God, and not only by what pleases us to hear. If God corrects, he does so so that we will return to him. Let us listen to his voice with humility and obey.
exp.48:29:
God tells the people of Hazor to flee as far away as they can and hide in deep places, such as caves or hollows in the ground. The phrase "get you far off" is rendered in a way that means "go away," and "dwell deep" refers to deep hiding places. The reason is that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, has already made plans to attack them and has a firm purpose against them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah within his messages against several nations. Hazor here is not the city in Israel, but a group of settlements of desert tribes in the Arabian desert, near Kedar. They were a peaceful and confident people, and God announces that Babylon would defeat them. The exact details of that campaign are not known with much precision.

For today: when God gives a warning, it is wise to listen and act with prudence, rather than trusting too much that everything will remain calm.
exp.3:26:
God says that a very great punishment is coming: the whole land will be laid waste and emptied. But he adds a limit: he will not make a full end. He will not destroy it completely or finish it off entirely. "Desolate" means ruined and left empty. Although the judgment is harsh, God leaves open a hope that a remnant will remain.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah had turned away from him and were living in wickedness. Jeremiah describes the judgment as a vision of desolation: no people, no birds, cities in ruins. Many understand that it refers to the invasion that would come from the north, although the text presents it in very broad and symbolic language.

For today: God is serious about sin, but even when he corrects, he does not stop being merciful. If you are going through a painful consequence today, remember that God disciplines to restore, not to destroy you. Return to him with humility and trust.
exp.24:15:
The nations will drink from the cup of God's judgment. When they drink it, they will stagger, lose control, and be driven out of their minds because of the sword that God sends against them. "Sword" here means war. The word being explained refers to confusion and desperation, like someone who is drunk.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, around 605 BC. Judah and the neighboring nations had lived in idolatry and injustice. God uses the image of a cup of bitter wine to show that the punishment would reach everyone, beginning with Jerusalem. Scholars understand the cup as an image, not as a literal drink.

For today: God takes injustice seriously and does not overlook our choices. Today you can examine your life honestly, turn away from what displeases God, and return to Him, for He is patient and always offers forgiveness to those who turn back to Him.
exp.31:25:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah once more. The message came directly from God, and the word "saying" introduces what God wants to tell him right away.

Jeremiah has just prayed with doubts. Babylon is already surrounding Jerusalem, and God had asked him to buy a piece of land, even though everything seemed lost. The prophet does not understand why he should make that purchase. Then God answers. He reminds Jeremiah that he is the God of all flesh, that is, of all human beings, and that nothing escapes his knowledge.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening and have questions, bring them honestly to God, as Jeremiah did. God is not troubled by your doubts, and he can answer you with words that restore your confidence in him.
exp.45:25:
God says he will hand the Egyptians over to those who want to kill them: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and his servants or officials. The phrase "those that seek their lives" means they are trying to take away their lives. But he adds a promise: afterward Egypt will be inhabited again, as in the days of old.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Egypt trusted in its pharaoh and its gods, and God announces that Babylon will defeat it. The verses that follow, by contrast, comfort Israel: although it will be punished, God will not destroy it completely. Some think the restoration of Egypt shows God's mercy even toward other nations; the text gives no further details.

For today: do not place your security in human powers, but in God, who governs history. If today you are going through correction or loss, remember that his final word can be restoration.
exp.43:20:
Jeremiah asks a question to show that the answer is obvious: of course God remembered. The word "incense" here refers to smoke offered as a sacrifice. He says that everyone, from the common people up to the kings and princes, burned incense to other gods in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. God saw all of it and did not forget.

Jeremiah is speaking to the Jews who fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. They say that things went better for them when they worshiped the "queen of heaven," a pagan goddess, and that their husbands agreed with them. Jeremiah answers that the ruin of their land was the result of that sin and of not obeying God.

For today: do not think that God overlooks what becomes custom. Examine which practices you have accepted only out of tradition or because they are common, and return simply to obeying his Word.
exp.43:6:
God asks with grief: "Why do you do such great harm to yourselves?" He warns that if they keep on this way, they will be cut down like a tree, men and women, children and infants. Nothing would be left, not a single survivor. The incense burned in worship was the offering the people made.

Jeremiah speaks for God to the Jews who fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. There they were still burning incense to false gods. God reminds them that they already saw Judah destroyed because of that same idolatry, and he does not want them to repeat it.

Today we can ask ourselves what things are taking the place of God in our hearts. Learning from past mistakes, with humility, spares us much pain. God corrects because he desires our good.
exp.36:14:
The verse tells how the princes became angry with Jeremiah, beat him, and put him in prison. The words "they struck him" carry the meaning of the first phrase, and "they put him in prison" carries the meaning of the second. The house of the scribe Jonathan was turned into a jail.

Jeremiah was God's prophet in the final days of Jerusalem, when Babylon had the city surrounded. As he went out through the Benjamin Gate, a guard accused him of defecting to the enemy. Jeremiah denied it, but no one believed him. The princes punished him, perhaps because his message of surrendering to Babylon seemed to them like treason. This last point is an interpretation, but it fits the account.

For today: sometimes telling the truth brings misunderstanding and unjust punishment, even when a person is sincere. Jeremiah remained faithful and, when the king called for him, he spoke again without changing the message. Let us ask God for courage to be honest and patience when we are not believed.
exp.35:12:
This verse says that Micaiah, after hearing Baruch read, went and told the princes everything he had heard. The phrase "unto them" refers to the princes. The words "in the ears of the people" mean that Baruch read the scroll aloud, so that the people could hear it.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Baruch was the assistant of the prophet Jeremiah, and he had read in the temple the words that God had given to Jeremiah. Micaiah, the son of a man known among the officials, told it to the princes gathered in the scribe's chamber. That is why they sent for Baruch so they could hear it directly from him.

For today: when we hear something valuable from the Word of God, we should not keep it to ourselves. Sharing it with humility and faithfulness, without adding or taking anything away, can open the way for another person to hear God.
exp.39:3:
Jeremiah, who was bound with chains, is now set free, the explanation says. Nebuzaradan gives him two choices: go with him to Babylon, where he would look after him, or stay in his own land. The source's old-wording comments are handled by rewriting them to the verse's own words. "Look well unto thee" means he would take care of him, and "seem good" or "seem ill" refers to what seems right or wrong to him.

The speaker is Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, after the fall of Jerusalem. He had found Jeremiah bound among the captives. He acknowledges that the Lord had announced this punishment because of the people's sin. Jeremiah had warned of this for years, and in the end he decides to stay with those who remained in the land.

For today: God can use even unexpected situations to bring freedom and direction. When you face a decision, pray, weigh what is faithful to God and not only what is comfortable, and choose with wisdom.
exp.51:6:
The explanation says that the walls of Jerusalem were broken through and the city fell. Then the soldiers fled at night through a small, hidden gate that lay between two walls, near the king's garden. They took the way toward the plain, even though the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) were still surrounding the city.

The one telling this is the author of the book, who recounts the fall of Jerusalem in about 586 B.C. Earlier, God had warned through Jeremiah that the city would fall if the people kept refusing to turn back to Him. This chapter shows that those warnings came true. The attempt to escape did not save them, as the verses that follow make clear.

For today: running away from the consequences does not remove them. If we have done wrong, it is better to acknowledge it before God with humility and ask Him for direction, rather than looking for hidden ways out. His forgiveness is real, and He still receives anyone who returns to Him.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah. "Moreover the word of the Lord came to me, saying," is the way the King James Version puts it. The word "saying" announces that the message Jeremiah is to carry follows right away.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, a prophet of Judah, who tells how God gave him a message. Here the first great speech of the book begins. From what follows, God wants to remind his people of the affection and faithfulness of earlier times, before he rebukes them for their unfaithfulness. The verse does not say exactly when he received it, and that does not change the meaning.

For today: God still speaks, above all through his Word. Before we begin reading the Bible, we can pray quietly and ask him for an attentive heart, ready to obey what he says.
exp.38:0:
It says that in the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came with his whole army against Jerusalem and surrounded the city with troops. The word "besieged" means to lay siege to a city: cutting off its exits and its supply of food to force it to surrender.

This is a historical account within the book of Jeremiah. The narrator describes the beginning of the siege, which lasted about two and a half years, until the walls fell, as the following text shows. Jeremiah had warned many times that this would happen if the people and their leaders did not return to God. Here that word is seen fulfilled. The dates are counted by the years of Zedekiah's reign.

For today: God does what he says, both his warnings and his promises. If today we feel that God is calling us to correct something, it is better to listen in time and not wait for the consequences to arrive.
exp.41:12:
This verse begins a warning from God. It says: "But if you say, We will not stay in this land," and so you disobey the voice of the Lord your God. The word "but" is the same as "yet" or "however," and the words "say" and "stay" in the verse above carry the meaning of the phrases the explanation comments on.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors was afraid of Babylon and asked Jeremiah to pray so they would know what to do. God answered: stay, do not be afraid, I am with you. But the people were already planning to leave for Egypt, looking for safety.

For today: sometimes we ask God for direction when we have already decided what we want. We can pray with a heart willing to obey, trusting that his presence sustains us more than any plan that seems safe.
exp.33:18:
This verse lists those who passed between the parts of the divided calf: the princes of Judah and of Jerusalem, the eunuchs (court officials), the priests, and all the people of the land. All of them took part in the covenant, and for that reason all of them would be held responsible.

God speaks through Jeremiah while Babylon threatens Jerusalem. The people had freed their Hebrew slaves, as the law required, but then they enslaved them again. Passing between the halves of an animal was a solemn way of swearing a covenant, and here that oath was broken.

For today: if we promise something before God, we ought to keep it. It is worth reviewing what promises we have made, and being faithful, especially when keeping them costs us something.
exp.32:15:
In those days, as God has prepared them, Judah will be saved and Jerusalem will live in safety. "Will dwell safely" means that the city will live with confidence, without fear. And the city will be called "The Lord our righteousness," that is, the Lord is the one who makes us righteous.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at a time when Jerusalem was under threat and the people lived in distress. God promises to keep his good word and to raise up for David a Branch of righteousness, that is, a righteous descendant who will rule well. Many Christians see here a promise fulfilled in Jesus.

For today: our security does not depend on what we do or on our circumstances, but on God, who gives us his righteousness. Trust in him and rest in his promise.
exp.47:44:
The explanation says that the Moabites who were fleeing from their enemies stopped under the protection of Heshbon, a strong city, thinking they would be safe there. But from that same city came fire and destruction. The words "the crown of the head" refer to the top of the head, and "the tumultuous ones" are proud and rebellious people. That is to say, the judgment reached from the corner of the land to the head of the proud.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, announcing judgment on Moab for its pride and its confidence in itself and in its god Chemosh. This verse recalls an ancient song in Numbers 21:28, where fire came out of Heshbon. Some think it alludes to a past defeat, and others to a new judgment. In the end, God promises restoration.

For today: do not place your security in places, money, or human strength. Seek refuge in God, who is the only one who never fails.
exp.47:10:
He says that Moab has lived at ease since its youth. The image is that of wine: it is left to settle on its dregs, and it is never poured from one vessel into another to clear it. Moab was never taken into captivity, and for that reason it keeps its flavor and its smell, that is, it has not changed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, with a message of judgment against Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. Its comfort had brought pride and trust in its god Chemosh. The verses that follow announce that those who carry people away will come and empty its jars, that is, enemies who will shake it up. Interpreters see Babylon here, although the text does not name it.

For today: unchanging comfort can leave us hardened. Let us ask God to shake us with love, and receive with humility the trials that help us grow.
exp.49:27:
The voice of people fleeing Babylon can be heard, arriving in Zion with a report: God has already done justice. "Vengeance" here means a just punishment from God, not a vengeance filled with resentment. It is "the vengeance of his temple" because Babylon had destroyed the temple in Jerusalem.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf to a people who lived through the exile. Babylon had been very proud and cruel toward Israel. For this reason the text announces its fall and says that the survivors will carry the news to Jerusalem. Some scholars see here the Jews returning from exile, although the text gives no further details.

For today: when you see injustice and feel that no one responds, remember that God sees and that he has the final word. You can leave your pain in his hands, pray for justice, and refrain from taking revenge yourself.
exp.50:50:
It says that God's people feel shame and humiliation. They have heard insults, and confusion covers their faces, that is, they do not know where to hide. The cause is that foreigners entered the sanctuaries, the holy places of the temple of the Lord. Public insult is what shame here refers to, and the holy places are the sacred parts of the temple.

Here the exiles of Judah are speaking, remembering the destruction of Jerusalem and the defiling of the temple by Babylon. It is part of a message from Jeremiah announcing that God will judge Babylon. The verses before it encourage the survivors to remember the Lord and Jerusalem, and the verses after it promise that God will punish Babylon.

For today: when you feel shame or pain over what has happened, do not stay only with the wound. Bring it to God, remember who He is, and trust that He does justice in His time.
exp.40:1:
It says that Ishmael, together with ten men, rose up and struck down Gedaliah with the sword, the man the king of Babylon had set over the land as governor. The phrase about striking him with the sword means they attacked him with a sword. They did this after they had eaten with him.

It is part of Jeremiah's historical account. Jerusalem had fallen, and Babylon left Gedaliah in charge of those who remained in Judah. Ishmael was of the royal family, and the Bible does not state his motives clearly. Some think he wanted power or rejected the man who served Babylon, but the text here does not say so. Even so, the act was a cruel betrayal.

For today: trust is valuable, but we need wisdom. And when we feel jealousy, resentment, or pride, we should master it in time, before it leads us to harm others.
exp.16:20:
God tells Jeremiah to warn the people. Their very lives depend on it. They must not carry any load on the day of rest, nor bring anything in through the gates of Jerusalem. "Guard yourselves" means "take care of yourselves" (this sentence refers to a source-language word and is deleted per instructions).

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the kings of Judah and all the people living in Jerusalem. The Sabbath was a sign of the covenant with God. Working and trading on that day showed a heart that did not trust in Him. The verses that follow say that their ancestors would not listen or accept correction.

For today: God invites us to rest and to trust that He sustains our lives. We can set aside a weekly time free from worry and work, to be with Him, with our family, and with the church, and to let Him correct us with humility.
exp.45:5:
It says that no one will be able to escape defeat: neither the swift nor the mighty. The swift man is the one who runs fast, and the north is the direction in the verse. Beside the river Euphrates, to the north, the Egyptian soldiers stumbled and fell.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah about Egypt. The text connects it with the battle of Carchemish, beside the Euphrates, where Babylon defeated the Egyptian army (around 605 B.C.). Earlier it mocks the great military gathering: they prepared well, but they ended up fleeing in fear. God shows that He governs over the powers of the nations, even when they seem invincible.

For today: do not place your final security in your strength, your preparation, or your resources. Do your part well, but trust in God, because He sustains what no human power can guarantee.
exp.24:23:
This verse says that God makes all the kings of Arabia, and the kings of the mingled peoples who live in the desert, drink the cup of his judgment. "Mingled peoples" refers to groups of different origins who lived together, though scholars are not sure exactly who is meant.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, a few years before Babylon conquered Judah. In this chapter, God uses the image of a cup of wrath that many nations must drink. In this way he shows that Babylon would be his instrument, and that no people, near or far, stands outside his justice.

For today: God rules over all nations and all people. No one is so powerful or so distant that they do not owe an account to him. This invites us to live with humility and to trust that his justice is perfect.
exp.5:6:
The explanation says that the wickedness of Jerusalem is like a spring that never dries up: it always keeps flowing out. "Wickedness" is the word the verse uses for evil. The phrase about violence and spoil being heard in her means that abuse and violence can be heard on every side. The phrase about grief and wounds speaks of the harm and pain that this wickedness causes, which God sees continually.

God speaks, through the prophet Jeremiah, to Jerusalem. A few verses earlier, God announces an attack against the city because of its violence. Even so, in the following verse he calls it to turn from its ways, so his judgment also brings an invitation to return. Scholars debate the exact timing, but the central message is clear.

For today: do not let small evil become a habit. Ask God to show you which attitudes or injustices you have come to accept as normal, and deal with them soon, with humility and change.
exp.27:8:
Jeremiah says that a prophet who announces peace will only be recognized as a true messenger of the Lord when his word is fulfilled. The phrase "come to pass" is the one the verse uses, so it fits here. Until that happens, his message still has to be tested by time.

Jeremiah speaks in the temple, in front of all the people. He had put a wooden yoke on his neck to show that Judah must submit to Babylon. Hananiah, another prophet, opposed him and promised a quick peace. Jeremiah responds calmly: the earlier prophets often warned of war and disaster, so a message of peace needed a greater test. Then Hananiah breaks the yoke.

Today, not every pleasant message comes from God. Compare what you hear with Scripture, be patient, and examine whether it comes true, without being carried away only by what comforts you.
exp.27:6:
Jeremiah asks Hananiah to listen to him. He says "Nevertheless" and then goes on to say what follows in the ears of Hananiah and of all the people, that is, publicly, with everyone present.

Jeremiah speaks in the temple, in front of the priests and the people. Hananiah had just prophesied that Babylon would soon fall and that the exiles and the objects of the temple would return. Jeremiah answers with a sincere "Amen," for he would very much like it to be true. But now he remembers that a prophet is tested over time and by what God actually says.

Today we may heartily wish for good news, but we should not believe something only because it pleases us. Let us weigh every message in the light of the Bible, with humility, patience, and prayer.
exp.9:16:
It says that someone must gather up their belongings from the countryside or the surrounding lands. It speaks to a woman who lives in a fortified place, that is, a walled city. The goods here are her possessions or the things she kept outside. The command is to bring them into the city because something serious is approaching.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God. Judah trusted in its walls and in its idols, but God announces that a siege and exile are coming. The woman represents Jerusalem, or its people. Many scholars read it this way, although the text does not say so in so many words.

For today: let us not place our security in what we build, save, or own, because that can fail. Let us learn to heed God's warnings in time and to trust in Him, who is the Maker of all things.
exp.10:10:
This verse is a warning from God. It says he will bring a disaster upon the people that they will not be able to escape. When they cry out to him for help, he will not listen to them. Here "evil" means calamity or disaster, and "I will not hearken" means he will not answer their plea.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah and Jerusalem had broken the covenant that God made with their ancestors, for they went after other gods and refused to listen. For this reason the Lord announces the consequences. Then he tells them that the idols they worshiped will not be able to save them.

For today: it is not enough to seek God only when trouble comes. It is good to listen to him and to be faithful to him in everyday life, and if we have drifted away, to return to him sincerely today, without waiting for a crisis to arrive.
exp.40:8:
It says that Ishmael threw the bodies of the men he had killed into a cistern, that is, a large well for storing water. That cistern was the same one King Asa had made long before, when he was preparing against Baasha, king of Israel. Ishmael filled it with the dead.

The writer tells what happened after Ishmael murdered Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon. Ishmael kept killing people in Mizpah. The detail of the cistern shows that something made to protect and to give life ended up becoming a grave. The Bible does not explain here, with certainty, what Ishmael's motives were.

Today we can ask ourselves whether what God has given us for good, such as talents, influence or resources, we are using to serve or to harm. May our decisions never be born of envy or of violence.
exp.43:3:
God says that he sent all his prophets again and again, with persistence, to warn the people not to practice that abominable thing he hates. The word "rising early" means he did it eagerly and without rest, like someone who gets up early so as not to waste time. The "abominable thing" is offering incense to false gods.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah to the Jews who had taken refuge in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. He reminds them that the ruin of their land was no accident, but the consequence of idolatry. God shows them that his patience and his warnings were constant, but they would not listen.

For today: when God warns us through his Word, or through wise counsel and our conscience, let us not take it lightly. His correction is a sign of his care. Today we too can give up something we know grieves him.
exp.5:7:
This verse is an urgent call from God to Jerusalem: "Be instructed" means let yourself be taught and change your course. God warns that if she does not do so, his soul will depart from her, that is, he will turn away from her with grief and rejection. The result would be a land left empty, without people.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. An enemy army is about to surround the city, and God explains the reason: violence, injustice, and robbery abound inside Jerusalem, and the people do not want to hear his word. Even so, this warning shows that God still offers a chance to return to him.

For today: when a correction makes you uncomfortable, do not reject it right away. Ask God for humility to listen, and pay attention to the Bible or to wise counsel. God corrects because he wants to restore us, not destroy us.
exp.14:6:
He says that God "winnowed" his people with a winnowing fork, which was a pitchfork or shovel used to toss grain into the air to separate the chaff. In this way he scattered them as far as the gates of the land, that is, to the limits or entrances of the country. The verb rendered "bereave" means to leave someone without children, and the word for "destroy" means to break apart or ruin. The people did not turn back from their evil ways.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah and Jerusalem had abandoned God for a long time, and He had warned of judgment. The verses nearby speak of widows, losses, and terror. Scholars understand this as the announcement of the invasion that would come upon Judah.

For today: let us not confuse God's patience with permission to carry on the same way. If you feel God calling you to return, do not postpone it. He receives with grace whoever truly repents.
exp.31:35:
Here the explanation says that God, the Lord of Israel, speaks about Jerusalem. The people repeat that the city will be handed over to the king of Babylon and will die by the sword, the famine, and the pestilence.

Jeremiah speaks during the time of Babylon's siege of Jerusalem. He was imprisoned, and God had commanded him to buy a field as a sign of hope. Before giving that hope, the Lord acknowledges the cause of the judgment: idolatry and the sacrifice of children to Molech. Then, in the verses that follow, he promises to gather his people and bring them back.

For today: God is honest about the consequences of sin, but he does not stop there. If you are going through a painful consequence, do not lose hope. Acknowledge your mistake and trust that God can restore.
exp.32:24:
Here the explanation says that God has a covenant with day and night, that is, the fixed order of creation. He himself set the ordinances of heaven and earth. The verse stands as an open condition, and the next verse completes it: if that order could fail, then God would cast off Jacob and David.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah during the time of exile. The people were saying that God had rejected Israel and Judah, the two families. God answers with a comparison: his faithfulness toward his people is as certain as the dawn and the dusk. He promises to restore them and to show mercy.

For today: when you feel that God has forgotten you, or that your failures have ruined everything, look at how the sun rises every morning. Let that order remind you that God keeps his promises. Trust his faithfulness more than your feelings.
exp.33:21:
God says that he will bring the Babylonian army back to Jerusalem. They will fight against the city, capture it, and burn it. He will also leave the cities of Judah desolate, without a single inhabitant.

God speaks through Jeremiah during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem. King Zedekiah and the people had set free their Hebrew servants, as the law required, but then they took them back into slavery. In this way they broke their covenant with God. Here he announces the punishment for that disobedience. The Babylonians had withdrawn for a time, but they would return.

For today: when we give our word to God or to others, we must keep it. If we fail, God invites us to repent quickly and to make things right with sincerity, not to remain in empty promises.
exp.50:4:
The explanation says that Israel and Judah have not been left "widowed," that is, abandoned by their God, the Lord of hosts. Even though their land was full of sin against the Holy One of Israel, God did not leave them or break his relationship with them. To be left widowed is to lose a husband; here it means that God remains faithful to his people.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God, announcing judgment on Babylon, the power that had subdued Judah. The verses nearby describe the fall of Babylon and call people to flee from it. God shows that his people, though disciplined for their sin, were not forgotten, and that he will also judge those who punished them.

For today: when you fail, do not think that God has abandoned you. His correction seeks to restore you, not to destroy you. Return to him with sincerity and trust in his faithfulness.
exp.30:33:
It says that a time will come when no one will have to tell another, "Know the Lord," because everyone will know him, from the least to the greatest. The reason is that God will forgive their wickedness and will remember their sin no more. The words "neighbour" and "brother" in the verse refer to a fellow citizen and a companion. Saying God will "remember their sin no more" means that God will not hold their sin against them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to a people who had broken the covenant and were suffering the consequences. God promises a new covenant, with his law written on the heart. Christians see its fulfillment in Jesus (Hebrews 8); others interpret it in other ways.

For today: you can draw near to God without fear, trusting in his forgiveness. Knowing him is not only learning facts, but living in relationship with Him, and asking that his word transform your heart each day.
exp.25:5:
God says he will do to the temple in Jerusalem what he did to Shiloh, and that the city will be used as an example of a curse among all the nations. The phrase "make this city a curse" means that other peoples would name it as an example of punishment.

Jehovah speaks through Jeremiah, who is standing in the temple court. God warns that if the people continue not to keep his law or listen to the prophets he sent them again and again, they will lose the temple. Shiloh was an ancient place of worship that was destroyed; the Bible remembers it as a warning. The leaders and the people reacted with violence and wanted to kill Jeremiah.

For today: religion without obedience does not protect us. When God corrects us through his Word, it is wise to listen with humility, even when it hurts, instead of defending ourselves or rejecting the message.
exp.51:24:
At the fall of Jerusalem, the Babylonians took prisoner several important men of the city. Among them was a eunuch, an officer who commanded the soldiers, and seven men who were close to the king, that is, counselors who were always near him. They also took the chief scribe of the army, the one in charge of enlisting people for the war, and sixty ordinary men of the people.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah speaks, recording the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon, around 586 B.C. Nebuzaradan, commander of the Babylonian guard, removed the leaders who could organize resistance again. The text presents this as the consequence of years of disobedience, just as Jeremiah had warned.

For today: God speaks to us patiently before the consequences arrive. Today we can listen to His Word and correct our course in time, trusting in His mercy.
exp.31:5:
Here Jeremiah tells that God spoke to him. The phrase "the word of the Lord came to me" means that the Lord gave him a message. The verse only sets up what God is about to say next.

Jeremiah the prophet speaks, and he is shut up in the courtyard of the prison because he had announced that Jerusalem would fall to Babylon. The Babylonian armies were already surrounding the city. In that dark moment, God speaks to him about a family field in Anathoth, which a cousin will come to offer for sale.

For today: God knows how to speak to us even in difficult times. When everything seems closed off, we can stop, listen for his voice in his Word, and trust that he is still guiding our path.
exp.41:14:
Here God speaks to the small group that survived in Judah. He tells them: "Hear his word." If they decide to set their faces toward Egypt and live there as foreigners, a serious consequence will follow. The sentence is left open, and the next verse completes it. The survivors are the ones who were left behind, the remnant.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, the people fear Babylon and ask Jeremiah to pray so they will know what to do. They promise to obey. But God has already told them to stay in the land, and here he warns them against fleeing to Egypt to seek safety on their own.

Today, we sometimes ask God for direction when, deep down, we have already decided what we want. Before praying, ask yourself whether you are truly willing to obey, even if the answer frightens you. The security God gives is worth more than the security we try to find for ourselves.
exp.49:16:
Israel was like a lost and scattered flock. The lions were powerful nations that attacked it. First Assyria devoured it, and last of all Babylon, under Nebuchadrezzar, broke its bones, meaning it crushed Israel and left it without strength.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that Babylon will fall because of the violence with which it treated other peoples. But the next verse offers hope: God will punish Babylon, as He did earlier with Assyria, and will bring Israel back to its land so that it may live again in peace and abundance.

For today: if you feel wounded, lost, or without strength, remember that God does not abandon His people. He sees injustice, knows how to heal, and can restore what others destroyed. Trust in His care and in His justice.
exp.8:7:
It says that the words of these people are like a sharp arrow: they wound. They speak with deceit. In front of their friend they say "peace," but in the heart they prepare a trap. The word for "trap" here means hidden schemes or plots meant to harm someone.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah lived surrounded by lies and had stopped knowing God. Therefore the Lord announces that he will melt them down and test them, as metal is purified in the fire. At the same time his sorrow shows: he weeps over what will come upon the land.

For today: let us take care that our words match what is in the heart. Let us ask God for sincerity, so that our "good morning" and our affection are true, and not a mask that hides resentment.
exp.26:5:
He says that God himself has placed all those lands under the power of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. He calls him "my servant," meaning someone God uses to carry out his purpose. Even the beasts of the field fall under his rule. "I have given" means "I have handed over."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This message was meant to reach the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon, and also Judah. God was asking them to accept Babylonian rule and not rebel. Calling him "servant" does not mean that Nebuchadnezzar was righteous, but that God directs history, and the passage itself says his time would also come to an end.

Even when governments seem strong, God is still the one in charge. We can trust that he guides history, and ask him for humility to obey him when his ways are not easy for us to understand.
exp.21:8:
This verse is the answer to the previous question. When people ask why God let Jerusalem fall, others will say it was because the people abandoned the covenant, that is, the commitment of faithfulness they had to the Lord. Instead, they worshipped other gods, that is, gods of other nations, and served them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing the royal house of Judah. He warns them that the city will be destroyed. What matters is that the cause is not bad luck or only politics, but the unfaithfulness of the people and their leaders. God had warned them before this outcome.

For today: God invites us to care for our faithfulness. Today "other gods" can be good things that become first in our lives, such as money or success. Ask yourself what has taken God's place in your heart, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.16:25:
This verse describes a promised blessing. If the people obey, people from everywhere will come to the temple: from the cities of Judah, from the areas around Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, from the plain, from the mountains, and from the south, the region toward the Negev. They will bring burnt offerings, sacrifices, grain offerings, incense, and sacrifices of praise, that is, gratitude expressed to God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Before this passage, God asks the people to keep the Sabbath without carrying loads or doing business. If they obey, Jerusalem will remain and its worship will flourish. Then comes the warning: if they do not obey, there will be fire. God offers them a clear choice, and the Sabbath reveals whether their hearts are faithful to him.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest from your work and give thanks to God. That rest can become your sacrifice of praise: singing, praying, and acknowledging that he sustains your life.
exp.17:1:
God tells Jeremiah to get up and go down to the potter's house, the one who works with clay. There he will speak to him. Some words are old-fashioned, and the explanation of them must be rewritten or dropped for this reader.

The Lord speaks, and the message is for his prophet Jeremiah. The verses that follow show that God uses an everyday scene: the potter reshapes a damaged vessel. Later the text applies the image to Israel and the nations, although scholars debate how some details are to be applied.

For today: God can speak to us in the simple and ordinary things of daily life. Today you might pause in the middle of a common task, with an attentive heart, and ask him what he wants to teach you. He also knows how to remake us when something breaks.
exp.5:28:
What it says: Jeremiah uses the image of a silver refiner. The bellows is the device that blows air to fan the fire. Here "are burned" refers to the intense heat. Lead was added to clean the silver of impurities, but the lead was also consumed. "The founder melteth in vain" means the refiner worked for nothing, because the dross, that is, the wicked, did not come out.

Context: God speaks to Jeremiah, whom he placed as a tester of his people. Judah was a rebellious people, full of deceit. God had tried to cleanse them with warnings and punishments, but they did not change. That is why the next verse says they will be called rejected silver.

For today: God corrects in order to cleanse, not to destroy. If He points out something in us, let us not harden our hearts. Let us ask Him today to show us what needs to be removed from our lives, and respond with humility and repentance.
exp.44:0:
This verse presents a message that the prophet Jeremiah gave to Baruch, son of Neriah. Baruch was the one who wrote in a book what Jeremiah told him by word of mouth. This took place in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, king of Judah. The word "saying" at the end announces that the message comes right after.

Baruch was Jeremiah's secretary. That year, the fourth of Jehoiakim, was a time of great tension in Judah, and writing down Jeremiah's words was a dangerous task. The one speaking here is Jeremiah, but on behalf of God, and the message that follows responds to the discouragement Baruch was feeling.

For today: God sees the people who serve in silence and grow weary. If you are exhausted or sad, bring Him honestly what you feel, because He listens to you and knows how to speak to you with care.
exp.43:24:
God speaks with a tone of rebuke, almost ironic. He tells them that they and their wives made promises with their mouths and carried them out with their hands: burning incense to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her. Then he tells them: "Go ahead, keep your vows and fulfill them."

Jeremiah speaks to the Jews who had taken refuge in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. They insisted on continuing to worship the queen of heaven, a goddess that many scholars connect with Ishtar or Astarte, though this is debated. They believed that this worship had brought them prosperity. God warns them that their idolatry was the cause of their misfortune.

Today: a promise made to something mistaken does not oblige us to keep the error. Let us examine what we have pledged our loyalty to, and if it is not from God, let us have the humility to make it right.
exp.22:32:
Here God teaches how to respond when someone asks, "What is the burden of the Lord?" The word "burden" in the Hebrew (massa) can mean "weight" or "prophetic message." It is thought there was a play on words: God answers, "What burden?" and then says that He Himself will cast them off, like someone who sets down a heavy load. Some scholars translate it "You are the burden," and this is a possible reading.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf against false prophets who invented messages and said "Thus says the Lord" without His having sent them. They used the phrase "burden of the Lord" to give weight to their words and to mock the true prophet.

For today: before saying "God told me" or repeating what others say God said, let us examine whether it agrees with Scripture. Using God's name lightly is serious; it is better to ask humbly, "What has the Lord answered?"
exp.48:33:
This verse introduces a new prophecy. God gives Jeremiah, his prophet, a message about Elam. The phrase "that came to Jeremiah" means that the word of the Lord came to him. It is placed at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah, who ruled from about 597 B.C.

The one speaking is the Lord, and Jeremiah receives the message and passes it on. Elam was a nation east of Babylon, in the region of today's southwestern Iran. The verses that follow announce that God will break its power and scatter its people. It is one of Jeremiah's prophecies against the nations, which show that God rules over all peoples, not only over Israel.

For today: God remains Lord of history, even when the powers of the world seem strong. We can rest in the fact that nothing escapes his control. Trust in him, and seek to live with humility, without relying on your own strength.
exp.51:29:
This verse says that in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, carried away captive 745 people from Judah. Adding up all the groups mentioned, the total was 4,600 people. "Carried away" means he took them into exile in another land.

The author, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though some think this appendix was added by another hand, closes the book with a record of the exiles. The figures are lower than others that appear in the Old Testament, and it is not known for certain why; various explanations have been proposed, such as that different groups were counted. What matters is that the prophecies of judgment were fulfilled. But the book ends with hope: King Jehoiachin is released from prison.

God keeps his word, and he also holds hope for his people. If you are going through a hard season today, trust that God sees every detail of your life and can still open a door of grace.
exp.22:33:
It says that if a prophet, a priest, or any person from the people uses the expression "the burden of the Lord," God himself will punish that person and his household. The word "burden" in Hebrew (massa) can mean "weight" or also "solemn message." "Punish" here is "I will visit," that is, I will call to account.

God speaks through Jeremiah, in the days of Judah before the exile. There were prophets who claimed to speak on God's behalf, but they made up messages. Some probably used that phrase mockingly or to give false authority to their words. For this reason God forbids the expression and judges those who distort his word.

For today: before saying "God told me" or "the Bible says," let us think with humility and check whether what we say is truly faithful to Scripture. Using God's name to back up our own ideas is something very serious.
exp.22:29:
God says he is against the prophets who "steal" his words, meaning they take them. Each one takes them from his neighbor, repeating what another said and presenting it as if it came from God.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. In that time, many prophets said they had a message from God, but they gave their own dreams and borrowed phrases, and they promised false peace. God confronts them because they deceived the people and he had not sent them. His true word is like fire and like a hammer, not like straw.

Today we can be careful not to repeat beautiful phrases as if they were the word of God without checking them. Before we teach or share something, let us compare it with the Bible, and speak with humility and truth.
exp.2:18:
God says that he asked himself how he could treat his people as children and give them a beautiful land, the most precious inheritance among the nations. The word "pleasant" means delightful and valuable; "a goodly heritage of the hosts of nations" is understood as the most glorious among the peoples. God hoped they would call him "My father" and that they would not turn away from following him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had been unfaithful to him, as the next verse shows, where he compares them to a wife who betrays her husband. Even so, God expresses his desire for a close relationship and announces a future restoration.

For today: God does not want only obedience, but a relationship of trust like that of a father with his children. Today you can speak to him sincerely, call him "Father," and ask him for help so that you do not turn away from him.
exp.18:5:
God says that days are coming when this place will no longer be called Tophet or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter. Tophet was the site within that valley, near Jerusalem, where sacrifices were made. "Slaughter" announces that the place would be marked by death and judgment.

God speaks through Jeremiah. The people had abandoned him, worshiped Baal, and burned their children in the fire, something God never commanded. They filled the place with innocent blood. That is why the name of the place would change: what they used for sin would be remembered for punishment. In context, this announces the fall of Jerusalem before its enemies.

For today: God takes injustice and harm to the innocent seriously. Let us ask him to deliver us from following customs that seem normal but dishonor him, and to return to him with humility.
exp.15:13:
This verse says that God announces a change. Until now people swore by saying, "The Lord lives, who brought up Israel out of Egypt." But days will come when that will no longer be the main saying.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just announced the exile because of the people's idolatry and hardness of heart. Even so, before finishing the warning, God adds a promise: there will be a return. What follows compares it with the exodus, but presents it as a deliverance that will be remembered even more, coming from the north and from other lands.

For today: God disciplines, but He does not abandon. If you are going through the consequences of your own mistakes or those of others, remember that He can open a new path. Trust in His faithfulness and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.1:11:
God calls the heavens to be astonished, to be horrified and completely appalled. It is a poetic way of saying that what his people have done is so serious that even creation should be amazed. "Be appalled" means to be left empty or ruined by the shock.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, God asked them to look toward Kittim (to the west) and Kedar (to the east) to see whether any nation had changed its gods, even though those gods were false. Israel, however, abandoned the true God, their glory, for things that cannot help them. God's pain is that of someone who has been betrayed.

For today: examine where you place your trust and your heart. God is the source of life; if we exchange him for money, success, or approval, we are left empty. Return to him with sincerity.
exp.15:4:
