God tells Jeremiah not to enter a house where there is mourning, not to go and weep with the family or offer them comfort. The reason is that God has taken away his peace, his mercy, and his compassion from this people. It is a harsh sign that the judgment is already unavoidable.

The Lord speaks to his prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people had rejected God again and again. That Jeremiah should not take part in the mourning was a public sign: there would be so many deaths that no one would be left to bury or comfort the dead. Scholars understand in different ways whether this also protected Jeremiah or only announced the judgment.

For today: God calls us to listen to him in time, before we harden our hearts. Today, through Christ, we can draw near to his mercy with confidence. Let us not let it pass; let us come to him with humility, and also comfort those who are suffering.
exp.22:8:
Here Jeremiah says that he is broken within because of the prophets. His bones shake, and he feels like a drunken man, that is, without strength and staggering. "Broken" means made into pieces. "The north" is the direction of the north. "The words of his holiness" are the holy words of God.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. God has just promised that he will bring his people back, but Jeremiah sees that many prophets and priests are false and are leading the people down the wrong path. That is why he trembles before the holiness of God and the seriousness of that sin.

For today: let us take God's Word seriously, and those who teach it. We can compare what we hear with the Bible, pray for our leaders, and ask God for a heart that grieves over sin, not one that ignores it.
exp.10:4:
He says that God will keep the promise he swore to Israel's ancestors: to give them a land "flowing with milk and honey," that is, fertile and abundant. "As it is this day" shows that the promise was already seen as fulfilled in the present. Jeremiah answers "So be it," meaning "Yes, let it be" or "I agree."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, and Jeremiah replies. God recalls the covenant made when he brought Israel out of Egypt, called an "iron furnace" because of the suffering of slavery. The people enjoyed the land, but they did not obey. So God reminds them that his faithfulness was joined to the call to obey.

For today: God has been faithful to you in many things. Respond as Jeremiah did, with a sincere "So be it," that is, with gratitude and with concrete obedience. Today, choose one thing God asks of you and do it.
exp.3:4:
This verse is a command to sound the alarm. The people are told to announce in Judah and in Jerusalem that the trumpet should be blown, that the people should gather together, and that they should run for shelter into the fortified cities, that is, the cities with walls. The word "declare" means to proclaim aloud.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, He called Judah to turn back to Him wholeheartedly, and warned that His anger would come like fire because of the people's wickedness. Now the warning becomes urgent: a disaster is coming from the north. The following passages describe it as a destroying lion, and many relate it to Babylon.

For today: do not ignore God's warnings or put off repentance until tomorrow. If you sense that something in your life or in your heart needs to change, return to Him today, with sincerity and humility.
exp.50:13:
God makes a solemn oath: "by himself," that is, by the most serious thing he can swear by. He promises that he will fill Babylon with men, as many as locusts, a plague that covers everything. Those enemies will raise a shout, the cry of victory of an army that conquers. The "hosts" here speak of the mighty armies of heaven and earth, under his command.

Jeremiah announces God's judgment against Babylon, the empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed his people. God himself speaks and says that this rich and proud city has reached its limit: the measure of your greed. The verses that follow remind us that the one who makes this promise is the Creator of all things.

For today: no human power, however rich or strong it may seem, stands above God. We can rest in knowing that he sees injustice and fulfills his word in his time, and we can also examine whether our own greed needs to be corrected.
exp.4:9:
God says that an invading army is to climb up the city's walls and destroy it, but without finishing everything off. The phrase about not making a full end means: do not wipe it out completely. He also commands them to take away the battlements, the projecting tops or parapets of the walls, because those defenses are not the Lord's: they do not belong to him and have no backing from him.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. First he describes a society marked by unfaithfulness and wickedness, and then he says the people rebelled and denied God, believing that no harm would come. Many understand the invaders to be the Babylonians, although the text does not name them here. The judgment is serious, but it is not total.

For today: let us not trust in defenses that God does not stand behind, such as pride, religious habit, or self-sufficiency. If God corrects, it is so that we will return to him, and even in discipline there is mercy.
exp.32:2:
Gód invites his people to call out to him, that is, to call on him sincerely and out of real need. He promises that he will answer and that he will show them "great and mighty things," meaning things that are vast and hard to grasp, things the person does not yet know. The word "mighty" can also be understood as things that are hidden or beyond the reach of human understanding.

The one speaking is the LORD, and he speaks to Jeremiah while the prophet is imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard. Jerusalem is surrounded by the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), and everything seems lost. Even so, God promises something beyond the ruin: in the verses that follow he speaks of healing and restoration. Scholars understand that promise mainly as applying to Israel at that time.

For today: when you feel shut in or without a way out, pray to God honestly. He will not always give the result you hope for, but you can trust that he hears and guides.
exp.49:1:
It says God commands that the announcement be made to all the nations, without hiding anything, and that a banner be raised as a signal, declaring that Babylon has already been taken. "Bel" and "Merodach" were the names of their chief god, and the carved images and idols they worshiped were the figures they bowed to. The text affirms that these gods were put to shame and broken in pieces.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had dominated Judah and destroyed Jerusalem, and it trusted in its power and in its gods. This message announces that its fall comes from the hand of the God of Israel. It is spoken as though it had already happened, to show that it is certain. The verses that follow speak of God's people returning in tears to seek him.

For today: Whatever we put in place of God, such as money, success, or power, sooner or later falls. Today you can ask yourself what you truly trust in, and place your hope again in God, who does not fail.
exp.1:19:
God says that long ago he broke the yoke and the chains that oppressed his people, that is, he freed them from slavery. But the people answered, "I will not serve." Instead of following God, they ran to the high places and gave themselves to idolatry under every leafy tree.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Judah of abandoning him after he had rescued them, and of seeking security in Egypt and Assyria and in false gods. High places and trees were common sites of pagan worship. The image of marriage shows the pain of a betrayed love.

For today: the freedom God gives us is not meant for living without him, but for serving him in love. Ask yourself what things you seek to feel secure or satisfied in place of God, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.34:5:
The Rechabites answer that they will drink no wine. The reason is that their ancestor Jonadab, son of Rechab, commanded them that neither they nor their sons should ever drink wine.

Here the family of the Rechabites speaks, the same people the prophet Jeremiah tested in the temple when he deliberately offered them wine. God uses this scene as an example: they faithfully obeyed a human father for generations, while Judah did not obey God, who spoke to them again and again. The point is not to teach that all wine is sin, but to show faithfulness.

For today: ask yourself whether you are as steady in obeying God as these men were in keeping their commitment. Choose one specific thing God has shown you today and carry it out firmly, even when no one sees you.
exp.22:34:
This verse says that people should ask one another in a simple way: "What hath the Lord answered?" and "What hath the Lord spoken?" The words "every one to his neighbour" and "every one to his brother" mean that each person speaks to his friend or neighbor. God is teaching them the right way to talk about his message.

God speaks through Jeremiah. At that time, some false prophets used the phrase "burden of the Lord" to give weight to their own ideas. God corrects this misuse, because they were twisting his words. That is why he asks them to ask again what he actually said.

Before repeating what others say God has spoken, it is wise to ask: what does the Bible really say? We can examine the Scriptures with humility and not use God's name to support our own opinions.
exp.24:10:
This verse says that the whole land of Judah would be left desolate and would be a horror to see. Also, these nations would have to serve the king of Babylon for seventy years. "Desolate" means an empty, abandoned place, and "horror" is something that leaves those who see it stunned.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After years of warning without being listened to, he announces that the people will suffer the consequences of their rebellion. He calls Nebuchadnezzar "my servant" because he would use him as an instrument of judgment, though that does not excuse the wickedness of Babylon. For this reason, after the seventy years, God would also judge Babylon. Scholars understand in different ways how to count those seventy years.

For today: God speaks clearly and is patient, but he takes our decisions seriously. If you have ignored one of his warnings, do not wait any longer: return to him today. Even judgment has a limit, and God remains the one in control.
exp.24:30:
It says that the noise of God's judgment reaches the most distant places on the earth. God has a dispute, that is, an accusation, against all the nations. He is the Judge of every person on the earth, of all humanity. The wicked are those who live without respecting God, and being given over to the sword means they will be handed over to the sword.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, a few years before Babylon conquered Judah. God had already warned that he would judge his own people, and here he makes clear that no nation will be free from giving him an account.

For today: God judges with justice, and no one escapes his gaze. This invites us to examine our hearts with humility, seek his forgiveness, and live with reverence toward him, without thinking ourselves free to answer before our Creator.
exp.11:3:
Here Jeremiah asks how much longer the land will suffer. It is dry, the grass looks withered, and the animals and birds have disappeared. The cause, he says, is the wickedness of the people who live there. They were saying: "He shall not see our last end," that is, "God will not see how we end up" or "Jeremiah will not see our final end." It can be understood in both ways.

Jeremiah speaks with God, complaining because the wicked seem to prosper while the land suffers. This takes place in Judah, probably when there was drought. Many people spoke about God with their mouths, but their hearts were far from him. Jeremiah was also rejected by his own family.

For today: you can bring your questions and your pain to God with sincerity, as Jeremiah did. And remember that God does see how we live and how we will end, so it is worth living with honesty before him.
exp.31:8:
Jeremiah tells that he bought the field of his cousin Hanameel, located in Anathoth. He paid by weighing out seventeen shekels of silver. In the verse your reader sees, "weighed him the money" refers to the silver being weighed out, because at that time coins were not used as they are today.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. He is imprisoned in the courtyard of the prison, because Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon. God had told him that his cousin would come to ask him to buy the field, according to the law of redemption within the family. When Hanameel arrived, Jeremiah recognized that it was the word of God. His purchase showed hope: someday the people would live again in that land.

For today: even when everything seems lost, we can take concrete steps of faith and obedience. Trusting God does not mean ignoring difficulty, but acting with hope in his promises.
exp.43:29:
God says that he will hand Pharaoh Hophra, king of Egypt, over to his enemies, to those who seek to take his life. He compares this with what happened to Zedekiah, king of Judah, whom God handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Seeking his life means trying to take his life, wanting to kill him. To hand over means that God allows him to fall into their power.

Jeremiah speaks to the Jews who fled to Egypt, disobeying God, thinking they would be safe there. God gives them a sign: if Egypt falls, they will know that his word is fulfilled and that they should not have trusted in that country. The history records that Hophra (Apries) lost his power in Egypt, though the details of his fall are told in several ways.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we trust as a refuge. Human powers change and fall, but the word of God endures. Let us seek his guidance before seeking security elsewhere.
exp.38:14:
This verse says that God had already given Jeremiah a message while he was still held in the court of the prison. The phrase "the word of the Lord had come" means that God had spoken to him before the Babylonians brought him out.

The author presents this detail as a step back in time. Jerusalem had already fallen, but the text recalls a promise made earlier to Ebed-melech, the Ethiopian who had defended Jeremiah (Jeremiah 38). The Lord is the one speaking, and he wants to show that he keeps his word to someone who acted with courage.

For today: God sees the acts of kindness we do, even when no one else notices them or when the things around us are falling apart. We can do what is right and trust that he will care for us in his own way and in his own time.
exp.48:7:
God warns the inhabitants of Dedan to flee and hide themselves in deep caves. "Deep caves" here refers to deep pits or hollows. "The calamity of Esau" is the ruin that comes upon Edom, since Esau was its ancestor. "Visit" here means coming to call someone to account, that is, to punish.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message against Edom. Dedan was a neighboring people, probably allied with or related to Edom, so it too was in danger. God shows that neither the reputation for wisdom of Teman nor hiding places could save Edom when its time came.

For today: we cannot hide from God or trust in our own wisdom or security. It is better to draw near to Him with humility and seek His forgiveness while there is still time.
exp.23:0:
God showed Jeremiah a vision: two baskets of figs set in front of the temple. This happens after Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had carried into captivity Jeconiah (son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah), the leaders of the people, the officials, and the craftsmen and smiths.

The Lord speaks, and Jeremiah tells it in the first person. This takes place around 597 B.C., when a first group of the people was taken into exile. God uses the image of the figs to explain what He thinks of those who were taken away and of those who stayed behind. The verse only sets the scene; the explanation comes later in the chapter.

For today: God does not judge only by appearances or by difficult circumstances. A painful situation may not be a sign of rejection on His part. We can trust that He sees us with care and that He keeps working even in hard times.
exp.30:37:
The explanation says that days are coming when Jerusalem will be rebuilt and dedicated to the Lord, that is, set apart for him. Its boundaries are marked: from the tower of Hananeel, on the north side, to the gate of the corner, which was probably on the northwest side. The phrase "built to the Lord" means that the city will belong to him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the section known as "the book of comfort." The people were under judgment and would soon be taken into exile. Even so, God promises restoration and a new covenant. The verses before this one assure that God will not completely reject Israel. The boundaries mentioned show that the promise is concrete. Some see it fulfilled in part with the return from exile, and others also look for its fulfillment in the future.

For today: God keeps what he promises even when everything seems to be in ruins. Today you can entrust your broken areas to him and ask him to rebuild them for himself.
exp.8:19:
He says the women should listen closely to what God speaks. He asks them to teach their daughters and their friends to sing "wailing", which are songs of mourning and sorrow, and "lamentation", that is, weeping expressed in words. It is not advice for easing pain, but a call to recognize how serious what is coming is.

Jeremiah announces God's judgment on Judah, and the disaster is so great that death enters even the palaces. In that culture there were women who led the mourning laments. Here God charges them to teach the lament to the next generation, because the grief will be very widespread.

For today: do not flee from grief or hide it. Learn to weep honestly before God, teach your children to do the same, and accompany those who suffer with your presence and your words.
exp.48:1:
This verse announces that God will bring a time of judgment on Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites. The sound of war will be heard, the city will be turned into a heap of ruins, and its towns (called "daughters" in some other versions) will be burned with fire. Destruction here means complete ruin. In the end, Israel will recover what had been taken from it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The Ammonites had taken over the territory of Gad, which belonged to Israel, as though Israel had no heirs. God does not overlook that injustice. Scholars debate exactly how and when this prophecy was fulfilled, but the message is clear: God judges pride and abuse.

For today: do not lose heart when you see injustice or abuse that seems to go unanswered. Trust that God sees, and avoid taking advantage of others, because He holds people accountable.
exp.1:22:
God asks his people how they dare to say they are not defiled and have never gone after the Baals, which were false gods of the Canaanites. He asks them to look at their conduct in the valley, probably a place where idolatry was practiced; some think of the valley of Hinnom, though this is not certain. He compares them to a swift young camel that runs back and forth without direction, driven by its desires.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah was denying its idolatry, even though its actions showed it. Earlier, God had said that its sin was engraved, meaning marked deeply and impossible to hide or wash away with simple rituals.

Today we can ask God to show us our hearts honestly. Instead of making excuses or comparing ourselves with others, let us acknowledge what we have done and return to him, for he forgives the one who repents.
exp.40:16:
It says that Johanan and the people who had been rescued went to live in Geruth-chimham, a place near Bethlehem. They did this as a stop, intending to continue on the way to Egypt. The verse's word "dwelt" means they settled there for a while. The name Geruth-chimham is usually understood as a place of lodging or an inn, though its exact meaning is uncertain.

Here the narrator speaks. Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, had been murdered by Ishmael. Johanan rescued the people, but he feared the Chaldeans would take revenge. That is why they were thinking of fleeing to Egypt. Later, in chapter 42, they ask God for counsel through Jeremiah, though it seems they were already inclined to leave.

For today: fear can lead us to decide before we pray. Before we act, let us seek God with a heart willing to obey, even if his answer is not the one we were expecting.
exp.31:17:
This verse says that God shows mercy to thousands of people, and also that the consequences of the wickedness of the parents reach their children. The word "thousands" is simply the number of people meant, and the phrase about the consequences falling "into the bosom" of the children is a way of saying that those consequences land on them. Then it calls God great, mighty, and the Lord of hosts, that is, the Lord of all the powers of heaven and earth.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, in prayer. Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon and he is a prisoner, but God had told him to buy a field as a sign that one day the people would return to their land. Jeremiah prays by remembering who God is.

For today: when everything seems lost, remember that God is merciful and at the same time just. Pray as Jeremiah did, trusting in God's character, and think too about the example you leave to those who come after you.
exp.7:6:
It says that even the birds of the sky know when it is time to migrate: the stork, the turtle dove, the crane, and the swallow return at exactly the right time. But God's people do not recognize "the judgment of the Lord," that is, what God commands and what He justly decides.

The passage records God speaking through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had turned to idolatry and injustice, and no one repented. God compares the instinct of the birds with the stubbornness of the people, who boast of being wise and of having the law, yet reject the word of the Lord.

For today: it is not enough to know things about God; we need to return to Him with humility. Today, think of an area where you sense God calling you to change, and respond with a sincere prayer and one concrete step.
exp.22:30:
God says that he is against certain prophets. The words "that use their tongues" refer to people who speak smooth, pleasing words, like someone who sweetens what they say. Then they declare, "He saith," meaning they speak as if God had given them that message. The wording of this line is somewhat difficult, and some translations understand it as "that use their tongues and declare, He says."

The speaker is the Lord, through Jeremiah. Judah was surrounded by prophets who said what the people wanted to hear, even though God had not sent them. Shortly before, God compares his word to fire and to a hammer that breaks the rock: it is powerful, not merely pleasant.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are looking for messages that comfort us or for the truth of God. It is wise to compare what we hear with the Bible, even when it makes us uncomfortable.
exp.32:19:
It speaks of God having a covenant (or pact) with day and night, that is, the fixed order in which they follow one another. And it asks: "Can you break it, so that there will no longer be day and night in their season?" The sentence is left unfinished here and is completed in the following verse. To "annul" means to cancel or undo. "In their season" means "at the right time."

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah, who was in a time of crisis for Judah. God promises to restore his people. He uses something no one can change, the order of days and nights, to show that his promise to David and to the Levites is just as certain.

For today: every sunrise is a reminder that God keeps what he promises. When you feel doubt or fear, look at the rising sun and rest in the fact that his faithfulness is firmer than any circumstance.
exp.13:13:
God answers Jeremiah and tells him that the prophets who speak in his name are lying. He did not send them, he did not command them, and he did not speak to them. What they announce is a false vision, divination, a thing of nothing, and a deceit that comes from their own heart.

Jeremiah had interceded for a people suffering from drought and famine. God tells him that he will not listen to their fasting. Jeremiah complains that the prophets promise peace and no war. Here God speaks and makes clear that these promises do not come from him. For that reason the people, who believed the deception, will also face the consequences.

Today it is wise to compare what we hear, even when it sounds spiritual or encouraging, with what the Bible says. That someone uses God's name does not prove that they speak on his behalf. A pleasant word is not always true.
exp.31:7:
Jeremiah tells us that his cousin Hanameel came to the courtyard of the prison, just as the Lord had already told him he would. He asked Jeremiah to buy his field in Anathoth, because Jeremiah had the family right to acquire it. The word "redemption" here means buying back a property so that it does not leave the family. When Jeremiah saw that everything was happening just as God had said, he knew the message came from Him.

Jeremiah was in prison, since Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon. God announced this purchase to him as a sign: although destruction and exile would come, one day the people would again buy and farm the land. Many understand this as a promise of hope.

For today: when God confirms his word step by step, we can trust him even in difficult times. Dare to take steps of faith, knowing that he keeps his promises.
exp.22:15:
This verse is a warning from God to his people. It tells them not to listen to prophets who bring them pleasant messages. The phrase "they make you vain" means that they fill people's heads with empty illusions and false hopes. Those prophets say whatever comes to their minds, not what God has actually told them.

God himself speaks, through Jeremiah, in a time of sin in Judah. The prophets of Jerusalem were living wickedly and encouraged the people to continue in their evil, telling them that everything would be fine and that no punishment would come. That is why God rebukes them so sharply, and the people were in danger for believing them.

For today: before accepting a spiritual message, let us compare it with the Bible. That a message is pleasant does not prove that it comes from God. Let us seek the truth, even when it sometimes confronts us.
exp.6:28:
God tells Jeremiah to cut off his hair and throw it away, and to raise a lament on the bare hills. It is a sign of mourning, because God has rejected this generation that provoked his anger. The verse uses the word "cut off," and the hills are the high places where the people carried out their rituals.

God speaks to the prophet Jeremiah just after telling him that the people will not listen to him. Judah had disobeyed, rejected correction, and practiced idolatry, even in the temple. Some understand that the cut hair may refer to the prophet or to the people; the text allows both readings.

For today: when we see that we are drifting away from God, or that others are, it is not enough to judge. God invites us to listen to his correction in time, and to weep sincerely and pray for those who have turned away.
exp.24:29:
God says that, like a lion, he will roar from heaven, from his holy dwelling, and his voice will be heard with force. "Roar" is the word used for a loud, deep cry. The ones who tread the grapes in the winepress are those who stomp on the grapes to get the wine; they sang and shouted while they trod. In this way, God will make his judgment heard against all the inhabitants of the earth.

God speaks to the prophet Jeremiah and commands him to announce this message. It comes after the image of the cup of God's anger, which the nations must drink. God begins the judgment with his own people, the city that bears his name, and then it reaches the other nations. Scholars often see here a judgment against wickedness and injustice.

God is holy and just, and he does not ignore evil. This invites us not to take his patience lightly, but to examine our hearts, repent, and return to him with humility.
exp.47:43:
This verse says that Moab will not be able to escape God's judgment. If someone flees in terror, they fall into a pit (a hole dug to trap animals). If they manage to climb out of the pit, they are caught in a snare (a trap made of rope). The phrase "the year of their visitation" refers to the time when God steps in to hold them accountable.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel, had become proud against God; it grew arrogant and rose up against Him. For this reason He announces its downfall. The images show that every attempt to escape only leads to another danger.

For today: let us not trust in our own cleverness or strength to escape the consequences of living in pride. It is better to humble ourselves now, ask God for forgiveness, and seek His mercy, because He is just, but He also forgives those who turn back to Him.
exp.4:18:
The explanation says that when the people ask why God has brought such misfortune upon them, the answer will be clear: you abandoned God and served false gods in your own land, so now you will serve foreigners in a land that is not yours. The phrase "gods of others" refers to the gods of other peoples; "strangers" means foreigners.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, shortly before the invasion of an enemy people (the text presents this as a punishment). Earlier in the chapter, the destruction of crops and cities has already been announced, but God makes clear that He will not finish them off completely. The punishment is not a whim: it responds to persistent idolatry. Even so, it leaves room for hope.

When something goes wrong for us, it is good to ask ourselves humbly whether we have put other things in the place of God. Not all suffering is punishment, but examining the heart always brings us closer to Him.
exp.4:27:
They have grown fat and sleek. That means they lived well fed and looked prosperous. "They have gone beyond the deeds of the wicked" means their evil went past every limit; they were worse than ordinary wrongdoers. They did not plead the cause of the orphan or the cause of the poor, that is, they did not do justice in the courts, and still things went well for them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses his people of getting rich through deceit and of taking advantage of the weakest. The next verse shows that God will not overlook this: he will call them to account.

For today: God pays attention to how we treat those who cannot defend themselves. Think of a vulnerable person near you, such as a child, an elderly person, or a worker who is underpaid, and look for a concrete way to help them or to speak up on their behalf.
exp.34:11:
This verse is a short phrase that marks a turning point. It says that God spoke to Jeremiah. The wording "came" is the older form of the verb, and it is simply a way of saying the word of the Lord arrived to him. Up to this point, the Rechabites had been telling how they obeyed their ancestor Jonadab. Now God himself takes up the word to say something.

The one speaking is the Lord, and the messenger is the prophet Jeremiah. The Rechabites had come to Jerusalem fleeing the Babylonian army, but they remained faithful to the command not to drink wine or live in houses. God uses this example to show that the people of Judah were not obeying him, even though he spoke to them again and again.

For today: before giving a lesson, God invites us to look closely. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are listening to his voice in the Bible with the same seriousness that others keep a promise made to their family.
exp.12:23:
God says he will scatter his people like chaff, the light husk of the grain that comes loose when it is threshed. The wind carries it away without any effort. The "wind of the wilderness" was hot, dry, and strong, so the image speaks of a quick scattering with no way back.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people had grown so used to evil that, as the text says, the leopard does not change its spots. God reminds them that they forgot the Lord and trusted in falsehood. The scattering is the result of that path. Many understand that it foretells the exile in Babylon.

For today: the habits we repeat shape us. Today you can honestly recognize some habit that pulls you away from God and ask him for help to change it. His correction seeks to bring you back to him.
exp.37:1:
Jeremiah says that God announces what will happen in Jerusalem. Whoever stays in the city will die by the sword, by famine, or by plague. But whoever surrenders and goes out to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) will keep his life. The phrase "his life shall be for a prey" means that, like the spoils of war, he will escape only with his life, with nothing more.

Jeremiah, God's prophet, speaks while Babylon besieges Jerusalem. Years of rebellion and of ignoring God brought this judgment. The officials hear it and become angry, because they believe his message weakens the courage of the soldiers. Jeremiah does not seek the harm of the people; he calls them to obey so that they may be saved.

For today: sometimes God asks us for something that wounds our pride, such as surrendering, asking forgiveness, or changing course. Hearing an uncomfortable truth can save us from greater harm. Let us pray for humility to obey, even when it is not what we want to hear.
exp.47:21:
This verse continues a list of cities of Moab on which God's judgment falls. Here the cities named are Dibon, Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim. It is an incomplete phrase, which continues into the next verse. Judgment here means punishment decided by God.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and the prophet announces that its fall will reach the whole country. The text names specific places, as if to say that no one will be left unaware. It is generally understood that Moab's pride and its trust in itself were part of the reason (see 48:7, 29).

For today: God knows places and people by their names, and nothing escapes him. We can trust that he sees injustice, and we can also examine whether we are trusting in our own strength instead of in him.
exp.10:16:
This verse says that God, who planted his people like a tree, now announces disaster against them. The phrase about pronouncing it is explained as meaning that he has declared a punishment. The cause is the wickedness of Israel and Judah, who brought harm on themselves, that is, they hurt themselves through their own choices. Burning incense here means offering it to the idol Baal, which is the act that provoked the Lord to anger.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, delivering God's message. The people had made a covenant with him, but they broke it by worshiping false gods. The image of the green and beautiful olive tree shows how greatly the Lord had blessed them. Scholars understand the fire mentioned in the previous verse as a reference to the judgment that was coming, though the details are interpreted in different ways.

God has given us everything good that we have. It is worth asking ourselves what things take the place that belongs only to him, and returning to him sincerely before those things do us harm.
exp.32:8:
God says that Jerusalem, his restored people, will be for him a name of joy, praise, and glory before all the nations. Those peoples will hear of the good that God does for them, and they will fear and tremble, meaning they will be amazed and filled with awe at so much goodness and peace.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who was then imprisoned, while Jerusalem was suffering destruction and the people were living in exile. In the midst of that pain, God promises to bring them back, to cleanse them from their sin, and to forgive them, so that their restoration will display his mercy.

For today: when God forgives you and lifts you up, your life can speak of his goodness. Tell someone, with humility and gratitude, the good that he has done for you.
exp.48:16:
It says that Edom will become a desolate place. "Desolation" means complete ruin and destruction. Whoever passes by it will be astonished, that is, left amazed and horrified, and will hiss, a gesture of shock or mockery at the ruin. The plagues are the blows and wounds left by the judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Edom, Israel's neighbor, lived in rocky mountains and felt secure and untouchable. God warns that its pride deceived it. The comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah shows that the punishment would be complete. Scholars agree on the general message, though they debate exactly when it was fulfilled.

Today we can learn that no human security, whether money, position, or strength, protects us from God. Examine where you place your trust. Cultivate humility, and rest in the Lord, who is the only truly firm refuge.
exp.22:14:
God announces a punishment for the false prophets of Jerusalem. He will make them eat wormwood, a plant with a very bitter taste, and drink bitter, poisoned water. These are images of suffering and judgment. The reason is that from them came a false religion without sincerity, which spread throughout the land.

The one speaking is the Lord, through Jeremiah. These prophets claimed to speak for God, but they lived in lies and adultery. Moreover, they encouraged the wicked with false promises of peace, so no one repented.

For today: it is not enough for someone to speak about God with confidence. It is wise to compare what we hear with the Bible and to consider whether that teaching leads us to change our lives or only leaves us feeling comfortable with our sins.
exp.8:8:
Here God asks two strong questions. "Visit" means to hold someone accountable or to punish them. "My soul avenged" means that God himself cannot remain indifferent in the face of such harm. The answer expected is: yes, he will have to intervene.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people used gentle words and spoke of peace with their neighbor, but they planned to deceive him. God had already said he would test them as metal is refined in a furnace. His judgment is not a whim; it arises from the lies and betrayal among them. The verses that follow also show the grief of God and of Jeremiah over what was coming.

Today we can examine whether our words match our hearts. God cares about truth and justice in everyday life. Let us ask his help to speak with sincerity and to treat others without a double face.
exp.10:7:
This verse says that the ancestors of Judah did not listen to God or pay attention to his voice. Instead of obeying, each one followed what his evil heart told him. "Imagination" here means their own desires and thoughts, or the stubbornness of the heart. That is why God says he will bring on them the consequences the covenant announced, because they did not keep it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He asks him to announce in Judah and Jerusalem the words of the covenant that God made with Israel when he brought them out of Egypt. God had warned them again and again, and even so the people refused to obey. For this reason the judgment that the covenant itself warned of is coming.

For today: God speaks to us with love and patience, but we can become used to ignoring him. Today you can choose to listen to his Word and obey one specific thing, instead of only following what seems right to you or what comes naturally.
exp.27:4:
This verse says that the prophet Jeremiah answered the prophet Hananiah. He did so in public, in the presence of the priests and of all the people who were standing in the house of the Lord. The house of the Lord is the temple in Jerusalem, and the Lord is the name of God. The word "answered" here means that Jeremiah then spoke, not that he argued.

Hananiah had just announced that God would break the power of Babylon within two years and bring back the exiles and the vessels of the temple. Jeremiah, who had announced a long period of submission to Babylon, responds calmly. He says "Amen," since he would wish it to be true, but he will soon make clear what God has shown him.

For today: when someone says what we would like to hear, we can respond with respect and without mockery, but also with honesty, measuring everything against what God has actually said.
exp.2:1:
God tells his people to look up at the hills, where worship of other gods was carried on, and to find a single place where they have not given themselves to idolatry. The high places were elevated sites where pagan worship took place. Judah sat along the roads like a nomad waiting in the desert for travelers, so the people sought allies and false gods. The verse speaks of spiritual unfaithfulness, and of land made dirty and unclean.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Judah. He uses the image of a broken marriage: the people have abandoned their God. Even so, the verse before invites them to return. The drought that follows is understood as the consequence of that unfaithfulness.

Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts. Honor him with sincerity, recognize those things, and return to him, who continues to call with love.
exp.2:4:
It says the people speak as if God were going to keep his anger forever. But the reality is shown: that people has spoken words of rebellion and has done all the evil it could. "Forever" is "for ever." "As much evil as you could" means that they held back in nothing.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He confronts them about their unfaithfulness, compared to that of a wife who betrays her husband. Just before, he invites them to call on him as "my Father." Many understand that the statement about anger reflects the people's excuse: to sin and think that God will not be angry, or that his anger will change nothing. The text is not entirely simple, and some read it differently.

For today: do not use God's patience as an excuse to stay in what is wrong. If there is something you know you must leave behind, come to him today with sincerity and ask him for forgiveness.
exp.49:41:
It says that an enemy army will come against Babylon armed with bow and spear. They will be cruel and show no mercy. The sound of their advance will be like the sea, and they will ride on horses, arranged in formation, every one ready, like one man going into battle.

Habla Jehová por medio del profeta Jeremías. Babilonia had been a proud empire that destroyed nations and carried Judah into captivity. God announces that judgment is now coming to her, and he compares it to what happened to Sodom and Gomorrah. The text says the enemy comes from the north. History mentions the Medes and Persians, but the passage does not name them here.

For today: God sees injustice, and nothing escapes him. If you are suffering because of someone powerful who has abused you, you can trust that God is just. And if you have power, use it with humility and compassion, because one day you will give an account.
exp.8:16:
God says that people should think carefully about what is coming, and that the mourning women should be called, that is, women who were paid to weep at funerals. He also commands that the skilled women be sent for, women who were good at singing laments. It is a command for them to come and wail.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the fall of Judah. Because of the people's disobedience, God announces punishment, scattering, and death. The call to the mourning women shows that the disaster will be so great that a public mourning will be needed, as for a whole nation that is dying. The prophet himself weeps with pain in this book.

For today: God invites us to take sin and its consequences seriously, without hardening the heart. Today we can acknowledge our faults with humility, grieve what hurts, and return to God in time, trusting in his mercy.
exp.47:31:
God says he will weep for Sibmah, a place in Moab famous for its vineyards. He compares his weeping to that of Jazer, another nearby town. The "branches" are the long shoots of the vine, which spread so far that they seemed to reach across the "sea" (probably the Dead Sea, though some understand it differently). The "summer fruit" is the summer harvest, and the "vintage" is the grape harvest. A "destroyer" came and swept everything away.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on Moab for its pride and its trust in itself. What is striking is that God takes no pleasure in it: he says he will weep and mourn for them, even though he judges them.

For today: God is just, but he also has compassion. When we see someone fall because of their mistakes, we should not celebrate. Better to pray for that person and show a tender heart, like God's.
exp.7:15:
From the region of Dan, in the far north, the snorting of the enemy's horses was heard. The strong sound a horse makes when it breathes is what this describes. The neighing of his strong ones made the whole land tremble. The invaders came and devoured the harvests, the riches, the cities, and the people.

The prophet Jeremiah announces God's judgment on Judah for its sin. The people expected peace, but terror arrived. Many understand the enemy from the north to be Babylon, although the text does not name it here. In these verses the voices of the people, of God, and of the prophet, who grieves over what is coming, are mixed together.

Today: do not trust in excuses or in human refuges. If God corrects you, return to Him soon and with sincerity, before the consequences reach your door.
exp.22:24:
God says that He has heard those prophets. They spoke lies, yet they used God's name to give authority to their words. Their excuse was: "I have dreamed, I have dreamed," as if a dream were the same thing as a message from God. Here, "prophesy" means speaking in God's name.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah. Earlier, He reminded the people that He sees everything and fills heaven and earth, so no one can hide from Him. These prophets were leading the people with dreams invented by their own hearts, and that drew them away from God, as had happened before with Baal. God does not condemn every dream, but the false use of His name.

Today we can test every teaching, impression, or "word" in the light of the Bible. Before saying "God told me," it is wise to ask for wisdom, to be humble, and to check whether it agrees with what God has already revealed in His Word.
exp.37:8:
Ebed-melec tells King Zedekiah that the men who threw Jeremiah into the dungeon have acted wickedly. A dungeon is a dark prison, a pit or cistern under the ground. He warns that the prophet would die of hunger there, because there was no more bread left in the city.

Ebed-melec speaks as an Ethiopian who served in the palace. Jerusalem was under siege by the Babylonians and there was a shortage of food. Some officials, angered by Jeremiah's messages, had put him into a cistern full of mud. Being a foreigner and of humble position, Ebed-melec dares to speak before the king, who was sitting at the Gate of Benjamin.

Today we can learn that speaking up for someone who suffers injustice is an act of faith. We may have no power or influence, but God can use our voice and courage. Ask yourself: whom can I defend this week?
exp.1:13:
These questions sound harsh. God asks whether Israel is a servant or a slave born in the house, that is, someone without rights who can be mistreated. Since he is not, God asks why he has been given over to plunder, that is, why he is seized and stripped like an animal that has been hunted.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier he said that his people committed two wrongs: they abandoned him, the fountain of living water, and dug broken cisterns. The question leads us to think that Israel was not destined to be a victim, since it was his son and chosen people. The verses that follow describe invaders who laid the land waste, and many understand that this was the consequence of turning away from God.

For today: when you feel that life is wearing you down, ask yourself honestly what things you are relying on for support apart from God. Return to him in prayer and in his Word, for only he gives water that never runs out.
exp.25:13:
Jeremiah tells the leaders and the people: "I am in your hands; do with me whatever seems good and right to you."

Jeremiah had preached in the temple that Jerusalem would be destroyed if the people did not change. Priests and prophets demanded his death. He defends himself before the officials: he does not take back his message, and he trusts that God will look after him. Right away he warns them that killing an innocent man would bring guilt upon them. The officials and the people acquit him.

For today: we can speak the truth with humility and without fear, leaving the outcome in God's hands. Whoever obeys God does not need to fight with pride or stay silent out of fear.
exp.50:15:
This verse says that God, with only his voice, makes a great quantity of water fall from the sky. He lifts up the clouds from the farthest places on the earth. He makes lightning along with the rain, and he brings out the wind from his storehouses, as if he kept it in storage rooms.

The prophet Jeremiah announces God's judgment against Babylon. Earlier, God promises to send against her armies as numerous as locusts. Here Jeremiah shows who the God who speaks is: the Creator who governs nature. Then he compares him with idols, which are human work, without life or spirit.

For today: when you feel small before problems or powers that seem enormous, remember that the God who governs the clouds and the winds also cares for your life. Trust him before anything that you or other people make to feel secure.
exp.27:5:
Jeremiah answers the prophet Hananiah by saying "Amen," which means "so be it." He wishes that God would fulfill what Hananiah announced: that the objects from the temple and the people taken away would return from Babylon. The people taken away by force into exile are the captives, and the objects are the articles of the temple.

Jeremiah speaks in the temple, in front of priests and the people. Hananiah has just said that God would break the yoke of Babylon within two years. Jeremiah had announced a long exile. His "Amen" does not seem to be approval, but a sincere wish that it would be true, although he then warns that a prophecy is tested when it comes to pass. Some also read it with a touch of irony; the text does not make this clear.

For today: we can wish for good news without ceasing to seek the truth. When messages sound appealing, it is wise to pray, to compare them with Scripture, and to speak with humility and compassion.
exp.38:9:
It says that Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, left some of the poorest people in the land of Judah, those who had nothing. Furthermore, he gave them vineyards and fields to work. "But" is the word for the old "empero," and the phrase about the "common poor" means the lowliest people, and "inheritance" refers to lands or properties.

This is part of the account of the fall of Jerusalem. The narrator tells that the Babylonians burned the city and took most of the people away into captivity. The poor were left behind, perhaps because they did not seem a threat, and so someone had to care for the land. The text does not explain the captain's exact reasons, so it is best not to claim more. It is striking that, in the middle of the ruin, the weakest received provision.

For today: God can care for the most needy even in times of crisis. We can ask ourselves whom we are overlooking and, where possible, help them with something concrete, such as food, work, or companionship.
exp.21:23:
God swears by his own life, which is the strongest oath possible. He says that even if Coniah were like a signet ring on his right hand, the most valuable and closest place, he would still pluck him off from there. The signet ring here was the king's seal, a symbol of authority. Coniah is another name for Jehoiachin.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had lived in injustice and idolatry, and God announces that Coniah, king of Judah, will be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar and taken captive to Babylon, together with his mother. His office would not protect him from the consequences.

For today: no position, success, or religious closeness frees us from being accountable before God. Rather than relying on what we are, it is wise to live with humility, listen to his correction, and turn back to him in time.
exp.28:25:
The passage says that God made Zephaniah a priest in place of Jehoiada, so that he would look after the temple. His task was to watch over any man who is "furious and prophesying," that is, someone who acts like a madman or out of his mind and claims to speak for God. That man was to be put in prison and in the stocks, a wooden device that held the body fast.

Here Shemaiah speaks, a false prophet exiled in Babylon. He wrote this letter to Zephaniah and the priests of Jerusalem to pressure them into silencing Jeremiah. Jeremiah had advised the exiles to settle down and wait, since the exile would be long. Shemaiah called him mad, but Jeremiah's message came from God.

For today: do not dismiss a message just because it is uncomfortable or unpopular. Test it against Scripture and ask God for wisdom before you judge.
exp.28:24:
This verse begins a message that God sends through Shemaiah of Nehelam. God says that Shemaiah sent letters in his own name to all the people in Jerusalem, to the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, and to all the priests. Letters means written messages, and Jerusalem is the city in which those people lived.

Jeremiah had written to the exiles in Babylon, telling them to settle there and wait. Shemaiah, one of those exiles, answered with letters of his own to oppose Jeremiah and to pressure the priests to silence him. God responds to that action, because Shemaiah was speaking as though he had authority without having been sent by God.

Today we can learn not to speak in God's name carelessly. Before advising or correcting others, it is good to compare what we say with the Bible and to pray with humility.
exp.31:10:
Here Jeremiah tells how he took the documents of the purchase of the field. The "deed of sale" is the contract. It was "sealed according to the law and custom," that is, closed in a legally proper way. "The open copy" was a copy left unsealed so it could be consulted. So there was one protected copy and another in plain view.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet of God while Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon and he himself was imprisoned in the court of the guard. God asked him to buy the field of his cousin in Anathoth, even though the land seemed lost. It was a sign that, after judgment, God would restore his people to that land.

For today: when everything seems uncertain, we can take concrete steps of faith, done with order and honesty, trusting that God keeps his promises even when we do not yet see the result.
exp.26:18:
This verse begins a message from God about the bronze objects that were still in the temple: the pillars, the "sea" (a large basin of water for the priests), the "bases" (wheeled stands for the basins) and the other vessels. "Vessels" here means utensils or containers.

Jeremiah speaks to the people and to the priests. Some false prophets were saying that these objects, which Nebuchadnezzar had earlier carried away, would soon be returned. Jeremiah warns them not to listen, because that hope was an illusion. God announces that what remained would also be carried off to Babylon. The message aims to lead Judah to submit and live, instead of staying deceived.

For today: Before believing a religious message that sounds pleasant, let us compare it with what God has said in his Word. The truth, even when it hurts, protects us and leads us to obey and to live.
exp.5:0:
This verse is a war alarm. God tells the people of Benjamin to flee from the middle of Jerusalem. They are to blow the horn (the ram's horn or trumpet) in Tekoa and raise a signal of smoke in Beth-haccerem. "North" is where the danger comes from, and great destruction comes with it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who was from the tribe of Benjamin. Judah had refused God's calls to return to Him. Tekoa and Beth-haccerem were places near Jerusalem, and they were used to send warnings. Scholars often connect the danger from the north with Babylon, although the text presents it in general terms.

Today we can learn to take God's warnings seriously. It is not wise to wait until the crisis arrives: listening in time, repenting, and returning to Him with humility is an act of wisdom.
exp.9:0:
This verse is a call to listen carefully. The word "Hear" means "listen," the name of the God of Israel is "the Lord," and "you" refers to the people being addressed. God speaks to the whole "house of Israel," that is, to all his people, and asks them to pay attention to what he tells them.

The book of Jeremiah records the messages God gave through this prophet to his people before and during the fall of Jerusalem. Here God speaks and prepares the message that follows: he warns Israel not to imitate the religious customs of other nations or to fear the signs of the heavens, and he reminds them that idols are the work of human hands.

Today, before we are carried along by what others fear, believe, or follow, it is good to stop and listen to God in his Word. Reading it attentively each day helps us live with trust rather than fear.
exp.51:5:
On the ninth day of the fourth month, the hunger in Jerusalem grew so severe that there was no longer any bread for the common people. The word "prevailed" here means that it became stronger, and "people of the land" refers to the inhabitants of the country in general.

This chapter is a historical account that summarizes the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, around 586 B.C. No one knows for certain who wrote it; some think it was Jeremiah and others think it was a later editor. It shows the end of the long siege, which Jeremiah had announced as the consequence of the people's disobedience.

For today: God speaks to us patiently before crises arrive, and it is wise to listen in time. In addition, this verse reminds us that the poorest suffer the most, so we can generously help those who are going hungry today.
exp.15:20:
This verse says that God himself is going to show his power. "I will teach them my hand" means he will make his strength visible in action, so that there is no room for doubt. "This once" means "now, on this occasion." The purpose is that they will know that his name is the LORD, that is, the true God, the Lord who acts.

God speaks here, responding to Jeremiah's prayer, in which Jeremiah has just said that the LORD is his strength and refuge. Jeremiah announces that even distant nations will recognize that the idols are a lie. God speaks in this way in the midst of judgment on Judah, which had followed false gods. Scholars debate exactly who the "them" refers to, whether Judah, the nations, or both.

For today: when something takes the place of God in your trust, whether money, success, or fear, hand it over to him. Ask him to show you his strength, and trust that you can truly know him.
exp.28:21:
This verse says that the exiles from Judah in Babylon will use the fate of two men as a curse. They will say: "The Lord make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire." "Carried away" refers to those taken into exile. "Roasted in the fire" describes an execution by fire ordered by the king of Babylon.

God speaks through Jeremiah to the exiles. Ahab and Zedekiah were false prophets who claimed to speak in God's name, but gave messages of peace that He had not sent them. The text says they also committed wickedness and adultery. This Ahab is not the king of Israel. The Bible does not tell more about how his death happened.

Today, this passage invites us not to believe every message just because it sounds spiritual or encouraging. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible and look for teachers who live with integrity.
exp.37:22:
He says that if King Zedekiah does not surrender, everything he loves will be lost. His wives and children will be handed over to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). He himself will not escape, but the king of Babylon will take him captive, and the city of Jerusalem will be burned. "Shalt be taken" means that he will be captured.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in a private conversation with King Zedekiah while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. God was asking him to surrender in order to save lives and the city. Zedekiah was afraid of his own officials and hesitated to obey. Jeremiah warns him that if he does not obey, the very women of the palace will say that his friends deceived him.

For today: obeying God out of fear of what others think usually costs far more than obeying him with humility. When God shows us a path, it is better to trust him now than to regret later having listened to the wrong voices.
exp.6:20:
God says to the people: "Add your burnt offerings to your other sacrifices, and eat the meat yourselves." The burnt offerings were burned completely on the altar, while the other sacrifices were partly eaten. God invites them with irony to gather everything together and eat it, as if it no longer had any worth to Him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to a people who carried out religious rituals but lived in disobedience. The verses that follow explain that the main thing God asked of them when He brought them out of Egypt was: "Listen to my voice." Many understand that He does not reject sacrifices in themselves, but rejects them when there is no obedience.

For today: faith does not consist only of attending, singing, or keeping religious customs. God seeks a heart that listens and obeys. Today you might ask yourself: "What is God asking of me that I have not yet obeyed?"
exp.51:26:
This verse tells that the king of Babylon ordered those prisoners to be punished and put to death in Riblah, a place in the region of Hamath, north of Israel. The words "struck" and "killed" point to an execution. Thus the people of Judah were left exiled far from their land.

The one who tells the account is the author of the book, who closes Jeremiah's prophecy with a historical summary. Many believe this chapter is very similar to 2 Kings 24 and 25. The prisoners were military leaders and officials, taken when Jerusalem fell. The account confirms that what Jeremiah had warned about for years came to pass.

For today: God speaks in earnest, and his warnings are not empty words. If he corrects us through his Word, it is wise to respond soon with humility. And even in dark times, we can trust that his mercy does not run out.
exp.25:15:
The explanation says that the civil leaders and the people defended Jeremiah before the priests and prophets who were accusing him. They declared that he did not deserve death, because what he had said came from the Lord. The "princes" are the leaders or officials of Judah. Being guilty of a crime deserving death is what the expression describes: committing an offense punishable by execution.

Jeremiah had preached in the temple that God would destroy Jerusalem if the people did not repent. The priests and prophets grew angry and demanded his death. Jeremiah answered calmly and warned that killing him would mean shedding innocent blood. Then the officials and the people recognized that he was speaking in the name of God. Afterward, some elders recalled the case of the prophet Micah.

For today: when an uncomfortable truth comes from the Word of God, let us not reject it out of irritation. Let us listen with humility, and if necessary, repent.
exp.31:41:
God says that just as he brought all the great evil of destruction and exile upon his people, so he will also bring them all the good he has promised. The "great evil" refers to the calamity they suffered, and "all the good that I have spoken concerning them" refers to the promises of restoration that he himself had announced.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by the Chaldeans (Babylonians), and Jeremiah was in prison. Even so, God commanded him to buy a field as a sign that one day the people would return and possess the land. The punishment was not God's final word, and his covenant remained firm.

For today: If God kept his word of judgment, he will also keep his word of hope. In the midst of trials, you can hold on to his promises and keep obeying with confidence, even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.4:17:
The explanation says that although God is going to punish his people very severely, he will not destroy them completely. The phrase "I will not make a full end with you" means there will be judgment, but a remnant with hope will also remain. The word "but" introduces the contrast.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people had left the Lord and served other gods. Because of this, the announcement is that a foreign army will invade the land, eat its harvests, and destroy its cities. Even so, in the middle of this strong warning, God leaves a promise: his discipline has a limit.

For today: when you face the consequences of your mistakes, do not think that God has already abandoned you. His correction is serious, but it is not the end. Return to him sincerely, because his desire is to restore you, not to destroy you.
exp.11:2:
Jeremiah tells God that He knows him completely: He has seen him and has tested his heart. Then he asks that the wicked be pulled away like sheep being led to the place of slaughter, and set apart for the day of punishment. The old word for "you have seen me" is also explained here: it simply means "you have seen me."

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. He is confused and hurt because the wicked prosper while he suffers for being faithful. His own neighbors had betrayed him. His prayer is very intense, and some understand it as a sincere outpouring of grief before God, not as a wish for personal revenge. God answers him afterward by calling him to persevere.

When it hurts to see the unjust doing well, do not keep your pain silent. Bring it to God honestly, trusting that He knows your heart and will do justice in his time.
exp.50:14:
This verse says that God is the Creator of everything. He made the earth by his strength, that is, by his great power. He established the world by his wisdom, meaning he made it firm and well ordered. And he stretched out the heavens with understanding, as one who spreads them out with perfect insight.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing God's judgment on Babylon, a rich and proud city that trusted in its treasures and its idols. The verses that follow contrast the living God, who governs the rain, the clouds and the wind, with the idols, which are a lie and have neither life nor breath.

For today: when you feel that money, power or anything fleeting gives you security, remember who holds up the world. Entrust your life to the wise and powerful God, and not to things that cannot save you.
exp.17:16:
It says God will scatter them with strength, like the east wind, a wind from the east that is dry and destructive. He will let them flee before their enemies. "I will show them the back, and not the face" means that God will turn away from them and will not look on them with favor. "The day of their calamity" is the time of their ruin and disaster.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah had forgotten him and were offering incense to empty idols. Because of this, they had turned away from the ancient, faithful paths. God announces the consequences of that abandonment. The following verses show that the people, instead of repenting, wanted to attack the prophet.

For today: when God corrects us through his Word, it is better to listen with humility than to defend ourselves or silence the one who speaks to us. Returning to God in time prevents much pain.
exp.30:36:
God says that it would be as impossible to measure all the heavens above or to search out the foundations of the earth to their depths. In the same way, it is impossible for him to reject the descendants of Israel completely. Although they had done wicked things, he affirms this.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were under judgment and suffering exile because of their unfaithfulness. Even so, in this passage about the new covenant, God assures them that his commitment to them will not come to an end. What follows announces that Jerusalem will be rebuilt for him.

For today: when you feel that your failures are greater than God's patience, remember that his faithfulness does not depend on your perfection. Return to him with sincerity, trusting in his promise and not in your merits.
exp.32:18:
God spoke again to Jeremiah. "The word of the Lord came unto Jeremiah" means that the message did not come from the prophet himself, but from God. It is a short phrase that marks the beginning of a new declaration. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "saying" announces that what He wants to communicate is coming.

Jeremiah is imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard, and Jerusalem is under threat from Babylon. Even so, God gives him words of hope about restoration. The verses before this one promise that there will not be lacking a descendant of David or priests who serve. This verse introduces the assurance that follows: God's faithfulness is as firm as day and night.

For today: when everything seems uncertain, seek the Word of God before the news or your fears. He continues to speak and fulfills what He promises, even in difficult times.
exp.22:2:
God promises that he himself will gather the sheep that were left of his people, that is, a remnant, from all the countries where he scattered them. He will bring them back to their folds, which are their homes or their land. There they will grow and multiply, that is, they will be fruitful and numerous.

The Lord speaks, and he does so in the midst of a severe warning against the shepherds, the leaders of Judah, who neglected and scattered the people. God confronts them, but also promises that he will not abandon his sheep. Afterward he announces new shepherds and a just King, a descendant of David. Christians see in him Jesus.

For today: if you have felt lost, far away, or hurt by bad leaders, remember that God cares for his people and knows how to gather them. You can return to him with confidence and seek a community where you are cared for with truth and love.
exp.19:1:
Pashur, a priest with authority in the temple, struck the prophet Jeremiah and left him bound in the stocks. The stocks were an instrument of punishment that held the body fast to humiliate and cause pain. They stood at the high gate of Benjamin, on the way up to the temple.

Jeremiah had just announced that God would bring judgment on Jerusalem for its disobedience. Pashur, in charge of order in the temple, would not listen to that message and tried to silence it by violence. Even so, the public punishment did not change what God had said, and Jeremiah went on speaking the next day.

Today, speaking the truth in love sometimes brings rejection or mockery. Let us ask God for courage to be faithful, and for humility to listen when his Word corrects us, neither silencing it nor resisting it.
exp.51:7:
This verse tells that the soldiers of Babylon pursued King Zedekiah, who was fleeing from Jerusalem. They overtook him on the plains of Jericho, a low area near the Jordan River. There his whole army was scattered: his soldiers abandoned him and each went off on his own. The phrase "overtook" means they caught him, and "was scattered" means his army broke apart and fled in every direction.

This final chapter of Jeremiah recounts the fall of Jerusalem. The text presents it as a historical record, and several scholars think its author may have been Jeremiah or another writer who gathered these events. For years Jeremiah had warned that the king should surrender to Babylon, but Zedekiah did not heed him. Here we see the result of ignoring those warnings.

For today: when we ignore the voice of God and trust our own plans, the support we thought secure can vanish. It is better to listen in time and obey with humility.
exp.13:17:
It says the situation is terrible everywhere. If a person goes out into the field, they see people dead from the sword; if they enter the city, they see people sick and weak from hunger. "By the sword" is the same as "slain with the sword," meaning killed in war. Also, the prophet and the priest "go about in a land that they know not": they move from place to place, but without understanding what is happening. Some understand that they were taken away as captives; others, that they wandered aimlessly.

Jeremiah speaks, a man who feels the pain of God and of the people. Judah suffers drought, hunger, and war because of its sin. The religious leaders gave false security and did not guide the people back to God.

For today: it is not enough to hold an office or to have a religious appearance. Seek God with sincerity, ask for wisdom, and acknowledge your mistakes, as the people do later in the text, so that you do not go about without understanding.
exp.48:28:
It says the enemies will carry off everything the people of Kedar had: their tents, their flocks, the curtains of their tents, their utensils, and their camels. Furthermore, they will cry out against them, "Fear is on every side," a phrase describing terror that comes from all directions.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Kedar were nomadic tribes of the desert, rich in livestock, who lived confidently and without defenses. God announces that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, would attack them. Scholars agree that the judgment falls on a people secure in themselves; the exact historical details of that campaign are not well known.

For today: our possessions and securities can disappear quickly. It is wise to guard the heart so that we do not trust in what we have, but in God, who sustains life when everything else is lost.
exp.3:27:
This verse says that the earth will mourn and the sky will grow dark. God gives the reason: what he has said and decided, he will carry out. The phrase "will mourn" means the earth will be in grief, the way people mourn when they lose someone they love. "I have not changed my mind, nor will I turn back" means that God will not change his plan or reverse his decision.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on Judah for its idolatry and rebellion, described as a land laid waste by an invading army. Many understand this to refer to Babylon, although the text does not name it here. Notice that God had earlier said he would not make a full end, meaning he will not completely destroy his people. His judgment is serious, but it leaves a door of hope open.

For today: God means what he says, both when he warns and when he promises. Do not take him lightly; it is better to respond in time with humility and return to him, for he is merciful.
exp.11:7:
God says that his people, his "heritage," turned against him like a wild lion in the thick forest ("thicket" is scrubland overgrown with brush). It roared against God, meaning it challenged him with its words and its conduct. That is why God says he "hated" it, a strong word that shows his painful rejection of that rebellion.

Here God himself speaks, through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah, whom God loved, had abandoned him and even opposed him. God laments that his people, instead of being a treasure, had become hostile. Some understand this "hating" as a wounded love that withdraws its favor, not as a hopeless hatred, since the book also promises restoration.

For today: God grieves when we reject him. If you notice hardness or rebellion in your heart, return to him with humility. He continues to offer forgiveness to anyone who repents.
exp.29:17:
God promises that he will bring back the exiles of the people of Israel, here called "Jacob." Their "dwellings" are their homes, and "captivity" is their exile. God will have compassion on them. The city, Jerusalem, will be rebuilt upon its own heap (its hill), and the palace will stand in its place, arranged in the right way.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were in exile, or were about to be, because of their disobedience. Others mocked Zion, saying that no one sought her. God answers with a promise of healing and restoration. Scholars see a partial fulfillment in the return from Babylon, and many Christians also see a broader hope in Christ.

Even if something in your life seems ruined or abandoned, God can rebuild it. Today you can bring that area to him with confidence and wait patiently for his mercy.
exp.25:22:
They sent men who brought Uriah back from Egypt, where he had fled, and took him before King Jehoiakim. Jehoiakim killed him with the sword and had his body thrown into the burial place of the common people, the cemetery of the poor and dishonored.

The narrator, who tells the story, relates what happened to Uriah, another prophet who announced the same message as Jeremiah against Jerusalem. He is mentioned to show the real danger Jeremiah faced. When Jeremiah speaks in the temple, some want to kill him, and Uriah's example shows that the king had already silenced a prophet through violence.

For today: telling the truth can cost dearly, and the powerful sometimes punish it. Even so, this scene invites us to be faithful to God with courage and not to measure success by human recognition. God does not forget those who suffer for obeying him.
exp.48:19:
Here he says that God invites us to hear his plan against Edom and against the inhabitants of Teman, a city known in Edom. The words for counsel and thoughts mean purpose and decision. The phrases about what has been settled and resolved mean that he has already decided it. The expression about the least of the flock can be understood as the youngest or weakest shepherds, or as the most insignificant ones; it is interpreted in several ways. Even they will drag the people away and lay waste to their dwellings, that is, their homes and pastures.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Edom was a neighbor of Judah and considered itself safe and wise. God announces judgment on its pride and violence, and compares its fall to that of Sodom and Gomorrah.

For today: let us not trust in our strength, fame, or security, because God is the only one who is truly powerful. Let us receive his Word with humility and live justly, knowing that he rules over all.
exp.7:2:
The explanation says that the survivors of this wicked people will prefer to die rather than to live. The words of the verse about choosing death over life are rendered here as the verse reads in the King James wording.
