"The rest" are those who remain alive after the judgment, and "the Lord of hosts" is the Lord, ruler over all power.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had worshiped the sun, the moon and the stars, and would not turn back to God even though they were called many times. For this reason he announces a harsh judgment: exile and shame. The verses that follow show that God still asks them why they do not return.

For today: let us not harden our hearts. If we feel that something is pulling us away from God, let us return to Him soon, because God still receives whoever truly repents.
exp.26:17:
Jeremiah says that if those prophets truly speak on behalf of God, then they should pray to the Lord that the sacred objects still left in the temple, in the king's palace, and in Jerusalem will not be carried off to Babylon.

Jeremiah speaks to the people, the priests, and King Zedekiah. False prophets were promising that Babylon would soon return what had already been taken. Jeremiah challenges them: if they truly listen to God, let them pray to prevent another loss. He insists that they submit to Babylon and live.

Today we can learn not to believe only what sounds pleasant. Before following a teaching, compare it with the Bible and seek God in prayer. God's truth is sometimes hard, but it leads us to life.
exp.14:1:
This verse says that when the people ask, "Where shall we go?", Jeremiah is to tell them the words of God: each person will receive the fate that falls to them. Some will die of disease or plague, others by the sword, others by famine, and others will be led away as captives to another country. The word for "sword" here means war or the blade of battle.

God speaks to the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had rejected God for a long time, and the passage points to the sins of Manasseh as part of the cause. God says that not even Moses or Samuel, great intercessors, would change the situation. Some understand "death" to mean plague; the text does not make this clear.

For today: do not take lightly God's voice when He calls you to return to Him. You can pray sincerely today, acknowledge something you have neglected, and ask Him for help to change, because His patience is real, but it must not be mistaken for permission to stay as you are.
exp.31:31:
This verse says that God is about to punish the city for all the wickedness of his people. It names everyone: the kings, the princes (leaders or officials), the priests, the prophets, the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. "Provoke me to anger" means to stir up his anger. No one was left out: both the leaders and the ordinary people.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon, and God explains why he allows that situation: the people had turned their backs on him for generations, even after receiving constant teaching and after defiling the temple with idols. Even so, in this same chapter God promises to restore his people.

For today: instead of blaming only others, we can examine our own hearts with humility. If we acknowledge our failings and return to God, we find his forgiveness and his loving correction.
exp.20:4:
God says that He Himself will fight against Jerusalem. The phrases "outstretched hand" and "strong arm" are images of power; they were once used to speak of how God delivered Israel from Egypt, but now they are turned against the people. The words "anger" and "fury" and "great wrath" show a very serious judgment. The word "you" in this verse refers to the people.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God to King Zedekiah while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. The king hoped that God would rescue him, but the people remained in sin and did not repent. God warns them that their resistance will not save them, because He Himself opposes that rebellion.

For today: we cannot ask for God's help while we ignore His voice. If there is something in our lives that God has shown us, the best thing is to turn back to Him with humility and sincerity, because He remains just and also merciful toward those who repent.
exp.24:12:
God says he will carry out against Babylon, "that land," everything he has declared against it. That includes what Jeremiah wrote down in this book about the nations. "Bring words" means to make them come to pass. "All nations" is the sense of the phrase "all the nations."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, around the year 605 BC. Judah had ignored his warnings for years. God announces that Babylon would be used to discipline Judah and other peoples, but that afterward Babylon too would have to answer for its own wickedness. The seventy years can be understood as a literal or approximate period; interpreters explain it in different ways.

God takes justice seriously and does what he says. We can trust that no injustice is forgotten before him, and so we can entrust our wrongs to him and live with humility, without repaying evil with evil.
exp.39:14:
Johanan tells Gedaliah, in private and in Mizpah, that he is willing to go and kill Ishmael without anyone finding out. He asks why Gedaliah should let Ishmael kill him, so that the Jews gathered around him would be scattered and the rest of Judah would perish. Here "to strike" means to kill, and "will be spilled" means that they will be scattered.

After the fall of Jerusalem, Babylon left Gedaliah as governor over those who remained in the land. Johanan and other military leaders warned him that the Ammonite king Baalis had sent Ishmael to assassinate him. Gedaliah did not believe them, so Johanan insists in private, concerned to protect the people who were left.

For today: when someone warns us of a danger, it is wise to listen with humility and to examine the facts in prayer. But we also learn that sincere concern does not justify settling a problem with violence or in secret. Let us seek wisdom and just ways.
exp.15:8:
God announces that he will take away the sounds of celebration from Jerusalem. The songs of joy will no longer be heard, nor the voices of the bridegroom and the bride at weddings. This would happen soon, "in your eyes" and "in your days," meaning while the people themselves were still living.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He commands him not to marry, not to attend funerals or feasts, as a sign to the people. The people had left God for other gods, and judgment was coming as a consequence. Even so, God gives warning in advance, and that shows his patience.

For today: let us not take everyday blessings and joys for granted. Let us thank God for them, and humbly examine whether our hearts still remain close to him.
exp.3:7:
God calls his people to put on mourning clothes, to weep, and to cry out in pain. Sackcloth was a rough cloth worn in times of grief or repentance. To lament means to mourn with songs or weeping, and to howl means to cry out in intense anguish. The reason is that the Lord's anger still remains upon them.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to the kingdom of Judah, warning that an invader is coming from the north, described as a destroying lion. The people had rejected God and still believed that everything would turn out fine. That is why the warning is serious, and weeping is the appropriate response.

Today, when God shows us that something is wrong in our lives, it is not wise to downplay it or distract ourselves. We can stop, confess with sincerity, and return to Him, trusting that his mercy remains open to those who humble themselves.
exp.21:11:
This verse says that Shallum will die in the foreign land where he is taken, and that he will never see his own land again. The word "carried" in the verse means that he will be taken away by force, that is, he will be sent into exile.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Shallum, also called Jehoahaz, was the son of King Josiah and reigned for a very short time. According to 2 Kings 23, the king of Egypt took him prisoner. God announces that there will be no return, and for that reason he calls for weeping over the one taken away more than over the one who has died. Then the text speaks of the injustice of kings who built palaces without paying their workers.

For today: having power or success is not enough; God looks at how we treat others. Today you can ask yourself whether you pay what is fair and whether you act with honesty and respect toward those who work with you.
exp.8:12:
God answers the question of why the land was left in ruin. The reason is that the people abandoned his law, the law he had set before them. They did not listen to his voice, nor did they live according to it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, the text asks who is wise enough to understand why judgment would come upon Judah and Jerusalem. God himself gives the answer: it was not by chance, but the consequence of disobedience. The following verse adds that they followed their own stubborn hearts and the Baals, false gods.

For today: it is not enough to have God's Word within reach; we must listen to it and put it into practice. You can choose one concrete command from the Bible that you have been putting off, such as forgiving, being honest, or setting aside time to pray, and begin to obey it today with humility.
exp.20:8:
It says that those who stay in Jerusalem will die by the sword, by famine, or by the pestilence. But whoever goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) who are besieging the city will live, and his life will be unto him for a prey. "His life shall be unto him for a prey" means that he will escape with his life, like someone who leaves a battle with only what he was able to save.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem to Nebuchadnezzar. The people had disobeyed again and again, and God sets before them a choice: the way of life or the way of death. It was a hard message, which many saw as betrayal, but it offered a way out to anyone who would believe.

For today: sometimes God asks us to trust his word even when it sounds difficult or humbling. Letting go of pride and obeying may be the path that saves us.
exp.4:14:
God tells Israel that he will bring against them a nation from distant lands. He describes it as strong and ancient, a people whose language you will not understand. Strong means powerful, and ancient refers to a people with a long history. The phrase about not understanding means you will not know their language.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had rejected his warnings, saying that no harm would come. So the judgment would be a foreign invasion. Many understand that it refers to Babylon, though the text does not give the name. Hearing a language you cannot understand was a sign of being left without protection and without a home.

For today: let us not take God's warnings lightly. He corrects because he wants us to return to him. If you feel his call today, do not harden your heart; ask him for forgiveness and trust in his mercy.
exp.49:10:
Babylon rejoiced and grew proud when she destroyed "my inheritance," that is, God's people and their land. The phrase "ye are grown fat" means that they swelled with arrogance. Babylon is compared to a heifer that leaps in the pasture, or to horses that neigh with pure delight. It was a proud joy, without compassion.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He had allowed Babylon to punish Judah, but she went too far: she enjoyed the violence and considered herself superior. For this reason God announces that he will raise up nations from the north against her. The verses that follow describe her shame and her ruin.

For today: God sees how we treat others, especially the weak. It is never good to rejoice in the harm of others or to boast of our power. Let us ask him for a humble and compassionate heart, and trust that he will do justice.
exp.18:4:
They built the high places of Baal, that is, altars on hilltops, to honor the god Baal. There they burned their own sons as an offering. "Holocaust" refers to offerings that were burned up completely. God makes clear that he never commanded this, never spoke of it, and never even thought of it.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah in the Valley of Hinnom, near Jerusalem. He accuses the kings and the people of abandoning him, worshiping other gods, and shedding innocent blood. For this reason he announces judgment on that place. Scholars agree that this refers to the sacrifice of children, although not all of them specify how widespread the practice was.

For today: We should examine whether what we do in God's name truly comes from him. Let us compare our customs with the Bible, and take care of the weakest among us, especially children.
exp.50:17:
They are vanity, meaning empty and without any real worth. They are "work of errors," that is, something fit for mockery. "Visitation" refers to the moment when God steps in to judge. When that time comes, the idols will be destroyed and will not be able to save anyone.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, passing on God's word against Babylon, a nation full of idols. Just before this verse, the Creator is shown sending rain, clouds, and wind. Then it says that the God of Jacob is the Former of all things. The contrast is clear: God creates; idols are only made by human hands.

For today: ask yourself what you are truly trusting in, whether money, success, or image. All of that can fail. Put your trust in the living God, who truly sustains your life.
exp.48:38:
It says that, although God will punish Elam, at the end of time he will bring back its people from captivity. "In the latter days" means "in the distant future" or "at the end." "Bring back the captivity" means "restore" or "bring back the exiles."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing the nations neighboring Judah. Elam lay east of Babylon, in what is today Iran. Before this verse, God announces severe judgment against them. Here he adds a promise of hope. The Bible does not explain in detail how or when it was fulfilled; some see it in historical events, and others in a future fulfillment.

For today: even when God corrects, his final word does not have to be destruction. We can trust that he is just and also merciful, and that he can restore what seemed lost.
exp.15:9:
God tells Jeremiah that when the prophet announces the punishment, the people will ask him in amazement: "Why has the Lord pronounced all this great evil against us? Or what is our iniquity? What is our sin that we have committed against the Lord our God?"

The Lord speaks to Jeremiah before the fall of Judah. God orders him not to attend feasts or times of mourning, as a sign that the end of joy in that land is coming. God already knows that the people will not acknowledge their guilt. In the verses that follow, he answers them: their ancestors abandoned him to serve other gods, and they have done even worse, following their own stubborn hearts.

For today: it is easy not to see our own sin. Let us ask God to show us honestly where we have drifted away from him, and let us listen without becoming defensive.
exp.10:14:
God asks with sorrow: what is my beloved people doing in my house, when they have committed so many wicked deeds? The holy flesh refers to the offerings from the temple sacrifices. God says that those offerings will not be able to remove the punishment, because the people were glad and boasted in their wickedness. The text is difficult, and some translators understand it in different ways, but the general sense is clear.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had as many gods as it had cities, and it worshiped Baal, and yet it kept going to the temple as if nothing were wrong. God had already said that he would not listen to their pleas, because religion without obedience is of no use.

For today: it is not enough to attend church or to perform rituals. God seeks a faithful heart, one that turns away from what is evil and loves him alone.
exp.40:12:
It says that the captives whom Ishmael was leading were filled with joy when they saw Johanan and his captains approaching. The phrase "the princes of the soldiery" refers to the leaders of the army, and "were glad" shows the relief of people who had been hoping for rescue.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah speaks. Ishmael had murdered Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, and carried off the people of Mizpah as prisoners. Johanan and his captains heard about it and went out to pursue him as far as Gibeon, beside the great waters, a place with a large pool. The captives saw in Johanan their deliverer.

For today: when someone goes through an unjust or frightening situation, our help can bring real joy. We can ask ourselves whom we might accompany, defend, or rescue through concrete action, without waiting for others to do it.
exp.14:7:
He says that God made there be more widows than grains of sand on the seashore. He sent a "destroyer" (an invading army) in the full "midday" sun, that is, in broad daylight, upon the mother and her children. Suddenly terror fell on the city. The word "destroyer" speaks of an attacker who lays waste.

God speaks through Jeremiah to Judah, his people. He had warned them many times, but they turned away and did not change their ways. God says he is "weary of relenting," that is, of holding back his judgment. Some believe this refers to the Babylonian invasion, though the text gives no further details.

For today: God speaks in earnest, but his patience is long. Do not harden your heart against his call. If something in your life is pulling you away from him, return today with sincerity, because God receives whoever turns back to him.
exp.48:23:
It says Damascus lost heart. To faint here means to be left without strength because of fear. The city wanted to flee, but a trembling seized it. "Anguish and sorrows have taken her" describes a sudden suffering that cannot be stopped, like that of a woman about to give birth.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This message is part of a series of warnings against nations neighboring Israel. Damascus, capital of Syria (Aram), receives news of a judgment that is approaching. Nearby passages mention cities that melt with fear at the "bad news." The text does not detail here who would carry out the punishment, and scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: the strongest cities can fall in a moment. Our true security is not in power, fame, or money, but in God. Today you can bring your fears to Him in prayer and trust in Him.
exp.45:7:
It says Egypt rises like the Nile when it swells and overflows. Its army rises up with pride and promises to cover the earth and destroy cities and their inhabitants. The explanation of "north" and "swells" is left out, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Jeremiah speaks of the battle of Carchemish, beside the Euphrates River. Egypt went out confident, but it was defeated by Babylon. The prophet describes that arrogance to show that God rules over the nations. The verses that follow say that day belongs to the LORD. Historians place this battle around 605 BC.

For today: human plans may seem unstoppable, but they do not have the final word. Before boasting in your strength or your plans, place them in God's hands and live with humility.
exp.18:1:
God commands Jeremiah to go out to the valley of the son of Hinnom, near the entry of the east gate of Jerusalem. There he is to proclaim aloud the message that God will give him. "Proclaim" means to announce openly. Some versions call that gate "the potters' gate," and it is not known with certainty what its exact name was.

The LORD speaks, and Jeremiah is his prophet. God sends him with the clay jar and with elders of the people and of the priests, so that they may be witnesses. The valley was a place where the people had worshiped false gods and shed innocent blood. For this reason God warns them of a judgment that is near.

For today: God calls us to speak the truth with courage and love, even when it is not popular. Ask him to show you what to say and when, and do it with humility and without fear.
exp.49:11:
It says that Babylon, here called the "mother" of its inhabitants, will be brought low and filled with shame. From being a great power, it will become the last of the nations.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, and says the message comes from the LORD. He addresses Babylon, which had destroyed Jerusalem and mistreated God's people. It mocked them and became full of pride. God announces that she herself will suffer the punishment for her arrogance and her sin.

For today: pride and cruelty may seem successful for a time, but God sees injustice. Today we can treat those with less power with humility and compassion, and trust that God will bring about justice in his time.
exp.51:22:
The passage says that on the ornaments of the bronze pillars of the temple there were pomegranates made of metal. On each side or row there were ninety-six, and in total there were one hundred around the network. Some explain that the ninety-six were seen on the four sides, and the hundred counted all the pomegranates on the ornament, but the text does not fully make this clear.

Here the narrator describes in detail what the Babylonians destroyed and carried away when they conquered Jerusalem, around 586 BC. This final chapter summarizes the fall of the city and the temple, as the fulfillment of the warnings that Jeremiah had given for years.

For today: God pays careful attention to what we do for Him, but no outward beauty can replace a faithful heart. Let us care for our relationship with God, not merely the appearances of our Christian life.
exp.29:2:
It says that God promises a time is coming when he will change the fortunes of his people.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah and commands him to write his words in a book. The people were under judgment and faced exile, or were already suffering it, and they needed hope. What was written would serve as a witness for the future. The words that follow speak of fear and anguish, so this promise comes in the middle of hard times. Some interpreters see it fulfilled in the return from Babylon, and others see a greater fulfillment still further ahead.

When everything seems lost, God remains faithful to what he has promised. You can hold on to his Word and wait with patience, knowing that he does not forget his own.
exp.50:31:
The explanation says that the fords, that is, the shallow places where the river could be crossed, were taken by the enemy. The reeds, which are the canes or rushes along the bank, were burned, and the soldiers of Babylon were left full of dread, not knowing what to do.

Jeremiah announces, on God's behalf, the fall of Babylon, the power that destroyed Jerusalem and led the people into exile. Many connect this with the conquest of 539 B.C., but the exact details of the fords and the reeds are not entirely clear. The message was a comfort for the exiles: God had not forgotten their suffering.

Today we can remember that no human power is eternal. If you feel oppressed or afraid before something that seems invincible, bring it to God in prayer. He sees the injustice and acts in his own time.
exp.41:1:
Here the people come to Jeremiah and ask him to pray for them. The phrase "let our supplication be accepted before thee" means that he would receive their request with attention. They note that "thy God" is the Lord, and that they are a remnant, that is, a small group that survived. They say they were many and now are few, as the prophet himself can see. The word "even" in the verse introduces the idea of "all this remnant" as a whole.

Here speak the military leaders, Johanan, Jezaniah, and all the people. Jerusalem had fallen before Babylon, and this group of survivors was frightened and without direction. They seek God's guidance through the prophet. Later, the story shows that they did not obey what God told them, so their request was not entirely sincere.

For today: asking God for advice is good, but we must be willing to obey his answer before we ask him. Today you can pray, saying: "Lord, tell me what to do, and I want to do it."
exp.47:25:
It says that God commands Moab to be "made drunk," that is, to be made to stagger under his judgment, like someone who drinks a cup of punishment. The reason is that Moab "magnified himself" against the Lord, in other words, he rose up proudly against Him. Therefore he will wallow in his vomit, an image of total humiliation. "Derision" means mockery or public shame.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and the chapter announces its fall because of its arrogance and its trust in itself. The following verse recalls that Moab also mocked Israel, the people of God.

For today: pride that defies God ends in shame. We can examine whether we trust our achievements more than Him, and ask Him for humility to depend on God each day.
exp.30:21:
God asks his people: "How long will you wander back and forth, rebellious daughter?" (the source word for "rebellious" means stubborn or defiant, so I'll keep it as "rebellious" since that word appears in the verse). He announces that he will create something new on the earth: "a woman will encircle a man." This phrase is difficult, and it has been understood in several ways: as a Israel that returns and seeks God with strength, as an unexpected situation of safety, or, in the Christian tradition, as a sign of the Messiah. There is no single certain explanation.

The Lord speaks to the exiles of Israel. Tenderly he calls them to return to their land, for he promises restoration, forgiveness, and a new beginning.

For today: if you are far away or going around in circles without direction, God does not reject you. He invites you to return, and he can begin something new in you. Today, pray with sincerity and take one concrete step toward him.
exp.37:26:
The verse tells how the princes came to Jeremiah and asked him what he had said with the king. Jeremiah answered them just as the king had instructed him. Then they left him alone, for the matter was not perceived, meaning that no one else knew what had really been discussed.

This passage is told by the narrator of the book. King Zedekiah had called Jeremiah in secret, and he feared the princes, who wanted to kill the prophet. Jeremiah had asked not to be sent back to the house of Jonathan, where he had nearly died. His answer was true, though he did not tell them everything. Some scholars see prudence in this; others debate whether it was the best course.

Today we can learn to be prudent and honest at the same time. We do not always have to tell everything, but we should take care that what we say is true. Let us ask God for wisdom to speak with sincerity and to protect what ought to be kept.
exp.29:7:
God promises that, on that day, he himself will break the yoke that weighs down his people. The yoke is the wooden piece placed on the necks of working animals. The straps that hold it in place are the ties that fasten it on. Foreigners are the peoples from other nations. The promise is that they will never again be enslaved.

The LORD of hosts speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. His people were suffering under foreign rule and in exile, and before this promise a time of great distress is described. Yet God announces deliverance. The verses that follow say they will serve the LORD their God and a king from the line of David. Some see this fulfilled in the return from exile, others in Christ.

For today: if you feel bound by fear, guilt, or some heavy burden, you can trust that God knows how to break chains. Bring that burden to him in prayer today, without fear.
exp.21:26:
Here it says that Coniah and his mother will desire with all their heart to return to their land, but they will not manage it. The phrase "lift up their soul" is an old expression that means to long for, to desire eagerly. In the verse above, the word "desire" is the one that carries this sense.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Coniah, also called Jehoiachin, was a king of Judah. God announces that he will be handed over to King Nebuchadnezzar and taken captive to Babylon. This happened because of the kingdom's disobedience. The text says he would die there, far from his homeland.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and God invites us to listen to Him in time. Even when we go through losses or difficult periods of exile, we can draw near to Him with humility, knowing that He hears us and cares for us.
exp.50:42:
It says that the cities of Babylon would be destroyed. Its land would be dry and desolate, a place where no one would live or even pass through. "Desolate" means completely ruined. "Son of man" simply means "a human being." "Dwell" means "live."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing what the LORD says against Babylon, the power that had subjected Judah. The passage, with images of sea and desert, shows that its great power would come to an end. Sheshach is a coded name for Babylon. God also calls his people to leave there and save themselves. Scholars discuss how and when each detail of this prophecy was fulfilled.

For today: nothing that humanity builds with pride is eternal. Today you can ask yourself where you are placing your security, and trust more in God, who endures forever.
exp.32:12:
This verse lists several regions of Judah: the cities of the mountains, the cities of the lowland, the cities of the south, the land of Benjamin, and the places around Jerusalem. In all of them, God says, flocks will once again pass under the hands of those who count them, that is, of the shepherds who number their sheep. Counting the flock is a sign of peace and prosperity.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who is in prison while Jerusalem is under attack by Babylon. It is a message of comfort for a people who will be taken into captivity. God promises to restore the desolate land and then announces the Messiah, the Branch of righteousness from the line of David.

For today: when everything seems ruined, God can still give back the ordinary and the simple. Trust that he keeps his word, and praise him now, even in the middle of trial.
exp.41:19:
This verse says that the people deceived themselves. The phrase about leading their souls astray means that they went off course and did harm to themselves. They asked Jeremiah to pray to God and promised to do everything God said. The phrase asking to be told means "let us know," and the phrase about putting it into practice means "we will do it."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors wanted to flee to Egypt out of fear. They asked God for guidance, but God told them to stay in the land. Jeremiah warns them that their hearts already seemed set on going to Egypt, even though they said the opposite.

For today: let us not ask God for direction if we have already decided not to obey. Before we pray, let us truly surrender our plans to him, and be willing to follow his answer, even when it is difficult.
exp.3:6:
Here a terrible enemy is described, advancing like a lion coming out of its hiding place. He is called the destroyer of nations, that is, someone who lays whole peoples waste. He comes to leave the land of Judah desolate, with its cities in ruins and no one living in them. The word "laid waste" means to destroy completely, and an "inhabitant" is a person who lives in a place.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing what God says. God warns Judah that the judgment is coming from the north because of their disobedience. Many understand that the lion refers to Babylon, although the text does not give the name here. The trumpet is meant to wake the people and move them to react.

For today: do not ignore God's warnings, hoping that everything will simply pass. If you sense that something in your life is drifting away from Him, do not put it off. Come to Him today with humility, ask for forgiveness, and correct your course, trusting in His mercy.
exp.39:4:
Nebuzaradan, the captain of the Babylonian guard, is said to have still been speaking with Jeremiah when he offered him another choice: to return to Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor over the cities of Judah, and to live with him among the people. He could also go wherever he thought best. The word "convenient" in the verse means suitable or agreeable. Then he gave him food and gifts, and let him go.

A Babylonian officer speaks here after the fall of Jerusalem. He had removed Jeremiah's chains and gave him freedom to choose. Jeremiah had announced this judgment for years. According to the text that follows, he went with Gedaliah to Mizpah, alongside those who remained in the land.

God can use even difficult circumstances to care for us and guide us. When you have to make a decision, pray, think about where you can serve best, and choose with humility, even if it is not the easiest or most impressive path.
exp.51:2:
It says that what happened to Jerusalem and Judah was no accident: God was angry because of their sin, and in the end he cast them out of his presence, that is, he removed them from their land and led them into exile. Also, King Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

This final chapter of Jeremiah summarizes the fall of Jerusalem, probably as the historical closing of the book. It tells how Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, did evil, just as earlier kings had. He rebelled against Babylon, and that brought the siege of the city. The text presents this as God's judgment for years of disobedience.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also warns us beforehand. If you feel God is calling you to correct something, do not put it off. Listen to him today, with humility, and return to him before the consequences grow.
exp.15:12:
God tells the people of Judah that he will drive them out of their land and take them to a country that neither they nor their ancestors have known. There they will serve false gods all the time, and God will not show them mercy. The word "favour" in the verse refers to kindness or mercy, and "other gods" means strange or false gods.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had abandoned God, worshiped idols, and followed the desires of their stubborn hearts, even worse than their fathers. This is the warning of exile. But the next verse shows that punishment would not be the final word: God promises to bring them back to their land.

For today: when we turn our backs on God, we end up serving other things that enslave us. We can return to him with humility today, trusting that his discipline seeks to restore us, not destroy us.
exp.9:9:
It says that, unlike idols, the Lord is the true God. He is alive, he is king forever, and at his anger the earth trembles. The nations cannot endure his fury, which is his righteous wrath and indignation. The verse's "fury" is his righteous wrath or indignation, and the nations are the peoples who cannot stand before it.

Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah, who saw the nations worship idols of wood covered with silver and gold. The prophet mocks those images, made by craftsmen, and contrasts them with the God who created everything. This verse is the center of that contrast.

For today: modern idols, such as money, success, or the approval of others, are also our own handiwork and cannot save us. Today you can place your trust in the living God, acknowledge his authority, and rest in the fact that he still reigns.
exp.19:2:
It says that the next day Pashur released Jeremiah from the stocks, a wooden device that held the body fast and punished it. Then Jeremiah announced to him that God no longer called him Pashur, but "Magor-missabib." This expression is usually understood as "terror on every side."

Pashur was a priest and an authority in the temple. He was angered by the message of judgment that Jeremiah preached, and he punished him. Jeremiah, without fear, spoke in God's name and gave him a new name that announced what would come: the invasion of Babylon and the suffering of the people.

For today: holding a religious position does not make us right. If someone corrects us with God's truth, it is better to listen with humility than to silence them or defend ourselves with pride.
exp.38:15:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian man. The message is that God will carry out his words against Jerusalem, for harm and not for good. "Before thee" means "in front of you": Ebed-melech would see with his own eyes that what was announced comes to pass.

God speaks through Jeremiah, who was being held in the courtyard of the prison. Ebed-melech, an official of the palace, had stood up for the prophet and helped pull him out of a cistern (chapter 38). This word came before the fall of Jerusalem. Although it announces judgment, it opens the way to a promise of protection for him, as seen in the verses that follow.

For today: God sees acts of courage and kindness, even when no one else notices them. If you do what is right and trust in Him, you can rest in the knowledge that He will not forget you, even in difficult times.
exp.51:0:
This verse introduces Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. He began to reign at the age of twenty-one and ruled for eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother is also named, Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah (she is not known to be the prophet Jeremiah, who was from Anathoth). The phrase "began to reign" means that he started to rule.

This final chapter of the book of Jeremiah reads like a historical summary, very similar to 2 Kings 24 and 25. It is not a speech from God, but an account that explains how Jerusalem fell. The verses that follow show that Zedekiah did what was evil, and that the judgment came because of the people's disobedience and their leaders. The details of his age and his mother place his reign in real history.

Today we can learn that holding an office or a position is not enough; what matters is obeying God. Let us ask him for humility to listen to his voice in time and not to harden our hearts.
exp.4:10:
This verse says that both Israel, the northern kingdom, and Judah, the southern kingdom, rebelled against God in a deliberate way. The word can be understood as "very treacherously": it was not a stumble, but a willful disloyalty.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, He announces that He will punish a people who abandoned Him, and that their walls will be torn down because they in fact do not belong to Him. Then their rebellion is shown: they denied God, said that no harm would come upon them, and despised the prophets.

For today: God does not settle for a faith of words alone. Honestly examine whether there is something you know God is asking of you and that you have decided to ignore. Return to Him soon, without excuses, because His patience seeks to lead us to repentance.
exp.37:0:
This verse tells us that four men heard what Jeremiah was saying to all the people: Shephatiah, Gedaliah, Jucal, and Pashur. "Heard" here means they heard it with their own ears. What Jeremiah said appears in the next verse.

The prophet Jeremiah was speaking in Jerusalem while the city was surrounded by the army of Babylon. He was announcing God's message: whoever surrendered would live, and whoever stayed would face grave danger. These four were officials of the kingdom. According to the text that follows, they became upset with his message and asked that he be put to death. We see that later, not in this verse.

For today: hearing is not the same as obeying. We can listen to a hard truth and become angry, or we can let it correct us. Let us ask God for a humble heart to receive his word, even when it is not what we want to hear.
exp.17:22:
Here Jeremiah speaks to God and tells Him that He knows well the plans of his enemies to kill him. He asks God not to forgive them or wipe away their sin, that is, not to let them go unpunished. The phrase "let them fall" means that they should be brought down before God's justice. The "time of your anger" is the moment when God acts in judgment.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. The people of his own town rejected him and plotted against him because he announced hard messages on behalf of God. This is one of his strongest prayers, sometimes called a "confession." Some see in it sincere pain brought before God; others, a cry that reflects the justice of prophetic judgment.

For today: when someone hurts you, you can bring your pain to God with complete honesty, without hiding what you feel. But leave justice in His hands, and remember that Jesus taught us to pray also for those who harm us (Matthew 5:44).
exp.7:13:
Here the people ask themselves, "What shall we trust in?" They propose to gather together and take refuge in the fortified cities to rest there. But then they admit that the Lord has left them without a voice or defense. The "cup of bitterness" is an image of bitterness and suffering, perhaps poisoned water. They acknowledge that all of this happens because they sinned against God.

Here the people of Judah speak, although some understand it to be the prophet Jeremiah speaking on their behalf. God has just said that judgment is coming because of their rebellion and because they did not even feel shame. The strong cities seemed like a way out, but the following text shows that the enemy would come anyway.

For today: when a crisis arrives, let us not first run to our human refuges. Let us honestly acknowledge our faults and return to God, who forgives those who repent.
exp.49:23:
The explanation says that Babylon fell like an animal that does not see the trap. Snares were laid for her, that is, nets or traps, and she was caught without realizing it. "You were found" means that they found her, and "caught" means taken captive. The reason the text gives is that she "struck against" the Lord, that is, she defied him and offended him.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on what God said against Babylon. This empire had dominated and destroyed other peoples, including Judah, and it felt secure. The message announces that God would call it to account. The Bible says that its pride and its wickedness had consequences. Scholars often connect the fall with the arrival of the Medes and Persians, although the text is written in poetic language.

Today we can remember that feeling secure does not mean being free from error. It is wise to ask God for humility and to examine our hearts before pride blinds us.
exp.47:4:
It says that the weeping of Moab will be so great that people will go up the slope of Luhith crying. At the descent to Horonaim, even the enemies heard cries of pain over the ruin. Luhith and Horonaim were places in Moab.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing a message from God about Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Moab trusted in its riches and in its god Chemosh, and for that reason judgment would come. Scholars are not certain of the exact location of Luhith, but the meaning of the verse is clear: the disaster would reach the whole territory.

For today: let us not put our security in money, in achievements, or in things that can disappear. Let us ask God to teach us to trust in Him first, and to live with humility and gratitude.
exp.46:0:
This verse is the introduction to a message from God. It says that the LORD gave a word to the prophet Jeremiah concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, struck Gaza, that is, attacked it or beat it down.

God is the one speaking, and Jeremiah is the messenger. Gaza was an important Philistine city. It is not known for certain which attack the verse refers to; scholars have understood it in several ways. What is clear is that the message announces a judgment that would come upon that region, as the verses that follow show.

For today: God sees the future and rules over all nations, even those that seem strong. We can trust that nothing escapes him. This invites us to live with humility and to place our security in him, not in human power.
exp.7:18:
The verse shows a cry that comes from a distant land. The people ask: "Is not the Lord in Zion? Is not her King there?" Then God answers with grief: why have they provoked him with idols? "Carved images" are idols that have been shaped by hand. "Foreign worthless things" are gods of other nations that are worth nothing.

Jeremiah writes before the exile in Babylon. Many understand that he hears in advance the weeping of those who will be carried into exile. The questions express surprise: how can this be happening to us if God dwells among us? God responds that the problem was their idolatry. Some think the voice asking the questions is Jeremiah's, and others think it is the people's. In any case, the grief of the prophet and the grief of God are mixed together.

Today: it is not enough to say "the Lord is with us" while we give our hearts to other things. Ask him to show you what has taken his place, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.6:19:
God says that his anger and his wrath will fall upon "this place," that is, Jerusalem and Judah. The punishment will reach people, animals, the trees, and the crops. "Is poured out" speaks of something that falls with force. "Shall burn" means that it will be a fire that no one will be able to put out.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. He says it in the temple in Jerusalem, where the people felt secure. But the whole family took part in worshiping "the queen of heaven," a foreign goddess. Many scholars connect her with Ishtar, though not all agree. God warns them that their sin would harm themselves.

Today: God is not satisfied with a religion that is only for show. Examine what things are taking the place of God in your home, and return to Him in humility before the harm grows.
exp.47:5:
The verse is an urgent command: flee to save your lives. It asks them to be like the broom bush in the desert, a solitary shrub with thin branches and no shade, that survives on dry ground. Some understand that it speaks of someone who flees with nothing and barely holds on; others, that it refers to hiding in remote places. The original text allows more than one reading.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God, announcing judgment on Moab, a people neighboring Israel. The following verses explain the reason: Moab trusted in its riches and in its god Chemosh, and not in the Lord. Because of this, destruction would come upon its cities.

For today: what we have, whether money, work or security, can fail. Today we can examine where we are placing our trust and return it to God, who does not collapse.
exp.30:27:
This verse says that God watched over his people with great care when it was time for judgment: to pluck up, to break down, to throw down, to destroy, and to afflict. "Throw down" means to overturn or tear apart what was in order, and "destroy" means to ruin. Now God promises that same devoted care for rebuilding: to build and to plant.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel and Judah had suffered judgment, above all through the exile in Babylon. Chapters 30 and 31 are a message of comfort and hope. God announces that punishment will not be the final word, but that there will be restoration and a new beginning.

For today: if you are going through a season of loss or correction, do not conclude that God has abandoned you. He is as faithful to build up as he was to discipline. Place your ruins in his hands, trust his timing, and cooperate with what he wants to build in you.
exp.22:0:
This verse is a strong warning from God. "Woe" expresses grief and condemnation. The "shepherds" are the leaders of the people, and the "sheep" are God's people. "Destroy and scatter" means that they ruin them and leave them dispersed, without care or direction. "Pasture" is the flock that God himself looks after.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The shepherds were the kings and rulers of Judah, and possibly other leaders as well. Through their bad example and their neglect, the people were lost and ended up scattered. The verses that follow say that God will hold them accountable, but he also promises to gather those who remain and bring them back to their land.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, in the church, the family, or the workplace, care for them with humility and truthfulness. And if leaders have failed you, remember that God is the Shepherd who does not abandon his people.
exp.50:5:
It says that God's people must flee from the midst of Babylon and save their lives, so as not to perish with her because of her wickedness. "Vengeance" here means justice: God is going to give Babylon what she deserves.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon was a powerful empire that had oppressed other peoples, including Judah. The previous verse recalls that God did not abandon Israel and Judah, even though they had sinned. For this reason God warns them to leave before the judgment on Babylon.

For today: God invites us to move away from any environment, habit, or relationship that pulls us toward evil. Ask him to show you something concrete you should turn away from, and take a real step today to get out of it.
exp.5:2:
The explanation says that shepherds will come to Jerusalem with their flocks. They will set up camp around the city, pitching their tents, and each will let his sheep graze in the part that falls to him. "To feed" means to give pasture to livestock. "Round about" means all around.

God speaks through Jeremiah and announces a judgment coming from the north. The "shepherds" here are usually understood as the leaders of enemy armies, and their flocks would be their troops. They surround the city as though it were a field to be divided among them. The "daughter of Zion" is Jerusalem, described as delicate and confident. Some scholars see here an image of siege; the text uses symbolic language.

For today: let us not confuse comfort with security. If God calls us to correct something, let us listen promptly, before the problems grow and surround us.
exp.7:5:
God says that he listened with close attention, but heard no one speaking what was true. No one repents of his wickedness or asks himself, "What have I done?" Each one keeps going his own way, like a horse that charges into battle without thinking or pulling back.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. God has just asked why his people do not return to him, even though whoever falls gets up again. Here he describes the hardness of their hearts: they have heard warnings, yet they keep moving forward without reflecting.

For today: before we hurry on with our own habits, it is good to stop and ask ourselves honestly, "What have I done?" If God shows us a mistake, we can repent quickly and return to him, who welcomes with grace whoever comes back.
exp.5:9:
Jeremiah asks to whom he can speak so that someone will listen. He says the people's ears are closed, shut up, as if they were not ready to receive anything from God. The word of the Lord strikes them as a reproach: they see it as something shameful or something they look down on. They take no pleasure in it.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. God had warned the people many times, but they remained hardened. Jeremiah feels the weight of speaking and not being heard, and in the verses that follow he says he is full of the anger of God.

For today: ask yourself whether you truly want to hear God or only want to hear what pleases you. Ask him for a heart willing to receive his word, even when it corrects you.
exp.23:3:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah again. The phrase "the word of the Lord came unto me" means that a message from God came to him. After asking him what he saw, God is going to explain the meaning of the two baskets of figs.

Jeremiah is the prophet speaking. God had just shown him two baskets in front of the temple. This happens after the king of Babylon carried some of the people of Judah into exile, around 597 B.C. God uses the image of the figs to explain what was happening to those who had been taken away.

For today: God does not leave us with only what we see. When something seems confusing or painful, we can ask him to help us understand it from his perspective and listen to his word with patience.
exp.48:34:
God says, the Lord of hosts, that he will break the bow of Elam. The bow was that people's main weapon, so it stands for their military strength. The phrase "the chief of their might" means that there lay the best of their power.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at the beginning of Zedekiah's reign in Judah. Elam was a nation east of Babylon, known for its archers. The message is part of the prophecies against several nations. The verses that follow say that Elam will be scattered and will suffer judgment. Scholars do not agree on all the historical details of how this was fulfilled.

For today: no human strength, whether money, power, or skill, is absolute. It is wise to trust God and not in what we think makes us invincible.
exp.9:4:
It says the idols of the nations are like a scarecrow in a cucumber field (this is one way to understand "palm": a wooden figure standing upright and stiff, though some think it refers to a smooth trunk like a palm tree's). They do not speak, they have to be carried because they cannot walk. That is why "do not be afraid of them": they can neither do harm nor help.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf to his people, Judah, who were surrounded by nations with idols and felt tempted either to fear them or to imitate them. The prophet describes how they are made: wood cut down, decorated with silver and gold, and fastened so it will not fall. He then contrasts all of this with the LORD, who has no equal.

For today: ask yourself what things frighten you or what you trust more than God, such as money, status, or the opinion of others. Everything we make ourselves falls short. Place that trust in the living God, who does hear and does act.
exp.14:15:
Jeremiah says that he found God's words and took them in, that is, he received them and held them deep within himself. Those words were a joy and delight to his heart. The reason is that he bore God's name: he was God's prophet, belonging to him.

The word "eat" in the verse is a figure of speech for taking something in fully and making it part of oneself. The phrase "the Lord of hosts" is a title that highlights the power of God.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the midst of rejection and mockery for announcing God's message. Before and after this verse he complains, asks for help, and feels deep pain. Even so, he remembers that God's word was his joy. Some think it refers to a moment of his calling, but the text does not say so with certainty.

For today: when you are tired or hurt, do not leave the Bible aside only as a duty. Read it slowly, as one who is nourished, and honestly tell God what you feel.
exp.11:11:
It says that destroyers came upon all the bare hilltops and high places of the wilderness. The "sword of the Lord" is an image of God's judgment, which reaches the land from one end to the other. "Spoilers" means plunderers or destroyers. "No flesh" means no human being; no one would have peace.

The Lord speaks, in the middle of Jeremiah's lament about the people of Judah. God calls the land "my vineyard" and "my heritage," and describes how invaders laid it waste because of the people's disobedience. Many understand this to refer to enemy armies, such as Babylon, though the text gives no names here.

For today: God takes seriously the direction we follow. His judgment is not whim, for He always calls people to repentance. Ask yourself whether there is something in your life that He is asking you to correct, and return to Him today with humility, trusting in His mercy.
exp.33:16:
God says that, since the people did not obey him when they proclaimed freedom to their fellow Hebrews, he will now proclaim a different kind of "freedom" for them: being left free to the sword, the plague, and the famine. To proclaim means to announce officially. Being "removed" means they will be shaken and scattered, becoming an object of horror before all the kingdoms of the earth.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem. The leaders had made a covenant to free their Hebrew servants, as the law required, but then they enslaved them again. In doing this they broke a promise made before God, in his house and with a solemn ceremony.

For today: God expects us to keep what we promise, especially when it comes to treating others with justice. Check whether there is any promise or debt of justice you have failed to fulfill, and seek to make it right with humility.
exp.33:14:
God reminds the people of Jerusalem that not long before they had done something good: they had turned back and set free their Hebrew servants. They did it with a solemn promise made inside the temple, "the house which is called by my name." The sentence explaining the two source-language words is removed, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah while Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon. The people freed their servants, as the law commanded, but afterward they enslaved them again. God holds them accountable for that betrayal, because they had sworn before him.

Today, this passage invites us to keep what we promise to God and to others. A good beginning is not enough if we later turn back. Let us ask him for help to be faithful.
exp.1:26:
It says the people call a piece of wood "father" and a stone "mother" or creator, that is, they call their idols that. The wooden block is "wood," and the back of the neck is the nape. They gave God their back, not their face. But when trouble comes, they ask: "Arise, and save us."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He accuses them of abandoning the living God to follow idols. With irony, he shows them as inconsistent: they ignore him in calm times and seek him only in crisis. In the verses that follow, he tells them to ask their gods for help.

For today: examine what you place your trust in, such as money, success, or approval. Seek God also in the good days, not only when there is distress, and trust that He still welcomes whoever returns with sincerity.
exp.23:4:
God tells Jeremiah that, just as good figs are precious, He will look with favor on the exiles of Judah. The people carried away into exile are the ones taken from their land, and the Babylonians are the ones who carried them off. God affirms that He sent them there for their good.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah after Babylon had taken the king and many leaders of Judah captive. God uses two baskets of figs: the good ones represent the exiles, and the bad ones represent those who stayed behind or fled. The promise is that He will watch over them, bring them back, and give them a heart to know Him.

For today: even when a crisis seems like punishment or total loss, God may be working for our good. Trust Him and turn to Him with all your heart.
exp.8:10:
God says that Jerusalem will be turned into heaps of ruins, a place where serpents live, that is, wild animals that take over what has been abandoned. He also says that the cities of Judah will be laid waste, that is, destroyed and empty, without any dweller, meaning without any inhabitant.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah had abandoned God's law and had not obeyed his voice, as the following verses explain. This announcement of judgment speaks of the destruction that would come at the hand of Babylon. Jeremiah says it with sorrow, since the text shows mourning and weeping over the land.

For today: God takes obedience seriously, but he also warns us with love. Today we can ask ourselves whether there is something he has told us in his Word that we are setting aside, and turn back to him with sincerity.
exp.4:19:
God commands the prophet to announce a message to the whole people. "House of Jacob" and "Judah" refer to God's people, that is, to the entire nation. The words for "declare" and "make it heard" are rendered here in the verse itself: the first means to announce or proclaim clearly, and the second means that no one can say they did not hear it.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah. The people had left God to serve other gods, and yet they wondered why hard things were happening to them. This verse is the introduction to a warning: what follows is a call to listen, for the people had eyes and ears, but did not want to see or hear.

For today: God speaks to us clearly, but sometimes we pretend not to hear. Today you can take a quiet moment, open the Bible, and ask God for a heart willing to listen and obey, without excuses.
exp.39:9:
He says that Gedaliah will stay in Mizpah to represent the people before the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) when they arrive. In the meantime, he encourages the Jews to gather wine, bread and oil, which are the fruits of the harvest, to store them in their storehouses, and to stay in the cities they had already taken.

Gedaliah is speaking, the man whom the king of Babylon appointed as governor over the few who remained in Judah after the fall of Jerusalem. The army leaders were uncertain and afraid, so he promises them that, if they submit to Babylon, they can live in peace and work the land.

For today: in uncertain times, God invites us to keep going with what is within our reach, to work with calm and to take care of what we have, instead of letting fear paralyze us. Doing well the tasks of each day is also a way of trusting.
exp.6:14:
God says he will cast the people of Judah out of his sight, just as he had already cast out their "brothers," that is, the tribes of the north. "Ephraim" was the largest tribe and stood for the whole kingdom of Israel. The phrase "cast out of my sight" means driving them away, taking away his favor and his closeness.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah trusted that the temple in Jerusalem would protect them, even though they kept living in disobedience. God reminds them that he had spoken to them many times and they did not listen. Israel, the northern kingdom, had already been taken captive by Assyria, and God uses that example as a warning.

For today: it is not enough to have religious things or to feel secure because of our tradition. God looks for a heart that listens and obeys. If you feel that God is speaking to you today, respond quickly and with humility.
exp.21:16:
It says that Jehoiakim had his eyes and his heart set only on his own gain. "Covetousness" is the desire to have more and more. He also sought to shed innocent blood, to oppress others and to do them harm.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jehoiakim, king of Judah, was building a luxurious palace while the people suffered. God compares him with his father Josiah, who defended the poor and the afflicted. For God, knowing Him is seen in doing justice. So He announces that Jehoiakim will have a dishonorable end.

For today: examine where you set your heart and your time. If you have any power, whether at home, at work or in the church, use it to care for others and not to take advantage of them.
exp.49:2:
This verse announces that a nation from the north will attack Babylon and leave its land desolate. The "north" is the direction the verse names, which the King James wording gives as "out of the north." Destruction that is total is what the word "desolate" means here. No people or animals will remain, because all of them will leave: "they shall remove, they shall depart, both man and beast."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Babylon, the empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and taken Judah into captivity. Its idols, Bel and Merodach, are called powerless. Scholars often see the Medes and Persians in this, although the prophecy also speaks of a broader fulfillment. Then God promises that Israel will return, weeping and seeking him.

For today: no human power, however strong it may seem, stands above God. We can trust that he does justice and restores those who return to him in humility.
exp.13:3:
This verse describes a severe drought. The ground split open into cracks because no rain fell, and the farmers, not knowing what to do, covered their heads. The word "chapt" in the verse means split or cracked open. The plowmen are the farmers. Covering the head was a gesture of shame, sorrow, and despair.

Jeremiah records this drought as part of a lament over Judah. Everyone suffers: the nobles, the farmers, and even the animals. Later, the people acknowledge their sin and cry out to God. Many understand this drought as a sign that the people had turned away from Him, although the text shows above all the pain and anguish of the people.

There are moments when our resources run out and we do not know what to do. Instead of hiding our faces in shame, we can lift them up and come to God with sincerity. He receives those who come with empty hands.
exp.48:13:
The prophet says he heard a message from God: a messenger was sent among the nations to call them to gather together against Edom. The word "rumour" in the verse means a report or a piece of news. The words "gather ye together" call the nations to come together, and "rise up to the battle" calls them to get ready to fight.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God against Edom, whose chief city was Bosra. Edom trusted in its mountains and its rocky strongholds, and believed it could not be touched. God announces that its pride will be brought low. Scholars understand in different ways how and when this was fulfilled, but the central message is clear: God rules over the nations.

For today: do not place your security in your position, your possessions, or your strength. All of that can fall. Live with humility and trust in God, who is the only refuge that never fails.
exp.31:26:
He says that the Lord is the God of "all flesh," that is, of all humanity, not only of Israel. Then he asks: "Is there any thing too hard for me?" Some translations read the question this way; the Hebrew word can mean "hard" or "wonderful," and for that reason it is rendered in several different ways.

God speaks to Jeremiah while Jerusalem is under siege by the Babylonians. Jeremiah, at God's command, had bought a field, and now he doubts and prays in confusion: why buy land if the city is going to fall? God answers by reminding him of his power. He announces judgment for idolatry, but later promises restoration.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, you can pray honestly, as Jeremiah did, and trust that nothing escapes him and nothing is impossible for him.
exp.28:29:
This verse is simple: it says God spoke to Jeremiah again. The phrase "the word of the Lord came" is an older way of saying that God gave him a message. It is a brief introduction to what follows.

Jeremiah had written a letter to the exiles in Babylon, and a false prophet named Shemaiah had sent them letters saying the opposite. The priest Zephaniah read that letter to Jeremiah, and then God gave him an answer. Here God is the one speaking, and Jeremiah is the messenger. The message that follows condemns Shemaiah for giving false hope.

For today: before believing any spiritual message, compare it with what God has said in his Word. Words that sound encouraging do not always come from God, and his truth sustains us even when it is hard.
exp.2:9:
Here, the explanation says that although Judah saw the punishment that fell on her sister Israel, she did not turn back to God with her whole heart. She only pretended, going along with it without sincerity. The point is that Judah's repentance was only on the surface.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel, the northern kingdom, had already been taken into exile because of her unfaithfulness, which the Scripture describes as spiritual adultery. Judah, the southern kingdom, saw this and yet carried on just the same. It is likely that this refers to shallow religious reforms, though scholars interpret it in different ways. God wants a true change.

For today: God is not satisfied with rituals or pleasant words. We can honestly ask ourselves whether our faith comes from the heart or is only a matter of habit, and ask him to give us a genuine repentance.
exp.50:34:
This verse is a cry for justice. Jerusalem, called the inhabitant of Zion, asks that the violence and the blood she suffered fall upon Babylon and Chaldea. "My flesh" speaks of her own wounded body, and "my blood" of the lives that were taken away.

Here the people of God speak, pictured as a mistreated woman. Earlier, they say that Nebuchadnezzar devoured them and left them like an empty vessel. God answers in the following verse: he will plead their cause and execute justice. The prophets present this as God's judgment on Babylon, not as mere human revenge.

For today: when you suffer injustice, you can bring your pain to God with sincerity, instead of taking revenge yourself. He listens to the wounded and knows how to act justly in his time.
exp.5:13:
The explanation says that the leaders treat the wound of the people as if it were something small. A serious break or injury is what is meant, and to treat it lightly is to handle it carelessly. They repeat "Peace, peace," but the peace they announce does not exist.

It is God speaking through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. He accuses prophets and priests of deceiving the people, because out of greed they told them that everything was well while sin kept growing. For this reason God later calls them to return to the ancient paths, but they answered: "We will not walk in it."

For today: do not settle for comforting words that ignore what is truly wrong. Ask God for humility to hear the truth, to recognize your wounds, and to return to his way, where there really is rest for the soul.
exp.25:23:
He says that Ahikam, son of Shaphan, protected Jeremiah so that they would not hand him over to the people to be killed. The phrase "was with" means that he supported and sheltered him. "Nevertheless" is the word that introduces the contrast with what came before, and "the people" here refers to those who wanted him dead.

The narrator tells us that Jeremiah had proclaimed judgment against Jerusalem and Judah, and this stirred up anger. Shortly before, it is told that King Jehoiakim had ordered the prophet Uriah put to death for saying the same thing. Jeremiah faced a similar danger. Ahikam was an influential man; his family appears in other passages helping Jeremiah. The Bible does not detail exactly how he protected him.

God can use particular people to care for those who speak the truth. We can be like Ahikam: to accompany and defend, with prudence, someone who suffers for doing what is right. And if you feel alone in your faithfulness, remember that God often provides support, sometimes in unexpected ways.
exp.49:35:
It says God will send judgment, like a sword, against the diviners of Babylon. They will be left "stupefied," meaning made foolish, because their predictions will fail. The sword will also fall on her "mighty men," her strong soldiers, and they will be "broken," that is, defeated and destroyed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had oppressed Israel and Judah, and trusted in its military power and in its wise men and diviners. God promises to defend his people, for their Redeemer is strong. Scholars understand that the passage announces the fall of Babylon, and some also see a broader meaning about judgment on all human pride against God.

For today: do not put your security in horoscopes, fortune-tellers, or your own strength. Trust in God, who cares for his people and rules over every human power.
exp.26:6:
The passage says that many nations will serve Nebuchadnezzar, his son, and his grandson, until the time comes when Babylon itself will be judged. Then other peoples and powerful kings will subdue her. The word "nations" in the verse above is the same word used for peoples in other translations, so both mean the same thing.

Through Jeremiah, God speaks to Judah and to the neighboring kings who wanted to rebel against Babylon. God affirms that He governs history and that, for a time, He allowed the power of Babylon. Its dominion would have a limit. The false prophets said the opposite and gave false hope.

Today we can remember that no human power lasts forever; only God remains. This invites us to be humble, not to trust messages that only tell us what we want to hear, and to seek God's voice with sincerity.
exp.24:32:
This verse says that on the day of God's judgment there will be many dead across the whole earth, from one end to the other. No one will mourn them, no one will gather them, and no one will bury them. They will lie on the ground like dung, that is, like worthless fertilizer.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, God had announced judgment on Judah and on many nations for their wickedness and their refusal to listen. Here it is shown that God is Judge of all humanity. The "shepherds" who come afterward are the rulers, who will also be judged.

For today: God takes justice seriously, and no one escapes it. Instead of ignoring his voice, we can repent with humility and trust in his mercy, which is still offered in Christ.
exp.29:13:
She says that Israel's "lovers," that is, the allied nations she had been seeking security from, have forgotten her and do not care for her. God says that he wounded her as an enemy would, with a harsh punishment, for the great multitude of her wickedness and her many sins. The phrase "for the multitude of thine iniquity" refers to the same idea of "because of," meaning the reason for the punishment.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Israel and Judah, who were living in crisis and exile. Their allies did not help them, and God explains that their suffering is connected to their rebellion. But the passage continues with a promise: God will judge their oppressors, and restoration will come.

For today: when the things or people we trust fail us, it is a good time to return to God honestly, acknowledge our faults, and ask him for healing. He corrects, but he also restores.
exp.45:16:
The Egyptian soldiers, defeated, cry out that Pharaoh is only a noise, like a man who made a great deal of commotion but let his chance slip by. The phrase about the king being a noise is usually understood as "a great noise" (other translations say "a commotion"). The appointed time would be the right moment to act or to resist.

Jeremiah announces the defeat of Egypt before Babylon, near the Euphrates River. The soldiers, who once trusted their king, now blame him for his empty words and his lack of action. Scholars discuss some details of the Hebrew text, but the general sense is that Egypt promised much and could not deliver.

Today we can learn not to place our trust in people who talk a lot and do little. Let us trust in God, whose word always comes to pass, and let us also be people who respond in time when He calls us.
exp.24:4:
God, speaking through his prophets, kept calling the people again and again: "Give up your evil ways and your wicked deeds, and live in the land that the LORD gave to you and to your ancestors forever."

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah. For twenty-three years he warned them, along with other prophets, but they would not listen. The call was an invitation to repentance: if they turned back to God, they could remain in their land. The phrase "forever" is understood as tied to their obedience, and some interpret it in different ways.

For today: God keeps calling with patience, not in a hurry to punish. If there is something in your life that you know does not please him, do not wait any longer. Listen to him today, take a concrete step of change, and trust that his mercy receives you.
exp.37:18:
King Zedekiah of Judah confesses to Jeremiah that he is afraid. He fears that the Jews who had gone over to the side of the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) will hand him over to them, and that they will mock him and mistreat him.

Jeremiah had just passed on a message from God: if the king surrendered to the leaders of Babylon, he himself would live, his family would be spared, and the city would not be burned. The king wanted to obey, but he was held back by fear of the people and of what they would say or do. Jeremiah answers him at once that they will not hand him over.

Today too we can know what God wants and still hesitate out of fear of mockery, rejection, or the consequences. This story invites us not to let human fear make our decisions for us, but to trust the word of God and take the step of obedience, even when it costs us.
exp.14:18:
God tells Jeremiah that if he turns back to Him, He will restore him and he will continue to stand before Him and serve Him. If he separates what is precious from what is worthless, he will speak as the mouth of God. Restoring means bringing back to its place, and what is worthless is that which has no value at all. In the end, the people must turn to the prophet, and not the prophet to the people.

The Lord speaks, answering Jeremiah, who has just complained bitterly. He feels alone, wounded, and rejected for preaching an unpopular message, and he even asks God whether he will be like a stream that dries up. God does not scold him harshly, but calls him to regain his confidence and faithfulness. Then He promises him protection.

For today: when you feel tired from doing what is right, tell God your pain honestly, but do not give in to whatever pulls you away from the truth. Ask Him to help you distinguish what is valuable from what is empty, and to speak with firmness and love.
exp.43:22:
Jeremiah tells the Jews living in Egypt that the disaster that fell on them was no accident. They offered incense burned in honor of other gods. By doing so they sinned against God, refused to listen to him, and did not follow his law, his commands, or the teachings he gave his people. The phrase "as at this day" means: "as you can see now."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of Jews fled to Egypt and kept worshiping the "queen of heaven," a pagan goddess. They believed this would bring them better fortune. Jeremiah answers that the ruin of Judah came from abandoning God.

Today we can ask ourselves where we look for security outside of God. Instead of blaming luck, it is wise to listen to his Word, recognize our mistakes, and obey him again with humility.
exp.41:0:
Here it says that all the military leaders, together with Johanan, Jezaniah, and all the people, from the least to the greatest, came near to Jeremiah. The word "came near" here is the verse's own wording, and the next verse explains why: they wanted him to pray for them.

The narrator tells what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. After the murder of the governor Gedaliah, the survivors were afraid of retaliation from Babylon. They seek out Jeremiah, the prophet, to ask for direction on God's behalf. Later it becomes clear that some were already thinking about going to Egypt.

For today: when you are afraid or do not know what to do, seek God's guidance with humility. But do not ask for direction only to hear what suits you; pray with the resolve to obey, whatever it is.
exp.8:22:
