God says that no one should take pride in their wisdom, their strength, or their wealth. Here, "boast" means to show off or to feel secure and superior because of something. These three things, wisdom, courage, and riches, were what the people believed would protect them.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah was living in sin, and judgment was drawing near, with death and destruction, as the verses before it show. Neither the wise, nor the strong, nor the rich would be able to save themselves. The verses that follow say what is truly worth rejoicing in: knowing God, who acts with mercy, justice, and righteousness.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our trust. Studies, work, or money are good, but they are not our foundation. Make time to know God through his Word and in prayer, because that is where true security is found.
exp.47:17:
It says that Dibon, an important city of Moab, must come down from its place of honor and sit in dry ground, without comfort. The reason is that the destroyer, an invader sent against Moab, has already come up against it and torn down its strongholds, that is, its defenses.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing God's message against Moab, a nation neighboring Israel. Throughout the chapter, Moab's pride and its trust in its wealth and strength are pointed out as the cause of its fall. Interpreters do not agree on who the exact invader was, but the message is clear: what seemed firm was going to collapse.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, success, or reputation. All of these can fail. Entrust your confidence to God and live with humility, because only He does not fall.
exp.28:7:
God warns his people not to be misled by the prophets and the diviners who live among them. He also tells them not to pay attention to the dreams they themselves dream. Being "deceived" means being led down a wrong path. "Diviners" are people who claim to know the future through means that God does not approve of.

Jeremiah writes a letter to the Jews who were carried off into exile in Babylon. God asks them to live normal lives, start families, and seek the good of the city. But some false prophets were telling them that the exile would end soon. God states that he did not send them, and that the return would come only after seventy years.

Today, before you believe a spiritual message, a "prophecy," or a hunch, check it against the Bible. If it does not agree with what God has already said, do not follow it, even if it sounds encouraging.
exp.9:22:
This verse says that a person cannot fully direct their own life or make sure of every step they take. The phrase "the way of man is not in himself" means that the course of a person's life does not rest in their own power. The one speaking recognizes that we need God's guidance.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks in prayer to God. He has just announced that the shepherds, that is, the leaders of Judah, did not seek the Lord and therefore failed. An invasion from the north is also foretold. Jeremiah admits human limitation and then asks that God correct him with justice, not with anger.

For today: before you make plans, pray and ask God for direction. Make your plans with humility, and trust that He can guide you even when things do not turn out as you expected.
exp.38:3:
What it says: When Zedekiah, king of Judah, and his soldiers saw that the Babylonians had already entered Jerusalem, they fled by night. They went out through a gate between two walls, near the king's garden, and the king took the road toward the wilderness, that is, toward the valley of the Jordan.

Context: The passage comes from the book of Jeremiah, describing the fall of Jerusalem after a long siege. Jeremiah had warned for years that God would allow this defeat and that surrendering was the best way out, but the king would not listen. Afterward, the Chaldeans caught up with him near Jericho.

For today: Running away from the consequences does no good when we would not listen to God's voice before. Today we can obey in time, acknowledge our mistakes, and return to Him in humility, because His word guides us better than our fear does.
exp.32:20:
It says that God's covenant with David is as firm as day and night. The word "annul" means to cancel or break. Just as no one can stop the order of day and night, no one will be able to cancel the promise that a descendant of David would reign, nor the promise that there would be Levites and priests serving God. "My ministers" refers to those who serve him in worship.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. The people were living through the disaster of the fall of Jerusalem and the exile, and it seemed that everything had been lost. God answers with hope: his word will stand. Christians see in Jesus, a descendant of David, the fullest fulfillment of this promise, though some interpreters understand it in other ways.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart, remember that God is faithful to what he has promised. Each sunrise can remind you that his faithfulness does not change, and that you can entrust your future to him.
exp.4:20:
This verse is a strong call from God to his people. He tells them to listen, though he calls them "foolish" and "without understanding." In biblical language, the "heart" is the mind and the will, meaning that they do not think or understand. They have eyes and ears, but they do not see or hear what God shows them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses Judah, which had left God to serve other gods. He warns them that this decision would have consequences. Then he asks them why they do not fear him, since he set limits to the sea by his power.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are really listening to God or only hearing words. Before reading the Bible or praying, we can ask him: "Lord, open my eyes and my heart." Then, obey what he shows us.
exp.28:3:
This verse is the opening of a letter. It says that the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, speaks to those who were carried away into exile. They were taken from Jerusalem to Babylon. The verse says "whom I have caused to be carried away": God acknowledges that the exile did not escape his control.

The prophet Jeremiah writes from Jerusalem, after the first deportation under King Jehoiachin. The letter is carried by two men sent to Babylon by King Zedekiah. The exiles expected to return soon, and God gives them instructions for a long stay.

God can speak to us and guide us even in places we did not choose. Instead of living while waiting for everything to pass, you can serve him today and do good in your present situation, trusting that he remains with you.
exp.4:21:
God asks his people whether they do not hold him in awe. He set the sand as the boundary of the sea, by a law that lasts forever. The waves rise and roar, but they cannot cross that limit.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He calls them foolish because, although they have eyes and ears, they do not understand. God reminds them of his power in creation to show that he deserves reverence, and that they have a rebellious heart that turns away from him.

For today: when you feel that your life is like a stormy sea, remember that God sets limits on what seems unstoppable. Respecting him and trusting him gives you peace, and it invites you to return to him with a sincere and humble heart.
exp.13:11:
God says that, even if the people fast, He will not listen to their cry. Nor will He accept their burnt offerings or their grain offerings. Here "consume" means to destroy. The "sword" is the weapon of war, "famine" is the scarcity of food, and "pestilence" refers to diseases that spread.

The LORD speaks to Jeremiah during a great drought and the threat of war. The people practiced religion on the outside, but in their conduct they remained far from God. The false prophets promised them peace without repentance. For this reason God tells Jeremiah not to pray for them.

For today: religious acts, such as praying, fasting, or giving, do not replace a heart that turns back to God. You might ask yourself honestly: is there something God is asking me to change while I only go through the outward motions?
exp.30:5:
This verse speaks of a future day when the watchmen, who kept guard from the heights of Ephraim, will give a joyful call. They will say: "Arise ye, and let us go up to Zion unto the Lord our God." The watchmen are the sentinels, and Zion is Jerusalem, where the temple stood. Ephraim names the tribes of the north.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He promises to restore Israel after the exile. The northern tribes had been divided and far from Jerusalem, but God announces that they will be brought back together to worship him together. Some see here a partial fulfillment in the return from exile, and others also a fuller fulfillment in the future.

For today: God knows how to gather what is divided and far away. We can draw near to him with hope, and also encourage others to say, "Let us go together to seek the Lord."
exp.50:62:
It says that, when he had finished reading the book in Babylon, Seraiah was to tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates River. The words "made an end of" mean "finished," and "bind" means "tie." The book contained the announcement of God's judgment against Babylon.

Jeremiah gives this command to Seraiah, an official who was traveling to Babylon with King Zedekiah. It was a symbolic act, like those prophets used to deliver a message. The book sinking represented the fall of Babylon, which would never rise again. Interpreters see in this the certainty of God's word, not a ritual with magical power.

For today: when evil seems great and unstoppable, remember that God has the final word. Trust in his promises and do not let fear defeat you, because he is faithful and just.
exp.32:3:
This verse says that God speaks, as the Lord and God of Israel, about the houses of Jerusalem and the palaces of the kings of Judah. Those houses were torn down by battering rams and by axes, that is, by siege machines used to break down walls and by tools used to destroy. The phrase "has said" in this verse means "has declared."

Jeremiah is imprisoned, and Jerusalem is surrounded by the army of Babylon (the Chaldeans). God acknowledges that the city suffers because of its wickedness, but in the same message he announces that he will not abandon it: he promises healing, forgiveness, and restoration.

For today: when you see something in your life or your family reduced to ruins, do not stay silent. God invites you to cry out to him, to acknowledge what needs to be corrected, and to trust that he can rebuild what seems lost.
exp.47:42:
It says that three dangers will come upon Moab: fear, the pit, and the snare. The "pit" is a trap dug in the ground, like the ones used to catch animals. The "snare" is a net or cord that catches. "Inhabitant" means someone who lives in a place. The idea is that there will be no way out.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring nation of Israel, and the preceding text says it was judged because it set itself up proudly against the Lord, that is, because of its pride and its rebellion. The verses that follow explain that whoever flees from one danger falls into another. It is poetic language about a judgment that is very real.

For today: pride makes us believe we do not need God, but in the end it traps us. Today you can be humble, recognize the things in which you have trusted yourself more than Him, and ask Him sincerely for direction.
exp.1:2:
God says that Israel was holy to Him, that is, a people set apart and dedicated. He compares it to the firstfruits, the first produce of the harvest, which belonged to God. Those who devoured Israel, meaning those who took advantage of it or attacked it, will be held guilty, and God promises that evil will come upon them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He tenderly remembers Israel's early days, when it followed Him through the wilderness like a faithful bride. This sets up a contrast: soon God will ask what wrong they found in Him that led them to turn away. It is an accusation, but one spoken with a tone of grief.

For today: God sees us as something precious and set apart for Him, not as an object of no importance. Today you can remember your first love and give God the first of your time, even if it is only a few minutes of prayer at the start of the day.
exp.41:9:
It says that if the people stay calm in Judah, God will build them up and plant them, and will not tear them down or uproot them. "Still" means to remain settled, without running away. "I repent me" does not speak of an error on God's part; many understand that it expresses his grief over the punishment he had to bring, and his desire to restore.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, the people were afraid of the king of Babylon and planned to escape to Egypt. Johanan and the leaders asked Jeremiah to pray, and ten days later this answer came: trust God and stay.

For today: when fear pushes us to look for quick ways out, we can stop, pray, and obey what God has already shown us. His protection often lies in trusting him, not in fleeing on our own.
exp.18:8:
It says that God will allow Jerusalem to be surrounded by its enemies, and that the hunger will be so terrible that people will come to eat their own sons and friends. The siege is the encirclement of the city; the extreme distress is the anguish of being pressed on every side; those who seek their lives are the ones who want to kill them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who announces judgment on Judah. The people had abandoned God, worshiped idols, and shed innocent blood in the valley of Ben-hinnom (see the verses before). This warning matches what is later described in Lamentations and in other texts about the siege of Jerusalem. It is presented as a consequence of rebellion, not as a desire of God to see them suffer.

For today: do not take God's warnings lightly. When He points out a wrong path, returning to Him in time is an act of mercy, not of weakness.
exp.3:10:
It says that a time is coming when people will speak of Jerusalem and its people in this way: a dry, scorching wind will blow from the bare heights of the desert upon "the daughter of my people," a tender way of naming God's people. Winnowing was throwing the grain into the air to separate the chaff from it, and cleansing was making it pure. But this wind is not for that purpose: it is too strong and only destroys.

God speaks through Jeremiah. The people believed that everything would be at peace, and false messages reinforced that belief. But God announces an invasion that many understand to be that of the army of Babylon, which comes from the north. Jeremiah himself is distressed by this word. The wind represents judgment for the people's unfaithfulness, not a gentle correction.

For today: let us not trust in an easy peace that avoids the truth. Let us ask God to show us honestly what we must correct, and return to Him while there is still time.
exp.3:3:
It says that the people of Judah and Jerusalem must "circumcise" themselves to God, but not in the body, rather in the heart. The "foreskins" are the skin that is cut away in circumcision; here it speaks of whatever blocks the heart from obeying God. If they do not change, God's anger will come out like a fire that no one can put out, because of the evil of their deeds.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier He had asked them to truly turn back to Him and to "break up the fallow ground," that is, to prepare the soil of the heart and not sow among thorns. Judah carried out outward rituals, but remained in sin. The verses that follow announce an invasion from the north.

For today: it is not enough to appear religious. Ask God to show you which attitude or habit is hardening your heart, and give it over to Him sincerely, letting Him change it from within.
exp.8:0:
Here the prophet wishes that his head were a spring of water and his eyes a fountain, so that he could weep day and night. He mourns for the slain of the daughter of my people, a poetic way of referring to the whole nation of Judah.

Jeremiah speaks, the one many call the weeping prophet. God had given him the task of warning Judah about its disobedience. The verses that follow speak of lies, unfaithfulness, and a people who did not know God. The slain may refer to those who would fall in the judgment that was drawing near; scholars mainly understand it this way. Jeremiah suffers with his people, even though he must announce the punishment to them.

For today: when we see sin and pain around us, let us not remain in criticism or indifference. Let us ask God for a sensitive heart, one that prays and weeps for others, and that is firm in the truth with love.
exp.16:6:
Blessed is the person who trusts in the Lord, that is, who places his security in Him. The word "man" here refers to any person, and "trusts" means has confidence. The second part reinforces this: the Lord Himself is his confidence, not just one more help among others.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, passing on what God said to the people of Judah. Just before this, God warns against trusting in other people and in one's own strength (flesh is his arm). That mistake is compared to a dry bush in the desert. This verse presents the contrast, and then the one who trusts in God is compared to a tree by the water.

For today: when a great worry comes, before looking only for human solutions, pray and hand it over to God. Asking others for help is not wrong, but let your final rest be in Him.
exp.45:17:
This verse says that God himself, the true King, swears by his own life that someone will come against Egypt. He compares this to Mount Tabor, which rises above the other mountains, and to Carmel, which stands up beside the sea. That is, the one who comes will be an overwhelming presence, impossible to ignore. "As I live" is a way of swearing an oath. "The Lord of hosts" means the Lord of all powers.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Egypt had been defeated, and its soldiers were fleeing, trusting in a pharaoh who let the appointed time pass by. Many understand that the one who comes is Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, used by God as an instrument of judgment. The text gives no further details.

For today: no human power, however great, stands above God. We can rest in the knowledge that he governs history, and trust in him more than in the leaders or security of this world.
exp.5:10:
Jeremiah says he is full of the Lord's anger and can no longer hold it in; he has grown tired of restraining it. That anger will fall on everyone: children out in the streets, groups of young men, husbands and wives, the old and the very aged. The very old are the ones who have lived a long time, and "taken" here refers to being captured in the invasion.

Jeremiah speaks, but he expresses God's feelings. Judah had spent years rejecting the warnings; its ears were closed. They despised God's word and lived in greed and deceit, including their religious leaders. The judgment would come through an invading army. Some understand the anger to be God's, and others understand that it also reflects the prophet's grief.

For today: let us not harden our hearts when God speaks to us. If something in his Word makes you uncomfortable today, listen to it with humility and change in time, before the consequences arrive.
exp.36:0:
This verse says that Zedekiah, son of Josiah, began to reign over Judah. He took the place of Coniah (also called Jehoiachin or Jeconiah), and it was Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon, who set him on the throne. The verse shows Nebuchadrezzar's authority in appointing him.

The one telling the story is the book of Jeremiah, which recounts these events as history. Judah was already under the power of Babylon, so Zedekiah was a subject king, not an independent one. The verses that follow explain why this matters: neither the king nor the people paid attention to the words that God gave through Jeremiah, even though they later asked him to pray for them.

For today: let's not wait until we are in trouble to seek God. Listening to and obeying his word in time is worth more than asking for prayer when it is already too late.
exp.1:3:
This verse is a call to listen. God asks the attention of all his people: "house of Jacob" and "families of the house of Israel" refer to the descendants of Jacob, that is, to the whole nation. "Hear ye" means "listen," and "the Lord" is the name of the Lord in this translation.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf. Just before this, God fondly recalls how Israel followed him in the wilderness, like a faithful bride. Then, in the verses that follow, he asks the people what wrong they found in him that led them to turn away and follow empty things, such as idols. This verse opens that complaint with tenderness and seriousness.

For today: before deciding or following what attracts us, we can pause to listen to the voice of God in his Word. Remembering how he has cared for us in the past helps us not to run after things that promise much and give nothing.
exp.31:22:
They came in and took possession of the land that was promised to them, but they did not listen to God's voice or live according to His law. They did not do what He commanded them. Because of this, God allowed all that disaster to fall upon them.

The prophet Jeremiah is the one speaking, praying to God. Babylon (the Chaldeans) had surrounded Jerusalem, and Jeremiah had bought a field by God's command. He remembers God's faithfulness in the past and acknowledges that the punishment came because of the people's disobedience. Then he asks, troubled, why God had told him to buy a field in the middle of that disaster.

For today: when we face difficult times, we can pray honestly, remembering what God has done and acknowledging our failures. Obeying Him is not a burden but the way to live well with Him.
exp.11:9:
It says that many shepherds, that is, rulers or leaders, ruined God's vineyard. The word for "trampled" means to trample underfoot, and the word for "portion" refers to the land or people that belong to God. What was precious to Him was turned into a lonely wilderness.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Judah. God laments that his people turned against him, and for that reason he allowed them to suffer. The "shepherds" are usually understood as kings and leaders, although some think they also include invading armies. Even so, the passage shows God's grief over what is lost.

For today: if you have any responsibility, whether in the family, the church, or at work, care with humility for those under your charge. And pray for leaders, that they will care for people and not destroy them.
exp.3:17:
It says that what is happening to Jerusalem is no accident: its own ways and its evil deeds brought about this result. The "wickedness" is its sin, and the "bitterness" is a deep pain that will reach the heart. The "watchmen" are soldiers who surround the city.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the Babylonian invasion. Judah had rebelled against God, and He warns that an enemy army is coming from afar. Immediately, the prophet expresses his own grief (the cry of anguish in his inner being), so the message joins justice and sorrow for the people.

For today: when we face painful consequences, it is wise to ask ourselves honestly whether there are decisions we should recognize and correct. God does not take pleasure in our pain; He invites us to return to Him with humility and to change direction.
exp.42:2:
Here the men say that Baruch, Jeremiah's assistant, is turning him against them. They accuse him of wanting to hand them over to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) so that they would be killed or taken away as prisoners to Babylon.

Azariah and Johanan speak, along with other proud men. After the fall of Jerusalem, they wanted to flee to Egypt because they were afraid of Babylon. Jeremiah had told them, on God's behalf, to stay in Judah. Instead of accepting the message, they called him a liar and blamed Baruch. The Bible does not say that Baruch did anything like this; it is their accusation.

When we do not want to hear an uncomfortable truth, it is easy to blame the messenger. Today we can ask God for humility to examine his Word with sincerity, even when it contradicts what we have already decided.
exp.49:32:
This verse says that God sees the suffering of his people. Israel and Judah, the northern and southern kingdoms, were oppressed, that is, treated with harshness and violence. Those who took them captive would not let them go. The verse says they "held them fast," meaning they kept them tightly bound, and to "let go" means to set them free.

The phrase "the Lord of hosts" shows his power over all things. This prophecy announces judgment against Babylon, the power that carried Judah into captivity. God promises to act on behalf of his people. The following verse calls him "the Redeemer," the strong one who defends their cause.

For today: if you feel trapped by an injustice or a burden you cannot shake off, remember that God sees your situation and is stronger than the one who oppresses you. Pray with confidence, keep doing good, and wait for his justice.
exp.30:38:
It says that a measuring line, that is, a cord used to mark out land and buildings, will continue to stretch out as far as the hill of Gareb and then will go around to Goah. "Hill" means the same as the word in the verse, "hill." It is not known for certain where Gareb and Goah were; they were probably places near Jerusalem, and scholars do not agree on their exact location.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He promises that Jerusalem will be rebuilt and dedicated to the Lord, even after the punishment. Measuring the city shows that God has a detailed plan to restore it. Earlier he said that he will not reject Israel forever, and this promise is part of the new covenant of this chapter.

For today: when you feel that your life has been left in ruins, remember that God knows how to restore with care and purpose. Place yourself in his hands and trust that he leaves nothing unmeasured.
exp.24:6:
This verse says that the people did not listen to God. The word "Yet" means "but," and "provoke me to anger" means to make him angry. "The works of your hands" refers to the idols they made and worshiped. In doing so, they were harming themselves.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. For many years, God had asked them to give up their evil ways, stop following other gods, and live in peace in their land. Since they paid no attention, God announces that he will bring Babylon, with its king Nebuchadnezzar, as the consequence of their rebellion.

For today: God warns us out of love, not to annoy us. If there is something in your life that you have put in God's place, such as money, fame, or an addiction, listen to his voice today and change course before it causes you more harm.
exp.21:4:
He says that if the king and his people do not obey what God has just commanded, God himself promises, with an oath, that the palace will become a desolation. The word "desolation" in the verse above shows what is meant: a place made empty and ruined. The phrase "I swear by myself" shows that God makes this promise with total seriousness.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing the king of Judah and his court. He had asked them for justice, to defend the oppressed and to care for the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. He offered them blessing if they obeyed, but he also warned them of the consequences if they did not. The warning seeks to bring them to repentance before it is too late.

For today: God is concerned with how we treat the weak. Today we can ask ourselves whom we can help or defend, and obey God's word through deeds, not only by hearing it.
exp.16:17:
Jeremiah asks God that his persecutors be put to shame and dismay, and that he himself not be. He asks that God bring upon them the day of evil, that is, a time of calamity, and that God destroy them with a complete and severe punishment.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here; he suffered mockery and threats for announcing God's word to the people. Earlier he says that he did not seek to be a prophet for his own pleasure, nor did he desire disaster; he only spoke what God gave him. This prayer is very harsh, and some see it as a desperate cry for justice rather than as a model of revenge.

For today: when you are hurt for doing what is right, you can tell God honestly your pain and your anger. Then leave justice in his hands and do not take revenge yourself.
exp.43:18:
What it says: The women of Judah explain that when they burned incense to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, their husbands knew about it and approved. Incense is the smoke of offerings burned on the altar; cakes are bread or pastry offered in worship; to worship her means to give her reverence.

Context: The speakers are Jews who took refuge in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. Jeremiah had called them to abandon idolatry, but they reject his message and blame their troubles on giving up this practice. The exact identity of the "queen of heaven" is debated; many connect her with a goddess of the ancient Near East, such as Ishtar or Astarte.

For today: It is easy to justify what we do by saying that everyone does it or that it has always been so. Let us ask God to show us the truth and obey him, even when custom says otherwise.
exp.13:8:
Here the people ask God why he seems to be like a man who is "astonied," that is, confused and unable to respond, or like a mighty warrior who cannot save anyone. Then they acknowledge that God is in the midst of them and that his name is "called upon" over them, meaning they are his people. They end by pleading: "leave us not," which means do not abandon us.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, praying on behalf of the people during a great drought. He acknowledges Israel's sin, but appeals to the character of God. In the response that follows, God says the people have not wanted to return to him, and he tells Jeremiah not to pray for them.

For today: when you feel that God is silent, be honest with him and pray with humility. Acknowledge your failings, remember that you belong to him, and ask for his help, but also allow him to correct your course.
exp.50:54:
It says that God himself is destroying Babylon and will silence the great noise of the city: its clamor, its pride, and its power. A "roar" is a loud noise. The enemy's "waves," or the invaders, will roar, and their voice will sound like great waters, that is, like a restless sea arriving with force.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on the words of the Lord. The message is addressed to Babylon, the empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and taken God's people into captivity. Those people needed to hear that God had not lost control and that he would bring about justice. Scholars understand in different ways how and when each detail was fulfilled, but the central message is clear.

For today: no human power, however great and noisy it may seem, stands above God. If you are suffering from something unjust today, you can trust that God sees and that he has the last word. Bring your worry to him in prayer.
exp.6:30:
The explanation says that the people of Judah built places of worship on high ground in Tophet, in the valley of Hinnom, near Jerusalem. There they burned their sons and daughters in the fire. The high places were elevated sites for worship, and Tophet is the name of the place. God says he never commanded this, and it never even came into his mind.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had already filled even the temple with pagan ideas, and now they were sacrificing children. Because of this, God announces judgment: that valley would be called the Valley of Slaughter. Scholars agree that this was a serious pagan practice, though they debate the details of how it was carried out.

For today: let us not invent ways of worshiping God according to our own customs. Let us compare what we do with what he teaches in his Word, and protect the youngest from anything that harms them.
exp.32:13:
He says that God promises to fulfill the good thing, that is, a promise of good, which he had already spoken to all his people, both to Israel and to Judah. "Behold, the days come" means that the moment will arrive. "Will perform" means that he will make it come true.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem and Judah lay in ruins because of God's judgment, and the people felt that everything was lost. God answers with hope: there will be shepherds and flocks again, and a branch of righteousness will come, a descendant of David. Many Christians see in him Jesus.

For today: when your situation seems like a desert, do not lean on what you can see, but on the faithfulness of God. He keeps what he promises, even though sometimes it takes longer than we expect. Today, remember one of his promises and trust in it.
exp.35:7:
This verse says that Baruch, the son of Neriah, did exactly what the prophet Jeremiah had commanded him. He read aloud from the scroll the words of the Lord in the Lord's house. The verse uses the name "the Lord" for God, and the scroll is the same writing that appears throughout this passage.

Jeremiah could not enter the temple, so he entrusted Baruch, his secretary, with reading what God had said to him. This took place on a day of fasting, when many people had gathered. The purpose was that the people would listen, repent, and turn away from their wrong ways, because God had announced serious judgment.

For today: Baruch's obedience was simple and complete, even when the message was difficult to deliver. We can ask God for the courage to do what He asks of us, without changing or softening His word.
exp.49:7:
God tells his people to run out of Babylon and out of the land of the Chaldeans. He asks them to be like the he goats, the ones that go at the front of the flock and open the way. In other words, they should be the first to leave, not left behind.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. His people were like a lost flock, poorly led by shepherds who had led them astray. God announces that Babylon will fall, attacked by an alliance of peoples from the north. For that reason he invites his own to leave before the judgment. Some scholars think this refers to the return from exile; others also see a broader message about turning away from evil.

Today we can ask ourselves what environment or habit draws us away from God. With his help, let us find the courage to leave that place and take the first step, even though others may still hesitate.
exp.38:13:
The verse says that the Babylonian officers had Jeremiah brought out of the court of the prison. They handed him over to Gedaliah, son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan, so that he would take him home. There Jeremiah lived among the people, now free from the prison.

The narrator tells what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar had ordered that Jeremiah be cared for, and his officers carried out the order. Jeremiah had announced this judgment for years and had been mistreated because of it. Gedaliah came from a family that had earlier protected the prophet (Jeremiah 26:24). The Bible does not explain all of Babylon's reasons, but the text shows that God looked after his servant.

God can care for those who are faithful to him even in very difficult times and through unexpected means. Today we too can keep obeying with integrity, trusting that God knows how and when to bring us relief.
exp.24:28:
God says that his judgment begins with Jerusalem, the city that bears his name. If he punishes his own people first, the other nations cannot imagine they will go free. "Unpunished" means left without punishment. "Sword" stands for war and destruction, and "the inhabitants of the earth" are the peoples of the world as it was known then.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the Babylonian invasion. For years Judah had rejected the calls to return to God. The cup they drink is a picture of divine judgment. The verses that follow show that God is the Judge of all nations.

For today: bearing God's name is not a license to live as we please, but a call to live with greater sincerity. We can ask him to examine our hearts and correct us without delay when he speaks to us.
exp.50:16:
Every person who worships idols is said to act like a fool, without knowledge. The craftsman who makes the image is the one who is shamed by it, and the carved figure is the idol itself. The cast metal idol is the image poured from molten metal. The explanation affirms that this idol is a lie, because it has no breath or life in it.

The prophet Jeremiah announces judgment on Babylon. Before this verse, he speaks of the Creator God who made the earth, the clouds, the rain, and the wind. After the verse, idols are set against the God of Jacob, who is the Former of all things. The message confronts trust in false gods and reminds readers who holds the true power.

For today, let us ask where we place our trust, such as in money, success, or the approval of others. None of these has life to save us. Today we can pray and hand that worry over to God.
exp.29:8:
This verse says that the people will no longer serve foreign oppressors, but will instead serve the Lord their God, and David their king, whom God himself will raise up. The phrase "David their king" in the verse above is the wording this comment is about; "but rather" is the meaning of the word "but" in that sentence. David died centuries ago, so many understand this as a future king from his line.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Israel and Judah, a people who were suffering punishment and exile. He promises to free them from their yoke, that is, from slavery. Christians often see in this "David" Jesus, a descendant of David. Jews interpret it in other ways, as a future king of that line.

For today: when you feel bound by guilt, fear, or a difficult situation, remember that God promises to rescue and restore. Serve him with confidence, because his king does not oppress but sets free.
exp.7:4:
God asks sadly why Jerusalem keeps turning away and staying in rebellion without stopping. A "perpetual backsliding" means a disobedience that never ends or changes. "They hold fast deceit" means they clung to lies and false securities. "They refuse to return" means they refused to come back to God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier he asked whether one who falls does not get up. That is, the normal thing is to return to the path. But the people did not repent or acknowledge their error. God compares them with the birds, which do know when to return, while his people ignore what God asks of them.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are holding on to some comfortable lie, such as excuses or bad habits. Returning to God begins with admitting, "I was wrong." He welcomes whoever comes back sincerely.
exp.12:16:
He says that if the people do not heed this warning, the prophet will weep in secret, with deep sorrow, because of their pride. His eyes will be full of tears because God's people, compared to a flock, will be carried away captive. The phrase "pride" in the verse means haughtiness, and "weep sore" means to weep very much.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on the message of the Lord to Judah. Earlier he had urged them to humble themselves and give glory to God, but they resisted. The verses that follow announce the exile. Some think the weeping belongs only to the prophet, while others hold that it also reflects the grief of God; the text allows us to see both.

When someone turns away from God out of pride, we should not look on them with contempt but with compassion. We can warn them with humility, pray for them, and weep over them with love, not with harshness.
exp.25:18:
Here the elders defend Jeremiah with a question: did King Hezekiah put Micah to death for prophesying disaster? No; rather, Hezekiah feared the Lord, that is, he held him in reverent awe, and prayed. Then God relented, that is, he changed course and did not send the punishment that had been announced. That is why they ask: if we harm Jeremiah, will we not bring great evil upon ourselves?

Jeremiah had announced in the temple that Jerusalem would be destroyed if the people did not return to God. Priests and prophets wanted to kill him. These elders recall what happened about a hundred years earlier with Micah, who said something similar. They understood that a harsh warning can be an opportunity for change.

For today: when a correction makes us uncomfortable, let us not react with anger. Let us listen with humility, pray, and ask God to show us whether we should change.
exp.48:15:
It says that Edom was deceived by its own pride. It lived in caves in the rock and in high places, and it felt secure, like an eagle in its nest up in the heights. But God says that from there he will bring it down. "Arrogance" and "pride" mean haughtiness and self-importance. "Rocks" are large stones.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Edom, a nation neighboring Israel. Its land was mountainous and hard to attack, and that gave it a false confidence. God announces that he will make it small and that it will be left desolate, as happened to Sodom and Gomorrah. Scholars do not agree on all the historical details of when this was fulfilled.

For today: pride makes us believe we are safe because of what we have or what we achieve. Today you can be humble and trust in God, not in your money, your position, or your strength.
exp.36:2:
The explanation says that King Zedekiah sent two men, Jehucal and Zephaniah the priest, to ask Jeremiah to pray to the Lord for them. The phrase "to the Lord our God" is the wording it quotes. Asking for prayer is what the king wanted.

The writer tells how Zedekiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had made king, did not listen to the word of God that Jeremiah spoke to him. Now Jerusalem is surrounded by the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). When the army of Egypt approaches, the Chaldeans pull back for a while, and the king wants the prophet to pray. He asks God for help, but without changing his heart or obeying.

Today we can notice how easy it is to ask for prayer only when we are in trouble, while ignoring what God has already told us. Praying is good, but it goes hand in hand with listening and obeying. Today, ask God for help, and also decide to do what you already know He is asking of you.
exp.49:42:
The explanation says that the king of Babylon received news of the reputation of the people coming against him, and fear paralyzed him. His hands grew weak and lost their strength. He felt anguish and intense pain, like that of a woman about to give birth.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had been a power that oppressed Judah. Now God announces that a people from the north will defeat it. Many understand this to refer to the Medes and Persians, though the text does not give names here. The message shows that no empire stands above God.

For today: when you feel that someone powerful is in control, remember that God is still the Lord of history. Trust in Him, act with justice, and do not place your security in human power.
exp.2:12:
God tells Israel to acknowledge its guilt. To "acknowledge" here means to admit, and to have "broken faith" means that it betrayed God. The phrase about having "scattered its ways among strangers" speaks of spreading its love and loyalty to other gods, under "every leafy tree," that is, in the shady places where pagan worship was practiced. And it did not obey his voice.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the northern kingdom, Israel, which was already in exile. Although he rebukes it, the invitation comes wrapped in mercy: God will not keep his anger forever, and he calls it to return, like a husband who longs to restore his people.

For today: God does not ask us to pretend that we are doing well, but to admit honestly where we have drifted away. Recognizing the wrong is not the end; it is the door back to a merciful God who receives us with grace.
exp.45:18:
God tells Egypt to pack its bags, as someone who must go into exile. "Packing for exile" means the belongings of someone who will be taken captive to another land. "Noph" is Memphis, a great Egyptian city. "Desolate" means a deserted and abandoned place. The city would be ruined and left without inhabitants.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. This message announces that Babylon would come against Egypt. Egypt trusted in its power and its fame, but God warns that its security was false. Scholars connect this prophecy with the campaign of King Nebuchadnezzar, although the exact fulfillment is understood in different ways.

For today: let us not place our security in money, prestige, or our own strength. All of that can fall suddenly. Let us seek refuge in God, who remains firm, and live attentive to his voice before troubles arrive.
exp.21:6:
He says God will send "destroyers," that is, those who bring ruin, each one with his weapons of war. They will cut down the choicest cedars and burn them. The cedars may speak of the trees of the royal palace, and also of the greatness and pride of Judah. Scholars understand the image in different ways.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing the house of the king of Judah. He warns that if they do not keep justice and the covenant, their palace will be left desolate. The verses that follow explain the reason: they abandoned God's covenant and served other gods. The text does not name the destroyers here, but the biblical story connects them with Babylon.

For today: let us not trust in what we have built, in power, or in prestige. What seems as firm as a cedar does not protect us if we turn away from God. Listening to his word and obeying it is what gives true security.
exp.35:31:
Jeremiah takes another scroll, that is, another book in the form of a rolled parchment, and gives it to Baruch, his scribe or secretary. Baruch writes again, taking dictation from Jeremiah, everything that King Jehoiakim had burned. Moreover, many other similar words were added.

God had commanded Jeremiah to put his messages in writing to call Judah to repentance. King Jehoiakim cut up the scroll and threw it into the fire, showing contempt for the message. God responds by ordering that it be written again and announcing judgment on the king and on the people who refused to listen.

For today: the Word of God is not destroyed because someone rejects it. If what God says makes us uncomfortable today, instead of ignoring it or pushing it away, we can listen to it with humility and respond with repentance and obedience.
exp.31:37:
This verse says that the people of Israel will be God's people, and that God will be their God. It is a promise of close relationship and of belonging to one another. The phrase "they shall be my people" is the same idea as "they shall be my people," and "to them" means "for them."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was about to fall to Babylon because of the people's disobedience, and God had allowed it. Even so, he promises to gather them again, bring them back to their land, and give them a heart and a way to fear him. This promise is repeated in other passages of the Bible, and many Christians see it fully fulfilled in the new covenant in Christ.

Today, even when you have failed or feel far away, God invites you to return to him. Take a few minutes to tell him sincerely: "You are my God, and I want to live as yours."
exp.42:6:
This verse tells how the group led by Johanan went down to Egypt, even though God had told them not to go. Tahpanhes is an Egyptian city, today written Tafnes, in the Nile delta. And the phrase "they obeyed not the voice of the Lord" means they ignored what God had commanded through Jeremiah.

After Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and Gedaliah, the governor, was killed, the people feared reprisals. They asked Jeremiah to pray, and they promised to obey God. He answered that they should stay in Judah and that God would protect them. But Johanan and the others said Jeremiah was lying, and they left anyway, taking him with them by force.

For today: sometimes we ask God for direction, but we have already decided what we want to do. Before we pray, let us ask ourselves whether we are willing to obey, even when his answer frightens us.
exp.48:10:
It says that God invites the fatherless to be left in his care, because he will provide for them. It also promises that the widows can trust in him. Here, "preserve" means keeping alive, caring for, and sustaining.

The message comes from the Lord through the prophet Jeremiah, and it is directed against Edom, the people descended from Esau. It announces that Edom will be completely destroyed and that its capital, Bozrah, will be left in ruins. In the middle of that judgment appears this sentence. Many read it as a sign that God cares for the most defenseless even when a nation falls. Others see it as a promise addressed to the families who will suffer the loss. The text does not clarify more than that.

For today: if you or someone close to you is living through a loss or a great need, you can entrust their care to God in prayer, and at the same time be the hands that help orphans and widows.
exp.43:15:
This verse is the people's answer of refusal to Jeremiah. They say: "As for the word that thou hast spoken unto us in the name of the Lord, we will not hearken unto thee." In other words, they refuse to obey what Jeremiah told them on God's behalf.

The ones speaking are the Jews who had gone to live in Egypt, men and women alike, including those who knew that their wives were burning incense to the queen of heaven, a pagan goddess. Jeremiah had just warned them that God's judgment would reach them because of their idolatry. Instead of repenting, they challenge him and defend their custom.

Today we might ask ourselves whether there is any word of God that we prefer to ignore because it makes us uncomfortable. Listening with humility, even when it hurts, is the first step toward returning to Him.
exp.47:33:
This verse describes a cry of grief heard throughout the land of Moab. Several towns are named, from Heshbon to Elealeh, Jahaz, Zoar and Horonaim. The phrase "as an heifer of three years old" probably refers to a young cow lowing loudly; some believe it is the name of a place. The waters of Nimrim, which gave life, will dry up or be left in ruin.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, known for its pride and its trust in its riches and its gods. God announces judgment on it, but he also shows sorrow: the prophet weeps over the ruin of its vineyards and of its joy.

For today: we should not trust in what seems secure, such as money or success, because everything can come to an end. And when others suffer, even those who went wrong, we can have compassion, as God did.
exp.51:28:
The verse says that in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, eight hundred thirty and two persons were carried away captive from Jerusalem. The phrase "carried away" means taken by force to another country, that is, deported into exile.

These are the final figures in the book of Jeremiah, which carefully records the three deportations of Judah. The one who records them looks back, now that Jerusalem has fallen. The numbers are small compared with other accounts, and scholars explain the difference in several ways: perhaps only a certain group of people is counted here. There is no single certain answer.

God warned through Jeremiah, and everything was fulfilled with exactness. His Word is worthy of trust, both in its warnings and in its promises. Today we can listen to him in time and obey him, knowing that he counts and remembers every person, even in the midst of pain.
exp.51:21:
It says that on top of each bronze column in the temple there was a decorative piece, called a capital, five cubits high (about 2.2 meters). It was surrounded by a bronze network and by pomegranates, also of bronze. The second column was the same.

Here the narrator describes the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, around 586 BC. He mentions in detail what the Babylonians carried away from the temple that Solomon built. The chapter closes the book of Jeremiah and shows that what the prophet had warned about came to pass. Scholars think the detail stresses how much was lost.

For today: beautiful and sacred things can disappear, and we should not place our security in buildings or religious symbols. Let us trust in God himself, who remains faithful even when everything else falls apart.
exp.21:14:
God asks a king whether he feels like a good ruler just because he lives in a luxurious palace with cedar walls. He reminds him that his father also ate and drank, that is, enjoyed a normal and good life, but in addition he "did judgment and justice," that is, he acted with uprightness and defended what was right. That is why things went well for him.

Jehovah speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Jehoiakim, king of Judah. He was building a large palace without paying his workers, while oppressing the people. His father, King Josiah, is held up as an example, because he cared for the afflicted and the poor. God says that this is truly knowing him.

For today: greatness is not measured by what we have, but by how we treat others. If you have a business or people under your charge, pay fairly and on time, and treat everyone with dignity.
exp.40:4:
They said that eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria. They came with their beards shaved, their clothes torn, and cuts on their bodies, signs of mourning and grief. They brought an offering and incense to take to the temple of the Lord, which lay in ruins.

The narrator tells what happened days after the murder of Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon. No one yet knew of the crime. These men were in mourning, probably because of the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, and they were going to worship God. Ishmael deceived them and killed them. The text does not fully explain his motives.

For today: even in the midst of grief, these men wanted to draw near to God. Let us bring our pain to Him honestly, but let us be prudent and not trust blindly someone who has not shown himself worthy of trust.
exp.1:10:
God asks whether any nation has ever changed its gods. He answers that none does, even though those gods "are not gods," meaning they have no real power. Yet his people did change their "glory," which is God himself, for something that "does not profit," meaning it neither serves nor helps.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Israel of abandoning him to follow idols. He asks them to look toward the west (the islands of Kittim) and toward the east (Kedar) to see that not even the pagan peoples acted this way. God speaks with pain, like someone who has been betrayed.

For today: we can exchange God for things that promise a great deal, such as money, success, or the approval of others, but these cannot sustain us. Today you can ask yourself what has taken God's place in your heart and return to him with sincerity.
exp.6:11:
The verse says that God invites his people to go to Shiloh, the place where his sanctuary once stood and where he first caused his name to dwell. He asks them to see what happened there because of Israel's wickedness. The phrase "go ye now" means "go now, then"; and the word "dwell" is the sense of "make his name dwell there."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people thought the temple would protect them, even though they lived in injustice, idolatry and deceit. Shiloh had been a center of worship in ancient times, and the Bible does not describe here how it was destroyed; God uses it as a warning: if Shiloh fell, Jerusalem can also fall.

For today: let us not trust in places, rituals or religious traditions as if they were a shield. God seeks a heart that obeys and lives in justice, not merely a presence in the temple.
exp.6:22:
The explanation says that the most important thing God asked of his people was obedience, not just rituals. "Obey my voice" means to act on what is said, not merely to hear it. The phrases "I will be your God" and "ye shall be my people" express a covenant relationship, of mutual belonging. "Walk ye in all the ways that I have commanded you" means living according to his instructions, and "that it may be well unto you" means that things may go well for them in life.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in the temple in Jerusalem. The people offered sacrifices, but they lived in disobedience. God tells them, with irony, to eat even the flesh of the burnt offerings, since without obedience those acts were of no value. Some understand that he does not reject the sacrifices, but places them in second place.

For today: it is not enough to attend church or do religious things. Ask yourself today: what has God asked me to do that I have not yet obeyed? Take one concrete step today.
exp.36:18:
Here Jeremiah asks King Zedekiah: where now are the prophets who said that Babylon would never come against you? "Your" refers to the people and the king; "prophesied unto you" means "announced to them on God's behalf."

Jeremiah speaks from prison, where they had put him for saying that Jerusalem would fall. The king consults him in secret, and Jeremiah repeats God's message to him without softening it. With this question he shows him that the prophets who promised peace were wrong, while what he had said was coming true.

For today: let us not seek only voices that reassure us. It is good to examine what we hear in the light of the Bible and to be willing to hear the truth, even when it is uncomfortable, because God corrects us to help us return to Him.
exp.50:60:
Jeremiah tells Seraiah that, when he arrives in Babylon, he is to look at the city and read aloud all the words Jeremiah has written against it.

Jeremiah is the prophet who is speaking. Seraiah was an officer who accompanied King Zedekiah on a journey to Babylon. The title "chamberlain" is uncertain: some think he organized the trip and the places where they would rest. Jeremiah asks him to read the message there, so that it would be clear that God would judge Babylon, the power that then ruled the world.

Today we can remember that no human power lasts forever, and that God's words are fulfilled in their time. When evil seems strong, trust in God and remain faithful, as Seraiah did, even in difficult places.
exp.24:18:
This verse continues the list of the nations to which Jeremiah was to give the cup of God's wrath to drink. Here Pharaoh, king of Egypt, is named along with his servants (his officials), his princes (his leaders), and all his people. The word "cup" stands for the cup of God's judgment, and drinking from it represents receiving God's judgment.

Jeremiah, the prophet of Judah, speaks here by recounting a symbolic vision that God gave him. The cup begins with Jerusalem and Judah, and then reaches other nations. The message is that God rules over all peoples, and that no king, not even the powerful Pharaoh, escapes his justice.

For today: no one stands above God, whether by their power or their position. We can live with humility, trusting that God is just, and examine our hearts without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.3:14:
It speaks of a voice that brings news from Dan, the far north of the land, and another that announces disaster from the hills of Ephraim, farther south. Disaster here means a great misfortune. They are messengers who warn, from place to place, that danger is already drawing near.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah and Jerusalem. The enemy comes from the north, and the news travels on, passing through Dan and Ephraim, right along the road to Jerusalem. God gives a clear warning because the people had turned away from Him, and before that He says: "Wash your heart clean of wickedness." Many understand the enemy to be Babylon, although the passage does not name it here.

For today: God warns before the consequences arrive. Let us not wait until the trouble reaches our door. If there is something crooked in our heart, let us go to God today and ask Him to cleanse us.
exp.21:15:
It says that Josiah, the king's father, defended the cause of people who were suffering and of those who had nothing. Because of this, it went well with him. A person who is "afflicted" is someone who suffers or is mistreated, and a "needy" person is someone who lives in want. Then God asks: "Is not this to know me?" That is, knowing God is not only talking about Him, but acting as He does, with justice and compassion toward the weak.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses Jehoiakim, king of Judah, who was building a luxurious palace with cedar and vermilion (red paint) while he oppressed the people and sought his own gain. God compares him with his father Josiah, who did practice justice. The verses that follow announce judgment on Jehoiakim.

Today, knowing God shows in how we treat the vulnerable. Think of someone close to you who is in need or being treated unfairly, and help them in a concrete way this week.
exp.10:19:
Jeremiah speaks to God. He calls him "the Lord of hosts," the one who judges with righteousness and "tries the reins and the heart," that is, he knows what is most inward: thoughts and feelings. He asks to see God's vengeance on his enemies, that is, that God would do justice. He says he has "revealed his cause" to God, which means he has placed his case in God's hands.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. He had just learned that the men of his own town, Anathoth, were plotting to kill him to silence his message. He did not know it, and he was like an innocent lamb. Scholars debate how to understand his request for vengeance; it is a cry for justice, not a command.

When you are treated unjustly, bring your case to God honestly, including your pain and anger. He sees the heart and can do justice better than you can, so there is no need for you to take revenge.
exp.50:47:
It says that the whole universe will rejoice when Babylon falls. The word "north" is what the verse above calls the direction the spoilers come from, so the explanation's sentence about the old word for north is rewritten here: the spoilers coming from the north are the armies that will come from that direction, and the Lord himself declares that he will send them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and taken its people into exile. God promises that this proud empire will also fall, and he encourages the exiles not to lose heart at news of war. Many understand that the army from the north refers to the Medes and Persians, although the text gives no further detail here.

For today: when you see that evil and injustice seem very strong, remember that God still governs history. Do not despair or take revenge. Trust that he will do justice in his time, and meanwhile remain faithful and keep your heart in him.
exp.9:5:
It says that there is no one like the LORD, the God of Israel. He is great, and his name is great in might. The word rendered "might" here speaks of real strength and power. "Like" means similar or equal.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to the people of Judah, who were surrounded by nations that worshiped idols. Just before this verse, he describes how an idol is made: from wood, decorated with silver and gold, and fastened so that it will not fall. Such idols cannot speak or walk. Jeremiah contrasts that powerlessness with the living God, to encourage the people not to fear false religions or be drawn in by them.

For today: when something seems greater than God to you, such as money, success, other people's opinions, or fear, remember that nothing can be compared to him. Set aside a few minutes today to tell him in prayer, "Lord, there is no one like you," and hand over that worry to him.
exp.14:14:
Here Jeremiah speaks to God with honesty. He tells God that He knows his situation, and he asks Him to remember him, to visit him (that is, to step in and look after him), and to avenge him (to do justice against those who persecute him). He also begs God not to let him suffer while God delays His anger, because he is bearing reproach and contempt for being faithful to Him.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, rejected and mocked for announcing God's message to a people who did not want to hear it. This is one of his most intimate outpourings. The verses that follow show that he loved God's word, but he felt alone and wounded by the mission.

For today: when you suffer for doing what is right, you can pray with complete frankness, without hiding your pain. Hand over to God your desire for justice, instead of taking it into your own hands, and trust that He sees your faithfulness.
exp.19:9:
Jeremiah says he heard the slander of many people. The phrase "fear on every side" was something he himself used as a warning. Now his enemies use it against him. They said, "Report him, and we will report him." Even his friends were waiting for him to stumble, that is, to fall or make a mistake. They thought they would trick him, overcome him, and take revenge on him.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. His message of judgment on Judah brought him mockery, rejection, and betrayal, even from people close to him. Just before this, the priest Pashhur had beaten him and put him in prison. Jeremiah felt worn out, but the word of God burned within him and he could not keep silent.

For today: if you are criticized or abandoned for doing what is right, do not hide your pain. Bring it honestly before God, as Jeremiah did, and ask him for strength to remain faithful. He sustains those who trust in him.
exp.33:4:
God tells King Zedekiah that he will not die in battle but will die in peace. When he dies, he will be honored as his ancestors were: burning spices or incense at the funeral, and people will mourn him with laments, crying out, "Alas, lord!"

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf while Babylon attacks Jerusalem. God announces that Zedekiah will be taken captive, but he promises that Zedekiah will not die by the sword. The Bible does not tell how this was fulfilled, and it is not clear how "in peace" should be understood here.

Even in times of judgment, God offers mercy to the one who listens. Today we can trust that his word is fulfilled, and respond with humility when he speaks to us.
exp.43:17:
The explanation says that the people, after they stopped burning incense and pouring out drink offerings to the queen of heaven, felt that they lacked everything and were dying by the sword and by famine. "By the sword" means by the sword.

The speakers are Jews who had taken refuge in Egypt, and they respond to Jeremiah with rejection. They believed that their past prosperity came from that worship. Scholars often think the queen of heaven was a goddess, but they are not sure which one. Jeremiah will explain to them that the ruin came because of their idolatry, not because they had abandoned it.

For today: sometimes we blame God or doing what is right for our difficulties, when the problem lies elsewhere. Before interpreting our trials, let us ask God for humility to see the truth and to return to Him.
exp.49:15:
The explanation says that Babylon will be left without those who sow and reap. "Cut off" can be read as "cut down" or "remove." The sickle is the curved tool used to cut the grain. The "oppressing sword" speaks of the violence of an oppressor. The foreigners who lived in Babylon, frightened by the war, would each turn back to his own people and his own land.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that Babylon, which had dominated many nations and mistreated Israel, would be judged for its pride and its sin. The verses that follow recall that Assyria and Babylon had devoured Israel, but God would also call them to account.

For today: God sees injustice and does not leave it unanswered forever. If someone has hurt you, trust that God is just, bring your pain to him, and avoid taking revenge on your own. Ask him to help you live with humility and to treat others well.
exp.3:19:
Destruction follows upon destruction, without end. The whole land lies in ruin. The reader is told that the tents and curtains, the coverings of the houses, fall in a single moment. The word "ruin" here means total destruction, a complete collapse.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, the prophet. He sees in vision the invasion coming from the north because of the sin of the people of Judah. His grief is so strong that he feels anguish in his heart. Some think the prophet speaks "my tents" on behalf of the people; others think God is the one speaking. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: the decisions we make have consequences, and God does not take pleasure when we suffer. If there is something in your life that you know needs to be corrected, do not wait for everything to collapse. Return to God today, with humility, and ask for his help.
exp.48:27:
This verse announces a judgment of God against Kedar and against the kingdoms of Hazor, desert peoples whom Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, was going to attack. God gives the command: "Arise, go up against Kedar and spoil the men of the east." The "men of the east" were nomadic tribes of the desert, to the east of Israel. The phrase "smite" means that he struck them down or defeated them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter gathers messages against several nations that were neighbors of Israel. These peoples lived confident in their tents, their flocks, and their remoteness, but God showed that none of them was beyond his reach. Scholars do not know in detail how this attack happened, but the text presents it as part of God's plan.

For today: there is no true security in what we possess or in living far from everything. Let us trust in God, who governs over all the nations.
exp.48:35:
It says that God will bring winds upon Elam from the four corners of the heavens, and will use them to scatter his people everywhere. "I will scatter them" is what the phrase means, as grain is winnowed to separate it. There will be so many exiled Elamites that no nation will be left where they do not go.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah. Elam was a people east of Babylon, known for its archers. God announces that he will break its bow, that is, its strength. The judgment comes because of its pride and its trust in its own power. The text does not detail all the historical events of its fulfillment.

For today: let us not place our security in our strength, money, or achievements, because everything can change. Let us trust in God, who governs the nations, and live with humility before him.
exp.28:26:
This verse is part of a question with a tone of rebuke. Someone asks Zephaniah: "Why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth, who prophesies falsely to you?" The word for a rebuke in the verse is "rebuked," which means correcting with authority, and "Anathoth" is Jeremiah's hometown.

The one speaking here is Shemaiah, a false prophet who was in Babylon. He wrote a letter to Jerusalem to pressure the priests. He wanted them to silence Jeremiah, because Jeremiah had sent the exiles an uncomfortable message: the captivity would be long, and they should settle down there. Shemaiah calls "false" the man who was in fact telling the truth from God.

For today: not everyone who sounds confident speaks the truth, and not every uncomfortable word is a lie. Before rejecting a correction, compare it with what Scripture says, and ask God for the humility to listen.
exp.1:30:
God calls his people to attention: "O generation, see the word of the Lord." He asks whether he has been to Israel like a wilderness, an empty and lonely place, or like a land of darkness, a place with no hope. Then he questions why they say, "We are lords; we will come no more unto thee."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah had left him to follow other gods and trust in themselves, even though he had cared for them and corrected them. His question is not seeking a technical answer; it reveals a wounded heart and shows that their abandonment had no just cause. The verses that follow show that they forgot him for a long time.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we drift away from God believing we do not need him. Remembering how he has cared for us helps us return to him with trust and humility.
exp.45:4:
It says God asks in wonder: "Why have I seen them dismayed and turned away back?" The Egyptian soldiers, even the bravest among them, were beaten down and fled without looking back. The phrase about running with all their strength is replaced here by the verse's own wording: "are fled apace" means they ran quickly and without stopping. The phrase about fear surrounding them on every side describes a terror that was all around them, as the verse says: "for fear was round about."

Jeremiah speaks a message from the Lord about Egypt. The verses before it show the army proudly preparing for war. Here we see the result: defeat. The text connects this with the battle of Carchemish beside the river Euphrates, where Babylon defeated Egypt. The message teaches that no human power is above God.

For today: do not place your security only in your strength, your money, or your preparation. Do your part well, but trust first in God, because He sustains what human effort cannot.
exp.3:18:
Jeremiah speaks with a pain so strong that he feels it in his body. "My bowels, my bowels!" and "my very heart" are old ways of speaking of the deepest part of a person. His heart pounds with anguish and he cannot keep silent, because he has heard the sound of the trumpet announcing war.

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, who sees judgment coming upon Judah for rebelling against God. Some think he speaks only out of his own pain, and others that he also expresses God's grief over his people. The text allows both readings. What is clear is that Jeremiah takes no pleasure in the punishment, but suffers because of it.

For today: when you see sin and its consequences, do not react with coldness or pride. Ask God for a heart that feels pain and prays for others.
exp.19:13:
He says Jeremiah wishes the day of his birth were cursed and never remembered with joy. It is a very strong expression of pain. The phrase about the day he was born means the day he came into the world. He does not curse his mother or God, but the day on which he was born.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking here, after being beaten and put in the stocks by the priest Pashhur for announcing God's message. He has just praised God, and suddenly he expresses his anguish. This mix of faith and despair may surprise us, but the Bible presents it with complete honesty. Job also spoke in a similar way.

For today: if you are exhausted or discouraged, you do not have to pretend to be strong before God. You can tell him honestly what you feel, even the darkest things. And seek the support of trusted people who will listen to you and walk with you.
exp.32:10:
This verse promises that in the places that are now empty, the voices of celebration will be heard again: weddings, joy, and people giving thanks to God because he is good and his mercy lasts forever. The bridegroom and the bride are the groom and the bride. "Return the captivity" means that God will bring his people back from exile, as he did at the first.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem and Judah were in ruins, and the people saw them as deserted, without people or animals. Jeremiah announces this message of hope while the punishment still weighs heavily. God promises to restore what seemed lost forever.

For today: when a situation looks empty or without a way out, you can keep thanking God for his goodness. He can bring back joy where there was pain. Today, write down one specific reason to thank him and say it to him in prayer.
exp.35:11:
He went down to the king's palace, to the secretary's room. There all the leaders were gathered, the princes, that is, the senior officials of the kingdom. Several are named: Elishama the scribe, Delaiah, Elnathan, Gemariah, Zedekiah, and the rest. A scribe was an official clerk of the government.

The narrator tells what happened after Baruch read aloud in public the message from God that Jeremiah had dictated. Micaiah, son of Gemariah, heard the reading and went to tell the officials. Some names, such as Gemariah and Elnathan, also appear in other accounts in the book, but we do not know for certain what each of them thought.

For today: when you hear the Word of God, do not keep it to yourself just because you heard it. Micaiah carried it to those who needed to know. Share it with wisdom and respect with someone who needs it.
exp.0:6:
God answers Jeremiah: "Do not say, I am a child." He explains that Jeremiah will go to every place where God sends him and will speak everything God commands him.

The Lord speaks, answering Jeremiah, who has just said that he does not know how to speak. God had just told him that he knew him and had set him apart before he was born to be a prophet. Jeremiah feels insecure, but God does not stop at his excuse. Immediately he promises to be with him and to put his words in his mouth.

For today: when God asks something of you and you feel very young, inexperienced, or unable, do not stay focused only on your limits. Obey step by step, trusting that God is with you and gives you what is needed for what he asks.
exp.26:14:
God says that He never sent those prophets. They speak as if they were speaking in His name, but they are lying. And that lie would have a terrible result: God would allow the people to be driven out of their land and to die, both they and the false prophets. The words "drive out" here mean to force out or banish, and "perish" means to die or be destroyed.

Jeremiah spoke to King Zedekiah, to the priests, and to the people of Judah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. Through Jeremiah, God asked them to submit to Babylon in order to save their lives. But other prophets promised that everything would soon be settled and that the objects from the temple would return. It was a comfortable message, but a false one.

Today, do not believe something just because it sounds pleasant or uses God's name. Compare what you hear with the Bible, pray for wisdom, and listen with humility, even when the truth is difficult.
exp.18:10:
God commands Jeremiah to say that He will break Jerusalem and its people, the way one breaks a clay pot that can no longer be mended. The place called Tophet was in the valley of Hinnom, and the burying in that place points to so many deaths that there will be no more room to bury anyone.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Jeremiah had broken a clay jar in front of the elders as a sign. The people had left God, worshiped idols, and burned incense to the stars. In Tophet, according to the text, innocent blood had been shed. The punishment came with the Babylonian invasion.
