For today: God takes injustice and idolatry seriously, but His warnings are also an invitation to return to Him. Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts, and repent sincerely while there is still time.
exp.35:22:
King Jehoiakim would listen as the scroll was read, and each time Jehudi had read three or four sections of it, the king would cut off those sections with a knife and throw them into the brazier, a kind of fire pan set on the hearth. He kept doing this until the whole scroll had been burned.

In context, God had told Jeremiah to dictate to Baruch his warning messages for Judah, in the hope that the people would turn back from their wrongdoing. It was winter, and the king was sitting near the fire. Instead of trembling before the word of God, as one would have hoped, he despised it and destroyed it. The verses that follow say that there was neither fear nor repentance.

For today: when the Bible makes us uncomfortable or corrects us, the temptation is to silence it or ignore it. Better to ask God for a humble heart, one that listens, acknowledges its mistake, and changes.
exp.51:32:
It says that the king of Babylon had Jehoiachin change out of his prison clothes, that is, he freed him from his appearance as a captive. Moreover, Jehoiachin ate at the king's table, always, every day of his life. The phrase "changed his prison garments" means that his prison clothes were exchanged for others, and "bread" refers to food in general.

This is the end of the book of Jeremiah, and it was most likely added by a later writer, since it speaks of events that happened after the fall of Jerusalem. Jehoiachin, king of Judah, had been held prisoner in Babylon for about thirty-seven years. The new king, Evil-merodach, treated him with kindness. Some see here a sign that God had not forgotten the family of David, although the text does not explain this.

For today: even in long times of difficulty, God can open a door of relief when we least expect it. We keep trusting and waiting, and we give thanks for small gestures of kindness.
exp.43:14:
This verse introduces a large group that comes together to answer Jeremiah. They were the men who knew that their wives were burning incense to other gods, the women who were standing there, and all the Jewish people living in Egypt, in the region of Pathros (southern Egypt). Burning incense means giving off fragrant smoke as an offering, and "other gods" means false gods.

Jeremiah had just warned them that God would punish them in the same way as Jerusalem. They had fled to Egypt, and yet they were still worshiping idols. Now they all respond together, and what they say next is an open rejection of God's word.

For today: it is easy to close our ears when the truth challenges our habits. Let us ask God for a humble heart that listens, even when his word asks us to change.
exp.22:38:
God says that, because of what the people did, he will "forget" them, meaning he will set them aside, and he will "pull them up" from his presence. He will also speak about the city, Jerusalem, which he had given to them and to their ancestors.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The Hebrew word for "burden" can also mean "message," and people used it mockingly or carelessly to speak of supposed messages from God, even though he had asked them not to do so. Some understand that they were mocking God's word; others understand that false prophets were making up messages. The text shows a serious judgment against the disrespectful use of his name.

Today we can be careful about how we speak of God. Before saying "God told me," it is wise to pray, to compare it with the Bible, and to speak with humility and respect.
exp.22:36:
This verse gives instructions on how to ask about God's word. The prophet should be asked with respect: "What has the Lord answered you? What has the Lord spoken?" These are simple questions, aimed at hearing what God actually said.

God speaks through Jeremiah to a people who often used the phrase "burden of the Lord." The Hebrew term can mean "message" or "burden," and it seems to have been used mockingly and carelessly. God corrects that habit and asks that what He said be repeated faithfully, without twisting it.

Today we can take care with what we say in God's name. Before claiming "God told me," it is good to return to the Bible, examine carefully what it says, and speak with humility. That way we do not use His name for our own ideas.
exp.47:2:
This verse describes a cry of anguish heard from Horonaim, a city of Moab. The words "spoiling" and "great destruction" speak of total ruin, like something shattered into pieces. It is as if the prophet hears from a distance the weeping of a people who are losing everything.

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, announcing what the LORD says about Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Moab trusted in its cities, its strongholds, and its pride, and the chapter declares that all of it will fall. Scholars do not agree on every historical detail of when and how this happened, but the central message is clear: no human strength is secure without God.

For today: check where you place your security, whether money, work, or achievements. Those things can fail, but God remains. Trust Him first, with humility.
exp.11:6:
God himself speaks and says that he has abandoned his house, that is, the temple and the land where he lived among his people. "Heritage" is the property received as an inheritance; here it refers to Israel, the people of God. The phrase "the dearly beloved of my soul" shows his deep affection for them. Even so, he gives them into the hands of their enemies.

Jeremiah complains that the wicked prosper. God answers him that his people have turned against him, and that even the prophet's own family will betray him. God suffers in judging, because he loves what he punishes. Scholars agree that this is about the judgment on Judah for its rebellion.

God takes no pleasure in punishment; his judgment is painful to him. Today we can trust that, when he corrects us, he does so with a heart wounded by love, and we can respond in time with sincere repentance.
exp.19:16:
He says that Jeremiah wished God, or whoever helped him, had put him to death before he was born. In that case his mother would have been his grave, and her womb would have stayed pregnant forever, so that he never came into the world. It is a very strong way of expressing deep pain.

The speaker is the prophet Jeremiah. He had just been beaten and placed in the stocks for preaching God's message (Jeremiah 20:1-2). He feels rejected, mocked, and worn out. His words are a sincere outpouring, almost a poetic lament. We do not know that God agreed with him in this; the Bible only shows his honest complaint.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, you do not need to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, as Jeremiah did. Then seek support from people you trust, and keep trusting that God hears you.
exp.38:5:
The explanation says that the king of Babylon had the sons of King Zedekiah killed in front of their father, in a place called Riblah. He also ordered the death of all the nobles of Judah.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah speaks, recounting the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. Zedekiah had tried to escape at night, but he was caught near Jericho. Jeremiah had spent years warning that surrendering to Babylon would save lives, but the king refused to listen. This scene is the sad fulfillment of those warnings.

For today: ignoring the truth out of fear or stubbornness often costs far more than we imagine. We can ask God for a humble heart that listens in time, even when the advice is hard.
exp.5:8:
He says that God, the Lord of hosts, will go through Israel the way a vineyard is gone over again after the harvest. The word "glean" means gathering again what was left behind, cluster by cluster. The phrase "the remnant of Israel" refers to those who were still left.

Then the grape-gatherer (the one who harvests grapes) is commanded to pass his hand over the branches once more and put whatever he finds into the baskets.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. The people kept on in injustice and would not listen. The image suggests a very thorough judgment: no one would escape by going unnoticed. Scholars disagree about who receives the command, whether Jeremiah or the invading army, but the underlying message is the same.

For today: do not put off God's correction. If something in your life troubles you as you read his Word, listen to it with humility and change in time, while there is still grace to return.
exp.23:8:
He says that God will hand over Zedekiah, his officials, and the rest of the people to become a mockery, a disgrace, an example, a proverb, and a curse among all the nations. "Mockery" means cruel ridicule. A "proverb" is a popular saying: their name would be used as an example of misfortune. "Driving" them away means that God will scatter them far off.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah after the first deportation to Babylon. With the image of two baskets of figs, the good ones are the exiles whom God will care for and bring back; the bad ones are Zedekiah and those who stayed behind or fled to Egypt. It was a judgment for their rebellion and their false sense of security.

For today: God is serious when he calls us to turn back to him, but he also offers a new heart. Do not harden your heart against his correction; return to him today with sincerity.
exp.33:3:
God speaks to King Zedekiah.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God while the army of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. The message is serious: the city would fall and the king would be taken away as a prisoner. But God leaves a door open to repentance. Some scholars think that the promise of dying in peace depended on Zedekiah obeying; the Bible does not fully make clear how it was fulfilled.

For today: even when we face the consequences of our mistakes, God continues to speak to us with mercy. If He shows you a hard truth, listen with humility; His correction always comes with an opportunity to return to Him.
exp.12:26:
God tells Jerusalem that he has seen all her sin. Her "adulteries" and her "fornication" are a picture of spiritual unfaithfulness: leaving God to worship idols. Her "neighings" recall a horse in heat, that is, an uncontrolled desire. The "hills" are the high places where idolatrous worship was carried out. At the end, God laments: "Wilt thou not be made clean? when shall it once be?", a cry of grief and of waiting.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a time of spiritual decline in Judah. Earlier, the people had forgotten God and trusted in a lie, that is, in false securities. God uses strong language because the people had broken their covenant with him, but his words also show a desire to see them made clean.

For today: God sees what we do in secret and still hopes that we will return. Today you can confess to him honestly whatever has taken his place in your heart and ask him to cleanse you.
exp.28:16:
God announces that he will send three blows upon the people who remained in Jerusalem: war, hunger, and disease. He compares them to figs so rotten that they cannot be eaten.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. A group had already been taken captive to Babylon, and those who stayed in Jerusalem, including King Zedekiah, considered themselves the favored ones. Moreover, they were listening to prophets who promised a swift peace. God tells them that his judgment is coming because they did not listen to the true prophets whom he sent to them again and again. The image of the figs appears in more detail in chapter 24.

For today: when God speaks to us, whether through his Word or through wise counsel, it is wise to listen in time and with humility. Feeling secure is not the same as being right with God. He corrects because he wants to heal us, and his mercy remains open to anyone who turns back to him.
exp.40:11:
This verse tells how Johanan and all the men who were with him went out to fight Ishmael, son of Nethaniah. They found him near the great waters at Gibeon. The explanation's comment on the wording is left out here, since the phrases it discusses do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah is speaking. Ishmael had murdered Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, and was carrying off the people of Mizpah as captives toward Ammon. When Johanan heard of this wickedness, he gathered the military leaders to rescue the people. According to the account, the captive people rejoiced and turned back to Johanan.

For today: when we see injustice against people who cannot defend themselves, God calls us not to stay silent or still. We can act with courage and wisdom, defending and helping those who suffer.
exp.48:5:
According to the explanation, after the punishment God will bring back the fortunes of the Ammonites. This means he will restore what they lost and bring them back to their land. The "children of Ammon" are the descendants of Ammon, a people neighboring Israel, east of the Jordan River.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Before this verse, God announces judgment on Ammon for its pride: they trusted in their valleys and their riches and thought no one would attack them. Even so, the final word is not only punishment but a promise of restoration. Scholars debate when or how this was fulfilled, and the Bible does not give details.

For today: God corrects pride and false security, but his final desire is to restore. If today you trust your resources more than God, return to him with humility. And if you are going through a correction, do not lose hope: his mercy has the last word.
exp.35:26:
This verse says that God spoke again to Jeremiah after King Jehoiakim had burned the scroll. That scroll contained the words Baruch had written while Jeremiah dictated them.

The phrase "the word of the Lord came" means that God gave him a new message. A scribe is someone who writes out or copies texts.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and then God addresses Jeremiah. The king rejected the warning and destroyed the scroll, but God protected Jeremiah and Baruch. Right away he orders them to write another scroll with the same words. Burning the paper did not change what God had said.

For today: do not be discouraged if someone rejects or scorns what is true. God's word endures. Perhaps today your task is to keep obeying with patience, trusting that God cares for his message and for those who are faithful to him.
exp.24:19:
This verse follows a list of nations to whom God commands that the cup of his anger be given to drink. Named here are "all the mingled people," meaning foreign peoples who were mixed together or allied; the kings of the land of Uz; the kings of the Philistines (the land of the Philistines is meant here); and the cities of Ashkelon, Azzah, Ekron, and what remained of Ashdod. Exactly who the "mingled people" were is not known for certain.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah, around 605 B.C. He warns that Babylon would come as an instrument of judgment, not only against Judah but against many neighboring nations.

For today: God rules over all nations, not only over his own people. This invites us to live with humility, not to trust in human power, and to listen to his voice in time, seeking his forgiveness and guidance.
exp.17:20:
Jeremiah asks God to hand the children of his enemies over to hunger and the sword. He asks that the women be left without children and become widows, that the men be put to death, and that the young men fall in battle. "To pour out through the sword" means to give them over to violence. The phrase about being cut down by the blade means the same thing as the sword.

Jeremiah is the one speaking. Some people of Judah, angry at his message, were planning to harm him (verses 18-20). He had interceded for them, and they repaid good with evil. This prayer is a very raw lament, and its words sound like a request for judgment, not an example of forgiveness. Many understand it as announcing the fall of Jerusalem.

For today: when you are wronged unfairly, you can bring your pain and your anger to God honestly, without taking revenge yourself. Then look to Jesus, who on the cross asked forgiveness for his enemies (Luke 23:34).
exp.28:2:
This verse tells us who carried Jeremiah's letter to Babylon: Elasah, son of Shaphan, and Gemariah, son of Hilkiah. King Zedekiah had sent them to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. The phrase "by the hand of" in the verse means "by means of." The names appear in the spelling used by this older version.

Jeremiah, a prophet in Jerusalem, writes to the exiles who were already in Babylon after the first deportation. These two men were traveling on official business, and so the letter reached the captives. What follows is God's message: they should settle down and live there, because the exile would be long. The Bible gives no further details here about these messengers.

God often uses simple means and ordinary people to carry his word. Today you can be a messenger too: a phone call, a letter, or a timely word of advice can encourage someone going through a hard season.
exp.39:13:
This verse tells how some men warned Gedaliah that Baalis, king of the Ammonites, had sent Ishmael to kill him. Johanan asks whether they really know this for certain, meaning with certainty. But Gedaliah did not believe them. The word "said" in this verse means "told him."

The ones speaking are Johanan and the military leaders. Babylon had left Gedaliah as governor over the Jews who remained in the land, and he lived in Mizpah. Johanan feared that if Gedaliah were killed, the whole group would scatter. Gedaliah, according to the text, thought the accusation was false. Ishmael did later murder him (Jeremiah 41), so his trust turned out to be a serious mistake.

For today: when someone warns us of danger, it is wise to listen with humility and ask God for wisdom. Being trusting is not wrong in itself, but ignoring a serious warning can cost dearly.
exp.13:7:
Jeremiah speaks to God in pain. He calls him the hope of Israel and the one who keeps his people in distress. But he complains: why does God seem like a stranger passing through, or a traveler who stops only for a night, with no intention of staying? The word "stranger" means someone who is only passing through.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, pleading for the people during a terrible drought. He acknowledges that they have sinned and asks God to act for the sake of his name. His complaint expresses what he feels, not necessarily what God is really like. Later, God answers that the people had turned away from him.

For today: when you feel that God is distant, do not stay silent. Bring your complaint to him with honesty and humility, acknowledge whatever needs correcting, and trust that he remains your hope.
exp.6:32:
This verse says that the bodies of the dead of Judah will lie thrown out, without burial. The birds and the wild animals will eat them, and no one will drive them away. "Drive away" here means to chase off or send away.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had built high places at Topheth, in the valley of Hinnom, to burn their sons in the fire, something God says he never commanded. Therefore he announces judgment: there will be so many dead that the place will be called the Valley of Slaughter. Not having a burial was a great dishonor in that time. The next verse speaks of the end of joy and of weddings.

For today: God takes human life and true worship seriously. We can examine whether what we do in the name of faith truly pleases him, according to his Word. And we can turn back to him with humility, knowing that his judgment is serious, but that he always calls people to repentance.
exp.16:16:
Jeremiah asks God not to become something that terrifies him. He says to God: "You are my hope," meaning that he trusts in God and looks to him for help when hard times come. The phrase "day of evil" refers to a time of distress, danger, or calamity.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. People mocked him and said: "Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come now!" Jeremiah announced judgment, and that is why they rejected him. He insists that he did not seek this work or desire the disaster, and that he spoke with sincerity before God. For this reason he clings to God as his refuge.

For today: when you are criticized or feel pressured for doing what is right, speak to God with complete honesty. Tell him your fear, and place your hope in him again, because he can sustain you when the difficult day comes.
exp.26:1:
God tells Jeremiah to make "bonds and yokes," that is, the straps and wooden pieces used to harness oxen to their work. He was to put them on his neck, as a sign that everyone could see.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah obeys as a prophet. The message was addressed to Judah and the neighboring kingdoms. With that yoke, God was showing them that they must submit to Babylon. The text names "Jehoiakim," but the rest of the chapter speaks of Zedekiah, and some scholars believe there is an old copying error in that name.

Today, God may ask us for obedience even when we do not fully understand his plan. This week, choose one concrete action that you know God is asking of you, and do it with humility, even if it costs you.
exp.21:5:
God compares the royal house of Judah to Gilead and to the top of Lebanon, places known for their forests and their beauty. They were like a treasure to Him. Yet the word "but" here is the key: despite that value, God warns that He will leave the house in desolation, with cities that have no inhabitants.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the kings of Judah. He had offered them a condition: if they practiced justice, the throne of David would remain firm; if not, ruin would come. Many understand that Gilead and Lebanon allude to the splendor of the palace, which was built with cedar wood.

For today: privileges and positions do not replace obedience. God loves us and gives us gifts, but He expects us to live with justice and humility. Today you can ask yourself: am I trusting in what I have, or in listening to and obeying God?
exp.30:16:
God tells Rachel, who is weeping for her lost children, that there is indeed hope for her future. "Thine end" means what comes after, the outcome of her story. "Border" means her territory, her land. Her children will return to their land.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Rachel appears as an image of the mothers of Israel who weep for their children carried off into exile. Ramah was a place near where the captives were gathered. God answers their grief with a promise of return, within a broader message of restoration for his people.

For today: when you go through a loss or a painful wait, you may weep without guilt, but you can also bring your pain before God and trust that he has the final word. His promise does not deny your sadness; it accompanies it with hope.
exp.1:31:
Can a young woman forget her jewelry, or a bride her wedding sash? In this verse God uses the comparison of a bride who would never forget her clothing and adornments. The words for "clothing" and "adornments" are the ones in the verse: the clothing is what she wears and the adornments are her jewelry and decorations, such as necklaces or ribbons (some translators think of a bridal sash or band).

God compares this to his people. Something as natural as remembering what belongs to you has become impossible for Israel, which has forgotten him for countless days.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He accuses them of ignoring correction, of rejecting the prophets, and of saying, "We are free, we will not return to you." His pain is that of a forsaken husband, and so he asks whether he had ever been a desert or a dark land to them.

For today: do not let everyday concerns fill your heart and make you forget God. Set aside a moment each day to remember him with gratitude, prayer, and his Word.
exp.49:19:
It says that when the time God has set comes, the guilt of Israel and Judah will be sought and will not be found. It does not mean they never sinned, but that God will pardon them completely. The word "shall be sought" means "shall be looked for" or "shall be searched out." The phrase "whom I reserve" refers to those God preserves, a remnant that remains.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on Babylon, which had subjected his people, and promises to bring Israel back to its land. Many understand that forgiveness is part of that restoration. Some Christians also see here a sign of the complete forgiveness God offers in Christ.

For today: if you have confessed your sin to God, you can rest in his forgiveness. Do not keep carrying guilt that he has already chosen to blot out. Come to him with humility and confidence.
exp.25:17:
It says that Micah, a prophet from the town of Moresheth, spoke in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah. His message from God was harsh: Zion, that is, Jerusalem, would be plowed like a field, the city would become heaps of ruins, and the mountain of the house would be like wooded high places overgrown with thickets.

Here some of the elders of the people are speaking. Jeremiah had just announced something similar in the temple, and the priests and prophets wanted to kill him. The elders recall the case of Micah (Micah 3:12) to defend Jeremiah: Hezekiah did not kill Micah, but listened, feared God and prayed, and God did not bring the punishment that had been announced.

A hard word from God can be an opportunity to turn back to Him. Before rejecting the one who corrects us, it is wise to listen with humility, examine our hearts, and pray.
exp.30:11:
The explanation says that God's people will return to their land and praise with joy on Mount Zion, that is, Jerusalem. "They will rush to the goodness of the Lord" means they will go eagerly toward the good things God gives: grain (the bread), wine, oil, and animals. A "well-watered garden" is a garden that is full of life, well cared for with water.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had been scattered into exile, and God promises to gather them and care for them like a shepherd with his flock. It is a message of comfort and hope for a wounded people. Christians often also see here a foreshadowing of the fullness God gives in Christ, although it is interpreted in different ways.

For today: if you are tired or hurt, remember that God knows how to restore. Go to Him with confidence, give thanks for what He gives you each day, and let Him care for you like a well-watered garden.
exp.31:28:
The explanation says that the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians who were already attacking Jerusalem, will enter the city and set it on fire. They will also burn the houses where the people offered incense to Baal and poured out drink offerings of wine or other drinks to false gods, which provoked the anger of God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon, and Jeremiah is in prison. God makes clear that this fall is no accident: the people had long been given over to idolatry, and the flat roofs of the houses were places where this worship was practiced.

For today: God sees what we do even on the rooftops, in what is hidden. It is worth asking ourselves what things are occupying the place that belongs to Him, and turning back to Him with sincerity before those things destroy us.
exp.4:2:
God says he looks for truth among his people, and he does not find it. Jeremiah tells God that he struck them and they did not feel pain; he nearly destroyed them, and still they would not accept correction. He says "you struck them" and "you destroyed them" and that they "refused to receive correction." Their faces were harder than a rock, meaning stubborn and without shame.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in prayer, just after God asked for a search of Jerusalem for even one honest person. God said that if such a person were found, he would forgive the city. Jeremiah sees that neither the poor nor, according to the verses that follow, the leaders want to obey. They said "As the Lord lives," yet they swore falsely.

For today: when God corrects us through hardships, his Word, or wise people, let us not harden our hearts. Let us ask him for humility to listen, to recognize our error, and to return to him sincerely, not merely with religious words.
exp.50:53:
This verse describes a cry heard from Babylon and a great destruction, a "quebrantamiento," in the land of the Chaldeans. The Chaldeans were the people who ruled Babylon. The word for this destruction means ruin, total destruction.

The prophet Jeremiah announces what God said about Babylon. This empire had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed Israel. God promises that no stronghold, not even one that reached to heaven, would save it. The verses that follow explain that God is the one who judges Babylon and gives it what it deserves.

For today: human powers may seem firm, but they are not eternal. If you suffer injustice today, you can rest in the fact that God sees and governs history. Trust in Him, do not repay evil with evil, and keep doing good with patience.
exp.28:31:
God says he will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite and his descendants. "Visit" here means coming to call someone to account. None of his family will live among the people or see the good that God will do for his own, because Shemaiah spoke rebellion, that is, he taught people to disobey God.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah at a time when the Jews were exiled in Babylon. Jeremiah had written to them telling them to settle there and wait seventy years. Shemaiah sent letters telling them the opposite, as if God had sent him. In this way he gave them a false hope. The text does not explain the exact details of how this punishment was carried out.

For today: before believing someone who claims to speak on God's behalf, compare what they say with the Bible. And if you teach others, do it with humility and truth, because God takes seriously the words we use in his name.
exp.42:10:
God says that Nebuchadnezzar will come and strike the land of Egypt. He speaks of three fates: some for death (plague or death in general), others for captivity (being taken away as prisoners), and others for the sword. The word "sword" here means war. The repeated phrase shows that none of this can be avoided.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. A group of Jews had fled to Egypt, thinking they would be safe there from Babylon, even though God had told them not to go. Jeremiah performs a symbolic act with stones hidden in Tahpanhes to show that Babylon would reach even there. God calls Nebuchadnezzar his servant because He uses him as an instrument, not because Nebuchadnezzar knows Him.

For today: there is no safe refuge far from the will of God. When we seek protection in human places or powers, instead of obeying Him, we deceive ourselves. Trusting God and following His guidance is true security.
exp.12:14:
The explanation says that the people must pay attention and not be proud, because God himself has spoken. The words "hear ye, and give ear" mean the same as "listen." The phrase "be not proud" means not becoming arrogant or thinking oneself superior. It is an urgent call to listen with humility.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on the words of the Lord to Judah and Jerusalem. Earlier, God announced a severe judgment on kings, priests, and the whole people because of their rebellion. Even so, in the verses that follow, Jeremiah invites them to give glory to God before the darkness comes, and he says he will weep in secret if they do not listen. His warning comes from pain, not coldness.

For today: when the Bible or our conscience confronts us, let us not defend ourselves with pride. Let us ask God for a humble heart, listen in time, and change our course.
exp.0:8:
God stretches out his hand, touches Jeremiah's mouth, and tells him that he has put his words in it. The phrase "he said unto me" is the same as "he told me." It is a gesture that shows Jeremiah will not speak on his own, but will carry God's message.

The Lord speaks, and he speaks to Jeremiah, a young man who has just been called as a prophet. Jeremiah felt very small and afraid, and he had said that he was only a child. God answers by promising that he will be with him and will deliver him. Then he gives him a very great task for his people and the nations. Many understand the touch on the mouth as a symbolic sign of his calling, not necessarily as something physical.

Today, when God asks us to speak or act and we feel unable, we can remember that he does not leave us alone. Before speaking, it is good to listen to his Word and let it guide what we say.
exp.8:4:
They deceive one another and no longer speak the truth. They have practiced lying so much that it is as if they had taught their tongue to lie. "Neighbor" here means a close companion or friend. "Iniquity" means bending what is good and doing evil with effort and persistence. They wear themselves out sinning.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, his people. He is grieved because lying had damaged the trust between neighbors and even between brothers. The verses that follow say that this falsehood grew out of refusing to know God. For that reason he announces that he will refine them as metal is melted and purified, although his sorrow over his people is evident.

Today we can examine our own words: do I exaggerate, conceal, or tell half-truths? Resolve to speak with honesty and kindness this week, even when it is costly. Ask God to help you become someone others can trust.
exp.6:15:
God tells the prophet Jeremiah to stop praying for the people of Judah. "Cry" means a strong, anguished plea. "I will not hear you" means that God would not grant what Jeremiah asked on their behalf at that time.

God speaks here in the well-known sermon at the temple. The people believed the temple would protect them, even though they worshiped idols, such as the queen of heaven, and did not live in justice. God reminds them of what happened at Shiloh and warns that judgment is coming. After a long time of rebellion and of refusing to change, the opportunity to repent was running out. Some scholars see here a judgment already decided; others see a sign of how serious their sin was.

For today: let us not trust in what is religious, such as a building or a custom, while the heart remains far from God. Right now we can turn back to Him with sincerity.
exp.14:8:
She who bore seven children, a full and blessed family, grows weak and fills with grief. Her sun sets at midday, meaning her happiness ends suddenly and before its time. She is put to shame and confounded. Those who survive, God will hand over to the sword before their enemies. The word for "weakened" here means she was worn down; the sword is the blade of war.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah did not turn back from their ways, and God announces judgment for that rejection. The mother probably represents the city or the nation; many understand it this way, though the verse does not say so with full clarity.

For today: God grieves that we ignore his call, but he always invites us to return. Do not harden your heart; if God speaks to you, respond today with humility and repentance.
exp.31:2:
This verse explains why Jeremiah was in prison. King Zedekiah had locked him up and challenged him: "Why do you prophesy like this?" Jeremiah was announcing that God would hand Jerusalem over to the king of Babylon, and that the king would take it.

The one speaking is the narrator, who recalls the king's words. Jerusalem was surrounded by the Babylonian army, and Jeremiah was in the guard's courtyard, next to the palace. The king was bothered by the message, since it discouraged the soldiers and he did not want to hear that his city would fall. Jeremiah, however, kept speaking what God told him.

For today: sometimes the truth is uncomfortable and tempts us to silence the one who speaks it. Let us ask God for humility to receive correction in time, without anger, and for courage to speak the truth with love even when it costs us.
exp.4:5:
It says that God will allow the people to be attacked as if by wild animals: a lion, a wolf, and a leopard (or tiger) that lie in wait around their cities. Whoever tries to go out will be torn to pieces. The word "striking" means hitting; "seized" means grabbed and torn apart. The cause is that their rebellions and acts of unfaithfulness toward God multiplied.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Judah. Earlier, Jeremiah looked first for the poor and then for the leaders, hoping to find someone who knew the way of God, but all of them had broken the yoke, that is, they refused to obey Him. The animals are a picture of the judgment that would come; many connect them with invaders, although the text does not name them here.

For today: rebellion almost never grows all at once, but little by little. Ask God to show you the areas where you have been giving in, and return to Him soon, before the habit hardens.
exp.37:6:
This verse tells how Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian man who served as an official in the palace, learned that Jeremiah had been put into the dungeon, which was a cistern or deep pit. At that moment the king was sitting by the gate of Benjamin, one of the gates of Jerusalem. The word "eunuchs" here probably refers to a court official, though some think it could also refer to his physical condition.

The narrator recounts how Jeremiah, for announcing God's message, was thrown into the mud by the leaders of Jerusalem. Ebed-melech, a foreigner, is the one who becomes aware of it and decides to act. The king was in a public place, where he could be spoken to.

Today, when we see an injustice, we do not need to hold an important position to speak up. Ebed-melech encourages us to raise our voices boldly on behalf of those who suffer.
exp.20:12:
God speaks firmly to Jerusalem and says that he is against her. He calls her "inhabitant of the valley, and rock of the plain," a poetic way of describing the city, settled among hills and ravines. The people feel secure and ask: "Who shall come down against us?"

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the days before Jerusalem fell. Earlier he had asked the house of David to do justice and rescue the oppressed. Since they did not obey, he now confronts them for their false confidence. Some believe "valley" refers to the city itself; others, to its location. It is not entirely clear.

For today: do not trust in your security, your position, or your resources. Practice justice and help those who suffer, because God looks at the heart.
exp.37:7:
This verse tells that Ebed-melech went out of the king's house and went to speak to him. He had heard that Jeremiah was in a dungeon, that is, a deep, dark cistern used as a prison. There was no water there, only mud. An official of the court was called a "eunuch," and the word "Ethiopian" indicates that he came from Ethiopia, a land south of Egypt.

The narrator tells that the leaders of the people had thrown Jeremiah there because they did not like his message from God. Ebed-melech, a foreigner with a position in the palace, saw the injustice and decided to act. The king was sitting at the gate of Benjamin, so Ebed-melech went to find him to defend the prophet.

For today: when we see an injustice, let us not wait for someone else to speak. Ebed-melech did not have the power of the leaders, but he used his position and his voice with courage. We can do the same on a small scale, defending someone who suffers mistreatment.
exp.30:2:
God says that he appeared to his people long ago. His message is: "I have loved you with an everlasting love," meaning a love that has no end and no beginning in time. Therefore, "with lovingkindness have I drawn you," which here means that God drew, sustained, and treated them with kindness even when the people failed.

Speaking through the prophet Jeremiah, God addresses Israel, which was going through exile and judgment, and many felt that God had abandoned them. This message of comfort reminds them that their history with God is rooted in love, and it promises that He will restore and rebuild them.

When you feel that your mistakes or your trials have pulled you away from God, remember that his love does not depend on your performance. Return to Him with confidence, knowing that his lovingkindness sustains you.
exp.26:21:
The explanation says that the sacred objects still left in Jerusalem would also be carried off to Babylon. There they would remain until God "visits" them, that is, until he takes notice of them and acts. Afterward God promises to bring them back and return them to their place. As for the words "I will restore them," the verse says "then will I bring them up, and restore them to this place."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. At that time, false prophets were saying that the objects from the temple would soon return. Jeremiah contradicts them: Babylon had already taken Jeconiah and the nobles, and more loss would come. Even so, God adds a promise of return. Traditionally this is linked to the return after the exile, although the text gives no dates.

For today: when you go through a loss or a long wait, do not take easy promises as hope. God may allow a difficult time, but his final word is not abandonment. Trust that he knows when to restore.
exp.1:28:
Another phrase means that they betrayed or deliberately failed in their commitment. God tells them that all of them, without exception, have been unfaithful to him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people worshiped idols of wood and stone, but when distress came they asked God for help. They defended themselves by saying they had done nothing wrong, and God responds by showing that their guilt is real and obvious.

For today: when God corrects us, it is easy to look for excuses or to argue. We can instead pray sincerely, acknowledge where we have failed him, and return to him, for he remains good and waits for us with patience.
exp.6:9:
God asks with sorrow and irony: how can they come to the temple, where his name is called upon, and say, "We are safe," while they keep on doing so many evils? The phrase "we are delivered" means "we are free from danger." "Abominations" are things that God hates.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people stole, murdered, swore falsely, and worshiped Baal, yet they thought the temple would protect them, as if their mere presence there were enough. God reminds them of what happened at Shiloh, where his sanctuary was destroyed because of the people's wickedness.

Today, going to church, praying, or invoking God's name does not replace an obedient life. Let us ask God to examine our hearts, and let us live in a way that is consistent with what we say we believe.
exp.41:16:
It says that all who decide to go to Egypt to live there as foreigners will die by war, famine, or disease. "Set their faces" means deciding to go; "sojourn" means living as a foreigner; "sword" is war; "pestilence" is a deadly plague. None of them will survive or escape the punishment.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem had fallen to Babylon, and the survivors of Judah were afraid and wanted to flee to Egypt. They asked Jeremiah to pray for them and promised to obey. God answers that they should stay in the land, and warns them that fleeing would not save them. Some scholars note that they were already inclined to go to Egypt even before hearing the answer.

We often look for security in a place or plan of our own, instead of obeying God. Before deciding something important, ask God sincerely, and be prepared to obey his answer, even when it is frightening.
exp.51:8:
The explanation says that the Chaldeans caught King Zedekiah as he was fleeing from Jerusalem. They took him before the king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, who was at Riblah, in the land of Hamath. There, "gave judgment upon him" means that he judged him and set out his punishment. "Took" means that they seized him.

Chapter 52 summarizes the fall of Jerusalem, and the author is not identified with certainty in this passage. For years Jeremiah had warned that Judah would fall if it kept rejecting God and refused to submit to Babylon. Zedekiah did not heed those words, and here what had been announced comes to pass.

For today: ignoring a clear warning does not make it disappear. If God speaks to us through his Word or through wise counsel, it is wise to obey in time, before the consequences arrive. His correction seeks to care for us, not to destroy us.
exp.30:8:
God says that his people will return from exile weeping, but that he himself will bring them back with mercy. He will lead them beside streams of water, along a straight path where they will not stumble. He is their Father, and Ephraim, a name that here stands for the people of the north, is his beloved firstborn son.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel was scattered by exile and defeat. This passage is part of a promise of restoration: God will gather the weak and the strong, the blind, the lame, and women who are expecting children. Some think the weeping is from repentance, others that it is from joy or from sorrow along the road; the text allows several readings.

If you feel far from God or have stumbled often, you can return to him with your tears. He does not reject you; he receives you as a father, guides you, and sustains you on the way.
exp.19:7:
Here Jeremiah says that every time he speaks on God's behalf, what he announces is destruction and ruin for the people. So instead of bringing him honor, the word of God brings him shame, insults, and mockery every day.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking just after the priest Pashur beat him and put him in the stocks for prophesying. Jeremiah feels exhausted and even confused with God, and he opens his heart to him with complete honesty. His message was unpopular, and he was paying the price.

For today: if being faithful to God costs you mockery or misunderstanding, do not pretend it doesn't hurt. Tell God about your weariness as Jeremiah did, and ask him for strength to keep being honest and faithful.
exp.47:41:
Moab will be destroyed until it is no longer a nation. The reason is clear: "he hath magnified himself against the Lord," that is, Moab became proud and rose up with arrogance against God.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and this chapter announces its judgment. Before that, the text describes an enemy that falls like an eagle on its cities, and then speaks of terror, pit, and snare, images of a trap from which there is no escape. The sin named here is pride before God.

Today we can examine our hearts: do we trust in our strength, achievements, or money as if we did not need God? Let us ask Him for humility and live thankful, knowing that all we have comes from Him.
exp.35:19:
This verse says that the officials went to the king, who was in the court, and left the scroll stored in the room of Elishama the scribe. Then they told the king, in person, everything the scroll said. The king's court is the palace yard, and the room is a chamber.

The scroll contained God's messages that Jeremiah dictated and Baruch wrote down. The officials were frightened when they heard them and decided to inform King Jehoiakim. Before this, they advised Baruch and Jeremiah to hide, perhaps because they feared the king's reaction. The Bible does not explain this in detail, so it is a reasonable assumption.

When God speaks to us through his Word, it is not wise to cover it up or soften it. We can carry it with honesty and respect, and humbly ask ourselves how we will respond, because ignoring it is also a decision.
exp.41:2:
This verse is the people's request to Jeremiah. They want God to show them the path they should follow and what they should do. The phrase "shew us the way" means that He would point out the right route for them. Notice that they say "the Lord thy God," not "our God."

The speakers are the army officers, Johanan, and all the people, a small remnant that remained after the fall of Jerusalem. They are uncertain and afraid, and they ask Jeremiah to pray for them. They promise to obey. However, later in the account it shows that they did not keep what they promised, and they went down to Egypt.

For today: asking for God's guidance is good, but we must do it with a heart willing to obey, even if the answer is not what we hoped for. Before we pray, let us ask ourselves whether we are truly open to whatever He says.
exp.9:2:
The explanation says that the religious customs of the neighboring peoples are worth nothing. Their practices and beliefs are what the verse calls "the customs of the people." The word "vain" means empty, without value. The prophet describes how they make an idol: they cut a tree out of the forest, and a craftsman shapes it with an axe, a tool for carving wood.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Israel, his people. The Israelites were surrounded by nations that worshiped idols and feared the signs of the sky, such as the stars. God warns them not to imitate those customs. The verses that follow show that the idol cannot speak, cannot walk, and cannot do either good or harm.

For today: let us ask ourselves which things made by human hands, such as money, fame, or success, have taken God's place in our hearts. Let us place our trust in the living God, not in what we ourselves make.
exp.32:16:
God promises that there will always be a descendant of David to reign over the people of Israel. "There will never be lacking a man" means that the line of kings will never come to an end. "Sits on the throne" speaks of ruling with authority. The words "to David" and "the Lord" are the same as the name of God, written in an older way.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were living through a painful time, close to the fall of Jerusalem, and it seemed that everything had been lost. God answers with hope: he announces the "Branch of righteousness," a shoot from David. Many Christians see here a promise fulfilled in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart, remember that God keeps what he promises, even when it takes time or seems impossible. You can rest in his faithfulness and pray with confidence, waiting on Christ, the King who never fails.
exp.19:5:
Here God, through Jeremiah, tells Pashur that he and his household will be taken away as prisoners to Babylon. There he will die and be buried, together with all his friends, to whom he had prophesied lies. "Those who truly love you" means those who valued him or followed him. "Captives" means prisoners taken in war.

Pashur was a priest and a senior official of the temple. He had struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks because he did not like his message of judgment. Jeremiah answers with the word of God, and this appears as an announcement of the Babylonian exile. Pashur was saying that everything was fine, but God was saying the opposite.

For today: let us not look only for words that make us feel comfortable. Let us ask God for humility to listen to his truth, even when it hurts, because true restoration comes from it.
exp.47:15:
The explanation says that Moab's ruin is very close and that the disaster is coming quickly. The word for "calamity" here means total destruction or utter defeat, and it refers to the disaster that awaits Moab.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, known for its pride and for trusting in its own strength and riches. In the past they boasted of being brave in war, but God, here called King and the LORD of hosts, declares that their power will not save them. Neighboring peoples are invited to mourn their fall.

For today: let us not place our security in what we have, in our strength or our success, because all of that can disappear quickly. It is wiser to live with humility and trust in God, who sustains what truly endures.
exp.29:19:
God promises that the people of Israel will live again as in the old days, secure and blessed. Their assembly, that is, the people gathered together, will be made firm and stable before God. And to "punish" those who oppress them means that God will act to hold them accountable for the harm they caused. "As before" means "as at the beginning."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This passage belongs to what is called the "book of consolation" (chapters 30 and 31). Judah faced ruin and exile because of its unfaithfulness, but God promises to restore the city, the temple and the joy of the people, and to renew the relationship: "You shall be my people, and I will be your God."

For today: if you are going through a time of loss or injustice, remember that God knows how to restore what is broken and also how to defend those who suffer. Trust in Him, and leave justice in His hands, without holding on to resentment.
exp.29:14:
God asks his people why they cry out in pain. A "wound" is a deep injury, and "hopeless" means there is no cure. God says this suffering comes because of the great wickedness and many sins of the people. "Iniquity" means doing what is evil and crooked.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Israel and Judah were in crisis, and their allies had abandoned them. God explains that the punishment was the consequence of their sin. But the message does not end here: later God promises to judge the oppressors and heal his people.

For today: when you suffer, do not stop at crying out. Ask God whether there is something you need to acknowledge, though not every suffering is punishment for a specific sin. If there is something, confess it sincerely, and remember that God corrects in order to heal, not to destroy.
exp.21:21:
It says the wind will carry off all the leaders of Jerusalem, as if they were worthless chaff. "Shepherds" here means the rulers and guides of the people. "Lovers" are the allied nations Judah trusted in, instead of God. Those allies will go into captivity, and the people will feel shame and confusion for their wickedness, that is, their evil.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Jerusalem, pictured as a woman. She did not listen to the voice of God, either in good times, and she sought security in other nations and in kings who fell. Some scholars see here an announcement of the fall before Babylon; the text gives no further details.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we truly trust. God speaks to us in good times, not only in crises. It is wise to listen to him before everything starts to totter.
exp.23:2:
God asks Jeremiah what he sees, and the prophet answers that there are two baskets of figs: some very good, and others so bad that they cannot be eaten. The word "said" in the verse means he told me, and the early figs are the first ripe figs of the season, very much prized.

The Lord speaks, and Jeremiah answers him. This happens after Nebuchadnezzar carried into captivity in Babylon King Jeconiah and many of the leaders and craftsmen of Judah. With this simple image, God wants to teach something about the exiles. He himself explains that he looks with favor on those taken to Babylon and has good plans for them, even though their situation may seem like punishment.

For today: do not judge your life only by what you see. A hard season can be a time when God is caring for you and preparing you. Ask him for eyes to see as he sees.
exp.5:20:
God says he will put stumbling blocks in front of his people, that is, things that will make them fall. The fall will reach everyone: fathers and sons together, and also the neighbor and the one who lives nearby. "Neighbor" here means a close associate or fellow person. "Perish" means to die or be destroyed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the invasion of Judah. The people did not listen to his word, they despised his law, and they thought sacrifices and incense were enough, even though their hearts were far from God. The verses that follow announce an army coming from the north. Scholars debate exactly who that people was, but the text presents them as an instrument of judgment.

For today: God is not satisfied with religious practices if there is no sincere obedience. It is worth asking ourselves whether we truly listen to his word and live it, and do not merely keep customs.
exp.45:13:
God commands an alarm to be announced in the cities of Egypt: Migdol, Noph (Memphis), and Tahpanhes. The message is "stand firm and get ready," because war, here called "the sword," is going to devour everything around you. The word "get ready" in that call means to prepare yourself. "The region" refers to the surrounding area.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah about the coming of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who would attack Egypt. Egypt trusted in its military strength, but the text says its strong soldiers would stumble over one another. The message shows that no human power stands above God.

Today we can learn not to rest only on our security, money, or strength. If God warns us in time, it is wise to listen and adjust our lives. Trusting in Him gives us a firmer foundation than any army.
exp.14:9:
Here Jeremiah laments with great pain. He cries out "Woe is me, my mother!" because he feels that being born brought him a life of quarrels and conflict with the whole country. The verse says "I have neither lent on usury, nor men have lent to me on usury," which means he never lent money at interest or borrowed that way, so he had no entanglements of debt with anyone, and yet everyone curses him.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the middle of a message of judgment upon Judah. Because he announced hard words on behalf of God, the people rejected him. His words are a sincere complaint, and God answers him right away with a promise to take care of him in times of distress.

For today: if people reject you for doing what is right, do not hide your pain. Tell God honestly, as Jeremiah did, and trust that he sustains you.
exp.14:12:
God says he will hand over the riches and treasures of the people to be plundered. "Give to plunder" means letting others steal and carry off everything. It will be "without any price": the people will receive nothing in return. And this will reach all their land (the "borders" are the boundaries or regions).

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The reason he gives is "for all your sins": the people had turned away from God. The verses before this are hard to understand, and some scholars debate exactly who is being addressed, but most see here a judgment on the nation.

For today: let us not place our security in money or possessions, because they can be lost. Let us seek God sincerely and live with a faithful heart.
exp.48:12:
God makes a solemn oath: Bozrah will become a ruin. It will be a thing of mockery and horror, a lonely place, and a word people use when they curse. "Desolation" means complete destruction, and "reproach" means shame or dishonor. Its neighboring cities will also be left in ruins forever.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in his message against Edom. Bozrah was an important city of that people. God says that Edom will be judged, as others were, and that it will not escape. Scholars understand the punishment as the consequence of its pride and its hostile treatment of Israel.

For today: God takes pride and injustice seriously, even when he is slow to act. Examine whether you trust in your own strength or in God, and treat others with humility and compassion.
exp.18:7:
God says he will leave Jerusalem turned into something that astonishes and terrifies. A horror is something that causes dread, and a hiss is a whistle of scorn or amazement. Those who pass by there will be stunned and will hiss when they see all its plagues, that is, its wounds and disasters.

God speaks through Jeremiah, who carries a clay jar to the Valley of Hinnom. There the people had practiced idolatry and shed innocent blood. God announces judgment because Judah turned away from him and would not be corrected. The jar that would later be broken would be a sign of that destruction.

For today: God is patient, but he takes seriously sin that does not change. Today you can ask yourself whether there is something in your life that God has shown you and you have ignored. Respond with humility and repentance while there is still time.
exp.50:20:
God says he will use someone as his "hammer" to break the military strength of his enemies: horses, riders, chariots, and those who rode in them. "Break in pieces" means to smash or shatter. Chariots and horses were the most powerful weapons of that time.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a long message against Babylon. Scholars debate who the "hammer" refers to: some think of Cyrus and the Medes and Persians, others of God's people or of a more general instrument. What is clear is that God directs history, and that Babylon, so feared, would not last forever.

For today: when evil seems invincible, remember that no human power is beyond God's control. Trust in him and do not let fear dominate you.
exp.2:11:
God tells the prophet to go and proclaim this message toward the north: "Return, Israel, you who have been unfaithful to me. I will not look at you in anger, because I am merciful, and I will not hold a grudge forever." The word "toward the north" points to the direction of the message, and "one who turns away from God by his own choice" describes someone who deliberately walks away from God.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Israel, the northern kingdom, had been taken captive by Assyria, and the message is directed toward that region. Even so, God offers them the chance to return. Judah, the southern kingdom, had seen that punishment and still carried on with a false repentance. But God asks that Israel acknowledge its sin.

Today we can draw near to God without fear of eternal rejection, but with sincerity. If you have walked away, acknowledge what you did and return. His mercy is a real invitation.
exp.1:21:
God says that, even if Israel tries to cleanse itself with bleach (a strong cleaning product) and a great deal of soap, its sin remains there, marked, that is, stained in a way that will not come out. No human effort erases that guilt.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses his people of having abandoned their love for Him to worship other gods, the Baals, in high places and under leafy trees. Even so, the people said, "I am not unclean." God uses strong images, such as that of a harlot and a good vine that turned into a strange one, to show the pain of betrayal.

For today: hiding guilt behind good appearances, religion, or one's own effort does not help. The healthiest thing is to honestly acknowledge what we have done and turn to God, who truly forgives and cleanses those who return to Him.
exp.45:9:
This verse says that day belongs to the Lord God of hosts, and that it will be a day of judgment against his enemies. It uses a strong image: the sword devours, is filled, and is made drunk with blood, that is, there will be a great slaughter. The place is the north, beside the Euphrates River.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks of the defeat of the Egyptian army, which was thought to be unstoppable, like a river that keeps rising. Historians often connect this with the battle of Carchemish, near the Euphrates, against Babylon. The text presents God as the one who rules over the nations, even though a human army is the instrument used.

For today: no human power is above God. If something seems enormous or unjust, trust that God sees everything and has the final word. Leave vengeance in his hands and seek peace.
exp.47:0:
God declares judgment against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. He names several Moabite cities: Nebo, Kiriathaim, and Misgab. All of them are described as ruined, put to shame, and dismayed. "Confounded" means left bewildered or humiliated. "Dismayed" means they lost all their strength. Some translators understand that Misgab may have been a stronghold or a high place, but this is not certain.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, but in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. This message is a warning to Moab, a nation that trusted in its pride, its strongholds, and its wealth. Later in the chapter, the text mentions that self-reliance. The exact historical details of how this was fulfilled are debated, so it is wise not to claim more than the text itself says.

For today: what seems strong, such as money, reputation, or achievements, cannot save us. Today you can examine what you truly trust in and give that place to God.
exp.38:16:
This verse is a promise from God to a particular person. It says that, on the day Jerusalem falls, God will rescue him and will not leave him in the hands of those he fears.

God speaks through Jeremiah, who was being held in the courtyard of the prison. The message is for Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian who served in the king's court. According to Jeremiah 38, he intervened to bring Jeremiah up out of a cistern. While God announces disaster on the city, he promises to look after this man. The following verse explains the reason: he trusted in God.

For today: when fear surrounds you, remember that God sees those who act with courage and trust in him. Do what is right today, even when it costs you, and leave the outcome in his hands, knowing that he cares for you.
exp.22:10:
God says that both the prophet and the priest are profane, that is, wicked or false in the way they live and serve. The most serious thing is that God found their wickedness even in his house, in the very temple, where reverence and truth were supposed to be.

Here the Lord speaks through Jeremiah. The prophet is distressed, almost reeling, over the corruption of the religious leaders. The land suffers because of the people's wickedness, and the guides who should have led them were leading them down the wrong path. That is why judgment comes upon them.

For today: it is not enough to be in religious places or to hold a spiritual office. God looks at the heart and at daily life. We can ask him to examine us and make us honest, and pray for those who lead in the church, that they may live with integrity.
exp.29:5:
It says that God invites the reader to ask an absurd question: whether a man can give birth. Yet the prophet sees men with their hands on their loins (the waist or the lower part of the back), like a woman in labor. Their faces are pale with fear. It is an image of very deep terror and anguish.

Jehovah speaks through Jeremiah to the people of Israel and Judah. A time of great distress is announced, probably tied to the fall before Babylon, although some also see in the passage a future fulfillment. But the immediate context is one of hope: God promises to deliver Jacob and break the yoke of his servitude.

Today, this text reminds us that God does not ignore our moments of fear and pain. Even when everything seems like anguish, he can turn them into a path toward deliverance. We can pray with honesty and wait in his promise.
exp.2:21:
God calls his rebellious people: "Return, backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings." The word "return" means to turn back, to change direction. The word "heal" speaks of healing a wound of the soul. The people answer: "Behold, we come unto thee; for thou art the Lord our God."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had been unfaithful to him, like a wife who betrays her husband, and had sought help from idols on the hills. Even so, God does not reject them: he invites them to come back. The verses that follow say that those idols are worthless and that salvation is found only in God.

For today: if you feel far from God, do not wait to get yourself in order first. Come back just as you are, with sincerity, and acknowledge that only he can heal what is broken in you.
exp.47:35:
It says that the heart of the one speaking sounds with sorrow, like the sound of a flute at a funeral, for Moab and for the men of Kir-heres. The reason is that the riches they had gathered were lost. The sound of the heart is a sound of grief and pain. Kir-heres is a city of Moab, and some believe it is the same as Kir-hareseth.

The one speaking is the LORD through the prophet Jeremiah, and he expresses grief over the judgment that is coming upon Moab. Earlier, their pride and their idolatry are described. Even so, a sincere sorrow is shown. Scholars debate whether the lament belongs to God, to the prophet, or to both.

For today: although God corrects pride and idolatry, his heart does not rejoice in anyone's ruin. We can pray that others will repent and feel compassion, instead of mocking when someone loses what they had put as their security.
exp.26:11:
Jeremiah tells King Zedekiah to bring his neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, that is, to submit to his rule and serve him and his people. In this way he will be able to live.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God. Judah was under pressure from Babylon, and some prophets were saying that they did not have to submit. Jeremiah states that this is a lie. God wanted them to accept this discipline in order to avoid death by war, famine, and plague. This applies to that specific historical moment, not to every government of every age.

For today: sometimes the wisest course is not the most comfortable one or the one we most like to hear. Before following a voice that promises easy solutions, let us ask God for humility, compare what we hear with the Bible, and be willing to obey even when it costs us.
exp.28:28:
This verse tells us that the priest Zephaniah read aloud, in the presence of the prophet Jeremiah, the letter that Shemaiah had sent him from Babylon. The phrase "in the ears of" means "for him to hear it." In this way, Jeremiah learned directly of the accusations against him.

Shemaiah was a false prophet among the exiles in Babylon. He had written to Jerusalem demanding that Jeremiah be corrected for saying that the captivity would be long. Zephaniah, a priest, received that letter, but instead of acting against Jeremiah, he read it to him. We do not know for certain why he did this; some think he respected Jeremiah or wanted to warn him. Afterward God answers and exposes Shemaiah.

Today we can learn not to react with fear to unjust criticism. The best course is to bring it honestly before God, who knows the truth and knows how to defend his own in his time.
exp.30:0:
This verse says that God promises to be the God of all the families or tribes of Israel, and that they will be his people. "Families" means the family groups or tribes. The phrase speaks of a close and mutual relationship: God belongs to them and they belong to him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were wounded by judgment and exile, but here God announces restoration. The words "at the same time" point to a future of renewal. The verses that follow explain the reason: God has loved them with an everlasting love and has dealt with them in mercy.

For today: our relationship with God does not begin in our effort, but in his steadfast love. If you feel far away or weary, you can return to him with confidence, because his desire is to be your God and to have you near.
exp.50:44:
God tells his people to leave Babylon and save their lives before his judgment arrives. "Come out of the midst of her" means to leave that city behind. "The fierce anger of the Lord" speaks of God's strong judgment against evil. "The Lord" is the name of God.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon was a powerful empire that had oppressed Israel and worshiped idols, such as Bel. God announces that he will judge Babylon and bring about its fall. His people were scattered among them, and God asks them to leave so they will not be caught up in that judgment. The historical details of how it was fulfilled are interpreted in various ways.

For today: God invites us not to settle into what opposes him. Today you can ask yourself what habit or environment is pulling you away from God, and take a concrete step to leave it, trusting that he cares for you.
exp.12:22:
It says that just as a dark-skinned person cannot change his skin, nor a leopard remove its spots, neither can the people do good on their own, because they are accustomed to doing evil. The word "Ethiopian" here renders the Hebrew term for a man from Cush, that is, the region south of Egypt. "Skin" is the outer covering of the body. "Accustomed" means used to something.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, before the fall of Jerusalem. After many warnings, the people kept on with idolatry and injustice. God uses this image to show how deeply rooted their sin was, and that punishment was drawing near.

For today: bad habits are hard to break by willpower alone. Recognize your need, ask God to transform you, and seek the support of other believers.
exp.35:13:
Here the princes, who were the high officials of the kingdom, send a man named Jehudi to fetch Baruch. They ask him to bring the scroll, that is, the rolled-up book in which were written the words of God that Baruch had already read to the people. Baruch takes it in his hand and goes with them.

The narrator recounts what happened after Micaiah reported to them what he had heard. Jeremiah, the prophet, had dictated those words to Baruch, his scribe. The officials wanted to hear them for themselves, because they were a serious message from God to Judah.

For today: when we hear that God's Word says something important, it is good to listen to it personally and attentively, without relying only on what others tell us. Let us open the Bible, read it calmly, and let it speak to us.
exp.11:14:
1) What it says: God promises that, after punishing the nations that were neighbors of Israel, he will return to them with compassion. He will bring each of them back to their own land, each to their own inheritance, which is the portion of land that belongs to them. "I will return" means that God himself comes back to them, and "I will bring them again" means that he restores them to their homeland.

2) Context: The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Those neighboring nations had mistreated Israel and, according to the text, had even taught his people to swear by Baal. God will judge them, but he leaves a door open: if they learn to follow him, they will be established among his people. If not, they will be destroyed.

3) For today: God's justice does not close the door to his mercy. If someone has hurt you or pulled you away from God, trust that God judges with justice. And remember that you too need his compassion. Pray today for someone you find hard to forgive.
exp.49:45:
It says that when Babylon is conquered, the cry of its fall will be so loud that it will shake the earth, and its outcry will reach all the nations. The phrase "nations" in this verse is the word the explanation refers to, and it simply means peoples or nations. The picture shows that the fall of this great power will not go unnoticed, but will shake the whole known world.

The one speaking throughout this passage is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces his judgment against Babylon, the proud empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed his people. God is presented as a lion that no one can stop, and he declares that no one can stand against him. Scholars often connect this with the fall of Babylon before the Medes and Persians, although some also see a broader meaning.

No human power, however great it may seem, is above God. We can trust that he does justice in his own time, and hand over with peace whatever worries us.
exp.10:1:
Here God commands that the words of "this covenant" be heard, that is, the solemn agreement He made with His people. And it is not enough to hear them: they must go and speak them to everyone, to the people of Judah and to those who lived in Jerusalem.

God speaks to Jeremiah, His prophet, and charges him to proclaim the covenant He had made with Israel when He brought them out of Egypt. From what follows in the chapter, the people had stopped obeying, and God was reminding them of what they had promised. It is not known with certainty which exact moment of Jeremiah's ministry this message corresponds to; some connect it with the reforms of King Josiah, but there are different opinions.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we merely know God's Word or truly listen to it in order to obey it. We can also ask with whom we might share what God has taught us.
exp.47:34:
It says that God will put an end to religious worship in Moab. There will no longer be anyone who offers sacrifices on the altars or who burns incense to their gods. It refers to the high places where the people practiced their worship.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring nation of Israel, which trusted in its riches and in its god Chemosh. The whole chapter announces judgment on Moab for its pride. The verses that follow show that even the prophet feels sorrow over that destruction, with images of mourning. Some scholars also see here a historical fulfillment, although the details are interpreted in different ways.

For today: examine what you truly trust in. Whatever we put in place of God, whether money, success, or religious customs, cannot sustain us. Seek God with humility and sincerity.
exp.30:28:
It says that a time is coming when people will no longer repeat a well-known saying. Sour grapes are green grapes, very acidic. The sensation after eating them, when the teeth feel sensitive and uncomfortable, is what the saying points to. The saying meant that children suffered the consequences of what their parents had done.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to a people battered by exile. Many used this saying to say: "We are paying for the sins of our ancestors." God promises to restore his people and announces a new covenant, in which each person will answer to Him for themselves. Interpreters debate how much of the saying was an excuse and how much was real pain; there were probably both.

For today: even if our family has left us wounds, we do not have to use them as an excuse. We can ask God for healing and decide with Him on a new path, taking on our own responsibility.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that the people did not ask, "Where is the Lord?", even though He brought them out of Egypt and led them through a very harsh desert. The phrase "shadow of death" means a dark and dangerous place. "Desolate" means without people. It was a land that no one usually passed through or lived in.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He complains to the people of Israel because their ancestors turned away from Him and followed empty idols. God reminds them of His past care: He freed them from slavery, looked after them in the wilderness, and brought them to a good land. Even so, they forgot Him.

For today: it is easy to forget God when things are going well. We can remember in prayer how He has helped us in hard times, thank Him, and seek Him every day, not only in times of need.
exp.50:30:
