It says that messengers will arrive one after another, running to tell the king of Babylon that his city has been captured on every side. Here "runner" means a messenger who travels on foot.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing what the LORD had decided against Babylon. This power had oppressed Judah and other nations. Many understand that the verse describes the fall of the city, and the Greek historian Herodotus recounts that it was taken quickly and by surprise, although the details are debated.

For today: no human power is eternal, however secure it may seem. We can trust that God acts with justice and in his own time. This invites us not to place our security in riches, fame, or strength, but in him.
exp.50:3:
This verse announces that many of the people of Babylon will die in their own land. "Chaldeans" is another name for the Babylonians. "Thrust through" means run through with spears, and "in her streets" shows that the blow will reach into the heart of the city.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. In context, Babylon had been an instrument of God, but it was also proud and cruel, and now it receives judgment. God promises that he has not abandoned Israel or Judah, even though they too had sinned. The verses that follow call the people to leave Babylon and save their lives.

For today: God sees injustice and does not forget it. That invites us to trust his justice instead of taking revenge, and to turn away from anything that drags us into living far from him.
exp.7:20:
He says the prophet is broken inside as he sees the harm done to his people. The word "broken" points to something shattered and wounded. The sentence "I am black" can be understood as deep grief, a heavy darkness of sorrow. The phrase "astonishment hath taken hold on me" means that horror seized him and left him without strength. "The daughter of my people" is a tender way of naming Judah.

The speaker is Jeremiah, though some think the voice of God can also be heard in the chapter. Judah had given itself to carved images and other gods, and judgment was coming. The people complain that the summer has passed and no rescue came. Jeremiah, instead of mocking, weeps with them.

For today: when we see the pain or sin of others, let us not respond with coldness or pride. Let us ask for a compassionate heart, pray for them, and look for ways to help them return to God, the true healer.
exp.12:25:
God says that He Himself will lift up the skirts of Jerusalem and leave them exposed for all to see, so that its shame will be seen. The word "skirts" refers to the edges of long clothing, and "ignominy" means public disgrace or shame. It is a strong image of humiliation.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. They had forgotten Him and trusted in a lie, that is, in idols and false securities. In the Bible, unfaithfulness to God is often compared to adultery. This image announces the consequences of that sin, but the closing question of the context ("how long?") shows that God still desires to cleanse them.

For today: God sees what we try to hide. Instead of covering our failures, we can confess them honestly to Him and return to Him, for He wants to cleanse us.
exp.47:9:
This verse says that cursed is the one who does the Lord's work deceitfully, that is, carelessly, halfheartedly, or with falsehood. Cursed too is the one who does not use his sword to shed blood. The word "sword" here means the blade of war, and "keep back" means to hold it back or restrain it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. The judgment on Moab was a task God entrusted to human executors, and it was not to be carried out halfheartedly. Some understand the "blood" as the warfare of judgment in that specific historical moment, not as a rule for all time.

Today, when we serve God, let us do it with sincerity and devotion, without pretending or leaving unfinished what he asks of us. Serve God with a whole heart and with perseverance.
exp.4:26:
It says that the houses of the wicked are full of deceit, like a cage full of trapped birds. Just as the hunter fills his cage with what he catches, they filled their homes with riches gained through traps and lies. With that, they became "great and rich," that is, powerful and prosperous.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He accuses people among his own nation who lay in wait and set traps for others. According to the verses that follow, they did not defend the orphan or the poor. God shows that these injustices do not go unnoticed and that there will be consequences.

For today: let us examine how we earn our money and how we treat the weak. Prosperity does not prove that God approves of everything we do. Let us ask God for honesty in our work and practical compassion toward those who have no one to defend them.
exp.35:28:
This verse is a message from God to King Jehoiakim. God reminds him of what he did: he burned the scroll where Jeremiah had written the warnings. Jehoiakim was angry because the scroll said that the king of Babylon would come and leave the land without people or animals. The word "shalt say" means "you shall say to him," and "destroy" speaks of wiping out the country.

The Lord speaks, and He speaks to Jeremiah so that he will tell the king. Baruch had written down the words that Jeremiah dictated. Jehoiakim rejected them by burning the scroll, but God commanded that they be written again. Burning the paper did not change what God had said.

Today we can learn that ignoring a warning does not make it disappear. If God's Word makes us uncomfortable, it is better to listen to it with humility and correct our course than to try to silence it.
exp.47:16:
This verse calls the neighboring peoples of Moab, and all who knew its reputation, to mourn its fall. The images of "strong staff" and "beautiful rod" stand for power and splendor: the rod was a symbol of authority, and the staff was a sturdy walking stick. The question "How is it broken?" expresses amazement that something so strong has fallen.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, announcing judgment on Moab, a nation neighboring Israel. The texts in this section point to its pride and its trust in its own riches and fortresses (for example, Jeremiah 48:7 and 48:29). The tone mixes sentence and sorrow, since the prophet himself weeps for Moab later in the chapter.

For today: nothing we admire or trust in, such as success, power, or fame, is as firm as it seems. Let us trust in God, not in our own strength, and learn to feel compassion, not mockery, when others fall.
exp.11:4:
If you have grown weary running with people on foot, how will you compete with horses? And if you stumbled in a land of peace, where you felt secure, how will you manage in the flooding of the Jordan?

"Compete" means to contend with someone or to face them in a contest. The "flooding of the Jordan" refers to the time when the river overflowed its banks, and the edge of the river was covered with thick brush where dangerous animals hid (some interpreters understand it this way).

Here God answers Jeremiah, who was complaining because the wicked were prospering and even his own family was betraying him. God tells him that the worst has not yet come. It is a firm answer, not one of immediate comfort, meant to prepare him for a harder ministry.

For today: small trials prepare us for great ones. Instead of giving up before the difficulties of the present, we can seek God, who strengthens us for what lies ahead.
exp.43:7:
This verse is part of a question God asks the Jews who had gone to Egypt. He charges that they provoke him with the works of their hands, meaning idols made by their own hands. Burning incense is offered in worship. Shame means public disgrace, and being cut off means they would be destroyed.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group fled to Egypt and continued to worship other gods. God reminds them that this same idolatry had already brought destruction upon Judah. He warns them so that they will not repeat the mistake.

For today: we can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts. Learning from past mistakes, and returning to God with humility, spares us from repeating the pain.
exp.41:6:
It says that ten days passed before God spoke to Jeremiah. The verse's wording "it came to pass" means "it happened," and "after" is the word used for the time that had gone by. The answer from God did not come right away.

After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors, with Johanan and the military leaders, asked Jeremiah to pray for them. They promised to obey God, whether what he said was good or bad. Jeremiah waited ten days until he received the word. The Bible does not explain why it was exactly ten days, so it is better not to invent a reason.

Today too, God sometimes seems slow to answer. That waiting can be a time to examine our hearts and ask ourselves whether we are truly willing to obey, even if the answer is not the one we want. Let us wait with patience and with a willing heart.
exp.15:16:
God says that his eyes are fixed on all the ways of his people, that is, on the way they live. Nothing they did escaped him, and their wickedness cannot be hidden from his sight.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He promises to bring Israel back from the lands where it had been scattered, but first he explains that the punishment is just: the people filled the land with idolatry, and God saw all of it. So judgment comes first, and restoration follows.

For today: we do not live hidden before God, and that can bring us either fear or comfort. We can stop pretending and honestly confess to him what is in our hearts. The One who sees us completely also offers forgiveness and a new beginning to anyone who turns back to him.
exp.13:20:
Here Israel asks God not to abandon his people. "Do not abhor us" means "do not reject us." "Do not disgrace the throne of thy glory" means that God should not let it fall into dishonor; the throne may refer to the temple or to Jerusalem, and it is interpreted in different ways. "Break not thy covenant" is: do not cancel your promise.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, praying on behalf of the people in the middle of a great drought. First they acknowledge their sin and that of their fathers. Then they do not rely on their own merits, but on the name of God and on his covenant, that is, on his faithfulness.

For today: when you have failed, do not hide from God. Come near with sincerity, acknowledge your mistake, and rely on what God is and on what he has promised, not on how good you yourself are.
exp.32:6:
God promises that he will bring back those who were taken away as prisoners, both from the kingdom of Judah and from the kingdom of Israel. He says "I will cause the captivity to return," that is, he will bring them back from exile. And he says "I will build them," so he will rebuild them as they were in the beginning, in their original strength.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks for God while he himself is imprisoned, as Jerusalem falls to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). The people were living with the consequences of their sin, and God had hidden his face from them. Even so, in the middle of the ruin, he promises healing, forgiveness, and peace. Scholars see this fulfilled in the return from exile, and many Christians also see its fullness in Christ.

For today: if you are going through a season of ruin or difficult consequences, God has not left you without hope. Draw near to him with sincerity; he restores, and he can rebuild what seemed lost.
exp.31:18:
He says that God is great in his plans and wonderful in what he does. His eyes are open, that is, he sees everything that people do. For this reason he gives to each person according to their way of living and according to the fruit of their deeds, in other words, the consequences of what they have done. The word "counsel" here means his purposes and his wisdom.

Jeremiah is praying to God. Babylon has Jerusalem under siege, and the prophet is a prisoner. Even so, God had asked him to buy a field, and Jeremiah prays by remembering who God is: Creator, faithful and just, the one who brought Israel out of Egypt.

For today: when you feel confused or see injustice, remember that God sees everything with clarity and nothing escapes him. You can trust that his plans are wise. It also invites you to live with honesty, knowing that your decisions matter before him.
exp.29:3:
This verse says that what follows are the words God spoke about Israel and Judah. It works as an introduction: God wants his message to be clear and clearly identified. "Israel" refers to the northern kingdom and "Judah" to the southern kingdom.

Here the Lord speaks, and he commands the prophet Jeremiah to write his words in a book. The people were under the weight of judgment and exile, but God promises that one day he will bring his children back to the land he gave to their fathers. The verses that follow show that before this restoration there will be a time of distress.

For today: God speaks to us and wants his Word to be kept and read. We can set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible and write down what God tells us, trusting that his promises are fulfilled even after difficult times.
exp.19:11:
Jeremiah speaks to God, whom he addresses as the Lord of hosts. He says that God tests the righteous, that is, examines them thoroughly. Jeremiah refers to the innermost part of a person, meaning the thoughts and the feelings. He asks to see God's judgment on his enemies, that is, for God to act justly. He says he has laid his cause before God, meaning he has entrusted it to him completely.

The prophet Jeremiah is the one speaking. His own friends were watching him and waiting for him to fall, because he announced harsh messages from God. He feels persecuted, but he trusts that God is on his side.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, tell God everything honestly, hiding nothing. Instead of taking revenge yourself, leave your cause in the hands of the one who knows your heart and the hearts of others as well.
exp.6:13:
God says that he will do to the temple in Jerusalem, where his name is called upon and in which the people trust, the same thing he did to Shiloh. The phrase "called upon my name" means that the place belongs to him and bears his name.

Jehovah speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people believed the temple would protect them, even though they continued living in injustice and idolatry. Shiloh had been an ancient center of worship in Israel, and God reminds them that this place was left in ruins. The details of its destruction are not explained here, but the message is clear: a holy place does not protect those who do not obey.

For today: let us not trust in outward things, such as a church, a tradition, or a religious custom, as if they guaranteed God's favor. Let us examine whether our hearts and our lives truly listen to him and obey him.
exp.50:35:
God promises his people that he himself will be their defender. "I will plead your cause" means that God will take up their case and do justice. "I will avenge you" means that he will punish the one who wronged them. The images of drying up Babylon's sea and its springs stand for Babylon losing what supported it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem and Zion have just complained that Nebuchadnezzar devoured them and left them empty like a vessel. God answers that cry. Some think the "sea" and the "spring" refer to the Euphrates River, which ran through Babylon, though they may also be a picture of his power in general.

When you suffer an injustice, you can bring your pain to God in prayer instead of taking revenge yourself. He sees, he hears, and he will do justice in his time.
exp.47:40:
It says that the cities and strongholds of Moab will be captured. The bravest soldiers, who seemed strong, will be overcome with so much fear that their hearts will be like those of a woman in labor, filled with pain and anguish. The word "taken" in the verse means seized, and the strongholds are walled places where people go to defend themselves.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing what the LORD says against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. The text gives as the reason that Moab grew proud against the LORD, that is, it became arrogant and rose up against God. The image of the eagle spreading its wings shows an enemy who falls swiftly. The text does not name the invader here.

For today: our walls, money, or strength do not give us true security if we live in pride. Today we can humble ourselves before God and place our trust in Him, who sustains those who seek Him.
exp.2:16:
This verse promises that a time will come when Jerusalem will be called "the throne of the Lord," that is, the place where God's rule is recognized. People from all the nations will gather there to honor his name. And they will no longer follow the "stubbornness of their evil heart," that is, their obstinacy and their habit of doing wrong. "Nations" is what the word "all the nations" means.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to a people who had turned away from him. But in the midst of the rebuke he offers hope: faithful shepherds and a restored future. He says that the ark of the covenant will no longer be spoken of, as if God's presence depended on an object. Interpreters debate whether this points to a spiritual fulfillment, a future one, or both.

For today: God does not want only rites or symbols, but a heart surrendered to him. Ask him to soften your stubbornness and teach you to truly obey him.
exp.10:21:
God announces that he will punish the men of Anathoth, that is, call them to account for what they have done. The young men will die by the sword, and their sons and daughters will die of hunger. It is a very harsh announcement of judgment.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. The neighbors in his own town, Anathoth, wanted to kill him so that he would stop prophesying. Jeremiah placed his case in God's hands, and God responds with this sentence. Some scholars connect it with the invasions that came upon Judah, but the text does not detail how it was fulfilled.

For today: when someone rejects you or attacks you for doing what is right, do not seek revenge. Commit your cause to God, who sees the heart and judges with justice. Remain faithful and let Him work.
exp.20:1:
Here King Zedekiah sends word asking the prophet Jeremiah to inquire of God on their behalf. Babylon, led by King Nebuchadrezzar, is attacking them. The king hopes God will do a miracle like those of the past, that God will act as he did before, and that the enemy army will withdraw. The word "perhaps" shows that he is not sure. "He" refers to Nebuchadrezzar.

The speakers are Zedekiah's messengers, Pashhur and Zephaniah, sent by the king. Jerusalem is surrounded and the king is afraid. But he seeks God only when danger arrives, without having turned to Him before. God answers through Jeremiah that He will not do what they hope, but that judgment will go forward.

For today: let us not wait for a crisis before seeking God. Let us draw near to Him with humility and sincerity from now on, without asking Him to approve what we have already decided.
exp.6:3:
It says not to trust in deceptive words. The people repeated three times "The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, is this," as a formula of security. God calls that idea a lie: the belief that the temple would protect them no matter how they lived.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who preached at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people worshiped there, but they oppressed the foreigner, the orphan and the widow, and followed other gods. God asked them to change their conduct, not merely to keep up their religious observances.

For today: attending church or using spiritual phrases is not enough to feel secure with God. Today you can ask yourself where in your life you truly need to obey, for example by treating with justice and kindness those who depend on you or who have less than you.
exp.7:1:
It says that bones taken out of the tombs will be scattered under the sun, the moon, and the stars, "the host of heaven." That was exactly what these people had loved, served, followed, sought, and worshipped. A "dunghill" is a heap of refuse or manure. The "face of the earth" means the surface of the ground. No one will gather them or bury them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. Judah had left God to worship heavenly bodies and idols. For that people, being left unburied was a terrible dishonor. The punishment shows how serious their idolatry was, and their own "gods" could not help them.

For today: examine what you give your love, your time, and your decisions to. What we put in God's place cannot save us. Return today to serving Him alone.
exp.2:22:
What it says: Here "vain" means empty, something that does no good. The "hills" and "mountains" were the high places where the people worshiped idols. "Salvation" means rescue or deliverance. The verse acknowledges that those places of false worship do not save; only the LORD, the God of Israel, can save.

Context: Jeremiah tells of a weeping heard on the heights, and God calls the rebellious children to return so that he can heal them. This verse is the answer of the repentant people, who admit their mistake. The lines that follow show their shame at having followed idols, just as their ancestors did.

For today: We can ask ourselves what things we have placed our hope in, such as money, success, or the approval of others. If they fail us, we can return to God sincerely, knowing that he does receive the one who comes back to him.
exp.41:8:
This verse is the beginning of God's answer. Jeremiah reminds everyone that he speaks in the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, the one they themselves asked him to bring their pleas to. "Present your supplication before him" means bringing their requests before God. "Said unto them" simply means "told them."

After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors, led by Johanan, was afraid of the king of Babylon. They asked Jeremiah to pray so they would know what to do. After ten days, Jeremiah brings them God's answer, just as they had asked.

When we ask God for direction, it is good to do so with a willingness to obey, even when the answer is not the one we hoped for. Prayer is listening, not only speaking.
exp.0:1:
It says that God spoke to Jeremiah in the thirteenth year of the reign of Josiah, king of Judah. The name of God is given in the verse as "the Lord," and the phrase about the word coming to him means that the message reached him and came to him. Josiah was the son of Amon. This verse marks precisely when Jeremiah's calling began.

The book is presented by a narrator or editor, who introduces Jeremiah as a prophet whose words come from God. Josiah was a reforming king, and many place that year around 627 B.C., although the exact dates are calculated in different ways. This verse and those that follow show that Jeremiah prophesied for about forty years, until the fall of Jerusalem.

For today: God speaks at concrete moments of history and of our lives. We can approach his Word with confidence, believing that he still guides those who listen to him, even in difficult times.
exp.24:33:
The explanation says that the shepherds and the principal ones of the flock, that is, the rulers and leaders of the people, must cry out loud and roll in the dust, as was done as a sign of mourning. Their time is over: they will be slaughtered and scattered. They will fall like a pleasant vessel, an expression usually understood as a precious and delicate vessel that breaks when it falls.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After years of warning Judah and the nations that they would not repent, he announces a judgment that will come from afar. The "shepherds" are the leaders, and their guilt is greater because they were meant to care for the people and did not.

Whoever has some authority, in the home, the church or the workplace, must care for those they lead with humility, because they will have to give an account to God.
exp.13:0:
This verse opens a new section of the book. It says that God spoke to Jeremiah about a great drought, that is, a time without rain. The name of God is "the Lord," and the word "came" means that the message reached the prophet.

Here Jeremiah is not speaking on his own, but presents what God made known to him. The verses that follow show the suffering of the people: Judah is in mourning, the cities have grown weak, and even the nobles cannot find water. In the Bible, lack of rain sometimes appears as a warning from God to a people who had turned away from Him. The text, however, here only announces the drought.

For today: when times of scarcity or pain come, do not stay only in complaint. Stop, pray, and ask God whether there is something you should correct or entrust to Him, trusting that He hears.
exp.37:3:
The leaders of the kingdom ask the king to put Jeremiah to death. They say his words "weaken the hands" of the soldiers and the people, that is, they take away their courage and their strength to fight. They accuse him of not seeking the welfare of the people, but their harm.

The princes, the leaders of Judah, are speaking while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. Jeremiah was repeating what God said: the city would be handed over, and whoever surrendered would save his life. They heard a message of defeat and betrayal; in truth it was a warning from God to save lives.

Today, we sometimes reject the truth simply because it hurts or contradicts what we want to believe. Before accusing the one who corrects us, let us ask ourselves humbly whether they speak with love, and whether God may be speaking to us through that voice.
exp.25:21:
This verse tells that King Jehoiakim sent a group of men all the way to Egypt, led by Elnathan, son of Achbor. They were going to fetch Uriah, the prophet who had fled there. The phrase "sent men into Egypt" simply means that he personally dispatched them to that country.

The narrator is the text of the book of Jeremiah, within a defense of the prophet. Uriah is mentioned as an example of what could happen to anyone who spoke the word of God with firmness. Jehoiakim did not want to listen to the message and preferred to silence the messenger. The text does not explain all the details of Elnathan's mission.

For today: when a truth makes us uncomfortable, it is tempting to attack the one who speaks it. Let us ask God for humility to listen to his correction, even when it comes by means we do not like.
exp.33:8:
This verse says that every Israelite was to give freedom to his Hebrew male and female servants. No Jew was to keep another Jew as a slave, because they were brothers. "Servant" here means a slave, or a person forced to work without freedom. The phrase "let go free" means released from service.

Jerusalem was surrounded by the army of Babylon. King Zedekiah made a covenant with the people to proclaim liberty. Jeremiah receives this word from God about that agreement. Some think the people acted out of fear and convenience, since the Bible does not fully explain it. What is certain is that afterward they changed their minds and enslaved them again.

For today: keep what you promise, especially when it comes to treating others with justice. Obeying God should not depend on the pressure of the moment, but on a heart that truly respects people.
exp.36:15:
This verse says that Jeremiah was put into the underground prison and into the cells, which were small rooms or narrow chambers. He stayed there for many days, that is, for quite a long time. The word for the prison means a dark, enclosed dungeon.

Jeremiah was a prophet of God in the final days of Judah, while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. He was accused of wanting to defect to the Chaldeans, but he denied it. The princes grew angry, beat him, and imprisoned him. His punishment came because he spoke what God commanded him, even though no one wanted to hear it. Later, King Zedekiah secretly sent for him to ask whether there was any word from God.

For today: being faithful to God can cost us misunderstanding or rejection. If this happens to you, do not lose heart. Remain honest, and trust that God sustains you, even in long and difficult times.
exp.28:8:
These men spoke in God's name and claimed to be prophets, but they were lying. God Himself makes this clear: "I have not sent them." "They prophesy to you" means they announce messages as if they came from God, and "falsely" means with a lie.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the Israelites who had been carried off captive to Babylon. False prophets were promising them that they would soon return home. God tells them that they should settle down, seek the peace of the city, and wait, because the return would come after seventy years. In this way He protected them from false hopes.

Today, not every message spoken "in God's name" comes from Him. Compare what you hear with the Bible, pray for wisdom, and be wary of anyone who only promises what you would like to hear. God is faithful, and His truth sustains us even when the wait is long.
exp.33:15:
The explanation says that the people of Judah first obeyed God and freed their Hebrew servants, but afterward regretted that decision. "Having treated my name with contempt" means they showed disrespect toward the God in whose name they had made the agreement. "Took them back again" means they enslaved again those they had set free, forcing them once more to serve them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was threatened by the army of Babylon. It seems that King Zedekiah and the people made a solemn covenant in the temple to free their Hebrew brothers, as the law required. But when the danger seemed to pass, they broke their promise. God judges them for not keeping what they had promised before Him.

For today: when we promise something to God or to others, let us not keep it only while it suits us. Think of a commitment you have neglected and ask God for help to keep it with integrity.
exp.12:1:
The explanation says that Jeremiah did exactly what God commanded him. He got the linen belt and put it on his waist. A belt or sash is what is meant by the girdle. The loins are the waist, the lower part of the back. The phrase "according to the word of the Lord" means "according to what God said."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, recounting his obedience. God asked him for a symbolic action, a kind of parable to be seen. Later the belt is ruined, and God uses it to show how Judah, which was meant to be joined to Him, had been corrupted by its pride. Some scholars debate exactly where the river in this account was located, but the central message is clear.

Obeying God sometimes involves doing things we do not fully understand. Jeremiah first obeyed, and afterward God explained the meaning. Today we can trust and take the next step that we know God is asking of us.
exp.25:10:
The priests and the prophets accuse Jeremiah before the officials and all the people. They say he deserves death, because he announced that the city would be destroyed. "Princes" refers to the leaders or officials. "Deserves" means he has already earned that punishment. "Laid waste" means stripped bare and ruined.

Jeremiah had preached in the temple that, if the people did not turn back to God, Jerusalem would become like Shiloh, a place where the sanctuary once stood and which now lies in ruins. The priests and the prophets felt attacked, since they believed the temple protected the city. They make the accusation, and the officials will act as judges.

For today: sometimes the truth that calls us to change makes us uncomfortable, and we prefer to silence the one who speaks it. Let us ask God for humility to listen to correction, instead of defending ourselves or attacking the messenger.
exp.22:25:
God asks a question filled with sorrow and firmness: "How long?" He is speaking about prophets who speak lies. He says they prophesy the deceit of their own heart, that is, their own ideas and inventions, and not what God has told them.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. The religious leaders of Judah were saying "I dreamed, I dreamed" and using the name of God to give comfortable and false messages. In this way they drew the people of God away, as they had done before with Baal. God reminds them that nothing is hidden from him, because he fills heaven and earth.

Today we can examine what we hear, and also what we say, in the light of the Bible. An impression, an experience, or a pleasant idea does not carry the same weight as the Word of God. Let us ask God for a humble heart to hear the truth, even when it is not comfortable.
exp.4:15:
It says that the arrows of this enemy people are as deadly as an open grave, ready to swallow everyone. The quiver is the case where the arrows are kept. And "mighty men" means that all of its soldiers are strong and fearless.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Israel had turned away from Him and did not believe that punishment would come. God announces that He will bring a foreign nation, whose language they do not know, as a consequence of their rebellion. Many understand this to refer to Babylon, although the text does not name it here.

For today: God is serious, but He is also patient. If there is something in your life that He has pointed out to you several times, do not ignore it. Today you can return to Him with sincerity, before the consequences arrive.
exp.36:13:
Jeremiah tells Irijah that it is false, that he is not defecting to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians, who had Jerusalem under siege). But Irijah, an officer in charge of the gate, does not believe him. He seizes Jeremiah and brings him before the princes, that is, the leaders of the government.

Jeremiah was a prophet of God, and he had warned that Jerusalem would fall. For that reason many regarded him as a traitor. He was heading toward the land of Benjamin, and the officer assumed the worst. The princes grew angry, beat him, and locked him in a makeshift prison. This shows that speaking God's truth is not always well received.

For today: sometimes we will be judged unfairly even when we are sincere. We can answer with truth and calm, and trust that God knows our hearts, even when others do not believe us.
exp.33:0:
This verse introduces a message from God to Jeremiah. It says that the word came when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, with his whole army and the kingdoms and peoples under his rule, was attacking Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. The verse shows the attack as happening at that moment, and the explanation of the wording is given in the note below.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in the last days of the kingdom of Judah, when Babylon was already surrounding the land. Soon after, God tells him to carry a message to King Zedekiah: the city would fall and he would be captured. The text presents this as the result of the people's disobedience, although the details of each cause are explained in other parts of the book.

For today: God speaks clearly even in times of crisis. When everything seems to be falling apart, it is worth listening to his Word with humility, even when it is not what we want to hear, and trusting that he is still in control.
exp.24:9:
This verse says that God will remove from the land the sounds of daily life and of celebration: joy, weddings, the noise of the millstones (the stones used to grind grain for bread), and the light of the lamps in the homes. In other words, everything would fall silent and dark, like an abandoned place.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah and the neighboring nations. For years the people refused to listen to his warnings or to give up idolatry. That is why God announces that he will use Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, as his instrument of judgment. He then notes that this domination would last seventy years, and that Babylon too would be judged.

For today: God speaks with love before he corrects, and listening to him in time spares us much pain. Today you can open the Bible with a heart ready to obey, and give thanks for simple things, such as food, light, and shared joy, which are his gifts.
exp.38:2:
The princes of the king of Babylon came into Jerusalem and took their seats in the middle gate. Several officials are named there. The word "sat" here means that they sat down, which is to say, they took control. Some of the names might be official positions, such as Rabsaris and Rabmag, and it is not certain what they mean. The name Nergal-sharezer appears twice, and it is not clear whether these are two people or a repetition.

The account tells of the fall of Jerusalem, which Jeremiah had announced for years. The Babylonians laid siege for a long time and then broke through the wall. That gate was probably a place of authority, and from there the invaders began to rule.

For today: God always fulfills what He says. If His Word warns us of something, it is wise to listen in time and correct our course with humility, before the consequences arrive.
exp.31:21:
This verse says that God gave the Israelites the land of Canaan, just as he had promised with an oath to their ancestors. The phrase "a land flowing with milk and honey" is a way of saying the land was fertile and abundant.

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, in a prayer to God. Jerusalem is surrounded by the army of Babylon (the Chaldeans), and Jeremiah remembers God's faithfulness in the past. Then he acknowledges that the people disobeyed, and that is why the punishment came.

For today: when you go through difficult moments, remember how God has kept his promises to you. And ask him for help to respond with obedience and gratitude, not with indifference.
exp.6:33:
God announces that he will silence, in the towns of Judah and in Jerusalem, the sounds of celebration: the voices of joy and gladness, and the voices of the bridegroom and the bride at their weddings. The words "I will cause to cease" mean "I will bring to an end." Ruin and total loneliness is the sense of the verse's word "desolate." The land would be left empty and lifeless.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in his message at the temple. The people mixed the worship of the LORD with idols, and even practiced terrible sacrifices at Topheth. God warns that judgment would come because of that rebellion. Many understand this as a reference to the Babylonian invasion and the fall of Jerusalem.

For today: let us not take lightly what God says about sin or his call to return to him. Examine whether there is something in your life that you keep tolerating, and come back to God sincerely, because he is the one who gives true joy.
exp.34:17:
Jeremiah speaks to the family of the Rechabites and tells them what God thinks of them. God commends them because they obeyed Jonadab, their ancestor (the word "father" here means the founder of the family). They kept all his commands and carried them out just as he gave them.

God himself had tested the Rechabites by offering them wine, and they refused it out of loyalty to their ancestor's command. Jeremiah uses their example to make a contrast: they obeyed a man, but Judah did not obey God, who spoke to them again and again. After this comes a promise for that family.

For today: if the Rechabites' loyalty to a human command was so firm, how much more should we listen to and obey the voice of God? Today you can choose a teaching from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice with steady commitment.
exp.10:6:
God says that He solemnly warned the ancestors of Israel, from the day He brought them out of Egypt until today. The word "protested" here means that He warned them with seriousness. "Rising early" means that He did it with eagerness, again and again, from the early hours. His message was simple: "Obey my voice."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah and of Jerusalem. He reminds them of the covenant He made with their fathers when He brought them out of Egypt. He does this because the people had turned away from Him. The verses that follow show that they also refused to listen, and for that reason the consequences of the covenant they failed to keep would come upon them.

God does not speak once and then withdraw; He insists with patience because He loves us. Today we can ask ourselves: am I listening to His voice in the Bible, in prayer, and in my conscience? Listening is not enough; we must obey. This week, read a passage calmly and put into practice one thing it shows you.
exp.21:20:
God says that he spoke to his people when things were going well for them, in their times of prosperity, that is, in the seasons of peace and abundance. But they answered, "I will not hear." God adds that this has been their habit since youth: they never paid attention to his voice.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses Jerusalem, which here appears as a woman with lovers, that is, allies and powers she trusted in instead of trusting in God. Before this verse, judgment is announced against the king of Judah. God reminds him that the disaster comes after many warnings that were ignored.

For today: let us not wait until a crisis arrives to listen to God. When things are going well, it is a good time to read his Word and obey it with humility.
exp.2:23:
It says that "shame," that is, disgrace, has devoured everything their fathers had worked for since they were young: their sheep, their cattle, their sons and their daughters. The word "youth" here refers to the time from one's early years onward. The word "shame" is a name given here to the idol Baal, whom the people served; many scholars understand it this way, though others read it only as shame.

The speakers are repentant Israelites, in a confession that the prophet Jeremiah puts on their lips. They acknowledge that worshiping the gods of the hills cost them everything and gave them nothing. That is why they end by saying that salvation is found only in the LORD.

For today: whatever we place above God, whether money, success, or pleasure, ends up costing us dearly. Today you can examine where you are investing your best strength, and return to God, who truly heals and restores.
exp.1:32:
God asks Israel: "Why do you dress up and adorn your way to find love?" Here "abonar" means to prepare or make something more attractive. Then he adds that she even taught her ways to the "wicked women," meaning she surpassed in wickedness even women of ill repute.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who seeks lovers, that is, foreign alliances and gods, instead of returning to her Lord. She makes great efforts to win over others, but she has forgotten God. Some understand "love" as political alliances; others, as idolatry. It probably includes both.

Today we can ask ourselves where we look for approval or security outside of God. Striving to please everyone, or trusting in fleeting things, leaves us empty. Let us return to God with sincerity; his love is not won by appearances.
exp.3:21:
It says that God's people acted with foolishness. A "fool" is someone without good sense, who ignores what matters. The "foolish children" did not truly know God. They were very skilled at doing evil, but they did not know how to do good. Those who "have no understanding" are the ones who lack discernment.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Judah. God grieves because he announces an invasion that will leave the land destroyed. The nearby verses use images of desolation, and many read them as a poetic way of showing how serious the judgment is. God explains the cause: his people did not know him.

For today: intelligence is not always wisdom. We can be very clever at business or personal advantage and still ignore God. Ask him to teach you to know him and to practice good, not just to know about him.
exp.47:46:
Although God judged Moab and its people were taken into captivity, the explanation says that one day their fate will change. The phrase about "the latter days" refers to the last days, or a time yet to come. With the words that close the verse, the message of punishment against this nation comes to an end.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab, Israel's neighbor, is warned because of its pride and its trust in its god Chemosh. The earlier chapters describe its ruin. This verse ends with a promise of restoration. Interpreters differ about when or how it will be fulfilled: some see it in the near future, others at the end of time.

For today: God corrects, but he takes no pleasure in destruction. Even in the harshest consequences, he leaves a door of hope open. If you are going through a hard season, trust that his final word is redemption.
exp.18:9:
God gives Jeremiah a command: he is to break a clay pot in plain view of the men who are with him. "Men" here means the men, and the "pot" is a jar of fired clay. It is a sign that everyone present could see and understand.

The LORD speaks, and he gives the order to the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, Jeremiah had taken some elders and priests to the Valley of Ben-hinnom, where the people had practiced idolatry and shed innocent blood. God wanted them to see a clear sign: just as a broken clay pot cannot be repaired, Jerusalem would be destroyed because of its rebellion. Some scholars point out that the jar was dry and hardened, which underlines how final the judgment would be.

Today we can learn that God speaks to us with seriousness and calls us to return to him while there is still time. Let us not harden our hearts; let us hand over to him today whatever pulls us away from him, and let him shape us.
exp.18:11:
God says that he will do to Jerusalem and to its inhabitants what can be seen in the place called Tophet: a place destroyed and defiled. The word "inhabitants" refers to those who live there; Tophet was a site in the Valley of Hinnom, outside the city.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah, who had just broken a clay jar in front of the elders. That image showed that the judgment would be irreversible. The people had abandoned God, worshiped other gods and, according to the passage, shed innocent blood. Tophet was a place tied to those practices, which is why God uses it as a symbol of what was coming.

For today: let us not take lightly turning to other loyalties. If anything occupies in our heart the place that belongs to God, it is wise to stop, repent and return to Him while there is time, trusting in His mercy.
exp.48:17:
It says that Edom will be destroyed like Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities, which were "overthrown," meaning utterly torn down. No one will live there, and no son of man will dwell in it, meaning no human being at all.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Edom was a neighboring nation of Israel, and it lived with confidence in its rocky mountains, as if it could never be reached. God denounces its pride and says that no height will free it from His judgment. Sodom is mentioned as an example of total ruin. Scholars understand in different ways how literal the fulfillment was, but the central message is clear.

For today: do not place your security in your achievements, your position, or your resources. Ask God for a humble heart, because only He is truly firm and no one can withstand Him.
exp.2:24:
They say the people recognize their shame and their guilt. "Lie down" means they are cast down, defeated. "Confusion" and "shame" speak of disgrace and dishonor, which cover them like a blanket. They admit they have sinned against God, they and their ancestors, from their youth until today, because they did not obey the voice of the Lord our God.

Here Israel speaks, the repentant people, responding to God's call in the preceding verses, which invited them to return to Him. They acknowledge that the hills and altars where they worshiped idols were vanity, and that salvation is found only in God. Some scholars see this as a genuine prayer of repentance, and others as the confession God was hoping to hear from them.

For today: confessing our failures honestly, without excuses, is the first step toward returning to God. He receives those who acknowledge their sin and wants to hear from them again.
exp.9:20:
The explanation says that the leaders of the people, called "shepherds," became foolish. It does not seek God, that is, they did not ask him for direction or take him into account. For this reason things did not go well for them, and the people they looked after were scattered, like sheep without a guide.

Here Jeremiah speaks, and in these verses he expresses the grief of Judah before the ruin that is coming. The broken dwelling and the lost children show a home destroyed, with its children gone. Interpreters often see in the shepherds the kings, priests and rulers. The prophet explains that the disaster came in part because they turned away from God.

For today: if you guide others at home, at church or at work, seek God first in prayer and in his Word. Without that, even the best plan can leave others confused and scattered.
exp.8:3:
The explanation says that lying and deceit had become so common in Judah that no one could trust anyone, not even a friend or a brother. The verse's word for the close companion or neighbor is the one the reader sees as "neighbour," meaning a neighbor or close friend. Deceit is spoken of as trickery, and lies as falsehoods. The phrase "every brother will utterly supplant" shows that betrayal reached even into one's own family.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, grieved over his people, and at the same time conveys the message of the LORD. Earlier he says he would wish to flee to the wilderness. The verses that follow explain that the people had learned to lie and did not want to know God. Some think the warning "trust ye not" describes the situation rather than being a general command to distrust everyone.

Today we can examine our own words. Before asking for trust, let us strive to be people who speak truthfully, including in small things, at home and at work.
exp.16:15:
Jeremiah tells God that he did not push himself forward to become a shepherd, that is, a leader of the people, and that he did not want the day of disaster to come upon them. "Pushed myself forward" means he got into this role without being called. "Disaster" means calamity. He affirms that God knows everything he said, because he spoke it before Him.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. He is accused of announcing judgments that do not come to pass, and people mock him, asking where the word of the LORD is. He defends himself before God, not before the people. He makes clear that his message was harsh, but he did not deliver it for pleasure or out of ambition. Some understand "shepherd" as his office as a prophet; the Hebrew term allows more than one translation.

When you are misunderstood for doing what is right, do not defend yourself with resentment. Bring your heart to God in prayer; He knows your motives and can give you peace.
exp.35:10:
This verse says that Micaiah, son of Gemariah and grandson of Shaphan, heard all the words of the Lord that were written in the book. The phrase "had heard" means that he had already listened to the full message. The sentence is left open, and the following verse tells what he did afterward.

Baruch, Jeremiah's helper, read the book with God's messages aloud, on a day of fasting and in front of many people in the temple. Micaiah was among the listeners. His father Gemariah had a room in the temple, from which the reading was done. Micaiah went right away to tell the palace officials what he had heard.

For today: when we hear the Word of God, it is not meant to be kept to ourselves. Micaiah took it seriously and shared it. We can ask ourselves what we are hearing from God today, and to whom we can share it with humility.
exp.2:17:
This verse promises that, in a future time, Judah and Israel will no longer be divided. They will walk together, and they will come back united from the land of the north, which is an old way of saying the north. They will return to the land that God gave as an inheritance to their fathers.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were divided into two kingdoms and had turned away from God. Israel had already been taken captive northward, to Assyria. God calls them to return and promises restoration, forgiveness, and unity. Interpreters differ on when it is fully fulfilled: some think of the return from exile, others of a future fulfillment.

For today: God heals divisions and brings back those who were lost. Ask Him to help you seek reconciliation with someone you have grown distant from.
exp.7:9:
God says he will give their wives to other men, and their fields to new owners. The reason is that everyone, from the lowest to the highest, is driven by dishonest gain. Greed means wanting to get ahead at any cost. Even the prophet and the priest, who should be leading the people, act deceitfully, practicing lies and fraud.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the Babylonian invasion. The people boasted of having God's law, but they did not live by it. This warning announces the consequences: the loss of families and land. Many understand it to refer to the conquest and the exile.

For today: it is not enough to own a Bible or hold a religious position; one must live with integrity. Examine your dealings, your work, and your money today, and ask God to help you correct any deceit or hidden greed.
exp.49:14:
It says a battle cry should be raised around Babylon. "Gave her hand" is an old expression meaning she surrendered, like someone who holds out a hand in sign of giving up. Her foundations fall and her walls are thrown down, that is, her strength and her protection. It is the vengeance of the Lord, that is, God's justice, and it asks that she be treated as she treated others.

The message comes from the prophet Jeremiah, who speaks on God's behalf. Babylon had destroyed nations and oppressed Israel, and judgment is announced against it because she sinned against the Lord. Some see here a fall of Babylon that was already near, and others also see a broader fulfillment. Scholars understand it in several ways.

For today: you can trust that God sees injustice and does not leave it without a response. This helps you let go of resentment and not take revenge yourself, leaving God to be the judge, and at the same time to examine your own treatment of others.
exp.40:6:
It says that Ishmael, son of Nethaniah, killed the men who came to the city. He cut their throats, that is, he slew them, and threw their bodies into a cistern, which was a pit for storing water. He did this with the help of the men who were with him.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah is speaking. Gedaliah had been appointed governor after the fall of Jerusalem, and Ishmael had murdered him. Those eighty men were coming in mourning, with offerings for the temple, and Ishmael deceived them with false tears to bring them into the city. The text does not explain his exact motive, and scholars only suppose it.

For today: deception can come with a friendly appearance and even with tears. Let us ask God for wisdom to discern, and never use false kindness to harm others.
exp.47:3:
It says that Moab was destroyed and broken to pieces. "Broken" means shattered, completely defeated. The most painful part is that the crying of her little ones was heard, that is, of the children, or perhaps of the weakest and most humble people of the city. Some older translations read the end of this verse differently, so there is not just one certain way to understand it.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, announcing what God says against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Moab trusted in its pride, its riches, and its fortresses. The message announces that this security will fall, and that ruin will come to cities such as Heshbon, Madmen, and Horonaim. The text describes the suffering with great vividness.

For today: God takes pride seriously, but he also hears the crying of the weak. We can examine what we truly trust in and be sensitive to the suffering of those who have no voice.
exp.49:37:
The explanation says that a great drought will fall on the waters of Babylon and they will dry up. The reason is that it was a land full of carved images, or idols, and its people became mad about them. Carved images are figures made to be worshiped, and to be "mad upon" them means to lose their good judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, announcing judgment against Babylon, the power that had destroyed Jerusalem. The "waters" may refer to the rivers and canals that sustained the city; some scholars also see a symbolic meaning. The sword in the previous verse and the desert that follows show that its fall would be total.

For today: idols are not always statues. Anything that takes the place of God, such as money, fame, or success, eventually leaves us empty. Today you can ask yourself what your heart holds above God, and give it to him sincerely.
exp.45:3:
This verse gives orders for war: harness the horses, mount up, put on the helmets, polish the spears, and dress in armor. The "helmets" here are metal headgear, and the "brigandines" are the body armor worn to protect the torso.

God speaks through Jeremiah about Egypt. Pharaoh Necho was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish, beside the Euphrates River, around 605 B.C. The orders sound like a call to get ready, but many read them with irony: Egypt prepares with everything it has, and still it will fall, as the verses that follow say. Some think it describes the preparation before battle; others see it as a mockery of Egyptian pride.

For today: we can prepare well and work hard, but our final security is not in our own resources. It is in God, who rules over all nations and all outcomes.
exp.30:20:
Here the people are told to set up markers and tall heaps of stones along the way, so that they do not lose the route back. Heaps of stones that serve as signs are called markers, and the road itself is the highway. The "virgin of Israel" is asked to pay close attention to the path by which she went into exile, because it is by that same way that she will return to her cities.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel was in captivity, and the Lord promises them restoration. He had earlier said that Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom, remains a precious son to him, and that he has compassion on him. The call to return comes from that love, not from rejection.

For today: if you have drifted away from God, he calls you to come back. Remember the point where you turned aside, take a concrete step toward him, such as prayer or asking forgiveness, and set up signs that help you not lose your way, such as daily Bible reading or a community of faith.
exp.35:4:
Jeremiah gives an instruction to Baruch, his assistant. He tells him that he is "shut up," meaning that he is prevented from moving freely, and so he cannot go into the house of the Lord, which is called here the temple. The word "commanded" means that he gave him a task to carry out.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. He had already dictated to Baruch all the words that God had given him, and now he wants them read in public. Jeremiah could not go to the temple, although the text does not explain in detail the reason for his restriction. God wanted the people to hear, to repent, and to be forgiven.

For today: when a limitation keeps you from doing what you would wish, do not sit idly by. Ask God what you can do with what you still have, and trust that He can use other people to carry forward His message.
exp.16:2:
He says God speaks to Judah, whom he calls "my mountain in the field," probably meaning Jerusalem and its land. He announces that their riches and treasures will be handed over to plunder. The verse's word "substance" means their possessions, and "high places" were elevated spots where people worshiped, often other gods. The reason is that sin spread throughout the whole territory.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had their sin deeply marked, as if engraved in iron, and they kept worshiping idols beside trees and hills. God announces the consequences: loss of wealth and of the land, and serving their enemies. He then contrasts this with trusting in people instead of in Him.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, possessions, or people. All of that can be lost. Trust God first and ask Him to be your true foundation.
exp.24:2:
Jeremiah reminds them that for twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of King Josiah, God has been speaking to him, and that he has repeated that message to the people again and again. The word "rising early" means doing it earnestly and from the start, never neglecting the warning. The people did not listen.

Jeremiah, God's prophet, speaks in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, when Nebuchadnezzar was beginning to reign in Babylon. He addresses Judah and Jerusalem. He reminds them that God had called them many times to turn from their evil way, and that the threat of judgment was not a sudden blow but the consequence of having rejected so many warnings.

For today: God often speaks with patience and more than once. If we sense that something in our life needs to change, let us not put it off. Listening humbly today, and obeying, is a way of responding to his love.
exp.24:24:
It says that God will also make the kings of Zimri, of Elam, and of the Medes drink the cup of his judgment. The word for north is used here for the direction the verse refers to. Zimri is a little-known place, and it is not known for certain where it was. Elam lay east of Babylon, and the Medes lay even further to the northeast.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, sent by God. In this chapter, the LORD announces that Babylon will be his instrument of punishment. The cup is an image of divine judgment, which reaches first to Judah and then to many nations. With this, God shows that he rules over all peoples, not only over Israel.

For today: no human power is beyond the reach of God. If you trust in kings, money, or fame, remember that only God is secure. Live with humility and obedience, knowing that he is just and also merciful to whoever turns back to him.
exp.5:3:
The explanation says that the enemies encourage one another to attack Jerusalem. Declaring or preparing battle means calling for war and getting ready to fight. "Against her" refers to the city, the daughter of Zion, the one under attack. "Let us go up at noon" means they want to attack at midday, in the full heat of the sun. Then they complain that the day is running out and the shadows of the evening are growing long, so they will not be able to attack in time. That is why, in the next verse, they propose attacking by night.

Jeremiah passes on what God showed him: an army from the north will come as judgment on Jerusalem. Here the prophet imitates the voice of the invaders, who are in a hurry and eager to destroy. The cause, according to the text, is the violence and wickedness in the middle of the city. Some understand the "woe" as mockery or the impatience of the enemies.

For today: let us not postpone the correction God asks of us. If today we feel his call to change, let us listen to it with humility, before the day is over.
exp.36:20:
This verse tells that King Zedekiah answered Jeremiah's plea. He had him taken out of the house of Jonathan and placed in the courtyard of the guard, a more open and less dangerous place. There they gave him a loaf of bread each day, taken from the bakers' street, until the city's bread ran out.

Jerusalem was under siege by the Babylonians. Jeremiah had announced that the city would fall, and for this reason he was accused and locked in a damp dungeon. He asked the king not to send him back there, for he feared he would die. Zedekiah, though weak and fearful, granted him some relief.

For today: God can care for us with simple provisions, even when the situation remains difficult. Jeremiah was not fully freed, but he received daily bread and protection. We can trust God day by day, and remain faithful to the truth even when it costs us.
exp.29:0:
This verse is an introduction. It says that what follows is a word that the Lord gave to Jeremiah. The phrase "came to Jeremiah" is the same as saying the word was given to him. And "saying" announces that God is about to speak right away.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is the prophet who receives the message. The verses that follow explain that God asks him to write it in a book and promises that he will bring Israel and Judah back from captivity. Many understand this chapter to be a message of hope for a people who had been punished. Scholars discuss which parts were fulfilled when the people returned from exile and which parts look further ahead.

For today: God speaks with purpose and wants his words to be preserved. We can read the Bible with confidence, trusting that he offers hope even after difficult times. Today, before you read, ask him to speak to you, and write down one promise that encourages you.
exp.21:28:
Jeremiah 22:29 repeats the word "earth" three times to draw attention with force. It is like a solemn cry: "Hear!"

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Coniah, also called Jehoiachin, was king of Judah and was taken captive to Babylon. God announces that his fate will be harsh and that none of his descendants will reign successfully on the throne of David. The whole earth is called to hear this judgment. Some understand it to refer to the land of Judah; others, to the whole earth as a witness.

For today: God speaks with seriousness, and it is worth listening before the consequences arrive. Today you can set aside a moment to read the Bible with a heart willing to obey.
exp.51:3:
It says that in the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came with his whole army against Jerusalem. They camped around the city and built siege towers and walls of attack on every side to surround it. "Camped against it" means they set up their camp there.

This chapter is the historical account that closes the book of Jeremiah. The one telling the story is not God speaking directly, but the writer recounting the events. It explains that Zedekiah did evil and rebelled against Babylon, and that the fall of Jerusalem came as God's judgment after much disobedience. This matches what Jeremiah had warned about for years.

For today: God is patient, but our choices have consequences. If you feel that God is calling you to correct something, do not put it off. Listen to His voice with humility and return to Him while there is still time.
exp.17:14:
God says that his people have forgotten him. Instead of worshiping him, they burn incense to emptiness, that is, to empty idols that are of no use at all. That idolatry makes them stumble on their paths, and it turns them away from the old, well-tested paths of their ancestors' faith. So they walk on untrodden trails, paths no one has traveled before and no one knows where they lead.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in the kingdom of Judah. Shortly before, he compares the faithfulness of nature, like the snow of Lebanon and the cold waters, with the unfaithfulness of Israel. It is a call to return, but also a warning of judgment, as the verses that follow show.

For today: when you notice that other things are taking God's place, such as success, money, or the approval of others, stop and return to the basics: prayer, his Word, and simple obedience.
exp.3:5:
Tell the people to raise a warning signal in Zion, to gather together and not stand still, because God is going to bring disaster from the north, a massive destruction. The old word for the north in the verse is one readers may not recognize, and the second term means total ruin or destruction.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing Judah and Jerusalem. Earlier He called them to return to Him wholeheartedly, but they did not do so. Now He warns of the judgment that is coming. Many understand that the enemy from the north was Babylon, though the text does not name it here.

For today: do not put off what God asks you to correct. If you feel He is calling you to come back to Him, respond today with humility and sincerity, before the consequences arrive. His warning is a sign of care, not only of anger.
exp.2:19:
The explanation says that the people of Israel betrayed God, just as a wife who is unfaithful to her husband betrays him. The words "treacherously departeth" mean breaking the promise of loyalty. The husband is the one she was bound to in faithfulness. The phrase "dealt treacherously" means that they acted with betrayal, failing to keep their word.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just recalled that he wanted to treat Israel as children and give them a good land, hoping they would be faithful to him. Here he expresses his pain because they left him. But the text that follows shows that it does not end in condemnation: God calls them to return and promises to heal them.

For today: if you notice that you have moved away from God, do not hide yourself. He grieves over betrayal, but he still invites you to come back. Today you can speak to him honestly, acknowledge where you have failed, and ask him to heal your heart.
exp.4:23:
They never stopped to think, in their heart, "Let us now reverence and honor the Lord our God." He is the one who sends the early rain (the autumn rain, for sowing) and the late rain (the spring rain, to ripen the harvest). He also keeps the set weeks of the harvest. Here, "fear" means reverence, not just being afraid.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Judah of having a rebellious heart. Just as the sea respects the limit of sand that God set for it, the people should have respected their Creator. But they took the blessings for granted and forgot who gave them.

For today: let us not take our daily bread for granted. Before eating, or when receiving good news, pause for a moment and thank God, aloud or in your heart. This simple gratitude keeps us humble and close to Him.
exp.50:40:
It says that Babylon, which the verse also calls "Sheshach," was taken and conquered. It was a city admired by the whole world, but now it causes dismay among the nations. "How is it taken" means that it was captured. "Sheshach" seems to be a coded name for Babylon, a kind of secret writing used in Hebrew; many scholars understand it this way. "Astonishment" means horror or amazement at its ruin.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment against Babylon, the powerful empire that had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed its people. The text shows that God is just and that no human kingdom, however great, is beyond his control. The nearby verses describe its fall with strong images, such as a feast that ends in a deathlike sleep and a sea that covers it.

For today: do not place your security in prestige, power, or success, because these pass away. Trust in God, who sustains what truly endures, and live with humility.
exp.31:15:
This verse tells how Jeremiah, after handing the deed of purchase to Baruch, son of Neriah, began to pray to the Lord. The "deed of purchase" was the document that proved the buying of a piece of land. Lord is the name of God, and "dí" and "á" are old spellings of "di" and "a".

Jeremiah speaks. Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon, and he himself was a prisoner. On God's command he had bought a field from his cousin, something that seemed absurd, since the land was about to fall into enemy hands. God told him to keep the documents in a clay jar as a sign that one day land would be bought again in Israel. Jeremiah, filled with doubt and wonder, brings everything before God in prayer.

For today: when what God asks of you seems to make no sense, do not hide your doubts. Pray honestly, remembering who God is and what he has done, and obey, trusting that his promises still stand.
exp.37:12:
This verse tells how Jeremiah was pulled alive out of the cistern. The men drew him up with ropes from the dungeon, which was a deep, dark cistern used as a prison. Afterward, Jeremiah remained imprisoned, but now in the court of the prison, a more open place and far less deadly.

The narrator recounts what happened. The leaders of Judah had thrown Jeremiah into the muddy cistern for predicting the fall of Jerusalem. Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian who served in the palace, spoke on the prophet's behalf before the king and rescued him. He put old rags under Jeremiah's arms so the ropes would not hurt him.

For today: God can use unexpected people and simple gestures to care for his own. Ask yourself whom you can help today with a practical act of compassion, even if no one notices.
exp.12:17:
God commands Jeremiah to tell the king and the queen to humble themselves and sit down on the ground, because the crown of their glory has already fallen from their heads. Sitting on the ground was a sign of mourning and humility. "Humble yourselves" means putting down pride.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah and to their royal family. He warns them that their arrogance will lead them into captivity. Many scholars think the "queen" was the queen mother, though there is no complete certainty about exactly who they were. The prophet himself weeps in secret for the people who will not listen.

For today: humility comes best when we choose it ourselves before life imposes it on us. Today you can acknowledge before God the areas where you have believed yourself self-sufficient, and ask him to teach you to depend on him.
exp.38:7:
This verse tells that the armies of Babylon, called Chaldeans, burned the king's palace and the houses of the common people. They also tore down the walls of Jerusalem. The word "burned" in this verse refers to setting the buildings on fire.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah records the fall of Jerusalem in the year 586 BC, according to the most widely accepted date. For years, Jeremiah had warned that if the people did not return to God, this judgment would come. The verses before this one show the sad end of King Zedekiah, and the verses that follow describe how many were taken captive.

For today: God speaks clearly and is faithful to his word, even when we do not always want to listen. If we feel that he is correcting us, let us not wait until everything falls apart; let us return to him today with humility, because his mercy remains open.
exp.50:1:
It says that God will send winnowers to Babylon, that is, people who fan the grain, the way someone tosses wheat into the air to separate the chaff. In this way they will leave her land empty. They will come against her from every side "in the day of evil," that is, the day of her disaster and judgment.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon was a powerful empire that had mistreated other peoples, among them Judah. God announces that this power will not last forever. The "destroying wind" of the previous verse and the image of winnowing show a judgment that sweeps away and scatters.

For today: no human power, however great it may seem, stands above God. If you see injustice today, trust that God governs history and in his time judges. Meanwhile, live with humility and justice, without relying on pride or on force.
exp.1:25:
It says that Israel will be put to shame, just as a thief is ashamed when he is caught in the act. That shame will reach everyone: the people, the kings, the princes (the leaders or rulers), the priests, and the prophets. No one is spared, not even those who were supposed to guide the people.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Judah of having left the living God to follow other gods. He compares them to a wild donkey in heat, running out of control. They answer stubbornly: "We have loved strangers, and after them we will go." Then they call a piece of wood "father," yet in their distress they ask God for help.

For today: it is not enough to turn to God only when there are problems. Examine what you place your trust in, such as money, success, or the approval of others, and return to God from now on, not only in the crisis.
exp.15:1:
God commands the prophet Jeremiah not to marry or have children in this place, that is, in the land of Judah. It is a personal instruction and a very hard one. "To take a wife" means to get married.

The Lord speaks and tells Jeremiah this a few years before the fall of Jerusalem (around 587 B.C.). His solitary life was a visible sign for the people: a judgment so terrible was coming that bringing children into that place would mean condemning them to suffering. The passage that follows describes death by disease, sword, and famine. Jeremiah bore that pain as a living message.

For today: God sometimes calls his servants to difficult and lonely paths. If you are going through one, remember that he sees your sacrifice and does not leave you alone. He also invites us to take his word seriously and not to ignore his warnings.
exp.42:0:
This verse says that Jeremiah finished speaking to the people. He had given them everything God commanded him to tell them, leaving nothing out. The verse stands as a pause before the people's response. The word "happened" would capture the sense of the verse's opening phrase, and "the Lord, the God of them" is the way the verse names God.

Jeremiah speaks after the fall of Jerusalem. The survivors, together with their leaders, had asked him to pray and to tell them God's will. He told them that they should remain in Judah and not flee to Egypt. As the following passage shows, the leaders accused him of lying and rejected the message.

For today: it is easy to ask for God's guidance while already having decided what we want to do. Before we pray, let us ask ourselves whether we are willing to obey even when the answer is not what we hoped for.
exp.22:6:
God announces that days are coming when people will no longer use as their main oath the familiar phrase: "As the Lord lives, who brought up the children of Israel out of Egypt." Swearing "as the Lord lives" was a way of affirming something with seriousness. The exodus will not be forgotten, but it will be overshadowed by something even greater.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, while Judah faced exile in Babylon. Just before this, he promises a righteous King, a descendant of David, who is called "The Lord our righteousness." Then he says he will gather his people from the north and from all the lands where he had scattered them, and bring them back. Many Christians see Jesus in that King.

For today: God does not stay in the past. If you are going through a season of loss or scattering, remember that he knows how to rescue again. Give thanks for his past works, but trust that he can still open a new path.
exp.21:10:
God announces that Shallum, son of King Josiah, went out of Judah and will not return. The phrase "who reigned in place of Josiah his father" means that he reigned in place of his father. "Went out of this place" refers to his being taken away from Jerusalem.
