The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Shallum is usually identified with Jehoahaz, who reigned only a few months and was taken captive to Egypt by Pharaoh Necoh (2 Kings 23:31-34). The previous verse explains the cause: the people abandoned their covenant with God and worshiped idols. That is why the consequences came.

For today: turning away from God has consequences, even when we have power or a good inheritance. Ask him today to keep you faithful, and to make your decisions just and honoring to his word.
exp.51:17:
The explanation says that the Chaldeans, the army of Babylon, carried off the bronze utensils that were used in the temple. The words in the verse refer to: caldrons (pots used for collecting ashes or for cooking), shovels (scoops for removing ashes from the altar), snuffers (the word is uncertain; probably bowls or vessels for sprinkling), bowls (vessels or basins), and spoons (ladles or small containers).

This is recorded in the final account of the book of Jeremiah, which describes the fall of Jerusalem around 586 B.C. The text goes through in detail what Babylon plundered, while the captain Nebuzaradan left the poorest of the people in the land. The emphasis on each object shows how much was lost.

For today: what we use to serve God can be lost, but he remains faithful. Value what you have today for serving, and trust not in places or objects, but in the Lord himself.
exp.47:37:
This verse says that on all the housetops of Moab and in its streets there will be nothing but weeping. The housetops are the flat roofs of the houses, where people used to gather. God says he broke Moab like a vessel that no longer pleases him, that is, it is no longer of use and it shatters.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and this message announces its judgment. The prophet even shows sorrow for them: the signs of mourning are shaven heads, wounded hands, and clothing of sackcloth. The texts speak of their pride and of how they trusted in their riches.

For today: do not place your security in what you have or in your own pride. All of that can be broken. Ask God for a humble heart, and learn to feel sorrow, not mockery, when others face the consequences of their mistakes.
exp.24:3:
This verse says that God sent all his prophets, again and again, to speak to his people. The phrase rising early and sending them means that he did it with persistence, starting early and never tiring. To incline the ear means to truly pay attention. The people heard the sounds, but they would not listen.

Here Jeremiah speaks to Judah and Jerusalem. He has been warning them for twenty-three years, since the thirteenth year of King Josiah. God was asking them to turn away from their evil ways and give up their idols. He reminds them that other prophets had also spoken, but the people paid no attention.

For today: God keeps speaking with patience. Today you can ask yourself whether there is something he has shown you in his Word that you have put off for later. Listen with humility and take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.2:20:
What it says: A voice is heard on the bare hills, a weeping and a pleading of the children of Israel. They weep because they have turned aside from the good way and have forgotten the Lord, their God. Going astray is living in a crooked manner, far from what is right.

Context: The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had betrayed him like an unfaithful wife, worshiping false gods on the high places. Many understand this weeping on the hills as the people's repentance, which the following verse confirms when God calls them to return and heal their rebellion. Some also see it as a lament of grief over their sin.

For today: When you notice that you have drifted away from God, do not hide or make excuses. Return to Him sincerely, with tears if needed, because He promises to heal those who come back.
exp.39:7:
This verse says that several leaders of the Jewish army came to Mizpah to meet Gedaliah, the governor. Their names are Ishmael, Johanan and Jonathan, Seraiah, the sons of Ephai, and Jezaniah, together with their men. The explanation of their origins (Netophathite and Maachathite) is removed here because the words do not appear in the verse above.

After the fall of Jerusalem, Babylon left Gedaliah in charge of the poor who remained in the land. These leaders had been scattered across the countryside and now came to him. The narrator only introduces them; in the next verse Gedaliah speaks and proposes that they live peacefully under Babylon.

For today: when times of crisis come, it is wise to seek the counsel of someone who leads with calm and not to act out of fear alone. But it is also good to listen carefully, because among those who come there may be both good and bad intentions, and we need to ask God for discernment.
exp.5:1:
God says that he has likened Jerusalem, called "the daughter of Zion," to a beautiful and delicate woman, that is, refined and accustomed to comfort. The wording of the verse is itself a clue: the comparison is set out as a deliberate likeness. The Hebrew verb here is hard to render, and other translations understand it as meaning that he will bring that beautiful daughter of Zion to ruin.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the invasion from the north by Babylon. He warns Jerusalem, which felt secure and at ease, that its beauty will not protect it. The shepherds with their flocks who come to camp are an image of armies surrounding the city.

For today: comfort and success are no guarantee of safety before God. Today you can ask yourself whether you have stopped listening to his warnings because you feel at ease, and return to him with humility before a greater shaking becomes necessary.
exp.51:18:
This verse describes the looting of the temple in Jerusalem. The Babylonians carried off the cups, the censers (for burning incense), the bowls, the pots, the candlesticks (holders for lamps), the basins (deep dishes), and the cups. Everything that was of gold and of silver was taken by the captain of the guard, that is, the chief of the king's soldiers.

It is the end of the book of Jeremiah, which repeats the account of the fall of Jerusalem around 586 BC. The narrator tells the events in detail, and many believe he adds this historical summary to show that the prophet's warnings were fulfilled. The people had trusted in the temple, but not in living faithfully before God.

For today: sacred things can be lost, but God does not depend on them. Take care of your relationship with Him, not only the outward side of your faith.
exp.29:6:
This verse speaks of a terrible day, so great in its anguish that there is none like it. It is called "time of trouble for Jacob", that is, for the people of Israel. But it ends with hope: Jacob will be saved out of that trouble. The word "none like it" means no other day compares to it, and "saved" means rescued.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were under the threat or weight of judgment and exile, and the verses before it describe a fear so great that men grip their loins (their waist) like a woman in labor. Interpreters disagree about whether "that day" refers only to the fall of Babylon and the return from exile, or also to a broader time in the future. The next verse promises to break the yoke and restore the people.

For today: even when a trial seems to be the worst of all, God can bring deliverance. We can ask him for help with confidence and wait on his faithfulness.
exp.13:4:
Verse 5 says that even the doe, an animal that is very tender toward its young, gave birth in the field and abandoned her newborn. She did not do this out of lack of affection, but because there was no grass to eat. The word "calved" in the verse means "gave birth," and the "calf" is the newborn fawn.

The prophet Jeremiah describes a great drought that fell upon Judah. The verses before this one show nobles, farmers, and servants ashamed because of the lack of water. Then Jeremiah prays to God and acknowledges that the people have sinned and rebelled. The drought is presented as a serious sign, and the text connects it with the spiritual condition of the people.

When crises come, we can be honest before God, as Jeremiah was. Instead of blaming others or hardening ourselves, we can acknowledge our failures, ask for forgiveness, and trust in his mercy.
exp.50:12:
It says that Babylon, the city that dwells by "many waters" (canals and rivers) and is full of riches, has already come to its end. "The measure of your covetousness" can be understood as meaning that her greed has reached its limit, or that God has already measured and cut off her greed, the way one cuts a thread. The word "dwellest" simply means "live."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah and to the nations. He announces that Babylon, which had harmed his people and his temple, will be judged. He mentions the kings of the Medes as the instrument of that judgment. The text presents this as the justice of God, not as a mere political event.

For today: riches and power do not protect us forever. It is worth asking ourselves whether greed is directing our decisions, and learning to trust God, to be generous, and to live with honesty, knowing that he is the true Judge.
exp.2:13:
This verse is a call from God to his unfaithful people. "Turn back" means returning to God wholeheartedly. "Backsliding children" are those who have drifted away from him. God says, "I am married unto you", meaning he remains bound to them in love. He promises to take one from a city and two from a family, that is, a remnant, and bring them to Zion, the place where he dwells.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Israel had worshiped idols "under every green tree", and yet God calls them to return. He reminds them that he is merciful and will not keep his anger forever. Some understand this as referring to the return from exile, while others also see a broader hope for the future.

For today: if you have drifted away from God, do not wait until you are perfect to come back. He calls you with tenderness. Acknowledge your failing sincerely and take a step of return today in prayer.
exp.31:14:
This verse is a promise from God: even though everything seems lost, one day people will again buy houses, fields and vineyards in that land. The word "possessed" in the King James wording means owned or held, as property is held. The phrase about "the Lord of hosts" is not in this verse, so the comment about it is removed.

Jeremiah speaks by the command of God. The armies of Babylon surrounded Jerusalem, and the prophet was in prison. Even so, God asked him to buy a field from his cousin. Jeremiah instructs Baruc to keep the documents in a clay jar, so that they would last a long time. It was a sign that there would be restoration after the judgment.

For today: when you pass through a dark season, do not stop trusting God or taking steps of faith. Plan with hope, pray sincerely, and leave the future in his hands, because he keeps his promises in his own time.
exp.44:2:
Baruch says he is worn out by grief. He feels that God has piled sorrow on top of his suffering. The phrase "I fainted in my sighing" means that he wore himself out with so much complaining and weeping, and still he found no rest.

God speaks through Jeremiah to Baruch, his assistant, who wrote down the prophet's words. This was in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when the messages were harsh and announced judgment. Baruch was overwhelmed, and perhaps he also wanted a safer life or a more important place. God does not ignore his complaint, but speaks to him frankly and promises to watch over his life.

When you feel tired and sad, do not hide your pain from God. Tell him honestly. And let him also examine your expectations, because trusting him is safer than chasing greatness.
exp.50:63:
It says that Babylon will be "drowned," that is, sunk like something that goes under the water and cannot come back up. She will not rise again from the punishment that God brings on her. "They will be weary" means they will be worn out, defeated, and without strength. The last sentence indicates that this is where Jeremiah's words in this book end.

Jeremiah gave Seraiah, an officer who was traveling to Babylon with King Zedekiah, a scroll with the announcement of that city's fall. He was to read it there, tie a stone to it, and throw it into the Euphrates. It was a symbolic act: just as the scroll would sink, Babylon would fall. Interpreters see here a sign that God judges proud empires, even though today they appear powerful.

For today: no human power is eternal. We can trust that God acts with justice, and so we do not need to fear those who seem invincible or live with envy or bitterness.
exp.49:44:
This verse calls for listening to the plan that God has decided against Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans. It says that even the smallest of the enemy's flock will drag them out, and that God will make their dwelling place desolate along with them, meaning their pastures or their home. The word "hear" in the verse means "listen," and the word for "flock" refers to a group of sheep.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing what the Lord has resolved. Babylon had dominated Israel and other nations. The chapter announces its fall before a people coming from the north. The king trembles, and God presents himself as the shepherd whom no one can resist. Some think that "the least of the flock" shows how easy the defeat will be; others see it as a picture of total humiliation.

For today: even when evil seems strong and impossible to stop, God still governs history. We can trust his justice, wait with patience, and not respond with pride or revenge.
exp.49:9:
It says that Chaldea, another name for Babylon, will be a spoil, that is, plunder that others will take. Those who plunder her will be fully satisfied, with everything they were seeking. The one who declares it is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and mistreated his people, and it felt proud and secure. God announces that he will raise up against her an assembly of nations from the north. The following verses explain the reason: Babylon rejoiced in destroying God's inheritance, that is, his people. Thus, judgment comes because of her pride and her injustice.

For today: let us not be deceived by the power of those who do harm. God sees injustice and has the last word. We can entrust our pain to him, refrain from seeking revenge, and live with humility, trusting in his justice.
exp.10:2:
This verse says that God commands Jeremiah to speak to the people on his behalf. The message is serious: "Cursed be the man that obeys not the words of this covenant." "Man" here means any person among the people, and "cursed" means that they are under the consequences of having rejected God. "Covenant" is the solemn agreement between God and his people.

The LORD speaks, and Jeremiah must repeat it to the people of Judah and of Jerusalem. This covenant had been given to their ancestors when God brought them out of Egypt. God reminds them that he kept his part faithfully, and asks them now to obey him. Scholars debate the exact moment when Jeremiah delivered this message, so it is not wise to state it with certainty.

Today we can remember that obedience to God springs from gratitude for what he has already done for us. We can ask him today to help us obey him in something specific.
exp.4:12:
Here it says that the prophets will become wind, meaning nothing but empty words, with no message from God. The explanation of the old wording: "Rather" is what the word "But" means here. And the phrase about it being done to them sounds like a wish that what they announce would happen to them.

These are probably words from the rebellious people, who mocked Jeremiah's warnings. They said that God would do nothing and that no harm would come. Some believe the statement is a kind of irony from God that turns back against them. Then God answers: his word in Jeremiah's mouth will be like fire, and the judgment would indeed come.

Today, when a truth from God makes us uncomfortable, it is tempting to call it exaggeration. It is better to listen with humility, compare it with the Bible, and let God correct our course in time.
exp.33:12:
God begins to speak and reminds them of something important: he made a covenant with their ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt, the house of slavery, that is, the place where they were enslaved. "The Lord" is God's name, and a covenant is a solemn, binding promise.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah to the people of Judah. They had freed their Hebrew slaves, but later changed their minds and enslaved them again. God reminds them that their freedom came from him, and that the law about releasing servants was part of the covenant. When the text says "brought them forth," it shows that the deliverance was a gift from God.

For today: if God has forgiven us and set us free, we should treat others with justice and compassion. Keeping what we have promised, even when it costs us, shows that we truly remember his goodness.
exp.50:38:
He says that God will prepare a feast for the Babylonians when they are at their most heated, that is, in the middle of their celebration and confidence. He will make them drunk, and they will rejoice, but they will end in a "perpetual sleep": death, without waking up. "I will make their feasts" refers to God's own action in arranging this.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment against Babylon, the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed its people. The images of lions, jackals and ruins show that its power will come to an end. Many think the feast is a figure of judgment, though history also records a feast on the night Babylon fell (Daniel 5). Scholars do not agree on whether this text refers to that exact event.

For today: do not trust in success, pleasure or power as though they were eternal. Live with humility, do justice, and rest in God, who governs every nation and cares for his own.
exp.7:7:
God asks how the people can say they are wise and that they have the law of the Lord. He says the pen of the scribes was used in vain, that is, without benefit. "In vain" means uselessly. There are two ways to understand this: either the scribes copied or interpreted the law falsely, or, although they wrote it, the people did not obey it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. Earlier he compared the people to the birds, which know their seasons, while they did not recognize God's judgment. They boasted of having the law, but they followed greed and deceit, and rejected his word.

Having a Bible, knowing verses, or going to church is not enough. Ask yourself today: which command of God have I read and still not obeyed? Ask him for humility to repent and put it into practice.
exp.12:0:
God tells the prophet Jeremiah to buy a linen belt, that is, a sash of fine cloth, and to put it around his waist. The waist, or the lower part of the back, is the place where the belt goes. He is also told not to wet it, that is, not to wash it or put it in water.

The one speaking is God, and Jeremiah is his messenger. God often teaches through symbolic actions, so that the people can see a message and not only hear it. Here a lesson begins about Judah and its relationship with God. The full meaning is explained in the verses that follow, so it is good to read them calmly. Some scholars debate details of how this action was carried out, but the central message is clear.

For today: obey God even when you do not yet understand the reason. Often he explains his purposes later, while you take the first step of trust.
exp.10:0:
This verse is the introduction to a new message. It says that God spoke to Jeremiah.

The one speaking is Jehovah, the God of Israel, and Jeremiah is the prophet who receives the message. From the verses that follow, we see that God asks him to remind the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem of the covenant they had with Him. Scholars disagree about the exact moment this message refers to, so it is not wise to claim a specific date. What is clear is that God speaks to call His people to obedience.

For today: before looking for what to do, let us learn to listen. Take a few minutes to read the Bible with an open heart, asking yourself: "Lord, what do you want to say to me, and how can I obey you today?"
exp.48:32:
It says that Hazor will become an abandoned place, where only jackals will live, animals that look like wild dogs. The phrase "a desolation for ever" means it will be left empty, without people. The old phrase "son of man" is an older way of saying "no man."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This message is against Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor, desert tribes who lived in confidence, without walls or gates, believing themselves safe. Hazor here is not the city in Canaan, but refers to those Arab settlements; scholars are not certain of their exact location. Babylon would be the instrument of judgment.

For today: the security that comes from our riches or our own strength is fragile. Let us place our trust in God, not in what we have, because only He truly sustains our life.
exp.22:27:
This verse says that a prophet who has only a dream should tell it as a dream, and the one who has received the word of God should announce it faithfully. The chaff is the dry husk that is left over; the wheat is the grain that gives food. God asks: what does the useless have to do with what gives life? They are very different things.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. At that time, several prophets said that God spoke to them in dreams, but they announced falsehoods that comforted the people. In this way they led the people away from God, as had happened earlier with Baal. God does not condemn every dream, but condemns speaking in his name without having his word.

Today we can examine what we hear or teach. Compare every opinion, feeling, or experience with the Bible. Whatever does not agree with it, do not present as the word of God.
exp.51:1:
This verse says that Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, did what was evil in the sight of God, just as Jehoiakim had done. The phrase "in the eyes of the Lord" means that God saw and judged his conduct. Jehoiakim was another king of Judah, known for his disobedience and for rejecting God's word.

This passage closes the book of Jeremiah with a historical summary. The writer, probably someone close to the prophet, explains why Jerusalem fell: it was no accident, but the result of years of rebellion. Zedekiah also rebelled against Babylon, and that brought on the siege of the city.

For today: our decisions carry weight, and copying the bad examples we see does not excuse us. It is worth asking ourselves whom we are imitating and seeking God sincerely before the consequences arrive.
exp.14:5:
Here God speaks to Jerusalem and Judah. He says: "You abandoned me and turned your back on me." Because of this, he announces that he will stretch out his hand against them and destroy them. The phrase "I am weary with repenting" means that God had already held back many times, giving more chances, but he will no longer do so.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before Judah fell to Babylon. The people had practiced idolatry and injustice for a long time, and the text mentions the sin of King Manasseh. God does not act suddenly: he had warned and waited, but the people did not return to him.

For today: God's patience is real, but it is not an excuse to put off change. If today you feel that you have drifted away from him, do not wait any longer. Come back, and trust that his mercy will receive you.
exp.6:16:
God asks Jeremiah a question: "Do you not see what they are doing?" He does not ask because He does not know, but so that the prophet will understand why the judgment is just. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem, and "streets" shows that the sin was public, not hidden.

God speaks to Jeremiah in the well-known message at the temple. He has just told him not to pray for the people, because they kept worshiping the "queen of heaven" and other gods. The verses that follow show that the whole family took part. God grieves, and He also warns that the greatest harm will fall on themselves.

For today: Ask God to open your eyes to see honestly what things occupy the place that only He should have in your life and in your home, and be steadfast in returning to Him.
exp.22:3:
God promises to give his people good shepherds, who will care for them and feed them. Thanks to them, the sheep will no longer live in fear, nor be frightened, nor will any of them be lost.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The leaders of Judah had scattered and neglected the people, and God is going to judge them. Afterward he promises to gather the survivors and bring them back to their land. The next verse points to a just King, a descendant of David, whom many Christians understand as a sign pointing to Jesus.

For today: God cares for those who are looked after and for those who look after others. If you have some responsibility over others, in your family, your church, or your work, serve them with tenderness and justice. And if you feel lost, trust that the Good Shepherd is searching for you.
exp.47:28:
We have heard of Moab's great pride. The verse piles up several similar words to stress the point: arrogance, swelling (being puffed up with oneself), pride, haughtiness, and the conceit of the heart. Everything points to an attitude of thinking oneself superior to others and not needing God.

It is part of Jeremiah's prophecy against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Here the prophet speaks, or God speaks through him, and announces judgment. Moab had mocked Israel and felt secure, but God sees its heart. The verses that follow show that God, even so, grieves over Moab and does not rejoice coldly.

For today: pride often grows when we feel secure or better than others. Today you can ask God to show you where haughtiness lives in your heart, and practice humility by listening more and recognizing that everything you have is a gift from him.
exp.41:21:
God, through Jeremiah, tells them with complete clarity that they will die by the sword, by the famine and by the plague. And it will happen in Egypt, the very place where they wanted to go to live as foreigners. The phrase "live as foreigners" here means to settle there as outsiders, and "plague" is a contagious sickness that kills many people.

Jeremiah speaks to the people who remained in Judah after the fall of Jerusalem. They had asked him to pray and promised to obey whatever God said. But they already had in mind to flee to Egypt, and when God told them to stay, they did not want to listen. That is why Jeremiah reminds them that they had promised something they did not intend to keep.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly seek the voice of God or only want Him to bless what we have already decided. Obeying is safer than running toward what only seems like a way out.
exp.13:1:
It says that all of Judah is in mourning because of the drought. And from Jerusalem rises a cry, a plea for help.

God speaks to Jeremiah because of a great drought. The verses that follow show nobles, servants, and farmers ashamed because there is no water and no harvest. Jeremiah presents this crisis as a painful situation, and in the context of the book many connect it with the people's turning away from God, though here the emphasis is on the suffering.

When crises come, we should not hide our pain. We can present it honestly to God, cry out to Him, and examine our hearts so that we return to Him with humility.
exp.49:8:
It says that God himself will raise up and bring against Babylon a company of mighty nations from the north (the north is the direction meant here). They will get ready for the attack, and Babylon will be conquered. Their arrows are like those of a skilled warrior who never comes back empty-handed; that is, they will not miss.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed Israel, and here God announces that this empire will also be held accountable. The verses before this one show a scattered people, and the verses that follow explain that Babylon falls because it rejoiced in destroying God's inheritance. Historians see the Medes and Persians in this, although the text gives no names.

For today: you can rest in the fact that God sees injustice and does not leave it unanswered forever. This invites you to trust him rather than take revenge, and to live with humility, remembering that no one stands above his judgment.
exp.47:18:
The explanation says that the people of Aroer should stand by the road and watch closely. There they will see those who flee and those who have escaped pass by. They should ask them: "What is done?" The words "á" and "acontecido" are just old spellings of "a" and "sucedido", so the sentence above should be rewritten for the verse's own words: the question "What is done?" is the wording the verse itself uses. Aroer was a city of Moab, beside the river Arnon.

It is a prophecy of Jeremiah, announcing God's judgment on Moab. The prophet describes the fall of Dibon and other cities. Aroer lies on the border, so it would be among the first to see the refugees arrive. The verses before it speak of pride and strength broken. Its neighbors were to mourn.

For today: let us not wait until the crisis reaches us. We can learn from what others have lived through, listen to their warnings, and correct our course in time, with humility before God.
exp.31:39:
It says God will make an everlasting covenant with his people, meaning a promise that never comes to an end. "I will not turn away" means he will not back out of it or stop doing them good. Furthermore, God will put a reverent and loving awe of himself in their hearts, so that they will not depart from him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Judah were about to be taken captive to Babylon because of their disobedience. Even so, God promises restoration. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of the new covenant, though this passage speaks first to Israel.

For today: if you feel weak or afraid of drifting away from God, remember that he does not only ask for faithfulness but also works in your heart. Pray each day, "Lord, keep my heart close to you," and trust that he sustains what he has begun.
exp.0:10:
God speaks to Jeremiah and asks him a simple question: "What do you see?" Jeremiah answers that he sees a rod of an almond tree, that is, a branch from that tree. The old wording in the text is a matter of spelling and grammar, not a difference in meaning.

The Lord speaks with Jeremiah, who had just been called as a prophet. God had just placed his words in Jeremiah's mouth. Then he goes on to say that he is quick to carry out his word. Many explain that in Hebrew the word for almond sounds something like the word for watching or staying awake, but that connection is an interpretation, not something the text states outright.

Today we can learn to look closely at ordinary things, asking God to teach us something through them. We can also trust that God keeps what he says, even when it takes time to be seen.
exp.42:3:
This verse says that Johanan, the army commanders, and all the people did not listen to the voice of the Lord. God had told them to stay in Judah, but they did not obey.

After Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and killed Gedaliah, the governor, the people were afraid of the Chaldeans. They asked Jeremiah to pray for them and promised to obey God. When God answered that they should stay in the land, the leaders said that Jeremiah was lying. Even so, they went to Egypt and took Jeremiah and Baruch with them.

Obeying God only when his answer pleases us is not true obedience. Before we ask him for direction, let us ask ourselves whether we are really willing to follow it, even when it frightens us.
exp.9:1:
God tells his people not to copy the religious customs of the nations around them. They also must not be frightened by the "signs of heaven," such as eclipses, comets, or the movements of the stars, even though the other peoples are afraid of them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Israel. Many in that time saw the stars as signs that directed their destiny, and this was mixed up with idolatry. The verses that follow show how absurd it is to worship idols made of wood, decorated and nailed down so they will not fall over.

For today: do not let fear of the future, horoscopes, trends, or the pressure of other people guide you. Trust in God, who is greater than any sign or circumstance, and ask him for wisdom before you follow what everyone else is doing.
exp.12:21:
God tells Judah that when they ask in amazement, "Why is this happening to me?", the answer is their great wickedness. The verse speaks of the edges of their clothing and the heels being exposed, a picture of shame and public humiliation, as happened to captives.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people have rejected his warnings, and an invasion is coming from the north. Some understand this to refer to Babylon. God wants Judah to understand that their suffering is not chance, but the consequence of their persistent sin.

For today: when trials come, it is good to humbly ask whether there is something we should acknowledge before God. Not every difficulty is punishment, but honesty opens the door to forgiveness and change.
exp.38:12:
This verse says that Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, sent for other important officers: Nebushasban, Nergal-sharezer, Rabsaris, Rabmag, and the rest of the king's princes. "Captain of the guard" was a high-ranking military leader. The names Rabsaris and Rabmag seem to be official titles, though it is not known with certainty what exact functions they held.

The one telling the story is the writer of the book, who recounts what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar had given a special order: to take care of Jeremiah and not harm him. These officers gather to carry it out, and they bring the prophet out of the courtyard of the prison to hand him over to Gedaliah.

For today: God can care for His own even in the midst of chaos and by using unexpected people. If you are going through a hard situation today, trust that God is still at work, even when you cannot see how.
exp.24:22:
This verse follows a list of peoples who must drink the cup of God's wrath. It mentions Dedan, Tema, and Buz, places and tribes of Arabia. The phrase about those who live at the farthest corners refers to people who live in the most remote regions. In some versions this line is translated as "those who cut the hair at their temples," as a custom belonging to those peoples, although scholars do not always agree on how to understand that expression.

The prophet Jeremiah, sent by God, speaks while Babylon was growing in power. God announces that his judgment will reach Judah and also many neighboring nations, great and small, near and far. No one stands outside his sight.

For today: God is just with everyone, and no one lives hidden from him. Instead of judging others with pride, we can examine our own hearts, live with humility, and seek his mercy in Christ.
exp.48:6:
This verse is a message from God against Edom. God asks, in a tone of rebuke, whether wisdom is no longer found in Teman, an important city of Edom. He asks whether their wise people no longer know how to give counsel and whether their understanding has been ruined.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Edom, a descendant of Esau, was known for its reputation for wisdom, and Teman was a symbol of that. God announces judgment and shows that not even human wisdom will be able to save them. The atmosphere is one of warning, because a disaster is coming.

For today: intelligence, experience, and good advice are valuable, but they do not replace God. Before relying only on your own plans, ask God humbly for direction.
exp.45:14:
This verse asks why the strong one of Egypt, that is, its mighty warrior, was swept away, and it answers that he could not stand because the Lord thrust him down. Some understand "your strong one" as a valiant warrior; others understand it as the bull Apis, an Egyptian god. The Hebrew text allows both readings, so we cannot be certain.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, will come to attack Egypt. Egypt trusted in its army and in its gods, but the message is that its defeat will not be only a military event; God himself allows it and directs it.

For today: human strength, whether money, position, or ability, is not a secure foundation. Today you can ask yourself what you are trusting in most and hand it over to God in prayer, asking him to be your true support.
exp.43:28:
God says he will give a sign to the Jews who went to Egypt. The sign is that he will "visit" them, that is, step in to punish them. In this way they will know that his words of judgment really come true. "For evil" means "for punishment." "Visit" here is not a friendly visit, but an intervention by God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. A group of Jews fled to Egypt in disobedience to God, and there they practiced idolatry, worshiping "the queen of heaven." God warns them that their punishment will be certain. The sign that follows is the downfall of the pharaoh Hophra, which is mentioned in the next verse. Scholars agree that it is a future sign, but they do not all date it the same way.

For today: God's words do not depend on what we think or wish. Today we can listen to him with humility and obey him, without waiting for the consequences to teach us the way.
exp.18:12:
God says that the houses of Jerusalem and the palaces of the kings of Judah will be made unclean, just like Topheth. This will happen because of the houses where, on their rooftops, the people burned incense to the stars, called "the host of heaven," and poured out drink offerings of wine to false gods.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Earlier, Jeremiah broke a clay jar in front of the people as a sign that God would shatter the city. Topheth was a place where idolatry was practiced, and God uses it as an image of judgment. The people had hardened their hearts and did not want to listen.

For today: examine what, or who, you give first place in your home and in your heart. God invites us to return to Him with humility, before habit hardens us.
exp.26:20:
This verse repeats that what follows is the word of God, not the opinion of the prophet. It speaks of the vessels that still remained in the temple, in the palace of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem. "Vessels" here means objects and containers of value, used in worship. The phrase "Thus saith" is like saying: "This is what God says."

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of God. Jeconiah and many nobles had already been carried off to Babylon, along with some objects from the temple. False prophets were claiming that everything would soon be returned. Jeremiah contradicts them: what remains will also be taken away, and God will bring it back in his own time.

For today: when someone promises quick and easy solutions, it is wise to ask what God really says. His word sometimes corrects us, but it also offers hope. We can trust that He keeps His times and does not forget us in our trials.
exp.25:19:
This verse introduces another prophet, named Urijah, the son of Shemaiah, from the town of Kirjath-jearim. He prophesied in the name of the Lord, that is, he spoke on God's behalf. He announced the same message of judgment that Jeremiah had spoken against Jerusalem and the land of Judah. The phrase "according to all the words of Jeremiah" means that his message matched what Jeremiah said.

Here some of the elders and common people speak up to defend Jeremiah, who was in danger of death because of his message. Earlier they had recalled Micah, whom no one put to death. Now they mention Urijah, but his case ended badly: according to the verses that follow, King Jehoiakim pursued him, he fled to Egypt, and they caught up with him. He is cited as an example of what could happen.

For today: telling the truth can be costly, and even so God calls us to be faithful. Let us ask him for courage, but also for wisdom and humility to speak with love.
exp.31:32:
He says the people turned their backs on God and not their faces toward him. Turning the neck away means refusing him, in the sense of turning your back on him. "Rising early and teaching" means that God instructed them again and again, with diligence and from early on. Even so, they would not listen or accept correction.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem is about to fall to Babylon, and God explains the reason: it was not for lack of warning, but because kings, priests, prophets and people rejected his word for a long time. Then he mentions their idolatrous practices, even in the temple.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we face God when he corrects us. Sometimes his voice comes through the Bible, a wise counsel or a restless conscience. A good practice is to respond with humility: to listen, acknowledge the mistake and change course without delay.
exp.14:19:
God promises Jeremiah that he will make him like a wall of bronze, strong and impossible to knock down, standing against the people. They will fight against him, but they will not be able to defeat him, because God will be with him to keep and defend him.

The Lord speaks to Jeremiah, who felt hurt and worn out by the rejection of his people. He had come to doubt God, calling Him unstable waters. God asks him to return to Him and speak the truth, without giving in to the pressure of the people. Then He gives him this promise of firmness.

For today: when you do what is right and others criticize you, do not depend on your own strength. Come to God honestly, even with your doubts, and trust that His presence sustains you. Being firm does not mean there will be no opposition, but that you will not be alone.
exp.25:12:
Jeremiah asks the people to change the way they live and act, and to obey God. If they do, the Lord "will repent" of the punishment he announced. This does not mean that God made a mistake, but that he changes his decision to judge when people turn back to him. "Hear" here means "listen and obey."

Jeremiah speaks before the princes and the people. The priests and prophets were accusing him of deserving death for announcing judgment against Jerusalem and the temple. He does not defend himself out of fear, but repeats that God sent him and offers a way out: return to God.

Today, when a word of God makes us uncomfortable, we can get angry or we can correct our course. Let us think of one habit or decision that does not please God, and take a concrete step of change today, trusting in his mercy.
exp.37:11:
Here Ebed-melech, a man from Ethiopia who served in the king's house, gives Jeremiah an instruction. He asks him to put the old, torn rags under his armpits, and under the ropes. This way the cords would not hurt his skin as he was pulled up. Jeremiah obeys.

It is Ebed-melech who speaks, the one who intervened to save the prophet, who was in a cistern or pit full of mud and close to dying. The king had given him permission to bring Jeremiah out. The text does not say why he was the only one who acted, but his courage and compassion are evident.

Today we can learn that love is also shown in small details. Ebed-melech not only rescued Jeremiah, but also took care that he would not suffer further harm. Ask yourself who you can help, and how to do it with tenderness and attention.
exp.37:17:
This verse says the opposite of the earlier promise. If King Zedekiah does not surrender to the princes of the king of Babylon, Jerusalem will be handed over into the hand of the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), they will burn it with fire, and the king himself will not escape from their hand. The word "go forth" in the verse means to go out to them and give yourself up.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in God's name to Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. Jerusalem was under siege. Jeremiah had already been imprisoned for saying that surrender was the way to save lives. The king consults him in secret, but he is afraid of what others will think.

For today: God shows us clearly the consequences of our decisions. Obeying him may be frightening and may cost us pride, but the fear of people should never weigh more than his word.
exp.37:10:
What it says: Ebed-melech gathered the men the king had given him and went to the palace, to a room under the treasury. There he took old, worn-out clothes and torn rags. Then he lowered them with ropes to Jeremiah, who was in the dungeon, a deep cistern full of mud.

Context: The narrator tells how Ebed-melech, a foreign official in the court, rescues Jeremiah. The leaders had thrown him there for announcing God's message, and the prophet could have died of hunger. Ebed-melech spoke with the king, obtained permission, and acted quickly.

For today: Ebed-melech did not only speak, he also did something concrete and careful. The rags were there so the ropes would not hurt Jeremiah. We can help others with simple actions, thinking of their pain and without waiting for someone else to go first.
exp.49:31:
The verse says the proud one, that is Babylon, will stumble and fall with no one to help him up. God promises to kindle a fire in his cities that will consume everything around them. The word "proud" here refers to someone who thinks himself above everyone else.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Babylon. This empire had oppressed Israel and Judah and refused to release the captives. God presents himself as the strong Redeemer who will defend the cause of his people. The fire can be understood as an image of judgment, and scholars debate how it was fulfilled in history.

For today: pride prepares us for a fall, but God cares for those who suffer injustice. Today you can ask him to free you from pride and trust that he defends the oppressed.
exp.31:43:
In the future, it says, people will once again buy fields with money. They will draw up a deed of purchase, seal it, and call in witnesses. This will happen in the land of Benjamin, around Jerusalem, in the towns of Judah, in the hill country, in the lowland plains, and in the south (the south is the Negev). Bringing back the captives means returning the exiles to their land.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon (the Chaldeans) is besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah is in prison. Even so, God commanded him to buy a field as a sign. It seemed like a pointless purchase, since the country was about to be conquered. But God promised that, after the punishment, he would restore his people.

For today: when everything seems lost, you can take small steps of faith based on God's promises. He is faithful and can restore hope where today you see only ruin. Trust and act with patience.
exp.25:16:
Some of the elders of the land stood up and spoke to the whole assembly of the people. "Assembly" here means a gathering, and "elders of the land" refers to older men who held authority and respect in the community.

Jeremiah had just preached in the temple that Jerusalem would be destroyed if the people did not repent. The priests and prophets demanded his death, but the princes and the people said he did not deserve to die. Then the elders step in and recall the case of Micah, who in the days of King Hezekiah said something similar and was not put to death. In this way they support Jeremiah with an example from history.

Today, when someone speaks an uncomfortable truth, it is good to listen with humility and not react with anger. And when we see injustice, we can raise our voices with wisdom, as these elders did.
exp.29:21:
This verse is a promise of relationship: God says that his people will truly be his, and that he will be their God. The phrase "ye shall be my people" means that they will be his people. It is a covenant phrase, like a promise of belonging to one another.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Israel were under judgment and in captivity because of their disobedience. Even so, in this chapter God promises to restore them, to punish their oppressors, and to raise up a ruler from among them. Some believers see here a sign of the Messiah; others read it mainly as a promise for Israel in its history. The verses that follow remind us that God also judges wickedness.

For today: God does not only want to forgive; he wants a close relationship. If you feel far away, draw near to him with a humble heart, and remember that his desire is to be your God and for you to live as his.
exp.15:18:
He says that Jeremiah turns to God and calls him his strength, his power, and his refuge when distress comes. He also announces that people from distant nations, "the ends of the earth," will come to God. They will acknowledge that what they inherited from their fathers, their idols, was a lie, something empty and without profit. The word "vanity" means something that has no worth or substance.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks in the middle of a harsh message of judgment against Judah for its idolatry. God has just said that he sees everything and will punish their sin. But here, in the midst of judgment, Jeremiah expresses trust in God and hope that other nations will also come to know him.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, run to God before things that promise security, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Ask him to be your refuge, and examine where you are placing your trust.
exp.49:34:
God says he will send a sword against all of Babylon. The word for "sword" in the original refers to war, and the verse names the Chaldeans as the people who ruled there. The judgment reaches the common people, the princes (the rulers) and the wise men (the advisers and experts). No one is left out.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had oppressed Israel and Judah and refused to release the captives. God presents himself as their Redeemer, the Strong One, who defends the cause of his people. These words announce the fall of Babylon, and the Bible presents that judgment as the justice of God.

For today: God sees injustice and does not forget it. If you are suffering or have been mistreated, you can entrust your cause to him and refrain from seeking revenge. And if you have power or knowledge, use it with humility and justice, because neither prestige nor human wisdom protects us before God.
exp.9:18:
Here someone cries out in pain: "Woe is me! I am wounded, and my sore hurts terribly." Then the speaker says they thought: "This is my sickness, and I must bear it." The words translated as "hurt" and "wound" in that reading are not explained here.

The speaker seems to be the people of Judah, or the prophet speaking on their behalf, facing the invasion and exile that God had announced. Interpreters understand this in different ways, but the next verse describes a ruined tent and lost children, so the pain is real. The cause is mentioned afterward: the shepherds, or rulers, did not seek the Lord.

For today: when pain comes, do not minimize it or bear it in silence. Be honest with God about your wound, and humbly examine whether there is something you should correct, without ceasing to trust in his mercy.
exp.34:14:
God says that he sent all his prophets to his people, again and again and with urgency. His message was: leave your evil way, correct your actions, and do not follow other gods. If they obeyed, they would keep living in the land God had given them. But they did not incline their ear, that is, they did not want to listen.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah to Judah and Jerusalem. God uses the example of the Rechabites, who faithfully obeyed their ancestor Jonadab in not drinking wine. If they honored the word of a human father, how is it that the people did not obey the God who had cared for them and spoke to them with such patience?

Today, God still speaks with patience, above all through his Word. A practical application: set aside a moment each day to read it and ask yourself what concrete change it calls for. Then obey without putting it off.
exp.32:14:
God says he will raise up from David's family a "Branch of righteousness." A branch is a new shoot, a sprout that comes up from a trunk that seemed dead. This descendant of David will rule with judgment, that is, with uprightness, and with righteousness throughout the land. The phrase "will cause to grow" shows that it is God who does this, not people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people were living through a very hard time, with Jerusalem threatened or destroyed and exile near. God promises to restore the land and to fulfill his good word. Christians see in this Branch Jesus, a descendant of David. Jews have understood it in other ways, as an ideal future king.

For today: when everything seems dry or without a way out, trust that God knows how to bring forth life and justice. Wait on him, and seek to live with uprightness and righteousness in your home and at your work.
exp.0:11:
God says to Jeremiah that he has seen well. The phrase "I will hasten my word" means that God watches over his word, stays alert to it, and hurries to see that what he has said comes to pass. "To perform it" means to carry it out, to make it come true.

God has just called Jeremiah as a prophet and shows him a rod of an almond tree. In Hebrew, the word for "almond tree" sounds like the word for "watching" or "being awake." The almond is one of the first trees to bloom at the end of winter. Through this, God assures a frightened young man that he is not speaking into empty air: what he has promised and warned will happen. Afterward comes the announcement of judgment that will come from the north.

We can trust that God does what he says. When one of his promises seems slow in coming, let us remember that he watches over his word, and in the meantime let us stay faithful with patience.
exp.45:8:
This verse describes the army of Egypt getting ready for war. The horses and chariots are called to advance with force, and the brave soldiers are called to come out. Cush is the region south of Egypt (often linked with Ethiopia), and Put and Lud are allied peoples who supplied soldiers. The phrase about those who handle the shield means they take up their shields, and the phrase about those who handle and bend the bow means they string their bows.

The one speaking is the prophet Jeremiah, passing on a message from God about Egypt. It refers to the battle of Carchemish, beside the river Euphrates, where Egypt faced Babylon. Egypt advances with pride, swelling like a flooding river, but the text that follows says that day belongs to the Lord, and that Egypt will be defeated. Some scholars debate details about the location of Lud.

For today: human strength, however great it may seem, does not decide the final outcome. Before you trust in your resources, plans, or strength, surrender them to God with humility and ask Him for wisdom.
exp.18:2:
God tells Jeremiah to speak to the kings of Judah and the people of Jerusalem. He announces that he is going to bring a disaster so terrible upon this place that everyone who hears of it will have their ears ring, that is, their ears will buzz or tingle from the shock of the news. Here "evil" means calamity, not wickedness.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in the valley of Hinnom, next to Jerusalem, with some elders as witnesses. God accuses the people of having abandoned him, of worshiping other gods, of shedding innocent blood, and of burning their children as offerings to Baal. For this reason he announces judgment.

For today: God takes injustice and idolatry seriously. Let us ask him to show us what things have taken his place in our hearts, and let us return to him before we harden ourselves.
exp.37:9:
This verse tells that King Zedekiah gives an order to Ebed-melech, a man from Ethiopia who worked in the palace. He orders him to take thirty men and bring the prophet Jeremiah up out of the dungeon, which was a cistern or deep pit, before he dies.

King Zedekiah is speaking in the middle of the siege of Jerusalem. Jeremiah had been thrown into the pit by his enemies for announcing messages from God that they did not like. Ebed-melech dared to speak up for him before the king. There is debate about why the king changed his mind so quickly; the text only shows that he gave in.

For today: when you see an injustice, do not stay silent. Ebed-melech, with no power or fame, spoke with courage and helped. Ask God whom you can defend or help this week.
exp.48:20:
The fall of Edom will be so severe that the earth will tremble, and the cry of its suffering will be heard as far as the Red Sea. It is a poetic way of saying that no one will fail to hear of what has happened.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Edom, a neighbor of Israel, appears here under the judgment of the LORD, who is compared to a lion advancing with power. The cities of Teman and Bozrah, both Edomite, are mentioned. The text does not detail all the reasons here, but other prophets speak of Edom's pride and its violence against Israel.

Today, this verse reminds us that God is just and that no human pride is strong enough to stand before Him. We can examine our hearts, lay down arrogance, and trust in God's justice instead of seeking revenge.
exp.1:8:
God says he will yet bring his case against his people. "I will enter into judgment" and "plead" are the language of a courtroom: God acts like someone formally making an accusation. He speaks not only to the people of that time but also to "your children's children," that is, to future generations. The word "yet" shows that God had already spoken to them before.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just recalled that he brought them into a fertile land, but they defiled it. Priests, teachers of the law, shepherds (leaders), and prophets stopped seeking him and followed Baal. This complaint is not from a God who wants to destroy, but from one wounded because his people exchanged what is good for what does not profit them.

For today: God speaks to us with patience before he corrects us. Honestly ask yourself whether anything has taken God's place in your life, and return to him today, before that habit passes on to your children.
exp.22:1:
What it says: God speaks to the "shepherds," that is, the leaders of the people. He tells them that they scattered and frightened the sheep, that is, they drove them apart and terrified them. Nor did they look after them, which here means caring for them and tending to them. That is why God says he will bring upon them the evil of their deeds, that is, he will call them to account for what they did.

Context: The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The leaders of Judah, above all its kings, had neglected and mistreated the people. The verses that follow show that God himself will gather his scattered sheep and give them good shepherds.

For today: If you have some responsibility over others, whether in the family, the church, or at work, care for them with tenderness and attention. Ask yourself: whom do I need to visit, listen to, or encourage this week?
exp.40:14:
This verse tells how Ishmael, the man who had murdered Gedaliah and led many captives away from Mizpah, managed to escape from Johanan. He got away with only eight men (according to the account, he had first come with ten, and two had died), and he took refuge with the Ammonites, a neighboring people.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah is speaking. After the murder of Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, the people were left in great fear. Johanan rescued the captives, but Ishmael escaped without paying for his crime. This left the people frightened and close to fleeing to Egypt.

For today: injustice sometimes seems to go unanswered, and that frightens us. Even so, fear should not lead us to decide on our own. Before acting, it is wise to stop and seek God's guidance.
exp.41:10:
God tells the people not to be afraid of the king of Babylon. "Be not afraid of him" means "do not be afraid of him." God promises, "for I am with you," that is, "I am with you," to save them and deliver them from the king's power, here called "his hand."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. After the fall of Jerusalem, a group of survivors feared Babylon's revenge and planned to flee to Egypt. They asked Jeremiah to consult God. The answer was to stay in the land, with the promise of protection and that God would build them up again.

For today: when fear pushes us to look for ways out on our own, we can stop and ask what God is asking of us. Obedience can be frightening, but his promise to be with us is firmer than any threat.
exp.0:16:
God tells Jeremiah to get ready and to get moving. "Gird up your loins" is an old expression: in those days people tucked up their robe with a belt so they could work or walk without getting in the way. God orders him to speak everything God commands him, without fear. The last sentence warns that if Jeremiah shrinks back before the people, God would allow him to be broken down in front of them.

The Lord speaks to the young Jeremiah as he calls him to be a prophet. Judah had turned away from God to worship idols, and Jeremiah was to announce the judgment that would come from the north. God promises that he will be with him, even though they will attack him.

For today: when God asks you to say or do something right, prepare yourself with prayer and determination, and do not let fear of what others think hold you back. Trust that his presence sustains you.
exp.31:3:
It says that King Zedekiah will not escape from the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians. He will be handed over to the king of Babylon, and the two will speak face to face, "mouth to mouth," and look at each other "eye to eye." It is a way of saying that Zedekiah will be captured and brought before him to be judged.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf. Babylon had Jerusalem surrounded, and King Zedekiah had shut the prophet up in the courtyard of the prison because he did not like his message. Jeremiah kept saying what God commanded him, even though he was punished for it.

Today we can learn that God's truth does not change because it makes us uncomfortable. It is better to listen to it humbly in time than to reject it and suffer the consequences later.
exp.4:25:
It says that among God's people wicked people were found. These people "lay wait," that is, they watched in secret, like the hunter who sets snares and traps to catch birds. But here the prey is not animals but men. These are people who plan and set traps against others.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Judah of not fearing Him, even though He gives them the rain and the harvest. The following verses explain the traps: deceit, unjust riches, and neglect of orphans and the poor. God does not overlook injustice within His own people.

For today: examine whether, in your work, your business, or your relationships, you take advantage of others through deceit or half-truths. Ask God for a heart that respects Him and cares for the weakest.
exp.21:18:
He says that King Jehoiakim will not have a dignified burial. He will be treated like a dead animal: they will drag him out and throw him outside the gates of Jerusalem, without honor. The phrase about being buried like a donkey means his body would be left without any ceremony, the way a donkey's would be. The word for wrongdoing refers to injustice or harm done to others.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, ruled with greed, violence, and oppression, very unlike his father. God announces that no one will mourn him. Scholars agree that this is a severe judgment; the Bible does not clearly describe how it was fulfilled, and some understand it as an expression of the dishonor that awaited him.

For today: power and wealth do not cover up injustice. Examine whether your decisions, at work or at home, treat others with justice and respect, and ask God for a humble heart that listens to his voice.
exp.4:11:
It says that the people denied the Lord. "They denied" here means that they rejected him or did not take him seriously. They said: "It is not he," meaning that God does not exist or does nothing. They thought no harm would come, neither war (the "sword," as the verse puts it) nor famine.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He accuses Israel and Judah of rebelling against him. The people felt secure and believed God would not judge them. So God says that his words in the prophet's mouth will be like fire, and the people like wood. Scholars understand that the verse points to the coming invasion of Babylon, though the text gives no further details here.

Today it is easy to live as if God does not see or does not matter, especially when everything is going well. We can ask ourselves honestly: do I listen to his word, or do I ignore it because it makes me uncomfortable? Let us return to him with humility before life forces us to.
exp.0:0:
It says this book begins with the words of Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah. He came from a family of priests who lived in Anathoth, a town in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, near Jerusalem. The name "Anathoth" in the verse is the older spelling of Anatot.

The book introduces its author and says where he came from. The verses that follow explain that God spoke to him during the reigns of Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah, up until the fall of Jerusalem. That is, Jeremiah served for about forty years in very difficult times. It is not known with certainty whether this Hilkiah is the high priest who found the book of the law in Josiah's time; many doubt it, and the Bible does not confirm it.

God does not call perfect people, but people with a concrete history, with family and with a place. He can use your origin, your work, and your surroundings to speak. Today, ask him how he wants to use what you already are and where you are.
exp.39:8:
Gedaliah swears an oath to the military leaders and their men. He tells them not to be afraid to submit to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). He asks them to stay and live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and he promises that it will go well with them. The quoted word "sware" in the verse above is an old form of "swore," meaning "made an oath," and the phrase "it shall be well with you" means "it will go well with you."

Jerusalem had already fallen, and many had been taken captive to Babylon. Babylon appointed Gedaliah as governor over the poor who were left behind. He speaks from Mizpah to calm the leaders who feared reprisals. His message agrees with what Jeremiah had taught: accept the situation and live in peace. However, the account goes on to a tragic ending, for Gedaliah was murdered.

When life changes in painful ways, God invites us not to act out of fear, but to live with diligence, peace, and trust in Him, day by day.
exp.35:29:
God announces judgment against King Jehoiakim. None of his descendants would hold the throne of David in a stable way, and his dead body would be left lying in the open, exposed to the sun by day and the frost by night, without a proper burial. "Descendants" here refers to his offspring.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jehoiakim had cut up and burned in the fire the scroll that contained God's warnings, as if destroying the message could cancel its fulfillment. His son Jehoiachin reigned only three months before being taken captive to Babylon. The biblical texts do not detail how Jehoiakim died, so we do not know exactly how this was fulfilled.

Today, ignoring, silencing, or rejecting what God says does not change the truth. When faced with an uncomfortable word of Scripture, we can choose the humility to listen and correct our course, rather than resisting it.
exp.16:10:
It says that whoever gathers riches unjustly is like a partridge that sits on eggs it did not lay. In the end, what he looked after does not belong to him. "Gathers" means collects or piles up. The end of life is the close of one's days, and a fool is someone who lacks sense. Those riches will leave him in the middle of his days, and at the end he will be seen as a fool. Scholars explain the image of the partridge in several ways.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. Shortly before, he reminded them that the heart deceives and that God examines everything. He gives to each person according to his deeds. For this reason he warns that gaining by injustice brings no security, and that only God is the true hope.

For today: before you earn money, ask yourself whether you are doing it with honesty. Work with integrity and entrust your security to God, not to what you have.
exp.38:10:
This verse says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had given an order to Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, concerning Jeremiah. The "commander of the guard" was a high official of the king. The order itself is given in the next verse.

The narrator of the book explains what happened when Jerusalem fell. While many were taken to Babylon, Jeremiah had announced for years that this would happen. Here we see that the Babylonian king gave instructions to protect him. The text does not explain why he did this; some think he had heard of Jeremiah's words about submitting to Babylon, but this is not stated here.

God can care for his faithful servants even in very difficult times, and even use people who do not know him. We can trust that he sustains us, even when everything around us seems to be falling apart.
exp.7:10:
They say the leaders treated the wound of the people as if it were something small. "Breach" is a serious break or wound, and "lightness" means treating it as trivial, not taking it seriously. They kept saying "peace, peace," but there was no peace.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, shortly before the fall of Judah. The prophets and priests, instead of calling for repentance, gave comforting messages while the people continued in greed and deceit. That is why God announces judgment, for they were not even ashamed.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we prefer words that soothe us or the truth that heals us. True peace begins when we acknowledge our sin, repent, and return to God, instead of covering the wound with pleasant phrases.
exp.33:1:
God commands Jeremiah to go to Zedekiah, king of Judah, and give him a clear message: Jerusalem is going to fall into the hands of the king of Babylon, and the city will be burned. "Burn" here means to destroy completely by fire. "Give into the hand" means to put under another's power.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of the LORD, the God of Israel. Babylon, with Nebuchadnezzar and his army, was already attacking Jerusalem and the cities of Judah that remained. God sends this word because the people and their kings had turned away from Him. Even so, the message goes on to include a personal word for Zedekiah: he would not die by the sword.

For today: God sometimes speaks hard truths, but He does so that we will listen and respond. If you feel corrected by something today, do not harden your heart; come near to God with humility.
exp.19:10:
He says that God stands with Jeremiah like a strong and fearsome warrior. Because of this, those who persecute him will stumble, that is, fall and fail, and they will not be able to overcome him. They will be deeply ashamed because their plans will not succeed. Their shame will be a lasting disgrace that no one will forget.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. He was tired of being mocked for proclaiming God's message. Even his friends hoped he would be proven wrong so they could take revenge. He wanted to stay silent, but the word of God burned inside him. Even so, in the midst of fear, he expresses his confidence that God defends him. How and when this would come about in his life, the text leaves in God's hands.

When you feel rejected for doing what is right, do not rely on your own strength. Ask God to sustain you, and trust that He is your defense.
exp.38:6:
This verse tells of the sad end of King Zedekiah. The Babylonians put out his eyes and bound him with fetters, which were metal chains for the feet, to take him away as a prisoner to Babylon. The last thing he saw before he was blinded was the death of his sons.

Here the narrator of the book of Jeremiah speaks, recounting the fall of Jerusalem. God had warned through Jeremiah that the city would fall if the king did not surrender to Babylon. Zedekiah would not listen and fled, but the Chaldeans caught up with him near Jericho. In this way what the prophet had said came to pass.

For today: ignoring the voice of God out of fear or stubbornness brings painful consequences. Today we can listen to his Word with humility and obey it in time, trusting that his guidance seeks our good.
exp.36:4:
The army of Pharaoh of Egypt had come out to help Judah. When the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), who had surrounded Jerusalem, heard the news, they withdrew from the city.

The one who narrates is the writer of the book of Jeremiah. King Zedekiah, who was weak and undecided, asked the prophet for prayer, but he did not want to obey his message. When the Chaldeans left, the people may have thought the danger had passed. However, God said through Jeremiah that Egypt would return to its own land and that Babylon would come back.

For today: do not confuse a passing relief with the true solution. When a crisis passes, do not stop seeking God or obeying Him. He wants us to trust in Him, not only in human help.
exp.1:1:
God orders Jeremiah to go and speak out loud to Jerusalem. The message is that God remembers her with affection. The words "youth" and "engagement" are the key ideas: youth is the time of early devotion, and engagement is the period of commitment before the wedding. God recalls when his people followed him in faith through the wilderness, a place without crops and without security.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. At the start of his ministry, God presents his relationship with Israel as a courtship. Before he rebukes her unfaithfulness, he recalls her first devotion. The verses that follow show that Israel was holy to God, and that those who harmed her would be judged.

Today, we can ask ourselves how our first love for God is doing. Even if we have grown cold, he remembers our beginnings with tenderness and invites us to return with confidence, without fear.
exp.9:17:
He says God himself will fling out the people who live in the land, as someone hurls a stone from a sling. To "fling out" means to throw them far away, that is, to pull them from their place. To "distress them" means to make them suffer. The phrase "that they may find it so" is hard: it may mean that they will feel the blow, or that, through their suffering, they will come to recognize what is happening.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment on Judah for its idolatry, and the verse that follows sounds like the people's lament before the destruction. Interpreters connect it with the exile to Babylon.

For today: when a hardship pulls us out of our comfort, we can ask God what he wants to show us. He can use pain to wake us up and draw us closer to himself, and he does not leave us alone.
exp.48:3:
Here God asks Ammon: "Why do you boast in your valleys?" The valleys were rich and fertile lands. The explanation says that this valley "came to ruin," meaning it had gone to waste. "Stubborn daughter" means a rebellious and obstinate daughter, a way of speaking about the nation of Ammon. She trusted in her riches and thought: "Who will come against me?"

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, with a message of judgment against the Ammonites, neighbors of Israel. Their capital was Rabbah. The verses before this one announce war and ruin upon her. Scholars debate which valleys are meant, but the idea is clear: Ammon felt secure because of what she had. Even so, the text ends with a promise of restoration.

Today we can ask ourselves what our security rests on. Money and achievements can fail. Let us trust in God first.
exp.8:9:
The prophet Jeremiah speaks, and in many passages he seems to express the grief of God as well. Judah was living in lies and betrayal, as the previous verse says. That is why God announces judgment: the land would be left in ruins. Even so, the message is not cold, but full of sorrow over what sin destroys.

For today: God does not rejoice in the damage that sin causes. We can ask Him to make us honest in our words, and to let us feel the pain that He feels, instead of being indifferent.
exp.4:7:
This verse compares the people of Judah to well-fed horses that, as soon as morning comes, are full of desire. Each man went after his neighbour's wife without any restraint, like a horse that whinnies and charges with no bridle to hold it back.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just said that the people abandoned him, swore by false gods, and fell into adultery. God had given them abundance, but they used it to sin. For this reason he asks whether he should not call them to account. Some understand the adultery literally and others also as spiritual unfaithfulness; the text allows both readings.

For today: what God gives us, such as health, work, or well-being, should lead us to thank him and to be faithful, not to live without control. Ask him to help you care for your marriage and to respect the marriages of others.
exp.28:0:
This verse introduces a letter that the prophet Jeremiah sent from Jerusalem to the exiles in Babylon. It was addressed to the elders who were still alive, to the priests, to the prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem. The word "carried away" means taken by force to another country.

Jeremiah speaks as a prophet of God. This happens after the first deportation, when King Jeconiah and many leaders and craftsmen were taken to Babylon, around 597 B.C. The people were wounded and confused, and the letter, carried by Elasah and Gemariah, would give them God's word for that situation.

God does not stay silent when we live through hard times or far from what we know. We can seek his word with confidence, because he has something to say to us also in the midst of trial.
exp.50:29:
The explanation says that Babylon's bravest soldiers no longer went out to fight. They stayed shut up in their strongholds, without strength, so frightened that they became like women, a phrase that speaks of fear and weakness in battle. Their houses were set on fire, and the bars of their gates were broken.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing what God has decided against Babylon. God calls the Medes and other nations to bring down that great city. The passage shows that no human power, however strong it may seem, can stop the Lord's plan. The exact historical details of the fall are understood in various ways.

Today we can remember that strength, money, or prestige are not a secure foundation. It is better to trust in God, who continues to rule above every human power.
exp.22:4:
