This verse promises that God will raise up, from the family of King David, a righteous Branch: a descendant like a new shoot growing out of a stump. He will be a King who prospers and who will rule with righteousness and justice throughout the land.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The kings of Judah had failed as bad shepherds, and the people were scattered in exile. God promises to gather his sheep and give them good shepherds. Christians see Jesus in this King; the original text speaks of a future descendant of David, and Jews understand it in other ways.

For today: when you see injustice or leaders who fail, do not lose hope. Trust that God keeps his promises, and try to treat others with justice in your own surroundings.
exp.25:2:
God tells Jeremiah to speak plainly to the people. He says "perhaps they will listen," that is, maybe they will hear. If each one leaves his evil way, God says that he will relent from the disaster he had planned to bring on them. This means he would change his decision to judge them. The word "turn" means to turn back or change direction.

God speaks, and gives Jeremiah the command at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah. Jeremiah is to go to the courtyard of the temple and say everything God commanded him, holding nothing back. The people had rejected the prophets again and again. Even so, God offers them one more chance before judging them. How to understand God's "relenting" is interpreted in several ways, but all of them show his willingness to forgive.

For today: if there is something in your life that you know does not please God, do not wait any longer. God still opens the door to anyone who wants to return to him.
exp.10:20:
This verse says that God speaks about the men of Anathoth, the town of Jeremiah. They wanted to kill him (they were seeking his life, that is, seeking to take his life), and they told him: "Do not prophesy in the name of the Lord, or you will die by our hand." In other words, they wanted to silence him with threats.

The Lord speaks, and he is answering Jeremiah after Jeremiah discovered the plot. The people of his own town, probably even people close to him, rejected God's message and wanted to silence the prophet. Jeremiah had placed his cause in God's hands, and here God answers him and announces that he will judge those who threatened him.

For today: if you are rejected for obeying God or speaking the truth, even within your own family or community, do not stay silent out of fear, and do not take revenge. Entrust your cause to God, as Jeremiah did, and trust that he sees and judges with justice.
exp.50:37:
They will roar together like lions, and they will yell like lions' cubs. The phrase "all at once" in the original is a way of saying "together, at the same time," and the word "roar" here means to shout loudly and fiercely. The image suggests a sound of strength and pride.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing what the Lord says against Babylon. God promises to defend his people, who had suffered at the hands of that empire. The verses that follow show that this roaring will not save them: they will be led away like lambs to the slaughter. Some understand this roaring as their arrogance, others as their despair at the fall; the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: do not let yourself be impressed by the noise and arrogance of the powerful. Their strength does not last forever. Trust that God sees injustice, and leave justice in his hands, while you keep acting with humility and uprightness.
exp.21:24:
God tells Jeconiah, king of Judah, that he will hand him over to those who want to kill him, the very people he is afraid of. They are Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and the Chaldeans. The phrase about those who seek his life means that they are trying to take his life. The phrase about those whose face he fears means that he is terrified of them.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Coniah, also called Jehoiachin, was a king who trusted in his power and his security. God warns him that even if he were as precious as a signet ring on his right hand, God would still tear him off. According to the context, he was taken captive to Babylon, and God judges him for the wickedness of his reign.

For today: do not place your security in your position, your money, or your reputation. All of that can disappear. Seek each day to humble yourself before God and to obey Him, because only in Him is true firmness found.
exp.42:8:
God tells Jeremiah to take large stones and hide them in the clay of a brick kiln, right at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, while the people of Judah watch. Tahpanhes is an Egyptian city. The instruction to hide the stones in the clay can be understood as burying them or setting them into the brick pavement.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. A group of Judeans had fled to Egypt out of fear of Babylon, disobeying God's word. With this action, God shows them that Egypt would not be a safe refuge either: Nebuchadnezzar, whom God calls "my servant," would come and set his throne over those very stones. Scholars debate the exact details of the place.

Today: running away from what God asks of us, looking for security somewhere else, does not protect us. It is better to obey and trust in Him, who is the true refuge.
exp.12:4:
He says Jeremiah obeyed God's command. He took the linen belt and hid it by the Euphrates, just as the Lord commanded him. Some of the wording is old: where the text says "I went," the older form is "fui," where it says "I hid it," the older form is "lo escondí," and "as the Lord commanded me" means "just as the Lord ordered me."

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, recounting a symbolic act that God asked him to perform. The belt represented the people of Judah, whom God wanted close to himself, but who became proud and drew away. Later the belt rots, as a sign of judgment for that pride. It is not known with certainty whether the journey was literal or a vision, and scholars have interpreted it in both ways.

For today: Jeremiah obeyed without yet understanding the meaning. We can practice that trust, doing with faith what God shows us, even when we do not yet see the reason why.
exp.36:19:
Jeremiah respectfully asks King Zedekiah to hear him. He pleads that the king not send him back to the house of Jonathan the scribe, because he fears he will die there. A humble request is what he is making, and "let my request be accepted before you" means "I hope you will consider my petition."

He speaks as God's prophet, who had warned that Babylon would defeat Jerusalem. For this he had been accused and locked away in a harsh place that had been turned into a prison. Jeremiah maintains that he has done no wrong and asks for fair treatment. The king agrees and has him kept in the prison courtyard, with a daily portion of bread.

For today: it is not a lack of faith to ask for help with humility and clarity when we suffer injustice. We can remain faithful to God, speak the truth with respect, and seek protection without bitterness.
exp.6:8:
God asks his people whether they can really steal, murder, commit adultery, and swear falsely. He also rebukes them for burning incense to Baal and following foreign gods they never knew. "Stealing" is taking what belongs to someone else, "adultery" is being unfaithful in marriage, "swearing falsely" is lying under oath, and burning incense is offering it in worship.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people believed they were safe simply because the temple was nearby, even though they lived in injustice and idolatry. God shows them that their religion was a facade. The verses that follow say that it is not enough to come to the temple and say "we are safe" if the heart remains in sin.

Today the message is clear: attending church or speaking well of the faith does not replace an honest life. Ask God to align your actions from Monday to Saturday with what you say on Sunday.
exp.36:17:
Here Jeremiah asks King Zedekiah a direct question: what crime did he commit to deserve prison? The phrases "I have sinned against you" and "I have done you harm" are not in this verse, so I have left those out. The words "they put me" and "the house of the prison" are likewise not quoted in the verse above, so I will simply say that he was kept in prison, the place where they held him.

Jeremiah is a prophet of God, and he speaks with the king, who had brought him out secretly to ask whether there was any word from the Lord. Jeremiah had already told him that Babylon would rule over them. They had imprisoned him for announcing that uncomfortable truth, while other prophets spoke only pleasing things.

For today: speaking the truth with respect can cost us dearly, but it remains the right thing to do. We can ask God for courage to be honest, without hatred or pride, and trust that He cares for those who are faithful to Him, even when they suffer injustice.
exp.28:14:
This verse records what the exiles were saying: "God has raised up prophets for us here in Babylon." The explanation of the word "raised up" is that God caused them to rise up, or stand up. The people leaned on those prophets to believe that their situation would soon change.

God speaks through Jeremiah, in a letter to the Jews taken captive to Babylon. He had promised them restoration after seventy years. But in Babylon there were prophets announcing an immediate return, and the people believed them. God warns that those words did not come from Him, and that judgment would still reach those who stayed behind in Jerusalem.

For today: it is not enough for someone to speak in God's name or to say what we want to hear. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and seek God with all your heart, with patience, even in difficult times.
exp.31:16:
Jeremiah begins his prayer by acknowledging who God is. He says that the Lord made the heavens and the earth by his great power and by his outstretched arm, a way of speaking about his strength in action. And he concludes that nothing is too hard for him, that is, nothing is impossible or too great for him.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking. Babylon had Jerusalem under siege, and everything seemed lost. Even so, God had told him to buy a field from his cousin, and Jeremiah obeyed and handed the deed of sale to Baruch. Afterward, puzzled, he prays. That purchase was a sign that one day the people would live again in their land.

When the situation looks closed, we can do as Jeremiah did: before listing the problems, remember who God is. Praying this way does not deny the difficulty, but it places it under the power of the One who created all things, and it helps us keep obeying with hope.
exp.28:23:
This verse is a brief command from God to Jeremiah: he is to carry a message to Shemaiah, a man from Nehelam. The text says nothing more about him here; the content of the message comes in the following verses. "Thus shalt thou also speak" means "you shall also say to him."

God speaks through Jeremiah to the exiles in Babylon. Earlier, Jeremiah had sent them a letter with God's word. Shemaiah, also in exile, answered by sending letters of his own to Jerusalem, and he pressed the priests to punish Jeremiah. God responds and confronts Shemaiah for speaking with an authority he did not have. Of Nehelam we know no more; some think it indicates his origin or family, but this is not certain.

Today we can learn not to speak in God's name lightly. Before we correct or silence others, it is wise to examine whether what we say agrees with his Word.
exp.38:4:
The army of Babylon pursued King Zedekiah, who had fled from Jerusalem, and caught up with him on the plains of Jericho. They captured him and brought him before Nebuchadnezzar, who was at Riblah in the land of Hamath. There Nebuchadnezzar passed judgment on him and pronounced his punishment.

The text is narrative; God does not speak directly here. After a long siege, Jerusalem fell. Zedekiah tried to escape at night, but he was caught. Jeremiah had warned many times that surrendering to Babylon was the way to save lives, and the king would not listen. Here what had been announced comes to pass.

For today: when God warns us through his Word, it is wiser to obey in time than to try to escape the consequences. Ignoring his voice out of fear or stubbornness only makes the fall more painful.
exp.18:0:
God tells Jeremiah to go to a potter and buy a clay jar, one of those that are already made and fired. He also asks him to take with him some of the elders of the people and some of the elders of the priests, that is, respected leaders who will serve as witnesses to what is about to happen.

The Lord speaks and gives his prophet Jeremiah an order that will be a living lesson. The verses that follow say that he will go to the Valley of Hinnom and there announce a judgment on Jerusalem. The jar will be a visible sign of that message. The details of the gesture are better seen in the rest of the chapter.

God sometimes speaks to us in ways that can be seen and touched. Today we can ask him to help us not to be only hearers, but to take his word seriously and let it correct our course before it is too late.
exp.45:19:
The explanation says that Egypt is like a very beautiful young cow, meaning a young, strong, and well-cared-for heifer. But destruction is approaching.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, passing on the message of the LORD. Egypt felt secure because of its wealth and power. Many understand that the enemy from the north was Babylon, which under Nebuchadnezzar advanced against Egypt. God shows that no nation is as strong as it believes itself to be.

For today: let us not put our security in what looks good, such as money, success, or fame. All of that can fall suddenly. Let us trust in God, who sustains what truly endures.
exp.20:0:
This verse says that God gave a message to Jeremiah when King Zedekiah sent two men, Pashur the son of Melchiah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, to make a request of him.

The phrases "came unto" and "sent unto him" are older ways of saying "came to" and "sent him" in today's English.

Context: Jeremiah is the prophet who speaks, and Zedekiah is the king of Judah. Babylon, led by Nebuchadnezzar, was attacking Jerusalem. The king wanted Jeremiah to consult God, hoping for a miracle. The verses that follow show that God's answer was not the one they were expecting.

For today: It is easy to seek God only when a crisis arrives. We can approach Him with steadiness and a willingness to obey, not only asking Him to get us out of trouble.
exp.17:10:
God tells Jeremiah to speak at once to the people of Judah and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. The message is that God is preparing a punishment against them, but He offers them a way out: that each one turn from his evil way and correct the way he lives and acts.

The Lord speaks after Jeremiah has watched the potter remake a damaged vessel. God teaches that He responds according to the attitude of the nations: if they repent, He holds back; if they harden themselves, judgment comes. That is why the warning is also an invitation. Nevertheless, the people answered with stubbornness.

For today: when you feel God correcting you, do not take it as rejection, but as an opportunity. Think of one specific habit you need to change, and take a step today to leave it behind, without waiting for tomorrow.
exp.49:38:
This verse says that Babylon will become an abandoned place. Wild animals of the desert will live there, such as beasts of the wild (wild animals), wolves, and ostriches. It will never again have inhabitants, not from one generation to the next.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Babylon, a powerful, idolatrous, and proud nation that had oppressed other peoples, including Judah. The text announces its judgment with the coming of a people from the north. Scholars debate how and when all this was fulfilled, since Babylon declined little by little over the centuries.

For today: no human power, however great it may seem, is eternal. We can trust that God is just and that he sustains those who suffer. It is also a good moment to examine what we put in God's place, because whatever is not God cannot give us lasting security.
exp.1:17:
It says that Judah seeks help in Egypt and in Assyria, as one who goes to drink water from their rivers. "The Nile" is the river of Egypt, and "the river" is the Euphrates, in Assyria. God asks sadly: what do you gain by going there?

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. His people had left the LORD and were looking for protection from foreign powers. Earlier, God says that Noph and Tahpanhes (Egyptian cities) had already hurt them. Interpreters explain the political details in various ways, but the central rebuke is clear: they abandoned God.

Today, when we are afraid or in need, it is easy to run to sources that seem secure: money, influence, or the approval of others. Ask yourself honestly: to which "river" do I go first? Seek God first in prayer, and then use the other resources wisely.
exp.47:24:
It says that Moab has lost its power. The "horn" was an image of strength and pride, like the horn of a bull or a deer. The "arm" stands for the ability to fight and defend oneself. If the horn is cut off and the arm is broken, Moab no longer has strength or defense. "Broken" means shattered.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, but what he says comes from the LORD. It is a message of judgment against Moab, a people who lived next to Israel. The verses that follow explain the reason: Moab exalted itself against God, that is, it rose up in arrogance, and it also mocked Israel. Scholars understand this language as a description of Moab's downfall, although not all of them agree on when or how it happened.

For today: human strength does not hold up when it turns into pride against God. Today we can ask ourselves what we trust in, and ask God for a humble heart that depends on Him.
exp.6:6:
The explanation says that God promises to let his people live in the land he gave to their ancestors, "forever." But this promise comes after an "if": if they change the way they live. Old words: "dí" is "di"; "á" is "a"; "forever" can be understood as "for a long time" or "from generation to generation."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people thought the temple would protect them, even though they oppressed the weak, killed the innocent, and worshiped idols. God asks them for a real change, not just trust in empty religious words.

For today: true faith shows in how we treat others. Think of someone near you who is in need, and help them with justice and kindness this week.
exp.40:0:
This verse tells how, in the seventh month, Ishmael, son of Nethaniah, came to Mizpah to visit Gedaliah. Ishmael was of royal descent, that is, of the king's family, and he came with ten men. There they ate bread together, which was a sign of friendship and hospitality.

The writer of the book then tells what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. The Babylonians had appointed Gedaliah as governor over those who remained in the land. Ishmael visited him, but, as the account goes on, his intention was to kill him. Scholars do not know his motives for certain; some think he wanted power, or that he acted out of jealousy.

Today the passage invites us to be wise. Being kind and trusting is good, but we should ask God for wisdom to discern people's intentions, without falling into constant suspicion.
exp.36:11:
It says that Jeremiah went out of Jerusalem to go into the land of Benjamin. The final phrase is difficult: "to separate himself thence in the midst of the people" can be understood as wanting to separate himself from the people, or as going there to receive a portion of his inheritance. Scholars translate it in different ways, so there is no single certain reading.

Context: The Babylonian army (the Chaldeans) had stopped besieging Jerusalem because the army of Egypt was coming. Some thought the danger had passed. But God, through Jeremiah, warned that the Chaldeans would return and burn the city. When Jeremiah went out, a guard accused him of defecting to the enemy, and they arrested him unjustly.

For today: Even when you are honest, sometimes you will be misunderstood or accused without reason. Jeremiah answered with the truth and remained faithful to God. Do the same: speak the truth calmly and trust that God sees.
exp.48:4:
God says he will bring terror on the Ammonites from every side. People will flee in disorder, each one straight ahead without looking back, and no one will stop to gather up those who are lost and scattered.

The Lord, the LORD of hosts, speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. This message is against Ammon, a people neighboring Israel. They trusted in their fertile valleys and their riches, and they said, "Who will come against me?" God warns them that this security is false.

For today: let us not place our security in money, in work, or in what we have. All of that can change suddenly. Let us trust in God, who gives true peace and does gather up the one who is lost.
exp.49:22:
This verse says that Babylon, which was like a mighty hammer striking all the nations, has now been cut apart and broken in pieces. It expresses amazement at how an empire so strong has become a wasteland, something the other nations look upon with horror. The word "was" is the simple past of "be," and "nations" refers to the peoples or nations of the earth.

The prophet Jeremiah announces, on God's behalf, judgment against Babylon. God had used this empire to correct other peoples, but Babylon was proud and cruel. Because of this, according to the text, it provoked the LORD. The verses that follow say that God himself brings about its fall.

For today: no human power lasts forever. If we have strength, money, or influence, let us use them with humility and justice, remembering that we answer to God. And if someone suffers from injustice, they can trust that God sees it.
exp.5:14:
Here God asks whether his people were ashamed of their horrible deeds. The answer is no: they no longer even knew how to blush. "Abomination" refers to things God detests. "I visit" here means that God will come to call them to account and to punish them. That is why it says they will fall along with the others who fall.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the fall of Jerusalem. He accuses everyone, from the least to the greatest, including prophets and priests, of greed and deceit. They kept saying "peace, peace" to calm the people, without addressing the real wound. God offers them the chance to return to the ancient paths, but they refuse.

For today: when our sin no longer hurts us, it is a warning sign. Let us ask God for a sensitive heart, and accept his correction with humility, before hardening drives us away from him.
exp.26:2:
God commands Jeremiah to send messages to five neighboring kings: Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon. The messengers those kings had sent to Jerusalem, to King Zedekiah, would serve to carry the word back.

Straps and yokes of wood, like the ones put on oxen, are the items Jeremiah was to place on his neck as a sign.

God speaks through Jeremiah. Those kingdoms were planning to rebel against Babylon, and God warns them, through a symbolic action, that by submitting to Babylon they would avoid a greater harm. Notice that the text mentions Jehoiakim at the beginning but speaks of Zedekiah, so some scholars believe there is a variant or a copying error in the name.

For today: before we cling to our own plans, it is wise to ask ourselves whether we are listening to what God says, even when it is not what we want to hear.
exp.28:11:
This verse says that the people, living far from their land, will again call out to God. The word "call upon" means calling to God asking for help. The phrase "go and pray" speaks of drawing near to Him in prayer. And God promises: "I will hearken unto you," that is, He will listen to them.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He writes a letter to the Jews exiled in Babylon. He tells them that the exile will last about seventy years and that God has not forgotten them. His plans for them are for peace and hope. The promise to listen is given within that setting: God will bring them back to their land.

For today: even in difficult times or far from what we know, we can pray with confidence. God listens. Today you can take a few minutes to speak to Him honestly about what weighs on you, remembering that He invites us to seek Him with all our heart.
exp.17:9:
It says that if a nation that God intended to bless does evil and does not obey his voice, God will change his mind about the good he had planned to give it. The word "repent" is used here, and in this verse it refers to a change of direction, not to a mistake on God's part. "Determined" here means "decided" or "planned."

Speaking through the prophet Jeremiah after the visit to the potter, who remakes the damaged vessel, God teaches that his warnings depend on how people respond. For this reason he calls Judah and Jerusalem to turn from their evil way, but they answer with stubbornness, set on following their own desires.

For today: let us not take God's blessings for granted while we live ignoring his voice. Today you can ask yourself in what area God is speaking to you, and obey him with humility, without hardening your heart.
exp.30:18:
Here he says Ephraim, that is, the people of the northern kingdom of Israel, acknowledges his sin. First he turned to God and felt sorrow for what he had done. Afterward he struck his thigh, a gesture of grief and regret, much like beating one's chest. The word "youth" refers to the sins of his younger days, and "shame" is the sense of disgrace. He feels confounded for bearing the shame of his past mistakes.

Here Ephraim speaks, lamenting his rebellion. This comes after God promises hope and restoration. God had said he disciplined him like a stubborn young bull, and the people respond with humility. Immediately God calls him "a dear son" and promises mercy.

For today: when you recognize your error, do not remain sunk in shame. Come before God with sincerity, for his discipline seeks to restore you, and his heart is moved to compassion for you.
exp.3:29:
This verse speaks to Jerusalem (Judah) as if she were a woman who has already been ruined. It asks her what she will do now. She dresses herself in bright red clothing, adorns herself with gold jewelry, and paints her eyes dark, but all of it is useless. Her lovers, that is, the nations she sought alliances with, despise her and want to kill her.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had turned away from Him and trusted in other nations. God had already announced judgment, and the invading army was drawing near. Many understand the lovers to be those allied nations, although the text expresses this in poetic language.

For today: no appearance, success, or human support can replace a sincere life with God. If today we trust more in what looks good on the outside, let us return to Him with humility.
exp.1:7:
It says that the spiritual leaders of Israel failed. The priests did not seek God, and they did not ask, "Where is the Lord?" The teachers of the law did not truly know him. The shepherds, that is, the rulers, rebelled against God. The prophets spoke in the name of Baal, a false god, and followed things that do not profit.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He has just recalled how he rescued his people from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness. But the people, and especially their leaders, forgot God and went after idols. For this reason God brings them to judgment, as in a lawsuit.

Today, it is not enough to hold an office, have knowledge, or keep religious customs. Ask yourself honestly: "Where is God in my life?" Seek to know him truly, not just to talk about him.
exp.27:7:
Jeremiah tells Hananiah that the prophets who came before, both his own and Hananiah's, announced hard things: war, affliction, and pestilence (that is, diseases that killed many people). They spoke of many lands and great kingdoms, and their message was usually a warning.

Jeremiah is speaking in the temple, in front of the people. Hananiah has just announced that God would break the power of Babylon within two years and that everything would soon be restored. Jeremiah replies with respect, but he reminds him that earlier prophets often brought difficult messages. For that reason, whoever announces peace should wait for events to confirm it.

For today: let us not accept a message simply because it sounds pleasant. Let us compare what we hear with the whole of Scripture, and be patient to see whether it comes true. Let us seek the truth of God, even when at times it is uncomfortable.
exp.44:1:
This verse opens God's message to Baruch. The words "Thus saith the Lord" were the way of announcing that what followed came from God. "Unto thee, O Baruch" shows that the message is personal, addressed to him by name. The phrase "thus saith" is the same as "says" or "said."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Baruch was his helper and wrote down what Jeremiah dictated to him, in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim. It was a difficult time, full of warnings of judgment. Baruch felt worn out and distressed, and God, who knew his complaint, decides to speak to him directly.

God does not see people as a faceless crowd. He knows your name, your weariness, and what you say inside yourself. You can be honest with Him when you are discouraged, and be attentive to His answer, even when it is not the one you expected.
exp.48:24:
This verse is a lament: someone asks with grief how it is possible that Damascus, the city of praise, the city that brought joy, has been left. The source's word for "left" is glossed by its own verb, and the old spelling note about the letter is not something the reader can see in the verse, so that sentence is removed. The sentence about other translations is also removed, since the reader's verse is the one above and no alternative wording needs to be mentioned. The exact sense of the original is not entirely clear.

God speaks through Jeremiah against Damascus, a city neighboring Israel. The verses before describe panic over bad news of war. The verses after announce judgment: fire and death. It is not known with certainty who speaks this lament: it may be the prophet, God, or someone from the city itself.

For today: no city, fame, or success is secure in itself. Put your trust in God, not in what looks strong, because only He endures.
exp.43:12:
God says that he will punish the Jews who went to live in Egypt, just as he punished Jerusalem. The three forms of punishment are the sword (war), famine, and plague (diseases that spread from person to person). "Visit" here does not mean a friendly call, but coming to call them to account.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. A group of Jews had fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem, even though God had told them not to go. There, moreover, they were burning incense to other gods. God warns them that Egypt would not be a safe refuge.

For today: running away from God does not keep us safe. When He asks something of us, trusting and obeying is safer than seeking protection on our own. If we have turned away, His Word invites us to return and to ask for forgiveness.
exp.33:13:
God reminds his people of an old law: when a Hebrew sold himself to another person because of debt, he was to serve six years and go free in the seventh year.

The explanation of the word "let ye go" is removed, as is the note about the older forms "ye" and "your," since those words appear in the verse your reader sees and need no comment.

The Lord adds that their ancestors did not obey or listen; in other words, they did not pay attention.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was threatened by Babylon, and King Zedekiah and the people had freed their Hebrew servants. Later they changed their minds and enslaved them again. God reminds them that this law was tied to the covenant made when he brought them out of Egypt. The verses that follow show that their disobedience was serious.

For today: if we make a promise before God, we should keep it even when it costs us. We can also ask ourselves whether we are treating with justice and compassion those who depend on us, such as employees or people in debt.
exp.6:12:
God says that the people have done all these evil things, even though he spoke to them again and again. The phrase "rising early to speak" means that God kept pressing them with urgency and persistence, like someone who gets up early so as not to waste time. Even so, they did not listen or answer when he called them.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah, probably at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem. The people believed the temple would protect them, even though they were living in injustice and idolatry. God reminds them of what happened at Shiloh, where the ancient sanctuary once stood, to warn them that a religious place saves no one without sincere obedience.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly listen to God or only go through the motions of religion. This week, set aside a few minutes to read the Bible calmly and ask him what he wants you to change. Then obey him in one concrete thing.
exp.49:36:
It says that the sword of judgment will fall on everything that gave Babylon its power: its horses, its war chariots, and its common people. The word "mingled people" refers to the mixed population, and it may include foreigners who lived there. The phrase "they shall become as women" means that its soldiers will be left without strength or courage. Its treasures will also be plundered.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces judgment against Babylon for its pride, its idolatry, and its mistreatment of God's people. The verses before include its wise men, diviners, and warriors, and the verses after speak of idols and desolation.

For today: let us not place our security in money, strength, or fame, because all of that is fragile. Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and hand our security over to God.
exp.9:7:
This verse says that those who follow idols become foolish and lose good judgment. The first quoted phrase in the source means that they become filled with a foolish confidence, and the second means that they become fools. The word translated as "vanities" means empty things, without value. The word for "wood" in the source refers to a piece of timber. So what an idol made of wood teaches is pure emptiness.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking to Israel, which was surrounded by peoples who worshiped images. Before this, he praises the LORD as incomparable, and afterward he describes how the craftsman covers the idol with silver, gold, and fine cloth. Even though it may look beautiful, it is still human work. In the end, Jeremiah contrasts it with the living and true God.

Today, an idol can be anything we trust more than God: money, fame, or success. Ask yourself: where am I seeking security? Lay it before God in prayer and trust Him.
exp.50:55:
It says that a destroyer has come against Babylon. Her brave soldiers were captured, and her bow, which is her weapon and her strength, was broken. The reason is that the Lord is the God who repays, that is, a God who does justice and gives each nation what it deserves. The verse's promise that he shall surely requite means that he will pay back according to what they have done.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to his people, who lived under the power of Babylon. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and oppressed many peoples. The message announces that this proud empire would not last forever and that God does not forget injustice.

For today: when you see wickedness that seems to go unpunished, do not take revenge with your own hands. Trust that God is just and will act in his own time. In the meantime, try to live with humility and to do good.
exp.5:21:
God announces that a people is coming from the "aquilón," an old word meaning the north. He also says that a great and powerful nation will rise up from the "cantones," that is, from the corners or far edges of the earth. It is a warning of invasion.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah was offering incense and sacrifices, but its heart was far from Him and it lived in injustice. For this reason God says that those rituals do not please Him. Many understand that the enemy from the north was Babylon, although the text does not name it here. Some scholars debate how this image was first applied.

For today: God is not satisfied with a religion that is only outward appearance. Examine whether your daily life, your dealings with others, and your obedience match what you sing and offer in church.
exp.43:19:
This verse is an introduction. It says that Jeremiah addressed the whole people: men, women, and all the people in general. The common people were the ordinary folk, the people as a whole. They had just answered him defiantly, and now the prophet is about to respond to them.

The Jews who fled to Egypt argued that worshiping the queen of heaven (probably a pagan goddess, though her exact identity is debated) brought them well-being. They said their troubles began when they stopped practicing that worship. Jeremiah, speaking on God's behalf, answers that the ruin came because of their idolatry and wickedness, not because they had abandoned it.

Today it is easy to blame the wrong thing when things go badly. It is worth pausing, listening humbly to God's correction, and returning to Him, rather than justifying our mistakes.
exp.2:0:
This verse recalls an ancient law: if a man divorced his wife and she married another man, he could not take her back again (Deuteronomy 24:1-4). Doing so would defile the land, that is, make it unclean. God compares this to Israel, who went off with many lovers, that is, other gods and alliances. Even so, God says: "return again to me."

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, which was practicing idolatry. He describes that unfaithfulness as adultery. What is striking is that, according to the law, returning would be impossible, yet God offers to receive his people back. Some see here a question with a tone of rebuke; the general sense is clear.

For today: if you have drifted away from God, do not think it is too late. He invites you to return with sincerity. You can pray, confess your failure, and begin again today.
exp.15:15:
God says he will send "fishers" and then "hunters" to seek out his people. They will catch them and hunt them everywhere: on the mountains, on the hills, and in the holes among the rocks. No one will be able to hide. The words for "north" and "hill" in the source are glossed here by the verse itself: "north" is not used in this verse, so the sentence about those words is removed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, before the exile in Babylon. Judah had fallen into idolatry and wickedness. This verse follows a promise of return to the land, but the text that comes next makes clear that judgment will come first. Some understand the fishers and hunters as the invaders who would lead the people into exile. Others also see a later search to restore them. There is more than one interpretation.

Today: we cannot hide from God, but there is no place where his mercy does not reach us. If you have turned away, return to him with sincerity.
exp.51:10:
The explanation says that the king of Babylon put out the eyes of Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. He bound him in chains, took him to Babylon, and kept him in prison until he died. The last thing Zedekiah saw was the death of his sons, according to the verse before.

Context: This final chapter of Jeremiah tells of the fall of Jerusalem, and it seems to summarize what is also recounted in 2 Kings 25. For years, Jeremiah had warned Zedekiah to surrender and listen to God, but the king did not obey. Here the narrator simply records the events: what God had said through the prophet came to pass.

For today: God's words are serious, and ignoring them has consequences. Today we can hear his Word with humility and obey in time, rather than hardening our hearts. His warning seeks to protect us, and it always offers a way back.
exp.12:10:
The explanation says that God joined all of Israel and all of Judah to himself, just as a belt clings to a person's waist. The "loins" are the waist or the lower part of the back. God wanted them to be his people, for his "fame" (his known name), his praise, and his honor. But they "did not listen," that is, they did not pay attention to him.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Earlier, Jeremiah had hidden a linen belt near the Euphrates River, and later he found it rotten and useless. With this image, God shows that his people, through their pride and by following other gods, had become spoiled.

God desires closeness with us, not just rules. We can ask ourselves today: am I truly clinging to God, listening to his voice, or have I been drifting away through pride or other priorities? Today you can return to him with sincerity.
exp.32:5:
God promises to bring health and medicine to Jerusalem. He says he will heal his people and show them abundant peace and truth. The phrase about bringing up healing means that God makes healing spring up or come forth, the way a wound is bound up. Here "reveal" means to make known, and "truth" points to something firm and trustworthy.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who was imprisoned at the time. Jerusalem was under siege by the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), and the houses were being torn down. God says this punishment came because of the people's wickedness, but it does not end there: immediately he promises to bring them back from captivity, cleanse them, and forgive them.

For today: even when you feel that everything has collapsed, whether because of your own mistakes or because of circumstances, God does not shut the door on you. You can draw near to him with sincerity, ask for forgiveness and healing, and trust that he knows how to rebuild what seemed lost.
exp.10:3:
God reminds the people of the covenant he made with Israel's ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt, which he calls the "iron furnace," a place of intense suffering. He asked them: "Obey my voice, and do them," and promised: "So shall ye be my people, and I will be your God." The phrase that means "do them" is explained as putting his commands into practice.

Here the LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, who must announce this message to Judah and Jerusalem. God reminds them of what they promised in the covenant, because the people were not obeying him. He warns that disobedience brings consequences, but he also reminds them of his faithfulness in rescuing them.

For today: God has shown us his love and wants a relationship with us, not just words. We can ask ourselves what God has already told us in his Word that we have not yet put into practice, and take one concrete step of obedience today.
exp.49:20:
It says that God commands an army to go up against Merathaim and against the inhabitants of Pekod, two names that here point to Babylon. "Waste and utterly destroy after them" means to pursue them until the task is finished. "Do according to all that I have commanded thee" asks for exact obedience to God's orders. According to many scholars, Merathaim and Pekod sound like Babylonian place names, but they also carry a play on words with their meanings: "double rebellion" and "punishment."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Babylon had oppressed Judah, and now God announces its fall. This is connected to the promise to restore Israel and forgive its sin.

For today: God is just and does not forget injustice, but he also forgives his own people. We can rest in the knowledge that he governs history, and leave in his hands the wrong that hurts us, without personal revenge.
exp.43:5:
It says that God poured out his anger with force on the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem. Because of this they lay in ruins and empty, and they stayed that way until now.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the Jews who had gone to live in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. He reminds them that he sent prophets again and again, but they would not stop burning incense to false gods. He tells them what happened so that they do not repeat the same mistake, and so that they see his warnings were serious.

For today: when God corrects us, it is because he loves us and wants to protect us. Let us listen to his voice in time, before the harm grows, and return to him with humility.
exp.30:7:
God says that He Himself will bring His people back from the north (the word "aquilón," which refers to the north wind or the northern region, is not needed here) and from the farthest places on the earth. He will leave no one behind: not the blind, not the lame, not the women who are pregnant or who have just given birth. They will return together, like a great company.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people of Israel were scattered and exiled because of their sin, but God promises them restoration. Ephraim names the northern kingdom, and the passage calls it God's firstborn, that is, a very beloved son. Many Christians also see here a foreshadowing of complete salvation in Christ, although this is understood in various ways.

For today: God takes special care of the weak and the weary. If you feel far away or without strength, you can return to Him with confidence, because He Himself seeks you out and walks with you on the way.
exp.43:25:
God says he swears by his "great name," that is, by who he is. His oath is that no Judean in Egypt will ever again invoke his name by saying, "As the Lord God lives," a phrase people used to affirm something solemnly. God takes away from them the right to use his name as if everything were fine between them and him.

Jeremiah speaks to the Jews who fled to Egypt, against God's command. There, together with their wives, they kept offering incense and drink offerings to the "queen of heaven," a pagan goddess, and they promised to keep doing so. God answers with a firm warning about the consequences of their idolatry.

For today: it is not enough to speak God's name with the mouth. He desires sincere faith, without dividing the heart with other idols.
exp.19:6:
He says Jeremiah feels deceived and overpowered by God. The word translated "deceived" can also be rendered "persuaded" or "enticed"; some understand it as "you deceived me." "Frustrated" means mocked, put to shame in his expectations. "Derided" means ridiculed with contempt. Jeremiah acknowledges that God was stronger and that he could not resist his call, but now everyone laughs at him every day.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks just after the priest Pashur struck him and put him in the stocks for announcing judgment on Jerusalem. Alone now, Jeremiah opens his heart to God with a very sincere complaint. Interpreters debate how strong the word "deceived" is, but all see here an honest prayer, not unbelief.

For today: when obeying God costs you mockery or weariness, do not hide what you feel. Tell it to him frankly in prayer, as Jeremiah did. God is not alarmed by your complaints, and he can sustain you even when you feel weak.
exp.28:4:
The explanation says that the exiles in Babylon are to live normally: to build houses and live in them, to plant gardens and eat what they produce. The verb translated here as "build" means "build," and the call to live in the houses is a call to dwell in them. Planting gardens means sowing trees and vegetables.

It is part of a letter from the prophet Jeremiah to the Jews carried captive from Jerusalem to Babylon. He speaks in the name of the LORD. Some false prophets were saying the exile would be short, but God tells them it will be long (Jeremiah 29:10 speaks of seventy years). For that reason he asks them to put down roots and not to live waiting for an immediate way out.

For today: even in difficult times, or in circumstances we did not choose, God calls us to live with faith, working, caring for our families, and serving where we are, without putting life on hold while we wait for things to change.
exp.5:26:
God tells Jeremiah that he has set him as a stronghold and a tower among his people. That means he is placed as someone who watches and tests. "You will know" means he will observe closely, and "you will examine their way" means he will assess how they live and what conduct they follow. Some versions render the word for stronghold as "tester of metals."

God speaks to Jeremiah just before the enemy invasion he announced. The people resist changing. For this reason, the prophet must look honestly at their condition, like someone testing metal. The verses that follow show the result: the people are like metal that is not refined.

For today: before judging others, examine your own way honestly before God. Ask him to show you what you need to correct, and respond with humility and obedience.
exp.7:19:
It says the harvest is over and the summer has ended, that is, the seasons when the fruit is gathered and the crop is expected. Even so, the people still are not saved, that is, not rescued from their distress. "Harvest" here means the gathering of the grain.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks with grief for his people, who suffer because of their idolatry and are under threat of judgment. The voices in the verse may be those of the people lamenting, although some think Jeremiah is expressing them on their behalf. The opportunities have passed and the rescue has not come. Afterward the prophet asks whether there is no balm and no physician to heal.

For today: do not put off turning back to God, because opportunities do not always come again. If you sense his call today, respond with humility and do not wait for the summer to pass.
exp.8:18:
This verse describes a cry of mourning heard from Zion, that is, Jerusalem. The people weep because everything has been destroyed, and they feel shame and bewilderment. A lament is a song of grief, and to be bewildered means to be ashamed and confused. They ask why they had to leave their land, and they say that their own homes have cast them out, as if they could no longer live in them.

God himself speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Just before this verse, he calls for skilled women to come and wail at funerals, because a great calamity is near. Many understand that it foretells the invasion and exile brought on by the people's sin, although the text presents it as an advance lament.

For today: when a loss leaves you confused, do not keep your pain silent. Bring it honestly to God, and also examine your heart, asking him to guide you back to himself.
exp.36:16:
This verse tells how King Zedekiah had Jeremiah brought out of prison and asked him a question in secret, in his own house: "Is there any word from the Lord?" Jeremiah answered that there was, and told him plainly that he would be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon.

Jeremiah was God's prophet in the last days of Judah. The officials had beaten him and put him in prison for saying that Jerusalem would fall. Zedekiah was afraid and wanted an answer, but he did not dare to hear Jeremiah openly. Even so, the prophet did not change the message to save himself from prison.

For today: God's truth is not always comfortable, but it must be spoken with honesty and love. And when we seek the voice of God, let us ask for the courage to obey it, not just curiosity to hear it.
exp.19:8:
He says that Jeremiah wanted to keep quiet: "I will not think about God anymore or speak in his name." But the word of God inside him was like a burning fire shut up in his bones. The phrase "I was weary with forbearing" means that he tried hard to hold it in and could not.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. He preached harsh messages on behalf of God, and every day people insulted him and mocked him. Even his friends were waiting to see him fall. Tired and wounded, he complains to God and thinks about giving up. Even so, at the end of the passage he trusts that God is with him.

For today: if you feel worn out from doing good or from speaking the truth, you can tell God honestly how you feel, as Jeremiah did. God does not become angry at your honesty. Ask him for strength to remain faithful, and surround yourself with people who encourage you.
exp.0:5:
Jeremiah responds to God with surprise and fear: "Ah, Lord God!" He says he does not know how to speak well because he is only a child. That word does not always mean a baby; it can refer to a young man without experience. Jeremiah feels too immature for such a great task.

God has just told him that He knew him and set him apart before he was born, to be a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah does not argue with the calling, but he feels he is not ready. Then God answers that he should not use that excuse, because He will send him, will give him what to say, and will be with him. Scholars do not know his exact age.

When God asks something of you and you feel small or incapable, do not stay in your excuses. What matters is not your ability, but that God goes with you. Take the step, trusting in his help.
exp.37:21:
It tells that the women of King Zedekiah's palace would be brought out before the officials of the king of Babylon. They themselves, in a tone of mockery or lament, would say that his "friends" had deceived him and overpowered him. "Your feet are sunk in the mire" means that they left him stuck in the mud, and "they are turned away back" means that they abandoned him.

The prophet Jeremiah is speaking to King Zedekiah while Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon. Jeremiah offers him a way out: surrender and live. He warns him with this vision of what would happen if he disobeyed God. The king was afraid of his people and of their criticism, and for that reason he hesitated.

For today: do not let fear of what others think keep you from obeying God. Advice that only seeks to please you can leave you stuck, but God's word, even when it is hard, leads to life.
exp.0:17:
God tells Jeremiah that he has made him like a fortified city, an iron pillar, and walls of bronze. These are images of strength and firmness. A fortified city is a city with defenses. The phrase about "against the whole land" is understood here as "against the whole country." That firmness will be needed in the face of the kings, the leaders, the priests, and the people of Judah.

God speaks when he calls Jeremiah, who was young and afraid. He entrusts him with a message of judgment against a people who worshiped idols. He knew they would reject him, so God promises him strength to endure. The next verse assures him: "they shall not prevail against thee; for I am with thee."

For today: when obeying God brings opposition or mockery, do not rely on your character alone. Ask God for the firmness that he gives, and go forward with humility, remembering that he is with you.
exp.5:5:
It says that God, the Lord of hosts, orders trees to be cut down and siege ramps raised against Jerusalem. A siege ramp is a mound of earth or wood built up to attack a city wall. Being "visited" here means receiving punishment, not a friendly visit. The reason is clear: violence and oppression are found within the city.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that an enemy army will come against Jerusalem. The nearby verses present this as the result of the people's constant wickedness: injustice, robbery, and harm. Even so, God calls them to turn back before He leaves the city desolate. His judgment comes with a warning and an open door.

For today: let us not downplay the injustice we see or practice. Ask God to show you where you need to change, and do it soon, treating those around you with justice and respect.
exp.10:11:
This verse says that when disaster comes, the people of the towns of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go out to cry for help to the false gods to whom they burned incense. But those gods will not be able to save them when they need them most.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had broken the covenant that God made with their ancestors, and had given themselves over to idolatry. God announces that the evil will come, and shows with irony that the idols they chose have no power to rescue them.

For today: it is easy to trust in things that seem to give us security, such as money, success, or the approval of others. When crises come, only God truly sustains. It is worth asking ourselves what we trust in first, and returning to Him with sincerity before the storm arrives.
exp.23:9:
God says he will send the sword, the famine, and the pestilence, that is, war, lack of food, and deadly disease. This will continue until they are consumed, that is, until they disappear from the land that he had given to their fathers and to them.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. In the vision of the two baskets of figs, the bad figs represent Zedekiah, his princes, and those who remained in Jerusalem or went down to Egypt. They did not listen to God, and for that reason this judgment would come. Historians and the biblical texts connect this with the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon.

For today: God speaks in earnest when he calls us to return to him. Let us not harden our hearts. If today you sense his voice, respond with humility, trusting that he corrects in order to restore those who repent.
exp.22:39:
This verse says that God will bring upon them a shame that will last forever and a disgrace so great that no one will be able to forget it. The words "reproach" and "shame" here refer to deep humiliation and dishonor.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah, at a time of great corruption. False prophets and the people were using the phrase "burden of the Lord" in a mocking way, or to give authority to their own ideas. Whether it refers to a message or a weight, God had asked them to stop using it. Since they kept speaking in His name without respect, the judgment is severe.

For today: let us be very careful about how we speak in God's name. Before we say "God told me" or use the Bible to support our own opinions, let us pray, study with humility, and speak with reverence.
exp.12:18:
It says that the cities of the Negev, the dry region in the south of Judah, were shut up, and no one could open them. The word "south" in the verse means the southern region. "Was carried away" means that it was taken into exile. All of Judah, without exception, was carried away into exile.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, with grief, on behalf of God. Earlier he called the people to humble themselves, because their pride would bring judgment. Here he describes that fall as though it had already happened. The shut-up cities may indicate that they were under siege, or that there was no one to defend or help them. This is interpreted in several ways. The message is that the punishment would reach everyone, even the most distant places.

For today: God warns us with love before the consequences arrive. If something in your life pulls you away from Him, such as pride, do not wait until you have lost everything. Humble yourself today, listen to His voice, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.35:15:
This verse tells how the officials, when they heard the message of the scroll, were afraid and looked at one another in alarm. "Afraid both one and other" in the verse above means that each of them was frightened, and that they were gripped by fear together. Then they said to Baruch that they would surely have to tell the king about everything they had heard.

The officials were the senior ranking men of King Jehoiakim. Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, had just read to them the warning words that God had given through the prophet. They understood that the message was serious and that the king needed to know it. Later on we see that the king reacted very differently.

For today: when God's Word touches our hearts, let us not ignore it or let it pass by. Let it move us to respond with reverence, and let us answer with obedience and humility.
exp.49:25:
It speaks of distant peoples, "from the utmost border," who will come against Babylon. They are told to open her storehouses, that is, her granaries or places where her wealth is kept. Then they must heap her up like piled grain or rubble, and destroy her completely. The remnant, meaning what is left behind, must not survive: nothing of her is to remain.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, announcing what the LORD says. Babylon had been God's instrument for judging other nations, but it grew proud and mistreated Israel and its temple. For this reason God now judges her. Scholars understand this as referring to the fall of Babylon before the Medes and Persians, though some also see a broader sense of final judgment.

For today: no human power, however great it may seem, stands above God. If you are suffering injustice, you can trust that God sees and will act justly in his time. And if you have some power or success, use it with humility.
exp.31:12:
This verse says that Jeremiah gave an instruction to Baruch, his secretary, and did so in front of everyone present. The phrase "I gave an order" is an old way of saying "I gave a direction" or "I commanded." "In front of them" means there were witnesses.

Jeremiah is speaking while he is imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard while Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon. God had asked him to buy a field from his cousin Hanamel, even though the land seemed lost. Jeremiah did everything with documents and witnesses, and now he passes on what God wants Baruch to do: keep the deeds as a sign that there will be restoration.

For today: when everything seems uncertain, we can act with faith and order, doing things with clarity and honesty, trusting that God's promises will be fulfilled in his time.
exp.43:9:
It says that the people of Judah, up to that day, had not humbled themselves or shown reverence for God. They also had not walked in God's law, which he had given to them and to their ancestors.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. A group of Jews had fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem, and there they were burning incense to other gods. God reminds them that the destruction of Jerusalem came because of that same idolatry, and that even so they had not learned the lesson.

For today: it is not enough to suffer the consequences of our mistakes; God invites us to acknowledge them with humility and return to him. Today you can ask him to show you something in which you have resisted changing.
exp.10:15:
God described his people as a green olive tree, lush, beautiful, and bearing good fruit. But with a great roar, like a storm or an army, God set fire to that tree, and its branches were broken.

The word "fair" in the verse is the one that indicates how something looks, and the phrase "called your name" means that this is how God described you or regarded you.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. The people had a special relationship with God, but they broke the covenant and worshiped Baal. That is why judgment comes. Some understand the "fire" as an enemy invasion; the text does not give exact details.

For today: having a good appearance or a good start in faith is not enough. God looks for constant faithfulness. We can ask him to examine us and help us remain in him with a sincere heart, not merely with religious habits.
exp.51:14:
Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard of Babylon, led away into exile the common people who were left in Jerusalem. The word "carried away" here means taken off into exile, and the phrase "the poor of the people" refers to ordinary folk, people without high office or position. He also took those who had defected to the side of Babylon.

This chapter is a historical account of the fall of Jerusalem, around 586 BC. The one who narrates it describes the judgment that Jeremiah had announced for years, because the people had turned away from God. It is not known with certainty who wrote it. It is very similar to 2 Kings 25.

For today: God takes his warnings seriously, but he never stops seeing ordinary people. If you are going through a loss or a hard change today, do not feel forgotten. Pray sincerely and trust him again.
exp.47:6:
It says that Moab trusted in its works (its deeds, strongholds and achievements) and in its treasures, and for that reason it too will be taken, that is, conquered. Its god Chemosh will go into exile, together with his priests and his princes. A god who cannot even save himself cannot protect anyone.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, announcing judgment on Moab, a neighboring people of Israel. The context shows a disaster that is near: weeping, flight, and cities destroyed. Moab trusted in its wealth, its pride, and its god, and not in the Lord. Scholars agree that the message is one of judgment, although they debate the historical details.

For today: examine what your security rests on. Money, success, or prestige can help, but they do not sustain the soul. Trust first in God, who does not fail or fall.
exp.43:8:
Here God asks a pointed question: "Have ye forgotten?" He reminds them of the wickedness of their fathers, of the kings of Judah, of their wives, and of themselves, committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. "Wickedness" here means evil deeds, above all idolatry.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the Jews who had fled to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. There they were still offering incense to other gods. God reminds them that this same idolatry had already brought judgment on their land, and warns them that repeating it will bring them further ruin.

For today: forgetting the past leads us to repeat the same mistakes. It is worth remembering our falls with humility, and the lessons God has given us, so that we return to Him sincerely and do not insist on paths that have already done us harm.
exp.26:10:
This verse says that any nation that agrees to submit to the king of Babylon and serve him, God will let remain in its own land. There it will be able to farm the land and live in it. A "yoke" is the wooden frame placed on the necks of working animals. The word "let remain" in the verse means that God will let them stay, and "till it" means they will work the land.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Judah and its neighbors faced the power of Babylon. False prophets claimed there would be no submission, but God says those words were a lie. Accepting the yoke was the way to survive.

Today we can learn to tell apart what sounds encouraging from what truly comes from God. Before following any voice, let us compare its message with Scripture and seek wise counsel. Sometimes humble obedience, even when it costs us, protects us more than an easy promise.
exp.30:15:
God tells Rachel to stop weeping. He asks her to hold back her voice from crying and her eyes from tears, because her labor and her pain have not been in vain. The word "salary" means reward. And he promises that her children will return from the land of the enemy, that is, from exile.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Rachel appears as a figure of the mother who weeps for her children carried away captive; she was the ancestor of Ephraim and Benjamin, northern tribes. This belongs within the promises of Israel's restoration. Later, Matthew 2:18 quotes the weeping of Ramah in another context, and interpreters relate it in different ways.

God does not mock pain, but neither does he let pain have the last word. Today you can weep honestly before him and, at the same time, hope that God is at work and that your faithfulness is not lost.
exp.12:15:
It says the people must give glory to God, that is, acknowledge and honor him, before it is too late. The "darkness" and the "dark mountains" are images of judgment and calamity: walking blindly and stumbling. The "shadow of death" is a deep and threatening darkness. The word "turn" here means "change into": they hope for light, but God would turn it into darkness.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, passing on the word of the Lord to Judah. The people were proud and resisted obeying. The following verse shows the prophet's grief, since the judgment would come in the form of captivity. Scholars agree that this is a warning given before the exile, although the exact date is debated.

For today: do not put off humbling yourself before God. If anything in your life has taken his place because of pride, acknowledge it today with simplicity and return to him, while there is still light.
exp.28:17:
God says he will punish those who remained in Jerusalem with war, hunger, and terrible diseases. He will make them an example to all the nations: a word of mockery, of curse, and of horror. The word "hissing" was a sound of scorn or amazement, and "reproach" means shame. Wherever they are scattered, they will be remembered in this way.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Some of the people had already been taken to Babylon, while King Zedekiah and others stayed behind in Jerusalem. They thought they were safe, but God compares them to rotten figs. The reason is given in the next verse: they did not listen to the prophets whom God sent to them again and again.

For today: when God speaks to us, whether through his Word or through others, we should not harden our hearts or feel secure without reason. Listening and obeying in time spares us much pain.
exp.0:3:
This verse says that God spoke directly to Jeremiah. The phrase "then the word of the Lord came unto me" is an older way of saying that the Lord's word came to him. Jeremiah does not invent the message; he states that he received it from God. Here his account of his calling as a prophet begins.

The one speaking is Jeremiah, in the first person. Earlier, the book explained that his ministry spanned about forty years, from the reign of Josiah until the fall of Jerusalem. With this verse, he moves on to tell how it all began. What follows is God's answer, in which He speaks of His purpose, and Jeremiah's reaction, in which he feels very young.

For today: God still speaks through His Word. Before wanting to do something for Him, we can stop and listen with humility. Opening the Bible with that desire changes the way we decide and the way we live.
exp.21:12:
God declares, with a warning cry, that woe is coming upon the one who builds his house and his chambers without righteousness and without rightness. The word "justice" here means acting with fairness and uprightness. The phrase "without wages" means for free, without paying. "Neighbour" refers to a fellow human being, the one beside us. In other words, it means taking advantage of someone else's labor without giving them their pay.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses the royal palace of Judah, right after speaking about Shallum, the son of Josiah. The next king, Jehoiakim, was expanding his luxurious palace with cedar and red paint, while exploiting his workers. God reminds him that his father Josiah did justice and things went well for him.

Today: if you have employees or work alongside others, pay them with fairness and on time. No progress, house, or business is worth anything if it is built on the abuse of others.
exp.35:16:
The princes of Judah, alarmed by what they heard, ask Baruch to explain how he wrote down all those words. They want to know whether Jeremiah dictated them. "Then they asked Baruch" is an older way of saying the same thing as the verse's "And they asked Baruch." And "from the mouth of Jeremiah" means that he wrote them down while Jeremiah was speaking them.

Jeremiah was prevented from entering the temple, so he sent Baruch, his scribe, to publicly read God's message. The princes heard the scroll and became alarmed, because it announced judgment. Before taking it to King Jehoiakim, they wanted to confirm where it came from. Afterward, they advised that Baruch and Jeremiah go into hiding, since the king might react with violence.

For today: when the Word of God unsettles us, let us neither ignore it nor argue it away. Let us listen with humility, and if need be, act with wisdom and courage to obey it.
exp.21:7:
This verse says that many people from other nations will pass by this city in ruins and will ask one another why God did such a thing to a city so great. The word "nations" is used here for the peoples around them, and the one who walks alongside you, a companion, is the person who goes with you.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the royal house of Judah. He warns them that their palace, beautiful as Gilead and Lebanon, will be destroyed. The verses that follow give the reason: they abandoned the covenant with God and served other gods. Many understand that the "city" is Jerusalem, although the text does not name it here.

For today: our decisions reveal what we love. Today you can examine which things you give first place and return to God sincerely, before what has been neglected becomes ruin.
exp.36:10:
This verse tells us that the army of the Chaldeans, meaning the Babylonians, stopped surrounding Jerusalem. They pulled back because the army of Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, was coming to help Judah. The phrase "it came to pass" here means that they lifted the siege for a time.

The one telling the story is the writer of the book. Earlier, God had told Jeremiah not to let the people deceive themselves into thinking the danger was over. The Chaldeans would return and burn the city. This is where the account of what Jeremiah did during that pause begins.

For today: a temporary relief does not always mean the problem has been solved. When a crisis passes, let us not become complacent or ignore what God tells us. Let us use the calm to listen to his voice and correct whatever needs correcting.
exp.25:7:
It says that when Jeremiah had finished telling everything the Lord had commanded him to speak, the priests, the prophets, and all the people seized him violently. "Seized him" means they took hold of him and arrested him. They were shouting, "Thou shalt surely die," that is, "You are certainly going to die!"

The context is Jeremiah's message in the temple, in the time of King Jehoiakim. God warned that if the people did not repent, the temple would be destroyed like Shiloh, a place where the tabernacle once stood. The religious leaders were offended because they trusted that the temple would protect them. They rejected the message and wanted to silence the messenger.

For today: God's truth sometimes makes us uncomfortable, especially when it touches our pride or our false sense of security. Instead of responding with anger, we can listen with humility, examine our hearts, and turn back to God.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that the word of God also came to Jeremiah during the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, and continued until the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, also a son of Josiah. That period ended when Jerusalem was carried away captive, in the fifth month. The phrase "It came also" means "it also happened," and "carrying away" refers to the exile of the inhabitants.

The one speaking is the writer of the book, who presents the setting of Jeremiah's ministry. Earlier he mentioned its beginning in the time of Josiah; now he summarizes his long labor up to the fall of Jerusalem. Many understand this to be about forty years, although the text does not give that number. In this way the reader knows that Jeremiah spoke in difficult times, full of warnings.

For today: God asks us for faithfulness even when we do not see quick results. Jeremiah kept speaking for years amid rejection. Today we can keep obeying God with steadiness, trusting that He sustains those who serve Him.
exp.51:19:
This verse describes the largest bronze objects in the temple: the two pillars, the "sea" (an enormous basin of water for the priests), and twelve bronze bulls that held up that basin. The "stands" were the supports with wheels. Solomon had made them, and the Babylonians carried them away. There were so many of them, and they were so heavy, that the weight of the metal could not be calculated.

This final chapter of Jeremiah tells, as a historical summary, the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 586 B.C. The captain of the guard, Nebuzaradan, plundered the temple. The scene shows the judgment that God had warned of because of the people's disobedience.

For today: What is most beautiful can disappear, and we should not place our security in buildings, achievements, or possessions. Let us set our hearts on God himself, who remains faithful even when everything else is lost.
exp.8:11:
This verse asks three questions: who is wise enough to understand what happened, to whom has God spoken so that he could explain it, and why has the land been left ruined and empty, so much so that no one passes through it? The word "desolate" in the verse means ruined and laid waste. A "wise man" is a person with understanding.

Jeremiah speaks with a broken heart over the judgment that is coming upon Judah. The questions remain open until God himself answers in the verses that follow: the people abandoned his law, did not obey his voice, and followed the stubbornness of their own hearts and the Baals.

For today: true wisdom begins when we recognize that our choices have consequences and that God speaks with clarity. Today we can ask ourselves in what area we are following our own path instead of his Word, and return to him with humility.
exp.22:31:
God says he is against those who tell false dreams as if they came from him. These "prophets" led the people astray with lies and with "flattery," which means empty praise meant to please people and say what they want to hear. God makes clear that he did not send them or give them any command, and that they did not help the people at all.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah, in the days before the fall of Judah. Several prophets were assuring everyone that all would be well, even though the people were living in sin. They said "Thus saith the Lord," but their words were made up or taken from others. God rebukes them for turning the people away from repentance.

Today we can compare what we hear, even when it sounds beautiful or spiritual, with what the Bible says. A true word from God may comfort, but it also corrects and leads us to obey him.
exp.27:2:
It says that, in just two years, God would bring back to Jerusalem all the vessels of the temple that Nebuchadnezzar carried off to Babylon. The phrase about bringing back refers to the same idea as the verse's "bring again." The phrase "within two full years" means "within two complete years."

The speaker is Hananiah, a prophet from Gibeon, in the temple, before priests and the people. He says he speaks on behalf of the Lord, but Jeremiah had announced a long exile. Hananiah offered a pleasant and quick message. Later, Jeremiah shows that Hananiah was not speaking on God's behalf.

For today: not every hopeful message comes from God. Before believing easy promises, compare them with what the Bible teaches and pray for discernment. God's true hope does not avoid reality, but sustains us within it.
exp.3:12:
It says that an enemy is approaching quickly and with great power. He comes up "as clouds," his chariots are like a whirlwind, and his horses are swifter than eagles.
