Then the people cry out, "Woe unto us!" because "we are spoiled," that is, they will be plundered and destroyed. Here "spoiled" means plundered.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, and the voice of God is also heard announcing judgment. Judah and Jerusalem had turned away from God. For this reason an invasion is coming, which many understand to be that of the army of Babylon, although the text does not give the name here. Then God calls Jerusalem to cleanse its heart so that it may be saved.

For today: do not wait for a crisis to arrive before you turn back to God. Ask him today to examine your heart, and sincerely let go of whatever you know does not please him.
exp.31:33:
This verse says that the people of Judah set their abominations, that is, their idols and detestable practices, inside the temple in Jerusalem. That was the place where God had put his name. By doing so they defiled it, that is, they made it unclean and dishonored it.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Jerusalem was under siege by Babylon, and Jeremiah was in prison. God explains why judgment is coming: the people, their kings, priests, and prophets did not listen to his warnings, though he spoke to them again and again. Even so, in this same chapter God promises to restore his people.

For today: God wants first place in our lives, which is now his house (1 Corinthians 6:19). We can ask ourselves what things we have let into our hearts that compete with him, and ask him for forgiveness and help to remove them.
exp.31:4:
He says that King Zedekiah will be taken to Babylon and will remain there "until I visit him," that is, until God acts again. Then comes a question: "if you fight against the Chaldeans, will it not go well with you?" That question expects the answer no, since it will not go well for them. "Chaldeans" is another name for the Babylonians.

The LORD speaks through Jeremiah, who was imprisoned because King Zedekiah could not bear his message. Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah said that resisting would be useless. Some understand "visit" as a possible time of God's care or judgment. The text gives no further detail here.

Today it reminds us that God tells the truth even when it is uncomfortable. We can ask him for humility to hear his correction in time, instead of resisting it out of pride or fear.
exp.25:6:
This verse tells us that the priests, the prophets, and all the people heard Jeremiah while he spoke in the temple. "The house of the Lord" is the temple in Jerusalem. The verse's word "heard" means they listened closely.

God sent Jeremiah to stand in the temple and warn the people that, if they did not obey, the temple would become like Shiloh, a place of worship that had been destroyed. God reminded them that he had sent prophets again and again, and they had not listened. Listening was not the same as obeying: they soon seized Jeremiah and demanded his death.

For today: hearing the Word of God is not enough; we must let it correct us. Let us ask God for a humble heart, so that we may receive with gratitude even what makes us uncomfortable.
exp.13:14:
This verse says that God speaks sternly against certain prophets. They spoke as if they came from God, but He had not sent them. They said there would be no war or famine, and God answers that these same prophets will die by war and famine.

"Sword" is the word here for war, and "consumed" means destroyed. Those two words were rewritten for you: the verse says "sword" and "consumed," and the sword means war.

The one speaking is the Lord, and He says it to Jeremiah. At that time there was a great drought and a threat of invasion. Jeremiah was praying for the people, but there were prophets who gave false comfort. God warns them that their lies will not stop the punishment, and that the people who believed them will also suffer.

For today: let us not believe something just because it sounds comforting or because someone with religious authority says it. Let us compare what we hear with the whole Bible and ask God for wisdom. The truth sometimes makes us uncomfortable, but it cares for us better than a pleasant lie.
exp.3:2:
God tells the men of Judah and Jerusalem to prepare their hearts like a field. Breaking up fallow ground means plowing land that has become hard or left unused so it is ready. Thorns are the weeds that choke the seed. There is no point in sowing before the ground has been cleared.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He calls His people to truly return to Him, not merely with words. Right after this, He asks for a change within, a renewal of the heart, and warns of coming judgment if they continue in their evil ways.

For today: before seeking new spiritual goals, ask yourself what thorns are in your life, such as resentments, habits, or excuses. Bring them honestly before God and let Him remove them, so that His Word can bear fruit in you.
exp.28:20:
God speaks against two men, Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah. They claimed to speak on God's behalf, but they were lying. God announces that he will hand them over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and that the king will put them to death before the eyes of the exiles. The phrase "prophesy a lie unto you" means that they announced lies to you as if they were true messages from God.

Jeremiah writes to the Jews who were taken captive to Babylon. Some false prophets were promising them a quick return, which went against what God had said through Jeremiah. The verses that follow say that their end would be remembered as a curse, and that God also knew about their wrongdoing. The Bible gives no further details about them.

Today we can learn to test what we hear in God's name. A pleasant message is not always true. Let us compare what is taught with all of Scripture, and pray for wisdom.
exp.45:21:
This verse says that Egypt, which was once thought to be strong, will now sound weak and frightened, like a snake that writhes and hisses while being attacked. An enemy army comes with axes, like woodcutters coming to clear a forest.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces that Babylon, coming from the north, will defeat Egypt. Many understand this to refer to Egypt's defeat before Nebuchadnezzar, and some connect it with the battle of Carchemish. The Egyptian soldiers trusted in their strength, but God showed that no human power stands above him.

For today: do not place your security in your money, your work, or your own strength. All of these can fail. Trust in God first and live with humility.
exp.37:23:
Zedekiah tells Jeremiah not to tell anyone what they discussed in private. If Jeremiah keeps it secret, they will not kill him. The phrase "Let no man know of these words" means that no one should find out about that conversation.

King Zedekiah is speaking, and he was afraid of his officials and of the Babylonians. Jeremiah had warned him that if he did not surrender, Jerusalem would be burned. The king wanted to hear from God, but he did not dare to obey in public. So he asks for silence and suggests to Jeremiah what to say if the officials ask questions.

For today: fear of other people can keep us from obeying God with courage. Let us ask him to give us faith to do what is right, even when it costs us, and to speak with truth and wisdom.
exp.40:9:
It says that Ishmael, after killing many, took captive all who had been left in Mizpah, including the king's daughters. These were people whom Nebuzaradan, commander of the Babylonian guard, had entrusted to Gedaliah. Ismael led them away with the intention of crossing over to the territory of the Ammonites, a neighboring people.

Context: the speaker is the narrator of the book of Jeremiah. Babylon had already destroyed Jerusalem, and Gedaliah had been appointed governor of those who remained. Ishmael murdered him through treachery. The Bible does not explain all his motives here; the text suggests he had ties to the Ammonite king, but does not detail it.

For today: violence and betrayal only bring more suffering to innocent people. When we face difficult times, let us seek God's will with humility and trust in Him, rather than settling things with resentment or ambition.
exp.4:3:
Here the prophet says: "I thought: surely these are poor people, lacking instruction; they act like fools because they do not know the way of the Lord, that is, what God commands and how he judges."

The quoted words in this explanation are not from the verse your reader sees, so I have translated the commentary around them rather than the wording itself. The phrase that means "have lost their reason" is not used in your verse, so I have left it out. "Poor" here seems to refer to simple folk without education.

Jeremiah speaks in the middle of a complaint to God. He sees that the people do not change, not even after punishment. At first he thinks the common people fail for lack of teaching. Then, in the next verse, he will go to the great men, but they too have broken the yoke, that is, they rebelled against God.

For today: learning God's word is important, but knowing it is not enough. Let us examine whether, besides knowing what God asks, we are willing to obey him and to receive his correction with humility.
exp.45:26:
Do not be afraid, God tells his people, and do not lose heart. He promises to rescue them from far away, that is, from the place where they are exiled, and also their children. He says that Jacob (another name for Israel) will return, will live in peace, will prosper, and no one will make him afraid.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. First he announces judgment on Egypt, which would be defeated by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. The Israelites lived under the weight of exile and the threat of foreign powers. God assures them that he will not abandon them: he will discipline his people, but he will not destroy them completely.

For today: when you feel weak or far from everything, remember that God remains faithful. You can speak to him honestly, ask him for comfort, and trust that he knows how to sustain you and lead you back to peace.
exp.6:23:
It says that the people did not listen to God or pay attention to him. Instead of obeying, they followed their own ideas, guided by a hard and evil heart. Paying attention with a willing heart to obey is what the verse's wording about the ear means; you can explain that the phrase refers to listening closely and being ready to obey. The "counsels" here are their own plans. Going backward and not forward means that instead of growing, they got worse.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, probably in the temple in Jerusalem. The people trusted in religious rituals, but they lived in disobedience. God reminds them that from the beginning he asked them for something deeper than sacrifices: that they listen to him and obey him. He sent them prophets again and again, and they ignored them.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we only fulfill our religious duties or whether we truly listen to God. This week, read a passage of the Bible calmly, ask God to speak to you, and decide to obey one concrete thing he shows you.
exp.14:10:
The Lord tells Jeremiah that surely what remains of him will turn out for good, that is, that his life will end in something good. He also promises that even the enemy will come to seek him and to plead with him in the difficult time and on the day of distress. The remnant, what is left over, is the part that survives.

Jeremiah has just complained to God: they curse him and see him as a man of quarrels, even though he never harmed them. Here God answers him with a personal promise. Translators and scholars understand this verse in several ways, since the Hebrew text is difficult, but almost all agree that it is a word of comfort for the faithful prophet in the midst of rejection.

When you suffer for doing what is right and feel alone, bring your complaint to God honestly, as Jeremiah did. He listens, answers, and promises to care for your future. Trust that the end of the one who is faithful to him is in his hands.
exp.19:14:
The explanation says that the man who brought the news to Jeremiah's father, "A man child is born unto thee," deserves a curse, because with that announcement he made him very glad. The phrase "brought tidings" means "brought news." It is a very strong cry, full of pain.

The speaker is the prophet Jeremiah. He had just been beaten and placed in the stocks for preaching God's message (Jeremiah 20:1-2). He is exhausted and discouraged. Even so, just before this, he had praised God, and then suddenly he falls into this complaint. The Bible shows his emotions without hiding them. This is not a teaching to curse others, but the sincere prayer of someone who is broken.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, do not pretend to be strong. Tell God honestly what you feel, as Jeremiah did. He listens, and you can also seek the support of trusted brothers and sisters.
exp.25:9:
When the princes of Judah heard about these things, they left the king's house and went up to the house of the Lord, and they took their seats at the entrance of the new gate of the Lord's house. This verse says that the leaders of Judah, the officials of the land, found out what was happening to Jeremiah. They left the king's palace, went up to the temple of the Lord, and took their seats at the entrance of the new gate, as if to hear the case and reach a decision.

Jeremiah had just announced in the temple that, if the people did not repent, Jerusalem would be destroyed as Shiloh had been. The priests, the prophets, and the people seized him and demanded his death. The officials came as authorities to judge. They would sit at the gates because legal matters were usually handled there, although the text gives no further details.

When someone tells us something uncomfortable, we should not react with anger. Before we judge, let us listen calmly, seek the truth, and compare what is said with what the Word of God teaches.
exp.32:0:
This verse says that God spoke again to Jeremiah. The phrase "the word of the Lord came" means that the message came from God. The phrase "the second time" shows that he had already spoken before, in chapter 32. The phrase "while he was yet shut up in the court of the prison" means that Jeremiah was still being held in a courtyard inside the palace. The word "saying" introduces what God is about to say.

God speaks, and Jeremiah is the one who receives it. The prophet was in prison for announcing that Jerusalem would fall to Babylon, something that troubled the authorities. Even so, God did not abandon him. He spoke to him in the middle of the crisis, and the message that follows brings hope and restoration for the people.

For today: even when you feel shut in by problems, God is not far away. You can pray with confidence, expect his voice, and listen to him through his Word, even when your situation seems to have no way out.
exp.36:3:
This verse says that Jeremiah was moving freely among the people, going in and out, because they had not yet put him in prison. The phrase "house of the prison" simply means the prison.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book. Jerusalem was under siege by the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). King Zedekiah did not obey God, yet he still asked Jeremiah to pray for them. The narrator makes clear that Jeremiah was still free, and it will soon be seen that they would soon imprison him. It is also mentioned that the army of Egypt came and the Chaldeans withdrew for a time, which gave the people false hope.

For today: we often seek God only when we are in trouble, without wanting to obey him the rest of the time. God invites us to listen to his word always, not only in crisis, and to obey it sincerely.
exp.11:1:
It says that God has allowed the wicked to prosper, like trees that are planted, take root, grow, and bear fruit. With their mouths they speak often of God. But their heart is far from Him. "Kidneys" is an old way of speaking of the most inner part of a person: their thoughts, desires, and emotions. "They act treacherously" means they behave with betrayal.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks, addressing God. He is confused and hurt, because he sees that false people live well, while he, who serves God, suffers opposition. He acknowledges that God is just, yet he dares to ask Him honestly. In the end, God answers him, but that comes later.

For today: You can bring your doubts to God with honesty, without pretending. And examine your own heart: let your faith not be only words, but a real closeness to Him.
exp.50:10:
He tells them to get ready for war: to polish the arrows and raise up the shields. God himself has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes so that they will attack Babylon and destroy it. This is the Lord's vengeance, that is, justice for what Babylon did against his temple in Jerusalem.

Jeremiah announces this message to a people in exile, or about to go into exile. Babylon seemed unconquerable, but it had destroyed the temple and oppressed Judah. The text presents God as the one who directs history and uses other nations to carry out his judgment. Historians know that Media and Persia played a part in Babylon's fall, although the details are explained in several different ways.

For today: when evil seems powerful and unstoppable, remember that God sees injustice and has the final word. Trust in his justice, without taking revenge into your own hands.
exp.3:30:
He says the prophet hears a cry of pain, like that of a woman giving birth for the first time. It is the "daughter of Zion," that is, Jerusalem and its people, who stretches out her hands asking for help and says that she faints because of the murderers, that is, the killers who have come to destroy. The word "faint" means that she has no strength left.

Jeremiah is the one speaking, announcing God's judgment for Judah's unfaithfulness. Earlier, the people tried to dress up and make themselves attractive to win allies, but it was in vain. Many understand that the invasion comes from the north, and it is later identified with Babylon. Jeremiah feels deep pain over what he announces.

For today: let us not wait until anguish comes to turn back to God. Today we can seek him with sincerity, instead of trusting in appearances or in human supports that fail.
exp.8:13:
They say that the people not only abandoned God's law, but also followed whatever their own heart devised. They also followed the Baals, who were false gods of the peoples of Canaan, tied to rain and harvests. That worship had been taught to them by their fathers. The word "imagination" here speaks of stubbornness and one's own desires, not of fantasy.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He explains why the land was laid waste: the people disobeyed his voice and his law. This verse shows the root of the problem, which was following their own impulses and inherited customs. That is why the judgment announced afterward comes.

For today: examine whether what you do comes from the Word of God or only from your desires and from what has "always been done" in your family. Compare it with the Bible, keep what is good, and humbly set aside what does not please God.
exp.28:5:
They say that the exiles in Babylon should build families: marry, have sons and daughters, and help their sons to marry too. "Take ye wives" and "take wives for your sons" refer to arranging marriages for their children, as was customary then, and "be increased, and not diminished" means that they should not shrink in number.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a letter to the Jews taken captive to Babylon. Some prophets were saying that the exile would be short. God tells them to live normally, because the stay would be long (the text speaks of seventy years ahead).

For today: even if you are in a difficult season or one you did not choose, God invites you to live with hope, to build relationships, and to sow life where you are, without becoming paralyzed while waiting for everything to change.
exp.24:5:
This verse is a call not to worship other gods. The phrase "go after" (in the sense of following or going behind something) is rewritten here as "follow," and bowing down in worship is simply the act of bowing down. The phrase "the work of your hands" refers to the idols that people made. God promises that if they give that up, he will do them no harm.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Judah. God had sent them prophets again and again, and they did not listen. He asked them to turn away from their evil ways and to keep living in the land he had given them. The next verse shows that they did not obey, and for that reason judgment would come.

For today: an idol can be anything that takes the place of God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Today you can ask yourself what has been capturing your heart, and place it back in God's hands through a sincere prayer.
exp.34:2:
Here Jeremiah tells that he obeyed God's command. He gathered Jaazaniah, his brothers, all his sons, and the whole family of the Rechabites.

Jeremiah speaks, and he does so by the command of the LORD, in the days of King Jehoiakim of Judah. God wanted to use the Rechabites as an example. Later it is seen that they were faithful to the command of their ancestor not to drink wine, and that faithfulness stood in contrast with the disobedience of the people of Judah.

For today: God values steady obedience. We can ask ourselves whether we are as firm in obeying God as others are in keeping their commitments. Today you can choose one concrete way to obey him better.
exp.10:17:
It says that God showed Jeremiah something he did not know, and that because of this he came to understand it. Then God made him see what his enemies were doing, that is, their actions and hidden plans.

Jeremiah speaks as God's prophet in Judah. The verses that follow show that some of his own people were plotting to kill him because of his messages. He was like an innocent lamb who suspected nothing, until God opened his eyes. Some scholars think these were people from his hometown, but this verse only speaks of "they."

Today we can ask God for wisdom to see reality clearly, without naivety or bitterness. When someone hurts or deceives us, we can do what Jeremiah did: bring our case to God in prayer, and trust that he judges with justice.
exp.29:12:
It says that no one pleads the people's cause to heal them, and that there are no remedies that bring results. It is an image of a serious wound: no one tends to it, and no medicine cures it. "Thy cause" means to defend or take charge of a case; "healing" is restoration to health; "healing medicines" are remedies that truly work.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the people of Israel and Judah, who faced the punishment of exile for their sin. God describes their condition as a wound that cannot be healed by human means, and says that even their allies will not help them. But in verse 17 he promises to restore their health. He first shows the seriousness of the situation, so that the people will stop trusting in false help.

For today: when your problem has no human solution, do not fill yourself with excuses or false remedies. Honestly acknowledge your need and turn to God, who can heal what no one else can.
exp.47:29:
God says he knows very well the rage of Moab, that is, its fury and its arrogance. But that anger will accomplish nothing. Its lies, that is, its boasting and false assurances, will not help it either. The phrase "it shall not be so" means that what Moab intends will not come to pass.

Here God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, in a message of judgment against Moab, a nation neighboring Israel. The preceding text speaks of its pride and haughtiness. God does not overlook that attitude. But afterward we see that God also grieves over the ruin that is coming, for he says he will weep for Moab.

Today we can remember that pride and empty words do not protect us. If we have trusted in our own strength or in excuses, it is wise to acknowledge this with humility before God, who sees the heart, and to seek his mercy.
exp.3:0:
God speaks to Israel and says: if you truly want to return, come back to me. If you put away your abominations from my sight, meaning the idols and practices that God detests, you will no longer wander from place to place, without direction or security.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had turned away from God and were seeking other gods. The verses that follow call for a sincere commitment: swearing by God in truth, with judgment and righteousness, and preparing the heart the way one prepares a field, without sowing among thorns.

For today: returning to God is not only feeling sorry, but letting go of whatever has taken his place. Ask him to show you one specific thing you should leave behind, and take that step today with sincerity.
exp.24:21:
This verse continues a list of nations that must drink the cup of God's anger. Here all the kings of Tyre and of Sidon are named, important cities of the Phoenician port, and also the kings of the islands "beyond the sea," that is, coastal lands of the Mediterranean.

The prophet Jeremiah, sent by God, speaks around 605 B.C. God announces that Babylon will bring judgment, first on Judah and then on many nations. The neighboring peoples will also answer for their pride and their wickedness. Scholars do not agree on exactly which islands are meant.

For today: God rules over all nations, not only over his own people. This invites us to live with humility, not to trust in power or riches, and to place our trust in God, who is just and patient.
exp.17:17:
Jeremiah's enemies say: "Come, let us devise devices against him." They think they do not need his message, because there will always be priests to teach the law, wise men to give counsel, and prophets to speak. "Let us smite him with the tongue" means attacking him with words, accusing or slandering him, and "let us not give heed to any of his words" means they will not pay attention to him.

The speakers are ordinary people who reject Jeremiah's message. He had announced judgment because of Judah's unfaithfulness, and instead of repenting, they prefer to silence him. Afterward, Jeremiah prays to God and reminds him that he had interceded on their behalf.

For today: when a correction makes us uncomfortable, it is easy to attack the messenger. Let us ask God for humility to examine what we hear, and if we are criticized for speaking the truth in love, let us bring that burden to prayer, as Jeremiah did.
exp.26:4:
God says that he made the earth, the people, and the animals. He did it with his great power and with his outstretched arm, which is a way of speaking of his strength in action. Furthermore, he gave it to whomever seemed meet to him, that is, to whomever he was pleased or willed.

Jehovah speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. Envoys from neighboring kingdoms had come to Jerusalem, probably to plan a rebellion against Babylon. God orders them to tell their kings that he is the Creator and that he decides to whom he gives dominion. Therefore, for now, Nebuchadnezzar would have that power.

For today: trust that God remains Lord over all, even when the world seems confused or unjust. Instead of depending on your own plans or on the powerful, pray, surrender to his will, and rest in his sovereignty.
exp.27:3:
It says that God will bring back Jeconiah, king of Judah, and all the exiles who were carried off to Babylon. The sentence "I will bring again" means the same as "I will bring back"; the carried-off ones are those taken away into exile; the "yoke" is the heavy burden of control that Babylon put on Judah. The promise is that this yoke will be broken.

The one speaking here is Hananiah, a prophet who presents himself as a spokesman for God, and he says it in the temple in front of the people. Jeremiah had announced that Babylon would rule for a long time. Later, the text shows that God had not sent Hananiah and that his message was false (Jeremiah 28:15-16). Hananiah offered quick relief, but it was not true.

For today: not every hopeful message comes from God. Compare what you hear with the Bible and ask for wisdom. True hope does not ignore reality, but rests on what God has actually said.
exp.49:13:
It says that all the archers must surround Babylon and shoot without holding back arrows. "Put yourselves in array" means get ready; "bend the bow" means draw the bow; "arrows" are the shafts shot from the bow; "spare no arrows" means do not hold back. The reason given is that Babylon has sinned against the Lord.

It is a prophecy by Jeremiah about the fall of Babylon, the empire that had destroyed Jerusalem. God speaks of judgment against a proud and cruel nation. The text does not clearly name the attackers here; many think of the Medes and Persians, and others also see a broader meaning. It stresses that this is God's justice, not simply human revenge.

For today: God sees injustice and does not overlook it. We can rest in the fact that he judges with justice, and so we do not need to repay evil with evil. Rather, we can pray for justice and live with humility.
exp.35:14:
The princes, that is, the leaders and officials of the kingdom, ask Baruch to sit down and read the scroll aloud, so that they themselves may hear it. The phrase "in our ears" means "before us." Baruch obeys and reads.

Baruch was Jeremiah's secretary, and he had written down Jeremiah's messages from God. He had already read the scroll to the people in the temple. Micaiah told what he heard, and the princes sent for him. Notice the respectful treatment: they invite him to sit down and they listen carefully. Afterward they become frightened, because they understand that the message is serious and that the king must know about it.

Today we can do the same with the Bible: listen to it calmly, without rush and with humility. Set aside a quiet moment, read a passage aloud, and ask yourself what God is asking of you.
exp.10:5:
In this verse, God orders Jeremiah to proclaim aloud, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, the words of the covenant. Proclaim means to announce publicly. Hear, and do them mean to listen and to put them into practice. Hearing is not enough: God asks for obedience.

The one speaking is God, and he gives the task to the prophet Jeremiah. The covenant is the commitment God made with Israel when he brought them out of Egypt: they would obey, and he would be their God. Jeremiah had already given his answer. The verses that follow explain why the message was urgent: their ancestors did not obey, and the people were still walking the same path.

For today: hearing God should lead us to act. Choose a teaching from the Bible that you already know, and decide today on one concrete step to live it out.
exp.1:14:
The young lions roared against Israel, lifted up their voice with force, and left the land desolate. Its cities were burned and had no one living in them. For "roared," the verse uses the word "roared" itself; for "inhabitant," it is the one who lives in a place.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on the words of God. He has just accused the people of two wrongs: leaving God, the fountain of living water, and digging broken cisterns. The "lions" are usually understood as enemy nations, such as Assyria or Egypt, though scholars debate exactly which ones. The passage presents the ruin as the consequence of turning away from God.

For today: when you feel emptiness or face problems, examine where you have placed your trust. Things that cannot sustain you, such as success or money, break apart. Return to God, who does satisfy.
exp.49:28:
God calls for archers to be gathered, all those who draw the bow, to surround Babylon with a camp, so that none escape. The phrase "to draw the bow" is what "bend the bow" means here, and "to camp" is to set up camp with an army around a city. God commands that Babylon be repaid according to what she did, because she rose up in pride against the Lord, "the Holy One of Israel."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, addressing the peoples who would attack Babylon. That nation had been cruel to Judah and had destroyed the temple. The text presents her as proud before God, and for that reason she receives judgment. Those who escape carry the news back to Zion.

For today: pride, the belief that we do not need God, puts us in danger. Today you can ask God for a humble heart and trust that he does justice in his own time, without you having to take revenge.
exp.47:13:
Jeremiah asks Moab a question that sounds like a serious mockery: "How do you dare to say that you are mighty and strong men for the war?" In other words, what right do they have to boast of their strength when disaster is already coming?

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah against Moab, a people who lived next to Israel. Moab trusted in its army, its riches, and its god Chemosh (Chêmos). God declares that none of these things will save them. The verses that follow say that their best young men will fall and that ruin is near.

For today: our strength, our money, or our abilities can fail. It is wise to examine what we truly trust in. We can work hard, but without placing our hearts in ourselves, and instead placing them in God, who sustains our lives.
exp.30:4:
It says that the people will once again plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria. Those who plant will enjoy the fruit of their labor. The sentence "they shall make common use of them" means they will be free to eat from what they planted. In the law, the fruit of a newly planted tree was not eaten until the fifth year (Leviticus 19:23-25), so this speaks of waiting and reward.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He addresses Israel, the northern kingdom, whose capital was Samaria and which had been taken into exile. In the middle of pain, God promises restoration, because he loves them with an everlasting love. The vines speak of peace, stability, and normal life returning.

For today: when you feel that what was lost will not come back, trust that God can restore hope. Keep sowing with patience in your family, your work, and your faith, knowing that God is faithful and can bring fruit in its time.
exp.37:14:
Jeremiah answers King Zedekiah with frankness. He tells him that if he reveals what God is thinking, the king might put him to death, and that if he gives him advice, the king will not heed it. The word "declare" means to make something known; "hearken" here means to actually listen and follow.

Zedekiah was the last king of Judah, and Babylon was already besieging Jerusalem. Shortly before this, the officials had thrown Jeremiah into a cistern for announcing the defeat. Now the king calls for him in secret, and the prophet, with good reason, is wary: he had already spoken before without anyone paying attention. Even so, the king immediately swears to protect him.

Today we can learn to be honest even when it costs us. And we can also ask ourselves whether, when we seek advice, we are truly willing to act on what we hear, even when it is not what we hoped for.
exp.5:23:
It says that the people of Judah heard news of the enemy army coming from the north, and fear left them paralyzed. Their hands being "gone limp" means they became weak and without strength, as if disarmed. Anguish seized them with an intense pain, compared to the pains of a woman in labor.

Here the prophet Jeremiah speaks, identifying himself with his people. God had already warned that an invader would come from the north, as a consequence of Judah turning away from Him. Many scholars see Babylon here, though the text does not yet name it. The verse shows the fear that comes when the warning is ignored.

For today: do not wait for a crisis to return to God. Heed His warnings with humility, and when fear leaves you paralyzed, bring it to Him in prayer.
exp.30:39:
This verse says that the whole area of the valley where dead bodies and ashes were, and the fields as far as the Kidron brook and the Horse Gate on the east, will be set apart for God. "Holy" means set apart for the Lord. And it will never again be uprooted or destroyed.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. He announces the restoration of Jerusalem after the punishment. The valley is probably the Hinnom Valley, a place associated with death and idolatry, although some scholars debate this. Even the most defiled place will be made clean. Some see a future fulfillment here, while others see a spiritual promise in the new covenant.

For today: God can make holy even what seems dirtiest or most lost in your life. Give him your story, including your most painful parts, and trust that he restores and sustains.
exp.24:31:
It says that God's judgment will spread from one people to another, like a huge storm rising from the most distant places in the world. The words for "people" and "the farthest corners of the earth" are not used in the verse; the sentence about them is removed. "The Lord of hosts" is a title that shows God as the Lord of all power.

Jeremiah speaks on God's behalf, probably shortly before Babylon came to rule the region. Before this chapter, the people of Judah had for years refused the calls to turn back to God. Here the message widens: God, as Judge of the whole earth, calls all the nations to account, and their leaders will also be held responsible.

For today: God takes justice seriously and does not overlook evil. You can examine your life with humility, correct what He shows you, and trust that He is a righteous Judge.
exp.26:13:
Here God warns the people not to listen to the prophets who were saying, "You will not have to serve the king of Babylon." The sentence that quotes their words is rendered here in plain terms, and the phrase about prophesying falsehood means that they speak falsehood in God's name. According to God, those messages did not come from Him.

Jeremiah, sent by God, speaks in the time of King Zedekiah of Judah. Babylon already controlled the region. Jeremiah urged the people to accept that yoke, that is, to submit, in order to save lives. The false prophets offered easy hope and said that everything would soon return to normal. But God's message was harder and more true.

For today: do not believe something just because it sounds pleasant. Compare what you hear with the Bible, pray asking for discernment, and accept God's truth even when it costs you, because His correction seeks your good.
exp.15:14:
It says that God will do something so great that people will swear by him in new words: "The Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel out of the land of the north." The word "north" refers to Babylon, from where the people would return. God promises to gather them from all the places where they were scattered and bring them back to the land he gave to their ancestors.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. The people had worshiped false gods, and for that reason God announces the exile. But in the midst of judgment he promises a new beginning. Just as the exodus from Egypt was the great memory of his rescue, the future return would be another act of salvation just as memorable.

For today: God disciplines, but he does not completely abandon. If you are going through the consequences of your mistakes, do not lose hope. Return to him sincerely, because he is faithful to restore and to make a new start.
exp.24:11:
God says that when the seventy years of service to Babylon are complete, He will call the king of Babylon and his nation to account for their wickedness. The sentence that explains one of the source phrases is rewritten here: God will come to judge them. He also says that the land of the Chaldeans will become a desolation forever, meaning a total and lasting ruin.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, around the year 605 BC. Judah had disobeyed God, and Babylon would be the instrument to discipline her. But Babylon was also responsible for its cruelty and pride. Many understand that "forever" speaks of a definitive fall, though some see it as prophetic language of great force.

For today: God sees injustice and does not leave it unanswered. We can rest in the fact that He judges with righteousness, so we do not need to take revenge. Entrust your grievances to God and seek to live with humility.
exp.19:0:
Pashur, son of Immer, was a priest who served as the chief governor, or the leading officer, in the house of the Lord. One day he heard Jeremiah speaking out the message God had given him.

The explanation here is that the title used for Pashur does not mean he was a king's son, but someone with authority, like the head or overseer of the temple.

The book of Jeremiah tells what happened after the prophet declared God's judgment on Jerusalem because of its disobedience. Pashur, because of his religious office, was responsible for keeping order in the temple. Instead of listening with humility, he responded with anger, as the verses that follow show: he struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks.

For today: holding a religious position or being respected does not make us immune to error. Let us ask God for a humble heart to listen to his Word, even when it troubles us or corrects us.
exp.47:14:
It says that Moab was destroyed. Its cities were laid waste, and its finest young men were led to the slaughter. The one who declares it is the King, the Lord of hosts, that is, the Lord who rules over all power.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks here, passing on God's word about Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. Moab trusted in its god Chemosh and in its military strength, and it boasted of being brave. The text announces that this confidence would not save it. Some historical details about how this judgment was fulfilled are not entirely clear.

Today, this verse reminds us that neither power, nor pride, nor idols can give us true security. It is worth asking ourselves what we truly trust in, and placing our hope in God, the only King who never fails.
exp.24:20:
This verse continues a list of nations. God names Edom, Moab, and the children of Ammon, neighboring peoples of Israel, located to the east and southeast of the Jordan River. The phrase "children of Ammon" refers to the Ammonites. In this list, all are called to drink the cup of God's wrath (v. 15).

The prophet Jeremiah, sent by God, speaks around 605 B.C., when Babylon was growing in power. God announces that his judgment would reach Judah first and then many neighboring nations. These peoples had their own history of pride and violence.

For today: God rules over all nations, not only over his people. We can live with humility, remembering that we all answer to him, and trust that his justice is perfect, even when we do not fully understand it.
exp.22:21:
If those prophets had stood "in my secret council," that is, in God's intimate counsel, they would have announced his true word to the people. In this way they would have helped them turn from their evil way and from the wickedness of their deeds. The phrase "had caused to hear" means they would have made the people listen.

God speaks through Jeremiah at a time when Judah had strayed. God accuses prophets who spoke comfortable and false messages without having been sent by him. It is clear that a true message does not lull the conscience to sleep, but calls for change.

For today: before accepting or repeating a spiritual message, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to God and invites you to correct your course. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and spend time with God in prayer and reading, so that you come to know his voice.
exp.51:33:
The explanation says that the king of Babylon gave Jehoiachin a daily provision of food, every day, for as long as he lived, until his death. The word for this daily allowance means a portion of food or sustenance. The phrase about receiving what was needed day by day means that he received what he needed each day.

The book ends with this historical detail, probably added by whoever gathered the words of Jeremiah. It tells that Evil-Merodach, king of Babylon, released Jehoiachin, king of Judah, after about 37 years in prison. Although he remained in exile, he was treated with kindness. Many see here a sign that the line of David had not disappeared, although the Bible does not explain this in detail at this point.

For today: even in times of loss or hard consequences, God can give small reliefs and daily sustenance. Learn to recognize and be thankful for those everyday provisions, and trust that God is still at work in your story, even when the outlook seems dark.
exp.20:5:
It says that God himself will strike the inhabitants of Jerusalem. A great plague will kill people and animals alike. "Inhabitants" means those who live in the city, and "plague" is a deadly disease that spreads quickly from person to person.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah. King Zedekiah had asked for a favorable word while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. God answers with judgment, because the people had turned away from Him. Even so, the passage ends by offering a way of life and a way of death: there was still a choice to be made.

For today: let us not harden our hearts when God corrects us. If He shows us a mistake, we can listen and turn back to Him with humility, because His warning is also an invitation to choose the path of life.
exp.0:13:
God tells Jeremiah that a calamity will come from the north. (The word "north" in the old wording is an archaic term for the north wind, so this is just the direction.) This disaster will be unleashed, like something released all at once, and it will fall on all the inhabitants of the land, that is, on the people of Judah and its cities.

The LORD speaks to Jeremiah, who had just been called as a prophet. He shows him the vision of a boiling pot tilting from the north. The verses that follow explain that God will call peoples from the north, and they say the reason is the idolatry and disobedience of Judah. Many understand this to refer to Babylon, although the text here does not name it.

For today: God warns before he acts. Let us not ignore the warnings; if anything in our lives is pulling us away from him, let us return to God sincerely, today.
exp.27:14:
Jeremiah speaks directly to Hananiah, another prophet, and tells him that God did not send him. Hananiah had made the people trust in a lie. The old spelling of the word "a" is not needed here, and the phrase "the face of the earth" is what the text means by the earth's surface.

Jeremiah had carried a wooden yoke to show that Judah must submit to Babylon. Hananiah broke it and promised that God would soon free the people. But God told Jeremiah to say that the yoke would be replaced with one of iron. Hananiah offered false hope, and the text tells us that he died that same year.

Today we can ask whether what we hear, even when it is pleasant, agrees with the Word of God. Not every comforting message comes from Him. It is wise to compare what we hear with the Bible, to pray with humility, and to prefer the truth, even when it costs us.
exp.2:2:
God had held back the rains because of the sin of the people. The "late rain" (the spring rain) was the one needed for the harvest to ripen. The people also had a "whore's forehead," that is, a brazenness typical of an unfaithful woman who no longer feels shame for what she does. And "you refused to be ashamed" means that they refused to admit their error.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to Judah. He compares the people to an unfaithful wife who went after other "lovers," that is, other gods. The drought appears as a warning from God, who still keeps inviting them: "return to me."

For today: when we feel that something is drying up in our lives, it is worth asking ourselves humbly whether there is something we should confess. God does not call us to humiliate us, but to restore us. Today we can return to Him with sincerity.
exp.19:17:
Here Jeremiah asks: why was I born? Only to see suffering and anguish, and to have my life consumed in shame? The sentence about the word for womb is explained in plain terms: it refers to the mother's body where the child is formed. "Toil" means hardship or exhaustion. "Shame" means mockery and disgrace.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks. God had called him to announce judgment, and the people mocked him. Shortly before this, the priest Pashhur struck him and put him in the stocks. Jeremiah, worn out, pours out his pain before God. The Bible does not hide this complaint, and many see it as a sincere prayer, not as a lack of faith.

When you are discouraged, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, as Jeremiah did. Then look for someone you trust who can stand with you and listen.
exp.39:2:
The verse says that the Lord did what he had warned he would do. He has brought the punishment, and the reason is plain: the people sinned against God and did not obey his voice, so this disaster came upon them.

The speaker is Nebuzaradan, the captain of the Babylonian guard, who is addressing Jeremiah after the fall of Jerusalem. It is surprising that a foreign officer would acknowledge that the Lord had announced all this. Some think he knew of Jeremiah's words, though the Bible does not explain how he learned of them. He then frees Jeremiah from his chains.

God speaks to us with patience, and his warnings are real. Today we can ask ourselves what correction we have ignored, and obey it humbly before the consequences arrive.
exp.48:37:
He says God will set his "seat", that is, his throne, in Elam, as one who comes to rule and to judge. There he will remove the king and the princes, that is, the rulers and leaders. "Jehovah" is God's name in this older version.

God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah, within messages addressed to several nations. Elam lay east of Babylon, in the region of present-day Iran. The text presents its fall as a judgment from God. But the following verse adds a promise of restoration "in the latter days". Scholars debate how and when this was fulfilled.

For today: God is the true King, and no human power lasts forever. We can trust that he judges with justice, but he also offers hope. Today you can hand over to him your worries about rulers and injustices.
exp.28:27:
It says that Jeremiah sent a message to the exiles in Babylon: the captivity will be long. So they should build houses and live in them, and plant gardens and eat their fruit.

The speaker here is Shemaiah, a false prophet who was in Babylon. From there he wrote to Zephaniah, the priest in Jerusalem, complaining about Jeremiah. He quotes Jeremiah's letter (chapter 29) as if it were a nuisance. For Shemaiah, that advice discouraged the hope of a quick return. Jeremiah was telling them that God would care for them even there.

For today: when you go through a hard season that will not end soon, do not put your life on pause. With God's help, keep working, caring for your family, and serving where you are, while still trusting his promises.
exp.45:6:
It is a question that God asks to draw attention. It compares a great army advancing with a river that rises and overflows. The Hebrew word for "rises" means that it lifts itself up and spreads out, like the Nile when it floods.

Jeremiah speaks on behalf of the LORD about Egypt. Pharaoh Necho led his army toward the Euphrates, and there he was defeated by Babylon, as the verses before this one show. Egypt boasted of being unstoppable, but God shows that its strength was not secure. Scholars generally agree about this battle, although some details are debated.

For today: We can be impressed by power, money, or success, and put our trust in them. But all of that can fall in a day. Let us place our trust in God, who does remain.
exp.40:3:
This verse tells us that a day had passed since the killing of Gedaliah, and that still no one had found out. In other words, Ishmael's crime was still hidden. The sentences that explain the wording of the older text are left out here, since the verse you are reading uses different words.

The book of Jeremiah recounts here what happened after the fall of Jerusalem. Babylon had appointed Gedaliah as governor over those who remained in the land. Ishmael, who was of the royal family, betrayed him and killed him in Mizpah. The narrator, who describes these events, shows us how deceit and violence could stay hidden for a time. Soon after, eighty pilgrims arrive in mourning, and Ishmael deceives them with false tears.

For today: what is hidden does not stay hidden forever, nor does it escape God. If we are tempted to conceal something wrong, it is better to confess it and act in truth, because God sees everything and forgives the one who repents.
exp.22:37:
The verse says that God had commanded the people not to use the expression "The burden of the Lord," yet they kept saying it. So God answers with judgment. The word "burden" comes from a Hebrew word that can mean a physical weight or a prophetic message.

The Lord speaks through Jeremiah. Some people used "the burden of the Lord" to mock, or to give authority to their own ideas, and the false prophets claimed to speak on God's behalf when he had not spoken to them. Many understand that the expression had become a play on words and a way of showing contempt for the true word of God. God warns them that treating his message this way will bring serious consequences.

Today we can be careful about how we speak of God. Before saying "God told me" or using spiritual phrases, it is worth examining whether we are honoring his word or only defending our own desires.
exp.15:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Jeremiah. "The word of the Lord came also unto me" is a way of saying that a message from God reached him. The word "Lord" here stands for God's name in the Old Testament. At this point the message itself has not yet been given; the verse only announces that God is about to speak.

The speaker is Jeremiah, a prophet who lived in Judah before the fall of Jerusalem. A phrase like this often begins a new message from God. In the verses that follow, God asks him to do something very hard: not to marry or have children, as a sign of the difficult times coming upon the people.

For today: God speaks, and listening to him is the first step. Before asking him for answers, we can set aside a moment to read his Word attentively and with a willingness to obey, even when it is not easy.

sum.46: God announces through Jeremiah that an invasion coming from the north, like a flood, will destroy the Philistines and reach as far as Gaza, Ashkelon, Tyre and Sidon. There will be so much terror that fathers will be unable to help their children. It is God's judgment: his sword will not rest until it accomplishes what he has commanded.
sum.29: God tells Jeremiah to write down his words. Although Israel and Judah are suffering great distress because of their sins, God promises to break their yoke, heal their wounds, and bring them back to their land. He will punish their oppressors, raise up a ruler from among them, and renew their relationship: "You will be my people, and I will be your God."
sum.40: Ishmael, a member of the royal family, murders Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, and kills many others as well, including pilgrims who had come to worship. He then takes the people captive, but Johanan catches up with him and rescues the people. Out of fear of the Chaldeans, they make preparations to flee to Egypt.
sum.48: God announces judgment on Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Hazor, and Elam for their pride and for trusting in their riches, their mountains, or their strength. No nation can escape when God decides to act. Even so, he promises to restore Ammon and Elam, and to care for the orphans and widows of Edom.
sum.25: God commands Jeremiah to warn the people in the temple that, if they do not repent, Jerusalem will become like Shiloh. The priests and prophets want to kill him, but the officials and the elders defend him, recalling Micah. God protects Jeremiah through Ahikam, and it is taught that God calls people to repentance.
sum.44: In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, God speaks through Jeremiah to Baruch, his scribe, who was worn out and full of sorrow. God tells him that He is going to tear down what He Himself built, so Baruch should not seek greatness for himself. Even so, He promises that his life will be spared wherever he goes.
sum.49: God announces through Jeremiah that Babylon will fall along with its idols, because it has been filled with pride and has mistreated his people. Israel and Judah, like lost sheep, will return weeping to seek God, and he will forgive them. God, their strong Redeemer, will defend their cause.
sum.14: God tells Jeremiah that the people of Judah will be punished for their rebellion, even if Moses and Samuel were to plead on their behalf. Jeremiah complains about the pain and rejection he suffers, but he finds joy in God's word. God calls him to return to Him and promises to make him strong, like a wall of bronze, and to rescue him.
sum.23: Jeremiah sees two baskets of figs: some very good, and others so bad they could not be eaten. God says the good figs are the exiles taken to Babylon, whom he will watch over, bring back to their land, and give a heart to know him. The bad figs are King Zedekiah and the people who stayed behind or fled to Egypt, and they will face judgment.
sum.12: God commanded Jeremiah to buy a linen belt and hide it by the Euphrates. Later he went back and found it rotten and good for nothing. Through this, God showed that the pride and idolatry of Judah and Jerusalem would leave them worthless, even though he had bound them to himself. He warned them to humble themselves before punishment and exile came, and Jeremiah wept for them.
sum.10: God tells Jeremiah to remind Judah of the covenant he made with their ancestors, but the people broke it and followed false gods such as Baal, so God announces punishment and will not listen to their cry. In addition, the people of Anathoth plan to kill Jeremiah, and God declares that they will be judged.
sum.22: God condemns the false shepherds and prophets who scattered his people with lies and false peace, and he promises to gather his remnant and raise up a righteous King from the line of David. His word is like fire and a hammer, and it is different from invented dreams. Those who twist it will face judgment.
sum.30: In Jeremiah 31, God promises to bring his scattered people back home, turn their weeping into joy, and rebuild them with everlasting love. He announces a new covenant: he will put his law in their hearts, everyone will know him, and he will forgive their sins. He also assures them that Israel will not be rejected forever.
sum.45: God announces through Jeremiah that the mighty army of Egypt will be defeated by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Neither its strength nor its gods will be able to save it. But to his people Israel he says, "Do not be afraid, for I am with you," and he promises to rescue them from captivity and discipline them without destroying them completely.
sum.39: Nabuzaradan, commander of the Babylonian guard, sets Jeremiah free and lets him choose where he wants to live. Jeremiah stays with Gedaliah, the governor appointed by Babylon, and many Jews return to the land. Johanan warns that Ismael intends to kill Gedaliah, but Gedaliah does not believe him.
sum.18: God tells Jeremiah to buy a clay jar and to take the elders of the people to the Valley of Hinnom. There he announces judgment on Jerusalem for its idolatry and for sacrificing innocent children. Jeremiah breaks the jar as a sign that the people will be shattered, and then he repeats the message in the temple: they would not listen to God.
sum.28: Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon: build houses, plant gardens, raise families, and seek the welfare of the city, because God promises to bring them back after seventy years, with plans for peace. He also warns them against false prophets, and God announces punishment for them and for Shemaiah.
sum.2: God compares the unfaithfulness of Israel and Judah to a wife who leaves her husband, yet still calls them to return, because he is merciful and does not keep his anger forever. He promises to restore them, give them good shepherds, and gather his people together. In the end, the people acknowledge their sin and declare that salvation is found only in God.
sum.33: While Babylon was attacking Jerusalem, Jeremiah warned King Zedekiah that the city would fall and that he himself would be taken away as a prisoner, though he would die in peace. The people had set their Hebrew servants free, but then they enslaved them again, breaking their covenant with God. Because of this, God says that they will receive "liberty" to face the sword, famine, and plague.
sum.34: God told Jeremiah to offer wine to the Rechabites, but they refused, because they faithfully keep the command of their ancestor Jonadab to live in tents and not drink wine. God uses their example to rebuke Judah, which did not obey his prophets, and he announces punishment for Judah, but he promises that the family of Jonadab will always serve him.
sum.3: God calls Judah and Jerusalem to turn back to Him wholeheartedly and to give up their wickedness, or an enemy army will come from the north to destroy the land. Jeremiah is distressed by the suffering he sees coming, and God explains that the people are foolish when it comes to doing evil. Even so, He promises not to bring a complete end to them.
sum.42: When Jeremiah finishes delivering God's message, the proud leaders accuse him of lying, and they take all the rest of Judah off to Egypt, disobeying the Lord. While they are in Tahpanhes, God tells Jeremiah to hide stones there and announce that Nebuchadnezzar will come to conquer Egypt and burn its gods. No one escapes God's judgment by running away from his word.
sum.19: Pashur, a chief priest, struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks because of his message. Jeremiah told him that Babylon would carry Judah off into exile. Then Jeremiah, worn down by the mockery, admitted that he could not keep silent about God's word. He trusted that God was with him, and he ended by cursing the day he was born.
sum.11: Jeremiah asks God why the wicked prosper. God answers that even greater trials await him, including betrayal by his own family. God laments that his people will be destroyed by their enemies, but he promises mercy and restoration. Whoever learns his ways will be blessed, and whoever refuses to obey will be uprooted.
sum.27: Hananiah prophesies that God will break the yoke of Babylon within two years. But Jeremiah replies that true prophets used to announce judgment, and that a prophet of peace will be known as genuine only if his words come true. Hananiah then breaks the wooden yoke, and God announces iron yokes in its place. Jeremiah tells him that God did not send him, and Hananiah dies that same year.
sum.9: God warns Israel not to imitate the nations or fear their idols, because they are the work of human hands, mute and powerless. Only Jehovah is the living God, the Creator of all things, and Jeremiah sees judgment coming upon Judah. He acknowledges that a person does not direct his own steps, and he asks to be corrected with justice.
sum.47: God announces judgment on Moab: its cities will be destroyed because it trusted in its riches and in its god Chemosh, and it grew proud against the LORD. The prophet himself weeps over its ruin. Even so, the passage ends with hope: at the end of time, God will bring back the captives of Moab.
sum.31: Jeremiah, who was being held prisoner while the Babylonians surrounded Jerusalem, buys his cousin Hanamel's field out of obedience, and he has the deeds of purchase stored in a clay jar. God explains that the city will fall because of the people's sin, but that one day he will bring them back, make an everlasting covenant with them, and people will once again buy land.
sum.41: After the fall of Jerusalem, the people and their leaders ask Jeremiah to pray for them and promise to obey whatever God says. Ten days later, God answers: if they stay in the land, he will look after them and protect them from the king of Babylon; if they flee to Egypt, war and famine will overtake them there. Jeremiah warns them that their promise was not sincere.
sum.36: King Zedekiah did not obey God, yet he asked Jeremiah to pray for them. God warned that even though the Chaldeans would withdraw for a time, they would come back and burn the city. Jeremiah was falsely accused, beaten, and thrown into prison, but he continued to tell the king the truth.
sum.7: God warns that Judah will be judged because its people rejected his word, clung to deceit and greed, and its leaders gave false peace without any shame. Even the birds know their seasons, yet the people do not understand God's judgment. Jeremiah weeps in grief and asks why there is no healing for his people.
sum.26: God tells Jeremiah to put on a yoke and to warn the kings of the neighboring nations, and Zedekiah as well, that they must submit to Nebuchadnezzar, to whom God has given those lands for a time. The prophets who say otherwise are lying, and whoever submits will live in their own land. The remaining objects from the temple will also be taken to Babylon, but God promises to bring them back someday.
sum.15: God tells Jeremiah not to marry, and not to attend funerals or feasts, as a sign that a terrible judgment is coming on Judah because of its idolatry, which is worse than that of its ancestors. But God promises that after punishing them and sending them into exile, he will bring his people back. In the end, even the nations will recognize that the idols are a lie.
sum.20: When Babylon besieged Jerusalem, King Zedekiah asked Jeremiah to inquire of God, hoping for a miracle. God answered that He Himself would fight against the city, and that whoever surrendered to the Chaldeans would live, while whoever stayed in the city would die. He also called the house of David to do justice and rescue the oppressed from the hand of their oppressor, because of their wickedness.
sum.35: God tells Jeremiah to write his warnings down on a scroll, hoping that the people will turn back from their wrongdoing. Baruch reads it aloud in the temple, but King Jehoiakim cuts it up and burns it, showing no fear. God protects Jeremiah and Baruch, and the word of God is written out again, this time with even more content.
sum.37: Jeremiah announces that whoever surrenders to the Chaldeans will live, but the officials throw him into a muddy cistern so that he will die. Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian, persuades the king and rescues him. Jeremiah pleads with Zedekiah to surrender, but the king is afraid, and Jeremiah remains in custody until the fall of Jerusalem.
sum.21: God tells Jeremiah to say to the king of Judah that he must practice justice and protect the oppressed, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow. If he does not obey, the palace will be left empty, and the city will fall because it abandoned the covenant with God. The kings Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Jeconiah are judged for their injustice and greed, and they will be taken into exile.
sum.4: God searches Jerusalem for even one honest person and cannot find one, because the people have rebelled, sworn falsely, oppressed the poor, and followed lying prophets. So he announces that a foreign nation will come to destroy them, though he promises not to finish them off completely. He reminds them that the sea obeys the limit he sets, yet they do not fear him.
sum.16: God accuses Judah of a sin so deep that it seems carved into their heart, and announces punishment. He blesses the one who trusts in Him, like a tree planted by the water, and warns about the deceitful heart. Jeremiah asks for healing, and God calls the people to keep the Sabbath, with the promise of blessing or of fire.
sum.8: Jeremiah weeps for his people, because lies, deceit, and the rejection of God's law have filled them with wickedness. God announces punishment: the land will be laid waste and the people scattered. Even so, He teaches that no one should boast in their wisdom, strength, or riches, but in knowing God, who delights in mercy and justice.
sum.17: God sends Jeremiah down to the potter's house to show him that he can reshape nations the way a potter reshapes clay, and that he changes his plans depending on whether people repent or not. Judah refuses to turn back to God and plots against Jeremiah, who cries out to God and asks him for justice against them.
sum.43: Jeremiah warns the Jews who were living in Egypt that Jerusalem was destroyed because of their idolatry, and that if they keep worshiping other gods, it will lead them to ruin. They refuse to listen and say they will keep honoring the "queen of heaven." God responds that his word will be fulfilled, and that only a few will escape.
sum.24: Jeremiah reminds Judah that for twenty-three years they rejected the warnings from God and from his prophets. Because of this, God will send Nebuchadnezzar, and the nations will serve Babylon for seventy years; afterward, Babylon will also be judged. Through the image of the cup of God's fury, God shows that his judgment will reach everyone.
sum.13: A great drought strikes Judah, and the people cry out and confess their sin. But God tells Jeremiah not to pray for them, because they still have not repented, and the false prophets are deceiving them with promises of peace. Even so, Jeremiah weeps and asks God not to abandon them, since only He can give the rain.
sum.5: God warns that a cruel army from the north is coming against Jerusalem, because the people are full of violence, deceit, and false peace. He offers them the chance to return to the ancient paths and find rest, but they refuse to listen, and God rejects their empty sacrifices. Jeremiah weeps and calls for mourning.
sum.38: Jerusalem falls to Babylon just as God had warned. King Zedekiah tries to flee, but he is captured, forced to watch his sons die, and then blinded and taken prisoner. Even so, God looks after Jeremiah, and He also promises to save Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, because he trusted in Him.
sum.51: Zedekiah rebelled against Babylon, and because of this Nebuchadnezzar laid siege to Jerusalem until hunger overcame the city. The city and the temple were burned, its treasures were stolen, and many people were taken into captivity. In the end, King Jehoiachin was released and treated with kindness, a small sign of hope.
sum.50: God announces that he will destroy Babylon for its wickedness and for what it did to Jerusalem, using other nations as his instrument. He calls his people to leave her and not to forget him, because he is the Creator and idols are worthless. Jeremiah orders this message to be read in Babylon and the book to be sunk in the Euphrates, as a sign of its fall.
sum.0: God calls Jeremiah, a young priest from Anathoth, to be a prophet to the nations, and promises to put his words in his mouth. Although Jeremiah says he is too young and feels afraid, God assures him that he will be with him to deliver him. Through two visions, the almond branch and the boiling pot, God announces that judgment will come from the north because of the people's idolatry.
sum.32: Jeremiah, still under guard, receives a promise from God: although Jerusalem lies in ruins because of its sin, God will heal it, forgive His people, and bring them back from captivity. Joy and flocks will return, and a righteous Branch from David's line will come. God affirms His covenant with David and the Levites, as firm as day and night.
sum.1: God reminds Israel of the love of her youth, when she followed Him through the wilderness, and asks what wrong they found in Him that made them abandon Him. His people left Him, the fountain of living water, for broken cisterns and for idols. Although they say, "We have not sinned," God announces judgment and shame.
sum.6: God sends Jeremiah to the gate of the temple to warn Judah not to put their trust in the temple while they continue to live in injustice, steal, murder, and worship idols. If they change their ways, they will remain in the land; if they do not, God will do to the temple what He did to Shiloh. God demands obedience rather than sacrifices, and He announces judgment and desolation.
